en: Having paid homage to Nārāyaṇa and to Nara, the most excellent of men,
and also to the goddess Sarasvatī, one should then utter the word "Victory.
Janamejaya said:
Having thus completed the marriage ceremony and being reunited with his kinsmen, what conversations did he hold? O Vaiśampāyana, recount them.
May this Mahābhārata—born from the lineage of Vyāsa, who is like a noble tree—be for you.

"Tell me here everything that Yudhiṣṭhira, with a joyful heart, said after the marriage was performed, as well as what they did in response to support those who might stumble on the path of worldly existence."
Dark as a cloud, with his mass of matted hair bound in a topknot, tall and staff-bearing, clad in the skin of a black antelope,
that foremost of poets was visibly purifying the worlds.

May Pārāśarya reveal his form on the sacred festival days. Om! I bow to Vyāsa, the grandson of Vasiṣṭha, the great-grandson of Śakti, the stainless son of Parāśara, the father of Śuka, and a treasure-house of asceticism.
Salutations to Vyāsa, who is a form of Viṣṇu; salutations to Viṣṇu, who is in the form of Vyāsa. Salutations again and again to the treasure-house of Brahman, the descendant of Vasiṣṭha.
Vaiśampāyana said:
Having performed the marriage of Abhimanyu, those heroes of the Kurus,
with their own parties delighted,
rested for four days and then departed contentedly.
Then they went to the assembly hall of Virāṭa;
that hall of the lord of the Matsyas was magnificent,
adorned with the finest jewels and excellent gems.
Having spread out their seats, those excellent kings of men approached Mālyavatī, who was fragrant with garlands.
Then, they both sat down upon the seats in front.
Both Virāṭa and Drupada were lords of men,
venerable as elders among the rulers of the earth,
and were the paternal grandfathers of Rāma and Janārdana.
But the hero of the Śini clan, together with the son of Rohiṇī, were in close proximity to the King of Pañcāla and very near to the King of Matsya.
Janārdana and Yudhiṣṭhira,
all the sons of King Drupada,
Bhīma and Arjuna, and the two sons of Mādravatī.
Pradyumna and Sāmba, both heroes in battle,
as well as the son of Virāṭa together with Abhimanyu—
all these heroes are equal to their fathers.
By virtue of their heroism, beauty, and strength,
the princes, the sons of Draupadī, sat down upon excellent seats adorned with gold.
When those great chariot-warriors were thus seated,
resplendent in their garments and ornaments, that prosperous city, filled with kings, shone brilliantly.
Then those heroes among men, having engaged in various conversations full of diverse topics, were like the sky filled with spotless planets.
They stood for a moment reflecting,
gazing intently at Kṛṣṇa;
and when they reached the conclusion of their discourse with Mādhava, they remained there.
Having been brought together there by Kṛṣṇa, the foremost of the Vṛṣṇis, for the sake of the Pāṇḍavas' cause,
those lions among kings listened in unison.
"His speech is of great meaning and great consequence," Kṛṣṇa said.
"It is known by all of you how this [man]..."
Yudhiṣṭhira was defeated by the son of Subala at dice through deceit, his kingdom was seized,
and a further agreement was made regarding their exile.
That those sons of Pāṇḍu, capable of conquering the earth by force, remained steadfast in truth— that conduct of theirs was a vow of formidable character, exactly as it was.
For six, seven, and indeed thirteen years— this most difficult period has been spent by the foremost of the Bharatas while remaining unrecognized in your presence.
All that was endured by those who, though engaged in the service of others' commands, patiently bore intolerable afflictions—
that is all known to you.
Since the kingdom has been obtained by their own kin through those who desired it,
and since things have come to this pass for King Yudhiṣṭhira, the son of Dharma,
as well as for Duryodhana, what now would be beneficial?
Reflect upon that which is righteous, appropriate, and glorious for both the Kurus and the Pāṇḍavas;
one should not desire that which is joined with unrighteousness.
Even the sovereignty of the gods belongs to the King of Dharma;
and this lordship over the earth, joined with dharma and purpose,
he would desire even in some small village.
For it is well known that the kingdom of kings is ancestral,
yet it has been seized by the sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra through deceitful conduct. Nevertheless, even so—
A great hardship of unbearable nature has been encountered,
yet Pārtha was not defeated in battle by those sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra through their own prowess.
Nevertheless, the king, together with his friends,
desires only their well-being— that which the sons of Pāṇḍu themselves have won by conquest.
Having oppressed the lords of the earth, that [wealth] was gathered together;
it is now sought after by these heroes among men—
the sons of Kuntī and the two sons of Mādravatī.
But these children, who are capable of withstanding their enemies, have been sought to be slain by those wicked and fierce men through various means,
as they desire to seize the kingdom.
And all of that is known to you exactly as it is:
having observed their greed to have increased,
as well as the righteousness of Yudhiṣṭhira.
Having also considered their relationship, form your opinions both collectively and individually;
for these men have always delighted in truth.
Having fulfilled that agreement exactly as prescribed,
they would otherwise, if treated by them in a contrary manner,
slay the assembled sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra.
Having heard of the king's mistreatment by them,
his friends should surround them and likewise oppose them with battle.
Being struck by them in battle, they might slay those very people; likewise, these men, abandoned by their kinsmen and slain according to dharma, might slay their enemies.
Nevertheless, it may be your thought that these [forces], being small in number, are not capable of victory; therefore,
let them all come together, united with their friends.
They will surely strive for their destruction;
even Duryodhana’s intention is as it is,
yet it is not known what he will actually do.
And since the opinion of another cannot be known,
what opinion do you consider most worthy of being undertaken?
Therefore, let this man of virtuous character depart from here.
A man who is pure, of noble birth, vigilant,
and capable as an envoy is fit for bringing about their pacification through the granting of half the kingdom to Yudhiṣṭhira.
Having heard the words of Janārdana—
which were consistent with dharma and artha, sweet and balanced—
his elder brother then took up his speech.
Having honored those words, O King,
Baladeva said:
"You have heard what was spoken by the elder brother of Gada."
The speech was both righteous and meaningful,
beneficial to Ajātaśatru and likewise beneficial to King Duryodhana as well.
For the heroic sons of Kuntī have renounced half of the kingdom and strive for his sake;
they were previously defeated and sent from here into the forest.
And having given the two sons of Mādrī, those heroes among the Kurus, half [of the kingdom], the son of Dhṛtarāṣṭra would rejoice exceedingly with us in happiness.
For having obtained the kingdom, those heroes among men,
when their enemies are properly engaged,
would surely enter into a state of peace and happiness.
Their pacification will bring welfare to the subjects;
thereafter, the destruction of the Kurus and Pāṇḍavas,
along with their kinsmen, will come to pass before long.
Therefore, strive for that which was spoken by Madhusūdana,
which is for the welfare of the entire world,
and also to understand the intention of Duryodhana.
And let a preeminent man go as an envoy to speak the words of Yudhiṣṭhira,
for the sake of their welfare as well as his own.
"It would be pleasing to me if someone were to go there for the sake of peace between the Kurus and the Pāṇḍavas.
Having addressed Bhīṣma, the hero of the Kurus, he—
And the high-souled son of Vicitravīrya,
Droṇa with his son, Vidura, Kṛpa,
and the King of Gāndhāra along with the Sūta’s son.
And all the other sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra,
who were preeminent in strength and preeminent in their knowledge of the scriptures,
remained steadfast in their respective duties.
When all these world-renowned heroes, learned in the scriptures and advanced in years, had assembled,
as well as the citizens and the elders who had gathered together.
Let him speak words accompanied by prostration,
so that they may bring about the welfare of Kuntī’s son;
and in all circumstances, let there be no deceit on your part.
For that kingdom was seized by those who relied on force from Yudhiṣṭhira, who had been won over by his beloved [wife],
while he was distracted during the game of dice.
Though being restrained by all the heroes of the Kurus and by his well-wishers, he— being ignorant of that [consequence]—
played and challenged him in return.
The descendant of Ajamīḍha challenged the son of the king of Gāndhāra, Matākṣa, to play at dice,
having indeed set aside both Karṇa and Suyodhana.
There were thousands of other gamblers there whom Yudhiṣṭhira might have been able to defeat;
yet, setting them aside, he [challenged] this son of Subala alone.
He challenged him, and was defeated by him at Akṣavatī while playing against his opponent;
for the dice were constantly turning away from him.
Though he was provoked and overpowered by force,
there is no fault whatsoever on the part of Śakuni in this matter;
therefore, let him speak his words only after bowing down.
For the son of Dhṛtarāṣṭra, the offspring of Vicitravīrya, is endowed with many stratagems; thus, he can be directed toward his own self-interest by that man.
Desire no war with the Kauravas;
summon Duryodhana through peaceful means alone.
An objective won through conciliation will prove beneficial.
"In battle, there will be misconduct; that is not the goal here.
Vaiśampāyana said:
While the hero among the Madhus was speaking thus,
That hero of the Śini clan sprang up instantly;
having censured those words of his, he spoke these words in great indignation.
Sātyaki said:
"As is the soul of a man, so does he speak;
according to the nature of your inner self, so do you speak."
There are indeed brave men, and likewise there are cowards;
both of these firm factions are seen among men.
Even within a single family, both the eunuch and the great chariot-warrior may be born.
"Just as a single tree possesses both branches that bear fruit and those that do not, O plow-bannered one, I do not find fault with the words you speak; rather,
O Mādhava, it is those who listen to your words whom I find fault with."

For how can one who speaks even a slight fault of the King of Dharma obtain the freedom from fear to speak in the midst of this assembly? Having challenged that high-souled one, those skilled in dice have defeated him.

How can there be a victory in dharma for those who, being ignorant of dice, play according to their own whims? If they had approached the son of Kuntī while he was playing with his brothers in the house and defeated him then, that would have been consistent with dharma for them.

Having summoned the king, who was always devoted to the dharma of the kṣatriyas, they defeated him through deceit; what indeed could be more wicked for them? And how can he, having made such a supreme wager here, now bow down to them?
Having been released from his forest exile, Yudhiṣṭhira has attained the station of his grandfather; even so, if he should desire the wealth of others,
he ought not to beg from them at all.
And how is it that they are devoted to righteousness and do not wish to seize the kingdom—
those who said the sons of Kuntī were recognized when they had completed their period of exile,
even though they had been entreated by Bhīṣma and the high-souled Droṇa?
They do not resolve to give the ancestral wealth to the Pāṇḍavas;
however, having compelled them by force in battle with my sharp arrows,
I shall cast them at the feet of the high-souled son of Kuntī.
If they do not resolve to bow down before the wise one,
they shall go, along with their ministers, to the abode of Yama—
[they who once covered] me, the sole hero intoxicated with pride, as I filled the ten directions.
The world considers him victorious as he fights upon the surface of the earth;
it is true that I am the disciple of Jaya, the conqueror,
were I to sever the heads of Bhīṣma and the others with my sword.
Indeed, they were not able to withstand the impetus of Yuyudhāna when he was enraged and eager for battle, just as mountains cannot withstand the force of the thunderbolt.
For who indeed [could stand] against the wielder of the Gāṇḍīva bow, and who against the one whose weapon is the discus, in combat?
Who indeed could withstand me, or who could endure Bhīma, so difficult to approach?
And there are the two Yamas, firm-bowed and of great splendor, who are like Yama himself;
and the heroes Virāṭa and Drupada, whose radiance is like that of Yama at the end of time.
Who, wishing to live, would dare to approach Dhṛṣṭadyumna, the son of Pṛṣata,
and these five sons of Pāṇḍu who increase the fame of Draupadī— men equal in stature to the Pāṇḍavas, equal in prowess, and fierce with pride?

And the son of Subhadrā, that great archer whom even the immortals could not withstand; and Gada, Pradyumna, and Sāmba, who are like Time, the thunderbolt, and fire— these we [shall oppose] against the son of Dhṛtarāṣṭra together with Śakuni.
"And having slain him in battle along with Karṇa, we shall consecrate the Pāṇḍava. No unrighteousness exists at all in slaying enemies who are assassins;
indeed, begging from one's foes is both unrighteous and disgraceful."
The arsonist, the poisoner, the one with a weapon in hand, the robber of wealth, and the abductor of land or wife— these six are indeed *ātatāyins* (assassins).
One should slay even an *ātatāyin* approaching, even if he be a teacher of the Vedānta.
One may strike back against one who seeks to kill; by that act, one does not become a slayer of a Brahmin.
Fulfill, without weariness, whatever desire lies in his heart. Let the son of Pāṇḍu obtain the kingdom surrendered by Dhṛtarāṣṭra.
"Either let Yudhiṣṭhira, the son of Pāṇḍu, obtain the kingdom today,
or else, all of them slain in battle, shall sleep upon the surface of the earth.
Drupada said:
"O mighty-armed one, it shall be exactly so; of this there is no doubt.
For Duryodhana will not surrender the kingdom through conciliation, nor will Dhṛtarāṣṭra follow him, being so fond of his son."
Bhīṣma and Droṇa [act] out of compassion, while the son of Rādhā and Saubala act out of folly;
however, Baladeva’s words do not accord with my understanding.
For this is what must first be done by a man who desires to follow a wise policy.

But the son of Dhṛtarāṣṭra must not be addressed with gentle words under any circumstances; for in my opinion, that man of evil intellect cannot be subdued by mildness. One might show gentleness toward a donkey, but one should employ severity toward cows.
"Even if I were alone, I would defeat that evil-minded Duryodhana; however, I shall send him forth first. I would never do this thing out of mere trust, for it is eternal [law]."
"I alone shall conquer the assembled foes once they have been arrayed.
I did not accept those words, preceded as they were by prostrations;
for a wicked man considers even gentle speech born of incapacity to be contemptible.
An ignorant person might perceive a conquered objective as being lost when there is still room for gentleness;
we shall act exactly in this way, and let effort be exerted here.
Let us dispatch messengers to our allies so that they may mobilize their forces for us.
"O Lord, let swift-moving messengers go to Śalya, Dhṛṣṭaketu, Jayatsena, and to all the Kekayas;
for Duryodhana will surely dispatch them everywhere."
We shall dispatch messengers quickly, without delay;
for Duryodhana will surely send those kings as well,
and those who have been approached first usually side with the one who first urged them.
"Therefore, hasten at the very first urging of these lords of men;
for it is my conviction that a great task must be undertaken by you.
Let Śalya be dispatched quickly, along with those kings who are his followers."
To King Bhagadatta, who dwells by the eastern ocean;
likewise to Amitaujas, Ugra, Hārdikya, and Āhuka;
and to Dīrghaprajña, Malla, and Rocamāna, O Lord.
"Let Bṛhanta and King Senābindu be brought here,
as well as Pāpajit, Prativindhya, Citravarman, Suvāstuka,
Bāhlīka, Muñjakeśa, and the lord of Cedi."
Supārśva, Subāhu, and the great car-warrior Paurava; those kings who belong to the Śakas, the Pahlavas, and the Daradas;
and those who are Kāmbojas, Ṛṣikas, and the inhabitants of the western marshlands.
Jayatsena and the King of Kāśī, as well as the kings of the Five Rivers;
the invincible son of Krātha and those kings who dwell in the mountains;
Jānaki, Suśarman, Maṇimān, and Pautimatsyaka.
The lord of Pāṃsurāṣṭra, the heroic Dhṛṣṭaketu, Auḍra, Daṇḍadhāra, the heroic Bṛhatsena,
Aparājita, Niṣāda, Śreṇimān, and Vasumān as well.
Bṛhadbala, Mahaujas, Bāhu the conqueror of enemy cities, King Samudrasena with his valiant son,
Adāri, Nadīja, and King Karṇaveṣṭa.
Samartha, Suvīra, Mārjāra, and likewise Kanyaka;
one of them,
Vīrabāhu, was preeminent in heroism and strength, as was Subāhu.
Vīrabāhu, the invincible Bhūmipa, Jālakīṭaka, Mahāvīra, Kadru, Nikara, Tumula, Kratha,
Nīla, Vīradharman, and the valiant Bhūmipāla.
Durjaya, Dantavaktra, Rukmī, Janamejaya,
Āṣāḍha, Vāyuvega, and King Pūrvapālī;
also Ārṣa, Devābudha, Sūta, and likewise Harihayopama.
Bhūritejas and Devaka, the son of Ekalavya, the Kārūṣaka kings, the heroic Kṣemadhūrti,
Udbhava, Kṣemaka, and King Vāṭadhāna.
Śrutāyu, Dṛḍhāyu, the valiant son of Śālva,
and the prince of the Kaliṅgas, who is fierce in battle—
let messengers be sent to these at once; for this is what I approve.
"O King, let this Brahmin, my priest, be dispatched immediately;
let this message be entrusted to him,
specifying how Duryodhana is to be addressed and how the king, the son of Śantanu, is to be addressed."
How Dhṛtarāṣṭra and Droṇa, the best among the wise, were to be addressed.
Vaiśampāyana said: When Drupada had spoken these words, he who was skilled in speech [replied].
There, the son of Vasudeva, that lion of the Vṛṣṇis, spoke these words.
Vāsudeva said:
"These words are fitting for the leader of the Somakas."

This brings about the accomplishment of the king’s purpose for the highly energetic Pāṇḍava; and this is our primary task, as we desire to follow a well-guided policy. For a man who acts otherwise would be truly foolish.

"However, our relationship toward the Kurus and the Pāṇḍavas is equal, whether those Pāṇḍavas behave as they please or otherwise. We were all brought here for the sake of the wedding, just as you were."
"Once the marriage has been performed, we shall go joyfully toward our homes.
You are the eldest among kings, both in age and in sacred learning;
we shall all remain here as your disciples, of this there is no doubt."
Dhṛtarāṣṭra always holds you in high esteem;
moreover, you are a friend of both the teachers Droṇa and Kṛpa. Therefore, do whatever you deem appropriate and fitting for this occasion.
O best of kings, dispatch him to the Kurus according to what is right;
may you yourself today send forth words that will accomplish the purpose of the Pāṇḍavas— words which,
being agreed upon by all of us, you shall indeed dispatch.
If that bull among the Kurus should first establish peace through righteous means,
the Pāṇḍavas will surely practice brotherly affection, thinking, "It is done.
Thus, there would not be a great destruction of the Kurus and Pāṇḍavas through their fraternal relations.
"Then, if the son of Dhṛtarāṣṭra, filled with pride, should act out of delusion,
you must first send messengers to others and afterwards summon us.
Then the dull-witted Duryodhana, along with his ministers and kinsmen— "
"The fool shall meet his end when the wielder of the Gāṇḍīva bow is enraged.
Vaiśampāyana said:
Then Virāṭa, the lord of the earth, having honored the descendant of Vṛṣṇi...
He sent him home with his attendants and kinsmen.
When Kṛṣṇa had departed for Dvārakā, those led by Yudhiṣṭhira,
as well as King Virāṭa, made all the necessary preparations for war.
Then Virāṭa, together with his kinsmen,
and Drupada, the lord of the earth, sent messengers to all the rulers of the land at the command of those lions of the Kuru race and the kings of Matsya and Pañcāla.
The immensely powerful kings, filled with great joy, assembled together.
Having heard that the vast army of the sons of Pāṇḍu was gathering,
the son of Dhṛtarāṣṭra likewise summoned the lords of the earth.
O King, at that time, when all the rulers of the earth were setting out for battle on account of the Kurus and Pāṇḍavas, the entire world became thoroughly agitated; indeed,
the earth was then crowded with armies consisting of the four divisions.
The forces of those heroes are arriving from here and there,
as if shaking this goddess Earth together with her mountains and forests.
Then the King of Pañcāla [addressed] his own family priest, who was advanced in both wisdom and age.
Then, with the consent of Yudhiṣṭhira, he sent messengers to the Kurus.
Drupada said:
"Among all beings, the living are the best; among the living, those who live by their intelligence are the best."

Among the intelligent, men are the best; among men, the twice-born (dvijātayaḥ) are superior. Among the twice-born, the learned (vaidyāḥ) are better; among the learned, those of perfected intellect (kṛtabuddhayaḥ) are superior. Among those of perfected intellect, the doers (kartāraḥ) are superior; and among the doers, the exponents of Brahman (brahmavādinaḥ) are the highest.
It is my conviction that you are the foremost among those of perfected intellect;
you are distinguished by your lineage, as well as by your age and your learning,
and in wisdom you are not inferior even to Śukra or Aṅgiras.
Everything is known to you: how that Kaurava behaved, and how Yudhiṣṭhira, the son of Kuntī and a Pāṇḍava, conducted himself;
and it is known to Dhṛtarāṣṭra that the Pāṇḍavas were deceived by their enemies.
Though entreated by Vidura, he still followed his son; for Śakuni, being skilled at dice and acting with deliberate intent, challenged the son of Kuntī—
who was pure, established in the conduct of a kṣatriya, and unskilled at dice.

Having thus deceived Yudhiṣṭhira, the son of Dharma, they will certainly not surrender the kingdom themselves under any circumstances. You, however, should speak words consistent with righteousness to Dhṛtarāṣṭra.
He will certainly turn the minds of his warriors [against you];
furthermore, Vidura will bring about that speech of yours,
and he will create a rift among Bhīṣma, Droṇa, and Kṛpa.
When the ministers are divided and the warriors have turned their backs,
it will be their task once more to bring them back to a state of single-minded focus. In the meantime, the sons of Pṛthā will remain at ease, their minds fixed in concentration.
They will perform military operations and the accumulation of supplies;
however, when your own people are divided and you yourself are faltering,
they will not carry out those military tasks for you in that manner— of this there is no doubt.
This purpose is perceived here as the primary objective:
that Dhṛtarāṣṭra, through this connection, might act according to your righteous words;
for you are endowed with dharma and would act righteously toward them.
By proclaiming the sufferings of the Pāṇḍavas to those who are compassionate,
and by speaking of the family dharma practiced by their ancestors to the elders,
he will divide their minds; of this I have no doubt.
"You have no fear from them, for you are a Brahmin learned in the Vedas; moreover, you are engaged in the task of a messenger and are especially venerable.
Therefore, by means of the Puṣya conjunction and at the moment of victory—"
"Let him go quickly to the Kauravas for the sake of accomplishing the purpose of the son of Kuntī.
Vaiśampāyana said:
Thus instructed by the high-souled Drupada, he set forth.

Accompanied by his disciples, the learned priest, endowed with virtuous conduct and skilled in the meaning of the treatises on statecraft, set out for the city named after the elephant (Hastināpura) for the benefit of the Pāṇḍavas toward the Kauravas.
Vaiśampāyana said:
Having dispatched their family priest to the city named after the elephant (Hastināpura),
they then sent messengers here and there to the various kings.
Having dispatched messengers elsewhere, that bull among men,
Dhanañjaya, the son of Kuntī and descendant of Kuru, set out for Dvārakā himself.
When Kṛṣṇa and Baladeva Mādhava had departed for Dvāravatī, [he proceeded].
Together with all the Vṛṣṇis and Andhakas, as well as the Bhojas by the hundreds,
King Dhṛtarāṣṭra’s son gathered all information regarding the activities of the Pāṇḍavas through dispatched messengers and spies.
Having heard that Mādhava had departed with excellent horses swift as the wind,
he proceeded toward the city of Dvārakā with a force that was not overly large.
On that very same day, the son of Kuntī, the joy of the Pāṇḍus, [also set out].
Dhanañjaya quickly went to the beautiful city of Ānarta.
Having traveled to Dvārakā, those two tigers among men, the descendants of Kuru,
beheld Kṛṣṇa asleep and approached him as he lay there.
Then, while Govinda was lying down, Suyodhana entered;
he sat upon an excellent seat at the head of Kṛṣṇa,
and having turned around, he gazed upon him as he sat upon his throne.
Then the high-minded Kirīṭin entered after him;
he stood behind Kṛṣṇa, bowing with palms joined in reverence.
Upon awakening, that scion of the Vṛṣṇis saw Kirīṭin before him.
Then he saw Suyodhana seated at the head of the bed; subsequently, that leader of the Yādavas beheld King Duryodhana,
the son of Vicitravīrya, stationed at the head.
Afterwards, Śauri of immeasurable splendor beheld Duryodhana;
having offered them a welcome and honored them as was fitting,
Madhusūdana then inquired about the reason for their arrival.
Then Duryodhana, as if laughing, said to Kṛṣṇa:
"In this conflict, you ought to grant me your assistance;
for your friendship is equal toward both me and Arjuna."
O Mādhava, our relationship with you is equal;
yet today, O Madhusūdana, I have approached you first.
The virtuous follow the precedent of those who came before them, honoring whoever arrived first.
"And you, O Janārdana, are today the most excellent among the virtuous in the world;
being ever esteemed, uphold the conduct of the righteous.
The Blessed Lord said:
"Welcome to you, O Gāndhārī! I did not know that it was you, Duryodhana. What is the purpose of your visit, and at what time did you arrive?"
"O Govinda, desiring to see you, I have come here before;
as one who seeks your favor, you ought to grant me your assistance.
Having heard those words of the son of Dhṛtarāṣṭra, the supreme among the best of gods—
Then Puruṣottama spoke these words to Duryodhana.
Kṛṣṇa said:
"There is no doubt in my mind that you arrived here first."
"But first, O King, it was Pārtha Dhananjaya who was seen by me.
Because of your prior arrival and because of his being seen first,
O Suyodhana, I shall provide assistance to both of you."
"The sacred tradition states that the choice [of the bride] must first be made by the suitors;
therefore, Pārtha Dhananjaya is worthy of the first choice.
There are hundreds of millions of cowherds equal in strength to my own frame."
Let all those warriors known as Nārāyaṇas,
who are skilled in combat, be the soldiers on one side; and let me alone, not fighting in the battle and having laid down my weapons, be on the other.
Having understood this, O son of Kuntī, and having reflected upon it again and again,
choose either them for assistance or me for counsel;
O Pārtha, whichever of these two is more pleasing to your heart.
"Therefore, may you choose first, for you are entitled to the first choice according to dharma.
Vaiśampāyana said:
Thus addressed by Kṛṣṇa, Dhanañjaya, the son of Kuntī, [chose].
In the midst of battle, he chose Keśava—

who is Nārāyaṇa, the slayer of enemies, the unborn one born among men by his own will— as his opponent, even though [Keśava] was not fighting, in the presence of all the Kṣatriyas, and even before the gods and Dānavas.
Then Duryodhana hemmed in that entire army;
and having obtained a thousand times a thousand warriors, O Bhārata,
and knowing that Kṛṣṇa had been carried away, he attained the highest joy.
Then King Duryodhana, taking that entire army with him,
approached the mighty son of Rohiṇī, who possessed formidable strength;
he then reported to him the entire reason for his arrival.
Then Śauri replied with these words to the son of Dhṛtarāṣṭra:
"O tiger among men, everything that was said by me previously at Virāṭa’s wedding must surely be known to you."
"O joy of the Kurus, O King, Hṛṣīkeśa was addressed by me with reproach for your sake,
saying again and again, 'The alliance is equal.
Yet Keśava did not accept those words that were spoken."
"I cannot bear to remain even for a moment without Kṛṣṇa;
I am neither a partisan of the Pārthas nor of Duryodhana.
This is my firm resolve, having considered Vāsudeva."

"You are born in the lineage of Bhārata, honored by all kings; go and fight according to the dharma of the Kṣatriyas, O bull among the Bharatas. Having been addressed thus, he then embraced Halāyudha.
Knowing that Kṛṣṇa had been carried away, he considered victory already won in battle. That king, the son of Dhṛtarāṣṭra, then advanced against Kṛtavarman,
who at that time gave him an army of one akṣauhiṇī.
Surrounded by that entire formidable army, the joy of the Kurus set out delighted, gladdening his friends.
Then Janārdana, the creator of the world, wearing yellow garments—
When Duryodhana had departed, Kṛṣṇa then said to Kirīṭin: "By adopting what resolve have I been chosen by you as one who will not fight? Arjuna replied:
"You are capable of slaying them all; of this there is no doubt.
O Supreme Person, I too am alone capable of slaying them, but you are renowned in the world, and therefore the fame shall go to you."
"I too am a seeker of glory; therefore, you have been chosen by me.
It has always been my heart's desire that you should act as my charioteer;
it behoves you to fulfill this wish, which I have long cherished."
Vāsudeva said:
"O Pārtha, this is fitting that you should vie with me;
I shall act as your charioteer, and let your desire be fulfilled."
Vaiśampāyana said:
Thus delighted, Pārtha, accompanied by Kṛṣṇa and surrounded by the foremost of the Dāśārhas, then returned once more to Yudhiṣṭhira.
Vaiśampāyana said:
O King, having heard the messengers, Śalya, surrounded by a great army and accompanied by his sons who were mighty chariot-warriors, marched against the Pāṇḍavas.
His military camp extended for nearly one and a half yojanas,
for that bull among men maintained such a vast army;
O King, he was the commander of an akṣauhiṇī, possessed of great heroism and prowess.
The heroes wore variegated armor and possessed variegated banners and bows;
all were adorned with variegated ornaments and had variegated chariots and mounts.
All wore variegated garlands and were decorated with variegated garments and jewels.
Hundreds of thousands of heroes, bulls among kṣatriyas, adorned with their own native lands' dress and ornaments, became the leaders of his army;
they seemed to distress all living beings and make the earth tremble.
Gradually causing his army to rest, he proceeded toward where the Pāṇḍava was.
Then, O Bhārata, having heard that the great car-warrior Mahāsena was approaching, Duryodhana rushed forth and personally honored him.
All of Śalya’s ministers, acting under the command of Duryodhana,
performed a pleasing service for Śalya that remained unknown to him;
and for the sake of honoring him, Duryodhana had assembly halls constructed.
In delightful regions, well-adorned and variegated with jewels,
various craftsmen prepared diversions; there, garlands, meats, foods, and drinks were provided with great honor.
There were wells of various shapes that increased the joy of the mind,
as well as ponds of diverse forms and water-houses;
having reached those assembly halls, he was honored like an immortal.

Accompanied by Duryodhana’s ministers, who attended to him appropriately in various places, he arrived at another assembly hall that possessed the splendor of the abode of the gods. There, garments, garlands, and abundant food and drink were provided.
Divine fragrances, pleasing to the nose and captivating to the mind, brought him joy;
and the king, full of devotion, beheld lakes together with their birds and deer.
There, he was endowed with auspicious and superhuman sensory objects.
He considered himself superior and held Purandara in contempt.
Then that bull among Kṣatriyas, filled with joy, asked his servants:
"Who were the men who built these halls for Yudhiṣṭhira?"
"Let the architects of the assembly hall be brought here, for I consider them worthy of a reward.
Let the son of Kuntī grant his permission; I shall bestow my favor upon them.
Thus they all reported everything to Duryodhana, filled with wonder.
When Śalya was overjoyed and even prepared to give up his life,
the ministers, perceiving that the king was then filled with joy,
revealed Duryodhana, who had been hidden there, to his maternal uncle.
Seeing him and recognizing that effort of his,
King Duryodhana— the best among men— was struck with wonder;
and the ministers also spoke of the King of Madra’s great amazement.
"O King, O Lord, this has been requested of you by Duryodhana;
O Ruler of the Earth, you ought to do what is pleasing for one who is worthy of such affection.
Having quickly seated him on his lap and smelled the crown of his head, the King of Madra—
Embracing him, he said with joy, "Let your desired object be accepted.
Duryodhana said:
"O auspicious one, be true to your word; let a boon indeed be granted to me."
"You ought to be the leader of my entire army.
Just as the Pāṇḍavas are yours, so indeed am I yours,
O Śalya."
"O Lord, you who are worthy of honor, worthy of protection, and worthy of devotion, favor me!
O Great King, O Bhārata, it is exactly as you say. Being pleased, I grant you this boon; it shall be so."
Vaiśampāyana said:
Śalya replied, "It is done; what else should be done?
And Gāndhārī likewise answered again and again, "It is done."
Śalya said:
"Go back to your own city, O bull among men, Duryodhana;
I shall go indeed to see Yudhiṣṭhira, the tamer of foes."
"O King, O lord of men, having seen Yudhiṣṭhira, I shall return quickly.
Duryodhana said:
"That bull among men, the son of Pāṇḍu, must certainly be seen by me."
"O King, O ruler of the earth, come quickly after you have seen the Pāṇḍava.
Śalya said:
"O Indra among kings, we are dependent upon you; remember the boon you granted us."
"I shall return quickly; may you be blessed, O King, go now to your own city.
Having thus embraced one another, both Śalya and Duryodhana spoke.
But having seen the Pāṇḍavas, O King, I cannot bring myself to act falsely.
Having thus taken leave of Śalya, he returned once more to his own city;
Śalya, however, went to the sons of Kuntī to report that deed of his. Having gone to Upaplavya and entered the military camp, he spoke.
Then Śalya beheld all those Pāṇḍavas there.
Having seen their maternal uncle, the king who is victorious in assembly, after a long time,
they all, together with Yudhiṣṭhira, rose from their seats.

Then, having met with the sons of Pāṇḍu, the mighty-armed Śalya accepted the water for his feet, the guest-offering, and the cow according to the prescribed rites. With palms joined in reverence and an undepressed mind, that righteous-souled one spoke to Śalya.

"Welcome to you, O King; please be seated on this seat. Thereupon Śalya sat down upon an excellent golden throne, and the Pāṇḍava then offered him water for his feet and the respectful guest-offering (arghya).

O Bhārata, having offered the *arghya* according to the prescribed rites to the King of Madra, the Pāṇḍava asked Śalya about his welfare, bringing him every comfort. He was surrounded by all those Pāṇḍavas who were practitioners of dharma.
Then that slayer of enemies, the King of Madra, having first performed auspicious rites,
embraced Yudhiṣṭhira with supreme joy;
likewise, he embraced the delighted Bhīma and Arjuna, as well as both the twins, his sister’s sons.
O Bhārata, Draupadī, Subhadrā, and Abhimanyu were there;
and as Śalya sat upon his seat, he spoke to the son of Pṛthā:
"O tiger among kings, O joy of the Kurus, is all well with you?"

"O best among victors, by good fortune you have been released from dwelling in the forest. O King, O Indra among kings, you have performed a most difficult feat by living in the desolate woods together with your brothers and this Kṛṣṇā."
While dwelling in that terrible life in concealment, he performed deeds most difficult to accomplish.
O Bhārata, for one fallen from his kingdom, there is only suffering; whence could there be happiness?
Indeed, this great misery has been brought about by the sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra.
"O King, scorcher of enemies, you shall obtain happiness after slaying your foes.
O Great King, lord of men, the true nature of the world is known to you;
therefore, my dear, not even the slightest trace of greed exists in you."
O Bhārata, follow the path of the ancient royal seers;
O dear Yudhiṣṭhira, be established in generosity, austerity, and truth.
O Yudhiṣṭhira, [practice] forbearance, self-control, truth, and non-violence.
Moreover, O King, this wondrous world is established in you;
you are gentle, generous, devoted to the Brahmins, a giver, and dedicated to righteousness.
O King, many dharmas witnessed by the world are known to you.
"O dear one, O scorcher of foes, this entire world is known to you. By good fortune, O King, O bull of the Bharatas, you have overcome this hardship.
By good fortune, O Indra among kings, I see you, righteous-souled as you are, together with your followers."
"O King, O Lord, you have accomplished what is difficult; you are a treasury of righteousness. Exertion, self-restraint, skill, vigilance, fortitude, and mindfulness—[these are yours].
Then the king told him of his meeting with Duryodhana."
And all that was heard, O Bhārata, as well as the granting of the boon—
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
"O King, you have performed a virtuous deed with a joyful inner soul."

O hero, that which was promised by you in words to Duryodhana—herein there is no distinction between Duryodhana and us. However, O lord of the earth, I desire one thing to be done; may prosperity be yours!
"O King, O best of beings, you ought to do even that which should not be done;
O hero, listen as I address you out of regard for me. For Karna always vies with the son of Pṛthā at the forefront of battle."
"O Great King, you are equal to Vāsudeva in battle; O best of kings, when the duel between Karṇa and Arjuna takes place,
O maternal uncle, Vāsudeva must perform the role of charioteer for Pārtha."
"O King, you must perform the duty of charioteer for Karṇa; of this there is no doubt.
In that role, O King, Arjuna must be protected by you if you wish to do what is pleasing to me. Furthermore, you must diminish the prowess of the Sūta’s son, which will bring us victory."
"O maternal uncle, you ought indeed to do this, even though it is something that should not be done.
Śalya said:
"Listen, O Pāṇḍava—may prosperity be yours—to what you say regarding that evil-souled one."
"For the sake of diminishing the prowess of the Sūta's son in battle,
I shall do that which is pleasing to you;
I will certainly be his charioteer in the conflict."
For he always considers me to be equal to Vāsudeva; therefore,
O tiger among the Kurus, I shall certainly speak words that are contrary and disagreeable to him when he desires to fight in battle.
"I shall be his charioteer at the head of the battle, O Pāṇḍava, so that he will be stripped of his pride and deprived of his splendor;
I tell you this truthfully, that he will be easy to slay."
"I shall do exactly as you have told me, my father;
and whatever else I am capable of, I will do to please you.
And as for the suffering that was endured by you together with Kṛṣṇā at the gambling match—"
Indeed, the harsh words uttered by the son of the Sūta,
the suffering caused by Jaṭāsura and Kīcaka, O you of great splendor—
all that Draupadī endured was exactly like the misfortunes experienced by Damayantī.

"O hero, all this suffering shall result in future happiness; you should not harbor resentment here, for destiny is indeed more powerful. For even great-souled ones, O Yudhiṣṭhira, encounter sufferings."
O lord of the earth, even the gods have experienced sufferings;
O king, ruler of men, hear how the gods, dānavas, gandharvas, kinnaras, uragas, and rākṣasas have likewise encountered suffering.
"O King, it is heard that the high-souled Indra, the king of the gods, experienced great suffering together with his wife, O Bhārata. Yudhiṣṭhira said:
"O Indra among kings, how did the high-souled Indra, together with his wife, experience such supreme and terrible suffering? This I wish to know.
Śalya said:

Listen, O King, to this ancient history of what occurred in the past, O Bhārata, regarding how Indra experienced suffering together with his wife. Tvaṣṭṛ was indeed a Prajāpati, the best of gods and a man of great asceticism.
Out of enmity toward Indra, he indeed created his son Triśiras;
that Viśvarūpa of great splendor sought the station of Indra with those three terrible faces, which resembled the sun, the moon, and fire.
With one [mouth] he studied the Vedas, with another he drank wine,
and with another he gazed upon all the quarters of the sky as if drinking them in.
He was an ascetic, gentle, self-controlled, and devoted to righteousness and austerity.
O subduer of enemies, he performed great, intense, and most difficult penance. Seeing the power of his asceticism and the strength of that one of immeasurable splendor,
Śakra, the wielder of the thunderbolt, fell into despair, thinking, "May this man not become Indra."
"How might he become attached to worldly enjoyments so that he does not perform great austerities?
How might the ever-increasing Triśiras swallow the entire three worlds?"—
having reflected thus in many ways, O bull of the Bharatas, the wise one [acted].
He commanded the Apsarases to entice the son of Tvaṣṭṛ, so that Triśiras might indeed become intensely addicted to the pleasures of desire. "Go quickly, act without delay, and seduce him! he said.
Clad in amorous attire, those fair-hipped women were endowed with captivating gestures;
all of them, possessed of coquettish charms and graced with beauty, said:
"May you be blessed; entice him and dispel my fear."
He might be Prajāpati, or indeed Candra, Vaiśravaṇa, or Yama;
or he might be Varuṇa with his noose in hand, or Dharma himself. For, O beautiful women, I perceive my own self to be unwell.
"O powerless ones, quickly destroy this most terrible fear!
The Apsarases said:
"O Śakra, we shall make such an effort to entice him."
"O slayer of Bala, so that you shall not incur fear from him—
let us go together, O Lord, to entice that treasury of asceticism who sits there as if burning with his very eyes."
"We shall strive to bring them under control and to dispel that fear.
Śalya said:
"Having been thus permitted by Indra, they went into the presence of Triśiras."
There, those beautiful women, tempting him with various gestures and displaying their dancing as well as the grace of their limbs, moved about;
yet the one of great asceticism felt no joy.
Having brought the senses under control, he became like the full ocean;
yet those [apsarases], having exerted the utmost effort, again approached Śakra,
and with palms joined in reverence, they all spoke to the king of the gods.
"O Lord, that most invincible one cannot be shaken from his fortitude;
therefore, O illustrious one, perform whatever task you have to do immediately thereafter.
Having thus honored the Apsarases and dismissed them, the high-minded Śakra—
He reflected upon the means for the slaying of that very high-souled one.
Thinking silently, the heroic and majestic King of the Gods,
the wise one, became resolved in his mind upon the destruction of Triśiras.
"I shall hurl my thunderbolt at him today; he shall soon cease to exist. A foe who has grown powerful must not be overlooked, even if he is weak, by one who is stronger.
Having reached this conclusion through the wisdom of the treatises, I have formed a firm resolve for his slaughter."
Then Śakra, filled with rage, hurled at Triśiras a thunderbolt that resembled Vaiśvānara, possessing a terrible form and inspiring fear. Struck violently by that thunderbolt, he fell down, slain.
Like the peak of a mountain cast down upon the surface of the earth, he lay there like an immovable mountain, struck by the thunderbolt; seeing him thus prostrate,
the Lord of the Gods found no peace, being scorched by his splendor.
Of terrible form, exceedingly fierce, intense, and of violent prowess,
though slain, he possessed blazing splendor and appeared as if still alive; indeed,
the heads of the one struck down in battle were truly marvelous, appearing as if living.

Then Śakra, his body trembling with extreme fear, remained there reflecting. At that moment, O Great King, a carpenter arrived at that forest where he had been struck down, carrying an axe upon his shoulder.
Three heads are born upon him, O Bhārata, appearing as three birds:
a partridge, a sparrow, and likewise a grey partridge;
indeed, his heads are born with the forms of all creatures.
There, the Lord of Śacī, the subduer of Pāka, saw a carpenter busily working nearby; he spoke to him in haste:
"Quickly cut off his heads; carry out my command."
The carpenter said:
"This tree has a massive trunk; indeed, this axe will not suffice to cut through it. Furthermore, I am unable to perform an act that is censured by the virtuous."
Indra said:
"Do not fear; quickly do as I say.
By my grace, your weapon shall indeed become like the thunderbolt."
The carpenter said:
"Whom may I know you to be, you who perform such terrible deeds today?
I wish to hear this; tell it to me in accordance with the truth."
Indra said:
"I am Indra, the king of the gods, O Takṣan; let this be known to you. Perform this as I have commanded, O Takṣan; do not hesitate."
"Indeed, Triśiras lies here slain by me; you too, know this for certain.
Having spoken thus, he bowed low with palms joined in reverence and uttered these words.
Takṣa said:
"O Śakra, how is it that you feel no shame for this cruel deed?
Having slain this son of a seer, do you have no fear of the sin of killing a Brahmin?
Indra replied:
"Afterwards, I shall practice the Dharma, which is extremely difficult to perform, for the sake of purification.
This enemy of great prowess has been struck down by me with the thunderbolt;
yet even now I am anxious, for I truly fear Takṣan."
"Quickly cut off their heads; I shall bestow a favor upon you. Men shall offer the head of your animal as a portion in sacrifices.
This is your favor, O carpenter; quickly do what is pleasing to me."
Śalya said:
Having heard those words of Mahendra,
the carpenter then severed the heads of Triśiras with his axe.
Then, as those [heads] were being cut off, Triśiras emerged; from all sides there came forth *kapiñjala* birds, *tittira* partridges, and *kalaviṅka* sparrows.
[He was the one] by whom he used to study the Vedas and drink the *soma*.
From that mouth, O King, kapiñjala birds quickly flew forth,
by which he seemed to gaze upon all directions as if drinking them in;
from that other mouth, O Pāṇḍava, partridges flew forth.
O bull of the Bharata race, the mouth of that three-headed one which had been drinking liquor then disgorged *kalaviṅka* birds;
once they were cut down, Maghavat became free from his fever.

Having granted the boon to the carpenter, the Lord of the Thirty-three (Indra) departed for the celestial realm (Tridiva) in great joy; the carpenter also went to his own home. Having reached his home, the carpenter did not tell this to anyone at all.
Then, for one year, they did not recognize the Tathāgata.
When the year was complete, the beings belonging to the Lord Paśupati cried out: "Maghavan is our lord; he is a slayer of a Brahmin!"
Then Indra, the subduer of Pāka, observed a formidable vow;
joined by the gods and the hosts of Maruts, he was fully engaged in asceticism upon the ocean, upon the earth, among the lords of the forest, and among women.
Having divided the Brahman-slaughter, he assigned it to them along with boons; and the Giver of Boons, having granted boons to the Earth, to the Ocean,
to the trees, and to women, cast off that Brahman-slaughter.
Then the Blessed One, purified and honored by the gods and the worlds,
approached the abode of Indra while being worshipped by the great seers;
having slain his enemy, the slayer of the foes of the gods considered himself to have accomplished his purpose.
Then Tvaṣṭṛ Prajāpati, having heard that his son had been slain by Śakra,
spoke these words with eyes bloodshot with rage:
"He who was constantly performing austerities, patient, self-controlled, and a master of his senses— "
"Since he has harmed my son who was indeed innocent,
therefore I shall produce Vṛtra for the sake of Śakra's destruction;
let the worlds behold my heroism and the great power of my asceticism."
Then let that evil-minded and wicked-souled lord of the gods behold [the consequence]:
having touched water and become enraged, the highly illustrious ascetic offered oblations into the fire and, having summoned the terrible Vṛtra, spoke to him.
"O enemy of Indra, grow by the power of my ascetic heat!
He grew, reaching up to the heavens, resembling the sun and Vaiśvānara;
risen like the sun at the end of time, he said, "What shall I do?"

Having been told, "Slay Śakra," he then departed for the celestial realm. Thereupon, O best of the Kurus, a most terrible and continuous battle then took place between Vṛtra and Vāsava, both of whom were filled with rage.
O best of the Bharatas, all the worlds were swallowed by Vṛtra,
that great-souled one whose energy was increased by Tvaṣṭṛ;
O Bhārata, he indeed seized all fragrances, sensory objects, and tastes.
Earth, wind, space, water, and light as the fifth—
O Great King, all this was seized by the high-souled Vṛtra;
then the heroic Vṛtra seized the lord of the gods, Śatakratu.
Opening his mouth, Vṛtra, filled with rage, swallowed him.
When Śakra had been swallowed by Vṛtra, the gods were then thrown into confusion;
those great beings created a yawn that would destroy Vṛtra.
Then, as Vṛtra was yawning, the slayer of Bala emerged from his opened mouth, having drawn back his own limbs;
from that time forth, yawning has resided within living beings in the worlds.
And all the gods rejoiced upon seeing Śakra emerge; then,
O bull of the Bharatas, a terrible battle once more commenced between Vṛtra and Vāsava, both of them enraged for a very long time.

When Vṛtra, endowed with strength through the power of Tvaṣṭṛ’s asceticism, grew powerful in battle, the wise Śakra then retreated. When he had withdrawn, the gods fell into a state of extreme despondency.
Having met with Śakra, O Bhārata, they were all bewildered by the splendor of Tvaṣṭṛ; deluded by fear, they consulted together with the sages, O King, considering, "What should be done?"
With their minds, they all went to the high-souled, imperishable Viṣṇu. Seated upon the peak of Mount Mandara, they all desired the slaying of Vṛtra.
Indra said:
Śalya said:
Listen to me, together with your brothers and Draupadī, to this supreme narrative, this ancient history that brings victory.
Having reflected thus, Śakra, the lord of the three worlds,
spoke these words again to the wise ones regarding the means for Vṛtra’s death:
"We have heard here that the entire world has been pervaded by that Vṛtra."
When the worlds had become like Vṛtra, fear came upon Indra. Then the majestic Indra, endowed with great splendor, gathered together with the deities and,
being full of energy, consulted them for the purpose of slaying Vṛtra.
"O gods, this entire imperishable world is pervaded by Vṛtra;
indeed, there is nothing that could serve as a counter-force against him.
For I was capable in the past, but now I am powerless."
"How indeed may I bring you prosperity? In my view, he is invincible;
he is radiant, high-souled, and possesses immeasurable prowess in battle.
He could swallow the entire three worlds, including the gods, asuras, and humans."
Therefore, O denizens of heaven, listen to this resolution of mine:
having approached the abode of Viṣṇu and met with that Great-Souled One,
we shall deliberate with him and discover the means for the destruction of that evil-minded one.
Śalya said:
When Maghavan had spoken thus, the gods, together with the hosts of sages,
then prostrated themselves before that high-souled one who is worshipped by all beings.

Afflicted by the fear of Vṛtra, they all went for refuge to the mighty god Viṣṇu, the protector worthy of seeking shelter; and, tormented by the dread of Vṛtra, they all spoke to Viṣṇu, the lord of gods:
"O Lord, the three worlds were traversed by you with your three strides."
O Viṣṇu, the nectar was brought back and the Daityas were slain in battle;
having bound the great Daitya Bali, Śakra was made the lord of the gods. You are the Lord of all worlds; by you all this is pervaded.
For you, O God, are Mahādeva, honored by all the worlds;
O supreme among the immortals, you are the refuge for all Gandharvas, Uragas, and Rākṣasas.
O supreme among the immortals, become the refuge for the gods, including Indra.
"O slayer of asuras, this entire world is pervaded by Vṛtra.
Viṣṇu said:
"The supreme welfare of you all must certainly be accomplished by me."
Therefore, I shall declare a means by which he shall cease to exist.
Go, along with the sages and Gandharvas, to where he who assumes all forms resides;
employ conciliation toward him, and then you will conquer him.
"O gods, by my splendor, Śakra’s path shall become accessible;
and remaining invisible, I shall enter his thunderbolt, that supreme weapon.
Go now, O best of gods, together with the ṛṣis and the gandharvas."
"Make peace with Śakra regarding Vṛtra without delay.
Śalya said:
"Thus addressed by the god, the sages and the thirty deities likewise [acted]."
Having come together and joined in concert, they went forth with Śakra as their leader;
they carried out the command of the Lord,
and then they encountered Vṛtra.
Then, all those of great majesty approached him,
who was blazing with splendor and scorching the ten directions,
as if swallowing the three worlds like the sun and the moon.
There the deities beheld Vṛtra together with Śakra.
Then the ṛṣis, having approached Vṛtra, spoke these kind words:
"O invincible one, this entire world is pervaded by your splendor."
"And you are not able to conquer Vāsava, who possesses great prowess; moreover,
a very long time has passed while the two of you have been fighting here,
and all creatures— including gods, asuras, and humans— are being oppressed."
"O Vṛtra, let there be eternal friendship between you and Śakra;
you shall obtain happiness and the eternal worlds of Śakra. Then, having heard the words of the ṛṣi, that exceedingly powerful Vṛtra—
Then the Asura, bowing his head to them all, said:
"O you all, highly blessed ones, and all you Gandharvas, you have heard everything that was said; now listen also to me, O sinless ones."
"How indeed shall there be a union between me and Śakra? For how, O gods, can friendship exist between us two who possess such dual splendors?
I wish to know this; let the best of sages speak."
The sages said:
One should desire to associate with the virtuous even once; thereafter, what is destined to be will surely come to pass.
One should not transgress against association with a virtuous person;
therefore, one should desire association with the virtuous. Indeed, association with the virtuous is firm and eternal.
For the wise man should speak of what is beneficial in times of difficulty;
association with a virtuous person is of great benefit.
Therefore, a wise man should never seek to harm one who is good.
Indra is esteemed by the virtuous and is the refuge of the great-souled;
for he is a speaker of truth, undepressed, a knower of dharma, and firmly resolute. Therefore, let there be an eternal alliance between you and Śakra.
"Thus, place your trust; let not your mind be otherwise.
Śalya said:
"Having heard the words of the great seer, the one of great splendor spoke to them:"
"O Blessed Ones, these ascetics must certainly be honored by me.
O gods, let everything that I say be done here;
then I shall do all that those bulls among the twice-born have told me."
O best of Brahmins, I am not to be slain by anything dry or wet, nor by stone or wood,
nor by weapon or thunderbolt, neither by day nor likewise by night—
even by Śakra together with the gods.

"This alliance with Śakra is always pleasing to me," [he said]. "So be it," the ṛṣis replied to him, O bull of the Bharatas. When the alliance had been thus established, Vṛtra became exceedingly joyful.
Then, having made a mutual pact, those sages of blazing splendor returned to whence they had come, along with Śakra and Vṛtra.
After a long time had passed, O Bhārata, Śakra reflected deeply.

Śakra, the slayer of Bala and Vṛtra, remained ever vigilant and filled with indignation, constantly contemplating means for the destruction of Vṛtra; anxious and searching for a vulnerability, he was always on guard.
Recalling the intention that had been formed by the sages regarding the peace treaty with Mahendra, and remembering the words they had spoken,
he once beheld that great asura on the shore of the ocean.
When the twilight hour had arrived, a moment both beautiful and terrible, the Blessed One then reflected upon the boon granted by the Great-souled One:
"This is the fierce twilight; it is neither night nor day."
He has indeed obtained a boon by which he is incapable of being slain even by the gods;
therefore, how should I act in this matter? I must constantly devise a means, for this Vṛtra, my all-robbing enemy, must necessarily be killed by me.
"If I do not slay Vṛtra today, having deceived that great asura—
him who is of great strength and massive body— it will not lead to my welfare.
While reflecting thus, Śakra called Viṣṇu to mind.
Then he beheld foam upon the ocean, resembling a mountain. "This is neither dry nor moist, and it is not a weapon;
I shall hurl this at Vṛtra, and he will perish in an instant."
Then he swiftly hurled that foam, together with the thunderbolt, at Vṛtra;
and Indra seized that foam which was the destroyer of Vṛtra. Having grasped it with his two arms, Śakra cast it upon the head of Vṛtra.
Having entered that foam, Viṣṇu then destroyed Vṛtra. When Vṛtra had been slain, the quarters became free of darkness,
a propitious wind blew, and all living beings then rejoiced.
Then the gods, along with the Gandharvas, Yakṣas, Rākṣasas, and Pannagas,
as well as the sages, praised Mahendra with various hymns. Honored by all beings, he comforted all beings in turn.

His enemies slain, his soul rejoicing, Vāsava, the knower of dharma, together with the deities, honored Viṣṇu, the foremost in the three worlds. Then, when the immensely powerful Vṛtra, the terror of the gods, had been killed—
Overcome by falsehood, Śakra became exceedingly dejected;
he had previously been overcome by Traiśīrṣā and by the murder of a Brahmin, and again by the spirits of Mahādeva crying out, "O slayer of a Brahmin!"
Repeatedly reviled by those who were fearless, the slayer of Bala and Vṛtra was overcome with shame; taking refuge at the edge of the worlds, his consciousness lost and his senses bewildered,
the lord of the gods could no longer distinguish himself, being overwhelmed by his own misdeeds.
He dwelt concealed within the waters, moving like a serpent.
Then, when the lord of the gods had vanished, oppressed by the fear of the sin of killing a Brahmin,
the earth appeared devastated, stripped of its trees, and its forests withered.
The rivers had their currents cut off and the lakes were devoid of water;
moreover, there was a great agitation among living beings caused by the lack of rain.
Even the gods and all the great seers were deeply terrified.
"The entire world, being without a king, is overwhelmed by calamities.
Either let a king be appointed today, or else let Mahendra be sought out.
Thereupon, the gods became terrified, wondering, "Who shall be our king?"
And even the celestial sages in heaven, deprived of the king of the gods,
did not set their minds upon the sovereignty of the gods.
Śalya said:
Then all the ṛṣis and the gods, the lords of the thirty-three, said:
"Let this illustrious Nahuṣa indeed be consecrated in the sovereignty of the gods;
for he is radiant, glorious, and ever righteous."
Having gone there, they all said: "O King, O Ruler of the Earth, become our king!
And the gods, the lords of the third heaven, [said]:
"O mighty-armed one, [protect] Nahuṣa."
O King, Nahuṣa, desiring his own welfare, spoke thus to those gods and hosts of ṛṣis who were accompanied by the ancestors:
"I am weak; I do not have the power to protect you."
"The king will be born powerful, for strength always resides in Śakra.
Then all the gods, led by the sages, spoke to him again:
"Endowed with the power of our asceticism, protect the kingdom in the triple heaven."

"There is indeed a terrible mutual fear among us, of this there is no doubt. Be consecrated, O Indra among kings; become the king in Triviṣṭapa over the gods, dānavas, yakṣas, ṛṣis, and likewise the rākṣasas."
Of the ancestors, gandharvas, and spirits who come within the range of your vision,
you shall take away their splendor as you look upon them; being thus powerful,
you shall always be the sovereign of all the worlds, placing righteousness at the forefront.
"Protect the Brahman-sages and the gods in heaven.
O Indra among kings, having been consecrated there in heaven, that king,
placing righteousness foremost, then became the sovereign of all the worlds.
When "Om" was uttered, Nahuṣa was then consecrated in the sovereignty of the gods. Having obtained a boon so difficult to acquire and having attained the kingdom in heaven,
he who had always been righteous became possessed by desire.
In all the celestial gardens and in the Nandana groves,
on Kailāsa, on the slopes of the Himavat, on Mandara and the Śveta mountain, on Sahya, Mahendra, and Malaya, and by the oceans and rivers.
Surrounded by Apsarases and attended by celestial maidens,
Nahuṣa, being the king of the gods, then sported in many ways,
listening to various divine stories that were enchanting to the ear.
All musical instruments and songs of sweet melody were played;
Viśvāvasu, Nārada, and the hosts of Gandharvas and Apsarases,
as well as the six seasons personified, stood in attendance before the Lord of the Gods.
A fragrant, pleasant, and pleasantly cool breeze blew from the Maruts. While the high-souled Nahuṣa was thus sporting,
the goddess, the beloved queen of Śakra, came into his sight.
Seeing her, that evil-minded one said to all the members of the assembly:
"Why does the goddess, the queen of Indra, not wait upon me?
I am Indra, the lord of the gods and likewise of the worlds."
"Let Śacī come to my dwelling quickly this very day.
Hearing that, the goddess became dejected and said to Bṛhaspati:
"O Brahmin, protect me from Nahuṣa; I have come to you for refuge."
"O Brahmā, you describe me as one endowed with all auspicious marks,
the beloved of the king of the gods, a partaker of supreme happiness,
united with the state of non-widowhood, a devoted wife faithful to her husband."
"You have previously spoken to me; make those words true indeed.
O Blessed One, O Lord, nothing false has ever been uttered by you before. Therefore, let that which was spoken by you be true, O best of the twice-born."
Then Bṛhaspati spoke to Indrāṇī, who was bewildered by fear:
"O Goddess, that which has been spoken by me shall certainly come true;
you shall soon see Indra, the king of the gods, arrived here."
"You must not fear Nahuṣa; I tell you this truly. I shall soon reunite you with Śakra. Then Nahuṣa heard that Indrāṇī had gone to him for refuge.
Then that king became enraged with Bṛhaspati, the son of Aṅgiras.
Śalya said:
"But perceiving that Nahuṣa was angry, the gods, led by the sages,"
They spoke to Nahuṣa, the king of the gods, who was terrible to behold:
"O King of the Gods, abandon your anger! O Lord, when you are enraged, the entire world—including the asuras, gandharvas, kiṃnaras, and great serpents—is struck with terror."
"O virtuous one, abandon this anger; those like you do not give way to wrath.
That lady is the wife of another; be gracious, O Lord of the Gods!
Turn your mind away from the sin of violating another's wife."
"You are the king of the gods; may it be well with you; protect your subjects with righteousness.
Thus addressed, he, deluded by desire, did not accept those words.
Then the lord of the gods spoke thus to the deities concerning Indra:

In the past, the illustrious Ahalyā, the wife of a seer, was violated by Indra while her husband was still alive; why was he not restrained by you? Indeed, many cruel deeds were committed by Indra in former times.
"Why was he not restrained by you from practicing dissimilarity [of conduct] and even from using deception?
Let the Goddess attend upon me; this is for her supreme benefit, and thus, O gods, it will always bring you well-being as well."
The gods said:
"O Lord of Heaven, we shall bring Indrāṇī just as you desire. O Hero, O Lord of the Gods, cast off this anger and be pleased."
Śalya said:
Having spoken thus, O Bhārata, those gods together with the ṛṣis then went to Bṛhaspati to speak the inauspicious words to Indrāṇī.
"O best of Brahmins, O most excellent of divine sages, we know that Indrāṇī has sought refuge in your house and has been granted protection by you. Therefore,
O one of great splendor, the gods along with the Gandharvas and the ṛṣis [seek your favor]."
They sought to appease Indrāṇī, saying, "Let her be given to Nahuṣa;
Nahuṣa, the king of the gods, is more distinguished than Indra and possesses great splendor. Let this woman of beautiful hips and excellent complexion choose him as her husband."
When this had been said, that goddess, shedding tears with a loud cry,
spoke these words to Bṛhaspati while weeping in distress:
"I do not wish to have the lord Nahuṣa as my husband."
"I have come to you for refuge, O Brahman; save me from this great fear.
When she had spoken these words, Bṛhaspati addressed the goddess.
Bṛhaspati said:
"O Indrāṇī, it is my firm resolve that I shall not abandon one who has come for refuge;
O blameless one, I shall not forsake you, who know the Dharma and are of virtuous character. Being a Brahmin, especially so, I do not wish to commit an improper act."
"Having heard the Dharma and being of truthful character, knowing the instruction of the Dharma, I shall not do this; go away, O best of gods!
Regarding this matter, listen to what was sung by Brahmā in the past."
His seed does not sprout at the time for sowing,
nor does the rain fall for him at the time for rain;
he delivers one who is terrified and has sought refuge to his enemy.
Seeking protection, he finds no refuge; the mindless man obtains food in vain,
and with his efforts ruined, he falls from the heavenly world.
The gods do not accept the sacrificial offering of one who surrenders a terrified refugee; moreover,
his offspring die prematurely.
His ancestors always remain in exile;
he delivers one who is terrified and has sought refuge to his enemy;
and the gods, led by Indra, hurl their thunderbolt at him.
Knowing this to be so, I shall certainly not give up this Śacī,
the world-renowned Indrāṇī, the beloved queen of Śakra;
for whatever is for her benefit would also be for my own benefit.
"O best of gods, let that be done; for I will not give up Śacī.
Śalya said:
"Then the gods spoke to him, the preceptor and the foremost of the Aṅgirases."
"How might this be well-conducted? Advise me, Bṛhaspati.
Bṛhaspati said:
"O auspicious goddess, let her entreat Nahuṣa for some interval of time."
"For this was indeed ordained by Indrāṇī, and so it shall be for us;
time creates many obstacles, and time will carry away time, for Nahuṣa is both arrogant and powerful, relying as he does on the boon."
Śalya said:
Then, when he had spoken thus, the gods were pleased and said to him,
"O Brahmin, this which you have spoken is excellent and for the benefit of all the inhabitants of heaven."
"O best of the twice-born, it is even so; let this goddess be propitiated.
Then all the gods, led by Agni, spoke these words calmly to Indrāṇī, desiring the welfare of the worlds.
"By you this entire world, both the stationary and the moving, is sustained.
You are a devoted wife and you are truthful; go now to Nahuṣa.
Desiring you, that king will soon perish."
"O Goddess, Nahuṣa and Śakra shall both obtain the sovereignty of the gods. Having made this resolution for the sake of accomplishing her purpose, Indrāṇī,
filled with shame, approached the dreadfully appearing Nahuṣa.
And having seen her, endowed with youth and beauty, the evil-minded Nahuṣa, his consciousness overwhelmed by lust, was filled with joy.
Śalya said:
Then, having seen her, Nahuṣa, the king of the gods, spoke to her at that time:
"O lady of radiant smiles, I am the Indra of even the three worlds. O lady of excellent hips, O woman of beautiful complexion, accept me as your husband."
Thus addressed by Nahuṣa, that goddess, devoted to her husband,
trembled, agitated by fear like a plantain tree in a gale;
she then paid homage to Brahmā, placing her joined palms upon her head.
Then he spoke to Nahuṣa, the king of the gods, who was terrible to behold:
"O Lord of the Suras, I wish to obtain something from you for a certain period of time;
for it is not known whether Śakra has arrived here, or what has become of him, or where he has gone."
"O Lord, if this truth is not understood after it has been realized, then I shall attend upon you; I tell you this truly. Having been addressed thus by Indrāṇī, Nahuṣa became filled with joy.
Nahuṣa said:
"O lady of beautiful hips, let it be as you tell me.
Once you have learned of my arrival, you must act accordingly; remember this as the truth."
Śalya said:
Released by Nahuṣa, that auspicious and ascetic woman then departed and went to the abode of Bṛhaspati.
Having heard her words, O best of kings, the gods, led by Agni, deliberated with one-pointed minds for the sake of Śakra;
they met with Viṣṇu, the powerful God of gods.
Agitated, those experts in speech addressed him with these words:
"O God of gods, Lord of the world, we do not know where Śakra, the lord of the hosts of gods, has gone, for he is indeed overwhelmed by the sin of Brahman-slaughter."
Unperceived by the hosts of gods, O Lord, you have gone and are not known;
yet you, O Lord of Gods, our progenitor and the Master of the world,
have assumed the state of Viṣṇu for the sake of protecting all beings.

"O best of the hosts of gods, since Vṛtra has been slain by your prowess, Vāsava is now beset by the sin of killing a Brahmin; please ordain his liberation. Having heard those words of the gods, Viṣṇu spoke.
"Let Śakra sacrifice to me alone; I shall purify the wielder of the thunderbolt.
Having worshipped me with the holy horse-sacrifice, the subduer of Pāka will return to the lordship of the gods, free from fear from any quarter."
"And by his own deeds, the evil-minded Nahuṣa shall meet his destruction. O gods, remain vigilant and endure this for some time.
Śalya said:
Viṣṇu dismissed the gods, who were led by the sages.
Having heard that auspicious and truthful speech of Viṣṇu, which was like nectar,
all the hosts of deities, together with their teachers and the ṛṣis, [departed].
To that place where Śakra was overcome with fear they approached;
there, O King, the great horse-sacrifice of the high-souled Mahendra was performed for the sake of purification, indeed as a remover of the sin of Brahman-slaughter.
O Yudhiṣṭhira, having divided the sin of Brahman-slaughter among trees, rivers,
mountains, the earth, and women,
and having distributed it among all beings and released it, the Lord of the Gods departed.
Free from fever and purified of sin, Vāsava became self-possessed; yet,

seeing that Nahuṣa was unshakable from his station, the slayer of Bala observed him to be unbearable for all beings due to the granting of the boon and his power that eclipsed the splendor of all creatures.
Then the heroic lord of Śacī vanished once more;
invisible to all beings, he moved about awaiting his time. When Śakra had thus disappeared, Śacī was overcome with grief.
"Alas, Śakra! the goddess then lamented, deeply distressed:
"If I have given gifts, if I have offered oblations, and if I have satisfied my gurus—if truth indeed exists within me—then let there be only one husband."
"I pay homage to this meritorious, divine, and celestial Night, which has begun during the northern course of the sun;
may my heart's desire be fulfilled. And there, she, being self-restrained, worshipped that divine Night.
By virtue of her devotion to her husband, she brought about a divine ear through the power of truth.
Having seen that goddess, the illustrious lady then replied:
"Show me that place where the king of the gods resides."
"Thus spoke the goddess Upaśruti; let the truth be seen through truth.
Śalya said:
"Then Upaśruti approached that beautiful and virtuous woman."
Seeing that goddess, endowed with youth and beauty, standing before her, Indrāṇī was greatly delighted; having honored her, she asked:
"I wish to know you; tell me, O lovely-faced one, who are you?"
Thus addressed by Indrāṇī, the goddess then spoke these words.
Upaśruti said:
"O Goddess, I am Upaśruti, and I have come into your presence."
"Gratified by your truthfulness, I have come to grant you a vision;
for you are a devoted wife, disciplined in self-restraint and observance.
I shall show you Śakra, the god who is the slayer of Vṛtra."
"Follow quickly; may prosperity be yours; you shall behold the best of the gods.
Śalya said:
"Then Indrāṇī followed after that goddess as she set out."
Having passed beyond the forests of the gods and many mountains,
and having crossed the Himalayas, he reached the northern side;
and having arrived at the ocean, which extends for many yojanas.
He reached a great island covered with various trees and creepers. There he saw a divine lake, filled with various birds, a hundred yojanas in width and just as many in length, and beautiful.
There, O Bhārata, were divine lotuses of five colors,
blooming by the thousands and celebrated by bees;
in the midst of that lake was a vast and auspicious lotus-pond.
Surrounded by a great lotus with a pale yellow,
upturned stalk, she entered together with her [sister] after piercing the stalk of the lotus; and there she saw Śatakratu (Indra) having entered among the fibers of the lotus root.
Seeing that Lord standing there in an extremely subtle form,
the goddess Upaśruti also assumed a subtle form;
and Indrāṇī praised Indra with his celebrated deeds of the past.
Then, while being praised, the god Purandara said to Śacī:
"For what purpose have you come? And how was I discovered?
By whom, O woman of excellent complexion, was I described to you as being here?"
Then she related Nahuṣa’s conduct:
"Having attained the sovereignty of Indra over the three worlds, he was filled with the intoxication of his own prowess; and that wicked-souled one, possessed by pride, spoke to me, O Śatakratu."
"Wait upon me!"—thus that cruel one has set a time for me.
O Lord, if you do not protect me, he will bring me under his control.
Tormented by this, O Śakra, I have come into your presence.
"O mighty-armed one, slay the fierce Nahuṣa, whose resolve is evil! O destroyer of Daityas and Dānavas, reveal yourself;
O Lord, regain your splendor and rule over the kingdom of the gods."
"And just as Vṛtra was slain by you, O Great King.
Śalya said:
Having been addressed thus by Śacī, the Blessed One then spoke again.

"This is not the time for valor, O beautiful lady, for Nahuṣa is more powerful than ever; he has been strengthened by the sages with offerings to the gods and the ancestors. I shall devise a plan in this matter, O Queen; you must carry it out."
"O auspicious one, this must be kept secret by you; it must not be told anywhere.
O slender-waisted lady, go and speak to Nahuṣa in private:
'O Lord of the World, come to me by means of this divine vehicle of the ṛṣis.'"
"Speak to him thus: 'In this way, I shall be pleased to come under your control.
Having been addressed in this manner by the king of the gods, that lotus-eyed wife said, "So be it," and then went toward Nahuṣa.
Then, having seen her, Nahuṣa was struck with wonder and spoke these words:
"Welcome to you, O lady of beautiful hips; what may I do for you, O girl of radiant smiles?
Devote yourself to me, who am devoted to you, O auspicious one; what do you desire, O high-minded woman?"
"O auspicious one, O slender-waisted lady, I shall do whatever task you have to perform.
You should feel no shame; trust in me, O fair-hipped one.
I swear by the truth, O goddess, that I will carry out your word."
Indrāṇī said:
"O Lord of the World, I await that time which has been appointed for me by you;
then, O Sovereign of the Gods, you yourself shall become my husband."
"O King of the Gods, attend to that task which is in my heart;
I shall tell it to you, O King, if you will do this which is pleasing to me. If you grant my words joined with affection, then I shall come under your control."

"O Lord of the Gods, I desire here an unprecedented vehicle for you— one that neither Viṣṇu, nor Rudra, nor the Asuras, nor the Rākṣasas possess— such as the steeds of Indra, or elephants, or chariots."
"O Great King, O Lord, let all the ṛṣis gathered together carry you in a palanquin, O King; for this indeed pleases me. You ought not to have an equal among either the asuras or the gods."
"By your own prowess, seize the splendor of them all through your very sight;
no one possessed of valor desires to stand before you.
Śalya said:
Thus addressed, Nahuṣa was indeed filled with joy at that time;
and the lord of the gods spoke these words to that blameless woman:
"O lady of excellent complexion, this vehicle you have mentioned is unprecedented."
"O Goddess, this is deeply pleasing to me; O fair-faced one, I am under your power.
For he who makes sages his mounts does not possess little heroism.
I am an ascetic of great strength, the lord of the past, the future, and the present."

If I were angry, the world would cease to exist; everything is established in me. O lady of pure smiles, all the worlds—gods, dānavas, gandharvas, kinnaras, uragas, and rākṣasas—are not a match for me when I am enraged.
Whatever I behold with my eye, I take away its splendor.
I am Indra among the gods and the supreme lord of the worlds;
in me reside the sacrificial offerings to the gods and the ancestors, as well as the eternal worlds.
"Therefore, O Goddess, I shall carry out your word; of this there is no doubt. All the Seven Sages, as well as all the Brahman-sages, will speak to me.
