Behold our majesty and our supernatural power, O lady of excellent complexion."
"By me all the gods, gandharvas, and dānavas have been deprived of their vigor;
whatever splendor I behold in each of them, that splendor I take away.
Having spoken thus to the goddess and having dismissed that lady of beautiful countenance, [he departed].
Then, O Bhārata, having reflected and by means of his strength and heroism, Nahuṣa dismissed the elephant Supratīka as well as Airāvata,
and [dismissed] the celestial chariot yoked with swans as well as the chariot yoked with horses.
But he, filled with great pride, having insulted the great sages and having placed those seers— who were established in their vows— upon his celestial chariot,
was unrighteous, powerful, and intoxicated by the pride of his boon.
That evil-minded one, acting out of lust, drove those sages about.
And she, having been sent forth by Nahuṣa, spoke to Bṛhaspati:
"The time limit that was set for me here by Nahuṣa has only a small portion remaining."
"Search for Śakra quickly; show compassion to me, your devotee.
"So be it," the blessed Bṛhaspati replied to her.
"O Goddess, you must not fear the evil-minded Nahuṣa."

For this lowest of men will not remain for long; having gone, O auspicious lady, he is slain by his violation of the great seers' vehicle and his ignorance of dharma. And I shall perform a sacrifice for the destruction of this evil-minded one.

"I shall reach Śakra; do not fear, may it be well with you. Then, having kindled the fire according to the rules, Bṛhaspati, possessed of great splendor, offered the supreme oblation for the sake of obtaining the king of the gods.
Having offered the oblation into the fire, he said, "O King, let Śakra be sought.
Thereupon, the blessed Lord Agni himself,
having assumed a wondrous female form, suddenly vanished.
Moving with a speed exceeding that of thought, he searched through the cardinal directions, the intermediate directions, the mountains, the forests, the earth, and the atmosphere;
and in the mere twinkling of an eye, he arrived before Bṛhaspati.
Agni said:
"O Bṛhaspati, I do not see the king of the gods anywhere. Water remains [everywhere], yet I do not venture to enter the water."
"O Brahmin, I have no access there; what else may I do for you?
Śalya said:
"The preceptor of the gods replied to him, 'Enter the waters, O you of great splendor!'"
Agni said:
"I shall not be able to enter the waters; my destruction will occur there.
I have come to you for refuge; may it be well with you, O one of great splendor."
Fire arose from water, the Kṣatra from the Brāhmaṇa, and iron from stone;
the all-pervading energy of these subsides within their own respective sources.
Bṛhaspati said:
O Agni, you are the mouth of all the gods; you are the bearer of the oblation.
You move hidden within all beings like a witness.
The seers call you the One, and they call you again as threefold.
O Consumer of Oblations, if this world were abandoned by you, it would perish instantly.
Having offered salutations to you, the Brahmins go to the eternal state won by their own deeds, together with their wives and even their sons.
O Agni, you alone are the bearer of oblations, and you alone are the supreme offering.
They worship you alone with sacrificial sessions and with sacrifices at the highest ritual. Having created these three worlds, O bearer of oblations;
When the time arrives, you blaze forth again as the source of this entire world;
O Agni, you alone become its foundation once more.
O Agni, they call you the clouds and you alone are the lightning;
for it is from you that the years emerge and consume all beings.
All waters are deposited in you, and this entire world is centered in you.
"O Purifier, there is nothing in the three worlds unknown to you.
Everyone resorts to their own source; enter the waters without hesitation.
I shall strengthen you with eternal Vedic mantras."
Śalya said:
Thus praised, the divine bearer of oblations, the supreme sage,
spoke these excellent words with great pleasure to Bṛhaspati.
"I shall show Śakra to you; I tell you this truth. Then Agni entered the waters—along with the oceans and the ponds—and arrived at that lake where the performer of a hundred sacrifices was hidden."
Then, O bull of the Bharatas, while searching for lotuses there as well,
he beheld the lord of the gods stationed in the midst of the lotus stalks.
Having returned quickly from there, he informed Bṛhaspati.
Then Bṛhaspati, accompanied by celestial sages and gandharvas, went to the Lord who was seated upon a lotus fiber with a body the size of an atom,
and he praised the slayer of Bala, the god, by recounting his ancient deeds.
O Śakra, the great asura Namuci, who was terrible, has been slain by you;
likewise both Śambara and Bala, of fearsome prowess. O Śatakratu, may you prosper and utterly destroy all your enemies.

"Arise, O wielder of the thunderbolt! Behold the celestial sages who have assembled here. O Mahendra, O Lord, having slain the Dānavas, the worlds have been saved by you, who relied upon the foam of the waters, augmented by the splendor of Viṣṇu."
O King of the Gods, Lord of the World, Vṛtra was slain by you in the past. You are the most excellent and worthy of praise among all beings;
there is no being here equal to you.
O Śakra, all beings are sustained by you;
you have established the greatness of the gods. Protect the gods and their worlds, O Mahendra, and attain strength.
Being thus praised, he grew gradually;
assuming his own form, he became endowed with strength.
And the god spoke to his preceptor Bṛhaspati, who stood before him.
"What task remains for you? The great Asura, the son of Tvaṣṭṛ, has been slain, as has Vṛtra of immense body, who sought to devour the worlds.
Bṛhaspati said:
"King Nahuṣa, a human being, having attained the sovereignty of the gods through the splendor of the hosts of celestial sages, oppresses us all most severely.
Indra said:

"How indeed did Nahuṣa obtain the kingdom of the gods, so difficult to attain? Endowed with what ascetic power, or possessed of what prowess, O Bṛhaspati, did he reach that state? Tell me all of that, as to how he attained the position of Indra."
Bṛhaspati said:
"O Lord of Gods, when you have perished, the entire world will be deeply distressed;
agitated by mutual fear, it will become a suffering realm without a ruler."
Then, by the gods together with the Gandharvas, the hosts of ṛṣis, and the fires,
the human king Nahuṣa was consecrated in the sovereignty of the gods.
The gods, being afraid, desired Śakra.
That great station of Indra has been abandoned by you.
Then all the gods, the ancestors, the ṛṣis, and the hosts of gandharvas gathered together.
Having gone there, they said to Nahuṣa, "O Śakra,
be our king and the protector of the world. Nahuṣa said to them, "I am not capable."
"Be strengthened by ascetic power and by splendor!
When the gods had spoken thus,
King Nahuṣa became possessed of terrible prowess.
Having obtained sovereignty over the three worlds, that evil-souled ascetic makes them his mounts and departs for other realms—
a most terrible being whose very glance is a poison that robs one of one's vital energy.
May you never see Nahuṣa at any time;
for all the gods, afflicted by fear of Nahuṣa,
wander about in hidden forms so that they may not be seen.
Śalya said:
While Bṛhaspati, the best of the Aṅgirases, was speaking thus, Kubera, the guardian of the world, [arrived].
Yama, the ancient son of Vivasvat, as well as the gods Soma and Varuṇa, arrived;
having assembled together, they spoke to Mahendra.
By good fortune, the son of Tvaṣṭṛ and Vṛtra have been slain;
and by good fortune, O Śakra, we behold you safe, unhurt, and with your enemy destroyed.
Having addressed them appropriately, Śakra urged them on regarding the interval concerning Nahuṣa:
"King Nahuṣa, of terrible form, is the ruler of the gods."
"Therefore, let assistance be given to me by you all;
for Mahendra, having met with the world-protectors, was indeed pleased in mind."
And he said to them:
"They replied, 'O Lord, Nahuṣa is of terrible form;
we fear him, for his very glance is poisonous.'"
"O King, if you should defeat Nahuṣa, then we indeed deserve a share, O Śakra.
Indra said, "Let it be so; may you be the lord of the waters."
May Yama and Kubera likewise receive this great consecration today along with him;
thus may we conquer our enemy, Nahuṣa of the terrible gaze.
Then Agni also said to Śakra, "Grant me a share;
I shall provide you assistance. To him Śakra replied, "O Agni, it shall be yours as well."
"In this great sacrifice, there is indeed one portion for Indra and Agni.
Having reflected thus, the blessed Mahendra, the subduer of Pāka,
likewise [appointed] Kubera as the lord of all Yakṣas and of wealth.
Then Śakra, the giver of boons, having honored them, bestowed the lordship over the ancestors upon Vaivasvata, and likewise the lordship over the waters upon Varuṇa.
Śalya said:
Then, as the wise Devarāja Nahuṣa was contemplating a means for his own destruction together with those very world-protectors,
the venerable ascetic Agastya appeared there.
Having honored the Lord of the Gods, he said: "By good fortune you indeed prosper through the destruction of Viśvarūpa and the slaying of the Asura Vṛtra.
By good fortune we behold the King of the Gods, Śatakratu, whose enemies have been destroyed."
By good fortune, Dharma remains established in the world; by good fortune, the worlds are firmly established. By good fortune, O Lord of Gods, we behold you; by good fortune, the worlds are renewed.
And by good fortune, O Purandara, Nahuṣa has fallen from the sovereignty of the gods.
"By good fortune, O slayer of Bala, I see you with your enemies destroyed.
Indra said:
"Welcome to you, O great seer; I am pleased by the sight of you."
"Accept from me water for the feet, water for sipping, a cow, and the guest-offering (arghya).
Śalya said:
"When that best of sages had been honored and was seated upon his seat,"
The Lord of the Gods, greatly delighted, questioned that bull among Brahmins:
"O Blessed One, O best of the twice-born, I wish this to be told:
how was Nahuṣa, whose resolve was sinful, cast down from heaven?"
Agastya said:
"Listen, O Śakra, to these pleasing words concerning how the evil-minded King Nahuṣa, arrogant in his strength and of wicked conduct, was cast down from heaven."
O God, best among victors, while carrying that evil-doing Nahuṣa, the illustrious celestial rishis and the stainless brahmin rishis, exhausted by their toil,
asked him about a doubt.
"O Vāsava, regarding these mantras proclaimed by Brahmā for the sprinkling of cows—
do they constitute authority or not?
Nahuṣa, his mind deluded by darkness, said to him, "They do not."
The sages said:
"You have set out upon unrighteousness and do not resort to dharma;
this is our authority, as it was previously declared by the great seers."
Agastya said:
Then, O Vāsava, while he was disputing with the sages, he—
afflicted by unrighteousness— struck me on the head with his foot.
Because of that, O Lord of Śacī, his splendor was destroyed and he was deprived of his glory.
Then I spoke to him, who was agitated and oppressed by fear:
"Since this Brahman was established by the ancestors and practiced by the Brahmarṣis..."
Because you defile that which is undefiled, because you touched my head with your foot,
and because you, O fool, have made the unassailable sages who are equal to Brahmā into draft animals and forced them to carry you, you are thus stripped of your splendor from heaven.

"O destroyer of sin, fallen and with your merit exhausted, you shall wander upon the surface of the earth for ten thousand years assuming the form of a great serpent; once those years are completed, you will regain heaven."

"Having seen Yudhiṣṭhira, born of your own lineage, you have been slain by a Brahmin's curse; enter heaven, O subduer of enemies! Thus has that evil-souled one fallen from the sovereignty of the gods."
But Nahuṣa, evil-minded, wicked-souled, and of sinful intent, said:
"By good fortune we prosper, O Śakra; that thorn in the side of the Brahmins has been slain.
Enter Triviṣṭapa and protect the worlds, O Lord of Śacī!"
Having conquered his senses and subdued his enemies, he was being praised by the great seers.
Śalya said:
Then the gods, surrounded by hosts of great seers, were exceedingly gratified.
The ancestors, the yakṣas, the serpents, and likewise the rākṣasas;
the gandharvas and the daughters of the gods, and all the hosts of apsarases;
the lakes, the rivers, the mountains, and the oceans, O lord of the people.
Approaching him, they all said: "By good fortune you prosper, O slayer of enemies!
By good fortune the wicked Nahuṣa has been slain by the wise Agastya;
by good fortune that man of evil conduct has been turned into a serpent upon the earth."
Śalya said:
Then Śakra, being praised by hosts of Gandharvas and Apsarases,
mounted Airāvata, the lord of elephants, who was endowed with all auspicious marks.
Pāvaka of great splendor, the great seer Bṛhaspati,
Yama, Varuṇa, and Kubera the lord of wealth— Śakra, the slayer of Vṛtra, was surrounded by all these gods.
Accompanied by Gandharvas and Apsarases, the Lord traveled through the three worlds.
Having united with Mahendrāṇī, the King of the Gods, Śatakratu,
the sovereign of the deities, protected the world filled with supreme joy.
Then the venerable Aṅgiras appeared there and worshipped the lord of the gods with mantras from the Atharvaveda. Thereupon,
the venerable Indra became filled with joy.
And then Atharvan granted him a boon:
"The name 'Atharvāṅgirasa' shall belong to this Veda;
for this shall indeed be its designation, and you shall receive a share of the sacrifice."
Having thus honored the Lord Atharvāṅgiras at that time,
O great king, Śatakratu, the king of the gods, dismissed him;
he likewise honored all the thirty deities and the sages whose wealth is asceticism.

O King, Indra, being greatly delighted, protected his subjects according to dharma. Thus did Indra, together with his wife, undergo suffering and live in concealment out of a desire to slay his enemies.
"You should not harbor resentment over this, O Indra among kings, that you have been afflicted in the great forest together with Draupadī and your high-souled brothers.
In this way, O Bhārata, O Indra among kings, you shall regain your kingdom."
Just as Śakra attained his status after slaying Vṛtra, O joy of the Kauravas, so too was the evil-conducted Nahuṣa— hater of Brahmins and wicked-minded—
struck down by the curse of Agastya and destroyed for eternal years.
"O slayer of enemies, in this way your wicked foes—
Karna, Duryodhana, and the others— will swiftly meet their destruction.
Then you shall enjoy this earth as far as the ocean."
O hero, O lord, accompanied by your brothers and Draupadī,
you should listen to this narrative concerning the victory of Śakra, which is equal in authority to the Vedas, while the armies are arrayed and you desire victory.
Therefore, O best among victors, I proclaim victory to you;
for high-souled men flourish when they are being praised, O Yudhiṣṭhira.
This is the end of the great-souled Kṣatriyas, O Yudhiṣṭhira.
Due to the transgression of Duryodhana and through the power of Bhīma and Arjuna,
a terrible destruction will soon take place in battle. He who, being self-restrained, recites this narrative of Indra’s victory—
Having shaken off all evil and conquered heaven, he rejoices both here and after death.
Such a man has no fear born of enemies, nor shall he be childless;
he shall encounter no calamity and attains a long life.
"In every case he attains victory and never suffers defeat.
Vaiśampāyana said:
"O bull of the Bharata race, the king was thus consoled by Śalya."

The best among the upholders of dharma honored Śalya according to the prescribed rites. Having heard the words of Śalya, the mighty-armed Yudhiṣṭhira, son of Kuntī, replied with these words to the King of Madra:
"You will undoubtedly perform the charioteership for Karṇa;
in that role, you must diminish Karṇa’s prowess with my praises.
Śalya said:
"I shall do exactly as you have told me;
and whatever else I am capable of doing, that too I shall perform for you.
Vaiśampāyana said:
Then, having taken leave of the sons of Kuntī, the illustrious Śalya, the lord of Madra and subduer of foes, departed with his army for Duryodhana.
Vaiśampāyana said:
Then Śalya, accompanied by his army, as if making the earth tremble,
went to the city of the son of Dhṛtarāṣṭra, Nāgasāhvaya;
thereafter, the hero Yuyudhāna, the great car-warrior of the Sātvatas, [proceeded].
With a great fourfold army, he approached Yudhiṣṭhira. His warriors, possessed of great heroism and gathered from various lands,
were heroes equipped with diverse weapons who brought splendor to the host.

With battle-axes, slings, spears, javelins, and mallets; with darts, double-edged swords, hatchets, barbed missiles, and stainless scimitars; and with arrays of swords, bows, and various kinds of arrows.
Washed with oil and gleaming, that army indeed shone;
the appearance of that host— which resembled a cloud and was adorned with those weapons— was like that of a cloud accompanied by lightning.
O King, that army of an *akṣauhiṇī* then entered Yudhiṣṭhira’s force and vanished within it, like a small river entering the ocean.
In the same way, the powerful bull among the Cedis took up an *akṣauhiṇī*.
Dhṛṣṭaketu approached the Pāṇḍavas of immeasurable prowess,
as did Jayatsena of Magadha, the mighty son of Jarāsaṃdha;
with an entire akṣauhiṇī of troops, he came to Dharmarāja.

In the same way, O king of kings, Pāṇḍya, surrounded by various kinds of warriors dwelling on the coastal marshlands of the ocean, approached Yudhiṣṭhira. His army was exceedingly vast in that gathering of forces.
O King,
Drupada’s army was then exceedingly beautiful to behold, well-attired and powerful; it was graced by brave men gathered from various lands and by his sons, who were great chariot-warriors.
Likewise, Virāṭa, the king of the Matsyas and commander of an army,
went to the Pāṇḍavas accompanied by mountain-dwelling rulers;
from here and there, they gathered around the high-souled Pāṇḍus.
Seven akṣauhiṇīs, crowded with various banners and eager for battle with the Kurus, gladdened the Pāṇḍavas;
likewise, they increased the joy of Dhṛtarāṣṭra’s son.
The lord of the earth, Bhagadatta, gave an army of one *akṣauhiṇī*;
his invincible force, filled with Cīnas and Kirātas who were like golden [images], shone like a forest of *karṇikāra* trees.
Likewise, O descendant of Kuru, the heroic Bhūriśravas and Śalya approached Duryodhana, each with a separate akṣauhiṇī;
and Kṛtavarman, the son of Hṛdika, arrived together with the forces of the Bhojas and Andhakas.
With an entire army of one akṣauhiṇī, he approached Duryodhana.
His force, with those tigers among men wearing forest garlands,
shone like a forest filled with intoxicated elephants at play.
And other lords of the earth, inhabitants of Sindhu and Sauvīra, headed by Jayadratha, arrived as if making the mountains tremble;
their vast army of one akṣauhiṇī then shone forth.
Being tossed by the wind like clouds of many forms,
Sudakṣiṇa the Kāmboja, along with the Yavanas and Śakas,
as well as the mighty-armed king, the lord of the Yavanas, arrived.
O lord of the people, he approached the Kauravya with an akṣauhiṇī;
his arrival of troops appeared like a swarm of locusts,
and having reached the Kauravya, it then vanished right there.
Likewise, Nīla, the resident of Māhiṣmatī, together with his blue-weaponed followers—
mighty protectors of the earth dwelling in the southern region—
and the two kings of Avanti, well-surrounded by those of great strength; ||| 05,019.023–05,019.024 ||| [he approached].
Each with a separate *akṣauhiṇī*, those two marched against Suyodhana;
and the five Kekaya princes, tigers among men and brothers born of the same womb,
gladdening the Kaurava, advanced toward him with an *akṣauhiṇī*.
O bull of the Bharatas, from here and there, three other armies were assembled by all those high-souled rulers of the earth;
thus, those eleven divisions belonged to Duryodhana.
Desirous of fighting the sons of Kuntī and crowded with various banners,
O King, there was no room left in Hastināpura at that time for the kings and the leaders of their armies, even considering only the principal ones, O Bhārata.

Then, O Bhārata, [he traversed] the land of the Five Rivers and the entire Kurujāṅgala, as well as the Rohitaka forest and the whole of the Maru desert, Ahicchatra, Kālakūṭa, and the banks of the Gaṅgā.
Vāraṇa, Vāṭadhāna, and the Yamunā mountain—
this vast region, abundant in wealth and grain,
became completely crowded with the army of the Kauravas.
There, the royal priest, who had been sent by the King of Pañcāla toward the Kauravas, beheld the army thus arrayed. Vaiśampāyana said:
Having approached the descendant of Kuru, Drupada’s family priest was honored by Dhṛtarāṣṭra, Bhīṣma, and Vidura;
having first spoken of all his well-being and likewise inquired after their health, he continued.
In the midst of all the commanders of the army, he spoke these words:
"The eternal dharma of kings is known to you all;
nevertheless, since it is already understood, I shall speak for the sake of providing this formal discourse."
Dhṛtarāṣṭra and Pāṇḍu were both renowned sons of one father;
there is no doubt that their paternal wealth was equal.
Those who are the sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra have obtained their paternal property.
"How is it that the sons of Pāṇḍu did not receive their paternal wealth? This being the case, you already know how, in the past,
the paternal property was not obtained by the sons of Pāṇḍu because it was withheld by the son of Dhṛtarāṣṭra."
Though they strove many times by means even that would end their lives,
those who still had life remaining could not be led to the abode of Yama;
and again, the kingdom was expanded by those high-souled ones through their own strength.
That which was stolen by deceit by the base sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra together with the Saubalas—
that deed was likewise approved by him; indeed,
he allowed us to dwell here in the great forest for thirteen years.
In the assembly hall, those heroes, together with their wives, were severely tormented;
likewise, in the forest, they endured various most dreadful afflictions.
And so it was in the city of Virāṭa, as if they had entered into another womb.
The highest degree of affliction has been reached by those great-souled ones because of their sins; yet,
casting all that previous transgression behind them,
those bulls among the Kurus desire only peace with the Kurus.
Having understood their conduct as well as the conduct of Duryodhana,
these well-wishers ought to conciliate Dhṛtarāṣṭra here;
for those heroes do not desire conflict with the Kurus.
The Pāṇḍavas desire their own [kingdom] so that the world may not perish.
Furthermore, whatever cause there might be for the Dhārtarāṣṭra to engage in conflict,
that cause should not be considered valid, for they are indeed more powerful.

Indeed, seven akṣauhiṇīs have assembled under the son of Dharma; desiring to fight with the Kurus, they await his command. Furthermore, there are other tigers among men who are equal to thousands of akṣauhiṇīs.
Sātyaki, Bhīmasena, and the two Yamas of great strength—
these eleven armies were gathered on one side;
and on the other side was the long-armed Dhananjaya, who assumes many forms.
Just as the Diademed One (Arjuna) surpasses all armies,
even so does the mighty-armed Vāsudeva of great splendor;
[consider] both the vastness of the armies and the prowess of the Diademed One.
"Having recognized the intelligence of Kṛṣṇa, what man would continue to fight?
Therefore, you all should give back what ought to be given, according to dharma and according to the agreement; let not this time pass you by."
Vaiśampāyana said:
Having heard those words of his, the highly effulgent Bhīṣma, advanced in wisdom, honored him at the appropriate time and spoke these words.
"By good fortune all the Pāṇḍavas, together with their kinsmen, are well;
by good fortune they have allies, and by good fortune they are devoted to dharma. By good fortune those brothers, the joy of the Kurus, desire peace."
"By good fortune, you do not intend to fight with Dāmodara.
What you have said is all true; there is no doubt of this.
Yet, it is my opinion that your speech is excessively harsh because of your status as a Brahmin."
Without doubt, those Pāṇḍavas have suffered hardships both in the forest and here;
and they have undoubtedly obtained their father’s entire inheritance in accordance with dharma.
Kiritin Pārtha is powerful, skilled in weapons, and possessed of great strength.
For who indeed could withstand Dhananjaya, the son of Pāṇḍu, in battle—
not even the wielder of the thunderbolt himself, let alone other archers? It is my conviction that he is capable of facing all the three worlds.
While Bhīṣma was speaking those words, Karṇa, filled with indignation, looked at Duryodhana and, having boldly interrupted him, spoke these words:
"O Brahman, there is nothing in this world that is not known by anyone who exists."
What is the use of that which has been said again and again?
In the past, for the sake of Duryodhana, Śakuni defeated [the Pāṇḍavas] at dice;
then, by agreement, Yudhiṣṭhira, the son of Pāṇḍu, went to the forest.
Disregarding that agreement,
O learned one, the king Duryodhana, relying on the strength of the Matsyas and the Pāñcālas, does not wish to give up his paternal kingdom; out of fear, he would not yield even a single step.
According to the law, however, one should give even the entire earth to an enemy;
if they desire their ancestral kingdom once more,
let them dwell in the forest for that period of time as promised.
Then let them dwell without fear in the lap of Duryodhana; for they would surely act upon this unrighteous resolve solely out of folly. Now, if those Pāṇḍavas, casting aside dharma, desire war—
"Having encountered these best of the Kurus, they will remember my words.
Bhīṣma said:
"O son of Rādhā, what deed of yours do you wish to have remembered by your speech?"
When Pārtha alone defeated six chariot-warriors in battle,
you witnessed that very deed as he was being repeatedly conquered;
O wise one, why did you not come to him right there in the city of Virāṭa?
"If we do not act exactly as this brahmin has said,
then we shall certainly be slain by him in battle and eat the dust;
Duryodhana, along with his ministers, will perish without a doubt."
Vaiśampāyana said:
Then Dhṛtarāṣṭra, having honored and propitiated Bhīṣma and having rebuked the son of Rādhā, spoke these words.
"Bhīṣma, the son of Śāntanu, has spoken these words for our benefit,
both in the presence of Duryodhana and in the assembly of the kings. This righteous soul, skilled in speech, will now speak further."
These words spoken by the high-souled Bhīṣma are for our benefit,
as well as for the benefit of the Pāṇḍavas and indeed for the entire world. Having reflected upon this, I shall send Sañjaya to the sons of Pṛthā.
"May you return today to the Pāṇḍavas without delay.
Having honored him, that descendant of Kuru dispatched him to the Pāṇḍavas;
then, having summoned Sañjaya into the midst of the assembly hall, he spoke these words.
Dhṛtarāṣṭra said:
"O Sañjaya, they say the sons of Pāṇḍu have arrived; go and ascertain whether they are at Upaplavya."
"You should also honor Ajātaśatru;
by good fortune, O sinless one, you have arrived at my village. My son has fallen under the power of death."
"O Sañjaya, you must tell Duryodhana, whose mind is stained by passion: 'O Sañjaya, having endured a period of hardship that was undeserved, all [the Pāṇḍavas] are now well.'"
"Peace for those virtuous ones who have acted with kindness, though they were treated falsely, will soon be found among us.
O Sañjaya, I am not anywhere [at enmity] with the Pāṇḍavas."
I have never seen anyone practicing any kind of deceit;
for having acquired all their prosperity through their own prowess,
the Pāṇḍavas bestowed it upon me alone.
For even upon close examination, I find no fault among them by which I might ever reproach the sons of Pṛthā;
they always perform their actions in accordance with dharma and artha.
Those who love happiness do not indulge in sensual desires, nor do they yield to heat, cold, hunger, thirst,
sleep, drowsiness, anger, joy, or negligence.
Having overcome [all obstacles] through both fortitude and wisdom,
the sons of Pṛthā strive for the union of dharma and artha;
they bestow wealth upon their friends at the proper time.
Their friendship does not decay from living together,
for the Pārthas act toward others according to what is fitting and beneficial;
indeed, there is no one among the faction of Ajamīḍha who hates them.
Except for the wicked, treacherous, and dull-witted Duryodhana, and the even more base Karṇa— for among them,
these [others] have no love for inferior pleasures.
O Sañjaya, a person of dull intellect strives to obtain a share of the splendor of those great-souled ones who possess blazing majesty.
Duryodhana, flourishing in happiness through his energy and exertion, considers that to be well-done;
for the fool thinks he has gained their share.
It is possible to seize the wealth of the living Pāṇḍavas—
of that Ajātaśatru whose path is followed by Arjuna, Keśava, Vṛkodara, and Sātyaki.
The two sons of Mādrī and all the Sṛñjayas are also there;
it would have been better for him to give [the earth] away before the battle,
for he alone, Savyasācin, could have conquered the entire earth.
The wielder of the Gāṇḍīva bow, standing upon his chariot, drove them away—
just as the high-souled Keśava Viṣṇu, the invincible lord of the three worlds, [did].
What mortal could stand before him—
he who is the most excellent and worthy of praise among all the gods, scattering showers of arrows with the roar of Parjanya?
Like swarms of locusts with swift speed, he,
on a single chariot with the Gāṇḍīva bow, conquered even the northern direction and the Uttara-kurus.
Savyasācin brought back their wealth and made the followers of the army pay tribute;
and it was Savyasācin who [conquered] the gods at Khāṇḍava.
The wielder of the Gāṇḍīva bow conquered those led by Indra;
Phalguna offered [the spoils] to the Fire-god,
increasing the fame and honor of the Pāṇḍavas.
There is no wielder of the mace equal to Bhīma today,
nor is there an elephant-rider equal to him; they say that on the chariot, he is not inferior to Arjuna.
Possessing the strength of ten thousand elephants in his arms,
well-trained, having incurred their enmity, and full of energy,
he would incinerate the sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra with his fury and speed.
Always intolerant and powerful, he could not be defeated in battle even by Vāsava himself in person;
he was highly intelligent, strong, and swift-handed.
Well-trained by Phalguna like two hawks tearing through flocks of birds,
let not the two sons of Mādrī enter among the Kurus here.
This full strength is ours alone; there is no third [force] equal to that of the Sātvatas. Moving with vigor in their midst, he is powerful.
Dhṛṣṭadyumna, the foremost of the Somakas, is here alone among the Pāṇḍavas along with his ministers;
having surrendered his very self, he is devoted to the victory of the Pāṇḍavas.
Who else could withstand Ajātaśatru,
he for whom that lion of the Vṛṣṇis would be the leader—
he who has lived with him, accomplished his purpose, and is now in the prime of his youth?
Virāṭa, the lord of the Śālveyas,
along with his sons, has always been devoted to the cause of the Pāṇḍavas;
I have heard that he is a devotee of Yudhiṣṭhira.
There are five powerful brothers, great archers, who were taken captive from the Kekayas;
they now desire the kingdom from the Kekayas.
And all the heroes of the lords of the earth, seeking battle, dwell with the sons of Pṛthā;
they have been assembled and stationed for the sake of the Pāṇḍavas.
I hear that there are brave and devoted men who, filled with affection, have taken refuge with the King of Dharma,
dwelling in mountain retreats and difficult strongholds.
Warriors on earth of noble birth and pure lineage,
as well as Mlecchas endowed with the prowess of various weapons,
have assembled and taken their positions for the sake of the Pāṇḍavas.
And King Pāṇḍya, immeasurable and like Indra himself,
accompanied by many great heroes,
has joined the high-souled one for the sake of the Pāṇḍavas.
A hero of the world with matchless heroic splendor,
from whom I hear that he learned the science of weapons under Droṇa, Arjuna, Vāsudeva, Kṛpa, and Bhīṣma.
He whom they call the peerless one, equal to Kṛṣṇa himself—
that Sātyaki— is intent upon the cause of the Pāṇḍavas; the Cedis and Karūṣas have also taken refuge with him.
Accompanied by all the kings with their full forces,
they beheld the Lord of Cedi in their midst, blazing like the sun, surrounded by splendor and glowing with majesty.
Having struck down the one who considered himself invincible in battle,
the foremost among those who draw the bowstrings on earth,
and the very spirit of all Kṣatriyas;
Violently crushing him with speed, Kṛṣṇa increased the fame and honor of the Yādavas as he struck down Śiśupāla in battle.
Considering Keśava to be irresistible there— He whose majesty all the lords of men, headed by the King of Karūṣa, used to increase— ;
Abandoning the lord of Cedi, they fled in chariots yoked with Sugrīva,
like other small animals upon seeing a lion.
Whoever would have advanced with force against him in opposition,
hoping for a duel with Vāsudeva,
lay dead, slain by Kṛṣṇa, his life departed.
Like a *karṇikāra* tree uprooted by the wind,
O Sañjaya, Keshava exerted his prowess for their sake.
O son of Gavalgaṇa, as I recall the deeds of that Viṣṇu, I find no peace;
for no other enemy could ever have withstood him.
For those for whom that lion of the Vṛṣṇis would be their leader,
my heart trembles with fear upon hearing that the two Kṛṣṇas have come together on a single chariot.
If my dull-witted son of perverted mind does not enter into a compact with those two,
O Sañjaya, then let them consume the Kurus.
O Indra and Viṣṇu, just as [you destroyed] the army of the Daityas; for in my view, Dhanañjaya is equal to Śakra,
and the eternal Vṛṣṇi hero is Viṣṇu himself.
The son of Kuntī, the Pāṇḍava Ajātaśatru, delights in dharma, is restrained by a sense of shame, is vigorous,
and is high-minded, yet he has been treated with deceit by Duryodhana.
If he were not angry, he might consume the sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra;
for I do not fear Arjuna, nor Vāsudeva, nor even Bhīma or the twins.
O charioteer, just as I am always more afraid of the king when he is inflamed with anger than I am of wrath itself,
so too am I fully endowed with asceticism and celibacy.
This mental resolve of his shall be fulfilled;
O Sañjaya, knowing that his wrath in battle is justified, I am today exceedingly afraid.
"Go quickly, dispatched by chariot,
and having approached the army of the Pāñcāla king,
inquire after the welfare of Ajātaśatru."
O dear one, having approached Janārdana, that noble minister of the heroic, you should speak to him again and again with affection.
"Ask after his health in my name;
Dhṛtarāṣṭra desires peace with the Pāṇḍavas. He would not fail to carry out any word of yours."
The son of Kuntī is the charioteer of Vāsudeva,
and Kṛṣṇa is dear to them and equal to their very selves; he is wise and ever intent upon their welfare.
Having gathered the Pāṇḍavas and the Sṛñjayas,
as well as Janārdana, Yuyudhāna, and Virāṭa,
you should inquire after their welfare in my name.
And all the five sons of Draupadī— whatever you deem appropriate for the occasion there, and whatever is for the benefit of the Bharatas, [you should do] toward the enemies.
"O Sañjaya, you should speak those very things in the midst of the kings—
that which would not cause fainting and would prevent war.
Vaiśampāyana said:
Having heard the words of King Dhṛtarāṣṭra, Sañjaya went to Upaplavya to see the Pāṇḍavas of immeasurable prowess. Having approached King Yudhiṣṭhira, whose soul is dharma, he—
Then, having first prostrated himself,
Saṃjaya, the son of a Sūta and the son of Gavalgaṇa,
spoke with confidence to Ajātaśatru.
"By good fortune, O King, I see you free from illness and accompanied by allies, equal to the great Indra himself.
Ambikā’s son asks after your well-being."
Is the wise and aged King Dhṛtarāṣṭra well? And is Bhīma, the foremost of the Pāṇḍavas,
as well as Dhanañjaya and those two sons of Mādrī, all in good health?
Is the princess Kṛṣṇā Draupadī—
truthful in her vows, the wife of heroes, and accompanied by her sons—
well in that place where you desire her to be? And is she high-minded?
"O Bhārata, desiring prosperity, [one obtains] desired objects.
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
"O Sañjaya, son of Gavalgaṇa, welcome to you!"
"O Sūta, with a joyful heart I greet you.
I assure you that I am free from ailment;
and I, O learned one, am well along with my younger brothers."
"O Sūta, having heard this long-awaited good news from the King, the elder of the Kurus,
I feel as though I have seen the lord of men in person."
O Sañjaya, as soon as he saw you, our aged grandfather— the wise, highly intelligent one, endowed with all virtues— was filled with affection.
"O dear one, is that Kauravya Bhīṣma well? Is his livelihood the same as it was before?
And is King Dhṛtarāṣṭra, along with his sons, well?"
Is the high-souled son of Vicitravīrya well?
Is the great king Bāhlīka, the descendant of Pratīpa, well?
And is the wise Sūtaputra well?
"O dear one, is Somadatta well?
And Bhūriśravas, who is true to his promise, and Śala? And Droṇa with his son, and the brahmin Kṛpa?"
Are these great archers also free from illness? O dear one, is the brahmin Śāradvata well?
They are possessed of great wisdom and purified by all the scriptures.
O dear one, do these foremost of archers on earth receive due honor? And are these bowmen also free from illness?
O Sañjaya, all those young archers on earth who exist in the kingdoms envy the Kurus,
for he who is so handsome dwells within their realm.
Is the son of Droṇa, that great archer of virtuous character,
well, O dear one? And is the highly wise prince Yuyutsu, the son of a Vaiśya woman, doing well?
"O dear one, is the minister Karṇa well— he who is obedient to the dull-witted Suyodhana? Are the elderly women, the mothers of the Bharatas, well?"
The master of the household, the wives of the servants,
the daughters-in-law, sons, nephews, sisters,
and grandsons— do they all remain free from deceit?
"O dear one, does the king continue to provide for the Brahmins their livelihoods as before and in accordance with tradition? Does the son of Dhṛtarāṣṭra grant me my rightful inheritance?"
O Sañjaya, does King Dhṛtarāṣṭra, along with his sons, overlook the transgressions against the twice-born? Does he not indeed oppress them?
I hope he does not overlook their deficient conduct as if it were merely the path of a cause;
for this is the supreme light in the world of the living.
The Creator has ordained prosperity for all people;
yet if these dull-witted ones do not restrain their greed,
there will be the total destruction of the Kauravas.
I hope King Dhṛtarāṣṭra, together with his sons,
desires to maintain his livelihood through the circle of his ministers; I hope they do not seek to live by means of creating dissension.
O dear one, I hope that all those Kurus, who appear as friends yet harbor ill-will and act as enemies under the guise of a single ally, do not speak evil of the Pāṇḍavas.
Does Droṇa, along with his son, and the heroic Kṛpa not speak any ill of us? Is the kingdom [secure] for Dhṛtarāṣṭra and his sons?
Having assembled, all the Kurus said:
"Having seen the gathered hosts of bandits, do they remember Pārtha, the leader in battle?"
O dear one, those arrows released from the tip of his bowstring by the wielder of the bow as he brandished it—
discharged from the *Gāṇḍīva* and roaring like thunder— [fell].
Do they perhaps remember those who were never crooked? Having seen him here, will anyone ever go against the current and return home from the arena?
For I have not seen anyone on earth— nor have I heard of anyone— equal or superior to Arjuna,
who possesses sixty-one sharpened, keen-edged arrows.
Well-attired and esteemed,
with mace in hand, the impetuous Bhimasena caused the hosts of enemies to tremble in the army.
Like an elephant in rut among the reeds,
Sahadeva, the son of Mādrī, paces about; do they perhaps remember him, the King of Kaliṅga?
He who conquered those assembled at Dantakūra with his left hand while striking with his right—
do they still remember him of great strength?
"O Sañjaya, son of Gavalgaṇa, as you look on, this Nakula has indeed been sent forth;
bringing them under my control, he has gone toward the western direction."
Do they perhaps remember this son of Mādrī,
who was involved in the calamity that occurred in the Dvaitavana forest during the ill-advised expedition to the cattle-stations?
Where Bhīmasena and Jaya liberated those who were fainting and fallen under the power of their enemies,
I followed behind and protected Arjuna.
The two sons of Mādrī and Bhīmasena, having cast down the hosts of enemies, returned safely; does he remember them? Does the wielder of the Gāṇḍīva remember them?
"O Sañjaya, surely it is not possible in this world to achieve victory through a single virtuous deed alone;
we must conquer with our whole soul."
"We are not able [to restrain] the son of Dhṛtarāṣṭra.
Sañjaya said:
"O Pāṇḍava, it is exactly as you deserve."
O best of the Kurus, you inquire after the Kurus and the Janas;
O Pārtha, those wise and excellent Kurus of whom you ask are well, my dear friend.
There are indeed virtuous elders among the sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra, O Pāṇḍava; know that there are also wicked ones among them.
For even Dhṛtarāṣṭra’s son might give [wealth] even to an enemy.
Whence could one deprive the Brahmins of their inheritance? That which you practice toward them is not righteous;
to act as if you were hostile toward those who are harmless is not good.
"O Dhṛtarāṣṭra, that unrighteous man, hating you who are of virtuous conduct, shall become a betrayer of friends along with his sons;
he does not grant his consent and suffers greatly."
The old man grieves within himself, O Ajātaśatru,
for he hears the Brahmins gathered together saying:
"Betrayal of a friend is the gravest among all sins."
O god among men, they remember you in the encounter with Jishnu,
the leader of warriors,
when the sound of drums and conchs has been raised high.
They remember Bhīmasena with mace in hand,
and they also remember the two sons of Mādrī as they charge through all directions in the midst of the battle.
"O King, those two great car-warriors, raining down showers of arrows incessantly upon the army, are unshakable in battle;
yet I do not think this is possible for any man alone."
The future is known as that which will come to be;
yet you,
O Pāṇḍava, though endowed with all these qualities, have encountered this affliction of such a distressing nature.
"You alone, O Ajātaśatru, must bring all this— and even more— into harmony through your wisdom;
for people would not abandon righteousness for the sake of desire."
All the sons of Pāṇḍu are indeed equal to Indra;
O Ajātaśatru, you alone, through your wisdom,
should bring about that peace by which they may obtain happiness.
The sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra, the Pāṇḍavas, the Sṛñjayas,
and whatever other kings are encamped there— you should establish peace for all of them in this manner.
O King Ajātaśatru, that which your father Dhṛtarāṣṭra spoke to me during the night—
along with his ministers and his sons— was these words, O King.
Having gathered together, listen to these words.
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
"The Pāṇḍavas and the Sṛñjayas have assembled."
O son of a Sūta, O son of Gavalgaṇa, speak those words to Dhṛtarāṣṭra that have been instructed by Janārdana, Yuyudhāna, and Virāṭa.
Saṃjaya said:
[He addressed] Ajātaśatru, Vṛkodara,
Dhanañjaya, and the two sons of Mādravatī.
I address Vāsudeva, the descendant of Śūra,
as well as Yuyudhāna, Cekitāna, Virāṭa,
and the aged lord of the Pañcālas.
O Dhṛṣṭadyumna, son of Pṛṣata, and O Yājñaseni,
all of you listen to these words of mine,
which I shall speak desiring the welfare of the Kurus.
King Dhṛtarāṣṭra, welcoming peace,
quickly prepared my chariot for the king along with his brothers, sons, and kinsmen.
May that be pleasing to the Pāṇḍavas; let there be peace. O sons of Pṛthā, you are endowed with all virtues through your steadfastness, gentleness, and uprightness.
Born into a noble family, they are compassionate, generous, restrained by a sense of shame, and possess certain knowledge of their duties;
it is not fitting for you to perform an inferior deed.
For such is your inner nature, O Bhīmasenas,
that it shines forth like a drop of collyrium upon a white cloth— whatever stain may have been yours.
Wherein the total destruction of everything is seen,
where the arising of evil is hell and one is established in non-existence—
who, knowing this, would ever perform such an action?
Where defeat is equal to victory,
those who have performed their duty toward their kinsmen are indeed blessed—
those who are your sons, friends, and relatives.
If they were to abandon their censured lives,
then the prosperity of the Kurus would surely be certain;
O Pārthas, if you remain and govern the Kurus.
Having led away all your enemies and subdued them,
let your life be equal to death; for it is not right that you should live by the slaughter of your kinsmen.
For who indeed, even with Keśava, could withstand you when you are joined by Cekitāna, protected by the arms of the son of Pṛṣata, and accompanied by Sātyaki— to conquer you?
Even having obtained the gods as ministers along with Indra himself,
who could overcome the Kurus, protected as they are by Droṇa and Bhīṣma, and by Aśvatthāman, Śalya, Kṛpa, and the others?
O King, who could withstand them in battle,
protected as they are by the son of Rādhā along with the lords of the earth—
the great army of King Dhṛtarāṣṭra’s son?
Who indeed is capable of slaying one who is inexhaustible?
Thus, whether in victory or in defeat,
I perceive no ultimate good whatsoever.
"How could the sons of Pṛthā perform an act devoid of dharma and purpose like base men of low birth? Therefore,
having bowed down, I shall propitiate Vāsudeva."
And to the aged lord of the Pañcālas,
with palms joined in reverence, I seek refuge in you all:
how may there be well-being for the Kurus and the Sṛñjayas?
For neither Vāsudeva nor Dhanañjaya would ever fail to carry out your word; when entreated, they would first give up even their lives— how much more so anything else?
Knowing this, I speak for the sake of accomplishment:
wealth, many jewels, a kingdom,
and vehicles of auspicious form.
"O best of men, it is not difficult for you to attain these [goals] while abiding by the command of the aged king— this is the view of the king, with Bhīṣma at his head."
"Whatever you think would be the highest peace here," Yudhiṣṭhira said,
"O Sañjaya, what words indeed do you hear from me?"
"O Sūta, you who desire battle yet fear it— non-battle is indeed better than battle;
for who, having obtained that [peace], would ever fight?"
O Saṃjaya, if the resolve of a man who does nothing were to succeed— whatever he might desire with his mind—
then no one would ever perform any action; this is known to me.
Other than through battle, there is much that is easier;
for what man, knowing this, would ever choose battle? Who, unless cursed by fate, would choose war?
O Pārtha, those who desire happiness perform actions that are not devoid of dharma and are beneficial to the world,
hoping for the happiness that arises from the fruit of their deeds.
Action is in truth a painful means to an end; yet he who seeks pleasure and wishes to avoid pain follows the sway of the senses' delight.
O Saṃjaya, who would desire one who destroys his family, who is like a blacksmith, and who has strayed from the indestructible Dharma? Covetousness for sensual pleasures torments one's own body.
One should abandon craving, which, when impelled by it, causes one to experience suffering— a craving that has departed from all phenomena— just as [fuel] is consumed by a fire of kindled brilliance.
The strength of the fire increases further by the attainment of the objects of desire, and likewise it is never satiated,
just as a kindled fire is not satiated by clarified butter.
Behold this vast accumulation of wealth belonging to King Dhṛtarāṣṭra, which we share with him;
such is his great delusion.
That we have been separated from the king—
who is not the master of his own body and does not listen to the sound of songs that are not auspicious— is indeed unfortunate.
He does not use unwholesome garlands or perfumes,
nor does he use unwholesome ointments; he does not wear unwholesome upper garments.
How could he drive us away from the Kurus?
Let him stay right here; this desire, which scorches my heart, will surely be cast off within my own body.
When a king himself is in a precarious position yet seeks security for others, that is not right;
he should regard their situation exactly as he regards his own.
Likewise,
he also approached others who had set fire to a nearby thicket in the dense forest during the heat of the summer season.
Just as an old man might grieve under the power of the wind,
so does King Dhṛtarāṣṭra today, who has attained sovereignty yet desires security at the end of the cold season.
For what reason, Sañjaya, does he lament,
having taken hold of his dull-witted, foolish, and unwise son, who is evil-minded and devoted to dishonesty?
Being himself untrustworthy, Suyodhana disregarded the words of Vidura,
the most trustworthy man; and King Dhṛtarāṣṭra, desiring to please his son, did the same.
Though he was awakening, he entered into unrighteousness alone—
[that man] who was wise, desirous of the welfare of the Kurus,
highly learned, eloquent, and possessed of virtuous conduct.
O Sūta, King Dhṛtarāṣṭra, out of a longing for his sons, did not remember Vidura among the Kurus—
he who was a destroyer of honor, self-indulgent, and envious.
Of one who is impetuous, who transgresses both wealth and dharma,
who speaks ill, who is subject to the power of anger,
whose soul is possessed by desire, and who is malicious in disposition.
O Sañjaya, King Dhṛtarāṣṭra, seeking to please his son— who was unleadable, devoid of merit, long-simmering in resentment, treacherous toward friends, and evil-minded— [acted thus].
O Sañjaya, as I looked on and abandoned both dharma and pleasure while gambling, the thought occurred to me at that very moment:
"If the Kurus do not come here, there will be total destruction."
Though Vidura spoke words of poetic wisdom,
he did not receive praise from Dhṛtarāṣṭra;
for they followed the intellect of the Kṣattṛ.
The hardship did not reach the Kurus at that time as long as they remained devoted to his wisdom;
for that long, there was prosperity for their kingdom.
O Sūta, listen now from me as I describe those ministers of Dhṛtarāṣṭra’s son who are greedy for that wealth:
Duḥśāsana, Śakuni, and the son of a Sūta.
O son of Gavalgaṇa, behold his delusion!
Though I examine it, I do not see how there may be well-being for the Kurus and the Sṛñjayas.
Having seized sovereignty from his enemies,
Dhṛtarāṣṭra— now that Vidura, the far-sighted one, has been sent into exile— indeed hopes for success together with his sons.
In that great sovereignty over the earth, free from rivals,
peace alone is not to be found;
for he considers his own interest to be already within his grasp and very near at hand.
That which Karṇa considers capable of being overcome in battle by Arjuna when he has taken up his weapons—
such great battles have indeed occurred before.
How was it that Karṇa did not become their island?
Both Karṇa and Suyodhana know this;
Droṇa knows it, and the Grandfather knows it as well.
And all these other Kurus who are there know that there is no other archer like Arjuna. All these Kurus indeed know this.
And those other rulers of the earth who were assembled there,
while Duryodhana was committing offenses and Phalguna, the tamer of foes, was absent.
Therefore, the son of Dhṛtarāṣṭra considers his wealth to be secure;
he thinks it possible to seize the Pandavas' sense of ownership with Kiritin, whose weapon is as long as a palm tree.
Having gone there to that battle, those who know him will not endure it;
for the sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra cannot remain when they hear the sound of the Gāṇḍīva bow being strung in the fray.
If Suyodhana thinks his purpose is already accomplished through the force of an enraged Bhīmasena,
even Indra himself, my son, would not dare to take this away from him.
O Sūta, sovereignty belongs to us as long as Bhīmasena lives,
as well as Dhanañjaya, Nakula, and my heroic Sahadeva.
O charioteer, if the aged king, together with his son, should adopt this understanding,
then [the world] will not be consumed by the wrath of the Pāṇḍavas in battle.
O Sañjaya, let not the sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra perish! You know the suffering that has befallen us;
honoring you, O Sañjaya, I shall forgive.
Whatever was formerly our relationship with the Kauravas, and whatever was our status under the sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra at that time—
let that continue to be exactly so even now.
"I shall attain peace just as you have said.
Let my kingdom be in Indraprastha; let Suyodhana, the foremost of the Bharatas, grant it to me."
Saṃjaya said: O Pāṇḍava, your conduct is eternally rooted in dharma;
it is heard of and seen in the world, O Pārtha.
Life is a great flux and impermanent; considering this, O Pāṇḍava, do not bring about your own destruction. If the Kurus will not grant you your share except through war, [then fight].
O Ajātaśatru, they offer you the practice of begging for alms within the kingdom of the Andhakas and Vṛṣṇis;
I consider this better than a kingdom obtained through war.
The life of a human being is short,
characterized by great outflows, constant suffering, and instability;
moreover, it is not commensurate with its allotted span of years.
Therefore, O Pāṇḍava, do not extend toward evil.
Desires indeed cling to a man,
O lord of men, as they are the root of obstacles to dharma.
A man who, being resolute, slays those [enemies] first gains irreproachable praise in the world. For here, O Pārtha, thirst for wealth is indeed a bond.
For one who pursues that [pleasure], dharma itself is impaired.
But he who chooses dharma is awakened;
for one who is greedy for sensual desires falls away due to his pursuit of worldly gain.
O dear one, by making the practice of dharma the foremost of his deeds,
he of great majesty shines like the sun; yet by the abandonment of dharma, even this very earth—
Having obtained [wealth], a man of sinful intellect perishes,
even though he has studied the Veda, practiced celibacy,
performed sacrifices, and given gifts to Brahmins.
Thinking it to be the supreme state,
he gave himself over to pleasures for many years;
indulging excessively in pleasure and what is dear, he—
He who does not perform the practice of yoga when his wealth is exhausted becomes excessively deprived of happiness; driven by the impulse of desire, he lies in misery.
Furthermore, one who is thus intent on purposeful conduct, yet having abandoned the Dharma, practices what is contrary to the Dharma—
being deluded and lacking faith in the world beyond;
Having left the body, the fool suffers after death;
for there is no destruction of actions— whether they be meritorious or sinful— in the world beyond.
First, merit and sin go to the doer;
afterwards, the doer indeed follows after them.
This applies to food that is given to Brahmins in accordance with the law.
Purified by faith, endowed with fragrance and flavor,
such is the deed of yours that is renowned among those who offer the *anvāhārya* feast with the most excellent sacrificial fees.
"O Pārtha, what must be done is being done here in this field; indeed, nothing remains to be done after death. You have already performed the task pertaining to the world beyond."
Great merit, praised by the virtuous,
abandons death, old age, and fear; it also abandons hunger, thirst, and all things unpleasant to the mind.
O lord of men, there is nothing whatsoever to be done there other than for the purpose of gratifying the senses;
such is the fruit of karma.
O Pāṇḍava, by being moderate and dear to the heart, do not for long cause both worlds to perish through the anger and the joy born of passion.
The praise that comes from reaching the end of one's actions—
truth, self-restraint, uprightness, and compassion—
is equal to the Aśvamedha and Rājasūya sacrifices thus performed.
Do not go again to the end of this sinful deed,
O sons of Pṛthā, if you shall thus perform a wicked act for a long time in this manner.
"O Pāṇḍavas, you shall dwell for many years in the forests, living a life of hardship for the sake of dharma,
having been previously bound to this exile."
That strength of yours was always dependent upon yourself; these Pāñcālas were your ministers,
as were Janārdana and the heroic Yuyudhāna.
King Matsya Rukmaratha with his sons,
Virāṭa along with his sons who are skilled strikers,
and those kings who were previously conquered;
They would all take refuge in you alone— you,
blazing with great allies and established in power,
placed at the forefront by Vāsudeva and Arjuna.
Intending to slay your enemies, you shall dispel the pride of Dhṛtarāṣṭra’s son in the midst of the arena;
why then would you increase the strength of your opponent?
Why, O Pāṇḍava, do you wish to fight at an inopportune time, having emaciated your own allies and dwelt for many years in the forests?
O Pāṇḍava, whether one is lacking in wisdom while fighting,
or whether one knows what is unrighteous, one deviates from the path of prosperity—
even if one is wise and understands the Dharma.
Or even if he departs from prosperity due to impetuosity,
O Pārtha, your mind is not fixed on unrighteousness;
you have committed no sinful deed out of impetuosity.
Surely, what is that cause for which you desire to perform this deed that contradicts wisdom—
a sharp, disease-born headache?
O Great King, drink this wrath which steals away fame, from which the fruit of evil arises, which is to be drunk by the virtuous but which the wicked do not drink; drink it and be at peace.
Who indeed would desire that which is followed by evil?
Forgiveness alone is better for you, not enjoyments,
wherein Bhīṣma, the son of Śāntanu, has been slain.
Where Drona has been slain along with his son, as well as Kripa, Shalya, Saumadatti, Vikarna,
Vivimshati, Karna, and Duryodhana.
"O Pārtha, tell me what kind of happiness that would be which you might find by killing these men;
even if you were to obtain this entire earth bounded by the oceans..."
For you cannot truly abandon old age and death, nor dear and unpleasant things, nor pleasure and pain, O King;
knowing this, do not engage in battle.
If you wish to perform such an act for the sake of your ministers' desire,
you should depart after handing over your own [kingdom] to them.
"Do not stray today from the path that leads to the gods.
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
"O Sañjaya, this is undoubtedly true."
"Righteousness is the best of actions," as you have said;
but having learned of me, O Sañjaya, you may censure me—
whether I practice righteousness or unrighteousness.
Where unrighteousness, assuming the forms of righteousness, appears as the entirety of dharma, and likewise where dharma, maintaining its own form, [is perceived];
The wise perceive him through their intellect;
thus, these two, in times of adversity, should always adhere to this mark: dharma and adharma.
O Sañjaya, understand that for whom the primary mark exists, for him there is authority; know that to be the duty in times of distress (*āpaddharma*).
But when the natural order has been subverted, by whatever means one performs the action—
One who is destitute should strive to accomplish it and seek to obtain it;
likewise, one established in his natural state should do so even when facing adversity.
O Sañjaya, both of these are to be censured.
For Brahmins who desire the non-cessation [of their lineage],
an expiation has been ordained by the Creator for those who,
in times of distress, engage in improper actions.
O Sañjaya, one should censure those who persist in improper actions for the sake of discerning the truth among the wise;
the conduct of the virtuous is always prescribed in this manner.
But those who are non-Brahmins and not learned—
one might well desire the total destruction of them;
for our ancestors and those who came before us lived for their sake.
Those grandfathers and others even further back than them,
who, seeking wisdom, performed their deeds—
I consider that there is no end to them, no end, no end.
Whatever wealth there is on this earth,
whatever belongs to the thirty gods in the world beyond,
the triple heaven of Prajāpati, and the world of Brahmā;
O Sañjaya, I do not desire that through unrighteousness;
for he is a lord of dharma, skillful, wise in policy,
a worshiper of Brahmins, and a man of intelligence.
Kṛṣṇa instructs the various and mighty Rājanya Bhojas;
for if I were to release him, I would be beyond reproach.
"If, while fighting, I should abandon my own duty,
let the highly illustrious Keśava say so;
Vāsudeva indeed desires the welfare of both."
For the Śaineyas, Caitrakas, Āndhakas,
Vārṣṇeyas, Bhojas, Kaukuras, and Sṛñjayas sit waiting upon the wisdom of Vāsudeva.
Having subdued their enemies, the Vṛṣṇis and Andhakas— Ugrasena and the others— are indeed bringing joy to their friends;
for all of them, led by Kṛṣṇa, are equal to Indra himself.
The wise Yādavas, whose valor was true, possessed great strength and abundant enjoyments;
and Babhru, the king of Kāśī, attained supreme prosperity.
Having obtained Kṛṣṇa as his brother and lord,
for whom Vāsudeva showers all desires,
just as a cloud pours rain upon living beings at the end of summer.
"O dear one, such is this Keśava;
for we know him to be one who understands the determination of actions. Kṛṣṇa is dear to us and the most virtuous."
One must not transgress the word of Keśava.
Vāsudeva said:
"O Sañjaya, there shall be no destruction for the Pāṇḍavas."
O Sūta, I desire their prosperity and the welfare of King Dhṛtarāṣṭra; I always wish for the growth of that king who has many sons.
"For my desire, Sañjaya, has always been this:
I would say nothing other than 'let them be appeased' toward them;
for I hear that this is also pleasing to the king."
I consider this to be appropriate for the Pāṇḍavas;
for indeed, O Sañjaya, peace— which is so very difficult to achieve— has been demonstrated here by the son of Pāṇḍu.
Since Dhṛtarāṣṭra, along with his sons, is greedy for this [wealth],
why should their quarrel not intensify here? O Sañjaya, as you move about here, discerning the truth of dharma—
And from me, and from Yudhiṣṭhira, O Sañjaya, you know— why then do you speak thus of the son of Pāṇḍu,
who is energetic and fulfilling his own duty?
For one who dwells according to the teachings, the family [is protected]; you have rightly declared the destruction [of the world] from a former age,
while this ritual procedure is being correctly observed.
The thoughts of Brahmins are diverse:
some say that success is achieved through action in the next world,
while others say that success is achieved through knowledge, having abandoned action.
Neither the Kṣatriyas nor even the Saṃjayas find [satisfaction]; one who does not eat would not be satiated by food and drink,
even if he were a learned man here who has understood what is known by the Brāhmaṇas.
Indeed, those sciences which accomplish action here have fruit, and not others;
among them, action here has indeed visible fruit.
One afflicted by thirst is quenched by drinking water;
this very principle is established by action alone,
and it is action that prevails there, O Sañjaya.
In this regard, whatever one might consider other than action to be virtuous,
the speech of that weak person is in vain;
for these gods manifest through actions in the world beyond.
By action alone does Mātariśvan move here;
by action alone, the sun rises constantly and unweariedly, ordaining day and night.
The moon approaches the months, the fortnights, and the conjunctions with the lunar mansions without weariness;
the fire, Jātavedas, consumes [its fuel] without weariness.
Being kindled and performing its work for the sake of all creatures,
the goddess Earth, unwearied, sustains this great burden by her strength.
Without weariness, the rivers swiftly carry their waters, satisfying all living beings;
without weariness, he of abundant splendor pours down rain.
Making the mid-air and the heavens resound,
he practiced the religious life with unwearied diligence,
desiring preeminence among the gods as the slayer of Bala.
Having abandoned pleasure and the dear things of the mind,
Śakra attained preeminence through that deed,
guarding truth and dharma with vigilance.
By practicing self-restraint, forbearance, equanimity, and kindness— all these together—
Maghavan attained the preeminent sovereignty over the gods.
Bṛhaspati practiced the life of a religious student;
concentrated and with a disciplined self, he acted according to the rule, abandoning pleasure and restraining his senses.
By that [merit], he attained the status of a god among the gods;
the constellations shine there by virtue of their deeds,
as do the Rudras, Ādityas, Vasus, and Viśvedevas.
King Yama, Vaiśravaṇa Kubera,
the Gandharvas, Yakṣas, and radiant Apsarases, as well as celibacy, the Vedas and their branches of knowledge, and sacred rites— [all these attend upon him].
Practicing this, the sages shine in the world beyond;
for he knows this Dharma of all people—
the Brahmins, the Kṣatriyas, and the Vaiśyas.
O Sañjaya, why do you, being wise among those who know, strive for the sake of the Kauravas,
when his eternal connection with the sacred traditions (āmnāyas) [is well known]?
Likewise, know that in the Aśvamedha and Rājasūya sacrifices,
he is further equipped with a bow, armor,
hand-guards, and chariot weapons.
If these sons of Pṛthā could find a means to deal with the Kauravas without slaughter,
then their protection of dharma would have been accomplished as a meritorious act.
O noble lady, if they, while engaged in their ancestral duty, should meet death by the power of destiny, having restrained Bhīmasena—
Fulfilling their own duties to the best of their ability—
even that would be a praiseworthy end for them;
or do you think otherwise?
For kings, the system of dharma operates either in war or in peace;
such is the very speech that I hear from you.
O Sañjaya, having first considered the division of the four social orders and your own duty,
and then having heard of the respective duties of the Pāṇḍavas;
Whether you praise or blame, whatever your mind inclines toward— let a Brāhmaṇa study, perform sacrifices, give gifts, and likewise visit the foremost sacred fords.
He may teach and also officiate at sacrifices for those entitled to do so; or he may accept gifts that are well-known [as appropriate]. A Kṣatriya, moreover, should study and also perform sacrifices.
He should give wealth, but not beg for anything;
he should not officiate at sacrifices for others, nor should he teach.
Thus is the ancient dharma of the Kṣatriya remembered.
Likewise, a member of the royal caste, having protected his subjects according to dharma, being vigilant, and having given gifts,
performed sacrifices, and studied all the Vedas;
Having taken a wife, the merit-maker should dwell in his home;
that righteous soul, having studied the Dharma, goes at will to the world of Brahmā by virtue of his merit.
A Vaiśya, having studied, should accumulate wealth through agriculture, cattle-rearing, and trade,
protecting it with vigilance and doing what is pleasing to the Brāhmaṇas and Kṣatriyas.
One who is virtuous in character and performs meritorious deeds may dwell in a house;
he should attend upon and honor the Brahmins,
for he is prohibited from performing sacrifices.
Always striving for prosperity and remaining tireless—
this is remembered as the ancient duty of a Śūdra. A king, protecting these [classes] with vigilance, [attains success].
Engaging all social classes in their own duties, free from personal desire and impartial toward his subjects,
he should not yield to unrighteous cravings.
If there should be someone superior to him—
one who is renowned and endowed with all dharmas—
then the protector of the earth should guard [him] with vigilance.
Enjoining the social classes to their own duties,
he, knowing [the truth], should instruct that wicked man;
for it would not be right if he were to harbor greed toward him.
When a cruel man, seizing power through the provocation of fate, covets another's land,
then this war among kings shall come to pass.
The armor, weapons, and bow produced therein— this work was created by Indra for the slaying of the Dasyus;
the armor, weapons, and bow were brought forth.
In that case, merit would be obtained through the slaughter of robbers;
yet this very fault has been committed by the Kurus in its most intense form—
by those ignorant of righteousness who fail to perceive what is truly dharma.
O Sañjaya,
it was not right that King Dhṛtarāṣṭra, together with his sons,
should have seized the wealth of the Pāṇḍavas so suddenly.
All those Kurus of their lineage pay no heed to the ancient dharma of kings,
where indeed a thief may carry off wealth unseen.
Or where one might seize [another's property] by force while being witnessed—
both of these, O Sañjaya, are censurable;
why then do you treat the son of Dhṛtarāṣṭra as if he were distinct?
He who, out of greed, considers this to be dharma—
that which he desires while following the sway of passion—
indeed regards his own duty as the seizing of another's wealth.
Those who know the rules say that this act is not theft;
rather, it was a share assigned to the Pāṇḍavas,
which the enemies would indeed seize from us without cause.
In this station, even death for us while fighting is praiseworthy; it is superior to the kingdom of another and is the ancestral duty of the Kauravas.
These are the ancient laws of the Kauravas.
O Sañjaya, you should report in the midst of the assembly those fools who have fallen under the power of death,
the dull-witted sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra who have been gathered together.
But this deed is even more wicked;
behold what has transpired among the Kurus in the midst of the assembly— the dragging of Draupadī, the beloved wife of the Pāṇḍavas.
That the Kurus, led by Bhīṣma, looked on with indifference as she— illustrious, endowed with virtue and good conduct—
was being obstructed by one who followed his lust while she was weeping.
If those Kurus, both young and old, had gathered together at that time to restrain the actions of that dull-witted man whose soul was consumed by desire, [the world would have been saved].
Dhṛtarāṣṭra would have done what was pleasing to me,
and he would have accomplished the welfare of his sons;
yet Duḥśāsana led him astray through his hostility.
In the midst of the assembly, she was led before her fathers-in-law; there, Kṛṣṇā spoke piteous words,
seeing no protector other than Vidura.
Out of sheer dejection, they were unable to speak in reply to the king in that assembly;
only the steward (Kṣattṛ), speaking words consistent with dharma, remained alone.
Having understood the dharma, he replied to the one of small intellect:
"If you did not speak such dharma in the assembly,
yet now you wish to instruct the son of Pāṇḍu."
But Kṛṣṇā performed this pure deed,
for it was indeed extremely difficult to accomplish, having entered the assembly hall;
by it she rescued the Pāṇḍavas from their distress.
Thus he saved himself, as a boat from the surge of the ocean,
when the son of the Sūta spoke to Kṛṣṇā while she stood in the assembly hall in the presence of her fathers-in-law.
"O Yājñasenī, no such refuge exists for you;
enter now the house of Dhṛtarāṣṭra’s son. Your husbands have been defeated and are no more."
And you, O spirited lady, choose another husband—
one who was once deeply rooted in the heart of Bibhatsu, most terrible, piercing the vital organs and cutting through the very bones.
From Karna, a wordy arrow of sharp brilliance was established in Phalguna’s heart,
as he was putting on his black antelope skins.
Duḥśāsana spoke these harsh words:
"All these are like sterile sesame seeds, ruined and gone to destruction for a long time in hell."
When Śakuni, the king of Gandhāra, spoke deceitfully at the time of the dice game, saying to the sons of Pṛthā,
"Nakula has been defeated; what do you have left?"
"Play with Kṛṣṇā Yājñasenī yourself!
You know all this, O Sañjaya;
such words as have been spoken here regarding the gambling match are indeed unfit to be uttered."
I myself, however, desire to go there to rectify this failed matter;
you know well the delusion of Dhṛtarāṣṭra’s son.
If, without sacrificing the interests of the Pāṇḍavas, I were to pursue peace with the Kurus— [I would do so] for the sake of that evil-minded man who follows the power of sin.
"May my conduct be meritorious and lead to great prosperity,
and may the Kurus be released from the noose of death—
even as I speak these wise words."
May the sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra observe this [conduct] which delights in dharma, is meaningful, and is non-violent; and may the Kurus honor me when I have arrived in their presence.
Know that the sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra have been utterly overwhelmed by Phalguna, the charioteer, and by Bhīma, who is clad in armor for battle, acting otherwise than they expected.
But the son of Dhṛtarāṣṭra utters fierce words against the Pāṇḍavas, who are being consumed by their own karma, being slow-witted, and already defeated.
Bhīmasena, mace in hand and vigilant,
reminded Duryodhana of his past transgressions at the proper time; for Suyodhana was like a great tree composed of wrath.
Skandha is Karṇa, Śakuni is its branches,
Duḥśāsana is the abundant flowers and fruit,
and the root is King Dhṛtarāṣṭra, who lacks wisdom.
Yudhiṣṭhira is a great tree composed of Dharma; Arjuna is its trunk and Bhīmasena its branches;
the two sons of Mādrī are its abundant flowers and fruit.
I am the root, as are Brahmā and the Brāhmaṇas;
Dhṛtarāṣṭra with his sons is the forest,
and O Sañjaya, the Pāṇḍavas are the tigers in that forest.
King Dhṛtarāṣṭra is the forest, and the sons of Pāṇḍu are considered tigers; O Sañjaya, the sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra have the nature of creepers, while the Pāṇḍavas are tigers among men.
A forest protected by a lion would not perish,
nor would a lion protected by a forest perish. King Dhṛtarāṣṭra is the forest, and the Pāṇḍavas are the tigers within that forest.
"Do not cut down the forest that contains the tiger; do not destroy the tigers from the forest.
A tiger is killed when the forest is gone; a forest is destroyed when there is no tiger.
Therefore, let the tiger protect the forest, and let the forest preserve the tiger."
"O Sañjaya, the sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra have the nature of creepers, while the Pāṇḍavas are like great *śāla* trees.
A creeper never grows without depending upon a mighty tree.
The sons of Pṛthā stand ready to serve, yet those subduers of enemies also stand ready to fight."
"Let the lord of men, Dhṛtarāṣṭra, do whatever must be done;
for the high-souled Pāṇḍavas, who walk the path of dharma, remain established in peace.
Knowing this, O wise one, you should report the truth regarding those powerful warriors."
Saṃjaya said:
"I take my leave of you, O god among the lords of men;
I am going, O Pāṇḍava—may it be well with you."
I hope that no crooked word has been uttered by me through some attachment of the mind,
[addressed] to Janārdana, Bhīmasena, and Arjuna.
Having taken leave of the two sons of Mādrī, Sātyaki, and Cekitāna, I depart; may it be well and happy with you. O kings, look upon me with a gentle eye.
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
"Permitted, O Saṃjaya, go in peace;
you have never done anything unpleasant to us."
We all— both they and we— know you to be pure-souled, seated in the midst of the assembly. O Sañjaya, you are a trusted messenger and very dear to us.
Possessing auspicious speech, virtuous conduct, and right view,
O Sañjaya, you should never be deluded in your mind,
nor should you become angry even when being told the truth.
You shall never speak words that strike at the vital points,
nor those that are harsh, nor praise that is bitter or sour; rather, you shall speak that which delights in the Dharma, is meaningful, and is non-violent.
O Sūta, I recognize this speech of yours;
you alone are our dearest messenger. Either Vidura or a second person should come here.
"For you have been seen by us frequently in the past;
you are a friend to Dhanañjaya, equal to his own self.
Having gone from here, O Sañjaya, do so very quickly."
You should attend upon those brahmins who are worthy of it—
those of pure vigor, endowed with virtuous conduct,
born of noble lineage, and possessed of all dharmas.
The Brahmins who study the Vedas, the mendicants, those who practice austerities, and those who dwell constantly in the forests—
these elders are indeed to be saluted in my name.
In the same way, you should speak of the welfare of the others:
the domestic priest of King Dhṛtarāṣṭra,
as well as his teachers and officiating priests.
And with them, O dear Sūta, you should associate appropriately and with well-being; likewise,
those elders who dwell there but are not learned in the Vedas.
Those wise ones, endowed with the power of virtuous conduct,
aspiring for us and mindful of us,
practice a measure of the Dharma according to their ability.
"Commend me to them as being well; and, dear father, inquire after their health, starting with the youngest. Then, with an undistracted mind and focused attention, he joined his palms in reverence.
One should offer salutations to them on my behalf—
those who live by means of legal proceedings in the kingdom,
and those who dwell in the kingdom while protecting it.
You should inquire after the welfare of all those farmers who support the world; they are beloved teachers, loyal, and obedient.
Desiring the Vedas, he practiced the life of a student;
Drona, who restored the fourfold science of weapons,
is to be saluted with respect when pleased.
Having mastered the sciences and being endowed with virtuous conduct,
he who once more fashioned the four-footed weapon—
swift and resembling the son of a Gandharva.
Having gone to the dwelling of Śāradvata’s son, you should inquire after the welfare of that Aśvatthāman,
the great chariot-warrior and the foremost among those skilled in weapons.
O Sañjaya, while repeatedly praising me,
you used to touch the feet of Kṛpa with your hand— [Kṛpa] in whom reside heroism, compassion, and asceticism.
Having grasped the feet of the best of the Kurus, report to us how [he] has conducted himself in wisdom, virtue, learning, courage, and fortitude.
There you should introduce me to Bhīṣma—
he who is the leader of the Kurus, whose eye is wisdom,
who is deeply learned, a servant of the aged, and possessed of great intelligence.
Having saluted that aged king,
O Saṃjaya, you should report to him that I am free from illness;
[and tell him] that the dull-witted Dhṛtarāṣṭra’s eldest son—
