O Sañjaya, you should ask after the welfare of Suyodhana— that fool, the rogue, and the one of sinful character by whom the entire earth was indeed ruled.
O Sañjaya, his younger brother Mandas was likewise of such character;
he too was a great archer and the most heroic among the Kurus.
"O dear one, you should inquire after the welfare of Duḥśāsana,
as well as those who are under his command and whatever other eminent kings there may be."
O Sūta, you must speak on my behalf to them all, as is appropriate, saying that everything is well;
for [I greet] the eminent poet who is undeluded regarding all matters.
Possessing great wisdom and endowed with all dharmas, he never takes pleasure in battle;
O dear one, you should inquire after the welfare of Vaiśyā’s son.
He who is peerless in cutting down and in gambling, whose dice are concealed and loaded, who is skilled at playing and knows the throws, and who is invincible in the reckoning of what must be staked.
"O dear one, you should ask after the welfare of Citrasena,
whose desire has always been this:
that there be no one among the Bharatas other than himself who attains peace."
May that wise bull among the Bāhlikas,
endowed with many excellent qualities, address me with a gracious mind as he did in the past.
He who is possessed of wisdom and is never cruel,
who always endures resentment out of affection—
he, Somadatta, is in my opinion worthy of honor.
The son of Somadatta, the greatest of Arhats among the Kurus—
he who is our brother, O Sañjaya, and my friend,
that great archer who is the best of chariot-warriors.
"O dear one, you should ask after the welfare of that Bhūriśravas, who is accompanied by his ministers—
he who is a great archer, the foremost and most excellent among chariot-warriors."
Having gone there, you should speak to him in my name;
likewise, Śalya— the great archer, the best and foremost among chariot-warriors— should be addressed with confidence in my words.
Sama, Śala, Rakṣitā, Pṛṣṭha,
Hrīniṣedha, Devitā, Matākṣa, Satyavrata, Purumitra, and Jaya.
O dear one, you should inquire after the welfare of all those who did not approve of my departure,
as well as the other youthful leaders of the Kurus.
"Whomever among our sons, grandsons, and brothers you may encounter,
you must convey my message that they are free from illness."
Those kings who were assembled by the son of Dhṛtarāṣṭra to fight the Pāṇḍavas—
some Vasātis, Śālvas, and Kekayas;
Likewise, the Ambaṣṭhas and the chief Trigartas,
the heroes of the east, north,
and south, as well as all those of the west and the mountains.
They are compassionate and endowed with virtuous conduct and discipline;
O dear one, you should inquire after the welfare of them all—
those elephant-riders, chariot-warriors, and horsemen.
And having reported that I am well to those great assemblies of noble foot-soldiers,
you should inquire after the health of all of them together.
Likewise, he should appoint ministers endowed with purposeful skill for the king, as well as gatekeepers and those who lead the army,
and those who are diligently engaged in calculating income and expenditure.
And those who deliberate on great matters:
Śakuni, the king of Gāndhāra from the mountains,
who is peerless in the art of dice-play and in causing ruin.
O Sūta, when you inquire after the welfare of that son of Dhṛtarāṣṭra, who is of perverted intellect and acts with pride, O dear one, you must ask him who,
as a hero, challenged the Pāṇḍavas with but a single chariot.
He who is invincible strives to conquer those who are deluded, being himself the peerless deluder of the bewildered;
O dear one, you should inquire after the welfare of Vaikartana.
He alone is the devotee, he is the teacher, he is the servant;
he indeed is the father, he is the mother, and he is the friend—
Vidura, of unfathomable intellect and far-sighted vision.

O Sanjaya, having approached our counselor, you should ask after his welfare, dear friend; and having saluted the aged Gandhari— who is like Kunti’s second mother— you should likewise inquire after her well-being.
O Saṃjaya, those aged women who are endowed with virtue and who are known as mothers—
having come together with all of them assembled;
To the elderly women, you should offer this greeting:
"O mothers of living sons, we hope your sons conduct themselves perfectly in their duties with a compassionate nature."
"Having said this, O Sañjaya, speak afterwards:
'Ajātaśatru is well, along with his sons.
And as for those wives of ours whom you know to be there, O Sañjaya..."
O dear one, you should inquire after the welfare of all of them—
whether they are well-guarded, fragrant, and blameless; and whether they dwell in their homes with vigilance.
O Sañjaya, my dear, having reported that I am well, you should ask them about their health,
and whether those auspicious women are receiving proper treatment from their fathers-in-law.
Conduct yourselves virtuously and with a compassionate nature, so that your husbands may be favorable to you;
establish such a mode of conduct for yourselves.
O Sañjaya, you know those who are our daughters-in-law there— those who have come from noble families, endowed with virtues, and blessed with offspring;
speak of them as well when you meet them.
"Yudhiṣṭhira, being well-disposed, has greeted you all: 'O daughters, embrace one another in your homes, O Sañjaya,
and having asked after their welfare in my name,'" he said.
May your husbands be auspicious and favorable toward you; may you be favorable toward your husbands. Adorned with ornaments, clothed in fine garments, and fragrant;
Free from loathsomeness, happy, and possessing enjoyments—
those whose appearance is graceful and whose speech is light— O dear one, you should inquire after the welfare of those women of the household.
To those sons of slave-girls who were the slaves of the Kurus, and to the many hunchbacks and lame men who depended upon them,
[he] spoke, saying that I was well.
You should inquire after his health, and ask about his lowliest servant:
"Does his ancient livelihood continue? Does the son of Dhṛtarāṣṭra still provide him with enjoyments?"
Out of compassion, Dhṛtarāṣṭra supports those who are maimed, the wretched, and the dwarfs;
likewise, he supports all the blind and the elderly.
There are many who live by their hands here;
having told them that I am well, you should inquire after their welfare, starting with the lowliest.
"Do not fear this suffering or this miserable life;
surely some evil was committed in former worlds.
Having subdued your enemies and favored your friends,"
"I shall provide you with clothing and food;
yet it is not possible for this to be told by one person alone,
for there are many groups of people from various lands."
Having been away for a long time and desiring to see [them] like a child,
I pay homage here, Sañjaya, to the sons of Bhīmasena;
may they grant my word as it has been spoken.
"Act in such a way that they may hear what is being spoken by you.
Indeed, there are [deeds] already performed by me for the sake of the brahmins; furthermore, alas, those yet to be are still proceeding."
I see them as being appropriately joined;
you should likewise report that very success to that king,
as well as those who are always without protectors and weak.
The fools strive only for their own sake;
therefore, O dear one, you should inquire after the welfare of those wretched men from us in every way, according to our word.
And those others who have taken refuge with the sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra,
having come from various directions, O Sūtaputra— having seen all of them as well, who are worthy of honor;
You should inquire after their welfare and well-being in this manner for all those who have arrived from the future and all the king’s messengers who have come from every direction.
O Sūta, having inquired after the welfare of them all,
you should afterwards say that I am well among them;
for there are no others like them upon this earth.
Those warriors who were obtained by the son of Dhṛtarāṣṭra are transient,
but my dharma is eternal; indeed, it is my very dharma,
possessed of great power, for the destruction of the enemy.
Furthermore, O Sañjaya, you should cause these words to be heard by Suyodhana, the son of Dhṛtarāṣṭra:
"That which burns the heart within your body..."
"O Kāma, may I instruct the Kurus so that they have no rivals;
there is no means for this,
nor could we ever become such as you desire."
"Either give me the city of Śakra itself,
or fight, O hero, chief of the Bharatas!
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
O Sañjaya, the Ordainer brings both the existent and the non-existent, the child and the aged,
the weak and the stronger, under his control. He bestows wisdom upon the child and childishness upon the wise.
The Lord, rising up in the east, bestows everything;
he is sufficient for making it known—declare it exactly as it is.
Then, having consulted with one another, they spoke the mantra with great joy.

O son of Gavalgaṇa, having gone to the Kurus and having saluted and clasped the feet of the mighty Dhṛtarāṣṭra, you should then inquire after his well-being. And when he is seated, surrounded by the Kurus, you should speak to him thus.
O King, it is by your very prowess that the Pāṇḍavas live in happiness;
O subduer of enemies, it was through your grace that those children obtained the kingdom.
Having first established them in the kingdom, do not now neglect them as they are on the verge of perishing.
"O Sañjaya, even all this together is not enough for any single person;
my dear, we live by uniting, so do not fall under the power of our enemies.
Likewise [regard] Bhīṣma, the son of Śantanu, the grandfather of the Bharatas."
Salute me with your head bowed while proclaiming my name;
and having offered your salutation, you must then say to our grandfather:
"The lineage of Śaṃtanu, which had sunk low, has been raised up again by you."
Therefore, O dear grandfather, act according to your own judgment in such a way that your grandsons may live together in mutual affection;
likewise, speak thus to Vidura, the counselor of the Kurus.
"O gentle one, speak words of non-war; Yudhiṣṭhira desires our welfare.
Furthermore, having repeatedly entreated the impatient Prince Suyodhana as he sits in the midst of the Kurus, you should say to him:"
Seeing me disregarding Kṛṣṇā alone when she had been brought into the assembly,
we endured that suffering so as not to slay the Kurus.
In this way, the Pāṇḍavas have endured successive afflictions from beginning to end.
The Kurus know all this, how we were powerful;
yet, O gentle one, when you exiled us clad in deerskins,
we endured that suffering so as not to slay the Kurus.

O scorcher of enemies, that which Duḥśāsana committed by entering the assembly hall and seizing Kṛṣṇā by her hair was done with your approval, and it was overlooked by us; now let us receive our own rightful share as is fitting.
"O bull among men, turn away your greedy mind from the property of others.
O King, in this way there will be peace and mutual affection. Grant us even a single portion of your kingdom, for we desire tranquility."
"Kuśasthala, Vṛkasthala, Āsandī, and Vāraṇāvata—let these be the places of residence for them;
let there be some fifth as well.
O Suyodhana, grant five villages to the five brothers."
"O wise Saṃjaya, may there be peace for us together with our kinsmen;
let brother follow brother, and let father be united with son;
let the Pāñcālas come together with the Kurus, smiling."
"I desire that we may see the Kurus and Pañcālas unhurt;
O dear one, O bull of the Bharatas, let us all be of good mind and make peace.
O Saṃjaya, I am indeed prepared for both peace and likewise for war."
"I am indeed capable of both mildness and severity toward both righteousness and worldly interests.
Vaiśampāyana said:
Having been thus permitted by the Pāṇḍava, Saṃjaya then departed.
Having carried out the entire command of the high-souled Dhṛtarāṣṭra,
Saṃjaya, O scorcher of foes, then departed quickly and reached Hastināpura in a single day, entering it at nightfall.
Having reached Hastinapura, he entered it quickly. Approaching the inner apartments, he spoke these words to the gatekeeper:
"Announce me to Dhṛtarāṣṭra, O gatekeeper."
"O gatekeeper, report to Dhṛtarāṣṭra that I have arrived from the presence of the Pāṇḍavas;
tell him that Sañjaya has come from the sons of Pāṇḍu— do not delay."
"O Kṣattṛ, if he is awake, you must announce me;
for I would enter only after being known to the lord of the earth,
since I have a matter of great urgency to report here."
Then the doorkeeper, having heard this, said to the king:
"If he is awake, let me announce the message of the Pāṇḍavas along with its reasoning, so that his feet may be saluted."
The gatekeeper said:
"O lord of the earth, salutations to you! This is Sañjaya, who has come to your door desiring to see you."
"A messenger has arrived from the presence of the Pāṇḍavas; O King, give orders as to what he should do. Dhṛtarāṣṭra said:
"Tell him that I am well and that Saṃjaya may enter at once; welcome to him!
I am never unavailable to him."
"O Kṣattṛ, why would he stand at my gate?
Vaiśampāyana said:
Then, with the king's permission, he entered.
The son of the Sūta approached the king, the son of Vicitravīrya, who was seated upon his throne in a great palace protected by wise, heroic, and noble men, with his palms joined in reverence.
05,032.007 Saṃjaya said: "O lord of the earth, I am Saṃjaya; salutations to you! O god among men, having gone to the Pāṇḍavas, I have now returned."
Having saluted you, the wise Yudhiṣṭhira, son of Pāṇḍu, inquired after your welfare; being well-disposed,
he also asks after your sons.
O King, are you pleased with your sons and grandsons, as well as with your friends, ministers,
and those who depend upon you for their livelihood?
Dhṛtarāṣṭra said:
"O dear Sañjaya, having approached you, I ask:
is Ajātaśatru Pārtha in good health?"
"Is that king well, along with his sons, his ministers, and his younger brothers— the Kauravas? Sañjaya said:
The son of Pāṇḍu, together with his ministers, is well;
moreover, he has accomplished even more than that which was previously in your mind—
he is wise and acts for the sake of dharma and worldly prosperity.
Learned, possessed of right vision, and virtuous,
he considers the compassion of the Pāṇḍava to be superior to righteousness,
and for him, righteousness is held to be superior to the accumulation of wealth.
O Bhārata, know that Pārtha does not pursue pleasure or what is dear if it is devoid of dharma;
even for one who does nothing, everything is accomplished.
Therefore, they say that the person is distinct from action: impelled by another, the person moves about,
like a wooden doll strung upon a thread.
Having seen this self-restraint of the Pāṇḍava,
I consider divine power to be superior to human effort;
and having observed this fault in your own conduct, [I think the same].
As long as a man desires [to live] for too long, so long does this man receive censure— a terrible result following from his feet, characterized by an ugly appearance.
But Ajātaśatru, having cast off evil like a snake sheds its worn-out and useless skin,
shines forth with his steadfast conduct.

Yudhiṣṭhira, having cast his sin upon you, O King, understand that he has abandoned the conduct of a noble man, which is consistent with dharma and artha, and is instead following the actions of his own [evil] nature.
O King, you have incurred reproach here in this world; let not sin cling to you there in the next. Therefore, you should pursue your purpose without them, even though it is uncertain.
Today you hope for [this] while being subject to the will of your son;
yet the great sound of unrighteousness resounds across the earth,
for this deed is not worthy of you, O foremost of the Bharatas.
One who is of inferior wisdom, of low birth, cruel, long-harboring enmity, and lacking steadfastness in the sciences of the kṣatriya— such a person,
possessing these qualities, cannot cross over calamities.
One who is of weak vigor and undisciplined,
though born of noble lineage, righteous, illustrious, learned, living in comfort, and self-controlled— [is surpassed by one who possesses these qualities and is resolute].
He upholds the two intertwined goals of dharma and artha;
he does not act otherwise than by the power of destiny.
For how could a wise man, the foremost bearer of sacred mantras, act differently?
One who is thus endowed with all mantras and not deficient in them should, when in distress, act without delusion, performing deeds that are not cruel and which promote both dharma and artha.
"These men of yours, too, who are knowers of the mantras, sit together here, ever intent upon their duties;
this is their firm and powerful resolve."
If Ajātaśatru had committed evil because of evil, the Kurus would not have perished prematurely for the sake of the destruction of the Kurus. But since he did not, they met their end.
He might perhaps wish to cast evil upon you;
otherwise, this censure would have fallen upon you in the world—
what else could it be but the domain of the lords?
Where Pārtha beheld the next world, he likewise transcended it; such is the one who is highly esteemed— of this there is no doubt, nor is it a human feat.
Having observed these qualities produced by karma,
and that existence and non-existence are both impermanent,
King Bali, finding no further shore;
He considered that there is no cause for it other than time.
The eye, the ear, the nose, the skin, and the tongue—
these are the seats of cognition for a living being.
These [desires], being indeed gratified, end with the destruction of craving;
one who is free from distress and devoid of suffering should drive them away.
But I do not consider this to be the action of a man.
When properly applied according to the rules, it develops;
born through the actions of the mother and father,
it grows through food provided in accordance with the prescribed method.
O King, he encounters the pleasant and the unpleasant, happiness and suffering,
as well as blame and praise;
yet another person censures him for his transgressions.
He praises only those of virtuous conduct;
he will surely reproach you for your opposition to the Bharatas,
and this will certainly be the end of all creatures.
If this were not due to your own transgression of duty,
O King, it would consume the Kurus like a fire consumes dry grass;
you alone, O King, are responsible for those whose sons have been born.
O lord of men, you will fall under the power of all the world; you boasted of your own willful nature at the time of the gambling match,
but see now that its ripening is nothing other than this.
O lord of men, O King, by favoring those who are unworthy and likewise by suppressing those who are worthy,
you have [lost] this vast and flourishing earth because of your weakness.
O descendant of Kuru, you are not able to protect me, for I have been dismissed by you and shaken off by the speed of the chariot;
O lion among men, exhausted, I shall lie down upon my bed.
In the morning, the Kurus assembled in the assembly hall to hear the words of Ajātaśatru.
Dhṛtarāṣṭra said:
"You are permitted; go to your dwelling and retire to your bed, O son of a Sūta. In the morning, the Kurus shall listen [to your words] in the assembly hall."
"Your words regarding Ajātaśatru have been spoken.
Vaiśampāyana said:
"The highly wise Lord of the Earth, Dhṛtarāṣṭra, spoke to the gatekeeper."
"I wish to see Vidura; bring him here without delay.
Sent by Dhṛtarāṣṭra, the messenger spoke to the Kṣattṛ:
"The great king, the lord, desires to see you, O man of great wisdom."
Thus addressed, Vidura reached the royal residence and said to Dhṛtarāṣṭra, "Inform the gatekeeper that I am here. The gatekeeper replied:
"O Indra among kings, this Vidura has arrived at your command;
he desires to see your feet—command me as to what he should do.
Dhṛtarāṣṭra said:
"Bring in the highly wise Vidura, who possesses far-sighted vision;
for I am never at an improper time for an audience with this Vidura.
The gatekeeper said:
"O Kṣattṛ, enter the inner apartments of the wise Great King; for the King never tells me that it is an inopportune time for you to have an audience. Vaiśampāyana said:
Then Vidura, having entered the residence of Dhṛtarāṣṭra,
spoke these words with palms joined in reverence to the king who was lost in thought:
"Having been thus addressed, the steward (Kṣattṛ) then entered and spoke to the king."
"I am Vidura, O man of great wisdom; I have arrived at your command. If there is anything that must be done, here I am—please instruct me. Dhṛtarāṣṭra said:
"O Vidura, Saṃjaya has arrived; having reproached me, he has departed.
Tomorrow, in the midst of the assembly, he will deliver the message of Ajātaśatru.
Today, I have not yet understood the words of that hero of the Kurus."
That burns my limbs and has caused me this sleeplessness;
tell me what you see here that would bring welfare to one who is awake and burning, for you, dear son, are indeed skilled in dharma and artha.
Since Saṃjaya has returned from the Pāṇḍavas,
my mind finds no peace as it should; all my senses have fallen into a state of natural agitation.
"Indeed, my only thought today is what he will say;
therefore, O Vidura, tell me all that exactly as it is—
everything you have to say by way of conciliation to Ajātaśatru."
"And how, O father, may it be for our welfare,
so that all wise men may become happy?
Vidura said:
Insomnia possesses one who is accused by a powerful person, one who is weak, one whose means of success are deficient, one whose wealth has been seized, one who is lustful, and a thief.
O lord of men, I hope you have not been touched by these great evils.
"I hope you do not burn with envy, coveting the wealth of others.
Dhṛtarāṣṭra said:
"I wish to hear from you words that are righteous and lead to the highest beatitude."
"For in this lineage of royal seers, you alone are esteemed by the wise.
Vidura said:
"The king is endowed with all auspicious marks, such that he might even rule over the three worlds."

O Dhṛtarāṣṭra, Yudhiṣṭhira has indeed been sent by you as your messenger; yet you are far more perverse, being governed by your own ill fortune. For he is a soul of dharma, skilled in righteousness, endowed with both radiant wisdom and insight.
Out of kindness, compassion, righteousness, and the power of truth,
and considering your own greatness,
he endures many afflictions at the hands of Duryodhana, the son of Subala, Karṇa, and likewise Duḥśāsana.
Having bestowed sovereignty upon these [senses], how can you desire prosperity? Self-knowledge, diligent effort, forbearance, constancy in dharma,
restraint of speech, and generosity— these are not found in their entirety within them.
O King, from a single tree come the sacrificial vessels:
the *sruk*, the *droṇī*, the *voḍhanī*, and the *pīḍanī*.
O King, understand this as I speak it to you.
From a single person, both the unreal and the real are born;
he practices what is praised and does not practice what is censured. One who is not an atheist and possesses faith—this is the characteristic of a wise man.
He whom anger, joy, pride, lack of shame, arrogance, and vanity do not distract from his purpose— he indeed is called wise.
He who represents himself as something other than what he truly is—
The sin committed by a gambler, or by a thief who robs his own soul—
[he] whose actions or secret counsel others do not know,
but who knows what has been done [by himself], he indeed is called wise.
He whose undertakings are not obstructed by cold, heat, fear, or pleasure—
whether in prosperity or adversity— is indeed called wise. He whose worldly wisdom follows after both dharma and artha is truly learned.
He who chooses wealth over desire is indeed called wise;
he who chooses wealth over desire finds wealth through liberation. Having thus considered the principles of statecraft, he is indeed called wise.

O bull of the Bharatas, the wise desire to act according to their ability and perform according to their ability; they do not hold anything in contempt. They understand quickly and listen for a long time.
Having understood the matter, he pursues it for its sake and not out of desire;
he does not involve himself in the affairs of others unless asked— this is the first mark of wisdom in a learned man.

Men of wise intellect do not long for what is unattainable, nor do they wish to grieve for what is lost; even in calamities, they do not lose their composure. Having made a firm resolve, he who sets out does not dwell in the midst of his undertaking.
He whose time is never spent in vain and who has his self under control is indeed called wise.
O bull of the Bharatas, the wise take delight in noble deeds, perform actions that lead to prosperity, and do not harbor malice toward what is beneficial.
He who does not rejoice in self-honor nor suffer from insult,
who is as unshakeable as a pool in the Ganges— he is called wise.
He is a knower of the reality of all beings and a knower of the yoga of all actions.
A man who knows the means for dealing with human beings is called wise; one whose speech is fluent, whose discourse is varied, who possesses reasoning and eloquence,
and who can quickly expound upon a text— he indeed is called wise.
He whose learning follows wisdom, and whose wisdom follows learning,
who does not transgress the noble boundaries of conduct— he shall receive the title of "wise man. But he who is unlearned yet arrogant, and poor yet high-minded [is otherwise].
One who seeks to obtain wealth through improper means is called a fool by the wise. He who abandons his own interest to pursue the interest of another,
and he who acts falsely for the sake of a friend— he too is called a fool.

The fool who, having attained a human birth— the open gateway to liberation— clings to household life, is known as one who has fallen after having ascended. He who desires those things he should not desire, and who hates those things he should desire;
They call him one of deluded mind who hates one who is powerful;
he makes a friend an enemy, hates his own friend, and harms him;
he undertakes wicked actions—he, they say, is one of deluded mind.
He procrastinates in his duties and doubts everything;
he takes a long time for matters that require haste—he is a fool, O bull of the Bharatas.
He does not offer the *śrāddha* to the ancestors, nor does he worship the deities.
He does not find a true friend; they call him one who possesses the marks of a fool. He enters uninvited and speaks much when unasked;
this lowest of men, with a deluded mind, places his trust in those who are vigilant.
He who, while behaving in such a manner himself, casts blame upon another for his fault,
and he who becomes angry while lacking self-control— that man is the most foolish of all, for he is ignorant of his own strength and devoid of both dharma and artha.
O King, he who desires that which cannot be attained through the state of actionlessness (*naiṣkarmya*), he who instructs one who is not a disciple, he who worships the void,
and he who serves a miser— these are called persons of deluded intellect.
Having attained great wealth, knowledge, or even sovereignty,
he who conducts himself without arrogance is called a wise man.
He alone enjoys his prosperity, while you wear beautiful clothes.
Who is more cruel than he who does not share with his dependents?
One person commits the sins, yet the multitude enjoys the fruit;
those who enjoy are released from blame, while the doer alone is stained by the fault.
An arrow released by an archer may kill one person or may not kill at all;
but the intelligence unleashed by an intelligent man may destroy an entire kingdom along with its king.
Having resolved upon two matters with one [insight], bring three under your control with four.

Having conquered the five, understood the six, and abandoned the seven, be happy. A single drop of poison kills one person, and by a single weapon only one is slain; but the leaking of a secret counsel destroys a king along with his kingdom and his subjects.
One should not eat delicious food alone, nor should one contemplate matters of state alone;
one should not travel the road alone, nor should one remain awake alone among those who sleep.
O King, that which you do not perceive is indeed singular and without a second.
Truth is the ladder to heaven, like a boat for crossing from this shore to the other.
There is but one fault in those who possess forgiveness, and a second is not found:
that people consider such a person, because of his forbearance, to be weak.
This fault of his should not be considered; for patience is the supreme strength.
Patience is indeed a virtue for the weak, and an ornament for the powerful. Patience is a means of subduing the world; what cannot be accomplished through patience?

What can an evil person do to one who holds the sword of tranquility in his hand? Fire that falls upon a place devoid of grass extinguishes itself. One who lacks forbearance will only join others with their faults and likewise afflict himself.
One quality is the highest good: forbearance. One alone is the supreme peace: tranquility. One alone is the highest vision: knowledge. One alone brings happiness: non-violence.
These two the earth devours, as a snake devours creatures dwelling in their holes: [the one who is angry and the one who is weak].
A king who does not oppose [the righteous] and a Brahmin who does not travel abroad—these two are the lowest of men on this earth bounded by the ocean.
A man shines resplendent in this world by performing two actions: [righteousness and learning].
They did not say anything harsh, nor did they seek any improper purpose;
for, O tiger among men, these two act out of reliance on others:
women who desire what they are desired by, and the world which worships those who are worshipped.

These two are sharp thorns that wither the body: he who desires while being poor, and he who is angry while lacking power. These two men in the world pierce the solar disc: [the one who gives and the one who receives].
The wandering mendicant who is not disciplined in yoga, and the warrior slain while facing the enemy—
these two do not shine because of their contrary conduct:
the householder who makes no effort, and the mendicant who is burdened with worldly affairs.
"O King, these two men stand above heaven:
the powerful man endowed with forgiveness, and the poor man who is generous. Two transgressions regarding wealth acquired through righteous means must be recognized."
Bestowing [gifts] upon an unworthy recipient and failing to bestow them upon a worthy one—
these two should be cast into the water with a heavy stone tied to their necks:
the wealthy man who does not give, and the poor man who lacks ascetic practice.
"O bull of the Bharatas, three courses of conduct for human beings are heard of;
those who know the Vedas understand them as the inferior, the middling, and the superior.
O King, there are three kinds of men: the highest, the lowest, and the middling."
One should employ them appropriately in the three kinds of tasks.
O King, there are only three who are without property: a wife, a slave, and a son;
whatever they acquire belongs to him to whom they belong.
The seizing of others' property, the violation of another's wife,
and the abandonment of a friend— these three faults bring about ruin;
they are the triple gateway to hell that leads to one's own destruction.

Lust, anger, and likewise greed—one should therefore abandon these three. One should not abandon these three who have come for refuge, even in times of peril: the devotee, the one who serves, and the one who says, "I am yours."
O Bhārata, the granting of a boon, the acquisition of a kingdom, the birth of a son,
and the liberation of an enemy from distress— these four are equal in value to one [other].
Indeed, these four belong to a king of great power.
The wise say these things are to be avoided; one should know them well:
one should not hold counsel with those of little wisdom, nor with those who procrastinate, the lazy, or the fickle.
"O dear one, let these four dwell in your house while you are established in the dharma of a householder and endowed with prosperity:
an aged kinsman, one who has fallen on hard times, and one of noble birth."
"A friend who is poor and a sister who is childless—
O Great King, Bṛhaspati declared these four things to be immediate [in their consequences] when asked by the Lord of the Thirty-three; learn them from me."
The resolve of the deities, the power of the wise,
the discipline of those perfected in knowledge, and the destruction of evildoers—
these four deeds bring about fearlessness.
When performed improperly, these bring fear: the fire-sacrifice of pride, the silence of pride,
study out of pride, and sacrifice out of pride.

O bull among the Bharatas, five fires must be served with diligence by a man: the father, the mother, the sacred fire, oneself, and the preceptor. By honoring these five alone in this world, one attains pure fame.
The gods, the ancestors, human beings, mendicants, and guests as the fifth—
these five will follow you wherever you go: friends, enemies, neutrals, those who depend on you, and those upon whom you depend.
If even one of the five senses of a mortal man has a flaw,
then his wisdom leaks away like water from the foot of a leather water-skin.
Six defects must be abandoned here in this world by a man who desires prosperity.
Sleep, lethargy, fear, anger, laziness, and procrastination—
a man should abandon these six like a leaking boat in the ocean.
One should avoid a teacher who does not instruct and a priest who has not studied the Vedas.
A king who does not protect, a wife who speaks unpleasantly,
a cowherd who desires a village, and a barber who desires the forest—
these six qualities must never be abandoned by a man.
Truthfulness, generosity, diligence, freedom from envy, forbearance, and fortitude—
these six perish in an instant through neglect:
cattle, service, agriculture, a wife, learning, and association with the low-born.
For these six always disregard those who have previously helped them: students who have been instructed disregard their teacher; those who have taken wives disregard their mother;
and men whose passion has departed disregard the woman they once loved; and those who have achieved their purpose disregard the means by which it was attained.
Like those who have crossed the wilderness seeking a boat, or the afflicted seeking a physician;
[one desires] health, freedom from debt, absence of exile,
and association with virtuous people.
One’s own self-reliant livelihood and dwelling without fear—
O King, these are the six joys of the world of the living. [But one who is] envious, pitiless, discontented, wrathful, and constantly suspicious [finds no such joy].
And one who lives off another's fortune— these six are constantly miserable.
Constant arrival of wealth, freedom from illness,
a beloved wife who speaks kindly, and...

O King, a submissive son and knowledge that brings wealth— these six are the joys of the world of the living for one who attains mastery over these six things that are eternally present within oneself.
One who has conquered the senses is never joined with evils, much less with calamities. These six live off these six; a seventh is not found.
Thieves live off those who are heedless, and physicians live off those who are diseased.
Women among those desiring pleasure; priests among those performing sacrifices;
kings among those engaged in disputes; and scholars among fools—these seven faults, which give rise to calamities, must always be abandoned by a king.
By these, for the most part, even firmly established kings are destroyed:
women, dice, hunting, drinking, and fifthly, harshness of speech; as well as great severity of punishment and the abuse of wealth.
There are eight preliminary signs of a man who is about to perish:
first, he hates the Brahmins; he enters into conflict with the Brahmins;
he seizes the property of the Brahmins; and he seeks to kill the Brahmins.
He delights in disparaging them and does not welcome their praise;
he does not remember them in times of need, and when asked for assistance, he shows malice. He in whom these signs are found will bring about our defeat.
A wise man, having understood these faults through his intellect, should avoid them.
O Bhārata, there are these eight sources of joy, like fresh butter;
when they are present, they are seen to be truly pleasant.
Meeting with friends, the great acquisition of wealth,
embracing one's son, union in sexual intercourse,
pleasant conversation at the proper time, and courtesy within one's own group— these are the joys.
The attainment of what is desired and honor in the assembly of people—
this house has nine gates, three pillars, and five witnesses;
he who knows it as presided over by the Knower of the Field (*kṣetrajña*) is a supreme sage.
O Dhṛtarāṣṭra, learn from me those ten who do not understand the Dharma:
the intoxicated, the negligent, the insane, the exhausted, the angry, the hungry,
the hasty, the timid, the greedy, and the lustful— these are the ten.
Therefore, a wise person should not become attached to these states of being.
In this very context, they cite this ancient history,
sung by Sudhanvan for the sake of the lord of the Asuras when he was seeking a son.
That king who abandons desire and anger,
who bestows wealth upon a worthy recipient,
who is discerning, learned, and swift in action—
The whole world regards him as an authority;
he knows how to inspire confidence in people,
and he inflicts punishment upon those whose faults have been recognized.
He who knows the proper measure as well as forgiveness— him,
such as he is, complete prosperity attends;
he never disregards anyone, however weak.
He who, when prepared, serves his enemy with deliberate intelligence and does not seek conflict with those possessed of strength,
but instead displays his prowess at the right time— he is wise.
Having encountered adversity, he is never distressed;
remaining vigilant, he seeks out effort;
and having conquered his self, he endures suffering when it comes.
For one who bears the burden of responsibility, his rivals are conquered;
[he avoids] fruitless exile from home,
alliances with the wicked, and the violation of another's wife.
He who does not practice hypocrisy, theft, backbiting, or the drinking of intoxicants is always happy;
he does not undertake the pursuit of wealth through agitation.
When questioned, he speaks only the truth;
he does not seek a dispute for the sake of mere gain;
nor does he become angry when not honored—he is undeluded.
He who does not find fault and shows compassion; he who, though weak, does not act as a guarantor; he who does not speak excessively and endures dispute;
He who never adopts an arrogant appearance and does not boast of his own prowess toward others receives such praise everywhere.
One who is not deluded does not utter anything bitter; even common people always act kindly toward such a person.
One who is tranquil does not inflame hostility.
He does not ascend to pride, nor does he sink into despondency; he feels no resentment thinking "I am in distress.
They call him of noble character the supreme and foremost of men.
He does not indeed take delight in his own happiness, nor does he feel satisfaction in the suffering of another;
having given, he does not later feel regret.
The virtuous and noble person does not boast of local customs, conventions, or the laws of his birth; rather,
he desires to flourish as one who knows both the higher and the lower.
Having attained [this state] everywhere and at all times,
he exercises sovereignty over the great multitude, yet he remains free from deceit,
delusion, envy, and evil deeds.
The wise man who avoids what is displeasing to the king, backbiting, enmity with a guild, and disputes with those who are intoxicated, insane, or wicked— he is preeminent.
Self-restraint, purity, devotion to the deities, auspicious rites, expiatory ceremonies, and various traditional sayings—
whosoever performs these as daily duties;
The deities favor his rise;
he enters into marriage with equals, not with inferiors;
and he forms friendships, conducts business, and engages in conversation with equals.
He places those distinguished by their virtues in positions of authority;
thus the policies of that wise man are well-guided.
He eats in moderation, having first distributed [food] among his dependents.
Having performed immeasurable deeds, he sleeps soundly;
when entreated, he gives even to his enemies.
Misfortunes abandon such a self-possessed man.
When his intended actions and those already undertaken are known to no other people whatsoever,
and when counsel is kept secret and properly executed;
Not even the slightest matter causes him distress—
he who is intent on the pacification of all beings,
truthful, gentle, charitable, and pure in disposition.
He is recognized as preeminent among his kinsmen,
like a pure, high-quality great gem;
that man who is deeply ashamed before himself.
He becomes the teacher of the entire world, possessing infinite splendor, well-disposed, and composed;
by his own radiance, he shines like the sun.
Born in the forest to King Pāṇḍu, who was consumed by a curse, these five sons of his are equal to five Indras;
they were raised and trained by you alone while they were still children.
O son of Ambikā, by granting them their rightful kingdom, you shall fulfill my command; thus, O dear one,
being happy and rejoicing together with your sons, you shall prosper.
"O lord of men, you shall not be subject to conjecture by either gods or humans.
Dhṛtarāṣṭra said:
"O dear Vidura, you who are pure and skilled in both dharma and artha, tell me what course of action you perceive for one who is awake and being consumed [by grief];
instruct me properly."
O noble-minded one, tell Ajātaśatru everything that was preceded by wisdom— whatever you consider to be beneficial and conducive to the welfare of the Kurus.
Suspecting evil and perceiving only evil,
I ask you with a troubled mind;
O sage, tell me all that according to the truth.
"Everything desired by Ajātaśatru [shall be accomplished]," Vidura said:
"O King, men who always speak pleasant words are easy to find."
One who speaks what is unpleasant yet beneficial, and one who listens to it, are both rare to find.
Whether it be auspicious or evil, hateful or dear,
one should speak that which is unsolicited to him whom one does not wish to see suffer defeat.
Therefore, O King, desiring your welfare regarding the Kurus, I shall speak to you;
listen to these words of mine as I utter them, which are conducive to your well-being and consistent with dharma.
O Bhārata, those actions that are undertaken falsely may yet succeed.
"Do not set your mind upon those actions performed without skillful means (anupāya).
Likewise, O King, even an action prescribed by yoga may fail if it lacks skillful means; therefore, a wise person should not let his mind be despondent over such a case."
One should examine the consequences in actions that entail consequences;
having deliberated thoroughly, one should act, and not proceed with impetuosity.
One should likewise scrutinize the consequence and the ultimate results of all deeds.

A wise man should either exert himself or not at all; he who does not know the proper measure regarding stability, growth, and decline— whether in respect to the treasury, the realm, or the army— does not remain established in his kingdom.
But he who perceives these aforementioned means of knowledge,
being disciplined in the understanding of dharma and artha, attains sovereignty.
One should not behave improperly simply because one has obtained a kingdom.

For lack of discipline destroys prosperity, just as old age destroys the most excellent beauty. Like a fish greedy for its appearance, it swallows the iron hook concealed by a choice morsel of food, without regarding the consequence.

That which can be swallowed, that which is swallowable, that which, once swallowed, is digested, and that which is wholesome upon digestion— that is what should be eaten today by one who desires prosperity. He who plucks unripe fruits from a tree [reaps no benefit].
He does not obtain the essence from them, and his seed perishes; but he who takes the ripe fruit when it has matured in due time obtains the essence from the fruit and fruit again from the seed.
Just as the six-legged bee gathers honey while protecting the flowers,
so should one take wealth from men without causing them harm;
one should pluck flower after flower, but never cause the destruction of the root.
Like a gardener in a grove, and not like a charcoal-burner,
a man should reflect upon his actions— considering, "What would come of me having done this? What would come of me not doing it?"— and then either act or refrain.
Some objects are such that they are eternally beyond human effort;
even the exertion of personal agency would be rendered useless regarding them. They are intent upon what is meaningless and turned away from what is meaningful.
A wise man swiftly undertakes certain matters that require little effort but yield great fruit, and he does not obstruct such things.
He who sees everything with straightforward vision, as if drinking it in with his eyes, [attains success].
Even when sitting in silence, the subjects are devoted to him.
A tree may be in full bloom yet bear no fruit; it may bear fruit yet be difficult to climb;
it may be unripe yet appear ripe, but it should never wither away.

He who gladdens the world in four ways— with his eyes, his mind, his speech, and his actions— the world in turn becomes well-disposed toward him. From whom living beings tremble, as deer do from hunters.
Even having obtained the earth bounded by the oceans, he falls away from it;
though he attained the kingdom of his fathers and grandfathers through his own splendor,
standing in misconduct, he causes it to fall like the wind dispersing a cloud.
When a king practices righteousness as it was practiced by the virtuous from the beginning,
the earth— filled with wealth and increasing prosperity— thrives. But when he abandons righteousness and practices unrighteousness, [the earth declines].
The earth contracts like a piece of leather placed over a fire; therefore,
the very same effort that is exerted in crushing an enemy kingdom should be applied to the protection of one's own kingdom.
One should acquire a kingdom through dharma and protect it through dharma;
having attained prosperity rooted in dharma, one neither abandons it nor is deprived of it.
Even from one who is mad and prattling, or from a crawling child, [one may learn].
One should extract the essence from everywhere, just as gold is extracted from stones;
a wise man should remain collecting the well-spoken words and good deeds of the intelligent from here and there, just as a stone-gatherer collects pebbles.
Cows see by means of their scent; Brahmins see by means of the Vedas;
kings see by means of spies; and other people see with their eyes.
A cow that is difficult to milk incurs much greater suffering.
Furthermore, O King, they do not even attempt to train a cow that is easy to milk;
nor do they heat a piece of wood that bends without being heated;
nor do they bend a piece of wood that is already naturally curved.

By this analogy, a wise man should bow before one who is stronger; he bows to Indra, he bows to whoever is more powerful. Cattle have Parjanya as their protector; kings have friends and kinsmen as their protectors.
Husbands are the kinsmen of women; Brahmins are the kinsmen of the Vedas.
Dharma is protected by truth; knowledge is protected by yoga.
Beauty is protected by grooming; lineage is protected by conduct.
Grain is protected by measuring; horses are protected by proper training;
cows are protected by constant supervision; and women are protected by their poor clothing.
It is my conviction that noble birth is no proof for one who is devoid of good conduct.
For even among those born in the lowest castes, conduct alone is what distinguishes them.
He who is envious of the wealth, beauty, heroism, lineage, happiness, good fortune, and honors of others suffers from an endless disease.
Fearing the performance of improper acts and the neglect of duties, and because of the disclosure of secrets at the wrong time—one should not drink that intoxicant by which one becomes intoxicated.
There are three kinds of intoxication: the intoxication of learning, the intoxication of wealth, and thirdly, the intoxication of noble birth.
These are the intoxications of those who are self-conceited; these very things are the self-restraint of the virtuous.
When the wicked are requested by the good for some task at any time, they do not perform even the slightest good deed for them at any time.
The virtuous consider themselves to exist even when they are unknown;
the virtuous are the refuge of those who possess self-mastery, and the virtuous alone are the refuge of the virtuous.
The virtuous are the refuge of the wicked, but the wicked are never the refuge of the virtuous.

The assembly is won by one who possesses fine garments; the quarters are won by one who possesses cattle; the road is won by one who possesses a vehicle; everything is won by one who possesses virtue. Virtue is preeminent in a person; it is that which perishes here [in this world].
He has no need for life, nor for wealth, nor for kinsmen.
O bull of the Bharatas, the food of the wealthy consists primarily of meat; that of the middle class, primarily of dairy products; and that of the poor, primarily of salt.
The poor always eat food that is far more excellent;
hunger produces a sense of sweetness, which is very difficult for the wealthy to find.
Generally, in this world, the affluent lack the capacity to eat.
But for the poor, O Indra among kings, even wood is digested;
for as great as the system is, and as extensive as it is,
so too is the suffering great, while happiness is not so.
For the lowest classes, there is fear of losing their livelihood; for the middle classes, fear of death;
but for the highest mortals, the supreme fear is dishonor. Among all forms of intoxication, such as that of drinking and the like, the intoxication of power is the most wicked.
For one intoxicated by the pride of power does not awaken until he has fallen; by the senses operating upon their objects without restraint,
this world is tormented by them, as the stars are by the planets.
For one who is conquered by the fivefold group of senses— which are innate and emaciate the self—
calamities increase like the moon, the lord of stars, during the bright fortnight.
He who desires to conquer his ministers without first conquering himself [is lost].
A king whose ministers are powerful overcomes his enemies; yet one who lacks self-control is brought to ruin.
He who first conquers himself by means of self-discipline will then conquer his ministers and his enemies without fail.

Prosperity attends to the utmost degree that man who has his senses under control, who has conquered his ministers, who wields the rod of punishment against those who deserve it, who acts after due deliberation, and who is steadfast.
O King, the body is the chariot of a man.
The self is not the controller; rather, the senses are its horses.
With these well-trained, excellent steeds, the wise man who is ever vigilant and skillful proceeds happily, like a charioteer.
These [senses], when unrestrained, are capable even of causing destruction,
like untrained and unruly horses on a road leading a bad charioteer; they perceive misfortune as fortune, and indeed fortune as misfortune.
The fool, led astray by the senses, considers great suffering to be happiness.
He who abandons both dharma and worldly purpose to follow the dictates of the senses will swiftly be deprived of prosperity, life, wealth, and wife.

He who is a master of his goals but is not a master of his senses falls from his sovereignty because of that lack of mastery over the senses. One should seek the Self by means of the self, with the mind, intellect, and senses restrained.
For the self alone is the friend of the self, and the self alone is the enemy of the self. The self is the friend of that self by which the self has been conquered;
that very self is the constant friend, and that very self is the constant enemy.
Like two large fish caught in a net made of fine mesh,
both desire and anger, O King, plunder one's wisdom.
He who, having carefully considered here the goals of dharma and artha, acquires the necessary requisites—
He who has gathered his resources indeed prospers constantly in happiness;
but he who, without first conquering the five internal enemies that exhaust the mind,
seeks to defeat other external foes, is himself overcome by those enemies.

For indeed, evil-minded kings are seen being destroyed by their own actions due to their lack of mastery over the senses and the resulting confusion of sovereignty; likewise, those who are sinless suffer because they do not abandon evildoers.
Equal punishment touches one due to association;
the wet is burned by the dry because of association;
therefore, one should not form an alliance with the wicked.
Calamity devours that man who, out of delusion, does not restrain his own rising enemies— the five senses— each with its fivefold purpose.
Freedom from envy, straightforwardness, purity, contentment, and pleasant speech [are the qualities of the self-restrained].
Self-control, truthfulness, and lack of exertion do not exist in the wicked.
Self-knowledge, lack of exertion, endurance, constancy in dharma,
guarded speech, and generosity— these, O Bhārata, are not found in the lowest of men.

The ignorant harm the wise with insults and slander; the speaker takes on the evil, while the one who forgives is liberated. Violence is the strength of the wicked; for kings, the power lies in the administration of punishment.
Service is the strength of women; forgiveness is the strength of the virtuous. O King, restraint of speech is indeed considered the most difficult of all;
for it is not possible to speak much that is both meaningful and varied.
Well-spoken speech of various kinds brings about prosperity;
yet that same speech, O King, when ill-spoken, results in misfortune.
A forest pierced by arrows or struck down by an axe grows back again.
A wound caused by speech— such as a loathsome or ill-spoken word— does not heal. While barbed arrows, reed-tipped shafts, and iron bolts can be extracted from the body,
the arrow of speech cannot be removed, for it lies deep within the heart.
Word-arrows fly forth from the mouth;
struck by them, one grieves day and night,
for they strike the vital spots of another.
A wise man should not entrust these matters to others;
for when the gods ordain defeat for a man,
they take away his intelligence, and he perceives things perversely.

When the intellect has become turbid and destruction is at hand, injustice appearing in the guise of justice does not depart from the heart. The gods do not take up a staff to protect one like a herdsman.
For whatever they wish to protect, they endow with intelligence;
yet this very intelligence has been clouded for your sons, O Bhārata,
by their hostility toward the Pāṇḍavas, and you do not perceive it.
"O Dhṛtarāṣṭra, let Yudhiṣṭhira— who is endowed with the marks of royalty and who might even be the ruler of the three worlds— be your disciple and your instructor;
for he is far superior to all your sons, being favored by destiny."
Endowed with splendor and wisdom, knowing the true nature of dharma and worldly purpose,
that best among the upholders of dharma— who, out of kindness and compassion,
endures many hardships out of respect for you, O Indra among kings— [is Rāma].
Dhṛtarāṣṭra said:
"Speak further, O one of great intelligence, words endowed with righteousness and purpose;
there is no satiety for me as I listen, for you speak of wonderful things here."
Vidura said:
"Bathing in all the sacred fords and straightforwardness toward all beings—
these two might be equal, or perhaps straightforwardness is superior."
O Lord, always practice straightforwardness toward your sons;
having attained supreme fame in this world, you shall obtain heaven after death. As long as a man’s merit is sung of in the worlds, so long does he dwell in heaven.
For that long, O tiger among men, he is glorified in the heavenly world.
In this regard, they also cite this ancient history:
the conversation between Virocana and Sudhanvan concerning Keśinī.
At the *svayaṃvara*, a maiden named Keśinī by name stood there, O King, peerless in beauty and desiring an excellent husband; then Virocana, the son of Diti, arrived at that place.
Desiring to obtain him from there, Keśinī spoke to the lord of the Daityas.
Keśinī said:
"O Virocana, are the Brāhmaṇas superior, or are the sons of Diti?"
"Why then does Sudhanvan not ascend the couch?
Virocana replied,
"O Keśinī, we are indeed the best and most excellent among the offspring of Prajāpati."
"Indeed, these worlds belong to us; who are the gods? Who are the twice-born?
Keśinī said:
"Stay right here, Virocana, let us wait in this assembly hall."
"Sudhanvan will arrive tomorrow morning; I wish to see you two together.
Virocana said, "O blessed lady, O timid one, I shall do exactly as you say."
"You shall see Sudhanvan and me together tomorrow morning,
when this night has passed and the solar disc has risen.
Then, O best of kings, Sudhanvan arrived at that place.
Where Virocana, O Lord, was staying together with Keśinī,
Sudhanvan approached the son of Prahlāda as well as Keśinī.
Seeing that the twice-born had arrived, O bull of the Bharatas, Keśinī—
Rising up, he offered him a seat, as well as water for the feet and the guest-offering. In the meantime, Sudhanvan appeared there and spoke these unsurpassed words to Virocana:
Sudhanvan said:
"O son of Prahlāda, I have touched your golden seat;
having attained oneness with it, I shall not sit together with you."
Virocana said:
"Let them bring a plank, or a grass mat, or even a cushion of kusha grass.
For you are not superior to me, whether by virtue of your qualities or by birth."
“O Sudhanvan, you are not worthy of sitting on the same seat as me.
Sudhanvan said:
“A father and son may sit together; likewise two brahmins or two kings.”
Only the two Vaiśyas and the two Śūdras, and no others, may sit among one another;
even your father, while seated, must wait upon me from below. You are but a child, pampered in the house; you understand nothing at all.
Virocana said:
"O Sudhanvan, let us put our question before those who know it, using as our stake whatever gold, cattle, horses, and wealth we possess among the Asuras."
Sudhanvan said:
"O Virocana, let the gold, the cattle, and the horses remain yours alone;
however, having made our two lives the wager, let us ask a question of those who know."
Virocana said:
"Where shall we two go now that our lives have been staked?
Indeed, I shall not remain among the gods, nor ever among men."
Sudhanvan said:
"Since our lives have been staked, we two shall go to your father;
for even for the sake of his son, Prahrāda would not speak an untruth."
Vidura said:
"Thus, having made their wager, Virocana and Sudhanvan, both enraged, then went to the place where Prahrāda was staying."
Having spoken thus, the two of them went toward the house of Prahrāda.
Having arrived there, they then beheld him, the lord of the Daityas. Seeing that they had come, Prahrāda was then filled with wonder.
Then the son of Diti asked both of them the reason for their arrival.
Prahlāda said:
"These two are seen here, with whom [in the past] no one has ever traveled together."

Like two enraged venomous serpents who have come here by the same path, why indeed do you travel together now when you did not travel together before? Therefore, Sudhanvan, I ask you this; do not speak falsely when asked.
"Virocana, I ask this of you: what friendship do you have with Sudhanvan?
Virocana replied, "I have no friendship with Sudhanvan; we have wagered our very lives."
"O Prahrāda, I ask this of you; do not answer my question falsely. Prahrāda replied:
"He is neither dappled, nor tawny, nor black, nor red."
Sudhanvan is subtler than the edge of a razor; who is fit to speak the Dharma? Whether you speak the truth or do not speak it, [it remains as it is].
"O Prahlāda, your blameless question shall bear fruit upon your head.
Prahlāda said:
"Let they bring water and the honey-mixture (madhuparka) for Sudhanvan."
"O Brahmin, you are worthy of worship; this white cow has been fattened for you.
Sudhanvan said:
"Water and the honey-mixture (madhuparka) were already offered to me on the road."
"O Prahlāda, answer truthfully the question we two are asking:
Are the Brāhmaṇas truly superior, or is Virocana? Speak the truth, O Lord of the Daityas, for truth is the highest austerity."
Prahrāda said:
"O Brahmin, whether you are his son or someone else, you stand as a witness between these two who are disputing; how could one such as I speak on their behalf?"
05,035.022d*0207_00 Vidura: Prahlāda spoke to the swan as he was approaching together with Āditya. 05,035.022d*0207_02 Prahlāda:

O Haṃsa, when Dhṛtarāṣṭra— the one of great wisdom, omniscient and pleasant to behold— and one who has sons, O Brahmin, both stand as witnesses and fall into dispute, how does dharma proceed between them?
Sudhanvan said:
"O wise one, you should give a cow to your own son, or whatever other wealth may be dear to him;
likewise, when two people are disputing, the truth must be spoken by you."
"Now, Sudhanvan, I ask you this: what would a false speaker dwell upon—whether he speaks the truth or even if it be falsehood? The swan replied:

If one who wanders with loose discipline like the ear of a cow should not explain the Dharma when questioned, O King, he falls away from Dharma; for him there is neither a higher world nor progeny. Dharma destroys these [transgressors], just as a river uproots the trees growing along its banks.
Those who, observing the Dharma, sit in silent meditation,

[the one who speaks] shall take half of the best [portion], while the doer [of the offense] shall receive a quarter. Among those members of the assembly, where the censurable is not censured, a quarter [of the fault] falls upon them.
By this, one becomes preeminent, and the members of the assembly are released from blame;
for where the blameworthy is censured, the sin falls upon the perpetrator.
—Prahlāda.
"O Dhṛtarāṣṭra, if one speaks falsehood out of delusion or even out of desire, what state does that evil speaker dwell in? I ask you this.
Sudhanvan said:
The night a woman is taken as a wife, the night one is defeated at dice,
and the night one dwells with limbs tormented by a heavy burden or speaks ill—
these nights one should spend shut out from the city, hungry at the outer gate.
Seeing many enemies and being a speaker of evil words,

one should dwell [in that state]; indeed, the speaker of evil words shall dwell for as many nights as he has been hostile, and for as many nights as a dear friend has died, and for as many nights as he is deprived of his entire wealth.
One kills five by lying about cattle; one kills ten by lying about cows;
one kills a hundred by lying about horses; one kills a thousand by lying about men.
By speaking a falsehood for the sake of gold, one kills both those born and those yet unborn.
"One destroys everything by lying regarding land; therefore, do not speak a falsehood concerning land.
Prahlāda said:
"O Virocana, Aṅgiras is indeed superior to me, and Sudhanvan is superior to you."
"His mother is superior to your mother; therefore, you have indeed been defeated by him, Virocana.
O Sudhanvan, this Sudhanvan is now the master of your life-breaths. Sudhanvan, I desire that Virocana be returned to you."
Sudhanvan said:
"Since you chose righteousness and did not speak a falsehood out of desire,
I therefore grant you back your son, O Prahrāda, who is so difficult to obtain."
"O Prahrāda, this Virocana, your son, has been given by me;
he shall perform the washing of my feet in the presence of the maiden.
Vidura said:
Therefore, O Indra among kings, you ought not to speak a falsehood for the sake of land. Do not go to your destruction along with your sons and ministers by pursuing [the enemy] against your sons.
The gods do not take up a staff to protect people like a herdsman.

But that which they wish to protect, they divide with their intelligence. For in whatever way a person directs his mind toward what is auspicious, in that same way all his goals are accomplished; there is no doubt in this.
The Vedic meters do not rescue one from evil who lives by deceit,
just as birds with fledged wings leave their nest.
The sacred hymns abandon him at the time of death:
intoxication from drink, quarreling, communal enmity, discord between husband and wife, and dissension among kinsmen.
They say that one should avoid what is disliked by the king, disputes between men and women, and any path that is dangerous; likewise,
one should avoid a sea-faring merchant who has previously been a thief.
A cheat with counting-sticks, a physician,
an enemy, a friend, and an actor—
these seven one should not appoint as witnesses in legal cases.
The Agnihotra performed with pride, the silence observed with pride, the study undertaken with pride, and the sacrifice offered with pride—
these four things bring about fearlessness.
Those who act improperly bring fear:
one who sets fire to a house, a poisoner, one who eats from a vessel belonging to a degraded person, a seller of Soma,
a maker of arrows, a spy, a betrayer of friends, and an adulterer.
An embryo-killer, one who violates the bed of his guru, and a twice-born man who drinks liquor;
one who is excessively harsh, a crow-like person, an atheist, and a reviler of the Vedas; one who seizes the sacrificial ladle, an outcast (vrātya), and even a wealthy miser—these [are excluded].
And those who, having been told "protect [this]," should cause harm, are all equal to slayers of Brahmins.
Gold is recognized by a grass-torch;
a noble man is known as virtuous through his conduct in the world.

A hero in times of fear, a wise man in times of financial distress; friends and enemies alike are tested in difficult calamities. Indeed, old age carries away beauty, while hope carries away fortitude.
Death [destroys] the vital breaths; malice, the practice of dharma; anger, prosperity; service to the ignoble, virtue;
lust, modesty; and pride destroys everything.
There is no wealth for the angry, no friend for the cruel,
no wife for the harsh, no happiness for the ignorant,
no modesty for the lustful, and no treasury for the lazy.
But for one who is unstable, nothing at all will succeed.
Fortune arises from auspiciousness, it increases through confidence,
it establishes its foundation through skill, and it is firmly established through self-restraint.
Eight qualities illuminate a man:
wisdom, noble birth, self-control, learning, valor, and moderation in speech.
Generosity according to one's ability and gratitude— O dear one, these qualities of great majesty are forcibly relied upon by a single quality.
When a king honors a man,
this single quality outshines all other qualities.
O King, these eight [qualities] exist in the world of men:
There are four illustrations of the heavenly world followed by the virtuous,
and four others which the virtuous follow.
Sacrifice, charity, study, and austerity—
these four are followed by the virtuous;
as are self-restraint, truthfulness, straightforwardness, and compassion.
The virtuous follow these four:
sacrifice, study, giving, austerity, truthfulness, forbearance, compassion, and freedom from greed; this is remembered as the eightfold path of Dharma.

Among these, the first group of four may be practiced even for the sake of hypocrisy, but the latter group of four does not abide in those who are not great-souled. That is no assembly where there are no elders.
Those who do not speak the Dharma are not elders;
that is not the Dharma where truth is absent;
and that is not truth which is permeated by deceit.
Truth, beauty, learning, knowledge, noble lineage, character, strength, wealth,
heroism, and eloquent speech— these ten are the sources of social association.
Now, he who would not speak at all, neither truth nor falsehood;
Those who, harboring malice toward the Dharma, sit in silence and meditate— of that [offense],
the most eminent member of the assembly shall incur one quarter, and a quarter shall fall upon the perpetrator.
A quarter falls upon those members of the assembly where the one deserving of censure is not censured.
In this case, the one free from sin becomes the best, and the members of the assembly are released;
the guilt goes to the perpetrator where one deserving of blame is censured. One who commits evil, having an evil reputation, reaps the fruit of that very evil.
One who performs merit and possesses a reputation for merit enjoys the fruit of merit alone. Therefore, a man of firm vows should not commit evil;
for evil, when committed again and again, destroys one's wisdom.
A man whose wisdom has perished constantly undertakes only evil;
merit increases wisdom when performed again and again,
and a man whose wisdom has grown constantly undertakes only merit.
Performing merit, one of meritorious fame goes to a meritorious state;
therefore, a person should practice merit with a well-composed mind.
A man who is envious, malicious, cruel, and a creator of enmity—
By practicing evil, one soon encounters great hardship;
but he who is free from envy, possessed of perfected wisdom, and always practices what is auspicious,
attains great honor and shines everywhere.
Without hardship he attains happiness and shines everywhere;
he who acquires wisdom from the wise is truly a scholar,
for having attained both dharma and artha, the wise man is able to prosper in happiness.
One should do during the day that by which one may dwell happily at night;
one should do during the eight months [of the dry season] that by which one may dwell happily during the rains;
one should do during the earlier stage of life that by which one may dwell happily when old.
One should do throughout one's life that by which one may dwell in happiness after death. People praise food that has been digested, a wife whose youth has passed,
a hero who has returned from battle, and an ascetic who has reached the further shore.

Whatever breach is covered by wealth acquired through unrighteousness remains uncovered; indeed, something else is torn asunder because of it. The teacher is the instructor for those who possess self-control; the king is the instructor for the wicked-minded.
Then Yama Vaivasvata, the teacher of those whose sins are concealed, declared:
"The origin of sages, of rivers, of noble lineages, and of great-souled beings, as well as the source of women's misconduct, must not be investigated."

O King, a Kṣatriya who delights in honoring the twice-born, who is generous, and who is upright toward his kinsmen, shares in heaven and protects the earth for a long time. Three kinds of men gather the golden flowers of the earth.
O Bhārata, those who are brave, learned, and know how to serve perform actions that are superior in intellect, middling in physical strength,
inferior in speed of movement, and the lowest in terms of bearing burdens.
Having placed sovereignty in the hands of Duryodhana, Śakuni, the foolish Duḥśāsana, and Karṇa, how can you desire prosperity?
O bull of the Bharatas, the Pāṇḍavas are endowed with every virtue.
"They behave toward you as toward a father; therefore, behave toward them as toward a son.
Vidura said:
"In this very connection, they cite this ancient history."

We have heard of the conversation between Ātreya and the Sādhyas. In ancient times, the Sādhyas, the gods, questioned that great seer of immense wisdom and rigid vows as he was wandering in the form of a swan.
"O great seer, we are the Sādhyas, the gods;
having seen you, we are unable to fathom you. By what we have heard, you are considered by us to be wise and intelligent."
"You ought to speak noble and poetic words.
The swan said:
"O immortals, this task has been heard by me."
Fortitude, tranquility, and adherence to truth and dharma—
having untied every knot of the heart,
one should bring both the pleasant and the unpleasant under the control of the self.

When reviled, one should not revile in return; for anger that is endured purifies one’s very self by itself, and one gains the merit of the other’s good deed. It consumes the reviler and secures for oneself the merit of his virtuous action.

One should not be abusive nor contemptuous of another; one should not be a betrayer of friends, nor should one serve the base; one should not be excessively proud, nor should one be of degraded conduct.
One should avoid harsh and biting speech;
for terrible words burn the vital organs, the bones, the heart, and likewise the life-breaths of men in this world.
Therefore, one who delights in dharma should always avoid speech that is harsh, cruel in form, piercing to the vitals,
and rough.
One should know that person who stabs others with the thorns of speech to be the most unfortunate among men,
carrying Nirṛti bound within his mouth.
If another were to pierce him from above with arrows that are exceedingly sharp and blazing like fire or the sun,
even while being thus pierced and overwhelmed;
The wise man should know: "He bestows my good deeds upon whomever he serves—whether it be a virtuous person, one who is not virtuous, an ascetic, or even a thief. (5.36.10a)
Just as a garment takes on the color of the dye,
so too does he fall under their influence;
but he who neither utters a dispute nor incites one [is not so affected].
He who, when struck, does not strike back nor cause others to strike,
and who feels no ill will toward one wishing to kill him— to such a person who has arrived, the gods look with longing.
They say that the unspoken is better than the spoken;
to speak the truth is the second [best];
to speak what is pleasant is the third.
One should speak what is righteous; that is the fourth [type of speech].
A person becomes like those with whom he converses, like those whom he serves, and like what he desires to become.

From whatever [object] one turns away, from that one is liberated; for by turning away from everything, one does not experience even the slightest suffering. One is neither conquered nor does one seek to conquer others.
He creates no enmity and harbors no resentment; he is of an even nature toward both blame and praise;
he neither grieves nor exults.

He desires the welfare of all and does not set his mind on their harm; he who is truthful, gentle, and self-controlled is a supreme person. He does not offer empty consolation, and having made a promise, he gives.
He who discerns both success and failure is a man of middle character.
Duḥśāsana, however, is one who strikes others but is not himself disciplined;
being ungrateful, he does not turn back from the power of his wrath.
He is not a friend to anyone, and moreover, he is evil-minded; these are the traits of the lowest man in this world.
Distrustful even of others' goodness, he suspects everyone of himself.
He who indeed rejects his friends is the lowest of men. One who desires his own welfare should serve only the best, and the middling when the time is right; but he should never serve the lowly.
One may indeed acquire wealth through the power of the wicked,
through constant exertion, wisdom, and human effort;
yet one does not truly obtain proper praise thereby.
He does not attain the conduct of great lineages.
Dhṛtarāṣṭra said:
"The gods envy those of great lineages."
"O Vidura, I ask you this question: who are those great families that possess an abundance of dharma and wealth, and are deeply learned?"
Vidura said:
"Austerity, self-restraint, knowledge of Brahman, performing sacrifices, holy marriages, and the constant giving of food."
Those very families in which these seven qualities exist and whose conduct is perfectly established are great lineages—
those whose conduct does not falter and whose lineage is not impaired.
Those distinguished families who, having abandoned falsehood, desire preeminent fame for their lineage, practice dharma through the purity of their conduct.
Through lack of ritual exertion, through improper marriages, through the neglect of the Veda,
and through the transgression of dharma, families fall into a state of non-nobility; likewise,
through the destruction of the property of the gods and the seizure of the property of Brahmins.
Families fall into ruin through the mistreatment of Brahmins;
O Bhārata, families fall into ruin through the contempt and slander of Brahmins, and also by the misappropriation of deposits.
Families well-endowed with cattle, men,
and horses do not count as true families if they are deficient in conduct; however, families that are not deficient in conduct are considered noble even if they possess little wealth.
They enter into the ranks of the noble and acquire great renown.
One should protect one's conduct with effort; for wealth comes and goes, but one who is diminished in wealth is not truly lost, whereas one who is ruined in conduct is utterly destroyed.
Families do not truly flourish through cattle, livestock, horses, or even highly prosperous agriculture if they are deficient in their conduct. May there be no one in our family who creates enmity.
O King's minister, may you not be a stealer of others' property, a betrayer of friends, a rogue, or a liar; nor may you eat before [offering] to the ancestors, the gods, and guests.

He who would kill a Brahmin among us, or he who would hate the Brahmins among us—he shall not enter our assembly; nor shall he who would destroy our cultivation. Grass, earth, water, and fourthly, kind speech—these are provided for all.
O King, O highly wise one, these things— offered with supreme faith as an act of hospitality— are never interrupted in the homes of the virtuous who are devoted to dharma and meritorious deeds.
O King, even a small chariot is indeed capable of bearing a heavy load, whereas other trees are not;
in this way, when properly joined together, they become capable of enduring the weight.
Other men are not so truly of noble lineage;
he is no friend from whom one fears in anger, nor is he a friend who must be served with suspicion.
That friend in whom one may place confidence as in a father— indeed,
that is true friendship, even if other [alliances] have been formed; for even if one is unrelated by blood, one should conduct oneself with the spirit of friendship.

He alone is a kinsman, he alone is a friend, he alone is one's refuge and ultimate resort— for a man of fickle mind who does not serve the elderly and whose intellect is ever wavering, the acquisition of friends is never stable.

Objects pass by those whose minds are fickle, who lack self-mastery, and who follow the dictates of the senses, just as swans abandon a dried-up lake. They become angry for no reason at all and become placid without cause.

This is the nature of the wicked: like a shifting cloud, they do not remain faithful to their friends even when they have been honored and have had their purposes fulfilled. Even when dead, the flesh-eating scavengers will not consume those ungrateful men.
One should indeed test friends, whether wealth exists or not;
