for it is only by not testing them that one learns the worth or worthlessness of friends.
From distress beauty fades, and from distress strength fades.
Through grief, knowledge perishes; through grief, one falls ill.
Through sorrow, that which cannot be obtained is lost, and the body is consumed by heat.
Enemies rejoice; therefore, do not set your mind upon grief.
Again a man dies and is born;
again a man declines and prospers;
again a man begs and is begged from.
Again a person grieves and is grieved for again:
pleasure and pain, existence and non-existence,
gain and loss, death and life.
In this world, they experience everything in turn;
therefore, the wise man should neither rejoice nor grieve,
for these six sense-faculties are indeed fickle.
Whatever occurs for them in whatever situation, from that very source his intellect flows away,
like water constantly leaking from a jar with a crack.
Dhṛtarāṣṭra said:
"The king Śikhin, whose body is emaciated, has been treated deceitfully by me;
he will bring an end to my foolish sons through battle."
"All this is perpetually agitated; this mind is perpetually agitated.
O high-minded one, tell me of that state which is free from agitation.
Vidura said:
O sinless one, I see no peace for you other than through knowledge and austerity, other than through restraint of the senses, and other than through the renunciation of greed.
One dispels fear by means of wisdom; one attains greatness through austerity.

Through service to the guru one finds knowledge; through renunciation one finds peace. Not relying on the merit of giving, nor relying on the merit of the Vedas, those seeking liberation wander here in this world, completely freed from passion and hatred.
At the conclusion of well-studied learning, of a well-fought battle, of a well-performed deed, and of well-practiced austerity, happiness increases. One attains well-spread beds;
Indeed, O King, they never find sleep when separated from one another; they find no pleasure in women,
nor do they take delight when praised by bards or heralds.
Those who are divided never practice the Dharma;
those who are divided do not attain happiness in this world;
those who are divided do not honor respect.
Those who are divided do not delight in tranquility;
indeed, wholesome advice spoken to them does not please them,
nor is their security and well-being ever established.
O lord of men, for those who are divided, there is indeed no refuge whatsoever other than destruction. Prosperity is to be expected in cattle, and asceticism is to be expected in a Brahmin.

Fickleness is to be expected in women; fear is to be expected from kinsmen. Even long threads, when numerous and equal, endure many strains because of their multiplicity—this is the analogy of the wise.
"O bull of the Bharatas, like firebrands, kinsmen smolder when separated and blaze when united. O Dhṛtarāṣṭra,
those who are heroes toward brahmins, women, kinsmen, and cattle— "
O Dhṛtarāṣṭra, like ripe fruit from its stalk, they are falling away.
Even a great, solitary tree, though strong and well-rooted,
can have its branches and trunk forcibly crushed by the wind.
Now, those trees that stand together in a grove, firmly established,
withstand even the swiftest winds because they rely upon one another;
in the same way, even a single man, though endowed with virtues, [is vulnerable].
Those who harbor enmity think they can overcome him, as the wind might uproot a solitary tree;
yet through mutual support and mutual reliance,
kinsmen flourish together like lotuses in a lake.
Brahmins, cows, women, children, and kinsmen are not to be killed; nor are those whose food one eats, nor those who have come for refuge.
Even for a great offense, their punishment shall be release.
Among humans, there is no other quality whatsoever for those who possess wealth equal to freedom from disease— blessings be upon you— for the sick are as good as dead.
[There is] no bitter headache born of illness;
O Great King, drink up this wrath— which is followed by evil, harsh, sharp, and fierce, and which the virtuous may drink but the wicked will not— and thus find peace.
Afflicted by disease, they do not care for fruits;
indeed, they do not find the truth within the objects of the senses;
the sick are perpetually beset by suffering.
They do not perceive wealth, enjoyments, nor happiness,
O King, for you previously disregarded my words when you saw Draupadī won at dice.
"Restrain Duryodhana from the gambling match at Akṣavatī;
the wise avoid the vice of gambling.
That is no strength which is opposed by gentleness."
A mixed dharma should be practiced with vigor; for prosperity that is cruel and unstable perishes, while that which is gentle yet mature passes down to sons and grandsons.
May the sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra protect the Pāṇḍavas, and may the sons of Pāṇḍu protect your sons; for the Kurus have one enemy and one friend, and they are of one counsel.
O King, may they live happily and prosper!
Today you have become the central pillar of the Kauravas;
the Kuru lineage depends upon you, O descendant of Ajamīḍha.
Protect the sons of Pṛthā, who are young and distressed by their forest exile,
while guarding your own fame, my dear son;
reconcile the Kauravas with the sons of Pāṇḍu.
Let not your enemies seek an opening against you;
O god among men, all of them abide in truth—
O lord of men, establish Duryodhana [in that same path].
Vidura said:
"O Indra among kings, O son of Vicitravīrya, Svāyambhuva Manu spoke of these seventeen types of men as those who strike at the sky with their fists."
He spoke to those very ones as they were bending Indra’s unbendable bow,
and likewise to the rays of light as they bent their unbendable feet:
"He who instructs one who should not be instructed, and he who becomes angry;"
He who excessively favors an enemy,
he who fails to protect his wife— may you be blessed—
and he who begs from one who should not be begged from, and he who boasts.
He who, though of noble birth, commits an unworthy act;
he who, being weak, is a constant enemy to the strong;
and he who speaks to one lacking faith;

O lord of men, he who desires that which cannot be desired, the father-in-law who expects laughter from his daughter-in-law, and he who, while living with his daughter-in-law, seeks honor from her; ||| 05,037.005a ||| he who desires that which cannot be desired, the father-in-law who expects laughter from his daughter-in-law, and he who, while living with his daughter-in-law, seeks honor from her; ||| 05,037.005a ||| he who desires that which cannot be desired, the father-in-law who expects laughter from his daughter-in-law, and he who, while living with
He who sows seed in another's field, he who excessively reviles a woman, and he who,
having received something, says, "I do not remember";
He who boasts after giving when being asked, and he who here attends upon the wicked with conciliatory words—
these follow after the Wind with nooses in their hands.
In whatever manner a person behaves toward someone, one should behave toward them in that same manner; that is the law.
One who acts with deceit should be treated with deceit.
Good conduct should be met with goodness; for old age robs one of beauty, hope robs one of fortitude,
death robs one of life, and envy robs one of the practice of dharma.
Lust destroys modesty and conduct; service to the ignoble destroys it; anger destroys prosperity; and pride destroys everything.
Dhṛtarāṣṭra said:
"When it is stated in all the Vedas that a person has a lifespan of a hundred years,
by what cause here does one fail to attain that full span of life?
Vidura said:

Excessive speech, excessive pride, as well as lack of generosity, O lord of men, anger, an excessive desire to know, and treachery toward friends— these six are sharp swords that cut short the lives of embodied beings.

These slay men, O Bhārata; it is not death [itself] that kills them— blessings be upon you— for he who approaches the wife of one who trusts him, he who violates the bed of his guru, the twice-born man who is the husband of a *vṛṣalī*, and he who drinks intoxicants.
One who issues commands, one who destroys the livelihood of the twice-born, one who is a messenger,
and one who betrays those who have come for refuge— all these are equal to killers of Brahmins; according to the sacred revelation (śruti), one must perform penance after associating with them.
A householder who is generous, whose speech is never rejected, who eats only the remnants of food, and who is non-violent; who does no harm, has abandoned strife, and is grateful;
The wise man who is truthful and gentle attains heaven. O King, men who always speak pleasant words are easy to find;
but one who speaks what is unpleasant yet beneficial, and one who listens to it, are rare indeed.

For a king who, relying on righteousness, sets aside what is pleasant or unpleasant to his master and speaks words that are disagreeable yet beneficial, is truly possessed of a companion. One should abandon an individual for the sake of a family; one should abandon a family for the sake of a village.

One should abandon a village for the sake of the district; one should abandon the earth for the sake of oneself. One should protect wealth for the sake of times of distress; one should protect one's wife even at the cost of wealth.
One should always protect oneself, even at the cost of both wife and wealth.
"In former ages, this gambling was seen to cause enmity among men. Therefore, a wise person should not practice gambling even for the sake of amusement.
O King, I have said this even at the time of gambling."
"O Prātipīya, such a statement is not at all fitting,
like medicine that is wholesome yet disagreeable to a sick man; it does not please you, O son of Vicitravīrya."
With crows you have defeated these peacocks with their variegated plumage— the Pāṇḍavas by means of the sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra—
concealing yourself among jackals while abandoning lions.
O lord of men, you will grieve when the time comes for that father who never becomes angry with a servant who is devoted and intent on his welfare.
In such a master, servants place their trust and do not abandon him in times of distress;
nor do they cause the obstruction of their livelihood.
If he desires to win over outsiders who were previously unknown,
his own trusted ministers, being restricted by their accustomed positions and deprived of their enjoyments, will abandon him.
Having first enumerated all his duties, and having established a livelihood consistent with his income and expenditure,
he should gather suitable companions.
For difficult tasks are indeed accomplished through companionship;
he who, having understood the intention of his master,
performs all duties without weariness.
A speaker of what is beneficial, affectionate, and noble; one who knows one's capacity and is to be pitied like one's own self—
such is Bāṇa, the fowler, the counselor, the solitary one who serves as a pillar.
One who is chronically ill and one who is quarrelsome— these seven types of servants one should abandon.
So too one who, when instructed, does not respect the command, and he who, when being appointed to a task, speaks back in opposition.
One who is conceited in his wisdom and speaks contrarily—
such a servant should be dismissed with the utmost haste. One who is not arrogant, not cowardly, and not procrastinating;
They say that an envoy endowed with eight qualities is one who is compassionate, gentle, unassailable by others, free from disease by nature, and possessed of noble speech.
A wise man should never go to another's house out of misplaced trust at an improper time;
nor should he remain hidden in a public square at night.

One should not desire a woman of royal caste, nor should one practice concealment regarding what was said in a sacrificial session; for one who has shared secret counsel and is associated with the wicked [is ruined].
One should not say, "I do not trust you";
rather, one should provide a statement based on a specific reason:
"The king is compassionate, but the king's servant is a harlot."
A son, a brother, a widow with young children,
and one who lives by the army and has already received his meal—
these indeed must be avoided in legal proceedings.
Ten qualities attend one whose nature is to bathe:
strength, beauty, purity of voice and complexion, and purity of touch, smell, and state.
Fortune, delicacy, excellent women,
virtues, and eating in moderation— these six attend upon health, longevity, happiness, and strength.
His offspring shall be unblemished,
and people shall not revile him as being a glutton, nor as one who is indolent or excessively voracious.
One should not allow these to dwell in one's house: those hated by the world, those full of deceit, the cruel, those ignorant of place and time, and those of undesirable appearance.
One who is miserly, abusive, and unlearned;
one born of low origins, who considers himself honorable though he is not; one who spits, who has created enmity, and who is ungrateful.
Even when one is severely distressed, one should never beg from these:
one whose actions are defiled, one who speaks excessively,
one who is constantly untruthful, and one whose devotion is unstable.
One should not associate with these six lowest of men: one who is excessively lustful, and those who are full of self-conceit.
For wealth is bound to companions, and companions are bound to wealth.
These two are bound to one another; they do not succeed without each other.
Having procreated sons and made them free from debt, and having provided some means of livelihood for them;
Having bestowed all his daughters upon suitable husbands,
he should dwell in the forest, desiring to live like a sage,
doing what is beneficial for all beings and bringing happiness to himself.

For a lord should indeed do this, for it is the root for the accomplishment of dharma and artha. For one who possesses intelligence, power, brilliance, courage, exertion, and resolve— from where can there be fear of returning [to worldly life]?
Behold the evils in a conflict with the Pāṇḍavas,
wherein even the gods together with Śakra would tremble;
enmity with one's own sons brings a life of constant anxiety.
The destruction of your fame and the joy of your enemies, the wrath of Bhīṣma and yours, O you who are like Indra,
as well as that of Droṇa and King Yudhiṣṭhira.
Having grown powerful, he would have destroyed this world,
like the white planet falling obliquely through the sky;
for there were your hundred sons, Karṇa, and the five Pāṇḍavas.

The sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra might rule the entire earth girt by the oceans, O King; yet the sons of Pāṇḍu are considered tigers in the forest. Do not cut down the forest while its tigers remain, nor destroy the tigers from the forest.
There would be no forest without tigers, and there would be no tigers without the forest;
for the forest is protected by the tigers, and the woods protect the tigers.
Likewise, those who are devoid of virtue do not desire to recognize the virtues of others.
Just as those of evil mind desire to know their own lack of virtue,
so one who desires the supreme accomplishment of his goals should practice dharma from the very beginning;
for prosperity does not depart from dharma, just as immortality does not depart from the heavenly world.

He whose self has turned away from evil and is established in what is auspicious has understood all this— both that which is primordial nature (*prakṛti*) and that which is its transformation (*vikṛti*).
He who pursues virtue (*dharma*), wealth (*artha*), and pleasure (*kāma*) at their proper times [is truly wise].

He who restrains the impulse that arises from anger and joy finds the union of dharma, artha, and kāma both here and in the hereafter; O King, he is a vessel for prosperity and is not bewildered in times of calamity.
Learn from me the five kinds of strength that men always possess:
that which is called the strength of arms is said to be the lowest form of strength; the acquisition of a minister—may you be blessed—is said to be the second strength.
Those who desire victory say that the acquisition of wealth is the third power;
however, O King, that which is his innate strength— derived from his father and grandfather—
is known as the fourth power, called the strength of noble birth.

O Bhārata, that by which all these [powers] are subsumed is called the power of wisdom— the most excellent strength among all strengths. For a man who might otherwise be capable of doing great harm to another person [is restrained by it].
Having incurred enmity with someone, one should not feel secure thinking, "I am far away";
for who that is wise would place trust in women, kings, serpents, Vedic study, those who serve the enemy, sensual enjoyments, or life itself?
For a living being struck by the arrow of wisdom,
there are no physicians, nor are there medicines; there are no fire-offerings or mantras, nor are there auspicious rites.
Neither the Atharvan priests nor the well-perfected physicians [can prevail];
O Bhārata, serpents, fire, lions, and high-born sons of noble families must not be disregarded by a man, for they all possess exceeding splendor.
Fire is a great brilliance in the world that remains hidden within pieces of wood;
it does not consume that wood as long as it is not ignited by others.
Indeed, when that very fire is produced by friction from the wood, it blazes forth.
Then that forest and others are quickly consumed by its brilliance;
even so, those born in noble families, possessing a splendor like fire,
though patient and showing no outward sign, lie dormant like fire within wood.
"You, along with your sons, possess the nature of creepers, while the sons of Pāṇḍu are considered to be like *śāla* trees.
A creeper never grows without depending upon a great tree, O King, son of Ambikā; you and your sons are like that forest."
Know, O dear one, that the Pāṇḍavas are lions in the forest;
for a forest devoid of lions would perish,
and lions would perish without the forest.
Vidura said:
"For the vital breaths of a youth depart when an elder approaches;
one recovers them again by rising to meet him and by saluting him."
Having offered a seat to the virtuous guest who has arrived,
and having brought water and washed his feet,
one should inquire after his well-being and announce one's own state.
Then, having observed [the guest], the wise man should offer food to one who possesses water, honey-mixture, and a cow,
but not to one who does not know the mantras and accepts them in his own home.
The noble ones say that life is a misfortune for one who, out of greed, fear, or stinginess for wealth,
acts as a physician, a surgeon, or one who has broken his vows of celibacy.
A thief, a cruel man, a drunkard, a killer of an embryo, one who lives by the army, and a seller of the Vedas—
even if such a guest is very dear, he is not worthy of the water offering.
Salt, cooked food,
curd, milk, honey, oil, ghee,
sesame seeds, meat, roots, fruits, and vegetables are not to be sold.
Red garments, all kinds of perfumes, and molasses—
[these are for one] who is free from anger, to whom a clod of earth and gold are equal, who has abandoned sorrow, and for whom strife and conflict have ceased.
Ceased from blame and praise, and indifferent to the pleasant and unpleasant,
this mendicant moves about like one who is neutral, subsisting on wild rice,
roots, inguda nuts, and vegetables.
With his self well-restrained, unprovoked in his fire-rites, dwelling in the forest and vigilant toward guests,
this ascetic is a bearer of the burden and a doer of merit.
Having done harm to an intelligent person, one should not feel secure thinking, "I am far away";
for the arms of the intelligent are long, with which they strike back when they have been struck. One should not trust the untrustworthy, nor should one place excessive trust even in the trustworthy.
Danger arising from misplaced trust cuts down even the very roots.
One should be free from envy, protect one's wife, share with others, speak kindly,
be gentle and sweet-spoken toward women, yet one should not fall under their control.

Women are said to be worthy of worship, highly fortunate, meritorious, and the very light of the home; they are the prosperity of the household, and therefore they must be protected with special care.
One should entrust the inner apartments to one's father and the kitchen to one's mother.
He should give away cattle as if they were himself; he should personally attend to agriculture;
he should have his servants carry out the practice of trade, and he should serve the Brahmins through his sons.
Fire arose from water, the Kṣatriya from the Brāhmaṇa, and iron from stone.
The all-pervading energy of those [virtuous men] subsides within their own sources; though born in noble families and possessing a brilliance equal to fire, these ever-present men,
full of forbearance and free from outward display, lie hidden like fire within wood.
That king whose counsel neither outsiders nor insiders know possesses eyes everywhere and enjoys sovereignty for a long time.
He should not speak of what he intends to do, but should reveal only what has already been accomplished.
In matters concerning dharma, kama, and artha, a secret counsel must not be disclosed. Having ascended to a mountain ridge, or having gone to a secluded palace,
or being in a forest free from people, there one’s counsel should be deliberated.
O Bhārata, one who is not a friend does not deserve to know the supreme secret counsel;
nor does an unwise friend, nor even a wise man who lacks self-control. A protector of the earth should never appoint someone as his minister without first having examined him.

For he whose ministers know all his undertakings— the desire for wealth, the protection of counsel, and every other action performed— is a king, O best of kings, who excels in dharma, artha, and kāma.
For that king whose counsel is kept secret, success is certain beyond doubt.
But he who, out of delusion, performs actions that are censured,
may even lose his life when those very actions lead to ruin.
The performance of praiseworthy deeds brings happiness;
the non-performance of those very same deeds causes great remorse.
Just as one who has not studied the Vedas is not worthy to perform a *śrāddha*, so too is he unfit for the rites.
O King, one who has not heard of the sixfold policy does not deserve to hear counsel;
for the earth is under the control of that ruler who knows its stability, growth, and decline, who understands the sixfold policy, and whose character is beyond reproach.

This earth, the bearer of wealth, belongs to him whose anger and joy are never in vain, who personally supervises his duties, and whose treasury is known through his own self-reliance; yet that lord of the earth is satisfied with the name alone and the royal parasol.
He should distribute wealth among his dependents; he should not be one who seizes everything for himself.
A Brāhmaṇa knows another Brāhmaṇa, and a husband knows his wife;
likewise, a king knows his minister, and a monarch knows another monarch.
An enemy who has fallen into one's lap, having come within the range of execution, must not be released.
One should wait upon him with humility and kill him when the opportunity for force arises;
for while he is not being killed, he causes fear, yet once he is slain, no further danger arises from him.
For from striking [others] indeed, fear arises from that almost immediately; therefore,
one must always restrain one's anger toward the gods, toward kings, toward Brahmins, and toward the elderly, children, and the sick.
A wise person should avoid useless quarreling, which is practiced by fools;
for such a person gains renown in the world and is not joined with misfortune. He whose favor is fruitless and whose anger is likewise useless—[is truly wise].
Women do not desire such a husband, just as they do not desire a eunuch for a spouse;
the wise man, and no other, understands that intelligence does not lead to the acquisition of wealth, nor does dullness lead to poverty,
for he knows the cyclical nature of the world's course.

O Bhārata, a fool constantly disregards those who are advanced in knowledge, virtue, and age, as well as those advanced in wisdom, wealth, and noble lineage— those of ignoble conduct, lacking in intelligence, envious, and unrighteous.
Misfortunes quickly come upon one who is harsh in speech and prone to anger; however, non-deceitfulness, generosity, the non-violation of agreements,
and speech that is properly directed, cause all beings to turn toward one.
One who is reliable, skillful, grateful, wise,
and upright gains a retinue even if his treasury is completely exhausted;
for he possesses fortitude, tranquility, self-control, purity, compassion, and speech that is not harsh.
And not betraying friends— these seven are the fuel-sticks of prosperity.
O lord of men, one who does not share, who is evil-minded, ungrateful, and shameless— that lowest of men should be avoided in this world.

He who, being himself at fault, provokes blameless people within his own circle does not sleep happily at night, like one living in a house with a snake. O Bhārata, when these [inner people] are corrupted, there will be a failure of security and prosperity.
One should always act to please them, just as one would toward the gods.
Those interests that are centered on women, those that arise from the first impulse,
and those centered on the ignoble— all of these have fallen into doubt.
Where a woman, where a gambler, or where a child exercises authority,
those regions sink helplessly like stone rafts in a river.
O Bhārata, those who are attached to worldly interests rather than to spiritual distinctions [perish].
I consider those to be truly wise who are indeed free from attachment;
for that man whom gamblers praise, whom wandering minstrels praise, and whom harlots praise, does not truly live.
Having abandoned those Pāṇḍavas of immeasurable prowess, who are supreme archers,
you have placed this great sovereignty of the Bharatas upon Duryodhana; therefore,
you shall soon see him fallen from that position.
[He was like Bali, who had been utterly deluded by the intoxication of sovereignty over the three worlds.
Dhṛtarāṣṭra said:
"This man is not the master of his own prosperity or adversity."
Like a wooden doll strung on a thread,
this world is surely under the control of what has been ordained by the Creator;
therefore, speak, for I am held fast by my ears.
Vidura said:
"O Bhārata, even Bṛhaspati, if he speaks words at an inappropriate time, incurs contempt for his intelligence and meets with dishonor."

One becomes beloved through generosity, another through pleasant speech; yet another becomes beloved through the power of counsel—whosoever is beloved, he remains beloved. One who is hateful is neither virtuous, nor intelligent, nor wise.
"O Bhārata, auspicious deeds are for one who is dear, while evil deeds are for one who is hateful.
O King, as soon as he was born, I told you:
'Abandon this one son, Duryodhana.'"
By the renunciation of those hundred sons there was growth for him;
by not renouncing them, there was the destruction of his hundred sons.
That growth which brings about decay is not to be highly esteemed.
Even a loss is to be highly esteemed if that loss brings about growth;
O Great King, that is not a true loss which brings about growth. However, that should be considered a loss here which, having been gained, causes much to be destroyed.
"Some are prosperous in virtue, while others are prosperous in wealth;
O Dhṛtarāṣṭra, one should avoid those who are increased in wealth but devoid of virtues.
Dhṛtarāṣṭra said:
"You speak everything that is consistent with the future and approved by the wise;
yet I cannot bring myself to abandon my son, for where there is righteousness, there is victory.
Vidura said:

One who is endowed with the qualities of intrinsic nature and is possessed of discipline will never inflict even the slightest injury upon living beings; whereas those devoted to slandering others take pleasure in the arising of suffering for others.
Constantly striving when in mutual conflict,
those whose vision is flawed face great danger in living together;
there is great fault in receiving wealth and great fear in giving it away.
Those who are indeed of a divisive nature, full of desire, shameless, and deceitful; those who are renowned as wicked and censured in social association,
and those men who are possessed of other great faults— one should avoid them.
When friendship ceases, affection for the base perishes; and whatever fulfillment of fruit there was, as well as whatever happiness existed in that friendship,
[the base person] strives to defame it and exerts effort toward its destruction.
Even when slight harm is done out of delusion, one does not attain peace;
having observed with a discerning intellect such association with the base, the cruel, and the undisciplined, a wise man should avoid them from afar.
He who favors a kinsman who is poor, distressed,
or afflicted enjoys increase in sons and cattle, as well as imperishable fame. Kinsmen must be made to prosper by those who desire their own welfare.
O Indra among kings, this leads to the prosperity of the family; therefore, act rightly.
O King, by performing acts of hospitality toward your kinsmen, you will be united with well-being.
For kinsmen must be protected, O bull of the Bharatas, even if they are devoid of merit.
How much more so, O Lord of the People, those who possess virtue and long for your favor? Grant your grace to the wretched Pāṇḍavas;
O Sovereign, let some villages be given to them for their livelihood.
"O lord of men, in this way you shall attain fame in the world. For you, being aged, must provide protection for your sons, my dear;
know that I too speak for your benefit and am a well-wisher of yours."
"O dear one, one who seeks prosperity should not engage in conflict with kinsmen;
pleasures should be enjoyed together with kinsmen, O bull of the Bharatas. There should be shared meals, conversation, and mutual affection."
One should perform one's duties together with kinsmen; there should never be any conflict with them in any way.
Kinsmen rescue one in this world, and kinsmen also cause one to sink.
Those who are well-conducted rescue one here, while those who are ill-conducted cause one to sink.
"O Indra among kings, O giver of honor, conduct yourself with righteousness toward the Pāṇḍavas;
surrounded by them, you shall become invincible to your enemies. For a kinsman who falls into decline after having approached a prosperous kinsman—"
Whatever was done by one who is sinking [in distress], he experiences that evil as equal [to the deed]. Like a deer encountering a hunter with a poisoned hand, he incurs that transgression;
O best of men, even later you will experience remorse.
Upon hearing that they have been killed or even slain, reflect upon that deed by which one,
having ascended the funeral pyre, might suffer remorse;
as long as life is uncertain, one should not perform such an act from the very beginning.
No man except for Bhārgava can remove this [evil],
for the capacity to comprehend what remains resides only in those possessed of intelligence.
If this evil was previously committed against them by Duryodhana...
O lord of men, that must be restored by you, the elder of the lineage;
having established them in their proper positions, O best of men, you shall become free from stain and worthy of worship by the wise in this world.
He who, having reflected upon the well-spoken words of the wise according to their results,
applies himself to his duties, abides for a long time in glory.
For knowledge, even when employed by the most skillful, is indeed ineffective if it is not properly applied.

Even if it is perceived, that which is unknown [to its consequences] does not grow; and even if known, the wise man who does not undertake what results in the arising of evil increases [in merit]. But he who follows after previously committed evil without reflection [is lost].
That person of dull intellect is cast down into misfortune for offenses against others. A wise man should recognize these six gateways to the disclosure of counsel;
one who desires the continuity of his interests should guard them constantly.
Intoxication, sleep, ignorance, and the form arising from the self;
placing trust in wicked ministers and even in an unskilled messenger—
knowing these to be the gates, the king who always keeps them closed [is secure].
One who is devoted to the practice of the three goals of life (trivarga) stands above his enemies. Indeed, without understanding the sacred scriptures and without serving the elders,
it is not possible to know dharma and artha, even for those equal to Bṛhaspati himself.
What is lost in the ocean is lost; what is spoken to one who does not listen is lost;

what is heard by one who lacks self-control is lost; and what is heard without the sacred fire is lost. Having examined it with discernment and repeatedly perfected it with intelligence, the wise man [should act].
Having heard, seen, and understood, a wise person should employ counsel.
Modesty destroys lack of livelihood; prowess destroys misfortune;
constant forbearance destroys anger; and good conduct destroys ill fortune.
O King, one should examine a family by its retinue, its fields, its dwelling, its service, and its food and clothing.
There is no turning back once desire has presented itself.
How much more so for one who has cast off the body yet remains stained by desire?
One should protect a physician who serves the wise, who is righteous, pleasant to behold, possessed of friends, and of good speech; as well as a true friend.

Whether of low birth or of noble birth, he who does not transgress the bounds of propriety— he who regards righteousness, is gentle, and possesses a sense of shame— is better than a hundred men of noble birth; and one who desires the continuity of his lineage should always protect these qualities.
Between those two whose mind meets with the mind, or whose secret intent meets with secret intent,
and whose wisdom meets with wisdom— their friendship never decays. But one who is evil-minded, lacking in cultivated wisdom, is like a well hidden by grass.

A wise person should avoid [such people], for in their presence, friendliness perishes. A learned man should not practice friendliness toward those who are arrogant, foolish, violent, reckless, or likewise devoid of dharma.
One should desire a friend who is grateful, righteous, truthful, noble, firm in devotion, self-controlled, established in stability, and not prone to desertion.
The failure to restrain the senses is no different from death.
Furthermore, excessive giving away may even cause the deities to falter.
Gentleness toward all beings, freedom from malice, forbearance, and fortitude— the wise declare these, as well as not insulting one's friends, to be conducive to longevity.

He who, relying on a very firm resolve, seeks to recover a wealth lost through poor management— that is the vow of a man of noble character; he understands how to provide remedies for the future while remaining steadfast in his determination in the present.

A man who knows the remainder of his past actions is not deprived of his goals; whatever he habitually practices through deed, mind, or speech, that alone carries him away. Therefore, one should perform what is auspicious.
Auspiciousness, ritual contact, disciplined application, sacred learning, exertion, and uprightness—
these bring about prosperity, as does the constant sight of the virtuous. Perseverance is the root of fortune, and of both the destruction of suffering and the attainment of happiness.
One who is great and free from despondency attains ultimate happiness;
O dear one, there is nothing more glorious nor more beneficial than this— for a powerful man, namely, forbearance at all times and in all places.
One who is powerless should forgive everyone; one who possesses power should forgive for the sake of dharma. For him to whom gain and loss are equal, forgiveness is always beneficial.
Even while enjoying pleasure, he does not fall away from dharma and artha.

One may indulge in such pleasures at will, but one should not practice the conduct of a fool. Prosperity does not dwell among those afflicted by suffering, the heedless, the nihilists, the lazy, the undisciplined, or those who are devoid of enthusiasm.
Those of wicked intellect, deeming a man endowed with uprightness, modest through his integrity, and lacking in power, treat him with contempt. [They likewise disregard] one who is exceedingly noble,
one who gives too much, one who is too heroic, and one who observes excessive vows.
Prosperity does not approach one who is conceited about their own wisdom out of fear;
nor does she dwell among those with excessive virtues, nor among those who are utterly devoid of virtue. She does not long for virtues, nor does she take delight in the absence of them.
Fortune, like a mad cow or a blind woman, remains fixed only in some particular place.
The Vedas have the Agnihotra sacrifice as their fruit; sacred learning has character and conduct as its fruit;
wives have pleasure and sons as their fruit; and wealth has giving and enjoyment as its fruit.

He who performs funeral rites for the sake of the afterlife with wealth acquired through unrighteous means does not enjoy the fruit of that action after death, because of the illicit acquisition of that wealth.
[This applies even] in wildernesses, forest fortresses, or during painful calamities and upheavals.
When weapons are raised, there is no fear for those who possess the remainder [of their merit]. Know that exertion, self-restraint, skill, vigilance, fortitude, mindfulness,
and undertaking an enterprise after due deliberation— these are the roots of prosperity.
Austerity is the strength of ascetics; the Veda is the strength of those who know the Veda;
violence is the strength of the wicked; and forgiveness is the strength of the virtuous.
These eight do not break a vow: water, roots, fruits, milk, [clarified butter, fuel, herbs, and honey].
The sacrificial oblation, the desire for a Brahmin, the word of a teacher, and medicine—
these one should not apply to another if they are contrary to oneself.
Recognizing that these things are contrary to oneself, one should not practice them toward others.
In brief, this is the Dharma; anything other than this proceeds from desire.
One should conquer anger with non-anger, conquer the wicked with goodness, conquer the miser with generosity, and conquer falsehood with truth.
One should place no trust in a woman, a rogue, a lazy person, a coward, a violent man, one who fancies himself a gentleman, a thief, an ungrateful person, nor in an atheist.
For one who is habitually respectful and constantly serves the elderly, [wisdom and merit increase].
Four things increase: fame, longevity, glory, and strength. Do not set your mind upon those gains that come through excessive suffering, by transgressing dharma, or by bowing down before an enemy.
An ignorant man is to be pitied; a childless couple is to be pitied;
offspring who do not eat are to be pitied; and a kingdom without a king is to be pitied.
Travel is the old age of embodied beings; water is the old age of mountains.
Non-enjoyment is the decay of women; the sting of words is the decay of the mind. Lack of sacred tradition is the impurity of the Vedas; the failure to observe vows is the impurity of a Brahmin.
The Vāhīkas are the impurity of the earth; untruth is the impurity of a man.
Curiosity is the impurity of a virtuous woman; living abroad is the impurity of women.
Silver is the impurity of gold; tin is the impurity of silver. Lead is to be known as the impurity of tin, and dross is the impurity of lead.
One should not conquer sleep with sleep, nor should one conquer a woman with desire;
one should not conquer fire with fuel, nor should one conquer liquor with drink. He whose friends are won over by gifts and whose enemies are defeated in battle—[he is truly victorious].
One whose wife is won over by food and drink—that man’s life is fruitful. Thousands live, and hundreds likewise live;
O Dhṛtarāṣṭra, abandon your desire, for there is no way one cannot survive.
Whatever rice, barley, gold, cattle, and women exist upon this earth—all that is not enough for even one person; seeing this, one does not become deluded.
O King, I tell you again: act with impartiality toward your sons.
"O King, if you possess equanimity toward your own sons and the sons of Pāṇḍu," Vidura said:
"He who, when entreated by the virtuous, does not falter;"
He accomplishes his purpose without losing his power; fame quickly approaches that virtuous man who is sufficient [in his conduct].
For the virtuous, when pleased, lead to happiness.
He who renounces even a great object if it is joined with unrighteousness remains untainted by reproach;
having cast off sorrows, he sleeps in happiness.
Just as a snake casts off its worn-out skin,
so one should cast off falsehood, self-exaltation, backbiting directed at the king,
and persistent deception toward a teacher; these are equal to the murder of a Brahmin.
Envy is a one-way path to death; excessive speech is the slayer of prosperity. Lack of service, haste, and boastfulness—these three are the enemies of knowledge.
So too are laziness, intoxication and delusion, fickleness, and idle gossip.
Stiffness, arrogance, and likewise a lack of generosity—these seven are indeed considered to be the constant defects of those who seek knowledge.
For one who seeks pleasure, where is knowledge? And for one who seeks knowledge, there is no pleasure.
One who seeks pleasure should abandon knowledge, or one who seeks knowledge should abandon pleasure.
Fire is never satiated with wood, nor is the great ocean with rivers; Death is never satiated with all living beings, nor is a beautiful-eyed woman with men.
Hope destroys steadfastness, Death destroys prosperity; anger destroys fortune, and miserliness destroys fame.
Neglect of protection, O King, destroys cattle.
A single angry Brahmin destroys a kingdom.
A goat, a bronze vessel, a chariot, honey, a game of dice, a bird, and a Vedic scholar— these should always be kept at hand.
An aged kinsman, one who has fallen into distress, and a friend—
may these always be present in your home:
a goat, a bull, sandalwood, a lute, a mirror, honey, and clarified butter.
Manu has declared that these auspicious items— poison, an udumbara fruit, a conch shell, gold, a navel-jewel, and yellow pigment (rocanā)—
should be kept in the house for the purpose of honoring the gods,
the brahmins, and guests, O Bhārata.
And this I tell you as the highest of all things, my dear son: the meritorious state that is most distinguished.
Never, out of desire, nor out of fear, nor out of greed—
One should abandon even one's life for the sake of the Dharma;
the Dharma is eternal, while pleasure and pain are impermanent.
Life is eternal, but its constituent element (dhātu) is impermanent.
Abandoning the impermanent, establish yourself in the permanent; for contentment is the highest gain—be satisfied. Behold those of great strength and great majesty!
Having ruled the earth filled with wealth and grain,
and having abandoned their kingdoms and vast enjoyments,
the lords of men have gone under the power of Death.
O King, men lift up their deceased son— who has been nourished by sorrow— and carry him out from their own homes,
with disheveled hair, weeping piteously.
They cast [the body] into the midst of the funeral pyre like a piece of wood;
another enjoys the wealth of the deceased,
while birds and fire consume the elements of the body.
Enveloped by both merit and evil, he goes to the other world accompanied by these two alone;
his kinsmen, friends, and sons turn back and leave him behind.
Just as birds, my dear, avoid trees that have neither flowers nor fruit,
so too does the karma performed by oneself follow a person who has been cast into the fire.
Therefore, a person should diligently accumulate merit little by little.
Above this world and below that [world],
there exists a great darkness, a blinding gloom;
indeed, it is the great delusion of the senses.
Awaken, O King, lest deception should overcome you;
if you are able, listen to these words as they truly are and act accordingly upon hearing them all.
You shall attain supreme fame in the world of the living;
you shall have no fear, neither here nor in the hereafter.
O Bhārata, the self is a river with sacred bathing places.
Truth is its water, fortitude its banks, and self-control its waves;
one who has bathed therein, being of meritorious deeds, is purified;
for the self is holy, and the waters are eternally water indeed.
Having made a boat consisting of fortitude, cross over the rivers of birth— rivers that have the five senses for their waters and are infested with the crocodiles of desire and anger—
by relying on your own kinsman, who is mature in wisdom and mature in dharma.
Having honored and propitiated one who is advanced in learning as well as advanced in age regarding what ought and ought not to be done,
he who consults such a person shall never be deluded.
One should guard the genitals and the stomach with fortitude, the hands and feet with the eyes,
the eyes and ears with the mind, and the mind and speech with action.
One should always be one who uses water for purification and always wear the sacred thread.
One who constantly studies the Veda, avoids the food of the outcaste, speaks the truth, and performs service for the teacher—
such a Brāhmaṇa does not fall from the world of Brahman.
Having studied the Vedas, having maintained the sacred fires,
having performed sacrifices, and having protected the subjects,
his inner self was purified by weapons for the sake of cows and Brahmins.
A Kṣatriya slain in battle goes to heaven;
a Vaiśya, having studied and having at the proper time distributed wealth among Brāhmaṇas, Kṣatriyas, and those who have sought his protection.
Having inhaled the merit-filled smoke purified by the *tretā* fire,
one enjoys the pleasures of the gods in heaven after death—
whether one be a Brahmin, a Kṣatriya, a member of the Vaiśya caste, or a Śūdra.
Worshipping these in due order according to the rule,
one becomes free from distress and, with sins burnt away, leaves the body and enjoys the pleasures of heaven when they are satisfied.
This dharma of the four castes has been declared to you;
now listen as I state the reason for it:
the son of Pāṇḍu is falling away from the duty of the Kṣatriya.
"Therefore, O King, employ him in the duties of royalty.
Dhṛtarāṣṭra said:
"It is exactly as you always instruct me."
"O gentle one, my mind also inclines exactly as you have told me;
yet, although I have always formed this resolve regarding the Pāṇḍavas,
upon encountering Duryodhana, it turns back again."
"No mortal is able to transcend destiny;
I consider destiny alone to be what is accomplished, while human effort is useless.
Dhṛtarāṣṭra said:
"O Vidura, if there is anything that has not yet been spoken by you, tell it to me as I am eager to hear; for you speak with wonderful eloquence. Vidura said:
O Dhṛtarāṣṭra, that ancient and eternal youth,
Sanatsujāta, declared, "O Bhārata, death does not exist.
He [will explain] to you all things— both secret and manifest— that reside within the heart.
"O Great King, he who is the best among all the wise shall proclaim it.
Dhṛtarāṣṭra said:
"What is there that you do not know, which the Eternal One might further tell me?"
"O Vidura, you yourself speak if there remains any wisdom within you.
Vidura said:
"I was born from a Śūdra womb; I do not venture to say anything other than this."
I know that eternal wisdom of the Kumāra;
for one who has entered the womb of Brahman is not to be censured by the gods even if he speaks what is most secret. Therefore, I say this to you.
Dhṛtarāṣṭra said:
"Tell me, Vidura, about that ancient and eternal one;
how may there be a meeting with him here in this very body?"
Vaiśampāyana said:
Vidura thought of that seer of rigid vows,
and knowing that he was being thought of, O Bhārata, he appeared before him.
And he received him with rites prescribed by rule;
then, once he was comfortably seated and rested, Vidura said to him:
"O Blessed One, there is a certain doubt in Dhṛtarāṣṭra’s mind."
"You ought to tell him that which cannot be told by me,
so that upon hearing it, this lord of men may transcend both pleasure and pain;
and just as gain and loss, the beloved and the hated do not affect him, so too shall old age and death."
They would endure fear and indignation, hunger and thirst, the intoxication arising from passion,
restlessness and lethargy, as well as desire and anger, decline and prosperity.
Vaiśampāyana said:
Then the wise King Dhṛtarāṣṭra,
having honored those words spoken by Vidura,
[addressed] the high-souled Sanatsujāta in private.
Desiring to attain supreme wisdom,
Dhṛtarāṣṭra asked:
"O Sanatsujāta, since I hear this..."
"The gods and asuras indeed practiced celibacy on the instruction that 'death does not exist';
for the sake of immortality, which of these two is now the truth?"
Sanatsujāta said:
"Some say there is immortality through action, while others say that death does not exist.
Listen to me as I speak, O King, so that you may have no doubt regarding this."
Both truths proceed from the Kṣatriya and others;
that which is considered delusion by the wise is death.
Indeed, I declare that negligence is death.
I declare that constant vigilance is immortality; indeed,
through negligence the Asuras were defeated, while through vigilance they become one with Brahman.
Death does not devour living beings like a tiger;
indeed, its form is not perceived at all.
Some, however, say that Yama is death, while others say it is something different from him.
The immortal self is established in celibacy;
as a god, he rules over the kingdom in the world of the fathers—
auspicious to the auspicious, inauspicious to the inauspicious.
From the mouth of men issues this death— anger, negligence, and the form of delusion—
wandering along wrong paths by means of the notion of "I."
No one attains union with the Self;
deluded and remaining under its sway,
those who have departed from here fall back into that [state].
Then the gods follow after him;
from this, death receives its name "mortality.
At the dawning of karma, there is attachment to the fruits of karma.
There they follow along and do not cross over death; because of their failure to understand the application of the true goal on all sides,
the embodied being proceeds by means of attachment to enjoyments.
That indeed is the great delusion of the senses;
for the pursuit of false objects is constant,
and the inner self is struck down by the pursuit of false objects.
Remembering them, he attends to sense objects on all sides; yet,
though he contemplates those things that tend to arise,
he destroys them by means of disregard, remaining unawakened [by their allure].

He indeed becomes like Death and devours as Death; thus knowing this, he who destroys his desires does not perish following after those desires, for a man who pursues desires perishes along with them.
Having cast aside desires, a person shakes off whatever passion (*rajas*) there may be.
This lack of light, the darkness (*tamas*) of living beings, is seen as hell;
they run as if being seized, going toward the abyss with their faces upturned.
Covetousness indeed strikes him first,
and then desire and anger seize him from behind;
these lead the foolish to death.
But the steadfast cross over death through their fortitude;
for a man of unconfused conduct in this world, what indeed can death do? It is like a tiger to one who is on straw.
O Kṣatriya, not conceiving anything else in his mind,
his inner self— though like a tiger upon a grass mat— is not learning [the truth] due to anger, greed, and delusion.
That which is this very death within your body—
having thus understood death as it arises,
and abiding in knowledge, one does not fear death here in this world.
He perishes within his own domain,
just as a mortal dies upon reaching the domain of Death.
Dhṛtarāṣṭra said:
Those very worlds of the virtuous which they say belong to the twice-born through sacrifice— most meritorious and eternal—
the Vedas proclaim here for the sake of others.
Sanatsujāta said:
"Knowing this, how indeed does one not go [to rebirth] through action? For it is by not knowing this that one goes there."
Likewise, the Vedas speak of the nature of reality;
that supreme Self does not come here again.
Dhṛtarāṣṭra said:
He proceeds along the path, having struck down other paths;
who appoints that unborn, ancient one?
If he [appoints] all this in due succession...
"What is his duty, or what is his happiness?
O learned one, tell me all that correctly," Sanatsujāta replied.
In this case, there is a great fault in the doctrine of differentiation;
for by means of beginningless conjunction, things become eternal,
and thus no deficiency whatsoever ever departs from them.
Through the yoga of non-origination, these states arise for the person;
or rather, that Blessed One is eternal,
who by means of the yoga of transformation creates the universe.
And thus he considered that to be its power; and when there is a connection with the meaning, the Vedas come into being. Dhṛtarāṣṭra said:
Those here who do not practice the Dharma in this world, and likewise those who do practice the Dharma— by such [neglect],
the Dharma is struck down by evil.
"Or does dharma indeed destroy evil?
Sanatsujāta said:
"In that case, both results are experienced."
Whether established in that [state] or otherwise, the wise one, by means of knowledge, eternally destroys both dharma and its opposite; this is established.
In this way or that, the embodied being encounters merit;
in this way or that, he encounters established evil.
Having gone [to their respective realms], both are experienced through karma as unstable.
Through his actions, he [the wise man] drives away unrighteousness with righteousness here in this world, whether it be good or evil; know that for him,
righteousness is the more powerful.
Dhṛtarāṣṭra said:
"Those worlds which they call the eternal realms of the twice-born who perform meritorious deeds according to their own dharma;"
"Describing their various courses and other matters besides these,
Sanatsujāta said: 'O learned one, this is not so, nor is it a deed that has been performed.'"
Those who have no rivalry regarding strength, as among the strong themselves,
those Brāhmaṇas, having departed from here, shine forth in the heavenly world.
For those who have no rivalry regarding dharma, that is the means for attaining knowledge of it.
Those brahmins, liberated from this world, go to heaven, to the celestial realm of Triviṣṭapa.
People learned in the Vedas declare that his conduct is perfectly right. One should not consider him as being excessively an outsider or an insider.

Wherever a Brahmin might think that food and drink are as abundant as grass and reeds in the rainy season, he should live there without distress. But where one who gives does not speak kindly and instead bestows inauspiciousness and fear, [he should avoid it].

He who does not cause distress to himself when another speaks ill of him acts as one who excels; he is superior, and no other person is so. Indeed, only a Brahmin is worthy of striking down his own inner self.
One should not enjoy the property of a Brahmin; that food is approved by the virtuous.
Yogins know that even items such as kusha grass, bark garments, or clothing constitute the property of a Brahmin.
Just as a dog constantly eats its own vomit to its own misfortune, [so it is for one who consumes the property of a Brahmin].
Thus they eat what has been vomited up, living off the very fruit of their own prowess.
A Brahmin should think, "I must always live in concealment," even while dwelling in the midst of his kinsmen; he should not let anything of his identity be known.
For what Brāhmaṇa would ever wish to destroy such an inner self—
one that is signless, immovable, pure, and free from all dualities?
Therefore, O Kṣatriya, the Brahman dwells within and perceives it.
What sin has not been committed by that thief who steals his own self, who represents himself as one thing when he is actually another?
By not grasping at anything, one becomes tireless, esteemed, and free from affliction.
Though instructed, he would not be like one who is truly instructed; such a Brahmin is a seer who knows the Brahman.
Those twice-born ones who are poor in worldly wealth but rich in the Vedas—know them to be invincible and unshakable, the very embodiment of the Brahman.
Whoever here may know all the gods who perform the *sviṣṭakṛt* offering,
he is not equal to that Brahmin toward whom one exerts oneself personally. But he whom they honor even though he does not exert himself is truly honored.
One who is being honored should not think highly of himself, nor should he be distressed by lack of honor;
for the world always functions according to its own nature, like the closing and opening of an eye.
When being honored, one should think: "In this world, the wise are those who show respect."
"Those fools who know not the Dharma, though they are experts in worldly treatises,
will not honor what is worthy of honor"— thus one who has been dishonored should reflect.
Indeed, honor and silence do not always go together.
For this world belongs to pride, and that [world beyond] belongs to pride; the wise know this.
Prosperity is the dwelling place of happiness in this world, yet it is also an obstacle.
For the prosperity pertaining to the Brahma-world is extremely difficult to attain for one who is devoid of wisdom, O Kṣatriya.
For the wise declare that she has many kinds of doors, difficult to guard:
truth, uprightness, modesty, self-control, purity, and knowledge.
The six means for warding off delusion.
Dhṛtarāṣṭra said:
"To whom does this silence belong? What indeed is silence?"
"O learned one, explain here the state of silence;
does the wise man attain silence through silence?
Sanatsujāta replied:
O Sage, how do they practice silence here? Since the Vedas, together with the mind, do not penetrate this [Reality], therefore it is called silence (*mauna*).
"O King Dhṛtarāṣṭra, just as the word of the Veda arose from that [source], so too does this [universe] shine forth through its identity with that. Dhṛtarāṣṭra said:
That twice-born man who studies the Ṛgveda, the Yajurveda, and the Sāmaveda is not tainted by sin even while committing evil deeds; he remains unstained. Sanatsujāta said:
Neither the Sāmans, nor the Ṛks, nor even the Yajus protect this wise man from evil action; I do not speak falsely to you: the Vedic meters do not deliver one from wrongdoing.
Like birds with fledged wings leaving their nest, the Vedas abandon that master of illusion who persists in illusion at the time of his end.
Dhṛtarāṣṭra said:
"O wise one, if the Vedas are not able to protect the knower of the Vedas,
then why is this eternal discourse of the Brāhmaṇas [still maintained]?"
Sanatsujāta said:
O one of great majesty, this world shines forth through the specific forms of that very [Self], such as names and so forth.
Having correctly pointed this out, the Vedas proclaim it;
they cite that universal diversity as being for that purpose,
namely austerity and sacrifice.
Through those two, the wise man attains merit;
having subsequently destroyed evil by means of that merit,
he is born with a self illuminated by knowledge.
Through knowledge, the wise man attains the Self;
otherwise, one who desires the fruits of the various classes of action takes upon himself everything performed in this world.
He who practices austerity in the forest, a sage subsisting on roots and fruits, enjoys the fruit there and returns again to the path;
for Brahmins, austerity is highly exalted, whereas for others, it is only to that extent.
This austerity alone becomes fully perfected and exceedingly prosperous;
the fruit of austerity practiced in this world is seen elsewhere. These worlds belong to the Brahmins who are self-restrained in their perfected austerity.
Dhṛtarāṣṭra said:
"O Sanatsujāta, tell us how asceticism, though already abundant, becomes exclusively perfected, so that we may understand it."
Sanatsujāta said:
This austerity alone is declared to be stainless;
when this is perfected, the austerity becomes truly successful, and not otherwise.
"O Kṣatriya, all this that you ask me has its root in asceticism.
Dhṛtarāṣṭra said:
"Through asceticism, those who know the Vedas attain the supreme immortality."

"Tell me of the stain upon austerity, O Sanatsujāta, for I have heard that there is a stainless austerity; by means of which I may know this secret, eternal [truth]. Whoever studies this single verse, it is equal to the merit of both [the study and the practice]."
Sanatsujāta said:
O King, he who possesses the twelve defects beginning with anger, as well as the six beginning with cruelty in this world—
The twelve qualities beginning with *dharma*,
which are known in the scriptures as the virtues of the twice-born,
are: anger, desire, greed, delusion, and the desire for knowledge.
Pity, envy, pride, grief, longing,
jealousy, and contempt— these twelve defects of human beings should always be avoided by a man.
O Indra among kings, each one of these attends upon individual men,
seeking an opening among them like a hunter among deer—
he who is boastful, covetous, and yet self-important.
One who harbors anger, one who is fickle, and one who fails to protect—
these six persons have arrived with evil natures; they do not act rightly even in great distress.
One who increases his own pleasure through the enjoyment of others,
one who regrets what he has given, one who is miserly and weak, one who praises his own group, and one who hates women;
These are seven other qualities of cruel conduct: righteousness, truthfulness, self-control, austerity,
lack of envy, modesty, forbearance, and freedom from malice.
Sacrifice, charity, fortitude, and sacred learning—
these twelve are the great vows of a Brāhmaṇa. He who should depart from these twelve [is fallen].
He may rule even this entire earth with three, two, or one [of these powers],
yet he should be known as one who possesses nothing of his own because he is distinguished [by detachment].
Self-control, renunciation, and vigilance—in these, immortality is established.
Those wise Brahmins who possess discernment declare that these have truth as their foremost quality.
The abandonment of faults constitutes vigilance, and that is considered to be eightfold.
Self-control is free from eighteen faults: opposition, the doing and not doing [of what is right],
falsehood, malice, desire for pleasure and wealth,
longing, anger, grief, thirst, greed, and indeed slander.
Envy, the desire to know [others' secrets], remorse, and attachment; epilepsy, excessive speech, and self-aggrandizement;
hatred for the world, conceit, quarreling, and the harming of living beings.
Censure, excessive speech, distress, intolerance, lack of steadfastness, failure to achieve one's aim, evil deeds, and violence— these are proclaimed [as the faults].
He who is free from these defects is called "self-controlled" (dama) by the virtuous.

Intoxication consists of eighteen faults, while renunciation possesses six virtues; these opposites are traditionally known as the faults of intoxication that have been described. However, renunciation is of six kinds, and among them, the third is the most difficult to perform.
By that [restraint], they indeed cross over suffering; when that is abandoned, victory is achieved.
One should avoid those faults of self-restraint that have been described. However, the sixfold renunciation is superior: having encountered what is pleasant, one does not rejoice.
When something unpleasant occurs, he never experiences distress;
nor does he ever speak words that would cause separation from his beloved wife and sons.
Whatever word he utters should be one that ought to be given to a petitioner who approaches him in need.
The second consists of *iṣṭāpūrta* (sacrificial rites and charitable works), which is constant through the yoga of detachment;
and the renunciation of desire, O King of Kings, is recorded as the third. By means of these, one should be vigilant; that [state] is also great and possesses eight qualities.

Truth, meditation, concentration, inquiry, and indeed detachment; non-stealing, celibacy, and likewise non-possessiveness—thus have the faults of intoxication been described; one should completely avoid those faults.
The abandonment of faults constitutes heedfulness, and that is considered to have eight qualities. They say that these qualities have truth as their foremost, for immortality is established in truth.
O Indra among kings, be one whose self is truth; for all worlds are established in truth.
One should perform the vow of austerity here even with a fault that has been committed;
this conduct established by Dhātṛ is indeed the truth and the vow of the virtuous. Even if one speaks what should not be spoken, that is remembered as the third quality.
He who, having renounced material things, does not employ them out of desire,
and for whom those things are neither employed nor used out of desire,
is not dependent on actions, just like a man of dull intellect who is a disciple.

Even one who possesses all virtues and is wealthy—if they understand this sixfold renunciation, nothing else remains [to be attained]. Heedfulness consists of eight faults; one should completely avoid those faults.
O Bhārata, one who is liberated from these five senses, from the mind itself,
and from the past and the future, shall indeed be happy. Being freed from these defects and endowed with these qualities, [he attains liberation].
Even when fully perfected, this austerity alone becomes truly prosperous.
O Indra among kings, regarding that which you ask me, what more do you wish to hear?
This is pure, it removes sin, and it wards off birth, death, and old age.
Dhṛtarāṣṭra said:
"People are most frequently described by means of the Vedas with the Purāṇas as the fifth;
likewise, there are others who possess four Vedas, and still others who possess three."
"Some have two Vedas, some have one Veda, and others likewise have no Ṛg-verses;
among them, which one would that be whom I might know as a Brāhmaṇa?
Sanatsujāta said:
"O King of kings, because one Veda was not understood, those Vedas became many; yet of that single Truth, O Indra among kings, some remain established in Truth.
Thus, without destroying the Veda, they exercise great wisdom."
Giving, study, and sacrifice—these proceed from greed for those falling away from truth; their resolve becomes futile. Therefore, sacrifice is extended only through the firm establishment of truth.
For one person [the goal] is accomplished by mind, for another by speech, and for yet another by action;
such a person, perfected through resolve, presides over his own intentions. Indeed, he should observe the vow of initiation with freedom from servility.
This name is derived from its root; it is indeed the supreme truth for the virtuous.
Knowledge is indeed direct perception, whereas austerity (tapas) arises as indirect perception.
One should know that a Brāhmaṇa who recites much is merely a "reciter of many [texts]."
Therefore, O Kṣatriya, do not think that one becomes a Brāhmaṇa merely by talk;
he who does not deviate from the truth—he alone should be known by you as a Brāhmaṇa.
O best among bipeds, the Vedic meters are indeed called *chandāṃsi*.
By means of their own free will, they exist there;
as those who know the meters, having studied them,
those noble ones have indeed gone beyond what is to be known through the Veda.
There is no one who is a knower of the Vedas; by means of the object of knowledge, they do not know the Veda, nor do they know the object of knowledge.
He who knows the Veda, he indeed knows the object of knowledge.
He who knows that which is to be known does not know the Truth;
he who knows the Vedas knows that which is to be known. Those who are learned in the Vedas do not know him, nor do the Vedas.
Nevertheless, those Brahmins who know the Veda perceive the Veda;
for the Vedas are indeed a portion of the share of the Abode.
For just as they speak of the branch of a tree,
and likewise of consciousness,
so too [they speak] regarding that reality which is the supreme self.
"O Kṣatriya, those known as the *chandāṃsi* (Vedic meters) were sung by Atharvan at the beginning of this creation of the ṛṣis;
those who have studied them are knowers of the meters."
O King, no one knows the knower of the knowable, nor the knowable itself; there is no one who is the knower of the Vedas,
nor indeed anyone who understands the Vedas.
He who knows the Vedas does not know that which is to be known;
but he who stands firm in truth, he knows that which is to be known. I recognize such a person as a true Brahmin, a wise teacher.
He who understands in this way indeed knows that which is supreme; for that is the supreme, and the Brahmin truly knows that supreme Brahman,
he who understands what has been declared by me as supreme.
He indeed comes to know the Supreme through gradual stages;
no search for him shall ever lead among adversaries. Without seeking Him in this Veda, one then beholds that Lord.
He who, having severed his doubt, declares all uncertainties—
toward him one should go for inquiry, neither to the east nor to the south, nor to the west, nor indeed to the intermediate directions in any way whatsoever.
One should remain silent and wait upon [the Self], nor should one stir even with the mind; for Brahman, which is indeed established within his inner self, will turn toward him.
For it is through silence that one becomes a sage, not by dwelling in the forest.
He who knows that syllable is called the best of sages.
Because he analyzes all meanings, he is called a grammarian (*vaiyākaraṇa*). He is likewise so called because he analyzes that [syllable] from its very root.
A man who perceives the worlds directly becomes an all-seeing one.
O Kṣatriya, a Brāhmaṇa established in truth indeed beholds Brahman;
likewise, O Kṣatriya, one established in knowledge and the other virtues also beholds Brahman.
"O learned one, I tell you this according to the sequence of the Vedas.
Dhṛtarāṣṭra said:
"O Sanatsujāta, as for this [teaching] which is for the sake of the Supreme..."
"You utter the divine speech, which is multiform and supreme— a discourse exceedingly difficult to obtain amidst worldly desires. Therefore,
O Kumāra, speak these words to me."
Sanatsujāta said:
"This Brahman which you ask me about and for which you are so exceedingly delighted cannot be attained by one who is in a hurry."

When the intellect has dissolved into the mind, that wisdom which is to be deeply contemplated is indeed attainable through the practice of celibacy (brahmacarya). I shall now declare that ancient, unmanifested wisdom.
And through their wisdom and their practice of celibacy, they attained perfection.
Dhṛtarāṣṭra said:
"That which is the eternal science of the Unmanifest;"
You speak of the perfection attained through celibacy;
indeed, you proclaim that primordial knowledge which is the embodiment of truth and which is acquired by the virtuous through celibacy.
"Having acquired that knowledge which is ever-present among teachers and elders, they abandon the world of mortals. Dhṛtarāṣṭra said:

"O Knower, tell me this: how can that celibacy (*brahmacarya*) exist by which knowledge can be directly realized? O Noble One, you dwell here without undertaking any [specific] activities at this time."
"How may one attain Brahmanhood and immortality? Sanatsujāta replied:
"Those who here in this world conquer their desires..."
Enduring the state of Brahman,
those who abide in pure being draw out their own selves from their bodies here, as one extracts a blade of grass from the *muñja* reed.
If all the desires that reside in the heart are completely liberated, then one is dead to death; therein one attains Brahman. O Bhārata, these two—the father and the mother—create this body.
That birth which is from the Teacher and the Instructor is true; it is free from old age and death.
For that birth which comes from the Teacher is indeed true and likewise immortal.
Therefore, a wise person should strive to attain that very [birth].
Those who, having entered here into the womb of the teacher and become embryos, practice celibacy,
they themselves become authors of the scriptures in this very world.
Having abandoned the body, they go to the supreme yoga—
that which covers the ears with truth,
making them attentive and bestowing immortality.
One should regard him as both father and mother;
knowing what he has done for him, one should never bear him malice.
A disciple should always hold his teacher in high esteem.
Desiring sacred study, pure and vigilant,
one should not practice pride nor harbor anger;
this is the first quarter of the life of a student of sacred knowledge (*brahmacarya*).

The pure person who acquires knowledge precisely through the sequence of a disciple’s conduct is said to have fulfilled the first quarter of this vow of celibacy (*brahmacarya*). One should do what is pleasing to the teacher, even at the cost of one's life or wealth.
The second quarter is said to consist of [proper conduct] through action, mind, and speech.
One should behave toward the teacher’s wife exactly as one behaves toward the teacher;
acting according to what is instructed and doing what is pleasing is called the third quarter.
Knowing that it was performed by the teacher, he thinks, "I have been cultivated";
being joyful toward that teacher, the third quarter is spoken of.
Recognizing what was done for himself by the teacher...
Having understood the goal, one thinks, "I have cultivated it"; the joyful mind directed toward that [thought] is indeed the third foot of the holy life (*brahmacarya*).
Having performed a service for his teacher here,
a wise man should not engage in gossip, nor should he think or say, "I am not doing this."

That indeed is the fourth quarter of the life of a religious student (brahmacarya). If, while he is living in this manner, something should befall him out of pride, thinking, "I have already done what was required for my teacher," [he fails].
"I think that the wise man does not do this;
indeed, that is the fourth foot of the holy life (brahmacarya). In due time, one obtains that foot as well as its meaning."
Then, one quarter [of the result] is obtained through association with a teacher,
another quarter through the application of energy,
another quarter through the study of the scriptures, and from that, one proceeds to the final quarter.
They say that for whom knowledge and the other [qualities]— the twelve forms,
as well as the other limbs and likewise strength—
bear fruit through union with the Teacher.
And by means of application to the goal of Brahman, one practices the holy life (*brahmacarya*).
Whatever wealth might accrue to one living in this manner,
that he should bestow upon his teacher.
Thus one attains the many-virtuous conduct of the virtuous;
such indeed is the conduct toward the teacher’s son.
Living in this manner, one prospers in every way here in this world.
He obtains many sons and established renown; the intermediate quarters and the cardinal directions rain for him,
and people dwell in this state of brahmacarya.
By this very practice of celibacy, the gods attained their godhood;
and the highly fortunate sages, being wise, reached the world of Brahmā.
By this same [practice], the form of the Gandharvas and the Apsarases came into being.

By this very practice of celibacy (*brahmacarya*), the sun is born for the sake of the day; just as those who desire various flavors [attain them] through the conjunction with the object of their longing, so too,
having understood this, these [beings] have attained such a state.
O King, even one who might cause [the body] to waste away or tear it apart,
while heating his entire body with austerity—
by this means, that wise man transcends childhood.
Thus, at the time of death, they obstruct death itself;
O Kṣatriya, those people win worlds that are finite, fashioned by their own actions.
The wise man attains all through that very Brahman;
no other path for reaching it exists.
Dhṛtarāṣṭra said:
It shines as if white, as if red, and likewise black, or like collyrium, or like a tawny-brown;
the Brahmin who is wise in this matter beholds it.
"What is the nature of that immortal, imperishable state?
Sanatsujāta replied:
"It does not appear as white, nor as red."
Moreover, that which is black, made of iron, and the color of the sun does not stand upon the earth, nor in the intermediate space;
it does not hold water within the ocean.
His form is not seen in the stars, nor is it dependent on lightning; it is not seen in the clouds,
nor in the wind, nor among the deities.
That is not seen in the moon, nor in the sun;
it is not in the Ṛg-verses, nor in the Yajus-formulas, nor even in the Atharvans; and it is not seen at all in the pure Sāman-chants.
O King, that which is seen neither in the *rathaṃtara*, nor in the *bārhata*,
nor indeed in the *mahāvrata* is certainly beyond the reach of darkness.
Even Antaka (Death) approaches at the time of destruction;
he assumes a form subtler than the edge of a razor,
yet his form is also greater than the mountains.
That is the foundation, that is the immortal, those are the worlds, that is Brahman, that is glory.
From that all beings were born, and into that they go at the time of dissolution.
That is the painless, great, and exalted glory.
The seers speak of the modifications of speech;
upon this all this world is established;
those who know that become immortal.
Sanatsujāta said:
Grief, anger, greed, desire, pride, and the longing for death;
envy, delusion, the desire to know [the faults of others], pity, malice, and contempt.
These twelve are great defects that destroy human life; each one of them, O Indra among kings, dwells within men. Possessed by these, a person of deluded mind commits evil.
Envious, fierce, harsh, and excessively talkative; harboring anger in his mind and boastful—
he who possesses these six qualities is indeed a person of cruel nature.
Even after obtaining wealth, they do not honor [others]; their agreement for shared enjoyment is treacherous; they are excessively proud, boastful after giving, and both miserly and weak.

One who praises excessively, one who hates women, and those who are always cruel— these seven are said to be of sinful character; yet righteousness, truth, austerity, and self-restraint [are the virtues].
Freedom from envy, modesty, forbearance, lack of malice, generosity, learning, steadfastness, and patience— these twelve are the great vows of a Brāhmaṇa.
He who does not fall away from these twelve [qualities],
even if requested by all this earth with three, two, or one [of its regions], shall rule it.
And it should be understood that he possesses nothing as his own;
self-control, renunciation, and vigilance—in these, immortality is established.
These belong to the wise Brahmins who have Brahman as their chief.
Whether true or false, slander is not praised for a Brahmin.
Those men who act in this way will surely find their place in hell.
