That intoxication which was previously described as having eighteen faults shall be his.
Hatred of the world, hostility, envy, false speech, lust, anger, dependence on others, slander, calumny,
loss of wealth, the desire to know [others' secrets], stinginess, and the harming of living beings.

Envy, delusion, excessive speech, loss of right perception, and malice— therefore, a wise person should never be intoxicated by these, for they are always censured. Indeed, six qualities are to be known as belonging to friendship.
They rejoice at what is pleasing and suffer at what is displeasing;
he who grants for a very long time to one who entreats— even that which should not be asked for— surely makes it a gift that ought to be given.

One who has requested [renunciation] and possesses a pure disposition deserves to renounce beloved sons, wealth, and his own wives; having abandoned all material things, he should not dwell here out of desire.
He enjoys his action, yet he does not obstruct his own aspirations; thus, possessing both substance and virtue, the renouncer is characterized by *sattva*.
Such a person withdraws the five elements from the five [objects].
Even when this is fully perfected, such austerity remains merely superior for those who fall away from *sattva*, being concentrated through mere volition;
for it is from the restraint of truth alone that sacrifices truly flourish.

For one person, [the goal] is achieved through the mind; for another, through speech; and for another, through action. A man who has accomplished his purpose through resolve is presided over by one who is free from resolve.
This is especially true of the Brahmin; hear from me something else as well.
One should teach this great [work], which brings glory;
the seers call it a transformation of speech. In this yoga, all this is established.
Those who know that become immortal;
O King, it is not by well-performed action alone that one attains this—
whether one speaks the truth, offers oblations, or performs sacrifices.
O King, by this a fool does not attain immortality, nor does he find peace at the time of his end; therefore,
one should sit alone in silence and not even stir with the mind.
Likewise, one should avoid both joy and anger arising from praise and blame.
O Kṣatriya, remaining right here, one enters and beholds Brahman. O learned one, I declare this to you according to the sequence of the Vedas.
All this, established throughout the day, shines forth;
the knower of the Self perceives it through the yoga of knowledge. In that [Self], this entire world is established.
Those who know this become immortal.
Sanatsujāta said:
That which is the pure, great light, shining with great glory—
The gods indeed worship that from which the *arka* shines forth;
the yogis behold him, the eternal Blessed One. From the radiant (*śukra*) Brahman proceeds [all things], and by the radiant Brahman it increases.
That pure light, unscorched in the midst of all luminaries, shines as the scorcher [of all];
yogis behold that Blessed One, the eternal. Then there are the waters, and from the waters, the midst of the ocean;
Both gods have taken refuge in the intermediate space; clothed in converging and diverging rays,
he supports both the earth and the sky.
Yogins behold that eternal Blessed One. In the beginning, he created the waters alone; then he cast his seed into them. That became a golden egg, radiant like the thousand-rayed sun.
In that [lotus] was born Brahmā himself, the grandfather of all the worlds;
yogins behold him as the eternal Blessed One. And both gods [perceived] the earth and the sky.
He sustains the quarters and the bright world;
from him the quarters and the rivers flow,
and from him the great oceans were fashioned.
Yogins behold that eternal Blessed One standing upon the wheel of the chariot, whose function is fixed and imperishable;
horses bear that divine and undecaying banner in the sky.
Yogis behold that eternal Blessed One;
his form does not abide within the realm of similarity,
and no one beholds him with the physical eye.
By means of wisdom, as well as by the mind and the heart—
those who know thus become immortal.
He who has supreme devotion for the Divine, and for the Guru as he has for the Divine...
For those purposes have been explained to you, and they shine forth for that Great-Souled One;
yogis behold that Blessed One, the Eternal.
[They see] the river of twelve groups, protected by the gods.
Desiring honey, they then move toward that which is terrible;
the yogins behold him, the Blessed One, the eternal.
Having gathered the honey, he drinks it for half a month like a bee.
Īśāna ordained that he should become the sacrificial oblation among all beings;
yogins behold him, the blessed and eternal one,
as wingless creatures alight upon the golden-leaved *aśvattha* tree.
Having become birds there, they fly away in every direction;
the yogins behold that eternal Blessed One. From the Full they draw forth full things; from the Full they have made full things.
They take from the full to the full; yet the Full alone remains.
Yogins behold that Blessed One, the Eternal. From Him indeed the wind has arisen, and into Him it always returns.
Therefore, both Agni and Soma are extended within that Prāṇa,
and within that [Prāṇa] into which they both go to their dissolution;
from that indeed is Vāyu extended.
Yogins behold that eternal Blessed One,
from whom indeed the wind has come and from whom the vital breath (prāṇa) has arisen; He is the foundation, He is the immortal, He is the worlds, He is Brahman, and He is glory.
From him all beings were born, and into him they go at the time of dissolution;
yogins behold him as the eternal Blessed One.
One should know that everything indeed proceeds from him; we are unable to describe each of those things.
Yogis behold that eternal Blessed One.
Prāṇa swallows Apāna; the Moon swallows Prāṇa;
the Sun swallows the Moon; and the Supreme swallows the Sun.

Yogins behold that eternal Blessed One. Just as a swan rising from the water does not lift one foot, if one were never to leave that officiating priest (ṛtvij), there would be neither death nor immortality.
Yogis behold that eternal Blessed One. The Person, the inner self, the size of a thumb, constantly departs by means of the yoga of the subtle body (*liṅga*).
Fools do not perceive that Lord, the worshipful, the primordial, who is the source of all forms and shines with splendor;
but the yogis behold him, the eternal Blessed One.
The fool who does not realize the Self abiding within himself revolves in the well of saṃsāra;
having abandoned the nature of the Self, he devours sense objects.
That person is indeed manifestly a donkey;
yogis behold him as the eternal Blessed One.
Thus that great-souled deity, the Puruṣa, swallows the fire.
Indeed, for one who knows that Person, his self does not perish here;
yogis behold that Blessed One, the eternal.
He who, having spread out thousands upon thousands of wings, might fly away—
Even if one were as swift as thought, one could not reach the center of that which is in the center.
Yogins behold that Blessed One, the eternal;
his form does not stand within the range of vision.
Those of perfectly pure being see him;
the wise one, intent on their welfare, should perceive him with the mind;
those who take refuge in him become immortal.
Yogis behold that eternal Blessed One;
mortals conceal themselves through their own training and their own conduct, as serpents hide in their holes.
Deluded people are bewildered by them; they cause confusion regarding the path for the sake of fear. Yogis behold that eternal Blessed One.
The existent (sat) is always honored by the non-existent (asat); how could there be death for that which is immortal?
Both truth and falsehood have their bond in the existent; the source of both the existent and the non-existent is one and the same.
Yogis behold that eternal Blessed One,
who is seen equally among human beings, neither through virtue nor through vice.
One should know this to be the same as the immortal;
thus disciplined, one should indeed seek that honey. Yogis behold that Blessed One, the eternal.
Neither excessive speech nor lack of study, nor the failure to offer the *agnihotra*, torments his heart; rather,
it is the mind that brings about the lightness characteristic of a Brahmin.
"Knowledge is its name; the wise, the practitioners of yoga, perceive that eternal Blessed One.
Thus, he who perceives the Self within all beings,"
When he is engaged here and there in various tasks, why should he grieve beyond that?
Just as one who stands at a great reservoir where water flows from all sides,
so it is for the Brahmin who possesses true knowledge regarding all the Vedas.
The Great Self, a person the size of a thumb,
is not seen though he is seated within the heart; unborn, moving, and unwearied by day and night.
Having realized this, the wise man remains serene:
"I alone am your mother, I am your father, and I am your son again;
I am the Self of all that exists and that does not exist."
"I am the grandfather, the elder, the father, and the son, O Bhārata. You all abide within my very self; you do not belong to me, nor do I belong to you.
The self alone is my station, and the self is my birth."
I am proclaimed in the Vedas as established in the ageless; subtler than the subtle, well-disposed, I am awake within all beings. They know me as the Father of all beings, seated within the lotus.
"O King, eat poison together with your ministers and certainly meet your destruction! Without what [is it that] the excellent black antelope skin is spread upon the navel?
Homage to the Ancient Being, to Viṣṇu, who is full bliss!
To the one whose splendor dispels all darkness, the cause of the universe—
Vaiśampāyana said:
Thus [spoke] Sanatsujāta and the wise Vidura.
As the king was conversing with him, that night passed away.
When that night had dawned, all those kings,
filled with joy, entered the assembly hall out of a desire to see the Sūta.
Desiring to hear the words of the Pārthas, which were consistent with dharma and artha,
all those headed by Dhṛtarāṣṭra went to the auspicious royal assembly hall—
broad, white as lime-wash, and adorned with golden courtyards.
It was radiant with moonlight, beautifully sprinkled with excellent water,
and strewn with lovely seats made of gold, wood, and even precious stones,
as well as ivory, all well-spread and provided with coverlets.
Bhīṣma, Droṇa, Kṛpa, Śalya, Kṛtavarman, Jayadratha,
Aśvatthāman, Vikarṇa, Somadatta, Bāhlika,
the highly wise Vidura, and the great car-warrior Yuyutsu.
O bull of the Bharatas, all those heroic kings together,
placing Dhṛtarāṣṭra at their head, entered that splendid assembly hall;
so too did Duḥśāsana, Citrasena, and Śakuni, the son of Subala.
Durmukha, Duḥsaha, Karṇa, Ulūka, and then Viviṃśati; Duḥśāsana, Saubala, Śakuni, Śala, and Tosalau—
these and many other kings, O bull of the Bharatas.
Placing the intolerant Duryodhana, the king of the Kurus, at their head,
they entered that assembly hall, O King, like the gods entering the abode of Śakra.
As those heroes with arms like iron clubs were entering, O King, [the hall shone].
O King, that assembly hall shone like a mountain cave filled with lions.
Having entered the hall, those great archers, who graced the gathering and possessed the splendor of the sun, took their seats upon costly thrones.
O Bhārata, while all those kings were seated,
the doorkeeper announced that the son of the Sūta had arrived:
"That very chariot which went toward the Pāṇḍavas is now approaching."
"A messenger has arrived swiftly for us on well-bred Saindhava horses.
Having approached, he quickly leaped down from his chariot and, adorned with earrings,
entered the assembly hall crowded with high-souled rulers of the earth.
Saṃjaya said:
"O Kauravas, know that I have returned from having gone to the Pāṇḍavas;
the Pāṇḍavas greet all the Kurus according to their respective ages."
The sons of Pṛthā saluted the elders and greeted their peers as equals; they addressed the youths with respect, honoring each according to their age.
Just as I had previously been instructed by Dhṛtarāṣṭra, I departed from here.
"Having gone to the Pāṇḍavas, I spoke; O kings, understand that.
My dear, Vāsudeva and Dhanañjaya spoke according to dharma.
Dhṛtarāṣṭra said:
"I ask you, Sañjaya, in the midst of these kings:
what words did Dhanañjaya, that leader in battle and one of undepressed spirit, speak, my dear,?"
"The great-souled one is the cutter-off of the lives of the evil-minded.
Saṃjaya said:
"Let Duryodhana hear these words."
That which the high-souled Dhananjaya Arjuna, about to fight with the permission of Yudhishthira, spoke while Keshava was listening.
Unafraid and aware of the power of his own arms,
the wise Kiritin, while about to fight in the vicinity of Vāsudeva, spoke thus to me:
O Sūta, speak in the midst of the Kurus to the son of Dhṛtarāṣṭra,
while that evil-minded, wicked-tongued Sūtaputra listens.

05,047.003d*0307_03 Whoever always hopes to fight me— 05,047.003d*0307_04 that dull-witted, extremely foolish man, ripened by time— 05,047.004a those kings who [wish] to fight with the Pāṇḍavas in battle;
Having been brought together, you should cause that king, along with his ministers, to hear the entirety of my speech as it was spoken while they were listening.
Just as all the gods now listen to the king of the gods who wields the thunderbolt in his hand,
so did the Pāṇḍavas and the Sṛñjayas listen.
Having heard these meaningful words spoken by the Diademed One,
Arjuna— the wielder of the Gāṇḍīva bow with eyes like red lotuses— spoke thus as he prepared for battle.
If Dhṛtarāṣṭra’s son does not relinquish the kingdom of King Yudhiṣṭhira of the Ajamīḍha lineage,
then surely some deed must have been committed by him in the past.
The evil deed committed by the sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra remains unrequited—
those who engaged in battle with Bhīmasena and Arjuna,
as well as with the two Aśvins and Vāsudeva himself.
Likewise, O King, by the Pañcālas and the Sṛñjayas,
by the grandson of Śini who held his weapon firmly,
and by Dhṛṣṭadyumna and Śikhaṇḍin.
And with Yudhiṣṭhira, who is equal to Indra himself,
who could consume the earth and heaven with his mere ill-will—
if the son of Dhṛtarāṣṭra considers that he can fight with them; [then let him do so].
The entire purpose of the Pāṇḍavas has been accomplished;
surely this Gāṇḍīva bow would consume them all. Do not act for the sake of the Pāṇḍavas' cause.
Come to battle if you so desire—
[remember] that bed of suffering which the virtuous Pāṇḍava, having been exiled, endured in the forest.
Through austerity, self-restraint, the protection of dharma, and wealth,
he shall experience even more grievous misfortune; the son of Dhṛtarāṣṭra, his life departed, shall lie upon his final bed.
By means of modesty, knowledge, austerity, self-restraint,
as well as by anger, the protection of dharma, and wealth,
the one of unjust conduct [overcame] the Kurus and Pāṇḍavas.
The evil-minded son of Dhṛtarāṣṭra, employing deceit as a pretext, overpowered him through the guise of devotion and sincerity,
and by means of asceticism, self-restraint, the protection of dharma, and force.

When the son of Dhṛtarāṣṭra, with his mind overwrought, releases that most terrible wrath upon the Kurus for many series of years, then he will regret the war.
Just as a blazing fire with black trails, well-kindled in the summer heat, would burn dry grass,
so shall he consume the army of Dhṛtarāṣṭra’s son.
When Yudhiṣṭhira, blazing with anger,
beheld Bhīmasena standing on the battlefield,
mace in hand and vomiting the poison of his wrath;
Then the son of Dhṛtarāṣṭra will regret that battle with the Pāṇḍava Durmarṣaṇa of terrible speed,
even though he is protected by kings who are like Indra himself.
[He saw] Bhīmasena, clad in armor and leading the army,
possessing his own distinctive marks,
the slayer of enemies, striking down the host like the God of Death himself.
Then that arrogant man will remember those words when he sees the elephants, resembling mountain peaks, struck down by Bhīmasena.
Then the son of Dhṛtarāṣṭra will regret that battle, seeing those with their frontal globes shattered, vomiting blood like elephants with broken temples;
he will enter [the fray] like a great lion entering among cattle.
When Bhīma, of terrifying form, approaches the sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra with mace in hand as their slayer,
then the son of Dhṛtarāṣṭra will regret the war.
Fearless in the midst of great terror, skilled in weapons,
and a crusher of enemy forces in assembly,
he would once with his chariot encounter floods of chariots.
When he, striking down the throngs of foot soldiers with his mace and crushing many armies with his might,
shall cast down the host of Dhṛtarāṣṭra’s son;
Then the son of Dhṛtarāṣṭra will regret that battle, as a hero cutting down a forest with an axe,
[seeing it] consumed like grass by a blazing fire.
Just as Dhṛtarāṣṭra’s son,
having beheld his own vast flood of troops like a ripened crop consumed by lightning, was overwhelmed with grief.
With its foremost heroes slain, turned away, afflicted by fear,
and for the most part with its warriors losing heart,
the army was consumed by Bhīmasena with the flame of his weapons.
Then the son of Dhṛtarāṣṭra will regret the battle,
as Nakula, the versatile warrior, draws more than a hundred arrows from his quiver with his right hand.
When the wise and preeminent charioteer [Arjuna] stands at the head of his chariot,
then the son of Dhṛtarāṣṭra will regret the battle—
having been accustomed to comfort, now lying in pain amidst the forests.
When Nakula, sighing heavily like an enraged venomous serpent, has lain for a long time,
then will the son of Dhṛtarāṣṭra regret that battle.
Having renounced their very selves for the sake of battle against the king,
those heroes, commanded by the King of Dharma,
rushed toward the army in resplendent chariots.
Having seen the five Kuru heroes— children who appear no longer like children, yet skilled in weapons— the son of Dhṛtarāṣṭra will later repent when he beholds them.
When he sees the Kekayas rushing forward, having abandoned their lives,
then the son of Dhṛtarāṣṭra will regret the battle—
when [the chariot] has its axle gone and its wheels silent.
Sahadeva, having mounted a chariot of gold and silver yoked with well-trained horses,
will strike down the heads of kings with floods of arrows.
When a great danger had arisen, seeing him standing in his chariot, skilled in weapons, turning about in the battle,
and rushing toward every direction;
Then the son of Dhṛtarāṣṭra will regret the battle—
[that man] who is restrained by modesty, skillful, truthful,
possessed of great strength, and endowed with all virtues.
The swift-acting Sahadeva, a powerful hurler of men, rushed toward Gāndhārī in that tumultuous fray when he beheld the sons of Draupadī, those great archers.
When he beholds those heroes, skilled in weapons and experts in chariot warfare,
approaching like snakes of terrible venom,
then will the son of Dhṛtarāṣṭra regret the war.
When Abhimanyu, the slayer of enemy heroes,
having mastered his weapons and being equal to Kṛṣṇa, plunged into the fray, raining arrows upon his enemies like a cloud.
Then the son of Dhṛtarāṣṭra will regret the war, when he sees that boy, who possesses no child-like valor,
falling upon the enemy host like Death itself.
Then the son of Dhṛtarāṣṭra will regret that battle when he sees the son of Subhadrā, who is equal to Indra and skilled in weapons;
for the Prabhadrakas are exceedingly swift and young.
When those who are confident and possess prowess equal to lions cast down the sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra along with their armies,
then the son of Dhṛtarāṣṭra will regret the war.
When Virāṭa and Drupada, those great car-warriors, having grown in strength, advance with their separate armies and behold the sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra together with their troops;
Then the son of Dhṛtarāṣṭra will regret the war,
when Drupada, skilled in weapons and standing upon his chariot in battle, begins to sever the heads of the youths.
When the enraged Virāṭa, the slayer of enemy heroes, cuts down [the bow] with arrows released from his bow,
then the son of Dhṛtarāṣṭra will regret the battle.
When he penetrates the enemy host at its vital points along with the Matsyas, who appear as if they were not cruel,
then the son of Dhṛtarāṣṭra will regret that battle.
When he beholds the eldest son of Virāṭa, who is of a compassionate nature, that chariot-warrior clad in armor at the head of the Matsyas for the sake of the Pāṇḍavas;
Then the son of Dhṛtarāṣṭra will repent for the battle,
when that foremost hero of the Kauravas, the best of men, the son of Śantanu, has been slain in combat by Śikhaṇḍin.
"Then our enemies would never hold us back;
I tell you this truly and without doubt:
when Śikhaṇḍin gathers together the chariot-warriors..."
When Bhīṣma, protected by his chariot-fender, advances in his chariot with divine horses, crushing the multitudes of enemy chariots,
then the son of Dhṛtarāṣṭra will regret the war.
When the wise one spoke that secret weapon to Dhṛṣṭadyumna, who was shining at the forefront of the army of the Sṛñjayas;
Then Drona, the son of Dhritarashtra,
will grieve when that immeasurable commander defeats the sons of Dhritarashtra with his arrows.
When the enemy-scorcher advances against Droṇa in battle, then the son of Dhṛtarāṣṭra will regret that war—
[he who is] modest, wise, powerful, and high-minded.
That illustrious preeminent leader of the Somakas—
those for whom that lion of the Vṛṣṇis serves as their guide— no other enemies could ever overcome.
And let him say in the world, "Do not choose me," for he is a minister peerless in battle, stationed upon his chariot—
the grandson of Śini, Sātyaki, whom we choose.
Possessing great strength, free from fear, and skilled in weapons; broad-chested, long-armed, and a destroyer;
peerless in battle and a supreme knower of divine missiles.
When the lord of the Śinīs was addressed by me, saying: "This grandson of Śini, armed with a weapon as long as a palm tree, a great car-warrior free from fear and skilled in weapons— "
Showering arrows upon his enemies like a cloud raining down,
and covering the warriors with a net of shafts,
the son of Dhṛtarāṣṭra will then regret the battle.
When that long-armed, great-souled one of firm bow resolves to fight,
[the enemy] is like cattle that, having caught the scent of a lion, [flee].
Enemies shrink away from him as they do from fire;
that great-souled one, long-armed and firm-bowed,
could shatter mountains and destroy all the worlds.
Skilled and dexterous in weaponry, swift of hand,
he shines like the sun stationed in the heavens; the artistry of the Yādava is variegated, subtle, and well-executed.
The conjunction of the lion of the Vṛṣṇis with the stars was great;
Satyaki is endowed with all those qualities which they call a praiseworthy conjunction.
When Suyodhana beholds in battle that golden chariot of Mādhava, yoked with four white horses, he will see it belonging to Sātyaki.
Then that dull-witted man of unrefined soul will suffer when he sees the fierce chariot, shining with gold and jewels,
yoked with white horses and bearing the monkey-banner.
When he sees him restrained by Keśava in battle,
that dull-witted man of unrefined soul will then suffer,
when he hears the fierce sound of the bowstring striking his palm.
That dull-witted man shall hear the great sound of the Gāṇḍīva being shaken by me in the great battle— a sound equal to the crash of a thunderbolt.
Then the foolish son of Dhṛtarāṣṭra,
evil-minded and with difficult allies,
was tormented in battle upon seeing his army enveloped in the darkness of a shower of arrows.
Like lightning flashing from a cloud, he split apart like a herd of cows at the front of the battle,
slaying thousands of enemies in their encounters.
When he vomits arrows of terrible form, like sparks of lightning— arrows that cut through bones and pierce the vital organs—
then the son of Dhṛtarāṣṭra will regret the war.
When the observer beholds the multitudes of arrows with sharpened tips released from the string of the Gāṇḍīva bow as they fall,
striking down elephants, horses, and armored warriors;
Then the son of Dhṛtarāṣṭra will repent for the battle,
when that fool sees the arrows released by his enemies being turned back by my own shafts.
When the wise man sees those being cut down by razor-sharp arrows flying crosswise,
then the son of Dhṛtarāṣṭra will regret the battle— when the *vipāṭha* shafts released from my arms [fall].
Then the son of Dhṛtarāṣṭra will regret that battle, when the twice-born cut off the heads of the youths like fruits from the tops of trees.
When the spectator beheld the warriors falling from their chariots, from great elephants, and from their horses,
struck down and cast upon the arena by his arrows;
Then the son of Dhṛtarāṣṭra will regret the war,
when he sees the sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra perishing before they have even reached the range of the enemy's weapons.
If he had not performed such deeds in battle on all sides,
then the son of Dhṛtarāṣṭra would have lamented over that war;
[for he has struck down] hosts of foot-soldiers and hosts of chariots on every side.
With my mouth wide open like Time with his bow drawn,
I shall drive away the enemies with showers of blazing arrows; then that dull-witted one will suffer.
When he sees his own army utterly bewildered by the chariot rushing through all directions, its dust obscured as it is mangled by the Gāṇḍīva bow;
Then the dull-witted Duryodhana will later suffer, seeing his entire army bewildered, its limbs severed, and deprived of consciousness.
With its horses, foremost heroes, and noble kings slain, with its winged steeds exhausted and its riders afflicted by fear, it cried out in distress—
being struck down and already destroyed.
Seeing that mass of scattered hair, bones, and skulls—
like the work of Prajāpati left half-finished—
he of dull intellect will then suffer remorse.
When the Gāṇḍīva bow, Vāsudeva, the divine Pāñcajanya conch, and the horses are upon the chariot,
and when that fierce [weapon] is completely uprooted from the earth—
In the great battle, as he is being violently shaken by me with a roar like the crashing of a thunderbolt,
that one of dull intellect shall hear the cry of "Gāñjī! for life.
The son of Dhṛtarāṣṭra shall see me, Devadatta, and his two inexhaustible quivers assembled together in battle,
as I strike down the gathered hosts of Dasyus.
When, at the end of the age, I shall set another age in motion and consume the Kauravas like fire,
then Dhṛtarāṣṭra, together with his sons, will be tormented.
Accompanied by his brothers, his sons, and his army,
he— deprived of sovereignty, under the sway of anger, and small-minded—
trembled when his pride had been brought to an end.
Later, Dhṛtarāṣṭra’s son will grieve bitterly.
Once, in the forenoon, when I had finished my prayers at the water's edge, a brahmin spoke these pleasing words to me.
"O Pārtha, you must perform a difficult task;
O Savyasācin, you must fight with your enemies.
Whether it be Indra himself, the wielder of the thunderbolt, riding his bay horses—"
Let him go before you in battle, slaying the enemies with a chariot yoked with Sugrīva; let Vāsudeva Kṛṣṇa protect you from behind.
And I chose Vāsudeva as my ally in this battle over Mahendra, who holds the thunderbolt in his hand; that Kṛṣṇa has been obtained by me for the destruction of the Dasyus.
I believe this was ordained for me by the gods,
O Kṛṣṇa: that victory over a man whom he would not even wish to conquer in his mind.
He will surely overcome all his enemies;
there is no concern regarding even the gods led by Indra among men.
He would seek to cross the ocean with his two arms alone.
He who would wish to conquer Vāsudeva in battle— that radiant Kṛṣṇa, the exceedingly heroic one, who is like the immeasurable great ocean of waters— [would seek to cross the unfordable sea].
He who should wish to split a mountain with his palm—
the vast, white mass of rock—
his very hand, along with its nails, would shatter.
Nor could he do anything at all to that mountain;
he might extinguish a blazing fire with his bare arms,
or even restrain the moon and the sun.
He who would wish to conquer Vāsudeva in battle would forcibly seize the nectar of the gods;
he who [would seize] Rukmiṇī, the daughter of the Bhojas, with a single chariot.
Having forcibly devastated the realm of kings,
he carried off his wife, who blazed with glory,
in whom was born the high-souled son of Rukmiṇī.
Having violently crushed the Gāndhāras and conquered all the sons of Nagnajit,
he forcibly released the screaming captive.
This Sudarśana, the ornament of the gods,
struck down the Pāṇḍya king at the gateway and likewise crushed the Kaliṅgas at Dantakūra.
By him, having been burned for many series of years, the city of Vārāṇasī became leaderless;
he whom others considered invincible in battle.
Having struck the Niṣāda king named Ekalavya as if Jambha had struck a mountain with great force,
he lies there lifeless, slain by Kṛṣṇa.
Accompanied by Baladeva, he struck down the wicked son of Ugrasena, who was scorching those among the Vṛṣṇis and Andhakas standing in their midst.
Having slain him, he gave the kingdom to Ugrasena;
and he fought Saubha, which was situated in the sky,
as well as the terrifying King Śālva with his illusory powers.
At the gate of Saubha he seized a *śataghnī* with his two arms; what mortal could withstand him?
There was a fortress named Prāgjyotiṣa.
In that city of the Asuras, which was formidable and unbearable, the mighty Naraka, son of the Earth,
seized the two auspicious jeweled earrings from the Ādityas.
Seeing that prowess of Keśava, the gods, together with Śakra, were unable to endure him; having assembled, they were afraid to seize him.
Knowing that Keshava’s strength and weapons were likewise irresistible, they urged Krishna to slay the bandits, being well aware of his nature.
Vāsudeva, the lordly one who possesses all perfections, promised to perform that difficult task;
having slain six thousand men at Nirmocana, he fulfilled his word.
Having suddenly severed the razor-edged nooses,
and having slain Mura and struck down the flood of Rākṣasas,
the hero went to Nirmocana as well.
Right there, a battle took place between him and the exceedingly powerful Viṣṇu;
slain by Kṛṣṇa, he lay there, his life-breath departed.
Like a *karṇikāra* tree shaken by the wind,
Kṛṣṇa took those two jeweled earrings and,
having slain Naraka, Mura, and Bhauma;
Surrounded by splendor and fame, the wise one of incomparable power returned;
there, the gods granted him boons.
Having seen that terrible deed performed by you in battle, may you have no fatigue while fighting,
and may you possess the power to move through both the sky and the waters.
"May weapons not pass through your body"—
thus Kṛṣṇa was fulfilled in his purpose regarding the immeasurable Vāsudeva of such a form.
The son of Dhṛtarāṣṭra hopes that by his own strength he can overcome Viṣṇu, who possesses great power, whose excellence of qualities is ever-present, and who is irresistible with infinite heroism.
For when that evil-minded one plots against him,
he endures it upon seeing us;
this situation has come to pass for both me and Kṛṣṇa.
He who thinks that by engaging in strife it will be possible to seize the Pandavas' sense of ownership [over their property]— let him go there to the battlefield and experience the consequences.
Having paid homage to King Śāntanava,
and likewise to Droṇa together with his son,
and to the peerless Śāradvata;
Desiring the kingdom, I shall fight; I consider his weapon to be restrained by dharma,
for he who fights against the Pāṇḍavas will be a practitioner of dharma.
Having been defeated by those cruel men in an unjust game of dice,
the sons of Pāṇḍu have indeed spent twelve years in the forest, undergoing the hardship ordained for them.
For a long time they have lived in concealment;
now that the Pāṇḍavas have suddenly regained their lives,
the sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra, established in their positions, cannot endure it.
If they should defeat us while we are fighting—
even with the gods led by Indra as our allies—
then unrighteousness, when practiced, is weightier than righteousness.
Thus, it is certain that there is no such thing as "done well," if this man were not bound by his actions,
and if he did not consider us to be superior.
I hope, with Vāsudeva as my second,
to slay Duryodhana along with his followers,
provided that this deed is not predestined for men.
No man’s own karma exists [independently]; having surely observed both this and that,
the defeat of Dhṛtarāṣṭra’s son is certain.
O Kurus, what I tell you is evident to you:
the sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra will cease to exist if they fight;
there is no way for the Kurus to escape except through battle. If you seek safety, [you must not fight].
There is no one left here among those who fight;
having slain the sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra along with Karṇa, I shall win back the entire kingdom of the Kurus.
"Whatever task you have to perform, do it according to your own station; enjoy your beloved wives and children.
For even among us there are such aged Brahmins."
They were learned, virtuous, and of noble birth;
they were experts in astrology and astronomy, possessing certain knowledge regarding the conjunctions of the lunar mansions.
Various divine mysteries, celestial questions concerning the movements of animals and the auspicious moments (muhūrtas),
and the great destruction of the Kurus and Sṛñjayas.
They announce the victory of the Pāṇḍavas;
for thus Ajātaśatru considers it:
that his purpose is accomplished for the sake of subduing his enemies.
Janārdana, that lion of the Vṛṣṇis, possesses direct knowledge of reality and perceives nothing with doubt;
and I too know the nature of what is yet to come.
I myself perceive this with my own intellect, remaining vigilant;
my ancient vision does not falter:
the sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra, though fighting, do not exist.
The Gāṇḍīva bow yawns even when not grasped;
my bowstring trembles even when not touched;
and my arrows leap forth from the mouth of the quiver.
And desiring to go again and again,
the sword, bright as silver, emerges from its scabbard like a serpent casting off its own worn-out skin.
From the banner, voices of fierce form speak:
"O Kiritin, when will your chariot be yoked?
And at night, packs of jackals cry out.
Then the *rakṣas* spirits emerge from the intermediate space;
deer, jackals, blue-necked peacocks, crows,
vultures, cranes, and hyenas likewise appear.
And birds with beautiful wings fly behind,
having seen the chariot yoked with white horses;
for I alone [shall overcome] all the kings and warriors.
Raining down arrows while employing various paths of weaponry, I shall lead them to the world of death,
just as a kindled fire consumes a thicket in the summer heat.
He released the Sthūṇākarṇa, the terrible Pāśupata,
as well as the Brahmāstra which Śakra knew, discharging them with great force while intent on the slaughter of Vegavat.
I shall leave nothing remaining of my subjects;
for this is the supreme state through which I shall attain peace. O son of Gavalgaṇa, tell them that my resolve is firm.

Furthermore, he constantly considered that by engaging in conflict with those ministers whom he had previously addressed as allies— even including the gods headed by Indra— he would be joined in strife.
Behold the delusion of this son of Dhṛtarāṣṭra:
the aged Bhīṣma, son of Śantanu, and Kṛpa;
Droṇa with his son, and the wise Vidura.
"Whatever all these say, let that be so;
may all the Kauravas be long-lived.
Vaiśampāyana said:
O Bhārata, when all those kings had assembled,
Bhīṣma, the son of Śāntanu, spoke these words to Duryodhana:
"Bṛhaspati and Uśanas once attended upon Brahmā."
The Maruts together with Indra, the Vasus together with the two Aśvins,
the Ādityas, the Sādhyas, and those who are the Seven Seers in heaven;
Viśvāvasu the Gandharva and the auspicious hosts of Apsarases.
Having paid homage, they approached the Grandfather, the elder of the worlds;
and having surrounded the Lord of All, the denizens of heaven sat down.
Taking away both the minds and the splendors of those denizens of heaven, [the two]—
"The two ancient gods, the sages Nara and Nārāyaṇa, have passed by.
Bṛhaspati asked the brahmin, 'Who are these two?
They do not wait upon you; tell us about them, O Grandfather.'"
Brahmā said:
"These two ascetics, who illuminate the earth and the heavens, blazing and radiant, have pervaded and transcended [all things] with their great power."
These two, Nara and Nārāyaṇa, have established themselves from one world to another;
exalted by their own ascetic power, they possess great being and prowess. Indeed, these two steadfast ones gladden the worlds through their deeds.
"Know, O Brahmin, that those two of great wisdom and subduers of enemies have become twofold for the destruction of the Asuras, being honored by gods and Gandharvas.
Vaiśampāyana said:
Having heard that, Śakra went to where those two were performing penance,
together with all the hosts of gods led by Bṛhaspati,
at which time a terrible fear had arisen among the inhabitants of heaven regarding the war between the gods and the asuras.
He requested a boon from the two high-souled ones, Nara and Nārāyaṇa.
O best of the Bharatas, they both then said to him, "Choose one.
Thereupon Śakra spoke to them: "Let assistance be rendered to us."
Then the two of them said to Śakra, "We shall do whatever you desire.
Accompanied by them, Śakra conquered the Daityas and Dānavas;
Nara, the scorcher of foes, having slain the enemies of Indra in battle.

Standing upon his whirling chariot, this Arjuna struck off with a broad-headed arrow the heads of hundreds and thousands of Paulomas and Kālakhañjas— specifically that of Jambha as he was devouring the sacrifice in battle.
On the far shore of the ocean, he shattered the city of gold after slaying sixty thousand Nivātakavacas in battle;
this conqueror of enemy cities, having defeated the gods along with Indra.
The mighty-armed Arjuna gratified the god of fire,
and likewise Nārāyaṇa slew many others there. Behold these two of great prowess as they encounter one another.

The heroes Vāsudeva and Arjuna, those two great chariot-warriors joined together, are the divine Nara and Nārāyaṇa, the ancient gods; so says the sacred tradition. They are invincible in the world of men, even by the gods and asuras led by Indra himself.
This Kṛṣṇa is Nārāyaṇa, while Phalguna is known as Nara.
Nārāyaṇa and Nara are indeed a single essence manifested in two forms.
For these two, through their deeds, attain the eternal and imperishable worlds.

They are born again and again in those very places at the time of battle. Therefore, O Lord, having sought refuge in these two illustrious ones, enjoy prosperity, O mighty-armed one, together with your sons, kinsmen, and relatives.
"Therefore, action alone must be performed," so said Nārada;
for he, the knower of the Vedas, explained all this to the circle of the Vṛṣṇis.
"When you shall see Keśava with the conch, discus, and mace in his hands..."
As Arjuna, the wielder of the terrible bow, takes up his weapons,
and the two great-souled Kṛṣṇas stand together upon a single chariot—
then, O dear Duryodhana, you will remember my words.
If this calamity were not present before the Kurus,
O dear one, your intellect would have been deluded from both worldly profit and dharma.
If you do not accept my words, you shall hear of many who have been slain.
For all the Kurus indeed revere your opinion alone;
yet you alone agree with the view of only three. And as for Karṇa, O bull of the Bharatas, he has been cursed by Rāma.
Of the ill-born son of a Sūta, of Śakuni Saubala,
and likewise of my mean and wicked brother Duḥśāsana—
Karna said:
"O Grandfather, you should not speak to me in the manner you have addressed me.
For I stand firm in the duty of a Kṣatriya, never having departed from my own dharma.
What other misconduct is there in me for which you reproach me?"
The sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra do not know of any transgression on my part anywhere;
O bull of the Bharatas, out of desire, greed, compassion, or affection,
I have never at any time committed any wrong against the son of Dhṛtarāṣṭra.
"I shall indeed slay all the Pāṇḍavas as they stand in battle.
How can peace ever again be established with those who were formerly hostile?
For I shall perform every task that is pleasing to King Dhṛtarāṣṭra."
"Likewise, he is firmly established in the kingdom of Duryodhana as well.
Vaiśampāyana said:
"But having heard the words of Karṇa, Bhīṣma, the son of Śantanu, spoke again."
Addressing the great king Dhṛtarāṣṭra, he spoke these words:
"As for what this man constantly boasts— that 'I shall slay the Pāṇḍavas'—
he does not possess even a sixteenth part of the power of the high-souled Pāṇḍavas."

The full merit of those Pāṇḍavas does not equal even a single fraction of this calamity that is coming upon your evil-minded sons. Know, therefore, that this is the work of that wicked son of a charioteer.
Relying upon him, your dull-witted son Suyodhana disregarded those heroes, the subduers of enemies who were sons of the gods. Furthermore,
what extremely difficult deed was performed by him in the past?

Having seen his beloved brother slain by Dhananjaya through valor in the city of Virāṭa— deeds which each of all those Pāṇḍavas had performed individually in the past— what was done by him [Karṇa] at that time?
For all of them are heroes skilled in weapons, and all have attained great renown;
they would rather renounce even the sovereignty over all the immortals than abandon victory.
Indeed, Dhananjaya has marched against all the Kurus assembled together.

"Having overwhelmed them, he seized the cattle; why was he absent at that time when your son was being carried off by the Gandharvas during the cattle-expedition? Where was the Sūta’s son then, who now acts like a bull?"
"But was it not also there that those Gandharvas were defeated by Pārtha, the high-souled Bhīma, and the two Yamas?
These many things of his, O bull of the Bharatas, are false."
"May it be well with you; [you are] always a boaster who destroys both dharma and artha.
Having heard these words of Bhīṣma, the high-minded son of Bharadvāja addressed Dhṛtarāṣṭra in the midst of the kings, honoring him:
"O King, let that which Bhīṣma, the best of the Bharatas, has said be done. You ought not to act upon the words of those who desire wealth for their own selfish ends.
I consider a reconciliation with the Pāṇḍavas before war is best."
"O King, the Pāṇḍavas are invincible even by the gods and asuras led by Indra.
Whatever words were spoken by Arjuna and reported by Sañjaya, I know that the Pāṇḍava will carry them all out."
"For there is no archer equal to him in the three worlds. But disregarding those meaningful words of Droṇa and Bhīṣma,
the king then questioned Saṃjaya regarding the Pāṇḍava.
At that very moment, all the Kurus lost hope for their lives when King Dhṛtarāṣṭra did not speak properly to Bhīṣma and Droṇa. Dhṛtarāṣṭra said:
"What did that Pāṇḍava king, the son of Dharma,
say upon hearing of these vast armies assembled for his sake?
What does Yudhiṣṭhira desire, as he prepares to fight out of intense resolve?"
Whose face among his brothers and sons does he look upon with anxiety?
Who indeed restrains him, saying, "Be calm," or "Desist from fighting," when that knower of dharma and practitioner of righteousness has been provoked to anger by the base through deceit?
Saṃjaya said:
"The Pāñcālas, together with the Pāṇḍavas, look toward the face of the king;
may you be blessed, for Yudhiṣṭhira instructs them all."

The separate throngs of chariots belonging to the Pāṇḍavas and the Pāñcālas welcomed Yudhiṣṭhira, the son of Kuntī, as he approached— Kuntī’s son, blazing with splendor like the sun rising through the darkness.
The Pāñcālas rejoice at Yudhiṣṭhira, who is like a rising mass of splendor; from the cowherds and shepherds upward,
the Pāñcālas, Kekayas, and Matsyas all rejoice at the son of Pāṇḍu.
Brahmin women, princesses,
and daughters of the Vaiśyas came together, playing, to see Pārtha clad in his armor.
Dhṛtarāṣṭra said:
"O Saṃjaya, tell us: with whom have the Pāṇḍavas allied themselves? With what strength are the Somakas, as if led by their general Dhṛṣṭadyumna?
Vaiśampāyana said:
Thus questioned in the assembly within the council of the Kurus, Gāvalgaṇi sighed very deeply and long, as if reflecting repeatedly; then,
due to fate and for no apparent reason, a faintness came over the Sūta.
Then, in the assembly hall within the royal council, a man announced:
"O Great King, this Sañjaya has fallen to the ground in a swoon;
he utters no word at all, his wisdom lost and his consciousness dimmed."
Dhṛtarāṣṭra said:
"Surely Sañjaya saw the sons of Kuntī, those great chariot-warriors;
his mind has been greatly agitated by those tigers among men."
05,049.013 Vaiśampāyana said:
Having regained consciousness and recovered his breath, Sañjaya spoke thus to Dhṛtarāṣṭra in the assembly hall amidst the gathering of the Kurus, O great king.
O Indra among kings, I have seen the sons of Kuntī, those great chariot-warriors,
emaciated by their confinement while dwelling in the palace of the King of Matsya. Listen, O Great King, to those with whom the Pāṇḍavas have now joined battle.
The heroic Dhṛṣṭadyumna attacked you in battle.
That righteous-souled one would never, under any circumstances, abandon the truth— neither out of anger, nor fear, nor desire, nor for the sake of wealth, nor from a motive of sophistry.

O Great King, by him who is the authority in dharma— the best among the upholders of dharma— Ajātaśatru has brought the Pāṇḍavas into conflict. There is no one on earth equal to him in the strength of his arms.
That wielder of the bow who indeed brought all the rulers of the earth under his control—
by that Bhīmasena the Pāṇḍavas have joined battle with you,
ever since they emerged from the house of lac and from the man-eater Hiḍimba.
Vṛkodara, the son of Kuntī, who was their island of refuge— when the King of Sindhu dragged away Yājñasenī,
there Vṛkodara, the son of Kuntī, became their island of refuge.
And because he liberated all those Pāṇḍavas who were gathered together at Vāraṇāvata while they were being consumed by fire, they have employed you against him; and because he,
while acting to please Kṛṣṇā, slew the Krodhavaśas.
Having entered the rugged and formidable Mount Gandhamādana—
upon which the strength of ten thousand elephants has been placed as the core of his two arms—
it is with that Bhīmasena that the Pāṇḍavas have joined you.

That hero who, accompanied by Kṛṣṇa as his second, having displayed his prowess for the sake of gratifying Jātavedas, formerly conquered Purandara while he was fighting; he who [conquered] Mahādeva himself, Giriśa, the wielder of the trident—
He gratified the God of gods, the Lord of Umā, through battle;
that wielder of the bow who brought all the world-protectors under his control—
with him as their victor in combat, the Pāṇḍavas have set out against you.
He who brought under his control the western quarter, where tens of thousands of Mleccha tribes dwell—
there Nakula stands as a warrior, a fighter of wondrous skill. With that handsome hero, a wielder of the most powerful bow, [you shall be encountered].
O Kauravya, the Pāṇḍavas have joined battle against you with the son of Mādrī,
he who by his prowess conquered the Kāśīs, Aṅgas, Magadhas, and Kaliṅgas—
against you, the Pāṇḍavas have joined battle with that Sahadeva.
On earth there are only four men equal in prowess to him:
Aśvatthāman, Dhṛṣṭaketu, Pradyumna, and Rukmin.
With that Sahadeva, the Pāṇḍavas have joined battle against you.

O bull of the Bharatas, that daughter of Kāśī, who was formerly a virtuous woman, practiced severe austerities in order to bring about the death of Bhīṣma even after her passing, by means of the younger of the two heroes among men, the one who brings joy to Mādrī.
The daughter of the Pañcāla king was born, and by divine providence she became a man again—
he who, O tiger among men, knew the virtues and faults of both women and men; he,
the Pañcāla who was fierce in battle, encountered the Kaliṅgas.
O Kurus, Śikhaṇḍin, having been initiated into the use of weapons, attacked you;
indeed, it was he whom a Yakṣa had transformed into a man for the sake of Bhīṣma’s slaughter. With that fierce and great archer, the Pāṇḍavas have assailed you.
The five Kekaya princes, brothers and great archers, heroes clad in polished armor, joined forces with you;
among them was he who has long arms, is swift in the use of weapons, steadfast, and whose valor is truth.
Therefore, you have a conflict with that hero of the Vṛṣṇis, Yuyudhāna;
and with that Virāṭa, who was at the time the refuge of the high-souled Pāṇḍavas,
the Pāṇḍavas have engaged in battle.
And he of great mind who was born for the destruction of Droṇa— by whom,
with Dhṛṣṭadyumna as their commander-in-chief, the Pāṇḍavas joined battle—
he was the king of Kāśī, a great chariot-warrior in Vārāṇasī.
He became their warrior, and with him they attacked you;
the Pāṇḍavas attacked with the high-souled sons of Draupadī— those who are invincible in battle even for children, and whose touch is like that of venomous serpents.
The Pāṇḍavas joined battle with that Abhimanyu, who was equal to Kṛṣṇa in prowess and equal to Yudhiṣṭhira in self-restraint;
and also with the highly illustrious Dhṛṣṭaketu, who was peerless in valor.
The great car-warrior Śaiśupāli, the son of Śiśupāla, was difficult to withstand when enraged in battle;
surrounded by an *akṣauhiṇī*, he joined the Pāṇḍavas, having sought their alliance against the Cedi king.
The one born of the Yadu clan who, having approached the Pāṇḍavas,
remains with them— he who is the refuge of the Pāṇḍavas as Vāsava is of the gods—
it is with that Vāsudeva that the Pāṇḍavas have joined you in battle.
Likewise, O bull of the Bharatas, Śarabha, the brother of the lord of Cedi,
together with Karakarṣa, joined those two;
as did both Sahadeva, the son of Jarāsaṃdha, and Jayatsena.
In battle, those two heroes, peerless chariot-warriors, stood firm for the sake of the Pāṇḍavas; and Drupada, possessed of great splendor and surrounded by a vast army,
stood ready to fight, having surrendered his very life for the sake of the Pāṇḍavas.
"These and many other kings from the east and the north— relying upon whom by the hundreds the King of Dharma remains established.
Dhṛtarāṣṭra said:
All these whom you have praised possess great energy;
yet all of them together on one side are equal to Bhīma alone on the other. Indeed, a great fear arises within me even more than from Bhīmasena himself.
O dear one, from that angry and intolerant man— who is like a great ruru deer from a tiger—
I stay awake through all the nights, sighing long and hot breaths;
terrified of Vṛkodara, O dear one, like a weak animal before a lion.

"O mighty-armed one, I do not see anyone in this army who can withstand him in battle— he who possesses a splendor equal to Śakra. Moreover, the son of Kuntī, the Pāṇḍava, is intolerant and firm in his enmity."
Laughing without cause, intoxicated, casting sidelong glances, and possessing a great roar;
endowed with great speed, great energy, mighty arms, and great strength—
he will bring an end to my dull-witted sons in battle.

Bearing his mace, Vṛkodara— like Death himself with staff in hand at the head of the Kurus in battle— assailed those seized by a paralysis of the thighs. He wielded that terrible mace, fashioned of refined iron and adorned with gold.
In my mind, I perceive him as if the staff of Brahmā were raised;
just as a lion of full-grown strength moves among herds of ruru deer,
so shall Bhīma range through my armies.
Of all my sons, he alone is of cruel prowess; he is a great eater, perverse, and always impetuous even in childhood. My heart trembles whenever I think of Duryodhana and the others.
Even in his childhood, those who fought against him were crushed as if by an elephant;
my sons have always been tormented by his prowess.
Indeed, that Bhīma is possessed of great heroism; when enraged, he is a conqueror of enemy cities.
That very same cause of division— terrible and of fearsome prowess— is like Bhīma himself,
as I behold him before me in battle, swooning with rage and devouring the ranks of men, elephants, and horses.
Equal to Droṇa and Arjuna in the use of missiles, equal to the wind in speed,
and equal to Maheśvara in wrath— who could slay Bhīma in battle?
O Sañjaya, tell me of the heroic Bhīmasena, who is incapable of enduring insult.
I consider it a great gain indeed that all my sons were not slain at once by that slayer of enemies,
that high-minded one by whom yakṣas and rākṣasas of terrible strength were struck down.
And how will a mere mortal withstand his impetuosity in battle— [he who is] the foremost among the mighty, such as Hiḍimba, Baka, Kirmīra, and others?
O Sañjaya, even as a child, he never remained under my control.
How much more so now, when the son of Pāṇḍu is tormented by my wicked sons?
He is cruel, and because of his cruelty, he might even break apart rather than bend;
with his sidelong glances and knitted brows, how can Vṛkodara be pacified?
With broad shoulders, peerless strength, and fair of hue, Bhīmasena stands as tall as a palm tree; in stature he exceeds Arjuna by a span.
In speed he surpasses horses, and in strength he surpasses elephants.
"Speaking softly and with honeyed eyes, the mighty Pāṇḍava is of middle stature"—
thus was the Pāṇḍava previously heard by me in my youth from the mouth of Vyāsa, exactly as he is in both form and valor.
With his iron mace, Bhīma— the best among strikers, impatient, ever-furious, fierce, and of cruel prowess— will, when enraged in battle, slay chariots, elephants, horses,
and men.
"O father, having previously been insulted by those who acted with hostility toward me,
how will my sons be able to withstand that iron mace— thick, well-jointed, gold-adorned, a *śataghnī* weapon that resounds with a hundred crashes?"

"O dear one, these fools, imagining themselves to be wise, desire to cross the ocean that has no further shore, no raft, and no bottom— a sea with arrows for its current and Bhīmasena as its treacherous whirlpool. Though I cry out to them, these children do not listen."
Those who perceive only the honey fail to perceive the perilous precipice;
those who will engage in battle with Vāyu in human form are surely impelled by the Creator like great beasts by a lion.
"O father, how will my sons be able to endure that iron club— four cubits long, six-sided, of immeasurable power, and painful to the touch—
when it is hurled by him as he whirled it about and split the heads of elephants?"
Licking the corners of his mouth and repeatedly shedding tears,
he aimed at the birds as they swooped down, uttering terrifying cries,
and roared back at the intoxicated elephants as they charged headlong toward him.
As he plunges into the chariot-paths, aiming at and slaying the foremost warriors—
like a blazing fire— my progeny might yet be saved;
for the long-armed one, creating a path while putting my army to flight, [advances].
With mace in hand, as if dancing, he will display the end of the age;
like a rutting elephant breaking down flowering trees,
Vṛkodara will enter the army of my sons in battle.
Rendering chariots devoid of men, stripped of banners, and with their poles shattered,
that tiger among men crushed both car-warriors and horsemen,
just as the force of the Ganges uproots various trees growing on its marshy banks.
O Sañjaya, my great army will enter [the fray], and surely my sons, afflicted by the strength of Bhīmasena, will fall under his control—
my sons, my servants, and even the kings themselves, O Sañjaya.
By him, the king of great heroism, having entered the inner apartments in former times with Vāsudeva as his companion, Jarāsaṃdha was struck down;
by that wise one, this entire goddess Earth was [conquered] by Jarāsaṃdha.
The powerful lord of Magadha brought them under his control and tormented them;
the Kurus fell [under his sway] through Bhīṣma’s prowess, and the Andhakas and Vṛṣṇis through his policy,
yet they did not come under his power— this was surely due to destiny alone.
Having gone there, he was slain by the son of Pāṇḍu, that hero endowed with mighty arms, who acted with speed even without weapons; what could be greater than that?
He was like a venomous serpent whose poison has been accumulated over a long period of time.
O Sañjaya, he will discharge his fiery energy upon my sons in battle,
just as Mahendra, the best of gods, destroyed the Dānavas with his thunderbolt;
Bhīmasena, mace in hand, will slaughter my sons.
I seem to see Vṛkodara rushing toward me, his eyes exceedingly copper-red, irresistible and unobstructible, with fierce speed and prowess—
though he is without medicine, without a bow, without a chariot, and without armor.
What man could stand before him as he fights with his two arms?
Bhīṣma, Droṇa, and this brahmin Kṛpa, the son of Śaradvat,
know it just as I do, for I am a knower of the prowess of that wise one.
Knowing the noble vow and desiring not to break their word,
those bulls among men on my side will stand at the head of the armies;
yet destiny is more powerful than all else, especially for a man.
Although I see their victory, I do not restrain my sons;
for those great archers, established in the ancient path of Indra,
will give up their lives in the tumultuous fray while protecting their royal glory.

"O dear Sañjaya, just as these sons of mine are my own, so too are the Pāṇḍavas; they are the grandsons of Bhīṣma and the disciples of Droṇa and Kṛpa. Whatever has been given or offered by us in reliance upon them, [that remains]."
Out of respect for his nobility, three elders performed the funeral rites for him;
for they say that for a Brahmin who takes up arms in battle seeking to uphold the duty of a Kshatriya, death is indeed the most excellent and supreme choice.
I indeed grieve for all those who wish to fight against the Pāṇḍavas;
that very danger which Vidura foretold at the outset has now arrived.
Yet, O Saṃjaya, I do not believe that knowledge can prevent the onset of suffering.
For even this exceedingly powerful knowledge can be destructive;
for even the sages, though liberated, seeing the welfare of the world,
become happy in happiness and likewise sorrowful in sorrow.
How much more so for me, who have been attached in a thousand ways to sons,
kingdom, wives, grandsons, and even kinsmen—
what indeed is the highest course of action for me now that this great danger has arisen?
Indeed, as I reflect upon it, I see only the destruction of the Kurus. This great calamity of the Kurus appears to have its beginning in the gambling match;
out of greed and a desire for power, this evil was committed by that fool.
"I think this is the inevitable nature of time as it moves inexorably forward;
like a rim fixed to a wheel, it is impossible to escape it.
What is to be done? How shall I act? Where indeed shall I go, O Sañjaya?"
"These dull-witted Kurus, having fallen under the power of Time, are perishing.
O dear one, when my hundred sons were previously slain, I was helpless;
how shall I now hear the wailing of women—how will death touch me?"
Just as a blazing fire, fanned by the wind, would consume the dry forest grass in the summer heat,
even so did the Pāṇḍava with mace in hand.
"Together with Arjuna, he will slay my sons.
Dhṛtarāṣṭra said:
"We have indeed never heard him utter any untruthful words."
Even the three worlds would belong to him who has Dhanañjaya as his warrior; yet,
though I reflect upon it incessantly, I do not see anyone who could withstand that wielder of the Gāṇḍīva bow in battle, even on his own chariot.

No one in battle is an equal match for the wielder of the Gāṇḍīva bow when he shoots heart-piercing arrows such as the *karṇin* and *nālīka*. Only if the two heroes, Droṇa and Karṇa— those bulls among men— were to oppose him, could they possibly withstand him.

"Skilled in weapons, the best among the strong, and undefeated in battles— because of their greatness, there is doubt in the world, yet for me there is no victory. Karṇa is compassionate and negligent, and the Teacher is aged and venerable."
Pārtha is capable, powerful, firm with his bow, and has conquered fatigue;
there would be a most tumultuous battle, yet he remains undefeated in every respect.
For all are heroes skilled in weapons, and all have attained great renown.
They might even renounce the sovereignty over all the immortals, but never their victory;
indeed, peace would surely come only through the death of those two or of Phalguna. There is no conqueror of Arjuna, nor is there any slayer of him to be found.
How can the wrath that has arisen against those dull-witted men be appeased?
Others also know weapons; they are both defeated and victorious. Yet, it is heard that Phalguna alone possesses absolute victory.
Having summoned the thirty-three gods, he gratified the fire-god at Khāṇḍava; he conquered all the gods, and I do not know of his defeat,
he whose charioteer in battle is Hṛṣīkeśa, who is equal to him in character and conduct.
"O dear one, his victory is certain, just like the victory of Indra;
for we have heard that the two Kṛṣṇas are joined upon a single chariot, and the bow Gāṇḍīva is strung— simultaneously, these three splendors have come together."
"We have no such bow, no warrior, and no charioteer;
yet those fools, following the will of Duryodhana, do not realize this.
O Sañjaya, even a blazing thunderbolt falling upon one's head might leave something remaining."
But the remaining arrows discharged by Kirīṭin, O dear one, cannot leave any survivor;
moreover, Phalguna appears as if he were shooting and as if he were slaying,
extracting heads from bodies with showers of arrows.
Moreover, the energy consisting of arrows, as if blazing on all sides when discharged from the Gāṇḍīva, would consume my sons' army in battle; indeed,
it would be terrified by the roar of Savyasācin's chariot.
The vast army of the Bharatas appears to me utterly terrified;
like a great fire, fanned by the wind and spreading in all directions, consuming a forest thicket, it will likewise consume my men with its mighty flames.
When the diadem-wearing Kirīṭin stands as an assailant in battle, vomiting forth volleys of sharpened arrows,
he is like the all-destroying Antaka created by the Ordainer.
Just as it may be, so shall he be unimpeded;
for when I have repeatedly heard those very many kinds of things in the assembly hall of the Kurus.
And thus, on all sides at the front of the battle,
this destruction indeed comes upon the Bharatas.
Dhṛtarāṣṭra said:
Just as all the Pāṇḍavas are valiant and desirous of victory, so too are their followers, who have renounced their own lives and are resolved upon conquest. Indeed,
you yourself must describe those valiant enemies to me.
The Pāñcālas, Kekayas, Matsyas, Māgadhas, and the lords of the Vatsa lands—
he who, being powerful, could bring these worlds under his control along with Indra himself, desiring them— Kṛṣṇa is that preeminent one of the world, intent upon the victory of the Pāṇḍavas.
Sātyaki, the descendant of Śini, quickly acquired the entirety of Arjuna’s science;
standing firm in battle, he scattered arrows like seeds.
And Dhṛṣṭadyumna, the Pāñcālya, a great car-warrior of cruel deeds, [was there].
"O dear one, that master of supreme weapons will wage war against my forces;
because of Yudhiṣṭhira’s wrath, Arjuna’s prowess,
the twins, and Bhīmasena, fear arises within me."
"O Sañjaya, a superhuman net has been spread out by the lords of men across the space;
they will destroy my army, and therefore I cry out. He is handsome, high-minded, fortunate, and endowed with the splendor of Brahman."

The son of Pāṇḍu is wise, possessed of well-performed wisdom, and righteous in soul; he is well-endowed with friends and ministers, and provided with those who are fit for employment and their supervisors;
he is further accompanied by brothers, fathers-in-law, and sons, all of whom are great chariot-warriors.
That tiger among men, the son of Pāṇḍu, is steadfast and discreet; he is compassionate, generous, modest, and his prowess is truth;
he is deeply learned, self-disciplined, a servant of the elders, and has conquered his senses.

What fool, desiring death and possessed of a deluded mind, would fall like a moth into that fire of the Pāṇḍavas— which is endowed with every excellence, blazing like a kindled flame, and scorching as it cannot be restrained?
"The king Śikhin, of slender form and the luster of pure gold, will bring an end to my slow-witted sons in battle.
O Kurus, understand this: I consider it best that we do not fight with them."
In battle, the destruction of the entire lineage will be certain.
This is my supreme peace, by which my mind is pacified:
if you desire non-battle, we shall strive for peace.
"Yudhiṣṭhira will not overlook us while we are training;
for he detests unrighteousness, making me himself the reason.
Saṃjaya said:
"O Great King, O Bhārata, it is exactly as you say:
the destruction of the Kṣatriyas in battle through the Gāṇḍīva bow is clearly foreseen.
But this I do not understand, regarding you who are ever steadfast."
"O knower of beings, if you should fall under the power of your son,
this is not the time for you, O great king, who have committed constant offenses,
for it was by you alone, O bull of the Bharatas, that the sons of Pṛthā were treated with deceit from the very beginning."
Those Kuru territories, including the Jāṅgala regions, have been taken over by them.
O hero, how will you recover this entire land that has been conquered? Your father was the best of men, a friend who had perfectly disciplined his self.
For one must abide by what is beneficial; one who acts with malice is not called a guru.
O Great King, hearing that they were defeated at the time of the dice game, you smiled like a child, thinking, "This is won! This is gained!"
In the past, you overlooked the Pārthas even as they were being addressed with harsh words, saying, "They are winning the entire kingdom. O Great King, you did not perceive the precipice;
yet the Kauravas, along with the Jāṅgalas, possess that ancestral kingdom of yours.

In the great battle they sought [victory], yet you did not consider the consequences; then you obtained the entire earth conquered by the heroes. This earth, acquired through the prowess of their arms, has been offered to you by the sons of Pṛthā.
"O best of kings, you think to yourself, 'This was done by me. Yet,
O best of kings, it was Pārtha who brought back your sons, who had been seized by the king of the Gandharvas and were sinking in a boatless sea."
And you smiled like a boy when the Pāṇḍavas had been defeated at dice, O King, as they were departing for the forest again and again;
[and you watched] Arjuna raining down many sharp volleys of arrows.
Even the oceans might dry up, how much more so those born of flesh?
Phalguna, the best of archers, hurls the Gandiva, the foremost of bows; and Keshava [wields] the Sudarshana among all weapons for all beings.
Vānara, Rocamāna, and Ketu— the best among those who possess banners—
these, borne by the white-horsed chariot in battle,
O King, will destroy us like the uplifted wheel of Time.
O King, O bull of the Bharatas, today this entire earth belongs to him who has Bhīma and Arjuna as his warriors; he is the king, O best of monarchs.
Thus, your army, mostly slaughtered by Bhīma, is sinking down.
Seeing this, the Kauravas, headed by Duryodhana, will go to their destruction; for,
O Lord, your sons and the kings who follow them will not achieve victory, being terrified by the fear of Bhīma, O Great King.
Today the Matsyas do not honor you, nor do the Pañcālas along with the Kekayas;
the Śālveyas and the Śūrasenas—all of them disregard you.
For all these have gone over to Pārtha, knowing the prowess of that wise one.
Indeed, because of their devotion to him, they have always been at odds with your sons; yet he,
who through unrighteous conduct caused suffering to the sons of Pāṇḍu— who were unworthy of death and endowed with virtue— still harbors hatred toward them even now.
"O Great King, this sinful man must be restrained by every possible means along with his followers;
I tell you this directly and openly, O Great King:
he is your son, and you ought not to grieve over this."

O Bharata, O Indra among kings, all this lamentation of yours regarding the Pāṇḍavas is as useless as it was when I and the wise Vidura spoke at the time of the gambling match, for you were like one who is powerless.
Duryodhana said:
"O great king, you must not fear; we are not to be grieved for by you.
O lord of men, O sovereign, we are capable of conquering our enemies in battle."
When Madhusūdana arrived with a vast army capable of crushing enemy kingdoms to see the Pārthas who had gone into exile in the forest,
there were the Kekayas, Dhṛṣṭaketu, and Dhṛṣṭadyumna, the son of Pṛṣata.
Many other kings followed as attendants of the sons of Pṛthā;
those great car-warriors gathered not far from Indraprastha,
and having come together, they censured you along with the Kurus.
O Bhārata, those kings, led by Kṛṣṇa, gathered together and sat around Yudhiṣṭhira as he sat clothed in deerskins;
they spoke of the task of reclaiming the kingdom.

O King, bull of the Bharatas, desiring to bring about the total destruction of you and your followers, Bhīṣma, Droṇa, and Kṛpa were then addressed by me when I was terrified by the fear of the destruction of my kinsmen.
"It is my conviction that the Pāṇḍavas will not abide by their agreement;
for Vāsudeva intends to bring about our total destruction.
With the exception of Vidura, all of you are to be slain by that high-souled one."

"And Dhṛtarāṣṭra, the knower of dharma, that best of the Kurus, must not be slain. Having brought about our total destruction, O dear one, Janārdana desires to establish a single kingdom for the Kurus under Yudhiṣṭhira."
In this situation, what is appropriate for us now: prostration, flight, or do we fight the enemy while completely abandoning our lives? For in battle, our defeat is certain.
For all the kings are subject to Yudhiṣṭhira’s will;
our kingdom is alienated, our friends are angry with us, and we have been censured on all sides by all the kings and by our own kinsmen.
There is indeed a fault in bowing down to one's kinsmen for eternal years;
however, I grieve only for my father, the lord of men, who has wisdom as his eye,
and who has fallen into suffering and reached infinite distress on my account.
"O best of men, you already knew long ago that your sons had besieged the enemies for my sake;
indeed, those great car-warriors have done so along with King Dhṛtarāṣṭra and his ministers."
"The Pāṇḍavas will avenge their enmity by the destruction of our lineage.
Then, O Bhārata, Droṇa, Bhīṣma, Kṛpa, and the son of Droṇa spoke,
perceiving that I was plunged into great anxiety with my senses distressed.

"O scorcher of foes, O lord of men, even if our enemies should attack us, we must not fear; for the enemies are incapable of conquering us in battle. Each one of us individually is capable of defeating all the kings of the earth."
"Let them come; we shall subdue their pride with sharp arrows.
For in the past, O Bhārata, all the kings were conquered by Bhīṣma alone with a single chariot when his father had died and he was filled with wrath."
Enraged, that best of the Kurus struck down very many of them;
then, out of fear, they sought refuge with this Devavrata.
This Bhīṣma is highly capable when joined by us in battle.
"Therefore, O bull of the Bharatas, let your fear of conquering the enemies depart. Such was the resolve at that time of those men of immeasurable energy;
for in former times, the entire earth was under the control of their enemies.
"Furthermore, these others are not capable of conquering us in battle today; for the Pāṇḍavas are now like birds with severed wings, devoid of prowess,
O bull of the Bharatas, and the earth remains established under our control."
"O scorcher of enemies, O best of the Kurus, know this: all these kings have been brought by me to a single purpose regarding pleasure and pain; they would even enter fire or the ocean for my sake."
They laugh at you here as if you were mad— distressed,
lamenting in many ways, and terrified by the boasts of others—
yet each one of these kings is individually capable [of defeating] the Pāṇḍavas.
Everyone considers themselves superior; let this fear that has come upon you depart.
Even Vāsava himself would not be able to destroy my entire army in its full strength, for it is of an inexhaustible nature, even by the self-existent Brahmā himself.
"Yudhiṣṭhira, having abandoned his city, begs for only five villages,
O Lord, for he is terrified of my army and of my power. And as for Vṛkodara, the son of Kuntī, you consider him capable."
"That is false, O Bhārata, for you do not know my full power. Indeed, there is no one on earth equal to me in combat with the mace;
none has ever surpassed me, nor shall anyone ever do so."
I am disciplined and accustomed to hardship, and likewise have mastered the sciences;
therefore, I have no fear of Bhīma or others anywhere. It is my certain conviction that there is no one equal to Duryodhana in the use of the mace.

"Blessings to you! It was fortunate that I encountered Saṃkarṣaṇa in battle—he who is equal to Saṃkarṣaṇa in strength and superior to anyone on earth. Bhīma would never have been able to withstand the blow of his mace in combat."
O King, that single blow which I might deal to Bhīma in my wrath would swiftly lead him to the terrible abode of Vaivasvata.
And I wish, O King, to see Vṛkodara with mace in hand.
For this has been my constant desire, long cherished:
that Vṛkodara, Pārtha, struck by my mace in battle,
shall fall lifeless upon the earth with his limbs shattered.
Even the Himavat mountain, were it struck but once by me with the blow of my mace, would shatter into a hundred thousand pieces;
and he likewise knows this of Vāsudeva and Arjuna.
"It is certain that there is no one equal to Duryodhana in the use of the mace;
therefore, let this fear of Vṛkodara in the great battle depart from you.
For I shall remove him [from the field]; do not be despondent, O King."
O bull of the Bharatas, once he has been swiftly slain by me, many chariot-warriors— both equal and superior in form— to Arjuna will launch their attacks:
Bhīṣma, Droṇa, Kṛpa, the son of Droṇa, Karṇa, and likewise Bhūriśravas.
Śalya, the lord of Prāgjyotiṣa, and Jayadratha, the king of Sindhu—
each one of these, O Bhārata, is capable of slaying the Pāṇḍavas;
yet together, they will send them to the abode of Yama in an instant.
"The entire army of the earth was unable to defeat Dhananjaya, the solitary son of Pṛthā—
no reason for this can be found.
Yet, by Bhīṣma, with volleys of arrows by the hundreds and thousands,"
"O Bhārata, with Droṇa, the son of Droṇa, and Kṛpa, Pārtha shall go to the abode of Yama; for the grandfather Gaṅgeya, born of Śantanu,
was equal to a Brahmarṣi and difficult even for the gods to withstand."
"O King, there is no one at all who can slay Bhīṣma;
for he was told by his gratified father, 'You shall not die against your will.
And Droṇa was born from the Brahman-sage Bharadvāja in a wooden vessel."

O great king, from Droṇa was born the son of Droṇa (Aśvatthāman), who is a knower of the supreme weapons; and this Kṛpa, the foremost of teachers, was born from the great ṛṣi Gautama from a clump of reeds—
it is my opinion that this illustrious one is also indestructible.

"O Great King, these three—Aśvatthāman, his father, and his maternal uncle—are indeed not born from a womb; and that hero stands on my side. All these, O Great King, are god-like great chariot-warriors."
O bull of the Bharatas, they could cause even Śakra distress in battle;
Arjuna is not capable of even looking at each one of them individually,
yet these tigers among men, when united, will slay Dhanañjaya.
"O Bhārata, in my estimation, Karṇa is equal to Bhīṣma, Droṇa, and Kṛpa;
and he was granted permission by Rāma, who said, 'You are my equal. Moreover, O Bhārata, Karṇa possessed two beautiful, auspicious earrings that were born with him."

O great king, that scorcher of foes was requested by Mahendra for the sake of Śacī; he was given an unfailing spear of supreme terror. How could Dhanañjaya live once he has been struck down by that spear?
"O King, my victory is certain, as if the fruit were already placed in my hand;
the total defeat of the enemies on earth is manifest.
For in a single day, O Bhārata, this Bhīṣma slays ten thousand."
O scorcher of foes, even those great archers Drona, Ashvatthaman, and Kripa were equal to him; and so too were the hosts of Samshaptaka kshatriyas,
who used to say, "Either Arjuna shall defeat us, or we shall defeat Dhananjaya."
O Lord, those kings consider themselves sufficient for the slaying of Savyasācin; O King, why then do you suddenly feel such distress? And if Bhīmasena were slain, O Bhārata, who else would fight?

O scorcher of foes, tell me that if you know it; for when the Pāñcālas have been broken, who else here would be able to stand? Your five brothers, as well as Dhṛṣṭadyumna and Sātyaki—[all these have fled].
"O King, those seven warriors of the enemy are their supreme strength;
whereas for us, there are Bhīṣma, Droṇa, Kṛpa, and the others— Aśvatthāman, Karṇa the son of Vikartana, Somadatta, and Bāhlika."
Śalya, the lord of Prāgjyotiṣa; then Jayadratha of Avanti;
Duḥśāsana, Durmukha, and Duḥsaha, O lord of the people;
Śrutāyus, Citrasena, Purumitra, and Viviṃśati.
Śala, Bhūriśravas, and both you and your son Vikarṇa—
O King, eleven Akṣauhiṇīs have indeed been assembled for me,
while those of the enemy are only seven; why then should I suffer defeat?

"Bṛhaspati has declared that one should fight an enemy whose strength is deficient by a third; O King, this army of mine is three times greater than those of the others. Furthermore, O Bhārata, I see many deficiencies in the forces of my enemies."
O lord of the people, O Bhārata, having fully understood all this— the emergence of my own many virtues, the excellence of my army,
and the inferiority of the Pāṇḍavas— you ought not to fall into delusion.
05,054.066 Vaiśampāyana said: Having spoken thus to Saṃjaya once more, O Bhārata, that conqueror of enemy cities, knowing that the time had come, desired to inquire further.
Duryodhana said:
"O Sañjaya, having obtained seven akṣauhiṇīs along with the kings,
what does Yudhiṣṭhira, the son of Kuntī, desire now that he is eager for battle?"
Saṃjaya said:
"O King, Yudhiṣṭhira was exceedingly joyful, longing for battle;
and both Bhīmasena and Arjuna, as well as the twins, were likewise not afraid."
Then the son of Kuntī, Bībhatsu, illuminating all directions with his divine chariot,
yoked it while desiring to test the mantra.
We beheld him clad in armor, like a cloud flashing with lightning.
Having meditated upon the mantras, he spoke with joy:
"Behold this omen, Sañjaya; we shall be victorious.
I perceive it exactly as Bibhatsu has told me."
Duryodhana said:
"You praise and welcome those sons of Pṛthā who were defeated at dice; tell me, what are the horses like on Arjuna’s chariot, and what is his banner?"
Saṃjaya said:
