O lord of the people, O illustrious one, Bhaumana, together with Śakra, Tvaṣṭṛ, and Dhātṛ, fashioned many wonderful forms.
Indeed, by means of divine illusion, they fashioned upon that banner forms of great value—
divine, massive, and yet light—
in order to please Bhīmasena; among them was Hanumān, the son of the Wind-god.
He shall place an image of himself upon that banner;
that banner indeed obstructed all directions for a distance of one yojana, both horizontally and upwards.
Though surrounded by trees, he would not become entangled;
for it was created as an illusion by the celestial architect,
just as Indra’s bow appears in the sky.
It is not of a single color, nor do we know what it truly is; yet,
fashioned by Bhauvana,
its form appears in many shapes.
Just as smoke, rising and obstructing the sky,
carries its fiery color upward,
so was this banner ordained by Bhauvana.
If there were neither burden nor obstruction,
those white, excellent steeds, swift as the wind, yoked to the chariot of variegated splendor and given by Divya, would have been present.
O Lord of Men, whether on earth, in the intermediate space, or in heaven,
the movement of these [beings] never fails;
for that hundred is always being filled.
Just as those previously granted boons were slain one by one,
so too do the large, ivory-colored horses, equal in prowess to him, shine as they are yoked to the king’s chariot.
The steeds of Bhīmasena were as white as rishya deer;
in battle, they possessed a speed equal to that of the wind.
Their limbs were dappled, and their backs were variegated like those of partridges.
Given by his brother Phalguna out of affection,
these horses, superior even to those of his heroic brother,
carry Sahadeva with joy.
To Nakula, the son of Mādrī and descendant of Ajamīḍha,
were given excellent bay horses, bestowed by Mahendra—
horses equal to the wind in strength and speed.
They carry the hero, the slayer of Vṛtra, like Indra;
and these noble steeds are his equals in age and prowess, and are matchless in speed.
"The large, divine horses Devadatta carry the princes, the son of Subhadrā and the sons of Draupadī.
Dhṛtarāṣṭra said:
"O Sañjaya, whom did you see there assembled for the sake of their respective causes—
those who will fight on behalf of the Pāṇḍavas against the army of my son?
Sañjaya said:
I saw Kṛṣṇa, the chief of the Andhakas and Vṛṣṇis, arrive there, along with Cekitāna and Yuyudhāna Sātyaki;
these two had joined the Pāṇḍavas, each with a separate akṣauhiṇī.
Both were renowned as great chariot-warriors (*mahāratha*) and considered themselves superior men.
Then the Pāñcālya king, surrounded by his ten sons—
heroes led by Satyajit and headed by Dhṛṣṭadyumna— arrived with an *akṣauhiṇī* division.
Drupada, increasing his honor and protected by Śikhaṇḍin,
arrived then, having concealed his form from all the troops;
so too did Virāṭa, together with his two sons, Śaṅkha and Uttara.
Accompanied by the heroes Sūryadatta and others led by Madirāśva,
as well as his brothers and sons, the protector of the earth took refuge with Pārtha, surrounded by an akṣauhiṇī of troops.
Jārāsaṃdhi the Māgadha and Dhṛṣṭaketu the king of the Cedis arrived separately, each surrounded by an akṣauhiṇī; likewise,
the five Kekaya brothers all had red banners.
Surrounded by an *akṣauhiṇī*, they have taken refuge with the Pāṇḍavas.
Of all these who were seen gathered there,
they are the ones who will fight against the army of Dhṛtarāṣṭra’s son for the sake of the Pāṇḍavas.
He who knows the human, divine, Gandharva, and Asura arrays—
that high-minded Dhṛṣṭadyumna stands at the head of his army.
O King, Bhīṣma, the son of Śāntanu, has been assigned as the portion for Śikhaṇḍin.
Virāṭa, along with the Matsya warriors skilled in striking, followed him;
the powerful lord of Madra was the allotted portion for the eldest son of Pāṇḍu.
Regarding those two, some there said, "In our opinion, they are unequal."
Duryodhana, together with his sons and his hundred brothers,
as well as the Easterners and the Southerners, were assigned to the portion of Bhīmasena;
whereas Karṇa Vaikartana was considered the portion of Arjuna.
Aśvatthāman, Vikarṇa, Jayadratha the king of the Sindhus,
and whoever else on earth considers himself a hero—
Arjuna Pārtha has assigned them all as his share.
The five Kekaya princes, brothers and mighty archers, having assigned the Kekayas themselves as their share, will fight in the battle. The Malavas, Shalvas, and Kekayas have been made their portion.
The two leaders of the Trigartas who were known as the Saṃśaptakas,
all the sons of Duryodhana, as well as those of Duḥśāsana,
and King Bṛhadbala— this was the portion assigned to the son of Subhadrā.
O Bhārata, the sons of Draupadī— mighty archers with banners adorned in gold— led by Dhṛṣṭadyumna, will advance against Droṇa. Cekitāna,
for his part, desires to engage Somadatta in a single combat of chariots.
Yuyudhāna desires to fight with Kṛtavarman, the Bhoja;
and the heroic Sahadeva, the son of Mādrī, who roars in battle,
has assigned his own share to your brother-in-law, the son of Subala.
Nakula, the son of Mādravatī, assigned a share for Ulūka the son of Kitava, as well as for the hosts of the Sārasvatas; and he likewise assigned shares,
O King, for whatever other kings shall advance against him in battle.
And by means of that summons, the sons of Pāṇḍu also arrayed them;
thus were their armies divided into their respective parts.
Whatever task you have to perform with your son, let that be done without delay.
Dhṛtarāṣṭra said:
"All my sons are as good as dead— those foolish, wicked gamblers—
who must face battle with the mighty Bhīma at the forefront of the fray."
All the kings of the earth, consecrated by the law of time,
shall enter the fire of the Gāṇḍīva like moths into a flame;
I consider the army already shattered by those high-souled ones with whom they have long harbored enmity.
Who will follow her in battle when she is broken by the Pāṇḍavas in combat?
For all [your warriors] are great car-warriors (atiratha), heroes, renowned, and majestic;
they are equal to the sun and fire in splendor and are victors in assembly.
Those for whom Yudhiṣṭhira is the leader and Madhusūdana is the protector,
and who have as their warriors the two heroic Pāṇḍavas, Savyasācin and Vṛkodara,
as well as Nakula, Sahadeva, and Dhṛṣṭadyumna, the son of Pṛṣata—
Sātyaki, Drupada, and the son of Dhṛṣṭadyumna; Uttamaujas the Pāñcālya, Yudhāmanyu who is difficult to conquer,
Śikhaṇḍin, Kṣatradeva, and likewise Uttara the son of Virāṭa.
Then Śveta, the son of Virāṭa, the banner-bearing commander of the army,
as well as the Kāśis, the Cedis, all the Matsyas, and the Sṛñjayas—
the son of Virāṭa, Babhru, and the Pāñcālas and Prabhadrakas— [all advanced].
Even Indra could not take this earth from those heroes who are steadfast in battle and capable of splitting even mountains, were they unwilling;
all of them are endowed with every virtue and possess a prowess that surpasses that of mortals.
"O Sañjaya, while I am crying out, my wicked son desires to fight.
Duryodhana said:
"Both of us belong to the same species, and likewise both of us are dwellers of the earth."
Then why do you consider victory for the Pāṇḍavas to be certain,
when there are the Grandfather [Bhīṣma], Droṇa, Kṛpa, and the invincible Karṇa,
as well as Jayadratha, Somadatta, and Aśvatthāman?
"Even Indra, accompanied by the immortals, was unable to defeat those high-souled, great archers in battle; how much less so, my dear, could the Pāṇḍavas?
Furthermore, O dear one, the entire earth was created for my sake against the Pāṇḍavas."

The Pāṇḍavas are not capable even of looking upon my men, who are noble, steadfast, heroic, and like fire itself, were they to attack them. For I am fully prepared to fight the Pāṇḍus along with their sons in battle.
O Bhārata, all those kings who desire to do what is pleasing to me will restrain them with a great multitude of chariots and my own nets of arrows, as if binding deer with a cord.
"The Pāñcālas, together with the Pāṇḍavas, will be pursued.
Dhṛtarāṣṭra said:
"O Sañjaya, this son of mine laments like one who is mad."
For Bhīṣma is not able to conquer Yudhiṣṭhira, the King of Dharma,
in battle; indeed, Bhīṣma always knows the strength of the illustrious Pāṇḍavas— those high-souled ones who know the dharma— along with their sons.
Since I did not report a conflict with those high-souled ones,
tell me again, Sañjaya, what their actions were;
who further incites those powerful Pāṇḍavas?
[They were] radiant, great archers, like fires fed with oblations.
Sañjaya said:
"O Bhārata, Dhṛṣṭadyumna always inflames these [warriors]."
"Fight! Do not fear the battle, O best of the Bharatas!
Whatever kings are there gathered with the son of Dhṛtarāṣṭra will encounter you in a tumultuous battle, a lake of armor."
"I alone shall seize all those who have gathered in battle, enraged and accompanied by their followers— like a fisherman seizing fish from the water—
including Bhīṣma, Droṇa, Kṛpa, Karṇa, the son of Droṇa, Śalya, and Suyodhana."
"And I shall restrain these [enemies] as the shore restrains the ocean, the abode of sea-monsters.
To him who was speaking thus, the righteous King Yudhiṣṭhira said:
"The Pañcālas, together with the Pāṇḍavas, acknowledge both your fortitude and your heroism."
"We have all ascended [to our chariots]; deliver us from this battle!
O mighty-armed one, I know you to be firmly established in the duty of a Kṣatriya, alone capable and sufficient for the Kauravas who desire to fight."
O scorcher of the foe, whatever you must ordain for us regarding the restraint of the Kauravas who have arrived before us— that shall be for our supreme welfare.

That man who stands at the front, displaying his prowess, for those who have retreated from battle, broken and seeking refuge— that man a hero would purchase for a thousand; such a state is indeed called "statesmanship" (*nīti*).
"You are a hero, a warrior, and one of great prowess, O bull among men;
you are undoubtedly the protector of those afflicted by fear in battles.
While the son of Kuntī, Yudhiṣṭhira, whose soul is dharma, was speaking thus—
Dhṛṣṭadyumna, free from fear, spoke these words to me:
"O Sūta, you should speak to all the warriors of Duryodhana throughout every land— the Kurus along with the Bāhlīkas, the Prātipeyas, and the sons of Śaradvat."
"Go quickly and speak to the Sūta’s son, as well as Droṇa with his son, Jayadratha, Duḥśāsana, Vikarṇa, and King Duryodhana, and likewise to Bhīṣma."
Approach Yudhiṣṭhira with only virtuous intent;
let not Arjuna, protected by the gods, slay you.
Quickly entreat that Pāṇḍava, the hero of the world.
"Quickly bestow the kingdom upon the King of Dharma; for there is no warrior whatsoever here on this earth such as Savyasācin, the son of Pāṇḍu, who is the most skilled among those who know weapons."
"For this divine chariot of the wielder of the Gāṇḍīva bow was fashioned by the gods;
it cannot be conquered by a mere mortal. Do not set your minds on battle.
Dhṛtarāṣṭra said:

The son of Pāṇḍu possesses the splendor of a Kṣatriya and has been a celibate student since his youth; the fools will encounter him in battle even as I lament. O Duryodhana, best of the Bharatas, desist from war!

O subduer of enemies, they do not praise war under any circumstances. Half of the earth is sufficient for you to live upon, together with your ministers; O subduer of enemies, grant to the sons of Pāṇḍu what is their due.
For all the Kurus consider it consistent with righteousness that you should desire peace with the high-souled sons of Pāṇḍu. O son, look instead at this army of your own.
"Your infamy has already been born, yet you do not perceive it due to delusion.
For I do not desire war, nor does Bāhlīka;
neither Bhīṣma, nor Droṇa, nor Aśvatthāman, nor Saṃjaya desires it."
Neither Somadatta, nor Śalya, nor Kṛpa desires battle;
neither Satyavrata, Purumitra, Jaya, nor Bhūriśravas likewise.
Upon whomsoever the Kurus, when oppressed by their enemies, might rely for support—[they all desire peace].

They do not rejoice in battle; therefore, my dear son, let that be pleasing to you. You do not act out of desire; rather, Karṇa is the one who makes you act, as well as the evil-souled Duḥśāsana and Śakuni, the son of Subala.
Duryodhana said: "Neither in you, nor in Droṇa, nor in Aśvatthāman, nor in Saṃjaya,
nor in Vikarṇa, nor in the king of Kamboja, nor in Kṛpa, nor in Bāhlika do I find [such confidence]."
"O Satyavrata, Purumitra, or Bhūriśravas,
or indeed among any others of your side, having placed the burden upon them, I challenge you. And I, O dear one, and Karṇa, having truly spread out the sacrifice of battle— "
O bull of the Bharatas, having consecrated Yudhiṣṭhira as the sacrificial victim,
the chariot was the altar, the sword the *sruva* ladle, the mace the *sruk* offering-spoon, and the armor the sacrificial hall.
My four lead horses constituted the *cāturhotra* ritual, the arrows were the *darbha* grass, and my glory was the oblation.
"O King, having performed the sacrifice of the self through battle against the son of Vivasvat,
and having conquered him, we two shall return together, surrounded by glory and with our enemies slain—
myself, O dear one, Karṇa, and my brother Duḥśāsana."
"Only these three of us shall slay the Pāṇḍavas in battle.
For either I, having slain the Pāṇḍavas, shall rule this earth;
or else, having slain me, the sons of Pāṇḍu shall enjoy this earth."
"O King, O Ruler of the Earth, I have renounced my life, my wealth, and my kingdom.
O Acyuta, I would never dwell together with the Pāṇḍavas—
not even for as long as it takes to pierce me with the point of a sharp needle, O Noble One."
"Even that much land should not be surrendered by us to the Pāṇḍavas.
Dhṛtarāṣṭra said:
"O dear one, I grieve for all of you; Duryodhana has been abandoned by me."
Those who follow you slowly as you proceed toward the abode of Vaivasvata—
the Pāṇḍavas, the best among strikers— will, having gathered together in battle, slay the very best of your warriors, just as tigers strike at herds of ruru deer.
The Bharata host appears to me as if turned back by Yuyudhāna,
like a terrified woman with disheveled hair being dragged away by a long-armed man;
meanwhile, Mādhava further replenishes the full force of Pārtha.

The descendant of Śini will stand in battle sowing arrows like seeds; Bhīmasena will be at the head of those fighting in the vanguard. All will take refuge in him as in a rampart that affords fearlessness from every side.
When you see the mountain-like elephants brought down by Bhīma—
shattered tusks, split frontal globes, and covered in blood—
beholding them in battle like crumbling mountains;
Terrified by the touch of Bhīma, you will remember my words;
seeing your army— its chariots and elephants destroyed— consumed by Bhīmasena like the course of a fire, you will remember my words.
A great danger shall come upon you if you do not make peace with the Pāṇḍavas;
you shall find rest only when you have been struck down by Bhīmasena’s mace,
like a vast forest cut down and laid low.
"In battle, you shall remember my words regarding the strength of the Kurus.
Vaiśampāyana said:
Having spoken thus, the king addressed all those lords of the earth.
Having addressed him thus, O Great King, he questioned Sañjaya again.
Dhṛtarāṣṭra said:
"What did those two high-souled ones, Vāsudeva and Dhanañjaya, say?"
"Tell me that, O one of great wisdom; I wish to hear your words.
Saṃjaya said:
"Listen, O King, to how Kṛṣṇa and Dhanañjaya were seen by me."
O Bhārata, I shall tell you what those two heroes said; O King,
with my palms joined in reverence and looking toward their toes,
I entered the inner apartments to report [the matter] to the two gods among men.
Neither Abhimanyu nor the twins ever go to that place where the two Kṛṣṇas, Draupadī, and the beautiful Satyabhāmā reside—
where both are intoxicated by honeyed wine and both are anointed with sandalwood paste.
I saw Keśava and Arjuna lying upon a single couch;
they were wearing garlands and excellent garments, adorned with celestial ornaments.
And there was a great golden seat, variegated with many jewels.
Spread with various coverlets, upon which those two subduers of enemies lay;
Janārdana, however, lay there using Satyabhāmā as his pillow. I observed Keśava’s feet resting upon Arjuna’s lap.
And when Arjuna, the great-souled one, was with Kṛṣṇā and Satyā,
Pārtha then assigned me a golden footstool.
Having touched it with my hand, I then sat down upon the ground.
The soles of Pārtha’s feet were marked with upward-pointing lines and possessed auspicious characteristics; there I saw those two beautiful feet raised from their footstool.
Surely, no trace of blemish exists within my own deeds.
When those two jewels among women, joined together, addressed me in turn,
I was filled with great wonder; my weapons seemed to gather in abundance,
and my hair stood on end upon seeing them both united.
Seeing those two dark-complexioned, tall, and youthful men, rising like the trunks of *śāla* trees,
seated together upon a single seat, a great fear entered me. Then, having seen those two bulls among men there, I reflected:

These two are equal to Indra and Viṣṇu; the dull-witted man does not perceive this, due to his reliance on Droṇa and Bhīṣma and because of Karṇa’s boasting. He whose mind abides by their command shall achieve success.
At that time, the resolve of Dharmarāja became my firm determination:
"Honored with food and drink, clothed and having received due hospitality,
I placed my joined palms upon my head and urged them to deliver the message."

With one hand accustomed to wielding the bow and arrow, Pārtha pressed down the foot marked with auspicious signs and urged Keśava forward. Rising up like the banner of Indra, he was adorned with every ornament.
Resembling the prowess of Indra, Kṛṣṇa,
who is the best among those who speak, addressed me with words that were gladdening and eloquent,
yet terrifying to the sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra— words that were gentle at first but ultimately most formidable.
The wise Keśava, having fixed his mind upon the thought of the external vital breath— who is dear and acts for the pleasure [of others]— uttered these words,
which were worthy of one capable of speech and endowed with perfect phonetic refinement.
"I heard that news which fulfilled my desires, yet later it withered my heart.
Vāsudeva said:
"O Sañjaya, speak these words to the wise Dhṛtarāṣṭra:"
While the chief of the Kurus was listening, and while Droṇa was also listening, O Sūta,
[speak] these words of ours: "Salute even the elders,
and after first asking about the welfare of those who are younger, give this reply."
Sacrifice with extensive sacrifices and give sacrificial fees to the brahmins;
rejoice with your sons and wives, for a great danger has come upon you. Renounce wealth for the sake of worthy recipients and obtain sons born of your desires.
"Go to those you love; for the king hastens toward victory.
This debt has grown great and will not depart from my heart—that Kṛṣṇā cried out 'Govinda! to me while I was dwelling far away."
"He whose bow is the Gāṇḍīva, composed of fire and invincible,
he who has me as his second— by that Savyasācin you have here incurred enmity.
Upon hearing these words of Kṛṣṇa, a great fear entered me.
But for one who perceives the greed currently existing in your son,
who would wish to challenge Pārtha, with me as his second,
unless he were even Purandara himself overtaken by Time?
He who could lift the earth with his two arms, burn these creatures when enraged,
and cast down the gods from heaven— he alone could conquer Arjuna in battle,
among gods, asuras, and humans, or among yakṣas, gandharvas, and serpents.
I do not see any Pāṇḍava who could advance against him in battle.
That great and wonderful feat which was heard of in the city of Virāṭa—
when one man [overcame] many— is sufficient proof of this.
When they were shattered by a single son of Pāṇḍu in the city of Virāṭa and fled in all directions— that was sufficient proof of his strength,
heroism, energy, speed, and lightness of hand.
"Neither lack of despondency nor fortitude exists anywhere other than among the sons of Pṛthā.
Sañjaya said:
Thus spoke Hṛṣīkeśa, gladdening Pārtha with his words.
Roaring like Indra, the subduer of Pāka, who rains at the appointed time in the sky,
Arjuna— known as Kirīṭin and Śvetavāhana— having heard Keśava’s words, spoke this great speech that caused the hair to stand on end.
Vaiśampāyana said:
Having heard the words of Saṃjaya, the lord of men, whose eye is wisdom,
then began to enumerate those words according to their merits and defects.
Having carefully analyzed the merits and defects with subtlety, the wise and discerning man,
desiring victory for his sons, determined their relative strengths and weaknesses according to the true nature of things through the essence of his intellect.
But when that wise lord of men had thoroughly considered those words regarding their merits and defects, he then began once again to calculate the relative strength of the Kurus and the Pāṇḍavas.
With his power and splendor, he [protected] the Pāṇḍavas against both gods and men; but toward the Kurus, and especially Duryodhana, he spoke with diminished power. Then he said to Duryodhana:
"O Duryodhana, this anxiety of mine never ceases."

O dear one, I do not approve at all of this conflict with the Pāṇḍavas— an undertaking that is so firmly adhered to by you, which will cause the destruction of the earth, and which is unrighteous, disgraceful, great, and terrible.
I consider this to be true, perceived directly rather than by inference:
all living beings feel supreme affection for their own offspring,
and they do what is pleasing and beneficial for them to the best of their ability.
In this very way, we generally observe that virtuous people,
having been benefited, often desire to return a great favor.
Remembering what was done for him at Khāṇḍava, Agni would act as his ally.
In this most terrifying encounter between the Kurus and the Pāṇḍavas,
Dharma and the other gods, having been summoned, will appear in great numbers among the Pāṇḍavas, overcome by a desire for victory.

Out of fear of Bhīṣma, Droṇa, Kṛpa, and the others, it is my conviction that they will display a fury equal to a thunderbolt, desiring to protect [him]. Those sons of Pṛthā, accompanied by the gods, cannot even be looked upon.
O tigers among men, those heroes who have mastered weapons and are full of prowess are human;
yet his supreme, divine bow Gāṇḍīva is unassailable,
as are his two great, divine, and inexhaustible quivers filled with arrows.
His divine banner bears the emblem of a monkey, its movement is unimpeded like smoke,
and his chariot has no equal in brilliance across the four quarters of the earth;
moreover, a roar resembling that of a great cloud is heard by the people.
A sound like a great thunderbolt, terrifying to his enemies,
which the entire world recognizes as superhuman in its prowess;
he whom the kings know to be a conqueror even of the gods in battle.
He appeared as if he were discharging five hundred arrows at once,
releasing them in the mere blink of an eye and striking them down at a great distance—
him whom Bhīṣma, Droṇa, Kṛpa, and likewise the son of Droṇa had praised.
Then Śalya, the king of Madra, as well as those men who stood as mediators,
[beheld] Pārtha— standing ready for battle, that tiger among chariot-warriors and subduer of foes— who was impossible for kings of superhuman prowess to defeat.
That Pāṇḍava, who with a single impulse shoots five hundred arrows, who is equal to Kārtavīrya in the strength of his arms—
that Arjuna, the great archer protected by Mahendra and Upendra— [is here].
"I see him as if he were slaughtering [the enemy] in this crushing great battle"—
thinking thus, O Bhārata, throughout all my days and nights, I have been sleepless and devoid of happiness, consumed by thoughts of peace for the Kurus.
"This immense destruction of the Kurus has arrived;
if there is no end to this strife other than through peace, then,
my dear son, peace always pleases me, not war with the sons of Pṛthā."
"For I always consider the Pāṇḍavas to be more powerful than the Kurus.
Vaiśampāyana said:
Having heard these words of his father, the son of Dhṛtarāṣṭra became exceedingly indignant.
Having summoned a great rage, he spoke these words once again:
"O best of kings, let that fear which you harbor— that the sons of Pṛthā, being assisted by the gods, might be invincible— be dispelled from your heart."
"O Bhārata, through freedom from desire and hatred, through absence of malice and greed,
and through equanimity toward all beings, the gods attained their divine status.
Thus spoke Dvaipāyana Vyāsa and Nārada of great asceticism.
And Rāma, the son of Jamadagni, told us this story in the past:
"O bull of the Bharatas, the gods never act like humans out of desire, greed, compassion, or hatred."

For if Agni, Vāyu, Dharma, Indra, and even the Aśvins were to act out of attachment to desire, the sons of Pṛthā would not have encountered suffering. Therefore, you should never entertain such anxiety.
O Bhārata, these gods are indeed ever-watchful over all states of being.
If, however, they are observed to act out of attachment to desire, hatred, or greed,
then that authority of the gods will not prevail among the gods themselves.
Constantly consecrated by me, Jātavedas, desiring to consume all the worlds, surveys them on every side;
or rather, he is the supreme splendor endowed with which the dwellers of heaven [shine].
O Bhārata, know that my power is even more incomparable than that of the gods;
O King, while the world looks on, I can, through the power of my mantras, stabilize the earth and the peaks of mountains even as they are being torn asunder.
This most terrible and loud-sounding [weapon], arisen for the destruction of this world of sentient and insentient beings, both moving and stationary,
I constantly pacify here with showers of stones and winds.
Out of compassion for all beings as I constantly behold the world,
chariots and foot-soldiers travel over waters that have been solidified by me;
I alone am the one who sets in motion the destinies of both gods and asuras.
"O King, whatever regions I travel with my akṣauhiṇī armies for any purpose,
there the waters flow for me wherever I desire.
Within my domain, O King, there are no dangers such as predatory beasts."

O King, even terrifying beings do not harm creatures while they are asleep because of me; the rain-cloud pours forth according to desire for those dwelling within my realm, all subjects are most righteous, and no calamities exist for me.
The Aśvins, as well as Vāyu and Agni together with the Maruts, and Dharma— the Slayer of Vṛtra and these others— do not venture to protect those who are hated by me;
for if they were capable of protecting my enemies by their power, they would do so.
For thirteen years, the sons of Pṛthā would not have experienced such suffering;
neither gods, nor Gandharvas, nor Asuras, nor Rākṣasas would have been able to protect one hated by me. I tell you this truth.
"Whatever I constantly intend, whether it be auspicious or inauspicious,
O scorcher of foes, this has never before failed me regarding both friends and enemies; and whatever I say, 'this shall come to pass,' it indeed comes to be."
"That which has occurred in the past cannot be otherwise; therefore, they know me as one whose word is truth.
This greatness of mine, witnessed by the world and renowned in all directions, has been spoken for the sake of consoling you, O King, and not out of self-praise."
"O King, I have never before been one to boast;
for it is an ignoble practice to praise oneself.
[I shall fight] the Pāṇḍavas, the Matsyas, and the Pañcālas along with the Kekayas."
"You shall hear that Sātyaki and Vāsudeva have been conquered by me;
just as rivers perish completely upon reaching the ocean,
even so shall they, along with their kinsmen, perish upon encountering me."
In me is supreme intelligence, supreme splendor, and supreme heroism;
my supreme knowledge and supreme yoga are distinguished above those [others].
And so too are Pitāmaha, Droṇa, Kṛpa, Śalya, and Śala.
"Whatever is known regarding the *astras*, all that exists within me.
Having spoken thus, O Bhārata, Yuyutsu, the subduer of enemies, having understood the duties at hand, questioned Saṃjaya once more regarding what was appropriate for the occasion.
Vaiśampāyana said:
Thus, disregarding that son of Vicitravīrya who was questioning him so intensely regarding the sons of Pṛthā, [he remained silent].
Karna spoke to the son of Dhṛtarāṣṭra, gladdening him in the assembly of the Kauravas:
"Since I falsely promised that weapon..."
Having previously learned that the city of Brahmā had been seized by Rāma, he then spoke to me thus:
"It shall not appear to you at the time of your death."
For even though I had committed a great offense, I was cursed by my preceptor, the great seer who was bowed in humility; yet he,
possessed of fierce splendor, was indeed capable of consuming me with his fire.
For the great seer’s mind was already inclined toward me even before he had seen the earth with its oceans,
owing to my own service and personal exertion.
Therefore, that weapon remains with me as a remnant;
thus, I am capable, and this burden is mine.
That grace of the Rishi lasted for but a moment.
Having conquered the Pañcālas, Karūṣas, and Matsyas, and having slain the Pārthas along with their sons and grandsons,
I shall attain the worlds won by the sword.
Let your grandfather remain by your side,
as do Droṇa and all the foremost among the lords of men; having set out with their respective principal forces, let them proceed.
"I shall slay the sons of Pṛthā; this is my burden.
To him who was speaking thus, Bhīṣma said:
"Why do you boast, O you whose intellect is overwhelmed by Time?"
"O Karṇa, you do not know that when the leader is slain, the sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra would be as good as dead;
for this was indeed accomplished by me while burning the Khāṇḍava forest."
Having heard of that deed by Dhananjaya, the second son of Kṛṣṇa, you and your kinsmen will indeed be able to restrain yourself.
And that power which the high-souled, blessed Mahendra, the lord of the thirty-three gods, had bestowed upon you—
now it lay fallen, shattered, and reduced to ashes.
You shall see him struck by Keśava with that arrow of yours which shines like a serpent’s mouth and has been carefully honored with the finest garlands.
Struck by the showers of arrows from the sons of Pāṇḍu,
O Karṇa, he shall go to his destruction along with you;
for he is the slayer of Bāṇa and the son of the Earth, O Karṇa.
Vāsudeva protects the wearer of the diadem—
he who is the slayer of enemies such as you and those even more formidable in the thick of a fierce battle.
Karna said:
"Without doubt, the high-souled lord of the Vrishnis is exactly as you have described him, and even more so."
"Let the Grandfather hear the fruit of whatever harsh words I have spoken:
I shall never again lay down my weapons in battle."
The Grandfather shall behold me in the assembly;
but when you have been silenced, all the rulers of the earth shall witness my power.
Vaiśampāyana said:
Having spoken thus, that great archer left the assembly hall and went to his own residence.
But Bhīṣma, O King, laughing in the midst of the Kurus, said to Duryodhana:
"The son of the Sūta is indeed true to his promise."
Likewise, why would he endure such a burden,
having arrayed his forces in counter-formation and pierced their heads,
while you behold the destruction of the world through Bhīmasena?
While the one whose banner is the sacrificial altar stands firm against the Āvantyas, the Kāliṅgas, the Jayadrathas, and the Bāhlikas,
I shall always slay the enemies.
When he, calling himself a Brahmin, discharged that weapon against the venerable and blameless Rāma, he slew warriors by the thousands and tens of thousands.
At that very moment, both righteousness and asceticism were destroyed by that lowest of men, the son of Vikartana;
even as King Bhīṣma was speaking these words.
When Karṇa had departed after laying aside his weapons,
the dull-witted son of Vicitravīrya,
Duryodhana, spoke to the son of Śantanu.
Duryodhana said:
Among all men who are equal and of equal birth,
how can you believe that victory will belong exclusively to those sons of Pṛthā?
We are indeed equal to them in heroism and prowess,
as well as in age, intelligence, and sacred learning; likewise in weaponry, in combat, in riding, in speed, and in skill.
"We are all of the same lineage, and we are all born of human wombs;
O Grandfather, you know how victory comes to the sons of Pṛthā,
neither from me, nor from Bhava, nor from Droṇa, nor from Kṛpa, nor from Bāhlika."
"Exerting my prowess against other lords of men, I shall begin my assault.
I am Karna, the son of Vaikartana, and my brother Duḥśāsana;
together we three shall slay the five Pāṇḍavas in battle with our sharp arrows."

Then, O King, having performed this most difficult task together and attained happiness, I shall satisfy the Brahmins with various great sacrifices accompanied by abundant sacrificial fees, and with cattle, horses, and wealth.
"Free from anxiety and with our fever departed, we shall go to heaven when the time arrives.
Then the great king Dhṛtarāṣṭra, deeply distressed in mind, spoke to Vidura,
the best among the wise, in the presence of all the kings.
Deluded by the noose of death and fallen under the power of Time,
O dear one, my son Duryodhana, together with Karṇa,
will be ensnared like deer caught in a net.
Like those seeking to cross water with their arms, my men in battle beheld their enemies there, crowded with chariots and elephants. Vidura said:
Then the Pāṇḍavas and Keśava will cast off their pride;
for the elders who perceive with certainty declare that the highest good lies here,
and that for a Brāhmaṇa in particular, self-restraint is the eternal dharma.
For him, generosity, forbearance, and spiritual accomplishment arise in accordance with reality;
self-restraint follows after generosity, austerity, knowledge, and sacred study. Self-restraint increases one’s vital energy; self-restraint is the supreme purifier.
But a man who is free from evil and possessed of increased luster attains greatness;
for there is always fear among living beings from those who are unrestrained, as if from carnivorous beasts.
And for the sake of restraining them, the Kṣatriya was created by the Self-existent One.
Among the four stages of life (āśramas), they say that self-restraint (dama) alone is the supreme vow. I shall declare its characteristics, of which self-restraint is the aggregate:
forbearance, fortitude, non-violence, equanimity, truthfulness, and uprightness.
Victory over the senses, fortitude, gentleness, modesty, steadiness,
lack of miserliness, absence of agitation, contentment, and faithfulness— O Indra among kings, he who possesses these qualities is considered a self-controlled man.
Desire, greed, pride, anger, sleep, boastfulness,
arrogance, envy, and grief— one who is self-controlled does not indulge in these.
Straightforwardness, honesty, and purity— these are the characteristics of one who is self-controlled.
One who is free from greed, desiring little, and not dwelling on sensual pleasures— that person is proclaimed as self-controlled, like the ocean.
He is well-conducted, perfected in virtue, serene in soul, a knower of the Self, and wise.

Having obtained honor in this world, he goes to a happy rebirth after death— he who has no fear of living beings and from whom all beings have no fear; he indeed is one whose wisdom is mature, renowned as the best among men.

Beneficial to all beings and friendly, people do not tremble before him; deep as the ocean, satisfied by wisdom, he remains tranquil. This is the conduct practiced previously and that which has been practiced by the virtuous.
Abiding in that very state, the self-controlled ones, devoted to tranquility, rejoice;
or, having established themselves in actionlessness (*naiṣkarmya*), satisfied by knowledge and with senses conquered,
moving about in the world while awaiting their time, they are fit for becoming Brahman.
Just as the track of birds in the sky cannot be perceived,
so too the path of the sage who is satisfied with wisdom is not seen. This is true even for one who, having abandoned his home, sets his heart solely upon liberation.
"His eternal worlds in heaven, consisting of light, are prepared for him.
Vidura said:
"He set a snare upon the ground for the sake of the birds here."
"O dear one, we have heard from our ancestors that once there was a certain fowler.
In his snare were caught two birds of equal strength;
taking hold of that trap, both those sky-dwellers flew away."
Seeing those two having ascended into the sky, the fowler then pursued them without despondency, following wherever they went;
thus he followed that hunter seeking the birds.

Then, O descendant of Kuru, a certain sage dwelling in a hermitage, having performed his daily rites, beheld those two moving swiftly through the sky while following the one who traversed the earth; at that time, the sage questioned him with this verse:
"O hunter, this appears to me as a wonderful marvel:
you are running on foot after two sky-dwellers who are flying through the air.
The fowler said:
"These two together shall carry away my single noose;
wherever they may dispute, there they shall come under my control.
Vidura said:
Having entered into a dispute, those two birds, bound by the noose of death and possessed of evil intellects, fell upon the earth after engaging in combat;
fighting with fury, they were subject to the power of the snares of death.
Approaching unperceived, the hunter then seized him. Thus,
those kinsmen who fall into mutual conflict over their interests come under the power of their enemies, like the two birds because of their quarrel.
Eating together, conversing together, inquiring after one another’s welfare, and meeting together—these are the duties of kinsmen; there should never be any discord.
At whatever time all are of good cheer, they should attend upon their elders.
Like a forest guarded by lions, they become unassailable— those who,
having acquired constant wealth, remain as if dejected; O bull of the Bharatas, such men surrender their prosperity to their enemies.
"O bull of the Bharatas, kinsmen, when separated, smolder like firebrands, but when united, they blaze; O Dhṛtarāṣṭra,
I shall tell you this other thing as it was seen by me on a mountain."
Having heard that, O Kauravya, act in such a way as will lead to your welfare.
We shall go to the Northern Mountain accompanied by the Kirātas,
as well as by god-like Brahmins skilled in magic, sorcery, and medicine.
On all sides of Mount Gandhamādana,
which was like a grove and filled with clusters of glowing medicinal herbs frequented by *siddhas* and *gandharvas*,
we all beheld honey that was yellow and not produced by bees.
Situated on a rugged mountain precipice, equal in size to a jar,
fiercely guarded by venomous serpents, and dearly beloved by Kubera—
it is that which, having consumed, a mortal man attains immortality.
"The blind regain their sight, and the old indeed become young"—
thus did those Brāhmaṇas, practitioners of the *jambha* spell, declare.
Then, O lord of the earth, the Kirātas, having seen that, began to make their request.
In that rugged mountain cave filled with serpents, they all perished;
bound by their hopes, they fell down, all deprived of life.
In the same way, this son of yours alone desires the entire earth.
Out of delusion, he sees honey but does not see the precipice;
Duryodhana, intent on fighting Savyasācin in battle,
does not perceive his splendor or prowess to be such as that.
Mounted upon a single chariot, he by whom the earth was conquered—
by whom Bhīṣma, Droṇa, and others were terrified despite their righteous conduct,
and who were shattered in the city of Virāṭa— what is there for you to see?
The hero who, while awaiting you, endures your gaze—
Drupada, the King of Matsya, and the enraged Dhanañjaya—
would leave nothing remaining in battle, like fires fanned by the wind.
"O Dhṛtarāṣṭra, take King Yudhiṣṭhira upon your lap;
for when two combatants fight in battle, victory is never certain for either.
Dhṛtarāṣṭra said:
"O Duryodhana, my son, understand that which I shall say to you:
like a traveler ignorant of the way, you consider yourself to be on the right path when you are actually on a wrong one;
for you seek to measure the splendor of the five sons of Pāṇḍu."
Just as one cannot perceive the supreme goal of the five great elements of immense power,
so too you are not able to understand Yudhiṣṭhira, the son of Kuntī, who is established here in the highest dharma.
And Bhīmasena, the son of Kuntī, to whom no one is equal in strength—
you regard him as the end of battle, like a tree facing a great wind;
he who is the best among all wielders of weapons, like Mount Meru among the peaks.
What wise man indeed would fight against the wielder of the Gāṇḍīva bow in battle?
And whom today would Dhṛṣṭadyumna of the Pañcālas not cut down,
as he releases arrows among the enemies like the King of the Gods hurling his thunderbolt?
And Satyaki, who is invincible and highly esteemed among the Andhakas and Vṛṣṇis,
being devoted to the welfare of the Pāṇḍavas, will destroy your army—
he who, by way of comparison, surpasses even the three worlds.

What wise man indeed would fight against that lotus-eyed Kṛṣṇa? For on one side are his wife, his kinsmen, and his relatives, along with himself and this entire earth; and on the other side is Dhanañjaya.
Vāsudeva, too, is invincible and self-controlled wherever the Pāṇḍava is;
that force where Keśava resides is unbearable even for the entire earth.
Stay, my son, according to the words of the virtuous friends who speak for your welfare.
Be patient with the aged Bhīṣma, the son of Śāntanu, our grandfather;
listen to me as I speak for the sake of the Kurus;
and [heed the words of] Droṇa, Kṛpa, Vikarṇa, and the great king Bāhlīka.
"You ought to regard these men exactly as you regard me;
for all of them, O Bhārata, are knowers of dharma and possess equal affection. This was so even when they were with their brothers in the city of Virāṭa."
Having abandoned their cattle, your army, utterly terrified, fell into disarray.
And that which is heard as a great marvel in that city—
the encounter of one against many— is sufficient proof of this.
"Arjuna did that; how much more so, then, could all of them?
Recognize your brothers and provide for them with proper livelihoods.
Vaiśampāyana said:
Having spoken thus to Suyodhana, the highly wise and illustrious Dhṛtarāṣṭra again questioned Sañjaya:
"Tell me, Sañjaya, what remained after Vāsudeva [had spoken]."
"What Arjuna said to you—indeed, I have a great curiosity regarding that.
Sañjaya said:
"Having heard the words of Vāsudeva, Dhanañjaya, the son of Kuntī..."
At that time, while Vāsudeva was listening, the invincible one spoke to the grandfather Śāṃtanava, to Dhṛtarāṣṭra, O Saṃjaya,
and to Droṇa, Kṛpa, Karṇa, and the great king Bāhlika.
[He addressed] the son of Droṇa, Somadatta, and Śakuni the son of Subala;
Duḥśāsana, Śala, Purumitra, and Vivimśati;
Vikarṇa, Citrasena, and King Jayatsena.
Vinda and Anuvinda of Avanti, and Durmukha the Kaurava, as well as Duḥsaha the ruler of the Sindhus, Bhūriśravas,
King Bhagadatta, and King Jalasaṃdha.
And those other kings who had assembled there to fight for the sake of the Kauravas—
desiring death, they entered the blazing fire of the Pāṇḍavas.
O Sūta, those who have been brought here by the son of Dhṛtarāṣṭra according to custom— with skillful greetings and salutations—
should be told in my name once they have assembled.
"O Sañjaya, you should say this in the midst of the kings to Suyodhana, the foremost of evildoers,
that intolerant and evil-minded prince:"
O Sañjaya, you should cause my son Dhṛtarāṣṭra— the evil-souled and excessively greedy one—
to hear all these words of mine in their entirety, along with his ministers.
Having thus established me, Dhanañjaya,
looking toward Vāsudeva, spoke these words which were meaningful and consistent with dharma:
The wise Pārtha, with his long eyes ending in red,
spoke these composed words as he had heard them from the great-souled Madhupravīra as he was speaking.
In the same way, you must indeed speak my words when the kings have assembled from all sides,
amidst the smoke of the fire of arrows and the roar of chariot-rims.
Since the oblation is not being performed in this great battle by means of the bow-sruva that robs the power of weapons,
come together and exert yourselves with diligence.
"O slayers of enemies, if you do not grant Yudhiṣṭhira his own desired share,
I shall lead you away with your horses, foot soldiers, and elephants."
Having rendered the inauspicious quarter of the ancestors [the south] with my sharp arrows,
I then took leave of the four-armed Hari and,
having paid homage to Dhanañjaya, departed with haste.
"O you of immortal splendor, I have arrived here with speed to deliver this great message into your presence.
Vaiśampāyana said:
When Duryodhana, the son of Dhṛtarāṣṭra, did not respond to those words and all remained silent, the lords of men rose up,
O great king, as all the kings upon the earth stood.
When [the assembly] was cleared, the king proceeded to question Sañjaya,
following the will of his sons and hoping for their victory, seeking the certain outcome regarding himself, his enemies, and the Pāṇḍavas.
Dhṛtarāṣṭra said:
"O son of Gavalgaṇa, tell us what is substantial and what is weak within our own army, whatever may be found here."
"You know everything about the Pāṇḍavas with great skill;
what among them is superior, and what among them is inferior?
You are the discernor of the essence of these two and the seer of all."
O Sañjaya, he who is skilled in both dharma and artha and knows how to reach a certain conclusion— when questioned by me, tell me everything:
which of those fighting in this battle are no longer present?
Saṃjaya said:
"O King, I would never say anything to you in private, for envy might overcome you."
"O descendant of Ajamīḍha, bring your father, whose vows are firm, as well as the queen Gāndhārī.
O lord of men, let those two dispel your resentment."
Those two are knowers of dharma, skillful, and knowers of certainty;
in their presence, I would speak that entire counsel of Vāsudeva and Arjuna to you.
Vaiśampāyana said:
When this had been spoken, Gāndhārī and Vyāsa arrived there;
they were brought here by Vidura and quickly ushered into the assembly hall.
Then, having understood that intention of his son Saṃjaya,
the blessed great sage Kṛṣṇa Dvaipāyana, who perceives the three periods of time and possesses great wisdom, approached Dhṛtarāṣṭra and spoke.
O Sañjaya, tell everything to Dhṛtarāṣṭra as he questions you,
exactly as you know it regarding all that he inquires about.
Regarding the true nature of Vāsudeva and Arjuna,
Sañjaya said:
"Arjuna and Vāsudeva are both highly honored archers."
Arising from desire and elsewhere, they are ordained for the sake of universal dissolution;

having taken their stand between heaven and earth, O Lord, that discus of Vāsudeva revolves by means of his illusory power (*māyā*), according to its proper application, for those possessed of wisdom.

Listen to me in brief regarding that which was concealed from the Pāṇḍavas, yet highly esteemed by them: having understood the strength and weakness of their forces. Mādhava [conquered] Naraka, Śambara, Kaṃsa, and the King of Cedi.
Janārdana, as if in play, has conquered those of terrible appearance;
Puruṣottama, the self-controlled one of exalted soul, brings the earth, the atmosphere, and the heavens under his own control by his mere will.
"O King, since you ask again and again concerning the Pāṇḍavas,
listen as I speak to you so that you may understand their relative strength— both essential and non-essential. Either the entire world on one side, or Janārdana on the other."
Janārdana is superior to the entire world in essence; Janārdana could reduce this world to ashes by his mere thought,
but the entire world is not able to reduce Janārdana to ashes.
Wherever there is truth, wherever there is dharma, wherever there is modesty, and wherever there is uprightness—there Govinda is; where Kṛṣṇa is, there is victory.
Puruṣottama [pervades] the earth, the atmosphere, and the heavens.
The inner self of beings causes them to act, like Janārdana when he plays;
it is my conviction that he could reduce the entire world to ashes in the blink of an eye.
Regarding this state of being, O King, concerning which you ask about the Pāṇḍavas—
Having made the Pāṇḍavas his sacrificial vessel, as if deluding the world,
Keśava desires to consume your foolish sons who are devoted to unrighteousness;
for Keśava is the wheel of time, the wheel of the universe, and the wheel of the ages.
By his own power, the Blessed One transforms incessantly time and death, as well as all that is moving and stationary;
the Blessed One alone is the sovereign— this I tell you as the truth.
Although Hari is the master of the entire world and a great yogi,
he undertakes actions to perform them like a weak laborer;
by means of that union with *māyā*, Keśava deceives the worlds.
Those men who take refuge in Him alone do not fall into delusion.
Dhṛtarāṣṭra said:
How do you know Mādhava, the Great Lord of all the worlds?
"Why do I not know him? Tell me that, Saṃjaya.
Saṃjaya said:
"O King, you do not possess true knowledge; my knowledge does not diminish."
One who is devoid of knowledge and overwhelmed by darkness does not recognize Keśava;
but through knowledge, my dear, I know Madhusūdana, who exists in the three ages,
the uncreated creator, the divine Lord, the source and dissolution of all beings.
Dhṛtarāṣṭra said:
"O son of Gavalgaṇa, what is this constant devotion of yours toward Janārdana,
by which you recognize Madhusūdana as the one who appears in the three ages?"
Saṃjaya said:
"I do not resort to illusion—blessings be upon you—nor do I practice dharma in vain.
Having attained a state of purity through devotion, I know Janārdana from the scriptures."
Dhṛtarāṣṭra said:
"O Duryodhana, take refuge in Hṛṣīkeśa Janārdana! O dear son, Sañjaya has returned to us; go for protection to Keśava."
Duryodhana said:
"If the Blessed One, the son of Devakī, intends to destroy the world while proclaiming his friendship for Arjuna, I will not go to Keśava today."
Dhṛtarāṣṭra said:
"O Gāndhārī, this evil-minded son of yours goes downward;
he is envious, wicked-souled, arrogant, and one who transgresses the words of those superior to him."
Gāndhārī said:
"O you who desire power, O evil-souled one, O transgressor of the commands of the elders! Having abandoned both your father and me for the sake of power and life, O fool!"
"Increasing the joy of your enemies and increasing my own grief,
you shall be slain by Bhīmasena and remember the words of your father.
Vyāsa said:
"O King Dhṛtarāṣṭra, you are dear to Kṛṣṇa; listen to me. Since Sañjaya is your messenger and he shall unite you with what is beneficial—he knows Hṛṣīkeśa, both ancient and indeed ever-new."
He who listens with one-pointed attention shall be liberated from great fear. O son of Vicitravīrya, those men who are shrouded by the darkness of anger and joy,
and who are not content with their own wealth, are bound by various kinds of snares.
Those deluded by desire fall again and again under the sway of Yama,
like blind men led by those whose eyes are blind, being guided by their own past actions.
This is the single path by which the wise travel.
"Having seen that, one transcends death; the great soul does not cling there.
Dhṛtarāṣṭra said:
"O Sañjaya, tell me, my dear friend, of the path that is free from fear on all sides."
"By going where, O Hṛṣīkeśa, may I attain supreme peace?
Saṃjaya said:
"One whose self is not disciplined could never know Janārdana, whose self is disciplined."
For the self, there is no means to accomplish its purpose other than the restraint of the senses. The abandonment of desire for the excited senses comes from vigilance;
vigilance and non-violence are, without doubt, the source of knowledge.
O King, be vigilant and strive to restrain your senses;
let not your intellect falter, but control it from whatever direction it wanders.
The wise know this constant restraint of the senses to be true knowledge.
This is both the knowledge and the path by which the wise proceed.

O King, Keśava cannot be attained by men who have not conquered their senses; rather, having understood him through the scriptures and through yoga, the self-controlled man finds delight in the ultimate reality.
Dhṛtarāṣṭra said:
O Sañjaya, tell me once more about the lotus-eyed one as I ask you;
for by knowing the meaning of his names and deeds, my dear, I may attain that Supreme Person.
Saṃjaya said:
"I have heard the auspicious etymology of that god's name; as far as I understand it, Keśava is indeed immeasurable."

Because he dwells within all beings, because he is the source of wealth (*vasu*), and because he is of divine origin, he is known as Vāsudeva; furthermore, because of his virility (*vṛṣatva*), he is called Vṛṣṇi.
Know, O Bhārata, that Mādhava is so named because of his silence (*mauna*), meditation (*dhyāna*), and yoga.

Because he is the dissolution of all principles (*tattva*), he is Madhuha and Madhusūdana. The word *kṛṣi* denotes the earth, and the syllable *ṇa* denotes bliss; because of his union with that state, the eternal one is Kṛṣṇa.

The Puṇḍarīka is the supreme abode, eternal, imperishable, and immutable. Because of that state, Janārdana is called Puṇḍarīkākṣa (Lotus-eyed). From him, the quality of goodness (*sattva*) does not deviate, and he is never deprived of goodness.
Because he consists of pure being (*sattva*), he is the Sātvata; because he arose from the bull (*ārṣabha*), he is the bull-eyed one (*vṛṣabhekṣaṇa*).
Since he was not born from a mother, he is the Unborn (*aja*); therefore, he is the Conqueror of Armies (*anīkajit*).
Because he is self-luminous among the gods and because of his self-control (*dama*), they know him as Dāmodara.
Through joy, through bliss, and through the sovereignty of happiness, he attains the state of Hṛṣīkeśa;
supporting heaven and earth with his two arms, he is remembered as Mahābāhu (the Long-armed One).
Because he never perishes below, he is therefore called Adhokṣaja.
Because he is the refuge (*ayana*) of men, he is remembered as Nārāyaṇa;
because he is the ancient abode (*purāṇasadana*), he is remembered as Purātana; and because he fills and is the abode, he is therefore Puruṣottama.
Because everything—both the non-existent and the existent—arises from and dissolves back into Him, one should proclaim the name of Hari; like a crow, one should contemplate the ultimate reality;
like a rooster, one should meditate; and like a crane, one should remain steady in all circumstances.

Because he always knows everything, they call him "All" (Sarva). Kṛṣṇa is established in truth, and truth is established in him. Govinda is the truth beyond truth; therefore, he is also named "Truth" (Satya).

Viṣṇu is called Jiṣṇu because of his striding and his victory; he is Ananta because of his eternity, and Govinda because of his knowledge of the senses (gavām). He makes the unreal appear as real, and thereby deludes all creatures.
"The Lord, who is thus constant in righteousness, together with the sages— the mighty-armed and infallible one— will surely come for the sake of compassion. Dhṛtarāṣṭra said:
"O Sañjaya, I truly envy those with sight who shall behold Vāsudeva nearby,
resplendent with his supreme form."
Illuminating the intermediate directions and the cardinal points,
Sañjaya spoke these words in the midst of the kings within the assembly hall.
The best of the Vṛṣṇis, shining with the Munis,
was uttering the speech of the Bharatas—
speech worthy of worship and bringing prosperity to the Sṛñjayas.
To those desiring prosperity, he is blameless and worthy of being grasped;
yet to those whose life-force has departed, his form is impossible to grasp— the sole hero of the Sātvatas as he rises up.
The leader of the Yādavas, the bull among men, the slayer and agitator of his enemies,
who indeed steals away the fame of his foes.
For the assembled Kurus were witnesses as that high-souled one, the slayer of enemies and most excellent,
spoke words of a non-cruel nature.
The best of the Vṛṣṇis beheld that most ancient seer, Vipracit, who deluded my followers—
a veritable ocean of speech and a vessel for the ascetics.
Ariṣṭanemi, Garuḍa, Suparṇa,
the lord of creatures, the abode of the world, the thousand-headed Puruṣa, the ancient one.
I take refuge in the one without beginning, middle, or end, whose fame is infinite, the uncreated creator and progenitor of Śukra,
the supreme refuge beyond all that is supreme.
The creator and progenitor of the three worlds,
as well as of the gods, asuras, nāgas, and rākṣasas,
he is the foremost among kings and the wise.
"I take refuge in him, the younger brother of Indra.
Vaiśampāyana said:
Janamejaya said:
When the virtuous Sañjaya had departed toward the Pāṇḍavas, what did my ancestors, the Pāṇḍavas, do there?
O best of the twice-born, I wish to hear all of this; please tell it to me.
When Sañjaya had departed, Dharmarāja Yudhiṣṭhira addressed Arjuna, Bhīmasena, the two sons of Mādrī his brothers,
as well as Virāṭa, Drupada, and the great car-warrior of the Kekayas.
Approaching the wielder of the conch, the discus, and the mace, he said:
"Let us go and entreat them so that Bhīṣma, Droṇa, and the wise Bāhlīka may proceed to the assembly of the Kurus."
"Let us not fight in battle with other Kurus;
this is our primary course of action, and this is our highest good.
Having spoken thus, they, being well-disposed, approached Janārdana.
Together with the Pāṇḍavas, the kings were like the immortals surrounding Marutvat;
likewise, all those bulls among men were difficult to withstand in the assembly.
Then Yudhiṣṭhira, the son of Kuntī, approached Janārdana.
Then, O King, Yudhiṣṭhira approached that bull among men,
the descendant of Daśārha and the preeminent leader of all the Sātvatas, and addressed him:
"O Janārdana, that time has now arrived for my friends."

I see no one other than you who could rescue us from these calamities. For it is by relying upon you, O Mādhava, that we remain fearless and press the son of Dhṛtarāṣṭra— along with his ministers and his own portion— to yield what is ours.
"Just as you protect the Vṛṣṇis in all calamities, O subduer of enemies, so too must the Pāṇḍavas be protected by you; protect us from this great danger.
The Blessed One said:
"Here I am, O mighty-armed one; tell me what you wish to say.
For I shall do all that you command, O Bhārata.
Yudhiṣṭhira said:

O Mādhava, you have previously employed conciliation mixed with mildness and even sternness; yet that was not based on justice, and for that reason we have been censured. You have heard what Dhṛtarāṣṭra and his sons intend to do.

"O Kṛṣṇa, all that Sañjaya has told me is indeed the opinion of Dhṛtarāṣṭra; he is his very self with his inner thoughts laid bare. An envoy reports exactly what he was told; he would deserve death were he to speak otherwise."
By refusing to give up the kingdom, he seeks peace with us while acting with a greedy and sinful mind, conducting himself in a manner unworthy of himself;
for we have already spent those twelve years in the forest.
"O Lord, by the command of Dhṛtarāṣṭra, we remained in concealment for one more year;
O Kṛṣṇa, we did not violate that agreement, for the Brahmins know this of us."
The aged King Dhṛtarāṣṭra does not perceive his own duty;
or, even perceiving it, he follows the command of the dull-witted one out of greed for his son.
O Janārdana, the king stands by the opinion of Suyodhana regarding us.

The greedy man acts falsely, even while behaving as if he were acting for his own benefit. O Janārdana, what indeed could be more painful than this, that I am unable to provide for my mother or for my friends?
"O Madhusūdana, with the Kāśis, Cedis, Pañcālas, and Matsyas as my allies,
and with you yourself as my protector, I requested only five villages:
Kuśasthala, Vṛkasthala, Āsandī, and Vāraṇāvata."
"And let there be some small portion here as our fifth settlement, O Govinda.
Let five villages or towns be given to us,
dear brother, so that we may dwell together in them and the Bharatas may not perish."
Yet that evil-minded son of Dhṛtarāṣṭra does not even grant them their due;
considering himself the sole master, what indeed could be more painful than this—
for one born in a noble family, grown old, yet still coveting the wealth of others?

Lust destroys wisdom; wisdom, when destroyed, destroys modesty. Modesty, when destroyed, obstructs righteousness; righteousness, when destroyed, destroys prosperity. Prosperity, when destroyed, destroys the person; for a person, the loss of self-mastery is death.
For kinsmen, friends, and officiating priests turn away from one who is devoid of wealth, just as birds, dear son, depart from a tree that has neither flowers nor fruit.
And this, dear son, is what death is: it is like falling from such a tree.
Relatives turn away like life-breaths from a deceased being;
Śambara declared no state more wretched than this,
wherein neither food for today nor for tomorrow is seen.
They say that wealth is the supreme dharma; everything is established upon wealth.
In this world, those who possess wealth live, while those men who are without wealth are as if dead.
Those who rely on their own strength attempt to strip a man of his wealth.
They destroy virtue, wealth, and pleasure, as well as that man himself.
Having reached such a state, some people chose death;
some departed for a village, some for the forest, and others set out for destruction.
Some develop madness; others fall under the power of their enemies;
some enter into servitude for the sake of another's wealth.
For such a man, this calamity is even more grievous than death itself.
The destruction of prosperity is the cause of that [misfortune] for him regarding both dharma and desire;
yet his death, which is in accordance with dharma, is the eternal path of the world,
which no one among all beings anywhere ever transcends.

O Kṛṣṇa, a person who is poor by nature is not so greatly afflicted as one who, having attained auspicious prosperity and grown accustomed to it, is later deprived of it. He has now encountered this great calamity solely through his own transgression.

He reviles the gods, including Indra, yet he does not reproach himself in any way; nor do all the scriptures prevail against him in his self-reproach. He becomes angry with his servants and shows malice toward his friends.
Then, wrath indeed takes hold of him, and he becomes further deluded. Having fallen under the power of delusion, he practices cruel deeds;
through that, he fosters a mixture of actions for the sake of the transgression of evil karma.
Confusion leads only to hell; that is the ultimate destination for those of evil deeds. If one does not awaken, O Kṛṣṇa, one goes only to hell.
Awakening for him is wisdom itself; he whose eye is wisdom does not perish.

For when a person has attained wisdom, he indeed examines the scriptures; being constant in the scriptures, he pursues dharma, and for him, modesty is the supreme limb. For one possessed of modesty loathes evil, and his prosperity increases.

As long as that illustrious man remains steadfast in dharma, with a tranquil soul and always engaged in the performance of his duties, he remains a true person; he does not set his mind on unrighteousness, nor does he dwell in sinful ways.

Whether shameless or deluded, neither woman nor man has any authority regarding dharma; such a person is exactly like a Śūdra. One who possesses a sense of shame protects the gods, the ancestors, and indeed himself.
Through that, one attains immortality; that is the ultimate goal of those who perform meritorious deeds.
O Madhusūdana, this very thing has been witnessed by you directly in me:
how, fallen from my kingdom, I dwell in these abodes.

"By any means whatsoever, we are not able to abandon our prosperity; therefore, if death should come to us while striving for this cause, that would be excellent. O Mādhava, that is our primary preference, as it would be for you as well."
May we enjoy that prosperity which belongs to those who are peaceful and equanimous.
In this regard, the ultimate limit of the exhaustion and arising of fierce deeds is this:
that having slain the Kauravas, we may enjoy those kingdoms.
"Furthermore, O Kṛṣṇa, even those who are unrelated, ignoble, and enemies should not be killed;
how much more so those who are such as these?
For they are our kinsmen in great number, our allies, and our elders."
Their slaughter is most wicked; what indeed is honorable in battle? This duty of the Kṣatriyas is sinful, yet we are kinsmen of the warrior class.
Whether it be our own dharma or unrighteousness, any other mode of livelihood is censured by us.
The Śūdra performs service; the Vaiśyas live by trade. We live by slaughter, while the begging bowl has been chosen by the Brāhmaṇas. A Kṣatriya kills a Kṣatriya; a fish lives upon another fish.
"O descendant of Daśārha, look how one dog kills another; such is the nature of dharma as it has come to pass.
O Kṛṣṇa, strife is constant in battle, and lives perish in the fray.
Strength serves merely for the sake of policy, while victory and defeat depend on chance."
O best of the Yadus, neither the life nor the death of living beings occurs according to their own will;
nor can happiness or even suffering be obtained before its appointed time.
For indeed, a single person may slay many, and many may likewise slay a single one.
A coward slays a hero, and one without fame slays the famous.
Victory is seen for both sides, as is defeat for both;
likewise, retreat is seen to result in loss and exhaustion.
In every way, battle is a calamity; who, while striking, is not struck in return?
And for one who is slain, O Hṛṣīkeśa, victory and defeat are equal. I consider that defeat is not at all distinguished from death.
O Kṛṣṇa, for one who might achieve victory, decline is certain;
in the end, even some other people will slay those who are dear to him—
his sons and brothers— as he becomes weakened in strength and falls into despair.
O Kṛṣṇa, a profound weariness with life arises from every side;
for those very heroes who are modest, noble, and compassionate are the ones slain in battle, while the common folk escape.
O Janārdana, even after slaying others, the latent tendency remains constant;
moreover, there is a sinful consequence here, and a remnant is left behind.
For that remnant, having gained strength, will leave no remnant at all.
And he strives for the total eradication [of enmity], desiring to bring an end to hostility. Victory breeds enmity; the defeated dwells in suffering.
Having abandoned both victory and defeat, one who is tranquil sleeps in happiness.
A person who has conceived enmity always sleeps in misery with an unpeaceful mind,
as if in a house with a snake;
he who destroys everything is deprived of fame.
He incurs eternal infamy among all beings;
for enmities do not subside even after a long time,
as there are always those who recount them, and men continue to be born into the family.
"Furthermore, O Keśava, enmity is not appeased by enmity;
rather, O Kṛṣṇa, it only increases further, like a fire fed with oblations. There is no peace otherwise; there will always remain some internal conflict until the very end."
For those who desire an interval [of peace], this fault is incessant:
for the mental anguish caused by human agency is a powerful affliction of the heart;
its pacification occurs either through its abandonment or through the withdrawal of the mind.

Alternatively, O Madhusūdana, if the accomplishment of the fruit [of our purpose] were to come about through the total destruction of our enemies, that would be even more cruel. But that peace which might be achieved through renunciation— that, without such slaughter, is indeed true peace.
Because of the uncertainty [of victory] and because of the total destruction of our enemies as well as ourselves,
we do not wish to abandon it, yet we do not desire the ruin of our lineage. In this matter,
peace through submission is indeed the weightiest course.
For those striving by every means who desire to avoid battle,
when conciliation is rejected, war— which is established as the lack of prowess—
ensues; through the repudiation of conciliation, a terrible conflict breaks out.
That [behavior] was observed by the wise to be like that of dogs at a cow-pen:
wagging the tail, growling, barking back, turning around, baring the teeth, and howling; thereafter, the battle begins.
In that case, O Kṛṣṇa, whoever is strong eats that meat after having conquered [the weak];
even so, among human beings, there is no distinction whatsoever.
In every respect, however, this is appropriate for the stronger toward the weak.
Disrespect and opposition arise because one who bows down is weak;
however, a father, a king, and an elder deserve honor in every way.
Therefore, O Janārdana, Dhṛtarāṣṭra is both to be honored and worshipped.
"O Mādhava, Dhṛtarāṣṭra’s affection for his son is powerful;
having fallen under the sway of his son, he will reject our prostration.
What do you think, O Kṛṣṇa, regarding what should be done next at this juncture?"
O Mādhava, how may we not fall away from both worldly purpose and dharma? For in such a crisis as this, O Madhusūdana, whom else but you, O Supreme Person, am I worthy to consult?
"Dear to us and desiring our welfare, you who know the course of all actions—
who indeed among us, O Kṛṣṇa, is a friend like you, who understands every certainty?
Vaiśampāyana said:
Thus addressed, Janārdana replied to the King of Dharma:
"For the sake of both of you, I shall go to the assembly of the Kurus;
if I may obtain peace there without sacrificing your interests."
"O King, may my merit from this great deed bear immense fruit;
may I release from the noose of death the agitated Kurus and Sṛñjayas,
the Pāṇḍavas and the Dhārtarāṣṭras, and indeed this entire earth."
Thus addressed, Dharmarāja replied to Janārdana,
the Supreme Person, at that time when his brothers were assembled.
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
"O Kṛṣṇa, it is not my opinion that you should go toward the Kurus;
Suyodhana will not act upon your well-spoken words.
For Suyodhana is evil-minded, as are Karṇa and the son of Subala."

The entire body of Kṣatriya kings is assembled here, following the will of Suyodhana; O Kṛṣṇa, I do not approve of your entering into their midst. For neither wealth nor divinity would please us, much less happiness.
"Nor shall you attain the sovereignty over all the immortals by obstructing you, O Mādhava.
The Blessed One said:
"O Great King, I know this wickedness of Dhṛtarāṣṭra’s son."
"We shall become objects of reproach among all the rulers of the earth;
moreover, all the kings combined would not be sufficient to stand before me when I am enraged, just as other animals cannot stand before a lion."
"But if they should proceed toward me with any improper act, I would consume all the Kurus; this is the resolve fixed in my mind. O Pārtha, my journey there shall never be in vain."
"Success may sometimes be achieved, or at the very least, there may be the state of being beyond reproach.
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
"O Kṛṣṇa, whatever pleases you, may you attain well-being among the Kauravas."
"I shall see you returned again, successful and in good health.
O Lord Viṣvaksena, having gone to the Kurus, bring peace to the Bharatas,
so that we may all live together with joyful minds and pure hearts."
"You are my brother and my friend, and you are dear to Bibhatsu and to me. You are free from suspicion because of our friendship; may you attain well-being for the sake of prosperity.
You know us, you know others, you know the matter at hand, and you know how to speak."

"O Kṛṣṇa, whatever is for our benefit, that should be said to Suyodhana. O Keśava, whatever beneficial words are consistent with righteousness— whether they be conciliatory or otherwise— you should speak those."
The Blessed One said:
"I have heard the words of Sañjaya, and I have heard yours as well.
I know everything—the intention that belongs both to them and to you."

Your intellect is grounded in dharma, while theirs is intent on enmity; whatever may be gained without war would be highly esteemed by you. Yet, O lord of the people, that is not the ultimate duty of a kṣatriya.
"All those belonging to the stages of life say that if a Kṣatriya should practice begging for alms,
victory or death in battle is his eternal destiny ordained by the Creator;
this is the specific duty of a Kṣatriya, and wretchedness is not praised."
"O Yudhiṣṭhira, it is not possible to maintain one's livelihood by resorting to wretchedness.
Exert yourself, O mighty-armed subduer of foes; slay your enemies! They are exceedingly greedy, bound by affection, and have lived together with you for a long time."
O scorcher of foes, O lord of the people, the sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra have made friends and established their strength; there is no possibility that they will treat you with equality,
for they consider themselves superior in power because of Bhīṣma, Droṇa, Kṛpa, and the others.
O King, subduer of enemies, as long as you treat them with gentleness, so long will they seize your kingdom—
not out of compassion, nor out of pity, nor for the sake of dharma or worldly gain.
"O subduer of enemies, the sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra were quite capable of fulfilling your desire; yet this was the very reason why the Pāṇḍavas did not feel remorse toward you,
even after they had performed such a difficult task as wearing only a loincloth."
In the very presence of his grandfather Droṇa, the wise Vidura,
the virtuous Brahmins, the king, the citizens,
and all the leaders of the Kurus as they looked on in truth.

O King, that wicked and cruel man felt no shame for his deed when he then deceived you— who were generous, virtuous, gentle, self-controlled, devoted to the Dharma, and faithful— to the game of dice through trickery.
"O King, do not show such affection for one whose conduct and character are so depraved;
he deserves to be slain by the whole world, how much more so by you, O Bhārata. Thus she pierced her younger brother with these unseemly words.
Boasting and filled with joy, he spoke with his brothers:
"Indeed, the Pāṇḍavas possess nothing here that is their own;
even their names and their lineage shall no longer remain."
After a long time, their defeat will come;
those people, having lost their true nature,
will revert to their original state when the wicked Duḥśāsana then instigates the gambling match.

Then the queen Draupadī, like one who is helpless, was dragged by her hair by that evil-minded man while weeping in the assembly hall before the gathering of kings; even in the presence of Bhīṣma, Droṇa, and others, she was repeatedly addressed as "O cow."
"All your brothers of terrible prowess have been restrained by you;
bound by the fetters of dharma, they did not do anything [in retaliation]. Uttering these and other harsh words, he spoke thus.
When you had gone forth into the forest, he boasted among his kinsmen;
but those who were gathered there, seeing you so innocent,
sat in the assembly hall with tearful throats, weeping at that time.
Neither did those kings, together with the Brahmins, applaud him;
rather, all the members of the assembly there censured Duryodhana. O crusher of foes, for one of noble birth, both censure and death are equal.
O King, death possesses great merit, whereas a life of reproach and a wretched livelihood do not.
O King, he is slain at that very moment when he becomes shameless;
and he is censured, O Great King, among all the kings upon the earth.
The killing of one whose conduct is such as this is an easy task; like a tree with severed roots, propped up only by a temporary support,
that ignoble and evil-minded man deserves to be slain by all the world like a serpent.
"O slayer of enemies, slay him; O King, do not hesitate.
O sinless one, this is entirely worthy of you and it is pleasing to me as well, that you should offer salutations to your father and to Bhīṣma."
But I, having gone to all the world, shall cut away the doubt of those who harbor dual sentiments regarding Duryodhana, O King; there,
in the midst of the kings, I shall proclaim my own manly virtues.
I shall proclaim your virtues as well as his transgressions; listen to my words as I speak here, which are beneficial and consistent with dharma and artha.
Having heard this, all the kings, the lords of various realms, [will respond].
They will believe in you, thinking, "He is a righteous soul and a speaker of truth," and they will come to understand how he acted out of greed;
furthermore, I shall censure him before the people of both the city and the countryside.
If, even when seeking peace among an assembly of the four varṇas including the old and the young, you do not attain righteousness there,
then the kings will censure the Kurus and Dhṛtarāṣṭra.
"O King, when he has been abandoned by the world and Duryodhana is slain, what task remains? Let whatever else must be done be performed.
Having gone to all the Kurus, I shall not let your interests suffer."

"I shall strive to bring about peace and observe their movements; having gone there and ascertained the activities of the Kauravas regarding the war, O Bhārata, I shall return for the sake of your victory."
"In every way, I anticipate battle with the enemies,
for all the omens appear to me in such a manner;
the beasts and birds are uttering terrible cries."
At the onset of night, amidst the foremost elephants and horses,
likewise, fire assumes terrible forms and displays many fearsome colors.
Then the terrible destroyer of the world of men would arrive here, were it not for the fact that weapons,
arrows, armor, and chariots [are at hand].
Having bestowed elephants and banners [upon them],
let all those warriors, having completed their training,
be diligent in the management of elephants, horses, and chariots.
"O lord of men, make all that which you must acquire for war complete and whole;
for Duryodhana is not able to give it now."
O King, it is by some small measure that you still live,
even though that prosperous kingdom of yours which was formerly yours has been seized at dice, O chief of the Pāṇḍavas.
Bhīmasena said:
"O Madhusūdana, speak in such a way that there may be peace for the Kurus;
do not terrify us with talk of war."

Impatient, ever-agitated, hating what is beneficial, and high-minded, Duryodhana must not be addressed with harsh words; you should deal with him through conciliation alone. By nature he is of evil character, and his mind is equal to that of bandits.
Intoxicated by the pride of sovereignty, he has created enmity with the Pāṇḍavas;
he is shortsighted, harsh, a reviler, and of cruel prowess;
long-simmering in his anger, unleadable, evil-minded, and fond of deceit.
He might even die, yet he would not break [his resolve] nor ever abandon his own opinion;
O Kṛṣṇa, I consider it most difficult to bring peace with such a man—
one who speaks ill even of his friends, has abandoned dharma, and is fond of falsehood.
