He indeed strikes down both the words and the minds of his friends; having fallen under the sway of anger and resorted to a wicked nature,
he pursues evil by his very nature, like a snake prodded by blades of grass.
For Duryodhana, with his entire army, is known to you in every respect— what his character is, what his nature is, what his strength is, and what his prowess is.
Formerly, the Kurus along with their sons, as well as we ourselves, were well-disposed toward him.

"O Madhusūdana, with Indra as our leader, we were rejoicing together with our kinsmen; yet, O Bhārata, through the wrath of Duryodhana, the sons of Bharata shall be consumed like forests by fires at the end of the winter season."
O Madhusūdana, these eighteen kings are renowned who utterly exterminated their kinsmen, friends, and relatives—
the prosperous Asuras, blazing as it were with their splendor.
At the time of the transition of the Dharma age, Bali was born;
Udāvarta among the Haihayas, Janamejaya among the Nīpas,
Bahula among the Tālajaṅghas, and Uddhata Vasu among the Kṛmis.
Ajabindu was the king of the Suvīras; Kuśarddhika, of Surāṣṭra; Arkaja, of the Balīhas; Dhautamūlaka, of the Cīnas;
Hayagrīva, of the Videhas; and Varapra, of the Mahaujasas.
Bāhu was the leader of the Sundaravegas; Purūravas, of the Dīptākṣas; Sahaja, of the Cedis and Matsyas; Bṛhadbala, of the Pracetas;
Dhāraṇa, of the Indravatsas; and Vigāhana, of the Mukuṭas.
Śama and Nandivega— these were the defilers of their lineages,
O Kṛṣṇa, who appeared at the end of the Yuga as the lowest of men within their families. May this [destruction] of ours, the Kurus, also come about at the end of the Yuga, brought forth by Time.
Duryodhana is a charcoal-brand of his lineage, the lowest of men and a person of sin;
therefore, speak to him gently and slowly, in accordance with righteousness and worldly purpose, avoiding harshness toward one of fierce prowess who is full of intense attachment to his desires.
O Kṛṣṇa, even if we must all become subordinates to Duryodhana, let us follow him by becoming humble; let not the Bharatas perish. Let there be a state of neutrality between us and the Kurus.
"O Vāsudeva, you must act in such a way that misfortune does not touch the Kurus. O Kṛṣṇa, the aged grandfather and those who are members of the assembly should be told:
'Let there be brotherly affection among the brothers; let the son of Dhṛtarāṣṭra be pacified.'"
"I speak thus because the king himself praises it; Arjuna does not seek battle at all, for there is great compassion in Arjuna.
Vaiśampāyana said:
Having heard these words of Bhīma’s— unprecedented in their gentleness— the mighty-armed Keśava, as if smiling,
regarded them as a mountain having become light or fire having become cold.
Then Śauri, the younger brother of Rāma, who bears the Śārṅga bow,
perceiving Vṛkodara to be overwhelmed with compassion, spoke to Bhīma as he sat there, enkindling him with words like the wind fanning a fire.
"O Bhīmasena, on other occasions you praise nothing but battle,
desiring to crush the cruel sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra who delight in slaughter; yet now,
O scorcher of foes, you do not sleep but remain awake, lying prostrate."
You always utter speech that is terrible, unappeased,
and harsh, sighing like one burning with fire-colored heat from your own wrath; O Bhīma, your mind is unpacified, like a smoky fire.
Sighing in solitude, you lie down like a weak man oppressed by a heavy burden;
yet some people who do not understand you consider you to be mad,
like an elephant that, having uprooted trees, lies down and devours them.
O Bhīma, you run about trampling the earth with your feet and groaning aloud;
you take no pleasure in these people and dwell in solitude, O Pāṇḍava;
you never welcome anyone else, whether by night or by day.
Suddenly you smile in secret as if weeping; placing your head upon your knees, you sit for a long time with eyes closed.
Again, you knit your brows as if licking your lips.
"O Bhīma, you are seen constantly; all that is caused by your wrath.
Just as the sun is seen in the east rising with its brilliance, and just as it is seen in the west when released, moving perpetually with its rays."
"Thus I speak this truth; there shall be no deviation from it: 'Ah! Approaching with my mace, I shall slay the intolerant Duryodhana.
It was with such a vow of truth that you grasped your mace in the midst of your brothers."
O scorcher of the foe, today your mind is fixed upon peace;
alas, now that the time for battle has arrived, you perceive things contrary to war—why does fear seize you, O Bhīma? Do you see these as unfavorable omens?
"O Pārtha, alas, you perceive adverse omens both at the end of your dreams and while awake; therefore, you desire peace. Alas, like a eunuch, you harbor no hope for manliness within yourself."
"You are overcome by dejection; therefore, your mind is disordered. Your heart trembles and your spirit sinks.
You are seized by a paralysis of the thighs; that is why you desire peace."

"O Pārtha, the mind of a mortal is indeed impermanent and fickle, like a seed-pod of the *śālmali* tree shaken by the force of the wind. This distorted intellect of yours is like human speech coming from cattle."
It plunges the minds of the sons of Pāṇḍu like those without a raft into the depths.
This is a great marvel to me, like the sliding of a mountain,
that you should speak such words as Bhīmasena could never equal.
"O Bhārata, having seen your own deeds and your birth in this family, arise! Do not yield to despondency, O hero; be firm.
This dejection of yours, O subduer of enemies, is not worthy of you."
"What a Kṣatriya does not obtain through his own prowess, he does not enjoy.
Vaiśampāyana said:
Having been addressed thus by Vāsudeva, he who was ever-wrathful and impatient—
Immediately thereafter, while in a state of composure like a well-trained horse, he spoke:
"O Acyuta, you perceive me as one thing when I intend otherwise;
for I am of exceedingly noble character and possess true prowess in battle."
"O Dāśārha, you have lived with me for a long time; do you know my true nature?
Or is it that you do not know me, like a shallow man who attempts to cross a deep lake? Therefore, you strike me with these improper words."
"O Mādhava, how could anyone who knows me as Bhīmasena speak such unseemly words to me, as you have deigned to say? Therefore,
O delighter of the Vṛṣṇis, I shall speak these words."
"My own manliness and strength are not equal to those of my enemies.
In every respect, this praising of oneself is not the conduct of a noble man;
yet, being driven by excessive insults, I shall speak of my own strength."
"Behold these two worlds, O Kṛṣṇa, from whom these creatures have come;
they are immovable and infinite, the foundations and mothers of all.
If these two were to collide suddenly like two rocks,"
"I could seize all these beings, including the moving and the unmoving, with my two arms.
Behold this space between my arms, which are like great iron bars;
I see no man who, having encountered them, would be released."

Even Himavat, the ocean, and the wielder of the thunderbolt, the slayer of Bala himself— even these three, exerting all their strength, could not protect one who has been assailed by me. I shall fight all the Kṣatriyas who have taken up arms against the Pāṇḍavas.
"I shall tread upon these [mountains] with the soles of my feet upon the earth.
For you do not fail to recognize my prowess, O Acyuta,
just as I have conquered kings and brought them under my control."
"If you do not recognize me now, like the radiance of the rising sun,
O Janārdana, you shall know me when the thickets of battle are pressed close,
O sinless one. Why have you reviled me with harsh words, like piercing a wound with a needle?"

"I speak this according to my understanding; know me to be superior even to him. You shall see, when the thick of battle has begun on that day of slaughter, elephants, chariot-warriors, and horsemen driven away by me."
Then you and the world shall behold me, enraged, slaying those bulls among Kṣatriyas and dragging away the very best of men;
my marrow does not fail, nor does my mind tremble.

"Even if all the worlds were enraged against me, no fear would exist within me. However, O Madhusūdana, it is out of friendship and compassion that I endure all these afflictions, lest the Bharatas be destroyed."
The Blessed One said:
"Desiring to know his disposition, I spoke these words out of affection; it was not out of reproach, nor from a desire for display of learning, nor from anger, nor from a wish to debate."
"I know your greatness, and I know what your strength is;
I also know your deeds, yet I do not despise you. O Pāṇḍava, I honor the excellence that you perceive within yourself."
I consider this [gift] to be a thousandfold even when bestowed upon you;
for such is your birth in a lineage honored by all kings,
and such as you are, O Bhīma, with your kinsmen and friends.
For people who desire to understand dharma that is subject to doubt, O Vṛkodara, cannot discern the sequence of divine and human causes;
yet it is that very [divine cause] which becomes the means for the accomplishment of a man's goals.
Even in his destruction, that very same human effort of his remains in doubt;
for things perceived in one way by poets who discern faults turn out otherwise,
like the gusts of the wind.
Even human action that has been well-deliberated, well-executed, and accomplished according to justice may be thwarted by fate; likewise,
even fate, though unaccomplished, is overcome by human effort.
Cold, heat, rain, hunger, and thirst, O Bhārata,
as well as whatever else is self-inflicted upon a person who is subject to destiny—
that is the characteristic found therein, and it is not subject to obstruction.
O Bhīmasena, O strong-armed one of great heroism and wisdom, for the world there is no other means of subsistence than action;
[the particle] *mātrā* is used here in the sense of restriction.

One who possesses such an understanding should engage [in action]; from the conjunction of both, the fruit will arise. He who, having formed this resolve, engages solely in actions, is not distressed by failure, nor does he experience joy upon success.
In this matter, Bhīmasena, this much alone is intended by me:
that absolute victory should not be expected for us in battle with the Kurus;
for even one whose reins are not too tightly drawn may find himself in such a reversal of fortune.
I speak this to you so that you do not fall into despondency or exhaustion.
O Pāṇḍava, when tomorrow comes, having approached Dhṛtarāṣṭra,
I shall strive to bring about peace without sacrificing your interests.

If they will bring about peace, then my fame shall be infinite; your desire will be fulfilled, and their highest welfare will be secured. But if they persist in their obstinacy and do not accept my word, [the consequences will follow].
"O Bhīmasena, in this battle against the Kurus, there will be fierce deeds indeed; in this war, the burden is placed upon you.
Arjuna shall hold the yoke, while the rest of the people must be carried."
"For I shall indeed be the charioteer for Bībhatsu when the battle occurs;
this is the wish of Dhanañjaya, for it is not that I do not desire the fight. Therefore, O Vṛkodara, fearing [the outcome], I seek your counsel."
"Stinging you with words that were not cowardly, I have kindled your splendor.
Arjuna said:
"O Janārdana, everything that ought to be said has already been spoken by Yudhiṣṭhira himself."
"O scorcher of enemies, having heard your words,
it appears to me that you do not consider peace to be easily achievable in this matter, O Lord—
whether due to the greed of Dhṛtarāṣṭra or the wretchedness that has come upon him."
You also consider human exertion to be fruitless;
yet, without actions, there is no arising of results through human effort.
Thus, this statement you have uttered is both true and not true.
And this should not be viewed as something that cannot be accomplished;
for what do you think is so difficult for us? Those whose actions bear no fruit are the ones who commit sins from the very beginning.
O Lord, when a task is properly accomplished, it becomes fruitful;
therefore, O Kṛṣṇa, act in such a way that there may be peace with our enemies. You are the supreme well-wisher of both the Pāṇḍavas and the Kurus.
O hero, just as Prajāpati acts for the sake of both the gods and the asuras,
so do you establish peace between the Kurus and the Pāṇḍavas;
I do not consider it difficult for you to carry out what is for our benefit.

If, O Janārdana, your purpose is thus to be accomplished, then by your mere coming you will surely achieve it; there is no doubt. But as for whatever else you intend to do against that wicked-souled hero—
"Everything shall come to pass exactly as you intend;
let there be peace with them, or whatever else it is that you desire.
O Kṛṣṇa, when this wish of yours is considered, it is our supreme authority."
That evil-souled man does not deserve death, along with his sons and kinsmen,
by whom that splendor was not tolerated when it was seen in the son of Dharma; and because he did not see a righteous means [to achieve his end], O Madhusūdana.
She was carried off by that cruel gambler through deceitful means. For how could a man born among Kṣatriyas, a wielder of the bow,
turn back when challenged, even when the loss of his life is imminent?

"O Vārṣṇeya, having seen those defeated by unrighteousness likewise exiled to the forest and facing execution, that Suyodhana has fled. And this is not surprising, O Kṛṣṇa, that you desire to act for the sake of your friends."
How indeed should the primary action be carried out—by gentle means or otherwise?
Or if you consider their immediate execution to be better, then let that very thing be done quickly; you should not deliberate further on this.

For you know, O Mādhava, how Draupadī was tormented in the midst of the assembly by that evil-minded man, and how even that was endured by him; yet he thinks, "May he indeed behave properly toward the Pāṇḍavas."
No understanding arises in me, like seed sown in barren soil. Therefore, O Vārṣṇeya, quickly do that which you deem appropriate and beneficial for the Pāṇḍavas— that which is our immediate duty.
The Blessed One said:
"It is even so, O mighty-armed Pāṇḍava, just as you say.
I shall bring about the welfare of both the Pāṇḍavas and the Kurus."
"O Bībhatsu, all this depends upon two factors.
For even a field that is fertile and well-prepared by a farmer will never yield fruit without rain, O son of Kuntī."
In that case, they might indeed speak of human effort, such as irrigation performed with exertion;
yet even there, one would certainly observe the drying up caused by fate.
This has been determined by the intellect of the great-souled ones of old.
The cause of the world is indeed joined with both destiny and human effort;
for I shall perform that [human effort] to the utmost of my personal exertion,
yet it is not possible for me to act against destiny in any way whatsoever.
For that evil-minded one acts having abandoned both righteousness and truth;
he does not feel remorse for such deeds.
Moreover, his ministers further increase that most wicked disposition of his.
Śakuni, the son of the Sūta, and his brother Duḥśāsana likewise— Suyodhana,
along with his followers, will not attain peace through the relinquishment of the kingdom,
O Pārtha, except by means of his slaughter.

Nor will the King of Dharma desire to relinquish [the kingdom] even through prostration; though entreated, that evil-minded one will not grant the realm. Yet, I do not think Yudhiṣṭhira’s command should be spoken to him.
O Bhārata, the purpose has been stated there by Dharmarāja;
thus, that Kaurava will not commit all those evils. And while they are not being committed, he shall become deserving of death by the world.

O Bhārata, he who thus mistreated all of you while you were still children, and by whom your kingdom was seized through that cruel and evil-minded act— he is indeed to be slain both by me and by the world.
The wicked man finds no peace upon seeing the prosperity of Yudhiṣṭhira;
O Pārtha, he has repeatedly attempted to sow dissension between us for your sake,
yet I did not accept that evil intent of his.
For you too, O mighty-armed one, know his supreme intention,
as well as my desire to do what is pleasing to the King of Dharma. Knowing both his own mind and mine, he [acted accordingly].
O Arjuna, you suddenly suspect me as if you were ignorant;
yet even that supreme, divine [weapon] has been mastered by you. O Pārtha, since this was ordained by destiny, how could there be safety from our enemies?

"O Pāṇḍava, whatever can be accomplished by me through speech or even through action, that I shall do, O Pārtha; yet I do not hope for peace with our enemies. How could one who desires such peace speak thus regarding the seizure of the cattle?"
Even though Bhīṣma entreated him when the year of the journey had passed,
they were defeated at that very moment when they were first conceived by you;
for Suyodhana was not satisfied even with a fragment or a mere moment.
"In every way, however, I must carry out the command of the King of Dharma;
furthermore, I must consider the evil deeds of that wicked-souled one.
Nakula said:
O Mādhava, many kinds of words, consistent with dharma and true to reality, were spoken by the King of Dharma, who knows the law and is generous; and O Mādhava,
having understood the king’s intention, Bhīmasena [acted accordingly].
The tranquility and the prowess of arms of the son of Mādhava have been proclaimed;
likewise, you have heard what was said by Phalguna as well. And your own opinion, O hero, has been stated by you more than once.
"O Supreme among Men, having heard all this and the opinion of others, you should do whatever you deem appropriate for the occasion; for,
O Keśava, one's judgment varies according to each specific circumstance."

"O subduer of enemies, a man must personally act when the time has arrived; for an objective conceived in one way often turns out quite otherwise. O best of men, the minds of people in this world are transient."
For our perceptions were indeed one way when we were dwellers of the forest, invisible; but they are quite another, O Kṛṣṇa, now that we are visible again.
Even so it was for us, O Vārṣṇeya, as we wandered in the forest at that time.
"O Hero, Janārdana, the devotion toward the kingdom is not as it is now;
for having heard that we have returned from our forest exile,
seven Akṣauhiṇīs have assembled through your grace."
For seeing these tigers among men, possessed of inconceivable strength and prowess, with weapons grasped in battle— who among men here would not tremble?
Therefore, you, in the midst of the Kurus, [should address] him who is filled with fear, preceded by words of consolation.
Speak words such that the dull-witted Suyodhana does not become distressed,
[regarding] Yudhiṣṭhira, Bhīmasena, the unconquered Bībhatsu,
Sahadeva, myself, you, and Keśava, O Rāma.
And the highly heroic Sātyaki, Virāṭa along with his son,
Drupada together with his ministers, Dhṛṣṭadyumna the son of Pṛṣata,
the valiant King of Kāśī, and Dhṛṣṭaketu the lord of the Cedis.
"Which mortal, bearing flesh and blood, would fight back in battle? By your mere arrival, O mighty-armed one, you will undoubtedly accomplish the desired goal for the King of Dharma alone."
O sinless one, Vidura, Bhīṣma, Droṇa, and Bahlika are capable of discerning what is beneficial when it is spoken by you;
they will also persuade Dhṛtarāṣṭra, the lord of men.
And as for that Suyodhana of evil conduct along with his ministers—
since Vidura is the listener of the matter and you, O Janārdana, are the speaker—
what purpose turning away from its course could they possibly not set back upon the right path?
Sahadeva said:
"O subduer of enemies, that which has been spoken by the king is indeed the eternal dharma; however, you must act in such a way that war itself may take place."
O descendant of Daśārha, even if the Kurus should desire peace with the Pāṇḍavas,
you would still have to engage them in battle.
For how could they endure seeing the princess of Pañcāla thus afflicted and brought into the assembly hall?
"O Kṛṣṇa, if Bhīma, Arjuna, and the righteous Dharmarāja were to abandon dharma, my wrath toward Suyodhana would be appeased by non-violence;
however, since they have cast aside dharma, I desire to fight him in battle."
"Speak my words, O Kṛṣṇa, to the unwise Suyodhana: 'You must dwell either in the forest in hardship or in the city named after the elephant. Sātyaki said:
"O mighty-armed one, the high-minded Sahadeva has spoken the truth.
Only upon the slaying of Duryodhana will there be peace for that wrath of mine. For you know how, upon seeing those clad in bark and deerskins in the forest..."
Even in you, O best of men, anger has arisen upon seeing the Pāṇḍavas in distress;
therefore, that which the heroic son of Mādrī, that bull among men,
has spoken as his word for all the warriors— that is the considered opinion.
05,079.008 Vaiśampāyana said:
While the high-minded Yuyudhāna was speaking these words,
a most terrifying lion-roar arose from all the warriors there on every side.
For all those heroes from every side, eager for battle, honored those words of the descendant of Śini, cheering him with cries of "Excellent! Excellent!
Vaiśampāyana said:
Having heard the king’s words, which were beneficial and consistent with righteousness and worldly purpose,
Kṛṣṇā— whose long black hair was flowing free— oppressed by grief, spoke to the descendant of Daśārha as he sat there. She was the daughter of King Drupada.
Having honored Sahadeva and the great car-warrior Sātyaki,
and seeing Bhīmasena so deeply despondent,
that high-minded woman, her eyes filled with tears and her mind exceedingly distressed, spoke these words.
"O mighty-armed Madhusūdana, knower of dharma, it is known to you how the Pāṇḍavas were deprived of their happiness by resorting to deceit,
O Janārdana, by the son of Dhṛtarāṣṭra together with his ministers."
And how Saṃjaya was made to hear the secret counsel in private by King Yudhiṣṭhira, O descendant of Daśārha— that too is known to you; and everything that was said to Saṃjaya has been heard by you.
"O father of great splendor, let five villages be given to us:
Kuśasthala, Vṛkasthala, Āsandī, Vāraṇāvata,
and some small settlement as the fifth, O mighty-armed one."
"O Keśava, this is what Duryodhana and his friends should be told. But having heard these words of the modest Yudhiṣṭhira, who desired peace, O Daśārha, Suyodhana did not act upon them.
O Kṛṣṇa, if Suyodhana should desire peace without the surrender of the kingdom, you must not enter into an agreement with him by going there under any circumstances.
For, O mighty-armed one, the Pāṇḍavas together with the Sṛñjayas will be capable [of victory].
To withstand the terrible and enraged army of Dhṛtarāṣṭra’s sons,
neither conciliation nor bribery can achieve any purpose among them;
therefore, O Madhusūdana, you should show no mercy toward them.
O Kṛṣṇa, those enemies who cannot be pacified by conciliation or by gifts—
against them, one who seeks to protect his own life must employ punishment.
Therefore, O Acyuta, a great punishment should be swiftly cast upon them.
O mighty-armed one, together with you, the Pāṇḍavas, and the Sṛñjayas— this [alliance],
O Kṛṣṇa, if carried out, would be capable for the sons of Pṛthā and bring glory to you as well; it would bring happiness to the entire warrior class.
O descendant of Daśārha, a Kṣatriya who has succumbed to greed must indeed be slain by a Kṣatriya who adheres to his own duty, or even by one who is not a Kṣatriya—
except for a Brāhmaṇa, my dear, even if he is established in every kind of sin.

"For the Brāhmaṇa is indeed the preceptor of all social orders and the one who eats the first portion of what is offered. O Janārdana, just as there is guilt when one who should not be killed is being killed, so too is guilt seen in the failure to kill one who deserves to be killed; thus know those who understand the Dharma."
"O Kṛṣṇa, act in such a way that this fault does not touch you,
O Daśārha, regarding the Pāṇḍavas along with the Sṛñjayas and their armies.
O Janārdana, out of confidence, I shall speak what has been said before once more."
"O Keśava, what woman on earth could possibly be like me?
She is the daughter of King Drupada, arisen from the middle of the sacrificial altar;
she is the sister of Dhṛṣṭadyumna and your dear friend, O Kṛṣṇa."

Having entered the lineage of Ajamidha, I have become the daughter-in-law of the high-souled Pandu and the queen of the sons of Pandu, who possess splendor equal to the five Indras. By those five heroes, five sons have been born to me, all of whom are great chariot-warriors.
O Kṛṣṇa, according to dharma, Abhimanyu was as much yours as he was mine;
yet here I am, having been seized by the hair and humiliated in the assembly hall while the sons of Pāṇḍu looked on and while you, Keśava, were still alive.
While the Kauravas, the Pāñcālas, and the Vṛṣṇis were still alive,
I was reduced to slavery by those wicked men and stood in the midst of the assembly hall,
while the Pāṇḍavas looked on, devoid of indignation and inactive.
"Save me!"—thus have you been longed for by my mind, O Govinda.
When the blessed king, my father-in-law, spoke these words to me:
"Choose a boon, O Princess of Pañcāla; in my estimation, you are worthy of a boon."
"O Keśava, when I said, 'Let the Pāṇḍavas be no longer slaves, but possessed of chariots and weapons,' they were sent forth into exile in the forest;
O Janārdana, you are well aware of such sorrows as these."
"Save me, O lotus-eyed one, along with my husband, kinsmen, and relatives!
Surely, O Kṛṣṇa, by law I am the daughter-in-law of both Bhīṣma and Dhṛtarāṣṭra; yet I have been reduced to slavery."
"Fie on the strength of Bhīmasena! Fie on Pārtha, the foremost of archers!
For here Duryodhana lives, O Kṛṣṇa, even for a single moment.
If I am worthy of your favor, and if you have compassion for me..."

"O Kṛṣṇa, let all your wrath be directed against the sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra. Having spoken thus, she— she whose outer corners of the eyes were dark— grasped her beautiful, deep-blue bow, which had a gentle curve at the end and a sharp point, and was perfumed with sacred fragrances.
Endowed with all auspicious marks and possessing the luster of a great serpent,
she of the noble hips took hold of his mass of hair with her left hand; then,
the lotus-eyed woman, moving with the gait of an elephant, approached the lotus-eyed one.
With eyes filled with tears, Kṛṣṇā spoke these words to Kṛṣṇa:
"O lotus-eyed one, this [hair] was seized by Duḥśāsana’s hand;
it should be remembered by you at all times when you seek peace with the enemy."
"O Kṛṣṇa, if Bhīma and Arjuna are so wretched as to desire peace,
then my aged father will fight along with his sons, who are great chariot-warriors;
and my five sons, O Madhusūdana, are possessed of great heroism."
Placing Abhimanyu at their head, they will fight with the Kurus;
if I do not see that dark arm of Duḥśāsana severed and covered in dust, what peace can there be for my heart?
Indeed, thirteen years have passed while I have waited,
keeping my resentment within my heart like a blazing fire;
my heart is being torn asunder, tormented by the arrow-heads of his terrible words.
"This one of mighty arms who today perceives the Dharma," having said this, the large-eyed Kṛṣṇā wept with great trembling,
her voice loud and choked with tears.
With her full and broad hips, she drenched her joined breasts,
shedding tears born of her eyes like exceedingly hot liquid that had turned to water.
To her, the mighty-armed Keśava spoke, offering words of consolation.
"O Kṛṣṇā, before long you shall see the women of the Bharatas weeping;
thus, O timid one, they will weep, their kinsmen and relatives slain,
their friends killed, and their forces destroyed— those with whom you, O passionate lady, are enraged."
And I, together with Bhīma, Arjuna, and the twins,
shall carry this out by the command of Yudhiṣṭhira and by the decree ordained by fate;
for the sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra are ripened by time and do not listen to my words.
They shall lie slain upon the ground, made into food for dogs and jackals;
for even Mount Himavat might move, the earth might split into a hundred pieces,
and the sky with its stars might fall, yet my word shall never be in vain.
The sky might fall, the earth might shatter, and the Himavat might crumble;
the ocean of waters might dry up, but my word, O Kṛṣṇā, can never be in vain. I promise you this in truth: O Kṛṣṇā, let your tears be restrained.
"Before long, you shall see your husbands, their enemies slain and endowed with glory.
Arjuna said:
"Today, you are the most excellent friend to all the Kurus."
O Keśava, you are a constant relative beloved by both sides; you are capable of ensuring the well-being of the Dhārtarāṣṭras through the Pāṇḍavas and of bringing about peace among them.
"O lotus-eyed one, slayer of enemies, go from here and speak to the intolerant Suyodhana on behalf of the Bharatas for the sake of peace; you must say that which ought to be said.
If what you say is consistent with dharma and artha, auspicious, and wholesome—"
"The fool will not accept what is beneficial; he will fall under the power of destiny.
The Blessed One said:
"That which is righteous, beneficial to us, and conducive to the well-being of the Kurus—"
"I shall go to King Dhṛtarāṣṭra with the desire to obtain [peace].
Vaiśampāyana said:
Then, when the darkness had departed and the pure sun had risen,
When the auspicious hour had arrived and the sun’s rays were mild,
in the month of Kaumuda, under the asterism Revatī, at the end of autumn and the onset of winter—
at that time when the crops were abundant and all was pleasant— the best of those endowed with spiritual strength arose, alert and composed.
Hearing auspicious, meritorious, and pleasant words from the esteemed Brahmins— just as Vāsava hears them from the ṛṣis—
he performed his morning duties, bathed, purified himself, and adorned himself.
Janārdana approached Vivasvat and Pāvaka;
having touched the hump of a bull, saluted the Brāhmaṇas,
and circumambulated the fire, he beheld auspicious omens before him.
Having assented to those words of the Pāṇḍava, Janārdana addressed Sātyaki, the grandson of Śini, as he sat there:
"Let the chariot be brought, along with the conch, the discus, and the mace."
Quivers, spears, and all manner of weapons [are ready];
for Duryodhana is evil-minded, as are Karṇa and the son of Subala.
Yet, even an ordinary enemy must not be disregarded by one who is more powerful.
Then, having understood that intention of Keśava, his attendants,
who bore the discus and mace, rushed forward to yoke the chariot. It was like the blazing fire of time, moving through the sky upon its path.
It was adorned with two wheels possessing the radiance of the moon and the sun; it was variegated on all sides with half-moons, full moons, fish, beasts, birds,
various flowers, and precious gems.
Adorned with various ornaments and diverse,
wonderful garments,
he was large and beautiful to behold, resembling the rising sun.
With its body variegated with jewels and gold, possessing excellent banners and beautiful flags,
well-equipped, invincible, and covered with tiger-skins,
it was the destroyer of the fame of enemies and the increaser of the joy of the Yadus.
With the horses Sainya, Sugrīva, Meghapuṣpa, and Balāhaka—
bathed and endowed with every excellence—
they further increased the majesty of Kṛṣṇa.
The chariot, with its Sughoṣa banner, was joined by the lord of birds;
it resembled the peak of Mount Meru and resounded like clouds and kettledrums,
protected by Dāruka, who was skilled in the art of charioteering.
Having performed a circumambulation, Śauri, adorned with ornaments suitable for his departure,
ascended the chariot like a meritorious man ascending a celestial vehicle (*vimāna*). Then, having caused Sātyaki to mount, Puruṣottama set forth.
Making both the earth and the intermediate space resound with the noise of the chariot,
the time of day suddenly became one from which the thick clouds had been dispelled;
an auspicious wind blew and the dust was stilled.
Auspicious beasts and birds, moving clockwise and favorably,
followed Vāsudeva on his departure;
they accompanied him from all sides with sounds containing words of auspicious meaning.
The cranes, woodpeckers, and swans [honored] Madhusūdana;
and the sacrificial fire, being fed with oblations of mantras and great offerings,
became smokeless with its flames turning to the right.
Vasiṣṭha, Vāmadeva, Bhūridyumna, Gaya, Kratha, Śukra, Nārada, Vālmīka, the Maruts, Kuśika, and Bhṛgu,
as well as the Brahman-sages and celestial-sages, [praised] Kṛṣṇa, the bringer of happiness to the Yadus.
They all turned together toward the younger brother of Vāsava, circumambulating him clockwise.
Thus honored by these highly fortunate and virtuous hosts of great ṛṣis,
Kṛṣṇa set out toward the abode of the Kurus.
Having paid homage to the deities and caused the Brahmins to pronounce blessings,
the lotus-eyed Acyuta set forth together with Sātyaki.
Yudhiṣṭhira, the son of Kuntī, followed after him as he was departing.
Both Bhīmasena and Arjuna, the two Pāṇḍava sons of Mādrī,
the valiant Cekitāna, Dhṛṣṭaketu the king of the Cedis,
Drupada, the king of Kāśī, and the great car-warrior Śikhaṇḍin.
Dhṛṣṭadyumna with his sons, Virāṭa, and the Kekayas—
these Kṣatriyas set out to escort that bull among Kṣatriyas.
Then, having followed Govinda, the righteous King Yudhiṣṭhira [returned].
Then, in the presence of the kings, the radiant one spoke these words:
"He who, being firm-minded and free from greed, would never follow an unjust path out of desire, fear, avarice, or for the sake of wealth; [he alone is a true man]."
Keśava is the knower of dharma, steadfast, and wise toward all beings;
he is the lord of all creatures, the god of gods, and possessed of great majesty.
To him, who is endowed with every virtue and marked by the Śrīvatsa, [I bow].
Embracing her, the son of Kuntī began to give her instructions:
"That woman who, from her childhood, has nurtured us—
she who is devoted to fasting and asceticism, and always intent on rites for well-being."
O Janārdana, she who was devoted to the worship of the gods and guests and to the service of her elders, who was affectionate and fond of her sons,
and who protected us here from the fear of Suyodhana— she is dear to us, O crusher of enemies.
Having crossed over the great oppression of death like a ship across the ocean,
O Mādhava, you should inquire after the welfare of her who, for our sake, has constantly endured sufferings that she did not deserve.
Comfort her greatly, who is overwhelmed with grief for her sons; having offered salutations, embrace the Pāṇḍavas while proclaiming their virtues,
O subduer of enemies, recounting the sufferings she has endured since her marriage to her fathers-in-law.
"O Kṛṣṇa,

subduer of enemies, will that time ever come when this reversal of suffering occurs, so that I may place my afflicted mother in happiness, for she suffers seeing humiliations to which she is not worthy?"
As we were departing for the forest, that miserable woman, longing for her son, ran after us; yet, abandoning her as she wept, we went to the woods.
Surely she does not die from her sorrows, O Keśava, if indeed she still lives.
O Kṛṣṇa, O Lord, she who is deeply afflicted by grief for her sons and honored by the people of Ānarta should be saluted by you on my behalf; furthermore,
she should be appeased and paid homage by you at the request of everyone.
Dhṛtarāṣṭra the Kauravya, and the kings of advanced age— Bhīṣma, Droṇa, Kṛpa, and the great king Bāhlika,
as well as the son of Droṇa, Somadatta, and all the Bharatas individually.
O Janārdana, honor them according to their age and their rank. O Madhusūdana, embrace Vidura— the highly wise counselor of the Kurus, whose intellect is unfathomable and who knows the Dharma.
Having spoken thus to Keśava in the midst of the kings, Yudhiṣṭhira,
having received permission and having circumambulated Kṛṣṇa, turned back;
but as he was departing, Bībhatsu [Arjuna] addressed his friend, that bull among men.
He spoke to the unconquered descendant of Daśārha, the slayer of enemy heroes:
"O Lord Govinda, that which occurred regarding our former determination in counsel concerning half the kingdom is known among all the kings."

If Suyodhana should give that to the King of Dharma with detachment, with reverence, and without contempt— O Govinda, O mighty-armed one— if he gives it, it would be pleasing to me, and they would be liberated from great fear.

"If, therefore, the son of Dhṛtarāṣṭra acts otherwise, being ignorant of the right means, O Janārdana, I shall surely bring about the end of the Kṣatriyas. When this was said by the Pāṇḍava, Vṛkodara rejoiced greatly.
Again and again, the son of Pāṇḍu trembled out of the force of his anger;
and trembling, the son of Kuntī let out great roars,
his mind overflowing with joy upon hearing Dhananjaya’s words.
Hearing that roar of his, the archers trembled violently,
and all their mounts discharged excrement and urine.
Having thus spoken to Keśava there, and having likewise declared his firm resolve—
Having been granted leave, he returned after embracing Janārdana.
When all those kings had departed, Janārdana,
joyful and mounted upon his chariot drawn by Sainya and Sugrīva, quickly pursued him.
Those horses of Vāsudeva, urged on by Dāruka, seemed to lick the path as they swallowed the sky. Then the mighty-armed Keśava beheld sages upon the road.
Blazing with Brahmanic splendor, they stood on both sides of the path;
having quickly descended from his chariot and offered salutations, Janārdana addressed all those sages in due order, honoring them.
Is all well in the worlds? Is the Dharma being properly practiced?
Do the three castes abide by the instruction of the Brahmins?
And is the worship of ancestors, gods, and guests being properly performed?
Having offered that worship to them, Madhusūdana spoke:
"O Blessed Ones, where have you attained perfection? What is your path here?
Or what is the task of the Blessed Ones? What may I do for you?"
"For what purpose have you, O Blessed Ones, come to the surface of the earth?
Thus addressed by Keśava, all the sages of rigid vows,
headed by Nārada, greeted Keśava in return.
The great seer Satyadevala with his head downward and garlanded with snakes;
Arvāvasu, Jānu, Maitreya, the powerful Śunaka,
Baka Dālbhya, Sthūlaśiras, and likewise Kṛṣṇadvaipāyana.
Āyoda-dhaumya, Dhaumya, Āṇi, Māṇḍavya, Kauśika, Dāmoṣṇīṣa, Triṣavaṇa, Parṇāda, Ghaṭajānuka,
Mauñjāyana, Vāyubhakṣa, Pārāśarya, and Śārika.
Śīlavān, Aśanidhātṛ, Śūnyapāla, Akṛtaśrama, Śvetaketu, Katthāma, Vaida, and Hiraṇyada—
approaching Madhusūdana, the son of Jamadagni spoke to him.
Having embraced Govinda in former times during his virtuous conduct,
the celestial ṛṣis who perform meritorious deeds, the highly learned brāhmaṇas,
and the ascetic royal ṛṣis all paid homage to him, O descendant of Daśārha.

O Janārdana of great splendor, the gods and asuras who witnessed the ancient battle have gathered from all sides, desiring to behold the assembled host of earthly kṣatriyas, as well as the courtiers and kings, and you yourself, O Truth.
"O Keśava, let us go to see this great spectacle;
O Mādhava, we wish to hear words endowed with righteousness and purpose as they are spoken by you among the kings of the Kurus, O scorcher of foes."
"O Keśava, we wish to hear the words spoken by you in the assembly, which were so sweet to hear; we wish to hear what the Kurus intend to do,
as well as what Bhīṣma, Droṇa, and others, and the high-minded Vidura, have said."
"And you, O tiger among the Yādavas, shall indeed assemble in that hall;
we wish to hear your divine words and theirs there, O Mādhava— words that are truthful and auspicious, O Govinda."

The earth, purified by the touch of your feet and freed from all wickedness, shall shine with the increase of Dharma and bestow joy upon us here. You have been bid farewell, O mighty-armed one; we shall see you again.
"Go without hindrance, O hero; we shall see you returned to the assembly hall, seated upon a celestial throne, endowed with strength and splendor.
Vaiśampāyana said:
As the son of Devakī departed, ten great car-warriors, destroyers of enemy heroes with mighty arms, followed him with weapons in hand;
and there were a thousand foot-soldiers and horsemen, O scorcher of foes.
"O King, there was abundant food and hundreds of other servants.
Janamejaya said:
"How did the high-souled Madhusūdana, the descendant of Daśārha, set out?"
"And what were the omens for that one of great majesty as he departed?
Vaiśampāyana said:
"These were the wonders that occurred at the departure of that high-souled one."
Listen to those divine, celestial, and portentous signs from me: even though there were no clouds, a thunderclap accompanied by lightning arose,
and immediately thereafter, Parjanya rained down heavily in a cloudless sky.
The great rivers flowed westward, and the best of the Sindhu rivers flowed toward the east;
all directions were reversed, and nothing could be discerned. O King, fires blazed up and the earth trembled.
Well-buckets and jars poured forth water by the hundreds;
yet at that time, this entire world was enveloped in darkness.
O King, neither the cardinal directions nor the intermediate points could be discerned due to the dust.
A great sound arose in the sky, yet no body was seen;
O King, in all lands this seemed like a marvel.
A wind from the southwest began to crush Hastināpura.
Shattering the trees in great numbers, harsh and with a terrifying roar—
wherever the descendant of Vṛṣṇi traveled on the road, O Bhārata,
there a pleasant breeze blew and everything moved in a clockwise direction.
A rain of flowers and lotuses fell in abundance;
the road became level, free from hardship, and cleared of kusha grass and thorns.
As he traveled here and there, O King, that mighty-armed one was accompanied by brahmins.

The giver of wealth is honored with offerings of honey-mixture (*madhuparka*) and flowers; women, meeting him on the road, scatter fragrant wild blossoms over that high-souled one who delights in the welfare of all beings.

O bull of the Bharatas, he passed comfortably through the delightful Śālibhavana, which was filled with every kind of grain and inhabited by the most righteous people; and as he went, he beheld many cattle-rich villages that were beautiful and pleasing to the heart.
Passing through cities and various kingdoms,
[the people] were ever-joyful and well-disposed, protected by the Bharatas;
they were not anxious about foreign armies and were unacquainted with calamities.
Then, as he was coming from Upaplavya, the people dwelling in the city gathered together along the road,
desiring to see Viṣvaksena. They all beheld him, their lord, like a well-kindled fire named Sunāman.
They honored that guest who had arrived from afar, for he was worthy of worship.
Having reached Vṛkasthala, Keśava, the slayer of enemy heroes,
found the sun’s rays scattered as the bright orb turned crimson.
Quickly descending from the chariot and performing his purification according to the prescribed rites, he gave instructions for unyoking the chariot and sat down for the twilight devotions.
Dāruka also, having released the horses and tended to them according to the scriptures, [performed his duties].
He cast off all his armor and, having released them, sent them away.
Having passed beyond all that, Madhusūdana said:
"For the sake of Yudhiṣṭhira’s purpose, we shall dwell here for the night."
Having understood his intention, the men constructed a dwelling for him;
in an instant, they prepared excellent food and drink.
O King, those who were the leading brahmins in that village [prepared it].
Noble, well-born, modest, and established in the conduct of Brahman,
they approached the high-souled Hṛṣīkeśa, the subduer of enemies,
and performed worship according to the rules, accompanied by benedictions and auspicious rites.
Having honored the descendant of Daśārha, who is worshipped in all the worlds,
they offered their jewel-adorned residences to that high-souled one. The Lord, having greeted them with due respect and saying "It is done," dismissed them.
Having approached their dwellings,
Keśava returned with them; there, after having fed the well-prepared Brahmins and having eaten together with them all, he dwelt happily for that night.
Vaiśampāyana said:
Having learned through messengers that Madhusūdana was approaching,
Dhṛtarāṣṭra, after honoring the mighty-armed Bhīṣma, spoke to him.
With his hair standing on end, he spoke these words to Droṇa, Saṃjaya, the high-minded Vidura, and Duryodhana along with his ministers:
"O joy of the Kurus, a great and wonderful marvel is being heard."
Women, children, and the elderly speak of it in every house;
others, having gathered together, discuss it with respect;
and various conversations concerning it take place in the courtyards and in the assembly halls.
The powerful descendant of Daśārha will come for the sake of the Pāṇḍavas;
that slayer of Madhu is in every way worthy of our honor and worship,
for he is the lord of all beings and the world depends upon him.
In that month of Mādhava, there is fortitude, heroism, wisdom, and vital energy.
That best of men should be honored, for he is the eternal Dharma;
indeed, when honored, he leads to happiness, but when unhonored, he brings misery.
If that subduer of enemies, the descendant of Daśārha, is satisfied with our attentions, we shall attain all our desires among all the kings. Therefore,
O scorcher of foes, make the necessary arrangements this very day for his worship.
"Let assembly halls be established along the road, provided with everything that fulfills every desire, O mighty-armed one, so that affection for you may truly arise in him.
Act accordingly, O son of Gandhārī; or what do you think, Bhīṣma?"
Then Bhīṣma and all the others spoke thus to Dhṛtarāṣṭra, the lord of men, honoring those words of his as supreme. Then King Duryodhana, having understood their consent, [acted accordingly].
He began to designate delightful sites for assembly halls;
then, in various beautiful regions,
they constructed numerous assembly halls in their respective parts, strewn with all kinds of jewels.
There were various seats endowed with diverse qualities,
women, perfumes, ornaments, and fine garments;
as well as excellent foods and drinks, and many kinds of edibles.
Then the king gave fragrant garlands; furthermore,
for the sake of their residence, the Kuru king provided a delightful assembly hall in the village of Vṛkasthala, adorned with many jewels.
Having thus arranged all these things, which were worthy of the gods and superhuman,
King Duryodhana then reported it to Dhṛtarāṣṭra.
Keśava [described] all those assembly halls and various kinds of jewels.
Without even considering [the consequences], the descendant of Daśārha arrived at that abode of the Kurus.
Dhṛtarāṣṭra said:
"O Kṣattṛ, Janārdana has come here from Upaplavya."
He dwells at Vṛkasthala and will arrive here in the morning;
he is the lord of the Āhukas, the leader of all the Sātvatas,
the high-minded, the one of great heroism, the great minister Janārdana.
Mādhava is the sustainer and protector of the prosperous Vṛṣṇi clan;
he is the Blessed One, the great-grandfather of even the three worlds,
whose wisdom the well-disposed Vṛṣṇis and Andhakas revere.
Just as the Ādityas, Vasus, and Rudras follow the wisdom of Bṛhaspati,
so shall I offer worship to that high-souled scion of the Daśārhas;
O knower of dharma, listen as I describe this to you in your very presence.

I shall give him sixteen golden chariots, each yoked to four excellent horses born in Bāhlīka, which are of a single color with very black limbs; as well as elephants that are ever-in rut, with tusks as long as plow-poles, and skilled in combat.
To each one of Keśava’s wives, I shall give eight female slaves; for each of these beautiful women, who possess the luster of gold and have not yet borne children,
I shall provide a hundred female slaves, and an equal number of male servants.
I shall also give him eighteen thousand sheep from the mountains, abundant and soft to the touch,
as well as thousands of skins produced in the land of China.
"I shall give those to him as well, for as much as Keśava deserves.
This pure, highly radiant jewel shines by day and by night;
I shall give that to him too, for Keśava truly deserves it."
"In a single day, even one [of these vehicles] can travel fourteen *yojanas*.
I shall give him that vehicle yoked with mules; moreover, I shall provide him with as many mounts as he has and as many men as he possesses."
"Then I shall always provide him with food eight times greater than this.
And all my sons and grandsons— with the exception of Duryodhana—
shall go out to meet the descendant of Daśārha, adorned and mounted upon polished chariots."
Thousands of beautiful courtesans, well-adorned and auspicious, will go out on foot to meet the illustrious Keśava;
even those from within the city who wish to do so will go forth to meet Janārdana.
And those auspicious maidens shall go forth unveiled to see him;
for the entire city, including its women, men, and children, gazes upon that high-souled Madhusūdana as subjects look toward the radiant sun.

"Let great banners and flags be raised in every direction," he commanded, "and let his path be sprinkled with water so that it is free from dust. And he further instructed that the house of Duḥśāsana was even more excellent than the house of Duryodhana.
Therefore, let this city be quickly prepared, thoroughly swept, and adorned.
For it is graced by palaces of beautiful form;
it is auspicious, delightful, and possesses great wealth for all seasons.
"Whatever jewel is in this house, both mine and that of Duryodhana,
whatever that descendant of Vṛṣṇi deserves— that should undoubtedly be given.
Vidura said:
"O King, you are highly esteemed even by the three worlds as the best of beings;
you are honored by the world and respected, O Bhārata.
That you, standing in the final stage of life, should speak thus—[is indeed worthy of you]."
"O King, through the scriptures or through sound reasoning, you are indeed firm and steadfast;
like light upon a polished stone, like the sun, or like a great wave in the ocean,
the great Dharma resides within you— thus the subjects have resolved."

O King, this world has always been permeated by the abundance of your virtues; therefore, together with your kinsmen, strive constantly to protect those virtues. Practice straightforwardness, lest you be ruined in many ways through childish folly.
"O King, that you wish to bestow upon Kṛṣṇa— your guest— so much as your kingdom, your sons, your grandsons, and even your most beloved friends; this and more,
as well as the earth itself, is worthy of the descendant of Daśārha."

"But you do not desire this for the sake of dharma, nor for the sake of doing what is pleasing to him; I swear this by my own soul, O Kṛṣṇa. This is a mere illusion, a falsehood, a deception, O giver of many sacrificial fees."
"I know your secret intention, O King, hidden by your outward conduct. The Pāṇḍavas, O monarch, desire only five villages each;
yet you do not wish to give them those—so who will bring about peace?"
"By means of wealth, you seek to win over the mighty-armed Vārṣṇeya; by this very stratagem, you wish to create a rift between him and the Pāṇḍavas.
Yet he cannot be won over by riches, nor by exertion, nor by disparagement."
"No one other than Dhanañjaya can accomplish this; this is the truth I tell you. I know the majesty of Kṛṣṇa, and I know his firm devotion to him;
I know that he would never abandon Dhanañjaya, who is as dear to him as his own life."
Janārdana will desire nothing other than a jar full of water, nothing other than water for washing his feet, and nothing other than inquiries regarding his welfare;
for such is the hospitable reception dear to this high-souled one, who is worthy of honor.
O King, let that which is due to him be performed for him, for Janārdana is worthy of honor. Keśava approaches the Kurus seeking their welfare;
O King, provide him with that very purpose for which he has come.

O Indra among kings, the descendant of Daśārha desires peace for you, for Duryodhana, and for the Pāṇḍavas; therefore, act upon his word. You are their father, O King, and they are your sons; you are old, while the others are but children.
Behave toward them as a father; for they indeed behave toward you like sons.
Having established peace between the Matsyas and Pañcālas and the Pāṇḍavas along with the Kurus, attain happiness according to dharma and achieve great fame.
Duryodhana said:
"Everything that Vidura has said regarding Kṛṣṇa is spoken truly;
for Janārdana is devoted to the sons of Pṛthā and cannot be alienated from them."
"O Indra among kings, whatever wealth of many kinds is to be given to Janārdana accompanied by marks of honor, that should never be given;
for Keśava does not deserve such a thing, as neither the place nor the time is appropriate."
"O King, Adhokṣaja will think, 'He worships me out of fear.
O Lord of the people, that which would cause humiliation for a Kṣatriya is not a deed a wise man should perform; this is my settled conviction."
"For that lotus-eyed god Kṛṣṇa is most worthy of worship;
this is known to me in every way regarding all three worlds. Yet, O Lord, nothing should be given to him, for such is the course of our business."
"War has been commenced; indeed, it does not subside without further conflict.
Vaiśampāyana said:
Having heard those words of his, Bhīṣma, the grandfather of the Kurus, [spoke].
He spoke these words to King Vaicitravīrya:
"Janārdana would not become angry whether he is treated with honor or dishonor; even when insulted, Keśava is not capable of despising another."
"O mighty-armed one, whatever task has been resolved upon by his mind cannot be made otherwise by any means whatsoever.
Whatever that mighty-armed one may say, that must be carried out without hesitation."
"Through the mediation of Vāsudeva, let there be a swift peace with the Pāṇḍavas. That righteous-souled Janārdana will certainly speak words that are consistent with dharma and purposeful.
Therefore, you, together with your kinsmen, should address him with pleasing words."
Duryodhana said:
"O King, O Grandfather, there is no possibility that I,
while living, could enjoy this entire prosperity along with them while they are still alive."
But listen to this very great task that I have resolved upon: neither to allow an opportunity for dissension, nor to permit his departure,
will I restrain Janārdana, the ultimate refuge of the Pāṇḍavas.

When he is bound, the Vṛṣṇis, the earth, and the Pāṇḍavas will likewise become subject to me; and he will arrive here tomorrow morning. In this matter, devise a means so that Janārdana does not perceive it correctly.
"And may no calamity whatsoever befall him; therefore, please explain this to me.
Vaiśampāyana said:
Having heard those terrible words directed toward Kṛṣṇā, [the sage spoke].
Dhṛtarāṣṭra, along with his ministers, became distressed and dejected.
Then Dhṛtarāṣṭra spoke these words to Duryodhana:
"O protector of subjects, do not speak thus; this is not the eternal dharma."
"For Hṛṣīkeśa is our messenger, our kinsman, and our beloved;
being sinless toward the Kauravas, how does he deserve imprisonment?
Bhīṣma said:
"O Dhṛtarāṣṭra, this son of yours, possessed of very dull intellect, is being enticed;
though entreated by groups of well-wishers, he chooses what is harmful rather than what is beneficial. This wicked man, who follows after evil, persists upon a path that is not the right one."

"Having disregarded the words of your well-wishers, you too follow his lead. Having encountered Kṛṣṇa, whose actions are effortless, this evil-minded son of yours, along with his ministers, shall cease to exist in an instant."
"I cannot, under any circumstances, bear to hear the speech of this wicked, cruel, and evil-minded man who has abandoned righteousness and is intent on misfortune.
Vaiśampāyana said:
Having spoken thus, the aged Bhīṣma, best of the Bharatas and of supreme prowess, full of great indignation, rose from that place and departed. Vaiśampāyana said:
Having risen in the morning, Kṛṣṇa performed his entire daily ritual;
then, permitted by the Brahmins, he set out toward the city.
O King, having then taken leave of that mighty-armed one as he was departing, [the people followed].
All those inhabitants of Vṛkasthala turned back;
the lotus-eyed one set out toward the abode of the Kurus,
and they followed the path as if swallowing the sky.

Urged on by Dāruka, the horses of that great-souled one [proceeded]; meanwhile, Duryodhana had prepared along the way, for the sake of Kṛṣṇa, abundant food, beds, garments, and likewise jewels of every kind.
The lotus-eyed one of great fame and mighty arms took no pleasure in those assemblies or the jewels as he approached the court of the Kurus.
As he arrived, the sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra, well-adorned, went out to meet him.
O King, with the exception of Duryodhana, all those led by Bhīṣma, Droṇa, and Kṛpa,
as well as the vast multitude of citizens, were eager to behold Hṛṣīkeśa;
some came in various kinds of vehicles, while others went on foot.
Having met on the road with Bhīṣma of unwearied deeds,
with Droṇa, and with those sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra, he proceeded to the city surrounded by them;
and for the sake of honoring Kṛṣṇa, the city was beautifully adorned.
The royal highways became strewn with many jewels;
O King, bull of the Bharatas, there was no one at home—
neither woman, nor elder, nor child— who did not desire to see Vāsudeva.
On the royal highway, men could not even find space upon the ground;
for indeed, O King, during Hṛṣīkeśa’s entrance,
even the most magnificent mansions were crowded with excellent women.
They appeared as if they were tottering on the surface of the earth under the weight [of the crowd];
likewise, those swift horses of Vāsudeva lost their speed on the royal highway, which was crowded with men.
That lotus-eyed subduer of enemies entered the white palace of Dhṛtarāṣṭra, which was adorned with lofty mansions;
having passed through three courtyards of the royal residence, Keśava arrived.
The subduer of enemies approached King Vaicitravīrya.
As the descendant of Daśārha arrived, the highly illustrious lord of men, whose wisdom serves as his eyes,
rose up together with Droṇa and Bhīṣma.
Kṛpa, Somadatta, and the great king Bāhlika—
all of them rose from their seats, honoring Janārdana.
Then, having approached the illustrious King Dhṛtarāṣṭra, [he spoke].
Vārṣṇeya immediately honored Bhīṣma with words.
Having paid homage to Madhusūdana, they performed their respective duties.
Having applied that sequence of duties among them, Madhusūdana—
There, Mādhava met with the kings according to their seniority; then Janārdana approached Droṇa along with his son, the illustrious Bāhlīka,
Kṛpa, and Somadatta.
There was a great, magnificent, and polished golden throne;
by the command of Dhṛtarāṣṭra, Acyuta sat upon it.
Then, [the king offered] a cow, the honey-mixture, and water to Janārdana.

The priests of Dhṛtarāṣṭra presented [the offerings] according to the prescribed rules. Having been shown hospitality, Govinda sat surrounded by the Kurus, joking with them all and establishing bonds of kinship with the Kurus.

Honored and worshipped by Dhṛtarāṣṭra, that highly illustrious subduer of enemies took leave of the king and departed. Having met with those Kurus in the assembly of the Kurus according to custom, he withdrew.
Mādhava approached the delightful residence of Vidura. Vidura, having approached Janārdana with every auspicious offering,
honored the descendant of Daśārha who was provided with all desired objects.
O lotus-eyed one, the joy that arises from the cause of your arrival—
Vidura, the knower of all dharmas, having offered hospitality to Govinda,
inquired after the welfare of the sons of Pāṇḍu regarding Madhusūdana.
To that wise friend who was pleased, most excellent in intellect, constant in dharma, free from fault, and intelligent,
he then related everything concerning the conduct of the Pāṇḍavas in full detail.
The descendant of Daśārha, who perceives everything directly, spoke to the steward (Kṣattṛ).
Vaiśampāyana said:
Then, in the afternoon, Janārdana approached Vidura.
Govinda, the subduer of enemies, approached his father’s sister.
Seeing Kṛṣṇa approaching, radiant as the clear sun,
Pṛthā embraced him around the neck and cried out, remembering the sons of Pṛthā.

Seeing Govinda, the scion of the Vṛṣṇis, after a long time as his companion among those virtuous beings, Pṛthā shed tears. Having offered hospitality to Kṛṣṇa, the lord of warriors, as he sat down, she spoke to him.
With faces parched and choked with tears,
they were those who, from their very childhood, had been devoted to serving their elders,
who were mutual friends, highly esteemed, and of one mind.
Deprived of their kingdom through deceit, those men worthy of honor have gone to the wilderness; having subdued anger and joy, devoted to Brahman and truthful in speech,
the sons of Pṛthā have abandoned their dear pleasures and left me behind as I weep.
And as they departed for the forest, they carried away my very heart along with its roots.
O Keśava, how did those high-souled Pāṇḍavas, who deserved no such fate,
dwell in the great forest, O dear one, which was teeming with lions, tigers, and elephants?
"Those children were deprived of their father and were constantly cherished by me;
how did they dwell in the great forest without seeing their parents?
[How did they endure] amidst the sounds of conchs, kettledrums, clay drums, and even flutes?"
O Keśava, from their childhood the Pāṇḍavas were always awakened in their home by the trumpeting of elephants,
the neighing of horses,
and the rattling of chariot wheels.

Being honored by the twice-born with the sounding of conchs and kettledrums, the resonance of flutes and lutes, and the chanting of "Auspicious Day," they in turn honored the brahmins with garments, jewels, and ornaments.
Honored by high-souled Brahmins with auspicious hymns— those worthy of worship who offered praise and blessings— they awoke upon the rooftops of the palaces, reclining on the skins of ranku deer.
Having surely heard the roar of the beasts of prey in the great forest, O Janārdana, those people— who do not deserve such a fate— can no longer find sleep;
[they are woken] by the sounds of kettledrums and clay drums, and the resonances of conchs and flutes.
O Madhusūdana, how did they— who were formerly awakened by the sweet sounds of women’s songs and by bards, panegyrists, and heralds singing their praises—
awaken now in the great forest to the cries of wild beasts?
Modest, firm in truth, self-controlled, and compassionate toward all beings,
he has brought desire and hatred under his sway and follows the path of the virtuous—
following the example of Ambarīṣa, Māndhātṛ, Yayāti, and Nahuṣa.
He bears the difficult-to-bear burden of the ancient royal sages— Bharata, Dilīpa, and Śibi Auśīnara; he is endowed with virtuous conduct and character, knows the dharma, and is true to his promise.
A king endowed with every virtue, who might even rule over the three worlds— Ajātaśatru, whose soul is righteous, possessing the luster of pure gold,
the most excellent among all the Kurus in terms of dharma, learning, and conduct.
O Kṛṣṇa, how fares Yudhiṣṭhira, who is pleasant to behold and long-armed?

And how fares Vṛkodara, that son of Pāṇḍu who possesses the strength of ten thousand elephants, whose speed is like the wind, who is ever impatient of insult, dear to his brother, and a doer of what is pleasing to him?
O Madhusūdana, he who is the slayer of Kīcaka along with his kinsmen,
the hero who slew the Krodhavaśas, Hiḍimba, and Baka,
is equal to Śakra in prowess and equal to the wind in speed.
Equal to Maheśvara in wrath, Bhīma is the foremost among strikers;
that scorcher of foes, the self-controlled and indignant son of Pāṇḍu, having set aside his anger, strength, and resentment, abides by the command of his brother.

O Janārdana, O Vārṣṇeya, tell me of that Bhīmasena, who is a mass of splendor, a great-souled one, a flood of strength, and possessed of immeasurable energy— one who is terrifying even by his mere appearance; how is Vṛkodara today?
O Acyuta, that middle Pāṇḍava with arms like iron clubs remains there;
O Keśava, though he has only two arms, that Arjuna constantly vies even with the thousand-armed Arjuna of old, O Kṛṣṇa.
That Pāṇḍava, who can discharge five hundred arrows with a single impulse,
is the equal of King Kārtavīrya in archery;
he is like the sun in brilliance and comparable to a great ṛṣi in self-restraint.
Equal to the earth in forbearance and possessing prowess like that of Mahendra,
he by whose valor, O Madhusūdana, this great, radiant, and celebrated sovereignty over all kings of the Kurus was acquired.
He whose terrible strength of arm the Kauravas revere,
that son of Pāṇḍu, whose valor is truth, is the best among all chariot-warriors;
having encountered him face-to-face in battle, no one would ever return alive.
He who is the conqueror of all beings, unconquerable, victorious, and infallible; he who is the refuge of the Pāṇḍavas as Vāsava is of the gods—
how is that Dhananjaya, your brother and friend, today?

Sahadeva is compassionate toward all beings, restrained by a sense of shame, and skilled in great weapons; he is mild, delicate, righteous, and dear to me— this great archer, a hero who shines in assembly.

O Kṛṣṇa, the youthful Sahadeva is devoted to serving his brothers and is skilled in matters of dharma and worldly affairs. O Madhusūdana, the brothers of that high-souled one, who himself possesses auspicious conduct, always honor his virtuous behavior.
O Vārṣṇeya, speak to me of my son by Mādrī, the heroic Sahadeva, lord of warriors, who honors his elder brother and is ever-desirous of serving me;
that Pāṇḍava is delicate, young, brave, and handsome.

O Kṛṣṇa, Nakula is dear to all his brothers like their own life-breath moving outside their bodies; he is a versatile warrior, a great archer, and possessed of great strength. Is he well, O Kṛṣṇa, my child who has been raised in happiness?
O mighty-armed one, shall I ever again behold Nakula— the one accustomed to comfort, undeserving of suffering, delicate, and a great chariot-warrior—
now that I have been separated from him for even the duration of a blink of an eye?
"O hero, I find no peace; behold me, for I still live today!
O Janārdana, Draupadī was my most beloved among all my sons—well-born, endowed with virtuous character, and possessed of every excellence."
The daughter of King Drupada, renowned for her truthfulness,
choosing the world of husbands over the world of sons— that speaker of truth abandoned her beloved sons and followed the Pāṇḍavas.
O Acyuta, how could Draupadī— who is born of a noble lineage, well-honored with all her desires, a sovereign lady, and the most auspicious of women—
be [thus treated] by her five husbands, who are heroes, strikers like fire itself?

O subduer of enemies, this is the fourteenth year that I have not seen Draupadī, the speaker of truth, who has been born to share in sorrow with those great archers, and who is now utterly wasted by the mental anguish caused by her sons.
"Surely a man does not enjoy happiness through meritorious deeds alone,
if Draupadī— who is of such conduct— does not enjoy imperishable happiness. Neither Arjuna nor Yudhiṣṭhira is dear to me as much as Kṛṣṇā."
When I saw Bhīmasena and the twins entered into the assembly hall,
nothing more painful than that had ever occurred before; yet even greater was my grief when I saw Draupadī standing in the windless space near her fathers-in-law.
Bringing her there by an ignoble man who followed the dictates of anger and greed,
all the Kurus beheld her in the assembly hall clad in but a single garment;
and right there were Dhṛtarāṣṭra, the great king, and Bāhlika.
Kṛpa, Somadatta, and the Kauravas alike were despondent;
in that entire assembly, I honor the Steward (Vidura),
for it is by conduct, O noble one, that one becomes distinguished, not by wealth nor by learning.
O Kṛṣṇa, the character of that high-minded, profound, and great-souled Vidura—
his very ornament— stands supporting the worlds.
And she, both afflicted by grief and yet joyful upon seeing Govinda arrived, [spoke].
She recounted all the various kinds of suffering in their entirety;
from birth onwards, she described the many diverse sorrows she had endured.
With her face bathed in tears and overcome with exhaustion, she reflected upon it all.
O subduer of enemies, O scorcher of foes, I wonder whether that gambling with dice and the slaughter of deer— which was practiced by former wicked kings— brings them any happiness;
for that would be the greatest of afflictions for me, along with my sons.
O scorcher of the foe, it burns me that Kṛṣṇā was so ill-treated by the sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra in the assembly hall in the presence of the Kurus;
and that she was banished from the city and forced into exile.
"O Janārdana, I am the abode of various kinds of sufferings;
O Keśava, living in concealment and being confined by children— O scorcher of foes, there could be no greater affliction for me than this."
"Deceived by Duryodhana, today marks the fourteenth year.
Even in the midst of suffering, there would be no happiness if the fruit of one's merit were not exhausted.
I have never made any distinction between the sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra and the Pāṇḍavas."
"By that truth, O Kṛṣṇa, may I behold you, with your enemies slain and enveloped in glory,
released from this battle along with the Pāṇḍavas;
for their essence is truly such as it has become, and they cannot be defeated."
I would rather reproach my father, and neither myself nor Suyodhana,
by whom I was handed over to Kuntibhoja like wealth by rogues— me, a young girl playing with a ball in my hand, who was given to you by my grandfather.
He, as a friend, gave her to his high-souled friend Kuntibhoja.
O scorcher of foes, I have been treated with contempt by my father and my fathers-in-law;
O Kṛṣṇa, I am utterly miserable—what fruit is there in my life?
05.088.064a The voice that spoke to me at night during the birth of Savyasācin said:
"Your son shall conquer the earth, and his fame shall touch the heavens;
05.088.065a having slain the Kurus in battle, Dhanañjaya shall obtain the kingdom."
Together with his brothers, the son of Kuntī will perform three horse-sacrifices;
I do not find fault with that, for salutations to Dharma, the creator! To the great Kṛṣṇa [be] eternal homage; Dharma sustains all creatures.
"O Vārṣṇeya, if dharma exists, then truth shall prevail;
and you too, O Kṛṣṇa, will bring all that to pass.
Neither widowhood, nor the loss of wealth, nor enmity shall overcome me, O Mādhava."

It brings such grief as does separation from one's sons; since I do not see Dhananjaya, the wielder of the Gandiva bow and the foremost among all bearers of weapons, what peace can there be for my heart?
This is the fourteenth year during which I have not seen Yudhiṣṭhira,
Dhanañjaya, Govinda, the twins, or Vṛkodara.
For those who have perished, men perform the *śrāddha* rite for the sake of their survival.
"In effect, O Janārdana, they are dead to me, and I am dead to them.
O Mādhava, speak thus to the righteous King Yudhiṣṭhira:
'Your dharma is being greatly diminished; O son, do not act in vain.'"
"O Vāsudeva, fie upon me that I live dependent on others! A life without a fixed foundation is better than a livelihood obtained through such wretched means.
Furthermore, you should speak to Dhanañjaya and the ever-vigilant Vṛkodara."

"The time has now arrived for that purpose for which a Kṣatriya woman gives birth. If, when this time has come, you let the time pass you by, you, though esteemed by the world, will commit a most cruel act."
If you are joined with cruelty, I shall abandon you for eternal years;
for when the time has arrived, even life itself must be relinquished. And the two sons of Mādrī, who are always devoted to the dharma of the Kṣatriyas, should be told this as well.
Choose enjoyments acquired through valor even over life itself;
for objects obtained through valor always delight the mind of a man living according to the dharma of the Kṣatriya, O best of men.
"Go, O mighty-armed one, and speak to Arjuna, the Pāṇḍava hero and the best among all wielders of weapons: 'Follow the path of Draupadī.
For you know them both exceedingly well, like two enraged Deaths."
For Bhīma and Arjuna could lead even the gods to their ultimate end;
yet such was the contempt shown toward them that Kṛṣṇā was dragged into the assembly hall,
and Duḥśāsana and Karṇa addressed her with harsh words.
Duryodhana approached the high-minded Bhīmasena while the leaders of the Kurus looked on,
so that they might see the fruit of his actions;
for Vṛkodara does not find peace once he has encountered an enmity.
Even after a very long time, Bhīma’s enmity does not subside;
for as long as that crusher of foes has not brought his enemies to their end,
the mighty-armed one shall find no peace during the nights.
The seizure of my kingdom was not a cause of sorrow for me, nor was my defeat at dice;
even the exile of my sons was not a cause of grief for me,
as long as I beheld the sons of the Kurus.

But when that large and dark-limbed woman, clad in a single garment, entered the assembly hall and heard those harsh words, what indeed could have been more painful than that? She was a woman of noble form, yet she was subject to her female nature, though she had always delighted in the duties of a Kshatriya.
In that manner, though she was possessed of protectors, Kṛṣṇā found no protector;
yet you, O Madhusūdana, are the protector of this daughter of a god, and you,
O Madhusūdana, are the protector of me and my sons.

Rāma is the best among the strong, and Pradyumna is a great chariot-warrior; yet even I, O Supreme Person, must endure such sorrow today while Bhīma— the invincible and never-retreating Vijaya— is still alive.
Then Śauri, the friend of the Pārtha, consoled his paternal aunt Pṛthā, who was overwhelmed by grief for her sons and was lamenting.
"O paternal aunt, what woman in the worlds could possibly be like you? he said.
The daughter of King Śūra, having entered the lineage of Ajamīḍha,
has become a woman of noble birth, as if she had gone from one lake to another;
she is a sovereign lady, endowed with every excellence, and highly honored by her husband.
A mother of heroes and a wife of a hero, endowed with all virtues,
O woman of great wisdom, one such as you is capable of enduring both happiness and sorrow.
Sleep and lethargy, anger and joy, hunger and thirst, cold and heat— [all these she endures].
Having conquered these, the heroic sons of Pṛthā will always be devoted to happiness;
having renounced vulgar pleasures, the sons of Pṛthā are ever fond of the joys of heroes.
Possessing great energy and great strength, they would not be satisfied with anything small.
The wise devote themselves to the extremes, while those who delight in vulgar pleasures seek the middle.
The wise endure both supreme hardships and human enjoyments that exceed the norm; the steadfast find delight in the extremes, not in the middles.
They say that reaching the end is happiness, while the interval between the two ends is suffering. The Pāṇḍavas, together with Kṛṣṇā, salute you;
having reported themselves to be well, they inquire after your health.
"You shall soon behold the Pāṇḍavas healthy, with all their goals accomplished,
lords of the entire world, having slain their enemies, and endowed with prosperity.
Thus consoled, Kuntī replied to Janārdana.
"O mighty-armed Madhusūdana, overcome by the mental agonies caused by their sons, they are gripped by the darkness born of ignorance; whatever may be beneficial for them,
O Kṛṣṇa, you should do exactly as you deem fit."

O scorcher of enemies, O Kṛṣṇa, through your non-violation of dharma and your lack of deceit, I recognize your power, as well as your truthfulness, your noble lineage, your steadfastness toward friends, and likewise your wisdom and valor.
In our family, you alone are dharma; you are truth; you are great austerity.
You are the protector; you are the Great Brahman; everything is established in you. Just as you have spoken, so shall it be; truth shall abide in you.
O unconquered one, you are the refuge for the Kurus, the Pāṇḍavas, and all the worlds;
O Vārṣṇeya, O Mādhava, you are the goal of all this.
O Keśava, such is your power and the strength of your intellect.
Having addressed her and circumambulated her clockwise, the mighty-armed Govinda set out toward the house of Duryodhana. Vaiśampāyana said:
Having taken leave of Pṛthā and having circumambulated her, Govinda Śauri,
the subduer of enemies, proceeded to the house of Duryodhana,
which was endowed with supreme splendor and resembled the palace of Purandara.

Janārdana entered that place furnished with various seats; having passed through three courtyards, he was not stopped by the gatekeepers. Then [he saw] a palace resembling a mass of clouds, as lofty as a mountain peak.
The highly illustrious one ascended the palace, which was blazing with splendor;
there he beheld the long-armed son of Dhṛtarāṣṭra seated upon his throne, surrounded by thousands of kings and the Kurus.
He saw Duḥśāsana, Karṇa, and Śakuni the son of Subala seated on their thrones near Duryodhana.
As the descendant of Daśārha approached, the highly illustrious son of Dhṛtarāṣṭra [rose].
He rose up together with his ministers, honoring Madhusūdana.
Having met with Dhṛtarāṣṭra’s son and his ministers, Keśava,
the scion of the Vṛṣṇis, greeted the kings there according to their seniority.
There, the infallible Lord Acyuta sat down upon a well-adorned couch made of Jāmbūnada gold, covered with various kinds of rugs.
Having offered a cow and the honey-mixture (madhuparka) to Janārdana on that [couch],...
Then the Kaurava offered him his home and his kingdom;
by the command of Dhṛtarāṣṭra’s son, a throne auspicious on all sides and adorned with every kind of gem had been prepared specifically for the sake of Kṛṣṇa.

There, all the Kurus together with the kings paid homage to Govinda, who was seated and possessed a radiance like the serene sun. Then King Duryodhana [addressed] the descendant of Vṛṣṇi, the best among victors.
He invited Keśava to a meal, but Keśava did not accept;
Janārdana did not accept.
Again and again, the Kauraveya invited him to a meal.
Although he was entreated repeatedly,
the Kaurava Duryodhana then addressed Kṛṣṇa in the assembly of kings, speaking first with mildness but ending in deceit, while addressing Karṇa.
"O Janārdana, why did you not accept the food, drinks, garments, and beds brought for your sake? You,
who are devoted to the welfare of both, gave assistance to both sides."
"O Mādhava, you are a kinsman and a beloved friend of Dhṛtarāṣṭra;
for you, O Govinda, know dharma and artha in their true essence in every respect. Therefore, O wielder of the discus and mace, I wish to hear the reason for this."
Thus addressed, the high-minded Govinda,
