whose voice was like the roar of a torrential cloud, at that moment raised his massive arm and replied—
speech that was not indistinct, nor swallowed, nor rejected, and free from confusion.
The lotus-eyed one spoke these excellent and reasoned words to the king:
"Messengers indeed enjoy their purpose and receive honor once their mission is accomplished;
O Bhārata, when I have fulfilled my purpose, you shall honor me along with your ministers."
Thus addressed, the son of Dhṛtarāṣṭra replied to Janārdana:
"It is not fitting for you to behave toward us in such an improper manner.
Whether you have achieved your purpose or not, O Madhusūdana, we [regard you as our friend]."
"O Govinda, we strive to worship you, yet we are not able;
nor do we know the reason, O Madhusūdana, why you did not accept the worship performed by us with such joy, O Puruṣottama."
"O Govinda, we have no enmity with you, nor is there any conflict;
therefore, having considered this, it does not behove you to speak such words.
Thus addressed, Janārdana replied to the son of Dhṛtarāṣṭra.
Looking toward him along with his ministers, the descendant of Daśārha, as if smiling, said:
"Neither out of desire, nor out of passion, nor out of hatred, nor for the sake of wealth, nor from a desire for argument, nor out of greed would I ever abandon dharma under any circumstances."

What wise man, being pleased by an offering made to him, would be willing to reject it? Whether the foods are those enjoyed out of mutual affection or those eaten in times of distress, O King, you do not show us affection, nor have we fallen into such distress.
O King, you have hated the Pāṇḍavas from their very birth without cause—
brothers who follow what is dear to you and are endowed with every virtue. Indeed,
this hatred toward the sons of Pṛthā is altogether unjustified.
The sons of Pāṇḍu are established in dharma; who is fit to say anything against them?
He who hates them hates me; he who follows them follows me. Know that I have attained oneness with the dharma-practicing Pāṇḍavas.
For he who, following desire and anger, seeks to oppose out of delusion,
and he who hates one possessed of virtues— him they call the lowest of men. He who, out of delusion or greed, seeks to harm kinsmen endowed with auspicious qualities, [is likewise base].

One who has not conquered himself and has not conquered his anger does not retain prosperity for long. But he who, through kindness, brings even those endowed with virtues— who are otherwise unpleasant to his heart— under his influence, remains established in fame for a long time.
"One should not eat the food of an enemy, nor should one feed an enemy. O King, you hate the Pāṇḍavas, yet the Pāṇḍavas are indeed my very life-breaths.
All this food, being tainted by evil intent, must not be consumed."
"The food of the steward alone must be eaten; this is the resolve fixed in my mind.
Having spoken thus to the impatient Duryodhana, the mighty-armed one then departed from that splendid residence of Dhṛtarāṣṭra’s son.
Having emerged, the mighty-armed and high-minded Vāsudeva went to the residence of the great-souled Vidura to take up lodging. Droṇa, Kṛpa, Bhīṣma, and Bāhlika then approached him.
The Kurus approached the mighty-armed Madhusūdana, who was staying in the house of Vidura, and said to him there:
"O Vārṣṇeya, we offer our houses along with their jewels to you."
The immensely radiant Madhusūdana said to those Kauravas:
"All of you may depart; my honor has been fully rendered by you. O best of the Kurus, this was not a matter of policy, but rather an act of worship toward us."
"And Duryodhana will not show you any affection.
Having been addressed thus by Kṛṣṇa, they departed, saying, "So be it.
When the Kurus had gone, the Kṣattṛ [Vidura] approached the unconquered Daśārha.
Then, with great effort, he honored him with all desired objects.
Thereupon, the Kṣattṛ brought forth many kinds of pure and excellent food and drink for the high-souled Keśava.

Having first gratified the brahmins with those [offerings], Madhusūdana Kṛṣṇa gave even supreme riches to those learned in the Vedas. When the best of the twice-born had finished eating, he sat upon an excellent seat.
Having become pure and well-restrained, Vidura brought the food;
endowed with supreme faith, he spoke these words:
"Be pleased, O Govinda, by our efforts; this is our greatest wealth."
Or otherwise, specifically, who else is worthy to honor you?
To the noble, wealth is as grass; to the hero, death is as grass;
to the dispassionate, a woman is as grass; and to the desireless, the entire world is as grass.
When he had finished eating, various bards and panegyrists praised that seated, unconquered descendant of Daśārha with many auspicious words;
then, together with his followers, he was like Vāsava among the Maruts.
He partook of pure and excellent foods brought by Vidura.
Vaiśampāyana said:
When he had eaten and was rested at night, Vidura spoke to him.
"That Great Soul whom noble beings desire after performing manifold austerities—
that God has arrived within the range of my vision.
O Keśava, Lord of the World, what hospitality may I now offer you?"
Kṛṣṇa said:
"I am the foremost among the poor upon the face of the earth.
Excellent, excellent, O one of great wisdom, you who are learned in all the scriptures!"
"You who are endowed with discipline, and in whom youth itself is seen—today I am pleased by your words; I grant [this], O joy of the Kurus.
Vidura said:

"Choose a boon; I shall grant you whatever is pleasing to your mind. "Grant me unwavering devotion to Keśava, a mind always fixed upon You, concern for righteousness, and birth in a noble family, O Madhusūdana."
Let there be no thought of another’s wealth, and let there be no thought of another’s wife;
O Lord, let the tongue never at any time be a slanderer of others.
Let the seat be crowded with one's own sons, and the home be filled with Brahmins.
O Madhusūdana, grant me a heart filled with the teachings of the scriptures.
May I be a giver of food in times of famine, a giver of gold in times of plenty, and a protector from fear when one is afflicted; O Kṛṣṇa, may these three be mine.
"Truth, purity, compassion, charity, and devotion to Janārdana—
these boons I request, O Mādhava, if you are pleased with me. This arrival of yours, O Keśava, was not undertaken for this purpose."
O Janārdana, that fool disregards both worldly interests and dharma;

he is impulsive, a destroyer of honor, yet desires honor for himself; he transgresses the instructions of the elders, violates the treatises on dharma, and being dull-witted and evil-minded, has fallen into arrogance.
O Janārdana, the wicked son of Dhṛtarāṣṭra is incapable of being led toward what is beneficial;
he is a slave to his desires, considers himself wise, betrays his friends, and is suspicious of everyone.
He is a non-doer, ungrateful, has abandoned righteousness, and delights in falsehood.
Deluded and of unrefined intellect, he is no master over his senses; following after his desires, he remains indecisive in all his undertakings. He is possessed of these and many other such faults.
Even when spoken to by you regarding what is for his welfare, he will not accept it due to his impetuosity.
O Madhusūdana, seeing the gathering of the kings' armies,
that foolish and unwise youth considers himself to have already achieved his purpose.
"It is certain that Karna alone is capable of conquering the enemies;
thus, the evil-minded son of Dhṛtarāṣṭra will not seek peace.
[This is true] while Bhīṣma, Droṇa, Kṛpa, Karṇa, the son of Droṇa, and Jayadratha [are present]."

They pursue an even greater course of action and do not set their minds on peace, O Janārdana. It is certain that the sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra, along with Karṇa, are unable even to look upon Bhīṣma, Droṇa, and Kṛpa; how much less can the Pārthas withstand them?
O Keśava, there was no agreement among all the sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra regarding you, who were striving for peace and desiring brotherly affection,
that the Pāṇḍavas should receive what is rightfully theirs from us.
"O Madhusūdana, where those who are thus resolved regard well-spoken words and ill-spoken words as equal,
there a wise man should not prattle, just as a singer does not perform before the deaf."

O Mādhava, it is not fitting for you to speak words to those who are ignorant, deluded, and lawless, just as a twice-born man should not speak to outcasts. This fool, relying on his strength, will not carry out your command.
"O Kṛṣṇa, the words you have spoken will prove meaningless for you among all those evil-minded men who are seated there; your entry into their midst does not please me."
O Kṛṣṇa, the contrary speech of these many evil-minded, undisciplined, and wicked-hearted men does not please you in their midst;
for they have failed to honor the elders and are arrogant due to their pride in wealth.
Out of pride in his youth and out of indignation, he will not accept what is for his own welfare; even if you speak of his strength, O Mādhava, though it be great,
he will have great suspicion toward you and will not follow your word.
"Arrogant due to his folly, he does not perceive the superior strength of the sons of Pṛthā.
'This cannot be overcome in battle today even by Indra together with the immortals'—
thus have all the sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra resolved, O Janārdana."
When they have thus been born [into their new state] and follow after desire and anger,
even your words, though capable, will become ineffective.
Standing in the midst of the elephant division, you are dull-witted;
The fool Duryodhana, his mind deluded, considers himself free from anxiety and thinks,
"This entire earth has been conquered by me."
The son of Dhṛtarāṣṭra hopes for a great kingdom on earth without rivals;
in him, peace alone is not to be found.
He considers his purpose already accomplished, though it remains bound. This earth, ripened by time, has been overturned;
for the sake of Duryodhana, they desire to fight the Pāṇḍavas.
All the warriors on earth have assembled here,
as have the kings together with the rulers of the land;
all of these have previously been engaged in enmity.
O Kṛṣṇa, the kings have been stripped of their essence by you;
out of fear of you, those heroes, though closely united with Karṇa, have taken refuge with the sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra.
Having renounced their very lives along with Duryodhana,
all those warriors were dispatched to fight the Pāṇḍavas,
having set their hearts solely upon either death or victory.
O hero of the Daśārhas, it is not my opinion that you should enter into their midst— those who are devoted to sensual pleasures, under the sway of wrath, and undisciplined.
When you have entered the midst of those many evil-minded ones seated together, O crusher of enemies, how will you prevail,
O mighty-armed one, for you are altogether difficult to overcome even by the gods?
"O slayer of foes, I know your power, your manliness, and your intelligence.
O Mādhava, the affection I have for the Pāṇḍavas is even greater toward you.
It is out of love, great respect, and friendship that I speak this to you."
"O lotus-eyed one, how can that joy of mine arising from the sight of you be described to you? For you are the inner self of all embodied beings.
Vaiśampāyana said:
Having heard the humble words of Vidura, the Supreme Person,
the Blessed Lord Madhusūdana, spoke these words.
The Blessed Lord said:
Just as one of great wisdom would speak, just as one who is discerning would speak,
so should a friend like you speak to a friend like me—
truthfully, consistent with dharma and worldly purpose, and appropriate for you.
"Thus have you spoken these words to me like a father and a mother;
they are true, appropriate, and fitting, exactly as you have told me. Listen now to the reason for my arrival, Vidura; be attentive."
"O Kṣattṛ, knowing all this— the wickedness of Dhṛtarāṣṭra’s son and the enmity of the kṣatriyas— I have today arrived among the Kauravas,
[finding] the entire earth overturned, along with its horses, chariots, and elephants."

He who would release [another] from the noose of death shall attain the highest dharma. If a man, striving to the best of his ability, is unable to accomplish a righteous deed, he nevertheless attains the merit thereof; of this I have no doubt.

"One who contemplates evil with the mind but does not approve of it through action does not obtain the fruit thereof; thus do those who know the Dharma understand. Therefore, O Kṣattṛ, I shall strive to bring about peace without deceit."
In this battle where the Kurus and the Sṛñjayas are perishing,
this most terrible calamity has arisen among the Kurus themselves;
it was brought about by Karṇa and Duryodhana, for all these others are their followers.
The wise know him to be cruel who does not approach a friend suffering from calamities and console him to the best of his ability;
for one should restrain a friend from an improper act even by seizing him by the hair.
One who has exerted effort to the best of one's ability becomes beyond reproach by anyone;
therefore, Vidura ought to accept that capable, auspicious, beneficial speech, which is consistent with dharma and artha, from Dhṛtarāṣṭra along with his ministers.

For I shall strive, without guile, for the welfare of the sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra, as well as that of the Pāṇḍavas and all the Kṣatriyas on earth. If Duryodhana should suspect me while I am thus striving for his welfare, [I shall act accordingly].
My heart will find joy, and I shall be freed from my debt;
for the wise know that one who does not intervene with every effort when kinsmen are divided is no friend at all, but stands as a neutral bystander.
"Let not the ignorant, foolish, and unfriendly say of me:
'Kṛṣṇa was capable, yet he did not restrain the enraged Kurus and Pāṇḍavas,' thinking that I have come only to accomplish the purpose of both sides."
Having exerted effort in this matter, I shall go among men free from reproach. For if, having heard my wholesome words endowed with dharma and artha,
that fool does not accept them, he will fall under the power of destiny.
If I were to act for the sake of the Kurus in accordance with what is right, without neglecting the interests of the Pāṇḍavas,
my conduct would be meritorious and of great significance.
And may the Kurus be released from the noose of death,
even as you speak words that are poetic,
rooted in dharma, meaningful, and non-violent.
The sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra would behold me as one who has attained power, and the Kurus would honor me upon my arrival;
moreover, even all the kings joined together would not be a match for me.
"Like other beasts standing before an enraged lion," Vaiśampāyana said,
"having spoken these words, the bull among the Vṛṣṇis then— "
On a bed of pleasant touch, he who brings happiness to the Yadus lay down to rest. Vaiśampāyana said:
While those two intelligent men were thus conversing at that time...
That night, auspicious and filled with stars,
passed away as the high-souled Vidura listened to various words endowed with dharma, artha, and kāma, and composed of diverse meanings, phrases, and syllables.
With appropriate stories concerning Kṛṣṇa of immeasurable splendor,
that night passed away for Kṛṣṇa as if he were unwilling to let it go.
Then, many bards and panegyrists, endowed with beautiful voices, [began to sing].
With the sounds of conchs and drums, they awakened Keśava while proclaiming the lineage beginning with Brahmā and ending with Vasudeva;
there, many bards and panegyrists praised Keśava.

Then, having risen, Janārdana, the bull of all the Sātvatas and scion of the Daśārhas, performed all his necessary morning duties. Having completed his water-rites and prayers, he offered oblations into the fire and adorned himself.
Then Mādhava worshipped the rising sun.
Then Duryodhana and Śakuni, the son of Subala,
approached the unconquered Daśārha as he stood performing his twilight devotions.
Let them report to Kṛṣṇa that Dhṛtarāṣṭra has arrived at the assembly hall,
along with the Kurus headed by Bhīṣma and all the kings of the earth:
"O Govinda, they entreat you, just as the immortals in heaven entreat Śakra."
Govinda greeted them with words of supreme sweetness;
having honored the son of Devakī as the immortals honor Śakra in heaven, they departed.
Then, when the sun had become clear, Janārdana, the scorcher of foes, gave gold, garments, cows, and horses to the Brahmins;
he bestowed jewels upon that unconquered scion of the Daśārhas.
Then, approaching him as he stood there, the charioteer paid his respects;
thereafter, Dāruka quickly presented himself before him in a great, radiant chariot adorned with small bells and yoked to the finest horses.
For him, that excellent chariot, renowned throughout the world, shone resplendent as it was yoked with the horses Sainya,
Sugrīva, Meghapuṣpa, and Balāhaka. Sainya had the luster of a parrot’s wing, while Sugrīva possessed the brilliance of the kiṃśuka flower.
Meghapuṣpa was of cloud-color, while Balāhaka was white;
Sainya carried him on the right, and Sugrīva carried him on the left.
Meghapuṣpa and Balāhaka were the two who bore him from behind.
Adorned with a lattice of jewels and fashioned by Viśvakarman,
the flagstaff mounted upon that chariot shone brilliantly;
upon it stood the son of Vinatā, touching the sun as if he were a celestial body.
On the banner of that virtuous hero, the enemy of serpents shone;
by that radiant and resplendent emblem of the king of birds, the preeminent chariot of that illustrious one was made beautiful.
With its golden lattices, banners, and golden standard,
that best of chariots shone like the sun risen at the end of time,
adorned with bird-emblazoned flags and canopies with golden lattice-work between them.
With various types of pillars and pathways, beautifully fashioned by Viśvakarman,
and adorned with coral, gems, gold, pearls, and beryl ornaments,
as well as clusters of hundreds of small bells with lattices of hair hanging between them.
Adorned with lotus-pools made of refined gold and with trees of burnished gold, that most excellent chariot shone,
as did its [decoration] of tigers, lions, boars, bulls, beasts, and birds.
With stars, suns, and golden elephants,
with thunderbolt-tipped goads and celestial chariots at the joints of its poles and the curves of its frame,
it possessed a towering central nave and a roar like the great sound of thunder.
Knowing that the divine chariot had arrived—
resounding like the thundering of massive clouds and adorned with every kind of jewel—
the high-minded Janārdana circumambulated the sacred fire and the Brahmins.
Having fastened the Kaustubha gem and blazing with supreme splendor, Kṛṣṇa— the descendant of Śūra and joy of all the Yādavas— surrounded by the Kurus and protected by the Vṛṣṇis,
mounted his chariot.
Vidura, the knower of all duties, ascended after the descendant of Daśārha—
the best among all living beings and the foremost among all upholders of dharma.
Then Duryodhana and Śakuni, the son of Subala, also [ascended].
With a second chariot,
they followed that scorcher of foes; Sātyaki, Kṛtavarman, and the great car-warriors of the Vṛṣṇis followed behind Kṛṣṇa with chariots, horses, and even elephants.
Their chariots, adorned with golden ornaments and yoked to excellent horses, resounded as they moved; those variegated vehicles shone beautifully,
and they proceeded along the great highway whose dust had been swept away and sprinkled with water.
At that time, the wise Kṛṣṇa, blazing with splendor, recounted the deeds of the royal sages.
Then, as the descendant of Daśārha departed,
single-sounding drums were beaten, conchs were blown, and all other musical instruments were played there.

Brave heroes of all the world, young men with the prowess of lions and subduers of enemies, surrounded the chariot of Śauri and followed him. Then, thousands of others followed, dressed in various and wonderful garments.
Carrying swords, spears, and other weapons, there were hundreds and thousands of warriors with axes in their hands who marched before Kṛṣṇa;
there were also more than a hundred excellent elephants and thousands of choice horses.
The people followed the unconquered hero of the Daśārhas as he proceeded,
desiring to see Janārdana arrived at the city of the Kurus; they went out with the old and the young, accompanied by their women, and stood along the roads for the subduer of enemies.
The palaces were repeatedly crowded by women leaning against the railings, appearing as if they would sway under their weight; meanwhile,
he was being honored by the Kurus and listening to various stories.
Honoring them as was fitting and observing them, he proceeded slowly.
Then, having reached the assembly hall, the followers of Keśava made all the directions resound with the blasts of conchs and the sounds of flutes.
Then that entire assembly of kings of immeasurable splendor trembled with joy in anticipation of Kṛṣṇā’s arrival. Then, as Kṛṣṇā drew near, the lords of men rejoiced.
Hearing that roar of the chariot, which resembled the thundering of a rain-cloud,
Ṛṣabha, the bull among all the Sātvatas, approached the gate of the assembly hall;
then Śauri descended from his chariot, which was like a peak of Mount Kailāsa.

Then, taking Vidura and Sātyaki by the hand, the highly illustrious one entered the assembly hall, which resembled the abode of Mahendra, appearing like a mountain cloud and blazing as if with splendor.
O King, like the sun, he shrouded the Kurus with his splendor;
with Vāsudeva at their head, both Karṇa and Duryodhana were positioned in front,
while the Vṛṣṇis and Kṛtavarman stood behind Kṛṣṇa.
Placing Dhṛtarāṣṭra at their head, Bhīṣma, Droṇa,
and all the others then rose from their seats, honoring Janārdana.
As the descendant of Daśārha approached, the high-minded one whose wisdom serves as his eye [Dhṛtarāṣṭra] followed.
Together with Bhīṣma and Droṇa, the highly illustrious one rose up. As the great king Dhṛtarāṣṭra, the lord of men, arose,
those thousands of kings stood up from all sides.
By the command of Dhṛtarāṣṭra, a seat auspicious on all sides and adorned with gold was prepared there for the sake of Kṛṣṇa. Duryodhana said:
"O Madhusūdana, having abandoned Bhīṣma and Droṇa, you have [given me] this—[what is this?
The Blessed One said:
"O Puṇḍarīkākṣa, for what purpose was this meal for a low-born man (vṛṣala) prepared?"

"O Indra among kings, you ask about food; why do you not ask about reverence? Food that has been digested is indeed gone, but reverence is undecaying and immortal. Even vegetables and fruits, when offered with reverence..."
My limbs find no delight in this nectar devoid of human touch;
rather, I would prefer the *hālāhala* poison, which, though it instantly takes life,
is pleasing when consumed by one whose eyebrows are knit in a frown of wealth.
"O dear one, birth is not the cause; virtues are the cause of excellence.
Even a *caṇḍāla* who is of good conduct, the gods know him as a Brahmin. The great sage named Vyāsa was born from the womb of a fisherwoman."
"A Brāhmaṇa is born through asceticism; therefore, birth is not the cause.
Smiling, the righteous Mādhava addressed the king, Bhīṣma, Droṇa, and the other kings according to their seniority.
There, all the kings, rulers of the earth, and the Kurus duly honored Keśava Janārdana as he entered the assembly hall.
Standing there in the midst of the kings, that descendant of Daśārha, the scorcher of foes, [shone forth].
The conqueror of enemy cities beheld the rishis stationed in the intermediate space.
Then, having gazed upon those rishis headed by Nārada,
the descendant of Daśārha addressed Bhīṣma, the son of Śāntanu, slowly.
"O King, the sages have arrived to witness this earthly assembly;
let them be invited with seats and abundant hospitality. Until they are seated, it is not possible for anyone else to remain."

"Let worship be quickly offered to the sages of purified souls. Seeing the ṛṣis standing at the entrance of the assembly hall, the son of Śāntanu then hurriedly commanded his servants, "Bring the seats!"
Then they brought from here and there large and spacious seats, polished and variegated with gems and gold;
and when they had been seated upon them and had received the guest-offering, O Bhārata.
Kṛṣṇa sat down upon his seat, and the kings likewise took their respective seats. Duḥśāsana gave an excellent seat to Sātyaki,
and Vivimśati gave a golden stool to Kṛtavarman.
Then, not far from Kṛṣṇa, both the high-souled Karṇa and Duryodhana sat down upon a single seat, filled with indignation;
and Śakuni, the king of the Gāndhāras, was seated there, protected by his Gāndhāra followers.
O lord of the people, the king sat upon his throne together with his sons; Vidura, however, the high-minded one, sat upon a jeweled seat covered with a costly deerskin, touching the seat of Śauri.

Having beheld the descendant of Daśārha after a long time, all the kings and lords of the earth were not satiated with looking at Janārdana, as if they were drinking nectar. Janārdana, dressed in yellow garments, resembled the flower of the flax plant.
He shone in the midst of the assembly like a gem set in gold.
Then everything became silent, for all minds were fixed upon Govinda;
no man there uttered a single word.
Vaiśampāyana said:
When all those kings were seated and had become silent,
Kṛṣṇa— possessing beautiful teeth and a voice like a drum— began to speak.
Like a cloud at the end of the summer heat, making himself heard by the entire assembly,
Mādhava looked toward Dhṛtarāṣṭra and spoke,
O Bhārata: "May there be peace between the Kurus and the Pāṇḍavas."
"O King, I have come to strive for this end of the heroes without further effort;
no other word of benefit need be spoken to you.
For everything that ought to be known is already known to you, O subduer of enemies."
"O King, today this family is the most excellent among all kings;
because of you in particular,
it is distinguished here as being endowed with learning and conduct, and possessed of all virtues."

O Bhārata, compassion, pity, mercy, and kindness, as well as straightforwardness, forbearance, and truth— these qualities are especially prominent among the Kurus. O King, such a great lineage as that remains steadfast in these virtues.
"Especially on your account, it is not fitting here for such an improper act to occur. For you, O best of the Kurus, are the foremost restrainer of the Kurus,
both toward outsiders and those within the family, O dear one, when they act falsely."
O Kauravya, those sons of yours, led by Duryodhana,
have cast virtue and profit behind them and act like cruel men;
they are undisciplined, have transgressed the bounds of propriety, and their minds have been stolen away by greed.
O bull among the Bharatas, you know this well regarding your own foremost kinsmen:
this most terrible calamity has arisen among the Kurus themselves;
if it is neglected, O Kauravya, it will destroy the earth.
"O Bhārata, this can be pacified if you so desire;
for I consider peace in this matter not difficult to achieve, O bull of the Bharatas.
Peace depends upon you, O King, and likewise upon me, O lord of the people."
"O Bhārata, these [allies] who have become your companions will likewise lead to the total destruction. O Kauravya, establish your sons; I shall establish the others.
For this is for the benefit of the Dhārtarāṣṭras and likewise for the benefit of the Pāṇḍavas."

O Indra among kings, for those who strive for tranquility and desire your teaching, your command must indeed be carried out by your sons along with their descendants; even though it may be difficult, they abide by your instruction for the sake of their own welfare.
O King, this is for your own benefit as well as for that of the Pāṇḍavas;
it is for me who strives for peace and desires your command.
Perceiving this yourself to be flawless, O Lord of the People, take the necessary measures.
But let the Bharatas remain your very own, O lord of men;
abide in dharma and artha, O King, protected by the Pāṇḍavas.
For such as they are, O ruler of men, cannot be overcome even with great effort.
For even Indra, accompanied by the gods, could not overcome you while you are protected by the high-souled Pāṇḍavas; how much less so mortal kings?
For there are Bhīṣma, Droṇa, Kṛpa, Karṇa, and Vivimśati.
Aśvatthāman, Vikarṇa, Somadatta, and Bāhlika;
Saindhava, Kaliṅga, and Sudakṣiṇa of Kamboja;
as well as Yudhiṣṭhira, Bhīmasena, Savyasācin, and the twins.

O slayer of enemies, O bull of the Bharatas, who indeed would fight in battle against those of great splendor— Sātyaki and the great car-warrior Yuyutsu— when they are joined by the Kurus and Pāṇḍavas? Who, with a perverted soul, would even attempt to fight them?
"O slayer of enemies, together with the Kurus and the Pāṇḍavas, you shall once again attain sovereignty over the world and invincibility against your foes. O lord of the earth,
the rulers of the earth who are equal to you will be yours."

O scorcher of enemies, even kings who are superior will enter into alliances with you. Thus, protected on all sides by your sons, grandsons, brothers, fathers, and friends, you will be able to live in happiness.
"O Lord of the Earth, having placed these very men at your head and having honored them as in the past, you shall enjoy the entire earth in its completeness.
For, O Bhārata, together with all these Pāṇḍavas and your own kinsmen,"

"You shall conquer other enemies; this is your entire self-interest. And you, O scorcher of foes, shall enjoy the earth acquired by them alone, provided that you prosper together with your sons and ministers, O lord of men."
O great king, in battle indeed a very great destruction is seen; O King, when there is destruction on both sides, what dharma do you perceive [in that],
whether the Pāṇḍavas are slain in combat or your own mighty sons?
"O King, O bull of the Bharatas, tell me whatever happiness you might find.
For all the Pāṇḍavas and your own men are heroes, skilled in weapons, and all long for battle; protect them from this great danger."
O best of kings, we shall not behold all the Kurus and the Pāṇḍavas together in battle—
those heroes on both sides, diminished and slain from their chariots by other chariot-warriors,
for all the kings of the earth have assembled here.
Overcome by the power of indignation, they might destroy these subjects. O King, protect this world so that these subjects do not perish;
for if you return to your natural state, O joy of the Kurus, there will be a remnant left.
O King, protect from great danger those who are pure, generous, modest, noble, and of virtuous birth, who assist one another;
may these rulers of the earth fare well as they meet with one another.
O bull of the Bharatas, O scorcher of foes, having eaten and drunk together, let them return to their respective homes, well-dressed and adorned with garlands,
after you have honored them and cast aside all resentment and enmities.

O bull of the Bharata race, let that very affection which you felt for the Pāṇḍavas when this end of life arrived be yours today, and forevermore. Those children, deprived of their father, were raised by you alone.
Protect them according to what is right, as well as your sons, O bull among the Bharatas;
for they must be protected by you, especially in times of distress. Let not your dharma, nor likewise your worldly prosperity, perish, O bull among the Bharatas.
"O King, having saluted you and sought your favor, the Pāṇḍavas have said to you:
'By your command, we, along with our followers, have experienced suffering;
these twelve years have been spent by us in the forest.'"

"Thinking, 'Our father will remain according to that agreement for thirteen years among people while remaining unrecognized,' we made this firm resolve, O dear one; and we did not violate that agreement, as the Brahmins know."
O bull among the Bharatas, abide by that agreement with us who remain steadfast;
O King, we have been constantly afflicted, so let us receive our share of our own kingdom.
You, applying yourself to both dharma and artha, ought to protect us properly.
"Beholding our heavy burden, we endure many afflictions;
may you therefore behave toward us as a mother and father. For the conduct of a teacher toward a disciple, O Bhārata, is even weightier than that of a parent."
We abide in you, and you likewise abide in us. For we, who have set out upon a wrong path, must be established by our father;
therefore, O King, establish us on the right paths and remain yourself upon your own path.
And your sons said to this assembly, O bull of the Bharatas:
"When the members of the council are knowers of dharma, it is not fitting here for anything improper to occur—
wherein dharma is overcome by adharma, and truth by falsehood."

While they look on, dharma is slain; the members of that assembly are themselves slain when dharma, pierced by adharma, enters the court. Indeed, those members of the assembly who do not extract the dart from it are themselves pierced.

O bull among the Bharatas, those who, observing the Dharma, remain silent and meditative, destroy these dharmas just as a river uproots trees growing along its banks; they speak what is truth, what is Dharma, and what is righteous.
"O Lord of Men, what else can be said by you other than giving? Or let those kings who sit here in this assembly speak, after having duly weighed both dharma and artha— if I am speaking the truth."

O bull among Kṣatriyas, release these Kṣatriyas from the noose of death; be at peace, O best of the Bharatas, and do not fall under the sway of wrath. Grant to the Pāṇḍavas their paternal share as is appropriate.
"Therefore, O scorcher of foes, having achieved your purpose, enjoy these pleasures together with your son.
You know that Ajātaśatru always stands firm in the dharma of the virtuous, and you know the conduct he maintains toward you and your son, O lord of men."
Though he was set on fire and cast out, he again took refuge with you alone;
yet it was by you, together with your sons, that he was exiled from Indraprastha. While dwelling there, he brought all the kings under his control.
O King, he made them look toward you alone and never turned away from you;
yet while he was conducting himself thus, as the son of Subala sought to seize his kingdom, wealth, and grain, he employed a supreme stratagem.
Having reached that state and beholding Kṛṣṇā brought into the assembly hall,
Yudhiṣṭhira— whose soul was immeasurable— did not waver from the duty of a kṣatriya.
"But I, O Bhārata, desire the welfare of both you and them."

O King, do not destroy your subjects by depriving them of dharma, wealth, and happiness. O lord of the people, restrain your sons who, through excessive greed, mistake evil for good and good for evil for themselves.
"The sons of Pṛthā stand ready to serve, yet these subduers of enemies stand ready to fight.
O King, O scorcher of foes, abide in that which is most beneficial for you.
All those kings honored those words in their hearts.
Indeed, no one there ventured to speak a word before him.
Vaiśampāyana said:
When those words had been spoken by the high-souled Keśava, [the assembly remained silent].
All the members of the assembly sat motionless, their hair standing on end.
"What man indeed would dare to offer a reply to this?"—
thus all those kings reflected within their minds.
When all those kings had thus become silent,
the son of Jamadagni spoke these words in the assembly of the Kurus:
"O King, listen without hesitation to this true parable."
Having heard this, accept what is beneficial if you deem it right. In ancient times, there was a sovereign king named Dambhodbhava who ruled over the entire earth; so we have heard.
Every day at the end of the night, having risen in the morning, that heroic great chariot-warrior would sit questioning the Brahmins and Kṣatriyas:
"Is there anyone superior to me, or perhaps someone like me, in battle?"
"Whether he be a Śūdra, a Vaiśya, a Kṣatriya, or even a Brāhmaṇa who bears arms"—
saying this, that king wandered over this earth,
intoxicated by great pride and thinking nothing of anyone else.
Then those compassionate physicians, brahmins who were fearless in every respect,
repeatedly forbade the king as he boasted again and again;
yet even though he was forbidden many times, he continued to question the twice-born ones.

Then the high-souled ascetics, endowed with Vedic vows, spoke to that king who was arrogant and intoxicated by his prosperity— those twice-born ones, blazing with anger as they addressed the monarch who was thus exalting himself.

Those two high-souled ascetics were seers who demonstrated the authority of the Vedas; between those two lions among men, there existed a friendship spanning many births. O King, you shall never be their equal.
Thus addressed, the king questioned those twice-born ones again:
"Where are those two heroes? What is their birth, what are their deeds, and who are they?
The Brāhmaṇas said:
"We have heard that Nara and Nārāyaṇa are indeed ascetics who have come to the world of men; fight with them, O King.
It is heard that both those high-souled ones are Nara and Nārāyaṇa."
On Mount Gandhamādana, they two are performing a fierce and indescribable penance.
Rāma said:
"That king, having mobilized a great sixfold army..."
Unable to endure it, he set out for where those two unconquered ones were;
having reached the rugged and formidable Gandhamādana mountain,
he searched and followed after those two unconquered ascetics.
Seeing those two best of men emaciated by hunger and thirst, their veins standing out, and worn down by cold, wind, and heat, he approached them,
touched their feet, and inquired after their well-being.
Having honored him with roots, fruits, a seat, and water,
the two of them invited the king, saying, "What may be done for you?
Thereupon, he recounted that entire sequence once again.
Dambhodbhava said:
"The earth has been conquered by my two arms, and all my enemies have been slain;
desiring a battle with you two, I have come to this mountain."
"Let this hospitality be granted, which I have long desired.
Nara and Nārāyaṇa said:
"O best of kings, this hermitage is free from anger and greed."
"For in this hermitage there is no fighting; whence could there be weapons, and whence could there be the crooked? Seek battle elsewhere; there are many Kṣatriyas on earth.
Rāma said:

Even though he was being addressed in this manner, O Bhārata, Dambhodbhava, who desired battle, spoke out once more; though repeatedly forgiven and pacified, he continued to challenge the two ascetics.
Then, O Kaurava, Nara took up a handful of reeds and said,
"Come, fight, O Kshatriya who lusts for battle!
Take up all your weapons and array your army."
"Indeed, I shall remove from you hereafter this desire for battle;
gird yourself in your armor and whatever other mail you possess,
since out of pride you challenge these people, headed by the Brahmins."
Dambhodbhava said:
"O ascetic, if you consider this weapon appropriate for us,
I shall fight with you by that very means as well, for I have come here seeking battle."
05,094.026 Rāma said: Having spoken thus, Dambhodbhava, together with his army, desiring to kill that ascetic, covered him from all sides with a shower of arrows.
As he discharged those terrible arrows capable of piercing the bodies of others,
the sage rendered them useless and warded them off with blades of grass.
Then the unconquered one loosed a formidable weapon made of grass at him.
That weapon was impossible to counter and appeared truly miraculous. With his supernatural power, that sage, who could strike by mere sign, pierced their eyes, ears, and noses with blades of grass.
Seeing the white sky covered with reeds,
the king prostrated at his feet and said, "May it be well with me.
Nara, the refuge of those seeking refuge, spoke to him, "O King!"

"Be devoted to Brahman, be righteous in soul, and never act in this way again. O King, a man such as you, mindful of the duty of a Kṣatriya, O tiger among kings, conqueror of cities, would not even conceive such a thought in his mind."

And do not, overcome by pride, ever insult anyone—whether they be inferior or superior; that, O King, is for your supreme benefit. One who is wise, free from greed, devoid of egoism, and self-possessed [attains this].

"O King, self-controlled, patient, gentle, and secure, protect your subjects. Never again insult anyone without first ascertaining their strength and weakness. Having received our permission, go in peace; do not act in this manner ever again."
"Ask after the welfare of the brahmins on our behalf with great earnestness.
Then the king, having paid homage at the feet of those two high-souled ones,
returned to his own city and practiced righteousness most diligently.
Furthermore, that deed which was performed by Nara in the past was truly great;
therefore, through his many virtues, Nārāyaṇa became superior. Consequently, as long as a weapon is not yet joined to Gāṇḍīva, the best of bows—
Therefore, O King, casting aside your pride, go to Dhanañjaya.
[The eight arrows are] Kākudīka, Śuka, Nāka, Akṣisaṃtarjana, Saṃtāna, Nartana, Ghora, and Āsyamodaka as the eighth.
Pierced by these, all human beings indeed go to their death:
desire and anger, greed and delusion, as well as intoxication and pride; likewise, envy and egoism—these are declared to be [the arrows] in sequence.
Maddened, they act perversely, deprived of consciousness and sense; these men sleep, leap about, and vomit;
they constantly urinate, weep, and laugh.
The qualities in Pārtha are innumerable, and Janārdana is even more distinguished than he.
You yourself know best Dhananjaya, the son of Kuntī;
those two who were Nara and Nārāyaṇa are none other than Arjuna and Keśava.
Know them, O Great King, to be two pre-eminent heroes, bulls among men:
the Creator of all worlds, the Lord who performs all deeds,
whose kinsman is Nārāyaṇa, and Arjuna, who is difficult to withstand in battle.

O Bhārata, who in the three worlds would dare to conquer that hero with the monkey-banner, the victorious Jiṣṇu, for whom there is no equal in battle? If you know this to be so, and do not suspect me otherwise—
Adopting a noble resolve, O Bhārata, make peace with the Pāṇḍavas.
If you consider it better that no dissension should arise between us,
then make peace, O best of the Bharatas, and do not set your mind on war.
"And your lineage, O best of the Kurus, is highly esteemed on earth;
let it remain so, may you be blessed, and consider only your own welfare.
Vaiśampāyana said:
Having heard the words of the son of Jamadagni, the venerable seer Kaṇva also spoke these words to Duryodhana in the assembly of the Kurus:
"Brahmā, the grandfather of the worlds, is indeed inexhaustible and immutable."
In the same way, those two lords, the sages Nara and Nārāyaṇa, are likewise [supreme]. For among all the Ādityas, Viṣṇu alone is the eternal,
unconquerable, immutable, perpetual Lord and Sovereign.
But others undergo death by signs: the moon, the sun, the earth, water, wind, fire, as well as space, the planets, and the hosts of stars;
and at the end of the world's dissolution, they always abandon the three worlds.
All indeed go to their destruction and are created again and again;
others— humans, beasts, birds, those born of animal wombs, and whatever others are known to roam the world of living beings— die in a mere moment.
For the most part, kings, having enjoyed prosperity until the end of their lives,
meet death in order to experience the fruits of their good and evil deeds. Therefore, you ought to make peace here with the son of Dharma.
"Let both the Pāṇḍavas and the Kurus protect the earth.
Suyodhana, one should not think 'I am strong';
for even the powerful are seen to be surpassed by those who are stronger, O bull among men."
"O Kaurava, among those who are truly powerful, mere physical strength does not constitute power;
for all those Pāṇḍavas possess divine prowess.
In this regard, they cite this ancient history."
While Mātali, the charioteer of the King of the Three Worlds, was desiring to give away his daughter and was searching for a bridegroom,
there was in his family a single daughter who was world-renowned for her beauty.
Renowned by the name Guṇakeśī, she was of divine form; in both splendor and physical beauty, she surpassed all other women. Mātali, together with his wife, [waited for] the time of her marriage.
Having understood this, O King, he reflected with focused intent: "Alas,
it is a reproach indeed that in the family of men who are of noble character, exalted, illustrious, and possessed of abundant strength, a daughter should be born."

The mother’s family, the father’s family, and that family to which she is given— by these three families a maiden brings uncertainty for the virtuous. Both the world of gods and the world of men [she surveys] with her mind alone as her eye.
Having dived into and searched through them all, no suitor has pleased me—
neither among the gods, nor the sons of Diti, nor the Gandharvas, nor humans; likewise,
I found no favor in many sages for the sake of a husband.
Having consulted with his wife Sudharmā during the night,
Mātali set his mind on going to the world of the Nāgas,
thinking: "Among gods and men, there is no bridegroom equal to Guṇakeśī."
"Someone will surely appear among the Nāgas who can be seen by his form.
Having addressed Sudharmā and circumambulated her clockwise,
he kissed the maiden on the head and entered the depths of the earth.
Kaṇva said:
While Mātali was traveling on the path, he encountered by chance the great seer Nārada,
who was going to see Varuṇa.
Then Nārada said to him: "O Sūta, where are you preparing to go—on your own business or by the command of Śatakratu? Thus was Mātali questioned by Nārada as they traveled along the path.
He related his entire matter to Varuṇa exactly as it was.
Then that sage said to him, "Let us go together;
I too am prepared to depart from heaven for the purpose of seeing the Lord of the Waters."
"I shall tell you everything while showing you the surface of the earth;
having seen some excellent place there, O Mātali, we two shall choose one,
Mātali and Nārada, after descending into the earth."
The two high-souled ones beheld the world-protector, the lord of the waters.
There, Nārada received worship befitting a celestial ṛṣi,
while Mātali likewise obtained honors equal to those of Mahendra.
Both of them, with joyful minds, having announced their business and being permitted by Varuṇa, wandered through the world of the Nāgas;
so too did Nārada among all the beings dwelling within the earth.
Knowing [all this], he gave an explanation of everything to the charioteer without exception.
Nārada said:
"O dear one, you have seen Varuṇa surrounded by his sons and grandsons."
Behold the prosperous abode of the Lord of Waters, auspicious on all sides!
This is the son of Varuṇa, the Lord of Cows, who is possessed of great wisdom;
he excels others here by virtue of his character, conduct, and purity.
This beloved son of his, Puṣkara, lotus-eyed and handsome to behold, has been chosen as a husband by the daughter of Soma,
whom they call Jyotsnākālī— the second Lakṣmī in terms of beauty.
The eldest son of the cow of the Sun is known and remembered as Kṛta. Behold this palace of Vāruṇī, which is made entirely of gold;
this is indeed the daughter of Varuṇa, the Surā who is renowned throughout the worlds.
"O friend of the Lord of the Gods, it is by attaining this [chariot] that the gods attained their divinity.
O Mātali, these blazing weapons of the Daityas, whose kingdom has been seized, are now seen here."
"O Mātali, these [objects] indeed revolve inexhaustibly;
they are employed through spiritual power and have been won by the gods.
Here, O Mātali, are the species of Rākṣasas and the species of Bhūtas."
And there were divine weapons fashioned by the ancient gods.
This fire of great radiance keeps watch in the lake of Varuṇa;
it is the discus of Viṣṇu, set in motion, smokeless and full of sacrificial luster.
This bow made of gāṇḍī wood, prepared for the destruction of the world, is constantly guarded by the deities; therefore it is called the Gāṇḍiva bow.
When a task arises, this [bow] exerts whatever strength is required.
By means of a power numbering hundreds of thousands, he constantly and firmly disciplines even those kings who are kinsmen of Rākṣasas and are beyond instruction;
for this first-born punishment was created by Brahmā, the teacher of the Veda.
"This great umbrella of the lords of men was proclaimed by Śakra;
the sons of the Lord of Waters hold this one of great splendor. This is the umbrella of the Lord of Waters, kept within the umbrella-house."
Cool water falls from all sides like a cloud raining;
this water, pure as the moon, has fallen from the umbrella and flows away,
shrouded by darkness so that it cannot be seen.
"O Mātali, many wonders of diverse forms are to be seen here;
however, your business may be obstructed by this, so let us go without delay.
Nārada said:
This city, situated at the navel-place of the world of the Nāgas,
is renowned as Pātāla, inhabited by Daityas and Dānavas. Whatever beings, whether stationary or moving, have reached this region together with the waters—
Entering, they cried out with a great roar, oppressed by fear.
There, the Asura Agni, who feeds upon water, blazes constantly;
he perceived himself bound, his soul held fast by his own activity.
05.097.004a Here, the nectar was deposited by the gods after they had slain their enemies;
05.097.004c from this, the waning and the waxing of the moon are clearly observed.
05.097.005a Here, at every change of the moon, the divine horse-head appears in due time.
It rises up, golden-hued, filling the world with its waters. Because all those forms of water fall there together,
this supreme city is known as Pātāla.

Airāvata, for the welfare of the world, takes water from this [ocean] and releases cool moisture into the clouds, which Mahendra then causes to rain down. Herein dwell sea-monsters (*timayaḥ*) of various forms and many different appearances.
Having drunk the luster of the moon from the waters, the aquatic creatures dwell there; O Sūta, struck by the rays of the sun, they resort to the depths of Pātāla and die during the day,
but they live again at night.
05.097.010a Here, at its rising, the moon is constantly surrounded by its rays;
05.097.010c touching the nectar through that contact, it restores life to embodied beings.
05.097.011a Here, those devoted to unrighteousness, bound and tormented by Time, [suffer].
The Daityas, their prosperity having been taken away by Vāsava, lived here.
Here, the lord of all beings, the great sovereign of all creatures known as Bhūtapati,
performed supreme austerity for the welfare of all beings.
05,097.013 Here dwell great sages, brahmins who observe the cow-vow, emaciated by their study and recitation of the Vedas; having cast off their lives, they have conquered heaven.
05,097.014 They always sleep wherever they may be and eat whatever food they may find.
Clothed in whatever manner he may be, such a person is said here to be observing the "cow-vow" (govrata).
Airāvata, the king of elephants, Vāmana, Kumuda, and Añjana—
these best of elephants were born in the lineage of Supratīka.
"Behold, Mātali, if any suitor here pleases you by virtue of his qualities, let us go and choose him with diligent effort.
This egg, placed in the water, is as if blazing with splendor."
Indeed, from the very beginning of creation, he neither sprouts nor creeps;
nor do I hear his birth or origin being described,
and no one knows his father or mother.
"Therefore, it is said that at the time of the end, a great fire shall arise,
O Mātali, and it will consume the entire triple world, including all things mobile and immobile.
Kaṇva said:
Having heard Nārada’s speech, Mātali then said:
"None of these pleases me; go elsewhere without delay.
Nārada said:
This great and excellent city, renowned as Hiraṇyapura,
belonged to the Daityas and Dānavas who move about employing hundreds of illusions; it was constructed by Viśvakarman with no small effort.

Created by Māyā with his mind, it rests upon the surface of Pātāla. Here, thousands of Māyās manifesting themselves, the highly powerful and heroic Dānavas dwell, having been granted boons in the past.
Neither Śakra, nor anyone else— neither Varuṇa, Yama, nor even the Giver of Wealth (Kubera)— is able to bring these Asuras,
the Kālakhañjas, and those born from Viṣṇupada under their control.
The Nairṛtas, the Yātudhānas, and those born from the Brahmaveda—
fanged and of terrifying form— they dwell as self-protectors; endowed with the power of *māyā*, they dwell as self-protectors.
The Dānavas known as the Nivātakavacas are intoxicated by the frenzy of battle; you know how even Śakra is unable to oppress them,
O Mātali, as have you yourself and your son Gomukha on many occasions.
The king of the gods, the lord of Śacī, together with his sons, has been utterly defeated.
Behold, Mātali, these dwellings made of gold and silver,
which have arrived here joined by means of skillful craftsmanship and according to the prescribed rules.
Some were green like lapis lazuli, others as beautiful as coral;
some were as bright as sun-crystal, and others radiant with the essence of diamond. Some appeared to be made of earth, while others again seemed to be composed of stone.
They appear like mountains and also like stars;
they shine with the form of the sun and resemble blazing fires;
variegated with networks of jewels, they are lofty and dense.
These cannot be fully described in terms of their form, substance,
or qualities, for they are perfected and endowed with excellent proportions. Behold the pleasure-gardens of the Daityas, as well as their couches.
There were precious and highly valuable vessels and seats,
as well as mountains with the luster of clouds, endowed with flowing springs of water, and trees that yield flowers and fruits according to one's desire, moving at will.
"O Mātali, is there any bridegroom here who might be pleasing to you?
Or, if you so desire, let us go to another region of the earth.
Kaṇva said:
But Mātali spoke to him as he was speaking in such a manner:
"O celestial sage, it is not my wish to do anything displeasing to the inhabitants of heaven;
for the gods and the Dānavas are brothers whose enmity is perpetual."
"How could I desire a connection with the faction of my enemies?
Let us go elsewhere; I ought not to look upon the Dānavas.
For I know myself to be such that I am characterized by a desire to give."
Nārada said:
This world belongs to the Suparṇas, those winged birds who feed on serpents; they experience no exhaustion in their prowess, their flight, or their burden-bearing.
O Sūta, this lineage was expanded by six sons of Vainateya:
Sumukha, Sunāman, Sunetra, Suvarcas,
Surūpa the king of birds, and Subala, O Mātali.
Indeed, hundreds and thousands of noble lineages of the kings of birds were increased through their offspring by those who became the founders of Vinatā’s clan,
born in the lineage of Kaśyapa and increasing his prosperity.
For all these are endowed with prosperity, and all bear the *śrīvatsa* mark;
desiring prosperity, they all likewise maintain their powers.
By their actions, however, these are Kṣatriyas—merciless devourers of those who enjoy their wealth.

Because they cause the destruction of their kinsmen, they do not indeed attain the status of Brahmins. O Mātali, I shall state their names according to their importance; listen, for this lineage is indeed praiseworthy, being protected by Viṣṇu.
Viṣṇu is the deity of these, and Viṣṇu alone is their ultimate refuge;
Viṣṇu is always in their hearts, and Viṣṇu alone is their constant goal. [They are] Suvarṇacūḍa, Nāgāśī, Dāruṇa, and Caṇḍatuṇḍaka.
Anala, Anila, Viśālākṣa, and Kuṇḍalin; Kāśyapi, Dhvajaviṣkambha, Vainateya, and Vāmana;
Vātavega, Diśācakṣus, Nimeṣa, and likewise Nimiṣa.
Trivāra, Saptavāra, Vālmīki, and likewise Dvīpaka;
Daityadvīpa, Sariddvīpa, Sārasa, and Padmakesara; Sumukha, Sukhaketu, Citrabarhas, and Anagha.
Meghakṛt, Kumuda, Dakṣa, Sarpānta, Somabhojana,
Gurubhāra, Kapota, Sūryanetra, Cirāntaka,
Viṣṇudhanvan, Kumāra, Paribarha, and likewise Hari.
Susvara, Madhuparka, Hemavarṇa,
as well as Malaya, Mātariśvan, Niśākara, and Divākara—
these sons of Garuḍa have been mentioned by me only by way of illustration.
They have been celebrated according to their preeminence, their fame, and their vital breaths.
If you have no liking for anything here, come, Mātali, let us go;
I will lead you to that region where you shall find something to your taste.
Nārada said:
This is the seventh layer of the earth, named Rasātala,
where resides Surabhi, the mother of cows, who was born from the nectar of immortality.
It constantly flows with milk produced from the essence of the earth—
a single, unsurpassed flavor formed from the essence of the six tastes—
just as in the past, when [the ocean] was overflowing with nectar, it vomited forth that very essence.
From the mouth of the Grandfather (Brahmā), that blameless woman arose;
as the stream of her milk fell upon the surface of the earth,
it formed a lake known as the Ocean of Milk, a supreme and most holy place of purity.
Surrounded on all sides like the edge of a mass of foam upon a flowering tree,
the best of sages dwell there drinking that foam;
O Mātali, they are known by the name Phenapa, and their food consists of foam.
They abide in fierce asceticism, before whom even the gods are afraid.
O Mātali, there are four other cows belonging to this [earth] who dwell in all the directions;
they are known as the guardians of the quarters, sustaining the very quarters themselves.
The daughter of Surabhi named Surūpā supports the eastern quarter;
she named Haṃsakā supports the southern quarter;
and the western quarter belonging to Varuṇa is indeed supported by Subhadrā.
O Mātali, she who possesses great majesty and assumes all forms constantly sustains the northern quarter,
which is righteous and known as Ilāvila, with a cow named Sarvakāmadughā (the Cow of Plenty).
Having churned the ocean with its milk mixed with the milk of these [cows],
and having made Mount Mandara the churning-stick, the gods together with the Asuras extracted Vāruṇī, Lakṣmī, and the nectar of immortality, O Mātali.
The king of horses, Uccaiḥśravas, and the Kaustubha jewel;
nectar for those who consume nectar, and *svadhā* for those who eat *svadhā*; and for those who feed on the immortal, Surabhi pours forth milk as ambrosia.
In this regard, an ancient verse sung of old by the inhabitants of the netherworld (Rasātala) is heard in the world and is chanted by the wise:
"Neither in the world of the Nāgas, nor in heaven, nor in a celestial chariot in the triple heaven (Triviṣṭapa)..."
"Such an exile would be as pleasant as dwelling in the depths of the netherworld.
Nārada said:
"This city named Bhogavatī is protected by Vāsuki."
Just as Amarāvatī is the preeminent city of the king of the gods,
so too stands this serpent Śeṣa, by whom this earth is always supported—
through his asceticism, which is foremost in the world, and through his great majesty.
His form resembles a mass of white clouds, adorned with various ornaments; possessing great strength, he bears a thousand heads and has tongues of flame.
Here, there are beings of various forms and various ornaments.
The sons of Surasā, the Nāgas, dwell there free from affliction;
marked with jewels, svastikas, and wheels, and bearing the signs of water-pots (kamaṇḍalu),
they number in the thousands, all powerful and fierce by nature.
Some had a thousand heads, some five hundred faces;
some had a hundred heads, and others even three heads;
some had two or five heads, and others likewise seven mouths.
Possessing great wealth and massive bodies, with coils as vast as mountain ranges— there are many thousands, millions, and billions of them here.
Listen now to me regarding the most eminent among those belonging to a single lineage of nāgas.
Vāsuki, Takṣaka, Karkoṭaka, Dhanañjaya,
Kālīya, Nahuṣa, both Kambala and Aśvatara, Bāhyakuṇḍa, the Nāga Maṇi, and likewise Apūraṇa and Khaga.
Vāmana, Cailapatra, Kukura, and likewise Kukuṇa;
Āryaka and Nandaka, as well as Kalaśa and Potaka; Kailāsaka, Piñjaraka, and the nāga Airāvata.
Sumanomukha, Dadhimukha, Śaṅkha, Nanda and Upanandaka,
Āpta, Koṭanaka, Śikhin, Niṣṭhūrika,
Tittiri, Hastibhadra, Kumuda, and Mālyapiṇḍaka.
The two *padmas*, the *puṇḍarīka*, the *puṣpa*, the *mudgaraparṇaka*,
the *karavīra*, the *pīṭharaka*, the *saṃvṛtta*, and the *vṛtta*; the *piṇḍāra*, the *bilvapatra*, the *mūṣikāda*, and the *śirīṣaka*.
Dilīpa, Śaṅkhaśīrṣa, Jyotiṣka, and Aparājita;
Kauravya, Dhṛtarāṣṭra, Kumāra, and Kuśaka; as well as Viraja, Dhāraṇa, Subāhu, Mukhara, and Jaya.
Badhira, Andha, Vikuṇḍa, Virasa, and likewise Surasa—
these and many others are known as the sons of Kaśyapa. O Mātali, look here to see if any among them pleases you as a husband.
Kaṇva said:
Mātali, having gazed intently and continuously at that one [Nārada],
questioned him there and became as if filled with joy.
"O Great Seer, tell everything to me who asks and desires to know;
for you, O Great Sage, possess knowledge of all things as clearly as a myrobalan fruit in the palm of your hand.
This man standing here before Kauravya and Āryaka—"
Resplendent and handsome, whose joy is this delighter of his family?
Who is his father and who is his mother, and to which serpent-king does he belong? To what lineage does he belong, standing as if he were its great banner?

"O divine sage, by my resolve, my fortitude, my beauty, and my youth, the husband of Guṇakeśī has entered my heart as my chosen lord. Having seen Mātali with a joyful mind because of the sight of Sumukha’s face, [she spoke thus].
Then he announced his majesty, his birth, and his deeds:
"I am born in the lineage of Airāvata, a king of serpents named Sumukha; I am the esteemed grandson of Āryaka and the daughter's son of Vāmana."
"O Mātali, this Nāga named Cikura was indeed his father;
not long ago, he was brought to his death by the son of Vinatā.
Then Mātali, with a pleased mind, spoke these words to Nārada.
"O dear one, this best of serpents is pleasing to me as a son-in-law. Indeed, let an effort be made in this matter, for I am truly delighted by him;
O sage, [let it be done] to give my beloved daughter to this lord of the nāgas."
Having heard Mātali’s words, Kaṇva said, "O best of sages, Nārada spoke to Āryaka, the king of the nāgas, O descendant of Kuru."
Nārada said:
"This is Mātali by name, the charioteer of Śakra, his beloved friend—
pure, endowed with virtuous conduct and qualities, radiant, heroic, and powerful."
He is the friend, counselor, and charioteer of Śakra;
his power is but slightly inferior to that of Vāsava in every battle.
He [shall mount] this supreme, victorious chariot yoked with a thousand bay horses.
In the wars between the gods and the asuras, he restrains them by his mind alone.
Having conquered with his horses, Vāsava conquers with his two arms;
when struck first by him, the slayer of Bala then strikes back.
He has a daughter of noble form, peerless on earth in beauty,
endowed with the qualities of goodness and character, renowned as Guṇakeśī.
O you of immortal luster, he is traveling through the three worlds with great effort for her sake.
"Sumukha, your grandson, is pleasing as a husband for your daughter.
O gentle one, best of serpents, if he pleases you, O noble one, do not delay;
let your mind be quickly resolved upon accepting the maiden."
"Just as Lakṣmī is in the family of Viṣṇu, and as Svāhā is in the family of Agni, so may Guṇakeśī, the slender-waisted one, be in your family. Therefore,
for the sake of your grandson, you should accept Guṇakeśī."
She is a worthy match for you, as Śacī is for the handsome Vāsava;
for we choose him on account of his virtues, even though he is fatherless,
out of great respect for you and likewise for Airāvata.
Because of Sumukha’s virtues— such as his character, purity, and self-restraint—
he has come in person and is prepared to give his daughter;
therefore, O Mātali, you too ought to show him honor.
Kaṇva said:
But Āryaka, though dejected and yet filled with joy, spoke to Nārada while his grandson was being chosen as king and his own son had met his death.
"How could I wish for Guṇakeśī as my daughter-in-law, O divine seer? This word of yours is not at all esteemed by me, O divine seer.
Who would not desire one who is the friend of Śakra and so well-endowed?"
But because of the weakness of the cause, O Great Sage, I reflect thus:
"O Father, O One of Great Splendor, my son, the progenitor of this body, has been devoured by Vainateya; it is for that reason indeed that we are afflicted with grief."
Furthermore, O Lord, as he was departing, Vainateya said:
"In another month, I shall devour Sumukha.
We know his resolve; it will certainly come to pass.
"Because of those words of Suparṇa, my joy has indeed vanished. Having heard these words spoken by Kaṇva regarding Garuḍa, [the King spoke].
Mātali, however, said to him: "I have already made up my mind in this matter;
your son Sumukha has been chosen by me as a son-in-law. This very serpent, together with me and Nārada, [is here]."
"O best of beings, go to Vāsava, the lord of the three worlds and sovereign of the gods, and see him;
through the remainder of his own purpose, I shall ascertain [the length of] his life,
and I will strive to thwart Suparṇa."
"And let Sumukha go with me to the Lord of the Gods for the sake of accomplishing our purpose; may it be well with you, O serpent!
Having been permitted by my grandfather, you may depart," so he said, O Bhārata.
Then, taking Sumukha by the hand, all those of great prowess beheld Śakra, the king of the gods, seated there in his great splendor;
and upon arriving there, the blessed Viṣṇu appeared with four arms.
Then Nārada related all of that to Mātali.
Thereupon Viṣṇu spoke to Purandara, the lord of the world:
"Let the nectar be given to him; let him be made equal to the immortals."
"O Vāsava, may Mātali, Nārada, and Sumukha obtain this desire of theirs according to their wish, through your grace.
Then Purandara, reflecting upon the prowess of the son of Vinatā, [spoke].
He said to Viṣṇu, "May you yourself grant him.
Viṣṇu replied,
"You are the lord of all worlds, both those that move and those that are unmoving."
"O Lord, who would venture to undo what has been given by you? What has been given is as if not given. Kaṇva said:
"Then Śakra granted supreme longevity to that serpent."
But the slayer of Bala and Vṛtra did not make him a partaker of the nectar;
however, having obtained the boon, Sumukha became truly fair-faced and,
having taken a wife, went toward his home as he desired.
Nārada and Āryaka, their purpose accomplished and filled with joy,
returned after having honored the highly effulgent king of the gods.
Kaṇva said:
O Bhārata, the mighty Garuḍa heard exactly what had occurred— that Śakra had granted a gift of life to the Nāga— and that bird,
having obstructed the three worlds with the great wind from his wings, [approached].
Suparṇa, extremely enraged, rushed toward Vāsava.
Garuḍa said:
"O Blessed One, why do you show such contempt regarding my hunger and fear?"

Having granted me the boon of acting according to my own will, you have now wavered. Since food has been ordained for all beings by the Creator, the Lord of all beings, why is it being withheld from me by you?
"This great elephant was chosen and the agreement was established by me;
O King, this vast progeny must be protected by him and by me.
But if this situation were otherwise, I would not venture to harm another."
"O King of the Gods, you sport according to your own will and as you please;
therefore, I shall give up my life, as will my attendants and those servants who dwell in my house. Be gracious, O Vāsava!"
Kaṇva said:
Having heard the words of Suparṇa, Sumukha then became Durmukha;
abandoning his [former] form, he turned pale and assumed the shape of a serpent.
Indra said:
"Having gone into the presence of Viṣṇu, I have merely touched his footstool;
O Vainateya, this was not done by me, so you ought not to be angry with me."
Having been granted safety by the powerful Viṣṇu,
that handsome son of Vinatā, having heard what was said by Purandara, spoke;
then Purandara addressed these words to Garuḍa.
"And this I deserve, O slayer of Bala and Vṛtra, and even more;
for though I am the lord of the three worlds, I have come to the state of another's servant.
While you remain, O Lord of Gods, Viṣṇu is no cause for my status."
"O Vāsava, King of the Three Worlds, sovereignty indeed rests eternally with you.
Yet, my mother is the daughter of Dakṣa and Kaśyapa is my father;
I too am fully capable of easily sustaining all the worlds."
My vast strength is unbearable even for all beings;
by me also was a most great deed performed in the conflict with the Daityas—
Śrutaśrī, Śrutasena, Vivasvat, and Rocanāmukha.

Prasabha and Kālakākṣa— these sons of Diti were also slain by me. But because I diligently attend to you while stationed upon your banner and carry your younger brother, for that reason you hold me in contempt.
Who else indeed is capable of bearing such a burden? Who else is more powerful?
Such as I am, with but a single portion of my strength, I could stir even the oceans;
yet, being superior, I carry this [burden] along with its kinsmen.
"O Vāsava, because I was deprived of food by you out of contempt, my dignity has been destroyed—
both toward you and toward these sons of Aditi who are endowed with strength and prowess."
"It is said that you are indeed the strongest among them all by far;
therefore, I carry you with only a portion of my wing, free from fatigue.
Reflect slowly upon this, dear one: who here is truly the stronger?"
Kaṇva said:
Having heard those words of the bird, which were terrible in their consequence,
the one who bears the wheel of the chariot spoke to Tārkṣya, agitating him who is otherwise unshakeable.
O Garuḍa, you consider yourself strong, yet you are very weak.
O egg-born one, it is enough that you praise yourself in our presence;
even the entire three worlds would be incapable of supporting my body.
I alone carry myself by my own power, and I support you;
you do not carry me with your arms—your boasting is in vain. First, try to carry this single arm of mine, the one on the right side.
"If you can support this single [hand] of mine, then your boasting shall bear fruit.
Thereupon, the Blessed One placed his arm upon his shoulder;
as soon as he was touched by the tip of [the Buddha's] fingernail, Garuḍa, the son of Kaśyapa, [was overcome].
Out of affection for the two of them, he placed the burden upon his own hands;
yet, though he endeavored to lift that weight, he was unable to do so by force. Afflicted by the load, he fell down, overwhelmed and deprived of consciousness.
For as much weight as there is in the entire earth together with its mountains,
he considered that to be the weight of a single branch of his body;
yet, though more powerful, he did not cause it pain by his strength.
Therefore, Acyuta did not destroy his life; however,
with his wings damaged, his body slumped, his mind bewildered, and overwhelmed by distress, the bird, oppressed by that heavy burden, then shed his feathers.
Bowing his head to Viṣṇu, that bird, the son of Vinatā—
distraught, overwhelmed, and dejected— spoke these few words:
"O Blessed One, by means of this embodied form which is worthy of the essence of the world..."

"I have been crushed upon the surface of the earth by your arm, which was released at its own will. O Lord, you ought to forgive me, a creature dwelling upon your banner— a bird agitated and consumed by the fire of your power."
"O Lord, O All-pervading One, your supreme power was not known by me;
therefore, I considered my own prowess to be peerless among others.
Then the Blessed One indeed showed his favor toward Garuḍa."
"Do not do so again," he said to him then out of affection;
and with his big toe, he hurled Sumukha onto the chest of Garuḍa.
From that time forth, O Indra among kings, he has lived together with the serpent.

Thus, overcome by the power of Viṣṇu, Garuḍa— the mighty son of Vinatā, O King, of great renown— suffered the destruction of his pride. In the same way, O son of Gāndhārī, you too [shall fall] as long as you oppose the sons of Pāṇḍu in battle.
As long as you do not encounter those heroes, my son, you shall live.
Bhīma, the best among strikers and the mighty son of Vāyu,
and Dhanañjaya, the son of Indra— who could they not slay in battle?
Viṣṇu, Vāyu, Śakra, Dharma, and both the Aśvins—by what means could you possibly behold these gods? Therefore, enough of this hostility; seek peace, O prince.
"You ought to protect your lineage by means of Vāsudeva as your refuge;
for this Nārada of great asceticism is a direct witness to all of this—
to that majesty of Viṣṇu who is the wielder of the discus and the mace."
Vaiśampāyana said:
Having heard that, Duryodhana, sighing with a frowning face and looking toward the son of Rādhā, then laughed aloud.
Disregarding those words of the seer Kaṇva, the evil-minded one struck his thigh,
which was shaped like an elephant’s trunk, and said this:
"Just as I have been created by the Lord, whatever is destined to be, and whatever my fate shall be."
"O Great Seer, I shall act accordingly; what will idle talk accomplish?
Janamejaya said:
"He who is obstinately intent on what is harmful and deluded by greed for the interests of another..."
Delighting in ignoble deeds, resolved upon death,
he was a bringer of suffering to his kinsmen, an increaser of grief for his relatives,
a giver of distress to his friends, and an enhancer of joy for his enemies.
"Why do his kinsmen not restrain him here as he stands on the wrong path—
neither a loving friend out of affection, nor the venerable Grandfather?
Vaiśampāyana said:
The word spoken by the Blessed One has been stated, as well as what was fittingly spoken by Bhīṣma;
listen also to that which has been spoken in many ways by Nārada.
Nārada said:
A listener who is a true friend is indeed difficult to find, and a well-wishing friend is likewise rare. For a friend remains where one stands; a kinsman does not remain there.
O joy of the Kurus, I see that the words of friends are worthy of being heard.
One should not persist in obstinacy, for obstinacy is truly terrible.
In this regard, they cite this ancient history as an example of how Gālava met with defeat through his persistence.
In ancient times, O Bhārata, Dharma himself, desiring to test Viśvāmitra as he was engaged in ascetic penance,
approached him having assumed the form of the venerable sage Vasiṣṭha,
one of the Seven Sages.

O King, hungry and famished, Viśvāmitra went to the hermitage of Kauśika; then, in great haste, he diligently cooked a sacrificial porridge (caru) of the finest food, yet he did not wait for it to be finished.

When that food had been eaten by him, which had been given by other ascetics, Viśvāmitra then approached with food that was still very hot. Having said, "I have already eaten; you stay here for a moment," the venerable one departed.
Then, O King, the immensely radiant Viśvāmitra remained standing right there;
holding that food upon his head with both hands, he moved along its side,
standing motionless like a pillar nearby, subsisting on air alone.
The sage Gālava exerted himself in serving him out of reverence,
great respect, affection, and a desire to do what was pleasing.
Then, when a hundred years were complete, Dharma returned once more.
Assuming the guise of Vasiṣṭha out of a desire for food,
he saw the wise Viśvāmitra, the great seer who subsisted on air, standing there with alms-food held upon his head.
Then Dharma accepted it; having eaten that food, which was likewise hot and fresh, he said, "I am pleased, O brahmin-sage," and that seer departed.
Having passed beyond the state of a kṣatriya, he attained the status of a brahmin.
Viśvāmitra was then delighted by the recitation of the Dharma;
and Viśvāmitra, being pleased by the service and devotion of his ascetic disciple Gālava, spoke to him as follows.
"O child Gālava, I have granted you leave; go wherever you desire.
Thus addressed, Gālava, pleased, replied with sweet words to the immensely radiant Viśvāmitra, the best of sages.
"What sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) shall I bestow upon you for this weighty task?
For a human rite is successful when it is accompanied by sacrificial fees;
indeed, one enjoys the fruits of the fees that have been distributed at its conclusion."
"In heaven, the fruit of sacrifices is said by the wise to be the sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā), which is peace. What shall I bring for the sake of my guru? Let the Blessed One speak.
But the Blessed One, though he knew [the answer], was won over by his service.
Viśvāmitra urged him repeatedly, saying, "Go, go! Addressed thus by Viśvāmitra with the repeated words, "Go,
go," Gālava replied many times, "What shall I give?"
But because of the ascetic Gālava’s persistent entreaties,
Viśvāmitra, his agitation slightly aroused, said this:
"Give me eight hundred horses, each with one ear black."
"Go, O Gālava, without delay, to those horses as white as the moon.
Nārada said:
"Thus addressed at that time by the wise Viśvāmitra..."
At that time, Gālava neither sat nor lay down, nor did he take food;
reduced to skin and bone, pale, and devoted to anxiety and grief,
he lamented excessively, consumed by his inner torment.
O Suyodhana, Gālava, distressed by his grief, lamented:
"Where are my well-nourished friends? Where are my riches and where my stores?
And where are my eight hundred horses, white as the moon?"
Whence can I have any desire for food, and whence can I have any desire for comfort? My desire even for life is severed; what is the use of my living?
I am beyond the ocean, or further than the farthest limit of the earth.
Having gone [to the forest], I shall release my soul; what fruit is there for me in life?
For one who is destitute, who has failed to achieve his purpose, who is abandoned by various fruits [of action], and who bears a debt—how can there be happiness through inaction?
For one who has enjoyed the wealth of friends and fulfilled their desired requests,
yet is unable to repay them, death is better than life. For one who says, "I shall do it," but fails to perform that duty after having made a promise—
The merit of sacrifices and charitable works perishes for one consumed by false speech.
There is no beauty in falsehood, nor is there progeny for the liar;
there is no sovereignty for the liar, so how could there be a fortunate rebirth?
Whence can there be fame for the ungrateful? Whence a place of standing? Whence happiness? For the ungrateful man is not to be trusted; indeed, for the ungrateful, there is no atonement.
The sinful man who lacks wealth does not truly live; how, then, can there be the maintenance of a sinner?
A wicked person who destroys what has been done for him certainly meets with destruction.
Such as I am— sinful, ungrateful, wretched, and even a liar—
I do not carry out the command spoken by my preceptor, even though his purpose has already been accomplished.
Having exerted this unsurpassed effort, I shall now relinquish my life-breaths;
never before have I made any request of the dwellers of heaven,
yet all the gods honor me at the sacrificial assembly.
