But I am going to Viṣṇu Kṛṣṇa, the best of the gods, the lord of the three worlds, the refuge of those who seek refuge;
from whom all enjoyments arise, pervading all the gods and asuras.
"Being self-restrained, I wish to see the imperishable Great Yogin.
When this was said, his friend Garuḍa, the son of Vinatā,
showed him [the Lord] and spoke to him with joy, desiring to do what was pleasing.
"In my view, you are a friend, and you are considered a friend by those who are friends.
When one has the means, one should provide what is desired according to one's wish;
and I have the means, O Brahmin, O twice-born son of Vāsava."
"I have already spoken for your sake, and my desire has been fulfilled by him.
Therefore, you may come; let us go, and I shall lead you wherever you please—to the far shore of the earth, O Gālava—go without delay."
Suparṇa said:
"I have been instructed by the Lord whose origin is unknown, O Gālava;
tell me which direction I should first go to see."
"O best of the twice-born, O Gālava, to which direction shall I go— to the east, the south, the western quarter, or the north?
It is from there that the creator of light for all the worlds first rises."
Where Savitṛ performs his penance at twilight for the sake of the Sādhyas;
where the primordial Intellect was born, by which this entire world is pervaded;
where the two eyes of Dharma reside, and where he himself is established.
The oblation offered through the mouths [of the gods] spreads in all directions;
this, O best of the twice-born, is the gate of the day as well as of the path,
where in former times the female progeny of Dakṣa were indeed born.
In that direction where the offspring of Kaśyapa have flourished,
from which the prosperity of the gods has its root, where Śakra was consecrated with the sovereignty over the gods, and where, O brahmin seer, the gods performed their ascetic penances.
For this reason, O Brahmin, this direction is called "East" (pūrvā):
because in former times it was first occupied by the gods; and for this very reason, it is the eastern quarter looked toward by those who came before.
One who desires happiness should perform the rites pertaining to the ancestors and the gods first;
it was here that the Blessed One, the creator of the worlds, formerly sang the Vedas,
and it was here that Sāvitrī was uttered by Savitṛ among those who discourse on Brahman.
O best of the twice-born, it was here that the *yajus* mantras were bestowed by Sūrya; here, Soma is drunk at sacrifices by the gods who have obtained their boons;
and here, the sacrificial fires, being satisfied, enjoy their own source.
05.106.012c Here, Varuṇa took refuge in the netherworld (pātāla) and attained prosperity.
05.106.013a O bull among the twice-born, here also shine forth the birth, the establishment, and the passing away of the ancient Vasiṣṭha.

05.106.014a Here, ten times ten births of the syllable *oṃ* arise; 05.106.014c where the Soma-drinking sages drink the sacrificial oblation at the Havirdhāna shed. 05.106.015a Where many wild animals, such as boars and others, have been consecrated in the forest.
Where Śakra has assigned portions for the sake of the deities,
there the fire-god Vibhāvasu, out of anger, consumes all those who are ungrateful— whether they be humans, asuras, or others— who have been established therein.
"This is the gateway to the three worlds, to heaven, and to happiness. This is the eastern quarter; enter it, if you so desire.
For I must do what is pleasing to him whose word I abide by."
"Speak, O Gālava; I shall go, for I am about to hear of another direction.
Suparṇa said:
"This [direction] was indeed formerly [established] by Vivasvat according to the scriptural injunctions."
The sacrificial fee given to the preceptor is called *dakṣiṇā*; furthermore, the word *dakṣiṇā* signifies the southern direction. Herein, the ancestral realm of these three worlds is established;
here, O twice-born one, the abode of the gods who subsist on steam (*uṣmapā*) is said to be located.

"Here, O twice-born one, all the gods always sit together with the ancestors; being worshipped in the worlds, they have attained an equal share [of the offerings]. This, they say, is the second door of Dharma."

Here, the determination of time is calculated in units of *truṭi* and *lava*. Here, the celestial ṛṣis, as well as the ṛṣis of the world of the ancestors and all the royal ṛṣis, dwell eternally, free from suffering.
In this state, both dharma and truth, as well as the fruit of one's actions, are observed;
O best of the twice-born, this is the destination of one whose self is exhausted by their own deeds.
O best of the twice-born, this is that direction which everyone eventually reaches.
But being enveloped by a lack of awakening, one does not perceive that happiness.
O bull among the twice-born, many thousands of Nairṛtas are created here as adverse sights to be beheld by those of undisciplined soul.

O twice-born one, here in the groves of Mandara and in the dwellings of the brahmin-sages, the Gandharvas sing songs that captivate the mind and the intellect. Having heard these Sāman chants sung in verse, Raivata [was moved].
Having lost his wife, his ministers, and his kingdom, he went to the forest. There, O Brahmin, Sāvarṇi and Yavakrīta’s son established a boundary which even the Sun does not transgress.
Here, the high-souled Rāvaṇa, the king of the Rākṣasas and descendant of Pulastya,
performed austerities and chose immortality from the gods;
here also Vṛtra, by his conduct, attained the status of Śakra’s enemy.
05.107.013 Here all the *āsravas* (outflows) arrive and again depart in five ways.
05.107.014 Here, O Gālava, men who have performed evil deeds are cooked;
here is the river named Vaitaraṇī, filled with crossings (*vitaraṇaiḥ*).
Having gone there, one reaches the end of suffering and the end of happiness. Having turned back here, the sun sheds sweet water;
and having reached the quarter of the *dhaniṣṭhā* constellation, it emits frost once again.
"O Gālava, in this place I formerly found two large creatures, an elephant and a tortoise, fighting as I wandered about, afflicted by hunger.
Here, the great Ṛṣi named Śakradhanu was born from the Sun."
They know him as the god Kapila, by whom the sons of Sagara were consumed. Here dwell the perfected ones named Śivas, Brāhmaṇas who have mastered the Vedas;
having studied all the Vedas along with their auxiliary branches, they attain the abode of Yama.
There is a city named Bhogavatī, protected by Vāsuki,
as well as by the nāga Takṣaka and likewise by Airāvata.
Here, at the times of departure [from life], a great darkness is encountered.
"O Gālava, this path of yours is one that cannot be pierced even by the sun or by fire itself; it leads to great torment. Tell me if you must go to the west, or else listen to my words."
Suparṇa said:
"This quarter belongs to King Varuṇa, the lord of cattle;
it is the eternal abode and the very origin of the king of the waters."

"O best of the twice-born, it is here that the sun himself later releases his radiance; therefore, this direction is renowned as 'Paścimā' (the West). It is here, moreover, that the sovereignty over aquatic creatures and the protection of the waters reside."
The blessed lord Kaśyapa consecrated Varuṇa as god.
Having drunk here all six juices of Varuṇa,
Soma— the dispeller of darkness— is born young at the beginning of the bright fortnight.
O twice-born one, here the Daityas, having been defeated by Vāyu and bound at that time, lay sleeping while sighing and being tormented by great serpents. Here the mountain receives the beloved Sun.
From that place where the evening twilight creeps forth,
named Asta, night and sleep emerge at the end of the day,
as if to take away half the lifespan of the world of living beings.

It was here that Śakra rendered the goddess Diti— who was sleeping and carrying her own offspring— devoid of her fetus, from which the host of Maruts was born. It is here that the root of the Himavat reaches the eternal Mandara.
Even in a thousand years, its end cannot be reached.
Here, having reached the shore of the ocean, the Surabhi cow pours forth her milk upon the golden mountain and the river of golden waters.

In the midst of this ocean, the headless trunk (kabandha) of Svarbhānu— who resembles the sun and seeks to destroy both the moon and the sun— is seen. Here also is Suvarṇaśiras, with golden hair, as he sings aloud.
A vast sound is heard from one who is invisible and immeasurable. Here stands a maiden named Dhvajavatī, the daughter of Harimedhas;
by the command of the Sun, she remained there, saying, "Stay! Stay! in the sky.
O Gālava, here the wind, as well as fire, water, and space,
release the painful touch of both day and night;
from this point onward, the course of the sun turns obliquely.
At this time, all the luminaries enter the solar orb;
having wandered together with the sun for twenty-eight nights,
they emerge again from the sun through conjunction with the moon.
Here is the eternal source of flowing rivers and the origin of the ocean; here abide the waters of the three worlds, supported by Varuṇa;
and here is the dwelling of Ananta, the king of the serpents.
05.108.017 Here is the unsurpassed abode of Viṣṇu, who is without beginning or end. 05.108.018 Here also is the dwelling of Pavana, whose friend is Anala;
05.108.018 here is the residence of the great ṛṣi Kaśyapa, the son of Marīci.
"This is the final path proclaimed for you by way of the cardinal directions.
Speak, O Galava, best of the twice-born; where shall we go? What is your intention? You have heard of three directions, O Brahmin; now hear also of the northern direction."
Suparṇa said:
Because one is delivered from evil by it, and because one attains the highest good through it,
it is called "Uttara" (the Deliverer) by the wise on account of its fruit of deliverance.
O Gālava, the path to the northern region of gold and its surrounding lands is considered the middle way between the western and eastern directions;
it lies in this most excellent northern quarter, O bull among the twice-born.
No person who is ungentle, undisciplined, or unrighteous dwells here.
Here, Nārāyaṇa Kṛṣṇa, Jiṣṇu the best of men,
and likewise the eternal Brahmā reside at the hermitage site of Badarī.
On this very ridge of the Himavat, Maheśvara dwells eternally together with Prakṛti and Puruṣa, possessing a radiance like the fire at the end of an eon;
he cannot be seen by the hosts of sages, nor likewise by the gods including Indra.
Neither by Gandharvas, Yakṣas, nor Siddhas— except for Nara and Nārāyaṇa—
is he perceived here; yet the glorious Viṣṇu alone, the thousand-eyed, thousand-footed, and imperishable one,
beholds him through his illusory power (*māyā*), though he possesses a thousand heads.

05.109.005c Here, among the Brahmins, Candramas was consecrated to the sovereignty; 05.109.006a here Mahādeva, having received the Gaṅgā as she fell, descending from the sky, gave her to the world of men, O best of those who know the Veda.
05.109.007a Here the Goddess performed austerities out of a desire to obtain Maheśvara;
05.109.007c here Kāma, Roṣa, Śaila, and Umā were born together.
05.109.008a Here, O Gālava, [the dwellings] of the Rākṣasas, Yakṣas, and Gandharvas [are located].
By virtue of his sovereignty, Dhanada was also consecrated on Kailāsa. Here is the delightful Caitraratha grove, here is the hermitage of the Vaikhānasas,
and here, O bull among the twice-born, are both the Mandākinī river and Mount Mandara.
05.109.010a Here the Saugandhika grove is guarded by the Nairṛtas; 05.109.010c it has grassy meadows, plantain trunks, and here the Saṃtānaka trees grow.
05.109.011a Here dwell the Siddhas who are ever intent on self-restraint and who move about at will.
O Gālava, here are palaces suited to one's desires and fit for enjoyment;
here dwell the seven Ṛṣis and the goddess Arundhatī. Here indeed stands Svāti, and its rising is recorded to occur here.
05.109.013a Here, having ascended the sacrifice, the Grandfather (Brahmā) stands firm;
05.109.013c the luminaries, including the moon and the sun, revolve here perpetually. 05.109.014a Here, the best of the twice-born guard the gateway known as Gāyantikā.
The great-souled sages named Dhāmas are speakers of truth; their origin, their form, and their accumulated ascetic merit are not known,
O Gālava, nor are the thousands of cycles of worldly enjoyments they have experienced.
O best of the twice-born, O Gālava, as a man enters further beyond that, he dissolves accordingly;
O bull among the twice-born, no one else has ever gone there before.
Except for the god Nārāyaṇa or the imperishable hero Jiṣṇu, [no one else could do so].
Here, that place called Kailāsa belonging to Ailavila is mentioned;
here, ten Apsarases named Vidyutprabhās were born.
O Brahmin, it was here that Viṣṇu, while performing his strides during the conquest of the three worlds, established the place known as Viṣṇupada, situated in the northern direction. It was here,
O best of the twice-born, that King Marutta performed a sacrifice.
O brahmin-sage, at Uśīrabīja, where the Jāmbūnada lake is located, the holy,
pure, and stainless lotus-pond of the great-souled brahmin-sage Jīmūta appeared in person from the Himavat mountains.
Having bestowed all that great wealth upon the Brahmins so as to bring it to a virtuous conclusion,
that great seer then chose the Jaimūta forest as his dwelling.
O bull among the twice-born, there the guardians of the quarters always wait upon him morning and evening.
"O Gālava, why indeed do they cry out, 'Whose duty is what?'?
O best of the twice-born, it is for this reason that this northern quarter is renowned as 'Uttarā' because of its other qualities,
and because it is superior (*uttara*) in all undertakings."

"O dear one, these four directions have been described to you in detail according to their sequence; yet you wish to go toward the direction of desire. O best of the twice-born, I am prepared to show those directions to you."
"O Brahmin, therefore ascend me, who am the entire earth, O twice-born one.
Gālava said:
"O Garuḍa, enemy of the lords of serpents, Suparṇa, son of Vinatā!"
"O Tārkṣya, lead me to the east, where the two eyes of Dharma are located. Go first to this direction which was previously proclaimed;
for you have stated that the presence of the deities is found therein."
"Herein, both truth and dharma have been correctly proclaimed by you.
However, I wish to meet with all the deities together;
furthermore, O younger brother of Aruṇa, I wish to see those gods once more."
Nārada said:
The son of Vinatā said to that twice-born man, "Mount [me].
Then the sage Gālava ascended Garuḍa at that time.
Gālava said:
"O devourer of serpents,
as you stride along, your form appears like that of the thousand-rayed Vivasvat, the sun, in the forenoon."
"O bird, I see the movement here of the trees driven by the wind from your wings as they follow after you, like those setting out together—
[the earth] with its oceans, forests, mountains, groves, and woodlands."
O sky-ranger, you appear as if drawing everything toward you with the wind from your wings;
the water, along with its fish, serpents, and crocodiles, is as if being lifted up into the sky by that great wind and the constant flapping of your wings.
I see fish of similar form— timis, timiṅgilas,
and serpents with human faces— as if they have been violently churned up;
moreover, my ears are deafened by the roars of the great ocean.
"I do not hear, I do not see, and I do not know the cause within myself.
Please proceed slowly and carefully, O bird, mindful of the sin of killing a Brahmin; for the sun is not seen, my dear, nor the directions, nor the sky."
"I see only darkness; I do not perceive your body.
O bird, I see your two eyes like two precious gems of noble birth, yet I do not see your body nor my own."
At every step, I see fire rising from the water;
it suddenly extinguishes my eyes, and they are restored once more.
Therefore, turn back, O son of Vinatā, for a great deal of time has passed as you have been traveling.
"O eater of serpents, I have no purpose whatsoever in going; turn back, O one of great speed, for I cannot withstand your velocity. For I have promised my preceptor eight hundred horses here."
"O bird, I see no path for the deliverance of these white horses with one black ear that possess the luster of the moon;
therefore, I have seen this path for myself: the renunciation of life."
"I have no wealth at all, nor do I have a friend possessed of wealth; yet even with great riches, this cannot be dispelled. Nārada said:
To Gālava, who was speaking thus— both much and piteously—
the son of Vinatā replied while continuing on his way, smiling:
"O brahmin-sage, you are not very wise, since you wish to abandon yourself."
Furthermore, time is not something artificial; for Time is the Supreme Lord.
Why was I not urged by you here previously?
There exists a great means by which this may be accomplished.
"This mountain named Ṛṣabha is upon the breast of the ocean;
having rested and eaten here, O Gālava, we shall return.
Nārada said:

Then, having alighted upon the horns of the bull, the twice-born bird and Gālava beheld there the Brahmin woman Śāṇḍilī, who was endowed with ascetic power. Suparṇa saluted her, and Gālava paid her due honor.
Addressed with that welcome, the two sat down upon a seat. She quickly prepared a meal, strengthened by sacrificial mantras;
having eaten it, both were so overcome by the food that they fell asleep on the ground.
Awakening after a moment, Suparṇa, desiring to depart,
beheld that ascetic woman living a life of celibacy, beautiful in all her limbs; indeed,
his mind was set upon seizing her, for she was like the goddess Śrī herself in person due to her beauty.

Then the bird saw himself with his body and limbs fallen away; though still possessed of a mouth and feet, that bird had become like a mere lump of flesh. Seeing him in such a state, Gālava was despondent and questioned him.
"What is this fruit born of your arrival here that you have obtained?
How long will our stay be here?
What indeed was meditated upon in your mind—that inauspicious thing which defiles the Dharma?"
"For this transgression of yours will not be a small matter.
Then Suparṇa said to the brahmin who was deep in thought, "O twice-born one,
I shall indeed carry this perfected woman from here to where Prajāpati resides."
"Where the god Mahādeva is, where the eternal Viṣṇu is,
where Dharma and Sacrifice are— there let this woman dwell.
Thus do I, bowing down with the desire to do what is pleasing, entreat you, O Blessed One.
"Indeed, this name was meditated upon by me while grieving in my mind;
thus, out of great respect for you, I have done what was unintended here. Whether it be well-done or ill-done, you ought to forgive me because of your magnanimity."
Then, being pleased, she said to those two—the lord of birds and the bull among the twice-born:
"Do not fear, O Suparṇa; you are Suparṇa, so cast off your agitation.
I have been reviled by you, my child, and I do not tolerate such censure."
That evildoer who would revile me would fall away from all the worlds; for by me,
who am free from all inferior marks and thus beyond reproach,
and who maintains right conduct, this supreme perfection has been attained.
Through proper conduct one obtains righteousness; through proper conduct one obtains wealth;
through proper conduct one attains prosperity; proper conduct destroys inauspicious marks.
Therefore, O long-lived Lord of Birds, depart from here as you please.
"Nor indeed should those women ever be censured, even if they are blameworthy,
if you desire to obtain both yourself and me through your own efforts;
for at that very moment, O eater of serpents, your body shall perish."
Indeed, through the grace of that very God of gods, by meditating upon him,
you shall once again become whole with all your limbs;
you shall become as before, endowed with strength and heroism.
Then his two wings became more powerful than before;
permitted by Śāṇḍilī, he returned the way he had come,
yet he did not find horses of such a kind.
Then Viśvāmitra, the best among speakers, seeing Galava standing on the road in the presence of Vainateya,
said: "O twice-born one, that object which was promised by you to me of your own accord— "
"The time for my liberation is as you, sir, may deem it; I shall wait for that further period of time accordingly. O Brahmin, let that path by which complete success is attained be heard."
Then Suparṇa spoke to the dejected Gālava, who was deeply distressed:
"Indeed, what Viśvāmitra has just said is now evident before my very eyes. Therefore come, O best of the twice-born; let us deliberate together, Gālava."
"Without having given it to the teacher, you will not be able to attain the full goal.
Nārada said:
"Then Suparṇa, the best of birds, spoke to the dejected Gālava:"
Because it was fashioned by Vahni upon the earth and likewise increased by Vāyu,
and because everything is golden, it is therefore called *hiraṇya*. For this reason, it is called *dhana*, since it bestows (*dhatte*) and sustains (*dhārayate*) this world.
This wealth remains eternal throughout the three worlds,
always present under the two Proṣṭhapadas, as well as under Śukra and the Lord of Wealth (Dhanapati).
Śukra takes away from men the wealth acquired through their own mental efforts.
It is guarded by Aja-Ekapād, Ahirbudhnya, and the Giver of Wealth (Dhanada).
Thus, O bull among the twice-born, that which is not to be obtained cannot be acquired;
and without wealth, there is no way for you to obtain the horses.
In this matter, request some king born of a lineage of royal seers for our sake— one who,
without oppressing his citizens, might fulfill our purpose. For there is a certain king born in the Lunar dynasty who is my friend.
"Let us go to him; for on this earth there is one who possesses such power:
a royal sage named Yayāti, the son of Nahuṣa, whose valor is truth.
When addressed by me and personally entreated by you, he will surely grant it."
His wealth was as vast as that of Kubera, the lord of riches;
thus, being wise, he purified his wealth through giving alone.
While they were thus conversing and reflecting upon what was appropriate, [the time passed].
When they arrived before King Yayāti at Pratiṣṭhāna,
the son of Vinatā accepted the hospitality, including the guest-offering (*argha*) and excellent food; and when questioned regarding the reason for his visit, he spoke.
"O son of Nahuṣa, this friend of mine, Gālava, is a treasury of asceticism;
he was the disciple of Viśvāmitra for tens of thousands of years, O King.
Now, having been permitted by him, this twice-born man desires to do you a favor."
The Blessed One said to him, "What heavy fee shall I give you?
When he had been told this repeatedly, he became somewhat angry;
yet, though knowing his own wealth, he spoke lightly, saying, "Give this."
"Give me eight hundred horses of pure birth, white as the moon, each with one ear black,
if you consider this, O Gālava, to be the price for the teacher's fee."
Thus spoke Viśvāmitra, whose wealth is asceticism, filled with wrath. This bull among the twice-born, tormented by great sorrow and unable to retaliate, has come to you for refuge.
Having accepted this alms from you, O tiger among men, he will be freed from his distress;
and having performed his final rites for his guru, he will practice great austerity.
Through a portion of that ascetic merit, he will also unite you with it.

He will fill you, who are already full through your own royal-sage asceticism. O lord of men, O ruler of the earth, as many hairs as there are on the horse, so many worlds do the givers of horses attain.
"You are a worthy recipient for this gift;
may it be received by you just as milk is held within a conch shell—unattached and pure.
Nārada said:
Thus addressed by Suparṇa with these most excellent and truthful words,
the king reflected attentively and, having deliberated again and again, resolved upon his course.
He was a performer of thousands of sacrifices, a donor, a lord of charity, and a sovereign.

Having seen his dear friend Tārkṣya and Gālava, the bull among the twice-born, as well as the illustration of ascetic power and the praiseworthy alms that had been described, Yayāti, the lord of Vatsakāśī, spoke these words:
Having bypassed other kings born of the Solar dynasty,
these two have arrived in my presence after considering their own wisdom;
today my birth has become fruitful, and today my lineage has been delivered.
"O sinless Tārkṣya, this region has today been delivered by you.
But I wish to say something, my friend: as you knew me before, I am no longer so wealthy, for my wealth, my friend, has been exhausted."
"O bird, I am not able to make your arrival fruitless;
nor do I dare to render the hope of this brahmin-sage in vain.
Therefore, I shall give that which will accomplish this task."
For one who approaches with hope and turns away disappointed indeed consumes his own lineage.
O son of Vinatā, nothing more sinful than this is spoken of in the world: either the destruction of hope or the words, "There is no gift."
For a man who has failed in his purpose and remains frustrated, yet is regarded as successful,
brings ruin upon his sons and grandsons by failing to fulfill the requests of those in need;
therefore, my daughter shall be the establisher of four lineages.
O Gālava, this daughter of Tārkṣya named Mādhavī proclaims all dharmas;
she resembles the daughters of the gods and promotes the practice of all dharmas for gods,
humans, and asuras alike.
"O fool, my daughter has been longed for by you because of her beauty; let her be accepted.
Kings will surely give even their kingdoms as her bride-price, so what need be said of eight hundred horses with black ears?"
"May you accept this daughter of mine, Mādhavī.
O Lord, may I indeed have a grandson; this is my boon.
Having heard those words of his, that brahmin of rigid vows—
Having accepted the maiden, Gālava, together with the bird,
said, "We shall see you again," and set out with the girl; meanwhile,
the bird thought, "This gateway to horses has been found."
Having spoken thus and taken leave of Gālava, he departed for his own abode.
When the king of birds had gone, Gālava, accompanied by the maiden,
went about considering what would be appropriate as the bride-price for kings.
He went in his mind to Haryaśva, the best of kings,
the highly heroic Ikṣvāku, who resided in Ayodhyā accompanied by a fourfold army,
endowed with treasuries, grain, and strength, beloved by his citizens and dear to the twice-born.
To him who was desiring offspring, practicing tranquility, and performing supreme austerity,
that brahmin Gālava approached Haryaśva and said:
"O Indra among kings, this daughter of mine shall increase your lineage through her progeny."
"O Haryaśva, let this woman be accepted as your wife for a bride-price (śulka).
I shall declare the price to you; having heard it, let it be considered.
Nārada said:
Then King Haryaśva, the best of monarchs, having reflected in many ways for the sake of progeny, sighed long and hot and spoke:
"She who is elevated in the six places that should be elevated, and slender in the seven places that should be slender..."
She is deep in the three deep places and red in the five [places]. The two hips, the forehead, the two armpits, and the nose—these six are prominent.
Her finger joints, hair of the head, body hair, nails, and skin are fine.
The voice, the physical constitution, and the navel—these three are declared to be deep. The palms of the hands, the soles of the feet, the corners of the eyes, the mouth, and the nails are red.
Five parts are long, four are short, five are subtle, and six are elevated.
That which has seven red parts, three broad parts, and three deep parts is praised; likewise,
the five long parts— the jaw, the eyes,
the arms, the thighs, and the nose— bestow happiness.
The four short parts on the back of the penis,
the neck, and the shanks are conducive to well-being; likewise, the five subtle things— the teeth, the finger-joints, and the hair— are beneficial.
The skin and the fingernails do not suffer pain in those who are afflicted;
furthermore, the chest, the collarbones, the navel, the nose, the mouth, and the region between the shoulders— these are the six prominences.
The corners of the eyes, the soles of the feet, the palms of the hands, the palate, the lower lip, and the tongue are red; indeed, such nails bring all happiness.
He belongs to the world of many gods and asuras, and he has seen many gandharvas.

"Endowed with many auspicious marks and capable of bearing many offspring, she is able to give birth to a son who will be a universal monarch (*cakravartin*). O best of the twice-born, speak the bride-price (*śulka*), having considered my wealth."
Gālava said:
"Give me eight hundred horses, each with one ear black, as bright as the moon, well-bred, and handsome in form."
"Then this auspicious, large-eyed woman shall become the mother of your sons, as the fire-drill is the source of sacrificial fires. Nārada said:
Having heard these words, King Haryaśva, deluded by desire,
spoke dejectedly to Gālava, the best of sages:
"I have two hundred horses of the kind you require at my disposal."
"Hundreds of other horses are to be sought, for my steeds range far and wide. Therefore, O Gālava, I shall indeed procreate but a single offspring;
may you fulfill this desire and grant me this boon."
Having heard this, the maiden spoke these words to Gālava:
"A certain boon was granted to me by a certain knower of Brahman:
'At the end of each birth, you shall become a maiden once again.'"
Therefore, having accepted these excellent horses, give me to the king;
for from the four kings, you will indeed have eight hundred sons,
and likewise, I shall have four sons.
"O best of the twice-born, let my destruction be carried out for the sake of my guru; such is my resolve, O brahmin, or do as you deem fit. Thus addressed by the maiden, the sage Gālava then—
He spoke these words to Haryaśva, the protector of the earth:
"O best of men, O Haryaśva, let this maiden be accepted;
for one-fourth of the bride-price, procreate a single son."
Having accepted that maiden and having greeted Gālava with joy,
he obtained at the proper time and place his desired son,
named Vasumanas, who was more wealthy than the Vasus themselves.
That lord of men became like a Vasu and a bestower of wealth.
Then, in due time, the wise Gālava returned and,
approaching with a joyful mind, spoke to Haryaśva.
"O King, this son born to you is like the rising sun.
O best of men, it is time for me to go to another king for alms.
Having remained steadfast in his word and steadfast in his manliness, Haryaśva [departed].
Because horses are so difficult to obtain, he gave Mādhavī back once more.
And Mādhavī, having again abandoned her radiant royal splendor,
became a maiden at will and followed behind Gālava.
"Let the horses remain with you for now," said the twice-born one;
he then departed with the maiden toward Divodāsa, the lord of subjects.
Gālava said:
"The protector of the earth, the lord and sovereign of the Kāśīs, possessed of great heroism—
the king of men known as Divodāsa, the son of Bhīmasena—
let us go there, O blessed lady; come slowly and do not grieve."
"He was righteous, devoted to self-restraint, and truthful, O lord of men.
Nārada said:
"Having approached him, that sage was honored by him in accordance with propriety."
Gālava urged that king toward the purpose of procreation.
Divodāsa said:
"O twice-born one, I have heard this before; why speak at such length?"

"O best of the twice-born, having heard this, this matter is indeed long desired by me. And it is highly esteemed by me that you have come to me in this way, bypassing other lords of men; and this will undoubtedly come to pass."
"O Gālava, that same wealth belongs to us as well, even for our horses;
I too shall beget but one son upon her, a king.
Nārada said:
Having said, "So be it," the best of the twice-born gave the maiden to the lord of the earth.
And the king accepted the maiden according to the prescribed rites. That royal sage took his pleasure with Prabhāvatī, just as the sun does.
As Vahni is to Svāhā, as that Vāsava is to Śacī,
as Candra is to Rohiṇī, as Yama is to Dhūmorṇā,
as Varuṇa is to Gaurī, and as the Lord of Wealth is to Ṛddhi;
Just as Nārāyaṇa is with Lakṣmī, as the ocean is with the Ganges,
as Rudra is with Rudrāṇī, and as the Grandfather is with Vedyā;
and as Vasiṣṭha, the son of Vasiṣṭha, was with Adṛśyantī and Akṣamālā.
As Cyavana begat [a son] upon Sukanyā, as Pulastya [begat one] upon Saṃdhyā,
as Agastya [begat one] upon the princess of Vidarbha, as Satyavat [begat one] upon Sāvitrī,
as Bhṛgu [begat one] upon Pulomā, and as Kaśyapa [begat one] upon Aditi.
Himavat was born of Menā, and Parāśara of Gandhavatī;
as Arcīka was born of Reṇukā and Kauśika of Haimavatī,
so Maudgalya was born of Candrasenā, and Kāśyapa of Aditi.
As Bṛhaspati was born of Tārā and Śukra of Śataparvā;
as the lord of the earth was born of Bhūmi and Purūravas of Urvaśī; as Ṛcīka was born of Satyavatī and Manu of Sarasvatī.
Duḥṣanta begot Dhṛti and eternal Dharma upon Śakuntalā; Nala begot [Indrasena] upon Damayantī; and Nārada begot [Senajit] upon Satyavatī.
Jaratkāru begot [Āstīka] upon Jaratkāru, and Pulastya begot [Viśravas] upon the western [wife].
As Urṇāyu was born of Menakā, and Tumburu of Rambhā;
as Vāsuki was born of Śataśīrṣā, and Dhanañjaya of Kumārī;
as Rāma was born of Vaidehī, and Janārdana of Rukmiṇī.
Pulastya was born of Bharadvājī Vṛtti, as was the eternal Dharma. While King Divodāsa was thus enjoying himself,
Mādhavī gave birth to a single son, Pratardana.
Then, when the appointed time had arrived, the venerable Gālava came to Divodāsa and spoke these words:
"May your lordship restore the maiden to me; let the horses remain."

"O Lord of the Earth, I shall go elsewhere for the sake of the bride-price. Then the righteous Divodāsa, the lord of the earth, remaining firm in truth, delivered that maiden to Gālava according to his agreement.
Nārada said:
In that very manner, having renounced her prosperity and become a maiden once more,
the illustrious Mādhavī, true to her promise, followed the brahmin Gālava.
Gālava, reflecting thus with his mind intent on his own task,
went to the city of Bhoja to see the king of the Auśīnaras. Having approached that monarch of true prowess, he spoke to him.

"This maiden will give birth to two sons for you who will become kings. O King, having fathered two sons who resemble the moon and the sun, you shall have attained your purpose both in this world and after death."

"O knower of all dharmas, as the price for these horses, which possess the luster of the moon and have one ear black, four hundred must be given to me. This undertaking is for the sake of my preceptor; I have no need for the horses myself."
"If it is possible, O Great King, let it be done without hesitation. You are childless, O royal seer; beget two sons, O ruler of the earth!
By means of the raft of a son, deliver your ancestors and yourself as well."
"O royal sage, he who enjoys the fruit of having a son is not cast down from heaven,
nor does he go to the terrible hell where those childless go.
Having heard this and various other things spoken by Gālava, [the king]—
Uśīnara, the lord of men, gave this reply to him:
"I have heard your words, O Gālava, just as you speak them.
But destiny is powerful, O Brahmin, for my mind is already inclined elsewhere."
"O best of the twice-born, I have two hundred such horses as these;
many thousands of others also roam for me.
Yet, O Gālava, I too shall beget but one son upon her."
"O twice-born one, I shall follow the path my son has taken, even at the cost of my own life;
O best of the twice-born, I would do this for you even with my very wealth. Indeed, my purpose is for the sake of the citizens and the people of the countryside, not for my own enjoyment."
"For a king who, out of desire, bestows another's wealth, O righteous-souled one, is joined neither with dharma nor with fame.
Therefore, I shall accept it; may you give her to me."
"For the sake of having an only son, [I seek] a maiden who resembles a daughter of the gods.
To King Uśīnara, the lord of men, who had thus spoken many auspicious words, Gālava, the best of the twice-born, paid his respects in return.
Having caused Uśīnara to accept [the maiden], Gālava departed for the forest.
Having obtained her, he took his delight in her, like one who has performed meritorious deeds enjoying sovereign splendor.
And he sported in the caves of the mountains and by the waterfalls of the rivers.
In various gardens, in forests and groves,
in delightful mansions and on the rooftops of palaces,
in windows and aerial chariots, as well as in inner chambers.
Then, in due time, a son was born to him, radiant as the morning sun;
he was widely renowned by the name Śibi, that best of kings.
Having attended upon him and having received [his leave], the brahmin Gālava—
Having set out for Kanyā, O King, he saw the son of Vinatā.
Nārada said:
Then Vainateya, laughing, spoke these words to Gālava:
"By good fortune, O twice-born one, I see you here having accomplished your purpose.
But Gālava, having heard these words spoken by the son of Vinatā,
explained that only a fourth part of his task remained indeed to be done.
Then Suparṇa, the best of those who fly, said to Gālava:
"You must not exert yourself further; this will not be accomplished by you.
For long ago, in Kanyakubja, the daughter of Gādhi, Satyavatī..."
Ṛcīka requested a maiden as a wife from him, and was thus addressed by him:
"O venerable Galava, let a thousand horses, radiant as the moon and each with one black ear, be given to me."
Ṛcīka, having said "So be it," went to the abode of Varuṇa;
having obtained the horses at Aśvatīrtha, he gave them indeed to the king. Having performed the Puṇḍarīka sacrifice, those [horses] were given by the king to the twice-born.
Having purchased two hundred of them from each of those [merchants], they were then obtained by the kings,
O best of the twice-born; furthermore, four hundred others that were being transported across the river were seized by the Vitastā.
"O Gālava, it is thus impossible to ever obtain that which cannot be obtained. Therefore,
O virtuous soul, offer this [maiden] to Viśvāmitra along with these two hundred horses, together with six hundred more."
"Then you shall be free from delusion and have accomplished your purpose, O bull among the twice-born.
Having said "So be it" to him, Gālava, together with Suparṇa,
took the horses and the maiden and approached Viśvāmitra.
Gālava said:
"Of these horses whose desired purpose is fulfilled, there are indeed six hundred;
let this maiden be accepted by you for two hundred of them."
"In this [queen], three righteous sons have indeed been born by royal seers;
may you also, O best of men, beget one more,
so that your number of horses may thus become a full eight hundred."
"Having indeed become free from my debt to you, I shall perform ascetic penance as I please.
Nārada said:
"But Viśvāmitra, having seen Gālava together with the bird..."
And he spoke these words to that maiden of beautiful limbs:
"O Gālava, why was she not given to me previously?
My four sons would have been the perpetuators of my lineage."
"I accept your daughter for the sake of obtaining a single son;
let the horses, having reached my hermitage, remain there entirely mine.
Then, the immensely radiant Viśvāmitra took his pleasure with her.
She gave birth to a son, Aṣṭaka, the son of Mādhavī.
As soon as that son was born, the immensely radiant Viśvāmitra endowed him with wealth and duties,
and likewise equipped him with those horses.
Then Aṣṭaka departed for his city, which shone like the city of Soma;
and Kauśika, having bestowed the maiden upon his disciple, also went to the forest. Gālava likewise, having bestowed the sacrificial fee upon Suparṇa, [departed].
With a mind full of favor, he spoke these words to the maiden:
"A son shall be born to you who is a lord of charity, and another who is a hero;
yet another shall be devoted to truth and righteousness, and yet another shall likewise be a performer of sacrifices."

"Come then, O lady of beautiful hips; your father has been delivered by your sons, as have the four kings and I too, O slender-waisted one. Then Gālava, having given leave to Suparṇa, the devourer of serpents, [departed].
Gālava quickly departed for Yayāti, the son of Nahuṣa;
having returned that maiden to her father, he indeed went forth to the forest.
Nārada said:
But that king, desiring once more to hold her *svayaṃvara*,
approached the hermitage at the confluence of the Gaṅgā and Yamunā;
having placed the daughter of Madhu upon his chariot, she was adorned with a garland of flowers.
Pūru and Yadu pursued their sister into the hermitage;
there occurred a gathering of nāgas, yakṣas, and humans, as well as of winged creatures, beasts, and birds that dwell upon the mountains, in the trees, and in the forests.
The forest was crowded with the lords of various regions and men, and it was surrounded on all sides by sages who were like Brahmā; yet,
as those suitors were being pointed out, that woman of excellent complexion [remained indifferent].
Having bypassed all those suitors, she chose the forest as her boon. Descending from the chariot and paying homage to her kinsmen, the maiden,
daughter of Yayāti, approached the sacred forest and practiced austerities.
By means of various fasts, initiations, and likewise observances,
she made herself light and became a wanderer among the deer;
her feet were soft and green, resembling sprouts of beryl.
She grazed upon the finest young grasses, both bitter and sweet,
and drank the excellent waters of sacred streams— cool, pure, and delicious.
In the forests where the lions, the kings of beasts, had departed,
and in the dense thickets now empty because they were freed from forest fires,
she wandered with the deer like a wild doe roaming the woods.
Restrained by her vow of celibacy, she practiced the extensive Dharma;
Yayāti as well, following the conduct of former kings,
lived for many thousands of years until he was joined with the law of time.
Pūru and Yadu were two lineages that flourished, O best of men; through them, the son of Nahuṣa, King Yayāti, established himself in this world and the next,
and now dwells gloriously in heaven.
The powerful king, equal to a great seer, enjoyed the foremost fruits of heaven; after a time spanning many thousands of years, rich in virtues, had passed,
while the illustrious royal seers and great seers were seated together.

Yayāti, his understanding clouded and his mind possessed by pride, treated all men, as well as the gods and the hosts of sages, with contempt. Then the god Śakra, the slayer of Bala, recognized him for what he was.
And all those royal sages exclaimed, "Fie! Fie!
Upon seeing the son of Nahuṣa, a reflection arose in them:
"Who indeed is this, whose king is he, and how has he come to heaven?"
"By what deed was he perfected? Where did he accumulate his ascetic merit?
How is he known to be in heaven, or by whom is he recognized? Thus did those kings dwelling in heaven reflect.
Having seen him, the hundreds of guardians of the celestial chariots and protectors of the gates of heaven, as well as the attendants at the seats, questioned one another regarding King Yayāti;
when questioned, they replied, "We do not know him."
For all of them, their knowledge being obscured, did not recognize that king.
Then, in an instant, the king became deprived of his splendor.
Nārada said:
Then, shaken from his place and fallen from his seat,
his mind trembling and assailed by the fire of grief, his garlands withered, his consciousness failing, and his crown and armlets fallen away—
Reeling with all his limbs collapsing, his ornaments and garments fallen away,
he was sometimes visible and sometimes invisible as he looked at them again and again; empty-minded and empty himself, he was about to fall to the surface of the earth.
"What impure thought, defiling to the Dharma, have I meditated upon in my mind, by which I have been moved from this place? Thus the king reflected.
Meanwhile, those kings, as well as the Siddhas and Apsarases, remained right there.
They beheld Yayāti fallen and without support.
Then, O King, a certain person arrived— the one who casts down those whose merit is exhausted—
and spoke to Yayāti by the command of the King of the Gods:
"Excessively intoxicated with pride, you hold no one in contempt; fallen from heaven through your arrogance, O son of a king, you do not even realize it—go, fall! he said to him.
Having uttered the words "May I fall among the virtuous" three times, the son of Nahuṣa,
the best among those who possess a goal, reflected on his destination as he was about to fall.
At that very moment, however, in the Naimiṣa forest, [he saw] the bulls among kings...
The king saw four [seated] there, and he fell into their midst:
Pratardana, Vasumanas, Śibi Auśīnara, and Aṣṭaka;
they were gratifying the Lord of the Gods with the Vājapeya sacrifice.
Smelling the smoke arising from their sacrifice as it reached the gateway to heaven, Yayāti descended toward the earth;
for the king perceived a river composed of smoke connecting the ground with the celestial realm.
Like one holding onto the Ganges as it flows, that lord of the earth, the king,
fell into the midst of his four illustrious and foremost brothers-in-law,
who were like the guardians of the world.
In the midst of the four sacrificial rites, amidst the great fires of that lion among kings,
the royal seer Yayāti fell as his merit was exhausted.
All the princes called him the very embodiment of splendor.
"Who are you, or whose kinsman are you? To what country or city do you belong?
Are you a yakṣa, or perhaps a deva, a gandharva, or even a rākṣasa? For you do not have the form of a human; what is the purpose you desire?"
Yayāti said:
"I am the royal sage Yayāti; my merit exhausted, I have fallen from heaven. Thinking, 'May I fall among the virtuous,' I have therefore descended here among you."
The kings said:
"O bull among men, let this which you desire be true for you;
may the fruit of our sacrifices and our merit be accepted."
Yayāti said:
"I am not a Brahmin whose wealth consists of gifts, for I am indeed a Kṣatriya;
nor is my mind inclined toward destroying the merit of others."
Nārada said:
At that very time, having seen Mādhavī who had arrived there in the course of her life as a deer-hunter, those kings saluted her and spoke as follows.
"What is the purpose of your coming? What command of yours shall we carry out?
For we are all your sons, O lady rich in asceticism, and must obey your orders.
Hearing those words of theirs, Mādhavī was filled with supreme joy.
She approached her father Yayāti and paid him homage. Seeing her sons bowing with their heads to the ground, the female ascetic spoke these words:
"O Indra among kings, these are your grandsons, my sons; they are not strangers to you."
"These will deliver you; this was ordained of old.
O King, I am your daughter, Mādhavī, who lived as a forest-dweller. I too have accumulated merit through dharma; therefore, please accept half of it."
"O King, because all men share in the fruit of offspring,
they therefore desire daughters' sons, just as you do, O lord of the earth.
Then all those kings bowed their heads to the mother.
Having saluted and paid homage to their maternal grandfather, the kings then spoke,
filling the earth with loud, incomparable, and affectionate voices,
as they sought to rescue their maternal grandfather who had fallen from heaven.
Then Gālava, having approached him, also said to the king:
"By means of an eighth part of my ascetic merit, may you ascend to heaven.
Nārada said:
Then, as soon as he was recognized by those virtuous ones, that bull among men,
the king, ascended [the chariot] without even touching the surface of the earth;
Yayāti, possessing a divine form, became free from all affliction.
Nārada said:
The lord of men returned to that place, the world of the gods;
without having fully pervaded that divine abode, he became free from his feverish distress.
Wearing celestial garlands and garments, adorned with divine ornaments,
and endowed with the quality of celestial fragrance, he did not touch the earth with his feet.
Then Vasumān first spoke these words aloud:
Renowned in the world as a lord of generosity, he then addressed the king:
"Whatever I have obtained in this world that is beyond reproach among all social classes, even that I shall give; may your majesty be united with it."
"May you be endowed with whatever fruit belongs to the practice of generosity, whatever fruit belongs to the practice of forbearance,
and whatever fruit belongs to my own act of bestowing [this gift].
Then Pratardana, that bull among Kṣatriyas, spoke these words:
Just as you have always delighted in dharma and have been constantly devoted to battle,
may you be endowed with that fame arising from the duty of a Kṣatriya which I have attained in this world,
as well as the fruit of the title "hero."
"By that truth that I always delight in the Dharma, go to heaven!
Thus spoke the wise Śibi Auśīnara in sweet words, [adding:
"Just as toward children, women, and those who are objects of amusement, so too [toward all beings]..."
"In battles, in falls, and likewise in calamities and misfortunes, never before have I spoken an untruth. By that truth, O King, ascend to the sky;
even as I [sacrifice] my life, my kingdom, my deeds, and my pleasures."
I would rather abandon my life than ever forsake the truth; by that truth, ascend into the sky!
Just as Dharma is pleased with my truth, and just as Pāvaka is pleased by my truth, and Śakra is pleased by my truth—by that truth, ascend into the sky!
Then the royal seer Aṣṭaka, the descendant of Kuśika and son of Mādhavī,
who was learned in dharma, spoke these words to him who had performed hundreds of sacrifices:
"O Lord, hundreds of Puṇḍarīka and Gosava sacrifices have been performed by me."
May you obtain the fruit of those sacrifices and Vājapeyas.
Neither my jewels, nor my wealth, nor other such possessions remain unused for sacrifices; by that truth, go to the sky.
"If I speak this truth, by that very truth, go!
For in whatever manner those grandsons of his addressed that lord of men,
in that same manner the king abandoned the earth and went to heaven."
Thus, all those kings together, by means of their meritorious deeds,
swiftly rescued Yayāti from his fall from heaven through their own dharma,
consisting of sacrifices and gifts, for they were indeed his grandsons.
"Born into four royal lineages and increasing their clans,
they cause their highly wise maternal grandfather to ascend to heaven.
The kings said:
"O King, we, who are endowed with the virtues of royal duty and possessed of all the qualities of righteousness, are your grandsons; ascend to heaven, O monarch.
Nārada said:
Having been established in heaven by virtuous kings who bestowed abundant sacrificial fees,
Yayāti, having given leave to his grandsons, ascended to the celestial realm;
and there he was showered with rain fragrant with various flowers.
Embraced by a meritorious wind of fragrant scent, having ascended to the immovable station won through the fruit of his grandson’s merit,
he blazed with supreme splendor, nourished by his own deeds.
He was celebrated with songs and dances by hosts of *gandharvas* and *apsarases*, welcomed with joy in heaven by the sounds of celestial drums,
and praised by various royal sages and *cāraṇas*.
Honored with the highest offerings and greeted by the gods,
he had attained the very fruit of heaven; then the Grandfather (Brahmā) spoke to him,
as if satisfying him with words, for his mind was tranquil and at peace.
O royal sage, you have built up the fourfold Dharma through worldly deeds;
therefore, this world of yours is imperishable, and your fame in heaven shall likewise be eternal.
Furthermore, today, by virtue of these well-performed actions here, [you have attained this].
The minds of all the inhabitants of heaven were shrouded in darkness, by which they did not recognize you; therefore, having failed to recognize you, you were cast down.
Yet, because of your very affection for your grandsons, you have been delivered and have come here.
"You have attained a station won by your own deeds—
a place that is immovable, eternal, meritorious, supreme, stable, and imperishable.
Yayāti said:
"O Blessed One, I have a certain doubt; you ought to sever it for me.
For I do not see anyone else worthy of being questioned, O Grandfather of the World. [This doubt has been nurtured] over the course of many thousands of years through the protection of my subjects."
"Through the floods of many sacrifices and gifts, a great fruit was earned by me.
How has it been exhausted in so short a time that I have been cast down?
O Blessed One, you know the eternal worlds that I have conquered."
"How indeed has all that of mine been utterly lost, O one of great splendor?
The Grandfather said:
"It was accumulated over the course of many thousands of years through the protection of your subjects."

O Indra among kings, the fruit that you had accumulated through the multitude of offerings and gifts at countless sacrifices has been exhausted by this very fault, because of which you have been cast down; for you were censured by the inhabitants of heaven due to your arrogance.
"O royal seer, this world does not become eternal through pride, nor through force, nor through violence, nor through deceit, nor through illusions. O King,
you must not hold in contempt those who are inferior, superior, or middling."
And regarding the royal seer Yayāti and his friends who desired prosperity:
indeed, for those consumed by pride, there is no equal anywhere. Those men who shall recount this account of his fall and his ascent—
"Even if they encounter difficulties, they will undoubtedly cross over them.
Nārada said:
"This fault was incurred by Yayāti in the past due to his pride."
O lord of the earth, because Gālava was so excessively persistent,
one must listen to those friends who desire one's welfare and seek one's prosperity. Indeed, one should not be obstinate, for obstinacy leads to ruin.
Therefore, O son of Gāndhārī, you too must abandon pride and anger. Make peace with the Pāṇḍavas, O hero; cast off your agitation, O King. May your majesty accept the truthful words of your friends.
"Having engaged in conflict with those capable [of victory], you will find yourself in a precarious position.
Vaiśampāyana said:
O best of kings, having been addressed thus by Nārada, Suyodhana—
He did not abide by that word; therefore, such was his end:
whatever he gives, O King, whatever he does, whatever austerity he practices, or whatever oblation he offers.
There is neither its destruction nor its diminution;
no other consumes it, for he alone is the agent.
This great narrative is considered unsurpassed.
Having observed those in the world who are deeply learned, free from anger and passion, and who have run in many directions,
the vision of the three aims (trivarga) pervades the earth.
"O King, this great and most meritorious account of Yayāti is such that by hearing it or causing others to hear it, men indeed go to heaven. Dhṛtarāṣṭra said:
"O Blessed One, it is exactly as you say, Nārada.
I too desire it to be so, O Blessed One, yet I am not its master.
Vaiśampāyana said:
Having spoken thus, O Bhārata, he then addressed Kṛṣṇa:
"O Keśava, you have told me that which leads to heaven, is conducive to the world, righteous, and just;
yet, my dear friend, I am not my own master, and what is being done is not pleasing to me."
"O Janārdana, my evil-minded sons will not heed me.
O mighty-armed Kṛṣṇa, O Supreme Person, strive to persuade my dull-witted Duryodhana, who transgresses the scriptures."
O mighty-armed Hṛṣīkeśa, he did not listen to the well-spoken words of Gāndhārī, nor of the wise Vidura,
nor of other well-wishing friends such as Bhīṣma and the rest.
O Janārdana, you yourself should instruct that evil-minded, cruel,
and senseless King Duryodhana of wicked soul; by doing so,
you would perform a very great service for your friends.
Then, turning back toward the impatient Duryodhana, Vārṣṇeya—
who knew the true essence of all dharma and artha— spoke these sweet words:
"O Duryodhana, best of the Kurus, listen to these words of mine."
O Bhārata, you are especially capable of this along with your followers;
O man of great wisdom, born into a noble family, it behooves you to do this rightly,
for you are endowed with learning and conduct and possessed of all virtues.
Those of base birth, evil nature, cruel, and shameless—
such as these would do this very thing, just as you think, my dear.
In this world, the conduct of the virtuous is observed to be joined with righteousness and purpose.
But for the wicked, O bull of the Bharatas, it is observed to be the opposite;
yet this contrary conduct is seen repeatedly in you. Furthermore, there is here a great and terrible consequence of unrighteousness that robs one of life.
O Bhārata, on many occasions you have brought disgrace upon yourself;
by avoiding that misfortune, O scorcher of foes, you will secure your own welfare, as well as that of your brothers, servants, and friends.
"You shall be liberated from this unrighteous and disgraceful act.
O tiger among men, O bull of the Bharatas, form an alliance with the Pāṇḍavas— those who are wise, heroic, highly energetic, self-possessed, and deeply learned."
That was indeed beneficial and pleasing to the wise Dhṛtarāṣṭra,
as well as to his grandfather Droṇa, the high-minded Vidura,
Kṛpa, Somadatta, and the wise Bāhlīka.
O lord of the people, O scorcher of foes, for Aśvatthāman, Vikarṇa, Saṃjaya, and especially for their kinsmen and friends,
as well as for the entire world, there would be peace and security, my dear.
"You are modest, born of noble lineage, learned, and compassionate. Remain, my dear son, under the instruction of your father and your mother, O bull among the Bharatas;
for they consider this to be the highest good, O Bhārata, that a father should instruct."
Everyone who has fallen into the greatest distress remembers the instruction of his father. My son, this meeting with the Pāṇḍavas is pleasing to your father;
O best of the Kurus, may it also be pleasing to you and your ministers. My son, let that be agreeable to you.
The mortal who, having heard the instruction of his friends, does not act upon it,
is burned at the end of its ripening, like one who has eaten the *kiṃpāka* fruit. But he who,
out of delusion, does not accept a word concerning the supreme good—
He who procrastinates and fails to achieve his purpose is later joined with remorse;
but he who, having heard of the supreme good, attains it as soon as it is reached,
casting aside his own opinions, prospers in happiness in this world.

He who, out of hostility, cannot endure the words of one who seeks his welfare, and instead listens to things that are contrary, falls under the power of his enemies. He who transgresses the counsel of the virtuous and follows the opinion of the wicked— [he is lost].
His friends soon begin to grieve for him who,
having abandoned his chief ministers, serves those of inferior character;
having fallen into terrible calamity, he finds no one to rescue him.

O Bhārata, he who associates with the wicked, whose conduct is vain, who never listens to his friends, who chooses strangers and hates his own kin— him the cow curses. You, O hero, having opposed those warriors, now seek protection from others.
O bull of the Bharatas,
who else on earth but you would hope for protection from others— passing over kinsmen who are great car-warriors equal to Śakra, yet are undisciplined, incapable, and foolish?
"O son of Kuntī, from birth onwards you have constantly humiliated them;
yet those Pāṇḍavas, being righteous-souled, have never been angry with you. O dear one, from their very birth, the Pāṇḍavas have been treated falsely by you."
O mighty-armed one, illustrious men have correctly followed this path in you;
O bull of the Bharatas, you too must likewise follow it toward your own principal kinsmen, and do not fall under the sway of anger.
O bull of the Bharatas, the undertakings of the wise are joined with the three goals of life;
when the three goals cannot all be attained, men pursue virtue and wealth.
But among those who are established in separate pursuits, the steadfast man follows virtue alone.
The middling person pursues wealth, while the fool pursues only sensual pleasure. He who, driven by greed, lets his senses run wild and utterly abandons Dharma,
perishes as he seeks to obtain both pleasure and wealth through improper means.
One who desires both pleasure and wealth should practice dharma from the very beginning;
for neither wealth nor pleasure ever departs from dharma.
O Lord of the People, they say that dharma itself is the means to achieve the three goals of life.

For one who desires [power] by that means grows quickly like a fire in dry grass. O bull of the Bharatas, you thus seek through improper means the great, blazing, and celebrated sovereignty over all kings, my son.

For he who behaves deceitfully toward those who act rightly, O King, hews away at his own self just as one cuts down a forest with an axe. An enemy must never be over-taxed, nor should anything ever be given to him.

For even those afflicted by suffering do not abandon their lives at any time. One should not thwart the resolve of that person whom one does not wish to see defeated; for the mind of the steadfast man who remains undaunted is fixed upon what is auspicious.
O Bhārata, one who has surrendered his very self should not cause harm even to another ordinary person in the three worlds,
let alone those bulls among the Pāṇḍavas;
for a man who has fallen under the sway of resentment perceives nothing at all.
For everything that is stretched out is eventually cut; behold the measure of things, O Bhārata!
My dear son, it is better for you to be united with the Pāṇḍavas;
for by being well-disposed toward them, you shall obtain all your desires.
O best of kings, while enjoying the earth conquered by the Pāṇḍavas,
you have cast the Pāṇḍavas behind you and hope for protection from others—
from Duḥśāsana, Durviṣaha, Karṇa, and Saubala as well.
O Bhārata, you desire prosperity by placing your sovereignty over these [sons of Pāṇḍu];
yet they are not sufficient for you in knowledge, nor likewise in dharma and artha,
nor are they insufficient in prowess against the Pāṇḍavas, O Bhārata.
"Indeed, all these kings together are not a match for you to even look upon the face of the enraged Bhīmasena in battle. O dear one, this entire army of kings is gathered here."
This Bhīṣma, as well as Droṇa, this Karṇa, and likewise Kṛpa;
Bhūriśravas, the son of Somadatta, Aśvatthāman, and Jayadratha—
all of these together are incapable of fighting against Dhanañjaya.
For Arjuna, when enraged, is invincible even by all the gods and asuras, let alone by humans or gandharvas; do not set your heart on battle.
Or rather, let some man be seen who can withstand the entire host of the Pārthiva army.
"If one could reach Arjuna in battle and return home in safety,
O bull of the Bharatas, what would be the use of this slaughter of men? Let that single man be sought out, by whose defeat all would be defeated for you."
Who among mortals could fight him who, at Khāṇḍavaprastha, conquered the gods along with the gandharvas, yakṣas, asuras, and pannagas? Likewise, a great wonder is heard of in the city of Virāṭa.
This is sufficient illustration for both one person and many:
that by whom Mahādeva Śiva was personally gratified in battle—
that invincible, unassailable, and unconquerable Jitṣṇu, the infallible one.
"You hope here in battle for the heroic and powerful Arjuna; but who would dare to challenge Pārtha when he has me as his second,
even if it were Purandara himself coming against him in person in combat?"
He who could lift up the earth with his two arms, burn these creatures in his wrath,
or cast down the gods from heaven— he alone might conquer Arjuna in battle.
Behold your sons, as well as your brothers, kinsmen, and relatives.
O best of the Bharatas, let these not perish on your account;
let there be a remnant of the Kauravas, and let this lineage not be destroyed. O lord of men, do not be called a destroyer of your kin, nor let your fame be lost.
The great car-warriors will install you alone in the position of crown prince,
and [they will establish] your father Dhṛtarāṣṭra, the lord of men, in the great kingdom. My dear son, do not disregard the royal fortune that is approaching and ready at hand.
By giving half [of the kingdom] to the sons of Pṛthā, you will attain great prosperity;
having made peace with the Pāṇḍavas and having heeded the words of your friends,
you will enjoy long-lasting blessings while being well-disposed toward your allies.
Vaiśampāyana said:
Then, O bull of the Bharatas, Bhīṣma the son of Śantanu, having heard the words of Keśava, spoke to the impatient Duryodhana.

"O dear one, you were addressed with these words by Kṛṣṇa, who desires the welfare of his friends: 'Reflect upon this, my son; do not fall under the sway of anger. O dear one, having failed to follow the counsel of the high-souled Keśava..."
"You shall never obtain what is better, nor happiness, nor prosperity.
O dear one, the mighty-armed Keśava has told you what is consistent with dharma and purpose;
follow that purpose, O King, and do not destroy your subjects."
Through your wickedness, while Dhṛtarāṣṭra is still alive, you will cause this blazing glory of the Bhārata lineage to fall among all the kings,
as well as yourself, along with your ministers, sons, cattle, and kinsmen.
By harboring evil thoughts toward Sahamitra, you will cause him to fall from life,
O best of the Bharatas, by transgressing the truthful and meaningful words of Keśava,
of your father, and of the wise Vidura.
"Do not, as a foolish man who destroys his family, go upon a wicked path;
do not bring grief to your aged father and mother.
Then Droṇa spoke these words there to Duryodhana:
"O dear one, Keśava has spoken words consistent with dharma and artha to you, who have fallen under the sway of indignation and are sighing again and again;
likewise has Bhīṣma, the son of Śantanu. Therefore, O lord of men, accept that advice."

"Wise, intelligent, self-controlled, desirous of your welfare, and deeply learned, they have both spoken words for your benefit; accept them, O scorcher of foes. O one of great wisdom, carry out what Kṛṣṇa and Bhīṣma have said."
"O scorcher of the foe, do not rely upon the words of those of feeble intellect who are inciting you; they will never accomplish your purpose,
for they will merely cast the enmity of their enemies around your neck in battle."
"Do not destroy all the Kurus, as well as your sons and brothers;
for know that where Vāsudeva and Arjuna are, that force is invincible. And this is the true opinion of our two friends, Kṛṣṇa and Bhīṣma."
"O dear one, O Bhārata, if you do not give [them] now, you will repent later.
Just as was said by the son of Jamadagni, Arjuna is indeed even greater than that;
for Kṛṣṇa, the son of Devakī, is difficult even for the gods to withstand."
"O bull among the Bharatas, what is the use of speaking further here of what is pleasant and dear to you?
All this has been told to you; do as you wish.
Indeed, O best of the Bharatas, I cannot bring myself to speak more to you."
In that interval between speeches, Vidura the Kṣattṛ also spoke these words,
looking toward the intolerant Duryodhana, the son of Dhṛtarāṣṭra:
"O Duryodhana, O bull among the Bharatas, I do not grieve for you."
But I grieve for these two elders, Gāndhārī and your father,
who will wander about helpless under the protection of you, their ill-wishing protector—
deprived of friends and ministers, like two birds with clipped wings.
"Having brought forth such a wicked man, a destroyer of his own lineage, those two will wander this earth as mendicants in grief.
Then King Dhṛtarāṣṭra addressed Duryodhana.
Seated together with his brothers and surrounded by kings, [Duryodhana was addressed:
"O Duryodhana, understand this which has been spoken by the high-souled Śauri:
accept it as exceedingly auspicious, conducive to prosperity and security, and imperishable."
"For with this companion, Kṛṣṇa of unwearied deeds,
we shall attain all our desired objectives among all the kings. Well-united with Keśava, go, my son, to Yudhiṣṭhira."
Perform the entire rite for well-being so that the Bharatas may remain free from harm. O dear one, go to the encounter by way of Vāsudeva as your ford;
I consider this to have arrived at the appointed time—do not let Duryodhana pass you by.
"If you reject Keśava, who is entreating you for peace and speaking for your sake, there shall be no escape from defeat for you. Vaiśampāyana said:
Having heard the words of Dhṛtarāṣṭra and having deliberated upon them, Bhīṣma and Droṇa spoke these words to Duryodhana, who was transgressing their commands:
"As long as the two Kṛṣṇas are unarmored, and as long as the Gāṇḍīva bow remains [inactive]..."
As long as Dhaumya does not offer the strength of our enemies into the sacrificial fire here,
and as long as the enraged Yudhiṣṭhira, that great archer restrained by his sense of honor, does not gaze upon your army, let this slaughter indeed cease.
As long as Pārtha is not seen stationed among his own ranks,
and as long as the great archer Bhīmasena does not range through the paths, gladdening the army, let this slaughter indeed cease.
"Let Bhīmasena, mace in hand, cease his conflict with the Pāṇḍavas only so long as he does not strike off the heads of the elephant-warriors in battle with his hero-slaying mace,
like the fruits of a great tree."
When they have ripened in due time, let this slaughter indeed cease:
Nakula, Sahadeva, Dhṛṣṭadyumna the son of Pṛṣata, Virāṭa, Śikhaṇḍin, and the son of Śiśupāla, all clad in armor.

As long as these men, skilled in weapons, do not enter like crocodiles into the great ocean while swiftly discharging their missiles, let this slaughter indeed cease; as long as sharpened arrows have not yet pierced the bodies of the kings.
As long as these do not enter, let this slaughter indeed cease;
as long as fierce vulture-feathered arrows do not fall upon the delicate bodies of the rulers of the earth, let this slaughter indeed cease.

Upon the chests of the warriors— smeared with sandalwood and agallochum and adorned with necklaces and golden coins— the great arrows of those skilled archers, who discharged iron shafts with great speed and long range, did not find their mark.
Let them be struck down by those who are easily distinguished; let this slaughter cease!
Let the elephant among kings, Yudhiṣṭhira, the King of Dharma, receive you with his two hands as you salute him with your head.
O bull of the Bharatas, Sudakṣiṇa placed his right arm— marked with the signs of a banner, a goad, and a flag— upon your shoulder for the sake of peace;
that arm was adorned with jewels and medicinal herbs, and its fingers were set with gems.
O bull of the Bharatas, let the mighty-armed Vṛkodara, whose shoulders are like the trunks of *śāla* trees, sit beside you as you are seated and stroke your back with his hand,
addressing you with gentle words for the sake of peace.
Saluted by those three— Arjuna and the twins— the king smelled their heads with affection and said, "O King,
having seen you united with your heroic brothers, the Pāṇḍavas."
"Let the lords of men shed tears born of joy;
let it be proclaimed throughout the royal capitals that all the prosperity of the rulers of the earth belongs [to you].
Enjoy the earth as a brother; be free from feverish anxiety."
Vaiśampāyana said:
Having heard those unpleasant words in the assembly of the Kurus, Duryodhana replied to the illustrious and mighty-armed Vāsudeva.
Having considered this, O Keśava, you ought to speak;
for you especially revile me alone,
O Madhusūdana, by speaking disparagingly of the sons of Pṛthā without cause.
"Why do you constantly reproach me, having considered the relative strengths and weaknesses?
You are the *kṣattṛ*, the king, the preceptor, and the grandfather; why do you all reproach me alone and not any other monarch?"
"I do not perceive any transgression on my part here;
yet all of you, together with the king, hate me. And I have committed no grievous offense, O subduer of enemies."
Reflecting upon it, O Keśava, I perceive even this most subtle point:
when the game of dice had been accepted by my beloved, the Pāṇḍavas were defeated by Śakuni and their kingdom was lost; what wrong did I do in that matter, O Madhusūdana?
Furthermore, O Madhusūdana, whatever wealth was lost there by the Pāṇḍavas,
that was then permitted to them by us alone;
nor was it our fault that they were defeated at dice.
O best of victors, why are the Pārthas—who are invincible—exiled to the forest?
By what reproach do they oppose their enemies?
O Kṛṣṇa, though the Pāṇḍavas are powerless, they rejoice as if against a foe.

"What have we done to them, or for what offense do the Pāṇḍavas, together with the Sṛñjayas, seek to slay the sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra? Yet neither by our fierce deeds nor by our words [have we provoked them]."
Terrified, we bow down here even out of fear of Śatakratu; yet,
O Kṛṣṇa, destroyer of enemies, I do not see anyone who, while abiding by the duty of a warrior,
would dare to conquer us in battle.
For Bhīṣma, Kṛpa, and Droṇa, along with their hosts, O Madhusūdana, cannot be conquered in battle even by the gods, much less by the Pāṇḍavas—
even if they were performing their own duty in the encounter, O Mādhava.
If we meet our death by the sword at the proper time, that will surely lead us to heaven.
O Janārdana, this is indeed the primary duty of us Kṣatriyas:
that we should lie down in battle upon a bed of arrows.

"O Mādhava, if we should attain the bed of heroes in battle without bowing down to our enemies, it shall not cause us grief. For what man born in a noble family, who conducts himself according to the dharma of the Kṣatriyas,"
Having thus considered one's livelihood in light of fear, one should not bow down to anyone here;
rather, one should exert oneself and never submit, for exertion alone is true manliness. Even if one should break at an improper joint, one must not bow down to anyone here.
Desiring their own welfare and seeking to grasp these words of Mātaṅga,
one such as I should bow to Dharma and to the Brahmins;
without thinking of anything else, one should act in this manner for as long as life lasts.

"This is the duty of Kṣatriyas, and this has always been my conviction. Furthermore, that share of the kingdom which was previously granted to me by my father cannot be recovered as long as I am alive, O Keśava."
O Janārdana, as long as King Dhṛtarāṣṭra remains alive,
we shall lay down our weapons and depend upon him for our livelihood, O Mādhava,
even if this kingdom— which was previously not to be given— has been bestowed upon me by another.
"O Janārdana, whether out of ignorance or even out of fear regarding me while I was still a child, O delighter of the Vṛṣṇis— that [kingdom] cannot be recovered by the Pāṇḍavas today,
O mighty-armed Keśava, as long as I am currently alive."
"For as much land as might be pierced by the point of a sharp needle, O Mādhava,
even that much of our earth must not be surrendered to the Pāṇḍavas.
Vaiśampāyana said:
Then, laughing, the descendant of Daśārha, his eyes clouded with anger, spoke these words to Duryodhana in the assembly of the Kurus:
"You shall obtain a hero’s bed; you will surely attain this desire."

"Be firm along with your ministers; a great conflict will take place. And as for what you think, O fool—that there is no transgression by me against the Pāṇḍavas—let all the lords of men understand that fully."
O Bhārata, while you were tormented by the splendor of the high-souled Pāṇḍavas,
this gambling match was ill-advised by you and Saubala.
And how, dear one, could your kinsmen— who are superior and esteemed by the virtuous— [have approved]?
Likewise, it is improper for one who walks the straight path to attend to that which is crooked through deceit.
O man of great wisdom, gambling with dice is the destroyer of the happiness of the virtuous; therein, dissensions and calamities arise among the wicked.
This terrible calamity, beginning with the game of dice, was brought about by you,
who acted without reflection alongside those of evil intent who disregard the conduct of the virtuous.
For who else would dare to wrong a wife belonging to his own kin in such a manner?
And having brought Draupadī—
who is of noble birth, endowed with virtuous character, dearer even than life itself,
and the queen of the sons of Pāṇḍu— into the assembly hall as you have described her, you have thus treated her with great humiliation.
All the Kurus know exactly what was said by Duḥśāsana in the assembly of the Kurus regarding the sons of Kuntī, those scorchers of foes, as they were departing into exile—
men who are always of upright conduct, free from greed, and ever-devoted to dharma.
What virtuous person would act so improperly toward their own kinsmen? Such cruel, ignoble, and harsh speech has been uttered many times by Karṇa, Duḥśāsana, and yourself.
Together with his mother, he exerted the greatest effort to burn those children at Vāraṇāvata, yet that plan of yours did not succeed;
for the Pāṇḍavas remained hidden there for a very long time.
Together with Mādrī at the house of a Brāhmaṇa in Ekacakrā,
the Pāṇḍavas were assailed by you with poison and serpent-bonds; though you strove with every means for their destruction, that effort of yours did not succeed.
"How can one who acts in such a manner, a doer of evil, deserve to remain in the kingdom? O defiler of your lineage, you shall be deprived of both your kingdom and your happiness,
for you have always harbored such thoughts and behaved with deceit toward the Pāṇḍavas."
"How is it that you have committed no offense against the high-souled Pāṇḍavas,
since you do not wish to give them their paternal share when they beg for it? O sinner, you shall be cast down and deprived of your sovereignty."
Having committed many unworthy deeds against the Pāṇḍavas like a cruel man, you, being of false conduct and ignoble nature,
now act with hostility toward your mother and father, Bhīṣma, Droṇa, and Vidura.
"O King, you have been told repeatedly, 'Be at peace,' yet you do not find peace.
For in peace there is a very great benefit for both you and Pārtha;
yet you do not take pleasure in it, O King—what else could this be but a deficiency of intellect?"
"O King, having disregarded the words of your well-wishers, you shall find no peace;
O ruler of the earth, an unrighteous and disgraceful act is being committed by you.
While the descendant of Daśārha was speaking thus to the intolerant Duryodhana, [the assembly broke up].
Duḥśāsana spoke these words in the assembly of the Kurus:
"O King, if you do not enter into peace with the Pāṇḍavas of your own accord,
the Kauravas will surely bind you and hand you over to the son of Kuntī."
"O bull among men, Bhīṣma, Droṇa, and your father will deliver you, Vaikartana, me, and these three others to the Pāṇḍavas.
