Having heard these words of his brother, Dhārtarāṣṭra Suyodhana—
Rising up in anger and hissing like a great serpent,
he set forth toward Vidura, Dhṛtarāṣṭra, the great king Bāhlika,
Kṛpa, Somadatta, Bhīṣma, Droṇa, and Janārdana.
Disregarding all these, that evil-minded and shameless man— unrefined, devoid of restraint, arrogant, and a despiser of those worthy of honor—
set out; and seeing that bull among men departing, his brothers [beheld him].
The kings and their ministers followed him from all sides as he rose up in the assembly hall, enraged and setting out with his brothers;
and beholding Duryodhana thus departing, Bhīṣma, the son of Śāntanu, spoke.

He who, having utterly abandoned both dharma and artha, approves of violent agitation, will soon be laughed at in his misfortune by his enemies. This wicked-souled son of Dhṛtarāṣṭra, a prince ignorant of proper means, [acts thus].
"Possessing false pride regarding the kingdom and following the sway of anger and greed,
O Janārdana, I consider this entire warrior class to have been ripened by Time;
for all these kings, together with their ministers, have followed [this path] out of delusion."
Then, having heard Bhīṣma’s words, the lotus-eyed and valiant descendant of Daśārha addressed all those headed by Bhīṣma and Droṇa:
"This is a great transgression on the part of all you elders of the Kuru lineage."
"O subduers of enemies, since you have forcibly constrained the dull-witted king from exercising his sovereignty, I believe that the time has come for action;
listen, O sinless ones, to how that which would bring about our welfare may be accomplished."

"O Bhāratas, that which I shall speak as beneficial is evident to you; it may be pleasing to you if it accords with your own inclinations. For the aged King of the Bhojas is indeed ill-behaved and lacks self-control."
Having seized the sovereignty from his father while he was still alive,
Kaṃsa, the son of Ugrasena, fell under the sway of wrath and was abandoned by his kinsmen;
yet, desiring the welfare of my relatives, I slew him in a great battle.
Furthermore, Āhuka was honored by us and our kinsmen,
and Ugrasena, the enhancer of the Bhoja royalty, was made king; for the sake of the family, all the Yādavas abandoned Kaṃsa alone.
"United, the Bhāratas, Andhakas, and Vṛṣṇis prosper in happiness.
Moreover, O King, the supreme lord Prajāpati spoke thus when the battle between the gods and asuras had been arrayed and their weapons were raised:
O Bhārata, when the worlds had become divided and were perishing,
the divine Lord, the creator and sustainer of the world, spoke:
"The Asuras, the Daityas, together with the Dānavas, shall be defeated."
The Ādityas, Vasus, and Rudras shall become the denizens of heaven;
and the gods, asuras, humans, gandharvas, uragas, and rākṣasas,
all well-prepared for battle, shall slay one another in this conflict.

"O scorcher of enemies, thinking, 'This entire existing world shall cease to exist in a mere moment through the destruction of the universe and all its inhabitants,' the Supreme Lord Prajāpati spoke thus regarding Dharma."

"Bind these Daityas and Dānavas and deliver them to Varuṇa. Having been thus addressed by the command of the Supreme Lord (Parameṣṭhin), Dharma then bound all those Daityas and Dānavas and handed them over to Varuṇa.
Having bound them with the nooses of Dharma and with his own nooses,
Varuṇa, the lord of the waters, remains vigilant in the ocean and constantly guards those Dānavas; likewise, he guards Duryodhana, Karṇa, and Śakuni, the son of Subala.
"Having bound Duḥśāsana as well, deliver him to the Pāṇḍavas.
One should abandon an individual for the sake of a family; one should abandon a family for the sake of a village;
one should abandon a village for the sake of a country; and one should abandon the whole earth for the sake of the self."
"O King, having bound Duryodhana, make peace with the Pāṇḍavas;
let not the Kṣatriyas perish on your account, O bull among Kṣatriyas.
Vaiśampāyana said:
Having heard Kṛṣṇa’s words, Dhṛtarāṣṭra, the lord of men,
spoke in haste to Vidura, who knows all duties:
"Go, dear son, to the highly wise and far-sighted Gāndhārī."
"Bring her here along with him; I shall persuade that evil-minded one. If she too can pacify that wicked-souled, evil-hearted man, we shall abide by the word of our friend Kṛṣṇa."
Even if she should point out the path to one overcome by greed—
a man of evil intellect with wicked companions— speaking words that are both capable and true:
"Will not a terrible and great calamity brought about by Duryodhana befall us?"
"May he bring peace for a long night, providing security and prosperity that is imperishable.
Having heard the king's words, Vidura, by the command of Dhṛtarāṣṭra, brought forth the far-sighted Gāndhārī.
Dhṛtarāṣṭra said:
"O Gāndhārī, this evil-souled son of yours, who transgresses your commands,
will lose both his sovereignty and his life through his greed for power."
"Like one who is undisciplined and lacks restraint, this fool has departed from the assembly with wicked and evil-minded men, having disregarded the words of his friends.
Vaiśampāyana said:
Having heard her husband’s words, the illustrious princess Gāndhārī, seeking the highest good, spoke these words: "Bring my son here quickly— he who is afflicted by his longing for the kingdom."
For sovereignty cannot be attained by one who is undisciplined and who destroys both dharma and artha; yet even so, this kingdom has been obtained by you in every way despite your lack of training.
Indeed, you alone are here highly censurable, O Dhṛtarāṣṭra, for your excessive fondness for your sons.
O King, he who, knowing his wickedness, follows after his wisdom,
is deceived by desire and anger and has fallen into delusion;
it is impossible for you now to turn him back by force.

Dhṛtarāṣṭra reaps the fruit [of his actions] for having bestowed the kingdom upon one who was foolish, childish, evil-minded, ill-aided, and greedy. For how could a high-minded man overlook dissension among his own kin?

"For when you are divided from your own kinsmen, your enemies will prevail over you. O Great King, since calamities can be overcome through conciliation or gifts, who would employ punishment against one's own people?"

By the command of Dhṛtarāṣṭra and at the word of his mother, the Kṣattṛ caused the impatient Duryodhana to enter the assembly hall once again. Desiring to obey his mother's words, he entered the assembly hall once more.
With eyes bloodshot from rage, sighing like a serpent,
Gāndhārī beheld her son who had entered and taken to a wrong path; reproaching him, she spoke these capable words.
"O Duryodhana, my dear son, listen to these words of mine,
which are for your benefit along with your followers, and which will result in happiness in the future.
O Duryodhana, best of the Bharatas, listen to what your father says to you."
"O Bhīṣma, Droṇa, Kṛpa, and Vidura, do this which is pleasing to your well-wishers!
By your making peace, honor will be rendered to Bhīṣma, to my father, to me,
and to our friends headed by Droṇa."
O highly wise one, O bull of the Bharatas, a kingdom cannot be obtained, protected, or even enjoyed through one's own mere desire;
for one whose senses are not under control cannot enjoy sovereignty for long.
But the wise man who has conquered his own self should protect the kingdom;
for desire and anger draw a person away from his goals. Having utterly defeated those two enemies, the king conquers the earth.

For this sovereignty over the world is indeed great; a kingdom is a coveted position that cannot be protected by those of evil nature. One who desires greatness should restrain the senses for the sake of wealth and dharma.
When the senses are restrained, the intellect grows like fire fed by fuel; for these [senses], when they cannot be controlled, are capable of destroying even one who is otherwise invincible,
just as unbroken horses that cannot be guided lead a bad charioteer astray on the road.
He who desires to conquer his ministers without first conquering himself— being one whose self and ministers are unconquered— he, lacking self-control, comes to ruin.
He who would first conquer his own self by means of self-discipline [is truly victorious].
Therefore, he does not seek to conquer his ministers or enemies in vain;
for prosperity attends one who has his senses under control, who has subdued his ministers, who wields punishment against the wayward, who acts with deliberation, and who is steadfast.
Like two large fish caught in a net with small mesh,
desire and anger, residing within the body, plunder one's wisdom;
for it is by these two that the gods who have gone to heaven closed the gateway to heaven.
Lust and anger increase for one who is afraid and remains unattached.
O King, he who knows how to properly conquer lust, anger, greed, hypocrisy, and pride, becomes the master of the earth.
A king who desires prosperity, righteousness, and the defeat of his enemies should be constantly intent on the restraint of his senses.
For he who, overcome by desire or anger, behaves falsely, [fails in these goals].
Whether among his own people or others, he will find no allies at all.
O dear one, united with the Pāṇḍavas— who are of one mind, possessed of great wisdom, heroic, and destroyers of their enemies— you shall enjoy the earth in happiness.
Just as Bhīṣma, the son of Śāntanu, and the great car-warrior Droṇa have both said,
my dear, that Kṛṣṇa and the Pāṇḍava are invincible— this is the truth.
Take refuge in the mighty-armed Kṛṣṇa, whose actions are effortless.
For Keśava, when pleased, brings happiness to both;
yet that man who does not abide by the instruction of his well-wishers who desire his welfare,
nor by that of the wise and learned, is a delighter of his enemies.

"O dear one, there is no auspiciousness in war, nor dharma or artha, much less happiness; nor is victory ever certain—do not set your heart on battle. For [this was said] by your father Bhīṣma, O highly wise one, and by Bāhlīka."
O subduer of enemies, fearing dissension, a share was given to the sons of Pāṇḍu;
today you behold the fruit of that gift,
as you enjoy the entire earth with its thorns removed by heroes.
"O subduer of enemies, grant to the sons of Pāṇḍu what is their due,
if you wish to enjoy half of the earth together with your ministers. Half of the earth is sufficient for your livelihood along with your ministers."

Abiding by the words of your friends, O Bhārata, you shall attain glory. For a conflict with the Pāṇḍavas— who are illustrious, self-possessed, wise, and masters of their senses— will, my dear, cause you to fall from great happiness.
"Restraint the anger of your friends and rule the kingdom as is fitting,
O bull of the Bharatas, after giving back their own share to the sons of Pāṇḍu.
Enough of this humiliation that has been inflicted for thirteen years."
"O one of great wisdom, pacify him who is inflamed by desire and anger;
he is not capable of [withstanding] the sons of Pṛthā, even though he desires your welfare— neither this son of a Sūta, firm in his wrath, nor your brother Duḥśāsana."
If Bhīṣma, Droṇa, Kṛpa, Karṇa, Bhīmasena, Dhanañjaya,
and the enraged Dhṛṣṭadyumna were to rise up, all living beings would surely cease to exist. O dear one, do not, overcome by indignation, cause the destruction of the Kurus.
Indeed, the entire earth has been touched by the prospect of slaughter for the sake of the Pāṇḍavas.
As for what you think, O fool— that Bhīṣma, Droṇa, Kṛpa,
and the others will fight with all their might— this is not possible today.
For sovereignty, joy, and a secure standing are equal for those who have conquered themselves—whether among the Pāṇḍavas or among you; yet, in that regard, dharma is even greater for you.
If these [Pāṇḍavas] should give up their lives out of fear of losing the king’s bounty, [then dharma prevails].
For they will not be able even to look upon King Yudhiṣṭhira. In this world, the attainment of wealth is never seen to come from greed for men;
therefore, enough of this greed, my dear son; be at peace, O bull of the Bharatas.
Vaiśampāyana said:
Disregarding those meaningful words spoken by his mother,
he set out once more in a fit of agitation toward the presence of those of undisciplined souls.
Then, having emerged from the assembly hall, the Kaurava consulted with the son of Subala, King Śakuni, who was skilled at dice.
Duḥśāsana spoke to Duryodhana, the son of Dhṛtarāṣṭra, and to Karṇa.
O King, if you do not come to an agreement with the Pāṇḍavas of your own free will,
then the sons of Pāṇḍu, having bound you, will hand you over to the son of Pāṇḍu, O Bhārata— namely,
yourself, Vaikartana, and me, these three, O bull of the Bharatas.

"O bull of the Bharatas, having heard those words of Duḥśāsana, Duryodhana, the son of Dhṛtarāṣṭra, sighed and spoke as if laughing: 'Bhīṣma, Droṇa, and even your father will deliver [the kingdom] to the Pāṇḍavas.'"
Having approached in private, he spoke again in secret counsel:
"This was the plan devised by Duryodhana, Karṇa, Śakuni the son of Subala,
and Duḥśāsana as the fourth."
"Before this Janārdana, acting with haste, seizes us along with King Dhṛtarāṣṭra and the son of Śaṃtanu,
let us ourselves forcibly capture Hṛṣīkeśa."

Having heard that the Vārṣṇeya has been seized by force—just as Indra seized the son of Virocana—the Pāṇḍavas will become despondent; they will lose their resolve like serpents whose fangs have been broken. They will be like tigers deprived of their claws. O tiger among men, having forcibly captured him, you shall be like Indra against the son of Virocana. Hearing that the descendant of Vṛṣṇi has been taken, the Pāṇḍavas will be heartbroken and will become devoid of energy, like snakes with shattered fangs.
For this mighty-armed one is the refuge and the armor for all of them;
when this bestower of boons, the bull among all the Sātvatas, is captured,
the Pāṇḍavas, along with the Somakas, will become devoid of effort.
"Therefore, while Dhṛtarāṣṭra cries out, let us bind this Keśava, who acts with haste, right here and fight our enemies.
[Let us thwart] the evil intention of those wicked and evil-minded men."
Satyaki, a wise man who understood gestures, quickly perceived his purpose;
having gone out for that reason, he stood with the son of Hridika and said to Kritavarman, "Quickly prepare the army!"
"Draw up your troops in battle array and stand at the door of the assembly hall clad in armor,
while I go and inform Kṛṣṇa of untiring deeds.
Having entered the assembly hall like a lion entering a mountain cave, the hero stood there.
He explained that intention to the high-souled Keśava,
and then he spoke likewise to Dhṛtarāṣṭra and Vidura;
smiling as it were, he declared this intention of theirs.
Devoid of righteousness and purpose, an action censured by the virtuous is what the dull-witted desire to perform here; yet it cannot be achieved in any way.
First, these foolish and evil-minded ones, having gathered together, will act with hostility.
Overcome by desire and passion, and following the sway of anger and greed,
these small-minded ones wish to seize this lotus-eyed one,
just as fools or the dull-witted would try to grasp a blazing fire with a cloth.
Having heard those words of Sātyaki, the far-sighted Vidura spoke to the mighty-armed Dhṛtarāṣṭra in the assembly of the Kurus:
"Just as Vārāṇasī was burnt, along with its horses, chariots, and elephants..."

But the bull among the people of Kāśī, along with his followers, has been slain by Kṛṣṇa. Likewise, having burned Nāgapura, the wielder of the conch, discus, and mace will himself become Kāleśvara and destroy the Kauravas.
For, though enraged, the slayer of Vṛtra did not prevail against him alone as he carried off the Pārijāta tree to bring joy to the Yadus;
having reached Nirmocana, he encountered six thousand powerful nooses.
Having approached the Kauravas, Vāsudeva carried them off;
having reached the gate of Saubha and shaken down the mountain with his mace,
Dyumatsena along with his ministers was struck down by Kṛṣṇa.

Because the Kurus still have a remnant [of merit], the lotus-eyed Acyuta, out of regard for dharma, continues to endure the evil deeds of those who are capable [of better], even though he is powerful. For if these men, together with the kings, desire Govinda—
This very day they shall all become guests of Yama;
just as the tips of blades of grass fall under the power of the mighty wind,
so shall all the Kauravas come under the power of the wielder of the discus.
"O King, O scorcher of foes, all your sons have reached the end of their time; they are now intent upon performing a deed that is both disgraceful and impossible— namely,
by seeking to overcome and forcibly subdue this lotus-eyed one."
Desiring to subdue this tiger among men— invincible and unassailable— they wish to seize him together, like the younger brother of Vāsava;
yet having encountered him, they shall cease to exist, like moths in a flame.
All these, though exerting themselves with reckless daring, are indeed not capable [of defeating him];
for Janārdana, if he so desires, could send them all— who are struggling against him—
to the abode of Yama, like an enraged lion dispatches deer.
"But this Kṛṣṇa would never, under any circumstances, perform a censurable act,
nor would Acyuta, the Supreme Person, ever deviate from dharma.
When Vidura had spoken thus, Keśava replied with these words:
Looking toward Dhṛtarāṣṭra while his friends were conversing among themselves, he said:
"O King, if these men, being enraged, should seize me by force,
or if I should seize them, O Ruler of the Earth, give your permission."
"I am indeed capable of restraining all these men when they are enraged;
yet, I would never under any circumstances perform a censurable or sinful act.
For, out of greed for the sake of the Pāṇḍavas, your sons will abandon their own self-interest."
If they desire this, then Yudhiṣṭhira,
together with his ministers and kinsmen,
has accomplished his purpose; indeed, he has achieved what was to be done this very day.
"O Bhārata, this very day I shall seize both these men and those who follow them,
and establish the Pāṇḍava king in the sovereignty. O King, this is my resolve, provided that such is his own determination."
Let the conchs resound together with the sounds of kettledrums and tabors;
let there be great auspiciousness for the sons of Pṛthā as they proceed without effort.
O King, if I were to seize [the wealth] from the sons of Pṛthā and give it to you, what wrong would that be?
"O Bhārata, O Great King, I would not have committed this censurable deed,
born of anger and evil intent, in your presence;
let it be as this Duryodhana wishes, O King."
"But I, O Bhārata, authorize all the oaths.
Having heard this, Dhṛtarāṣṭra addressed Vidura:
"Bring that wicked Suyodhana, who is greedy for the kingdom, here quickly."
"If I am able to bring him back once more onto the path, along with his friends, his ministers, his brothers, and his followers,"—
then the Kṣattṛ caused Duryodhana to enter the assembly hall again.
Then King Dhṛtarāṣṭra addressed Duryodhana, who was unwillingly surrounded by his brothers and kings,
and encompassed by Karṇa, Duḥśāsana, and the other monarchs.

O cruel one, abounding in evil, accompanied by those who assist in base deeds— having joined with such wicked companions, you wish to perform a sinful act that is impossible, disgraceful, and censured even by the virtuous.
Just as a fool like you, a defiler of his lineage, would resolve,
so do you— having joined with evil companions— desire indeed to seize this lotus-eyed one, who is invincible and difficult to approach.
O fool, you seek him whom even the gods, together with Indra, cannot compel by force— just as a child seeks the moon;
he who [cannot be overcome] by gods, humans, gandharvas, asuras, or serpents.

He cannot be withstood in battle; you do not realize that he is Keśava. Wind is difficult to grasp with the hand, the moon is difficult to touch with the hand, the earth is difficult to hold upon one's head, and Keśava is difficult to seize by force.
When Dhṛtarāṣṭra had spoken thus, Vidura the Kṣattṛ also spoke,
looking toward the intolerant Duryodhana, the son of Dhṛtarāṣṭra:
"At the gate of Saubha, there was a lord of monkeys known by the name Dvivida."
With a great shower of stones, he covered Keśava.
"O Duryodhana, listen now to these words of mine:
desiring to seize Mādhava, he has exerted himself with every effort."
There, he was unable to be seized; yet you seek him by force.
Six thousand great asuras, having bound him with nooses, were unable to seize him while he was being released; yet you seek him by force.

Naraka, together with the Dānavas, was unable to capture Śauri when he had gone to Prāgjyotiṣa; yet you seek to seize him by force. Having slain Naraka in battle, he whose lifespan lasts for many yugas and years—

Having taken thousands of maidens, he married them according to the prescribed rites. For by him, while still a child, Pūtanā was slain; likewise, O bull of the Bharatas, Govardhana was lifted up for the sake of the cows.
Ariṣṭa and Dhenuka, as well as the exceedingly powerful Cāṇūra,
and Aśvarāja have been slain, along with Kaṃsa who was practicing for his own destruction; and Jarāsaṃdha, Vakra, and the heroic Śiśupāla.
Bāṇa was slain in battle and the kings were destroyed; King Varuṇa was conquered, as was the Fire-god of immeasurable splendor;
and by carrying off the Pārijāta tree, the Lord of Śacī himself was defeated.
While reclining upon the single ocean, he slew Madhu and Kaiṭabha;
having entered another birth, he likewise slew Vālī and his other brothers, such as Kumbhakarṇa and the rest, in battle.
Having installed Vibhīṣaṇa and taken Sītā, the princess of Mithilā,
he protected the kingdom— its thorns removed— in accordance with the law;
and having entered another birth, Hayagrīva was likewise slain.
This one is the agent and is not created; he is the cause even in human effort.
Whatever this Śauri desires, that he can accomplish without exertion. You do not recognize that Govinda, the infallible one of terrible prowess.

Like an enraged venomous serpent, an unconquered mass of splendor, you shall cease to exist along with your ministers upon attacking the mighty-armed Kṛṣṇa, the doer of effortless deeds— just as a moth perishes upon reaching a fire.
Then, disregarding those words, the wicked ones led by Duḥśāsana— deluded by divine illusion and intent on restraining Kṛṣṇa, mistaking him for Suyodhana— bound him with a net of ropes.
Having released the king who was crying out, they were filled with wonder;
this [verse] is seen as an addition in some manuscripts, but it appears incoherent.
"How did this come to be?"—it was like a marvel.
Vaiśampāyana said:
When Vidura had spoken thus, the heroic Keśava, the slayer of enemy hosts, addressed Duryodhana, the son of Dhṛtarāṣṭra.
Whenever you see the monkey-bannered one,
the middle Pandava wielding his bow in battle,
or Vṛkodara whirling with mace in hand;
"Then, at that time, you shall give away the entire earth.
Suyodhana, because of your delusion, you think, 'I am alone';
and having thus insulted me, O evil-minded one, you desire to seize me."
"Right here are all the Pāṇḍavas, as well as the Andhakas and Vṛṣṇis;
right here are the Ādityas, the Rudras, and the Vasus, along with the great ṛṣis.
Having spoken thus, Keśava, the slayer of enemy heroes, laughed aloud.
As that high-souled Śauri smiled, all the gods together suddenly issued forth from him like flashes of lightning;
the thirty deities, each the size of a thumb, emitted sparks of fire.
Brahmā was situated on his forehead, and Rudra appeared upon his chest;
the world-protectors were in his arms, and Agni was born from his mouth.
All of them bore fierce weapons and were endowed with divine bodies.
The Ādityas, the Sādhyas, the Vasus, and also the two Aśvins;
the Maruts together with Indra, and likewise the Viśvedevas;
and they also assumed the forms of Yakṣas, Gandharvas, and Rākṣasas.
Likewise, Saṃkarṣaṇa and Dhanañjaya appeared from his two arms;
then Arjuna, the archer, appeared on the right, and Rāma, the wielder of the plow, on the left;
while Bhīma, Yudhiṣṭhira, and the two sons of Mādrī appeared at his back.
Then the Andhakas and Vṛṣṇis, headed by Pradyumna,
stood at the forefront of Kṛṣṇa with their great weapons raised—
the conch, discus, mace, spear, Śārṅga bow, plow, and the sword Nandaka.
All manner of uplifted weapons were seen blazing forth on every side from all the arms of Kṛṣṇa;
likewise, they issued from his two eyes, his nose, and his two ears in every direction.
Extremely fierce flames of fire, accompanied by smoke,
burst forth from his pores like the rays of the sun;
he was glorious, possessing a thousand feet, a hundred arms, and a thousand eyes.
At that time, the earth and the world of the *nāgas* were seen below his ankles;
the moon and sun were his two eyes, and all the planets were situated all around him;
and all the higher worlds were established within his belly.
The rivers and the oceans were the sweat of that Great-Souled One;
all the mountains were his bones, and the trees were indeed his body hairs.
The twinkling of his eyes was day and night, and the autumnal [season] was upon his tongue.
Beholding that terrible form of the high-souled Keśava,
the kings, their minds filled with terror, closed their eyes—
with the exception of Droṇa, Bhīṣma, and the highly intelligent Vidura.
To the highly fortunate Saṃjaya and to the sages whose wealth is asceticism,
the Blessed Janārdana granted divine vision.
There, O King Dhṛtarāṣṭra, a marvel occurred as he [regained] his own two eyes.
The lords of men, together with the ṛṣis, were filled with wonder and praised Madhusūdana as he sat there, having obtained divine vision through his desire to behold the universal form of Vāsudeva.
The Blessed One bestowed divine eyes upon Dhṛtarāṣṭra;
Dhṛtarāṣṭra, the son of Ambikā, beheld the supreme form.
Then the gods, along with the Gandharvas, Kinnaras, and great serpents [were present].
And the highly fortunate ṛṣis, accompanied by the world-protectors,
having bowed their heads to the god and standing with palms joined in reverence, praised him, saying:
"O Lord, withdraw, withdraw your anger!"
And this form which has been displayed, established within myself—
until all these worlds on earth, together with the hosts of gods, have gone to destruction.
You are the creator and the transformer; you alone provide complete protection. This entire world, both stationary and moving, is pervaded by you.
Of what measure are these rulers of the earth? What is their prowess, and what is their valor?
"O mighty-armed one, for whose sake you displayed this divine form,
such words were uttered by the Lord together with the gods.
Having seen that great marvel of Mādhava in the assembly hall, [they spoke thus].
The divine drums resounded and a rain of flowers fell.
"O lotus-eyed one, you alone are the Lord of the entire world;
therefore, O best of the Yādavas, you ought to show me your favor."
"O Blessed One, I choose once more the disappearance of my eyes.
Vaiśampāyana said:
"I have seen you; I do not venture to see anyone else here."
Then the mighty-armed Janārdana said to Dhṛtarāṣṭra:
"O joy of the Kurus, let your two eyes become invisible.
And the entire earth trembled, and the ocean was agitated as well.
O bull of the Bharata race, the kings were filled with supreme wonder.
Then the evil-minded Duryodhana, together with Karṇa and other wicked men,
became terrified at heart upon seeing the form of Mādhava.
Then that tiger among men,
Śauri, the lord of all the worlds, the subduer of enemies who is worshipped by all the gods, withdrew his own divine, wonderful, variegated, and magnificent form.
Then, taking Sātyaki by the hand as well as the son of Hṛdika,
Madhusūdana departed, permitted by those sages. Thereupon,
Nārada and the other sages vanished and went away.
While that clamor was occurring, a marvel then took place:
seeing him set out, the Kauravas along with the kings followed that tiger among men, just as the gods follow Śatakratu.
Reflecting upon that entire circle of kings, the immeasurable-souled Śauri emerged from there like a fire accompanied by smoke;
then he departed on a great, radiant chariot adorned with small bells.
Dāruka appeared, driving a chariot that was adorned with a network of gold, light, rumbling like a cloud,
well-equipped, bright, covered with tiger-skin armor,
and yoked with the horses Sainya and Sugrīva.
In the same manner, the great car-warrior Kṛtavarman,
the hero son of Hṛdika who is esteemed by the Vṛṣṇis, was seen mounted upon his chariot.
As the descendant of Śūra, the subduer of enemies, stood ready at his chariot and prepared to depart, [the people gazed upon him].
The great king Dhṛtarāṣṭra spoke once more:
"O Janārdana, you behold all this power that resides in my sons;
it is directly before your eyes, O crusher of enemies, and nothing is hidden from you."
O Keśava, knowing that I desire peace for the Kurus and am striving toward it, you ought not to harbor excessive suspicion regarding this state of mine;
O Govinda, even by sons devoid of virtue, I have been benefited.
O Lord of the Three Worlds, since your feet have been saluted by me without effort,
I have no sinful intention toward the Pāṇḍavas, O Keśava;
for you already know the words that were spoken by me to Suyodhana.
"O Mādhava, all the Kurus and the kings of the earth know that I am striving for peace with every effort.
Then the mighty-armed one spoke to Dhṛtarāṣṭra, the lord of men.
Droṇa, the grandfather Bhīṣma, the steward Vidura, Bāhlika, and Kṛpa—
you have all witnessed firsthand what occurred in the assembly of the Kurus,
and how that fool, like one lacking in discipline, repeatedly rose up in anger.
"King Dhṛtarāṣṭra speaks of himself as being powerless.
I take my leave of you all; I shall go to Yudhiṣṭhira.
Thus addressed, Śauri, that bull among men, mounted his chariot and prepared to depart.
The great archers, preeminent heroes, and bulls among the Bharatas followed him:
Bhīṣma, Droṇa, Kṛpa, the Steward (Vidura), Dhṛtarāṣṭra, and Bāhlika;
as well as Aśvatthāman, Vikarṇa, and the great chariot-warrior Yuyutsu.
Then, in a great, radiant chariot adorned with small bells,
he set out while the Kurus looked on, to see Pṛthā, his father’s sister.
Vaiśampāyana said:
Then, having entered her house and saluted her feet,
he related in brief what had occurred in the assembly of the Kurus.
Vāsudeva said:
Various kinds of reasoned speech have been spoken by both the sages and myself, which ought to have been accepted; yet he did not accept it.
All this is now ripe for its time, falling under the sway of Duryodhana.
The entire warrior class will be consumed in an instant by the fire of Pārtha.
I take my leave of you; I shall depart quickly for the sake of the Pāṇḍavas.
What words of yours should I speak to those sons of Pāṇḍu on your behalf?
"Tell that to me, O lady of great wisdom; I wish to hear your words. Kuntī said:
"O Keśava, you should speak thus to King Yudhiṣṭhira, whose soul is righteous:"
"Your dharma is greatly declining; O son, do not act in vain!
O King, like that of a dull-witted and unlearned *śrotriya*, your intellect—though devoted to recitation—perceives only dharma."
"Examine your duty according to how you were created by the Self-Existent One:
the Kṣatriya was created from the chest, subsisting on the strength of his arms,
for the constant performance of fierce deeds and the protection of his subjects."
Listen now to a single analogy which I have heard from the elders:
in ancient times, Vaiśravaṇa, being pleased, offered this earth to the royal sage Mucukunda, yet he did not accept it.
"I desire that I may enjoy a kingdom won by the strength of my own arms.
At this, Vaiśravaṇa became both pleased and amazed. Thereupon, King Mucukunda ruled over the earth.
O Bhārata, he who is devoted to the duty of the Kṣatriya and has properly acquired [his status] through the strength of his own arms—
indeed, when subjects, well-protected by the king, practice their duty here in this world,
the king obtains a fourth part of that merit.
If the king practices righteousness, he is fit for divinity;
if he practices unrighteousness, he goes to hell. By means of his own duty, the science of government (daṇḍanīti) restrains the four castes.
When the king conducts himself perfectly and in its entirety according to the science of government (daṇḍanīti), he properly employs [his subjects] and restrains them from unrighteous acts;
at that time, the most excellent period known as the Kṛta Yuga prevails.
"Is time the cause of the king, or is the king the cause of time? Let there be no such doubt in you: the king is the cause of time;
the king is the creator of the Kṛta age, as well as of the Tretā and Dvāpara ages."
The king is the cause of the fourth age;
by being the cause of the Kṛta age, the king enjoys heaven eternally. By being the cause of the Tretā age, the king does not enjoy heaven eternally.
By initiating the Dvāpara age, he partakes of his portion accordingly; by initiating the Kali age, the king incurs excessive sin. Consequently, that evildoer dwells in hell for eternal years.
Time becomes the cause; an impermanent king dwells [in power]. For by the fault of the king, the world is afflicted, and he is the one [responsible] for that world.
"Observe the duties of kingship inherited from your father and grandfather;
for this which you wish to abide by is not the conduct of royal seers.
Indeed, one who is overcome by despondency cannot be established in compassion."
The king obtained some small fruit arising from the protection of his subjects;
for neither Pāṇḍu, nor I, nor your grandfather ever previously employed that wisdom with which you now conduct yourself.
Sacrifice, charity, austerity, heroism, and the continuation of progeny—
greatness, strength, and vigor were always desired by me. Humans and gods constantly offered *svāhā* and *svadhā*.
When properly propitiated, the auspicious ancestors and deities constantly desire for their sons long life, wealth,
and offspring; [they expect] from them charity, study, sacrifice, and the protection of subjects.
Whether this be dharma or adharma, you were born with it by the very fact of your birth.
You are learned men born into a noble family, yet, my dear, you are afflicted by a lack of livelihood.
For you are like hungry beings wandering the earth seeking a heroic lord of charity.
Having attained [these goals] and being satisfied, they depart; what dharma is greater than that?
Having obtained a kingdom in this world, a righteous man should win over others through gifts, others through force, and others through pleasant speech from every side.
A Brāhmaṇa should practice begging for alms; a Kṣatriya should protect [the people];
a Vaiśya should acquire wealth; and a Śūdra should serve them.
Alms-seeking is forbidden to you, and agriculture is not at all appropriate for you.
"You are a Kṣatriya, a protector from injury, one who lives by the strength of his arms. O mighty-armed one, raise up once more your ancestral portion that has been submerged!
[Do so] through conciliation, bribery, sowing dissension, punishment, and through statesmanship."

"What indeed could be more painful than this, that I, deprived of my kinsmen, must look to the alms of others after giving birth to you, O delighter of your enemies? Fight according to the duty of a king; do not let your ancestors sink into ruin."
"Do not go, with your merits exhausted, to a miserable state along with your younger brothers.
What is the use of life for one who is being struck down by enemies?
Kuntī said:
In this regard, O scorcher of enemies, they cite this ancient history, the conversation between Vidulā and her son,
wherein she spoke of what is beneficial and how one may attain even more.

Illustrious, spirited, and born of noble lineage, Vibhāvarī was devoted to the duty of the kṣatriyas; she was blessed, discerning, and far-sighted. Renowned in the assemblies of kings, she was learned in sacred texts and possessed of great erudition.
Indeed, the truthful Vidurā reproached her own biological son,
who had been defeated by the King of Sindhu, was lying down with a dejected mind,
was joyless, ignorant of righteousness, and a source of increased delight for his enemies.
"You were not born from me, nor were you born from your father; from where have you come? You are a man devoid of passion, a mere branch, a person whose means are impotent.
For as long as you live, you shall be hopeless; bear the burden for the sake of what is auspicious."
Do not despise yourself; do not sustain yourself with so little. Set your mind on what is auspicious; do not fear, but steady yourself.
Arise, O coward! Do not lie there thus defeated.
Delighting all his enemies, devoid of pride, and causing grief to his kinsmen—such is the man. Indeed, a small stream is easily filled, and the paws of a mouse are easily filled;
likewise, a base man is easily satisfied, for he finds contentment even with very little.
Even by breaking the enemy’s fang, go quickly to your death; or even by facing danger to your life, exert your prowess! As you move about, watch for a vulnerability in the enemy like a hawk.
Whether crying out or remaining silent, whether in the sky or on the ground, why do you lie there like a ghost, as if struck by a thunderbolt? Arise, O coward! Do not remain thus defeated.
Do not go to your end like a wretched man; let yourself be known by your own deeds. Do not be mediocre, nor inferior, nor base; stand firm and exalted.
Blaze for even a moment like a firebrand of *tinduka* wood.
Let not one who desires to live be like a smokeless fire of chaff or a crow’s nest; it is better to blaze for a moment than to smolder for a long time.
Let no woman be born in the house of any king who is as harsh as a donkey yet as soft as a mare.
Having performed human duties and having run the race to its very end,
one attains freedom from debt to Dharma and does not reproach oneself. Whether they have failed to obtain their goal or have obtained it, the wise do not grieve.
He commits acts of immediate retribution and does not value his own life;
exert your prowess or go to that certain destination. Placing Dharma before you, my son, for what purpose do you live?
"O eunuch, your sacrifices and charitable works are indeed destroyed, as is all your fame;
the very root of your enjoyment is severed—for what purpose do you live?
An enemy should be seized by one who is sinking, or by one who is about to fall from his thighs."
Even when his roots are completely severed, he should not despair in any way;
lifting up the yoke, he should pull it along, remembering the conduct of a noble steed. Exert your strength and pride, and recognize your own manliness.
Raise up the family that has sunk, for it is indeed because of you;
he whose great and wondrous conduct men do not proclaim is merely a heap-increaser, neither woman nor man.
He whose fame is not celebrated for generosity, austerity, or heroism; nor for learning, or the acquisition of wealth—he is merely his mother’s excrement.
Whether by sacred knowledge, austerity, prosperity, or valor, [he is so].
He who indeed surpasses other men by his deeds is truly a man;
you should not, however, seek the wretched livelihood of a beggar with a skull-bowl—
a cruel, disgraceful, miserable way of life fit only for a base person.
That man whom his enemies would rejoice over— him who is emaciated,
despised by the world, and possessed of inferior food and clothing— who brings about the loss of wealth, who is wretched, short-lived, and insignificant.
Having encountered such a kinsman, a relative does not thrive in happiness;
we shall surely perish through lack of livelihood, having been exiled from the kingdom, deprived of all the pleasures of desire, fallen from our station, and destitute.
"O Sañjaya, I have given birth to you as a source of strife under the name of 'son'— one who brings disrepute among the virtuous, the destroyer of his family lineage,
devoid of indignation, lacking in energy, bereft of prowess, and a bringer of no joy."
"Let no woman ever give birth to such a son as this!
Do not merely smoke; blaze up intensely and strike down your enemies! Blaze at the heads of your foes, even for a moment or an instant!"
A man is truly such only as long as he is indignant and intolerant; one who is patient and devoid of indignation is neither woman nor man.
Indeed, contentment destroys prosperity, as does compassion.
Both in the fear of non-exertion and in exertion, one who is devoid of effort does not attain greatness. Release yourself from these sinful deceptions by means of your own self;
having made your heart as hard as iron, seek once more your own true nature.

Because he withstands the city [of the senses], he is called a *puruṣa*; they say that he who lives here like a woman has a meaningless name. [This applies not] to one who is heroic, of vigorous spirit, and who moves with the stride of a lion.
Even when he has passed away according to destiny, his subjects rejoice in the distribution of his bounty—
he who, having abandoned his own dear pleasures, seeks after prosperity,
and thereby brings joy to his ministers before long.
The son said:
"What indeed would the entire earth be to you if you did not see me?
What use would ornaments be to you, or what use enjoyments, or even life itself?"
The mother said:
"May those who hate us today attain the worlds intended for the wicked;
and may our friends go to those worlds intended for those who have disciplined their souls."

Do not follow the way of life of those who are abandoned by their servants, who subsist on the alms of others, who are wretched and lacking in strength. O dear one, let the Brahmins and your friends live depending upon you.
O Sañjaya, that man upon whom all beings depend for their livelihood— just as living creatures depend on the rain-cloud, or the gods depend on Indra—
is one whose life is truly meaningful, like a tree laden with ripe fruit.
The life of that hero is truly well-lived in this world, whose kinsmen prosper through his valor and dwell in happiness, just as the thirty gods do through Śakra;
he who sustains himself by relying on the strength of his own arms.
He gains fame in this world and a blessed state in the next.
Vidura said:
"Now, in this situation, do you wish to abandon human effort?"

In no long time you will travel the path frequented by the base. For they know that a Kṣatriya who, desiring life, does not display his brilliance through valor to the best of his ability is nothing but a thief.
Meaningful, appropriate, and virtuous words do not reach you at all, just as medicine fails a man who is about to die. Indeed,
there are many people in the service of the King of Sindhu who are well-contented.
Out of weakness, the fools sit idle, awaiting a flood of calamities; yet,
having gathered allies and exerted effort here and there,
others will follow them upon seeing your prowess.
Forming an alliance with them, frequent mountain fastnesses while awaiting your time of misfortune; for this Sañjaya is not ageless or immortal,
yet by name you are he, and I do not perceive that [immortality] in you.
"O son, let your name be true to its meaning for me; do not let it be a meaningless one.
A Brahmin spoke of you as a child who possesses right view and great wisdom:
'Having encountered great hardship, this one shall again attain growth.'"
Remembering his words, I hope for your victory;
therefore, my son, I speak to you and shall say it again and again:
for when another's purpose is accomplished, those who have aided him are themselves gratified.
For one who follows the meaning within these systems, the accomplishment of that purpose is certain.
Whether there be success or failure for my ancestors, O Sañjaya, knowing this, set your mind on battle; do not retreat.
Śambara declared that no state whatsoever is more wretched than this:
where neither food for today nor for tomorrow morning is to be seen.
He said that this is a greater misery than the slaughter of husband and sons.
That which is called poverty is indeed a gradual death.
I was born into a great family, as one who has come from one lake to another; a sovereign lady through all my auspicious qualities, I was most highly honored by my husband.
Formerly, when my circle of friends saw me adorned with costly garlands and ornaments and clothed in well-washed garments, they beheld me now fallen into such great distress.
And when you see both me and my wife so exceedingly weakened, [you will understand our plight].
"O Sañjaya, there will be no purpose for your life at that time;
what is the use of life to you when you see us abandoning our slaves, laborers, servants, teachers, officiating priests, and family chaplains due to a lack of livelihood?"
If I do not see here today that praiseworthy and glorious deed for you as I did before, what peace can there be for my heart? If I were to say "no" to the brahmins, my heart would break.

"I have not said 'no' to a Brahmin, neither for myself nor on behalf of my husband; we are those who should be sought as refuge, not those who seek refuge in others. Having lived by depending on another, I shall now abandon my life."
Be our shore where there is no shore; be our boat where there is no boat. Establish us in a place where there is no place, and restore us to life when we are dead.
All those enemies shall be overcome by you, provided you do not wish to live.
If you instead adopt such a cowardly way of life,
dejected in spirit and with a ruined mind, then abandon this sinful livelihood;
for by the mere slaying of a single enemy, a hero attains renown.
By the very slaying of Vṛtra, Indra became Mahendra;
he obtained the Māhendra cup and became the lord of the worlds. Having proclaimed his name in battle and challenged his armored enemies, he [attained this].
When a hero, having either routed the vanguard of the army or slain a preeminent man,
obtains great glory through fair combat,
at that very moment his enemies tremble and bow down before him.
Having abandoned their own selves in battle, those base men, being helpless, filled [the world] with the fulfillment of all their desires—
whether it be a kingdom subject to violent downfall or even the uncertainty of life itself.
For the virtuous leave a remnant of an enemy who has been humiliated;
considering sovereignty— which is like the gateway to heaven or even like nectar—
to be blocked by enemies on a narrow path, one should strike among the foes like a flaming torch.
"Consume [the earth] by conquering my enemies in battle at the head of the fray;
restraining the other castes and subduing all evildoers,
slay the foes in war, O King, and uphold your own duty."
May the illustrious enemy never behold you in such piteous distress,
surrounded by our grieving [kinsmen] and the shouting foes;
may I not, myself dejected, see you standing there so wretched.
Having dwelt with the maidens of Sauvīra, take pride in your own merits as you did before;
do not fall under the power of the maidens of Sindhu.
You are young, endowed with beauty, learning, and noble lineage.
If one such as you, illustrious and world-renowned, were to act otherwise,
I consider that death itself would be better for you than being like an ox when the burden must be carried—
were I to see you speaking pleasant words to another.
What peace can there be for my heart if he follows behind?
No one born in this family has ever walked behind another;
you ought not, my dear son, to live as a follower of another.
For I know the eternal heart of the Kṣatriya,
which was proclaimed by those of old and even those more ancient, as well as by those of later times and even those more recent; it is eternal, immutable, and fashioned by Prajāpati.

"Whosoever here is a Kṣatriya, not yet born [into that state], yet knows the duty of a Kṣatriya, should not bow down to anyone out of fear or out of regard for his livelihood. He should rather exert himself; he should not bow down, for exertion alone is manliness."
He might break even at an improper time, yet he would not bow down here to anyone;
like an elephant in rut, that high-minded one would roam about,
always bowing to the Brāhmaṇas and to Dharma alone, O Sañjaya.
"Restraining the other castes and striking down all evildoers—
whether with companions or alone— he should remain thus for as long as he lives.
The son said:

O my mother, you have forged my heart as if out of black iron—cruel, possessed of a mind for enmity, and intolerant. Alas! Such is the conduct of the kṣatriyas, wherein they treat me as if I were a stranger.
Just as a mother of evil intent might urge her son toward battle,
so do you, O lady, speak such words to your only son. What indeed would all the earth have gained had it not seen me?
"What use have you for ornaments, what use for enjoyments, or even for life—
especially now that my beloved son has been slain?
O mother, out of delusion you reproach your own beloved son, especially so."
Mātali said:
"For all undertakings of the wise, my dear, are for the sake of dharma and artha; it was with this very purpose in mind, Sañjaya, that I urged you."
"This primary time has arrived, endowed with its proper sequence;
if you do not undertake your duty when this time has come, you will act most cruelly, your character having become unsuitable."
O Sañjaya, if I were not to speak to you when you are touched by infamy,
I myself would become your greatest and most intimate enemy.
They say that the affection of a she-ass for her young is both powerless and without cause.

Abandon this path censured by the virtuous and frequented by fools; for there is indeed a great ignorance to which these creatures have resorted. If you were to possess virtuous conduct, by that you would become dear to me.

One should act with one who is endowed with the qualities of dharma and artha, and never with anyone else; with one who is devoted to both the divine and the human, and whose conduct is practiced by the virtuous.
For he who takes pleasure in such an undisciplined son or grandson [brings ruin].
Moreover, for one who lacks the effort to rise [and act], the fruit of offspring is in vain;
he who takes delight in a son who is ill-behaved and of wicked intellect.
For those lowest of men who neither perform their duties nor avoid censurable acts obtain no happiness, either in this world or the next.
O Sañjaya, a Kṣatriya is created for battle and for victory in this world.
Constantly engaged in fierce deeds for the protection of his subjects,
whether conquering or being slain, he attains the same world as Indra;
yet that bliss does not exist even in the holy abode of Śakra in heaven.
When a kṣatriya, having brought his enemies under his control, enjoys happiness,
it is because that high-minded man, though repeatedly humiliated here by his burning resentment,
desires to conquer his foes.
Whether by sacrificing one's own life or by utterly defeating one's enemies,
the happiness that is obtained thereby is not found elsewhere;
for true peace is never attained here, O Sañjaya.
How else could there be peace for him?
For in this world, a wise man desires even a very small amount of what is unpleasant; he for whom there is little that is dear in the world certainly has little that is unpleasant.
"Moreover, due to the absence of a beloved, a man does not attain what is auspicious;
he inevitably meets with non-existence, just as the Gaṅgā reaches the ocean.
The son said:
"O mother, you should not speak such words to your son, especially not these. Show only compassion here, remaining as if dull-witted and mute.
The mother said:

Therefore, my joy is even greater because you perceive things in this way; that you urge me with such a challenge—I indeed urge you back in turn. Moreover, I shall honor you once I have truly slain all the Saindhavas.
"I see that your complete victory is indeed destined to be yours.
The son said:
"How can there be victory for me, who am without treasury and without allies?"
"Having recognized this terrible state within myself by means of my own self,
my inclination toward kingship has turned away, as if from heaven itself for one who has committed an evil deed. Do you perceive some such means [to remedy this]?"
"O you of mature wisdom, explain this correctly to me as I ask;
for I shall carry out all that instruction exactly as prescribed.
Mātali said:
One should not despise one's own self on account of former failures;
for some goals come into being after not having existed, while others, having existed, perish.
Furthermore, goals should not be undertaken out of mere impatience by those who are very foolish.
O dear one, for all actions, there is always impermanence in their fruit.
Those who know that it is impermanent do not come into being, yet they continue to exist;
whereas those who do not act at all never come into being.
In the absence of effort, there is a single result: the non-existence of the fruits of actions;
whereas if there is effort, the result is twofold—it either comes to pass or it does not—for one who has already understood the impermanence of all things.
O Prince, prosperity and abundance will be repelled by adverse circumstances;
therefore, with a mind that is always free from distress, one should resolve: "It shall come to pass," and remain ever vigilant, alert, and intent upon deeds that lead to well-being.
O dear son, when auspicious rites are performed before wise kings together with Brahmins and lords, their prosperity increases swiftly;
Fortune turns toward them just as the sun rises toward the east.
You have demonstrated many illustrations, skillful means, and encouragements;
I see that you have shown your true form. Now, you ought to exert your manly effort to achieve the desired human goal here.
"Those who are angry, greedy, impoverished, insulted, or dishonored,
as well as those who are competitive— keep an eye on whoever such as these may be. By this means, you shall break apart great assemblies."
Like the wind of great velocity rising up and scattering the clouds,
you should be one who gives them precedence, rising early and speaking kindly;
they will surely do what is pleasing to you and place you at their head.

As soon as an enemy perceives his rival as one who has renounced the will to live, he trembles before him like a snake that has entered his house. If, having recognized such prowess, one does not bring that foe under control, [he becomes a source of danger].
One should counter his criticisms with one's own; in the end, that will come to pass.
By gaining a foothold through such debate, there will be an increase in wealth;
for friends seek out and take refuge with those who possess wealth.

Moreover, O dear one, even kinsmen abandon one whose purpose has failed; they may take refuge with such a person, yet they despise him as well. He who places his trust in an ally whom he has made an enemy—[such a man is lost].
"Therefore, it is indeed possible that he might obtain the kingdom.
The mother said:
"A king should never feel fear in any kind of calamity."
Even if one should be divided, one must not behave as if divided;
for when they see that the king is divided, the entire realm,
the army, and the ministers all become divided in their resolve.
Some resort to his enemies, while others abandon him once again; some who were previously insulted seek to strike him down,
yet those who are his most intimate friends remain by his side.
Powerless and longing for their own welfare, like cows whose calves have been tied up, they grieve for him who is grieving, just as kinsmen grieve for those who have perished.
Were they not honored by you before? Are they not considered your friends?
Those who covet the kingdom when the king has fallen into calamity—
do not let them incite your friends, nor let them abandon you once you have been torn asunder.
This was said by me, desiring to test your power, manliness, and intelligence.
Consoling me as one who is strong might console the weak,
she spoke thus: "If you understand this, and if I speak correctly, then,
O Sañjaya, assuming a stern demeanor for the sake of victory, arise!"
"We have a great store of treasure unknown to you;
I alone know it, and no one else. I shall bestow it upon you.
Furthermore, O Sañjaya, you have more than a hundred friends."
O Hero, those who share in both joy and sorrow, who are worthy of a hundred, and who never turn back—
such indeed are the companions for a man who desires to prosper; they are ministers who crush the enemy, even when he rises up but slightly.
The son said:
Whose speech is such that even upon hearing it, the darkness of a person of small intellect would not be dispelled— speech consisting of words and syllables of such wonderful meaning?
"This burden must be borne by me in the water; I must flow down the slope, since you, who perceive the past and the future, are my guide.
For I am desirous of hearing your words again and again."
Repeating various words in response, I remained silent again and again,
like one who is not satiated by nectar obtained with difficulty from a kinsman;
now I shall exert myself for the restraint and defeat of my enemies.
Kuntī said:
Like a well-bred horse struck and urged on by the arrows of her words,
he performed everything exactly according to her instruction.
This terrifying and supreme incitement, which increases one's vital energy,
should be made to be heard by a king who is despondent and oppressed by enemies;
this history named "Victory" (Jaya) ought to be heard by one who desires victory.
Having heard this, one swiftly conquers the earth and crushes one's enemies;
this is indeed a rite for the procreation of sons and the birth of heroes. A pregnant woman who hears it repeatedly will certainly give birth to a hero.
A hero in knowledge, a hero in austerity, a hero in self-restraint, and an ascetic;
blazing with Brahmanic splendor, esteemed for his virtuous reputation;
radiant, endowed with strength, highly fortunate, and a great chariot-warrior.

For his sake, a Kṣatriya woman gives birth to a hero of true prowess— one who is bold yet invincible, a conqueror who is never defeated, a restrainer of the wicked, and a protector of those who walk the path of dharma.
"O Kṛṣṇa, having heard these words of his mother, Sañjaya engaged in battle with the enemies and certainly achieved victory. Kuntī said:
"O Keśava, you should say this to Arjuna: 'When you were born in the lying-in chamber, I was seated in the hermitage, surrounded by women.
Then, a voice of divine form and enchanting beauty arose in the sky.'"
"O Kuntī, this son of yours will be equal to the thousand-eyed Indra. He shall conquer all the Kurus assembled in battle;
and with Bhīmasena as his second, he will overturn the world."
"Your son shall conquer the earth, and his fame shall touch the heavens. Having slain the Kurus in battle with Vāsudeva as his ally,
he will recover his lost paternal inheritance."
Accompanied by his brothers, the illustrious one will perform three horse-sacrifices.
O Śvetāśva, you must act exactly as the voice spoke.
[Act] toward that Bibhatsu, Savyasācin, who is true to his promise, O Acyuta.
"O descendant of Daśārha, just as I know him to be so powerful and invincible,
let it be exactly as those words have spoken. O Vārṣṇeya, if there is such a thing as dharma, then it shall come true."
"And you too, O Kṛṣṇa, will bring all that to fulfillment;
I do not doubt the word that was spoken.
Homage to the Great Dharma; Dharma sustains all creatures."
This must be said to Dhanañjaya and to Vṛkodara, who is ever-exerting:
"The time has now arrived for that purpose for which a Kṣatriya woman gives birth;
for those bulls among men do not falter when they have encountered enmity."

Your mind has always known the disposition of Bhīma; that crusher of foes does not find peace until he brings his enemies to their end. Indeed, as long as that mighty-armed one does not achieve this, he shall find no rest even during the nights.
O Mādhava, O Kṛṣṇa, speak to the auspicious and illustrious Kṛṣṇā, the daughter-in-law of the high-souled Pāṇḍu, who possesses specialized knowledge of all dharmas:
"O highly fortunate one, born of an illustrious lineage, this is indeed fitting for you."
Since you have behaved toward all my sons exactly as is fitting,
both sons of Mādrī— who are devoted to the dharma of the Kṣatriya— should be told that wealth is indeed acquired through prowess by those who delight in the dharma of the Kṣatriya.
Choose enjoyments acquired through valor even over life itself;
for objects obtained through valor always gladden the heart of a man who lives according to the dharma of the Kṣatriya, O best of men.

And while you were looking on, Pāñcālī—she who honors all dharmas—was addressed with harsh words; who indeed could forgive that? Neither the seizure of the kingdom nor the defeat at dice is such a sorrow.

Neither the exile of my sons nor their departure is the cause of my grief; rather, it is that when Bṛhatī, who was dark-complexioned, born of noble lineage, renowned, and possessed of supreme knowledge of all dharmas, was weeping in the assembly at that time—
I heard harsh words, which I consider even more painful than that:
that Kṛṣṇā, though possessed of noble form and always devoted to the duty of a warrior, found no protector at that time, despite being one who truly has protectors.
"O mighty-armed one, speak to that Arjuna, the best among all wielders of weapons and a tiger among men, saying: 'Follow the path of Draupadī.
For you know them both exceedingly well, like the two Yamas, the End-makers, when enraged."
For Bhīma and Arjuna could lead even the gods to their ultimate end; yet such was the contempt shown toward them that Kṛṣṇā was brought into the assembly hall,
and Duḥśāsana addressed harsh words to Bhīma.
While the Kuru heroes are looking on, you should remind them of that once more;
O Janārdana, you should inquire after the welfare of the Pāṇḍavas along with their sons and Kṛṣṇā, and tell them again that I am well.
"Go upon a path free from harm; protect my sons.
Vaiśampāyana said:
Then Kṛṣṇa, having offered his salutations and performed a circumambulation of her, departed.
The mighty-armed one, with the playful gait of a lion, then emerged from there;
he then dismissed Bhīṣma and the other bulls of the Kuru race,
and having placed Karṇa upon his chariot, he set out together with Sātyaki.
Then, as the descendant of Daśārha departed, the Kurus gathered together and conversed about the great wonder and supreme marvel concerning Keśava:
"The entire earth has been utterly bewildered and bound by the noose of death."
"Because of Duryodhana's folly, they said, 'This is not possible.
Then, having departed from the city, that best of men proceeded on his way and deliberated with Karṇa for a very long time.
Having dismissed the son of Rādhā, the delighter of all the Yādavas summoned Aśvatthāman and consulted with him again and again;
then, with great speed, he quickly urged the horses forward.
Driven by Daruka, those horses, possessing great speed and the velocity of thought or the wind, went as if drinking up the sky;
having swiftly traversed that distance like swift-flying hawks.
Highly extolling the sun, they brought him to Upaplavya, where he held the Śārṅga bow.
Vaiśampāyana said:
Having heard the words of Kuntī, the great car-warriors Bhīṣma and Droṇa—
They spoke these words to Duryodhana, who disregarded their commands:
"O tiger among men, you have heard in the presence of Kṛṣṇa the meaningful, composed, righteous, and unsurpassed speech uttered by Kuntī."
The sons of Kuntī will do that which is approved by Vāsudeva;
for they can never be pacified, O Kaurava, without the kingdom,
since the Pārthas were then tormented by you while bound by the bonds of dharma.
And Draupadī was treated so in the assembly by them— that was endured by you—
once they had obtained Arjuna, who was skilled in weapons, and Bhīma, who had achieved his exertion,
as well as the Gāṇḍīva bow, the two quivers, the chariot, and the banner.
Yudhiṣṭhira will not forgive Nakula and Sahadeva, who are endowed with strength and heroism, nor his ally Vāsudeva;
this has been witnessed by you, O mighty-armed one, as it was done by the wise son of Pṛthā.
Previously, in the city of Virāṭa, we were all defeated in battle;
yet [Arjuna], having invoked the Raudra weapon, burnt the Dānavas of terrible deeds, the Nivātakavacas, in combat with the fire of his weapons.

"Karna and these others, as well as you yourself, armored and mounted on your chariot, were rescued during the cattle-expedition; that is sufficient proof. Cease hostilities, O best of the Bharatas, and make peace with your brothers, the Pāṇḍavas."

Protect this entire earth, which has fallen into the jaws of death! Go to that tiger among men— your eldest brother, who is virtuous in character, affectionate, gentle of speech, and pure— casting away all sin from here.
If you are seen by the Pāṇḍava with your bow laid aside,
with a serene brow and radiant countenance, peace will have been established for our lineage. Therefore,
approaching that prince together with your ministers and embracing him—
"O subduer of enemies, salute the king as you did before.
Let Yudhiṣṭhira, the son of Kuntī and elder brother of Bhīma, receive you with both hands out of affection as you offer your salutation."
May Bhīma, the best among strikers, with shoulders, thighs, and arms like those of a lion, and with long, rounded, mighty arms, embrace you with his two arms;
and then may Guḍākeśa, whose neck is like a lion’s and whose eyes are like lotus petals, [embrace] you.
Let Pārtha Dhanañjaya, the son of Kuntī, offer his salutations;
and let those two tigers among men, the twin sons of Aśvinī, who are peerless in beauty upon this earth,
rise to honor you with affection as if you were their preceptor.
"Let the kings, headed by the Daśārhas, shed tears born of joy;
O King, cast aside your pride and reunite with your brothers.
Then, together with your brothers, rule over the entire earth."
Embracing one another with joy, let the kings depart from each other.
Enough of this war, O Indra among kings; listen to the reasons of your friends.
For the certain destruction of the kṣatriyas in battle is clearly foreseen.
O hero, inauspicious celestial bodies, fierce beasts and birds,
and various portents foreboding the destruction of the Kṣatriyas are appearing;
these omens, in particular, indicate our own ruin here.
For your army is being struck by blazing meteors,
O lord of people; your mounts are joyless and seem to be weeping,
while vultures hover around your troops on all sides.
The city is not as it was before, nor is the royal residence;
jackals, uttering inauspicious cries, frequent the blazing quarter of the sky.
Follow the words of your father, your mother, and of us who desire your welfare.
O mighty-armed one, both peace and exertion depend upon you.
O crusher of foes, if you do not follow the words of your friends,
you will grieve when you see your army tormented by the arrows of Pārtha.
And when you hear the great roar of the powerful Bhīma shouting in battle,
you will remember my words and the twang of the Gāṇḍīva—
if these words of mine prove to be false for you.
Vaiśampāyana said:
Thus addressed, he became despondent; with a sidelong glance and downcast face, knitting his brows together, he said nothing at all.
Seeing him thus dejected and looking at one another closely,
those two bulls among men spoke these further words.
Bhīṣma said:
"Against one who is obedient, free from malice, devoted to the Brahmins, and true to his promise—that son of Pṛthā—we shall have to fight; what indeed could be more painful than this?
Droṇa said:
O King, my great respect and humility toward the ape-bannered Dhanañjaya are even greater than those I feel for my son Aśvatthāman;
yet, I shall fight against that Dhanañjaya who is dearer to me than a son.
Having followed the duty of a warrior, shame on this livelihood of a kshatriya!
For there is no other archer in the world equal to him;
by my grace, that Bibhatsu is superior to all other bowmen.
One who betrays friends, one of evil disposition, an atheist, one who is crooked, and a rogue— such a person does not receive honor among the virtuous, like a fool who has arrived at a sacrifice.
Even when being restrained from evils, the evil-minded person desires to do evil.
Even when urged by evil, one whose nature is virtuous desires what is good; for these people, though acting with improper conduct while following after what is pleasing,
lead only to harm, O best of the Bharatas, because of their faults.
"You were told by the elder of the Kurus, by me, by Vidura,
and likewise by Vāsudeva that this was for your own welfare, yet you did not accept it.
Thinking only 'I have strength,' you are rashly attempting to cross over [the ocean]."
Like the current of the Gaṅgā with its crocodiles and timingalas during the summer heat,
you now regard the sovereignty of Yudhiṣṭhira as if you had merely put on a garment today, or as if you had greedily obtained a discarded garland.

Who, while established in his kingdom, could surpass the Pāṇḍava Partha, who dwells even in the forest accompanied by Draupadī and surrounded by his brothers bearing weapons? For all kings stand at his command like servants.
Having reached that abode of Ailavila, the King of Dharma shone resplendent;
having attained the residence of Kubera and obtained its jewels,
the Pāṇḍavas now desire sovereignty after having seized your prosperous kingdom.

We have given gifts, offered oblations, studied the Vedas, and satisfied the Brahmins with wealth; know that our lives have passed and we have accomplished all that was to be done. But you, having abandoned happiness, kingdom, friends, and riches—
By engaging in conflict with the Pāṇḍavas, you will meet with great calamity;
for the goddess Draupadī, who speaks the truth and observes fierce vows through her asceticism, prays for the victory of that Pāṇḍava— you shall not defeat him.
How will you defeat the son of Pāṇḍu, whose counselor is Janārdana and whose brother is Dhanañjaya— the best among all wielders of weapons—
and whose allies are Brāhmaṇas who are steadfast and have conquered their senses?
How will you defeat that heroic Pāṇḍava of fierce asceticism?
I shall speak again what must be done by one who desires prosperity,
when his friends are sinking into an ocean of calamity.
"Enough with fighting those heroes; be pacified for the sake of the Kuru lineage. Do not go to destruction along with your sons, ministers, and army.
Dhṛtarāṣṭra said:

Surrounded by princes and likewise by ministers, O Sañjaya, Madhusūdana, the slayer of enemy heroes, having placed Karṇa upon his chariot, set forth. What did he say to the son of Rādhā while seated on the seat of the chariot?
"O Saṃjaya, tell me what conciliatory words Govinda employed toward the Sūta's son;
for at that time, Kṛṣṇa, whose voice was like the roar of a flood or a cloud, spoke to Karṇa—
whether softly or sharply— relate all of that to me."
Saṃjaya said:
[He spoke] words that were sequential, smooth, gentle, pleasant, consistent with dharma, truthful, and beneficial.
O Bhārata, listen to me as I recount those heart-captivating words which Madhusūdana, whose self is immeasurable, spoke to Rādheya. Vāsudeva said:
O Rādheya, you have served brahmins who have mastered the Vedas;
you have questioned them regarding the true meaning of reality with self-restraint and without malice.
It is you alone, Karṇa, who knows the eternal doctrines of the Vedas.

For you alone are thoroughly established in the subtle treatises on dharma. Regarding the son born of an unmarried girl (*kānīna*), the son born of a pregnant bride (*sahoḍha*), and he who is born of a maiden— those learned in the scriptures declare that the man who marries her is his father.
"O Karṇa, you were born in such a manner; by law you are the son of Pāṇḍu.
According to the injunctions of the *dharmaśāstras*, come, for you shall become king.
For the sons of Pṛthā are on your father’s side, and the Vṛṣṇis are on your mother’s side."
"O bull among men, recognize these two alternatives:
either go from here with me today, O dear one, so that the Pāṇḍavas may recognize you as the son of Kuntī born before Yudhiṣṭhira."
The five Pāṇḍava brothers will grasp your feet,
as will the five sons of Draupadī and the unconquered son of Subhadrā; likewise,
kings and princes have assembled for the sake of the Pāṇḍavas.
All the Andhakas and Vṛṣṇis shall grasp your feet.
They shall bring golden jars, as well as silver and earthen ones;
likewise, all medicinal herbs, all seeds, all gems, and all creepers.
"Let the kṣatriya women and the princesses bring the materials for the consecration.
And at the sixth hour, Draupadī shall likewise approach you;
let Dhaumya, that best of the twice-born whose self is disciplined, offer oblations into the fire."
"Today let the twice-born Brahmins, learned in the four Vedas,
consecrate you as you stand upon a tiger skin,
together with the family priest of the Pāṇḍavas and likewise the five Pāṇḍava brothers, those bulls among men."
"The five sons of Draupadī, as well as the Pāñcālas and the Cedis,
and I myself shall consecrate you as king, the lord of the earth. Let King Yudhiṣṭhira, the son of Kuntī, be your heir apparent."
Holding a white fan, that righteous-souled one of firm vows—
Yudhiṣṭhira, the son of Kuntī— shall ascend the chariot.
And the mighty Bhīmasena shall hold over you a great white umbrella.
O son of Kuntī, once you have been consecrated,
Arjuna, the son of Kuntī, shall drive your chariot— which resounds with the tinkling of hundreds of small bells, is covered with tiger skins, and is yoked to white horses.
Abhimanyu will always remain close to you,
as will Nakula, Sahadeva, and the five sons of Draupadī;
the Pāñcālas and the great car-warrior Śikhaṇḍī shall follow after you.
"I and all the Andhakas and Vṛṣṇis shall follow you,
O lord of people, as will the Daśārhas, your attendants, and the Daśārṇas. O mighty-armed one, enjoy the kingdom together with your brothers, the Pāṇḍavas."
Mount the chariot together with your brothers, the Pāṇḍavas;
accompanied by prayers, burnt offerings, and various kinds of auspicious rites,
let the Draviḍas along with the Kuntalas go before you.
Let the Āndhras, the Tālacaras, the Cūcupas, and the Veṇupas,
as well as the Sūtas and Māgadhas, praise you today with many hymns;
and let the Pāṇḍavas proclaim the victory of Vasuṣeṇa.
Surrounded by the sons of Pṛthā like the moon by the stars,
O son of Kuntī, rule the kingdom and bring joy to Kuntī. Let your friends rejoice, and let your enemies be distressed.
"May you today have brotherly affection with your brothers, the Pāṇḍavas.
Karna said:
"O Keśava, without doubt you speak thus out of friendship and affection for me."
"O Vārṣṇeya, both out of friendship and out of a desire for my own welfare,
I acknowledge everything; according to the laws of righteousness (*dharma*), I am the son of Pāṇḍu, just as you consider me to be, O Kṛṣṇa, in accordance with the injunctions of the *dharmaśāstras*."
"O Janārdana, the maiden conceived me from the Sun;
and at the word of Āditya, she abandoned me once I was born. Thus was I born, O Kṛṣṇa; by law, I am the son of Pāṇḍu."
But I was cast aside by Kuntī in such a way that it was not well for me;
for as soon as the charioteer Adhiratha saw me, he took me home and,
out of affection, O Madhusūdana, gave me to Rādhā.
Out of affection for me, milk immediately flowed from Rādhā;
she accepted my urine and excrement, O Mādhava.
How could one like me perform the removal of her bodily waste?
A knower of dharma, constantly devoted to listening to the treatises on dharma,
even Sūta Adhiratha recognizes me as his son;
and out of affection, I too always recognize him as my father.
For he, O Mādhava, out of love for his son, had the birth rites and other ceremonies performed for me according to the rules prescribed in the scriptures, O Janārdana;
and he had the name Vasuṣeṇa bestowed upon me by the twice-born.
O Keśava, when I had reached youth, I married wives; O Janārdana, sons and grandsons were born to me from them. O Kṛṣṇa, my heart has become bound to them by the fetters of desire.
"Neither for the sake of the entire earth, nor for heaps of gold,
O Govinda, would I venture to speak a falsehood out of joy or fear,
since I am supported by Duryodhana within the family of Dhṛtarāṣṭra, O Kṛṣṇa."
For thirteen years, I have enjoyed a kingdom free from thorns;
and together with the Sūtas, I have repeatedly performed many sacrifices. Marriages and alliances have also been contracted by me along with the Sūtas.
"O Kṛṣṇa, it was by relying on me that Duryodhana made his preparations for weapons and entered into hostilities with the Pāṇḍavas, O Vārṣṇeya. Therefore,
O Acyuta, I shall be the one who advances against him in a single combat of chariots in battle."
Highly delighted, he chose the supreme hostility toward Savyasācin;
for whether out of fear of death or imprisonment, or even out of greed, O Janārdana,
I cannot bring myself to act falsely toward the wise son of Dhṛtarāṣṭra.
"For if I do not go today for a duel with Savyasācin,
O Hṛṣīkeśa, there will be infamy for both me and Pārtha.
Without doubt, O Madhusūdana, you would speak for the sake of our welfare."
"Without a doubt, the Pāṇḍavas would do everything under your command;
therefore, O Puruṣottama, you should establish a rule for this counsel.
I consider this to be beneficial here, O delighter of all the Yādavas."

If that righteous king, firm in his vows, should know me to be the first-born son of Kuntī, he will not accept the kingdom. And even if he were to obtain that great kingdom, O Madhusūdana, I would [not allow it].
"O subduer of enemies, I would rather bestow this prosperous kingdom upon Duryodhana alone;
let that very Yudhiṣṭhira remain the eternal king, righteous-souled as he is,
with Hṛṣīkeśa as his leader and Dhanañjaya as his warrior."
O Mādhava, the earth and its kingdom belong to him who has Bhīma the great chariot-warrior, Nakula, Sahadeva, the sons of Draupadī,
Dhṛṣṭadyumna the Pāñcālya, and the great chariot-warrior Sātyaki.
Uttamaujas, Yudhāmanyu, and Somaki Satyadharmā;
Cekitāna the king of Cedi, and the unconquered Śikhaṇḍin;
and likewise the Kekaya brothers, who have the color of indragopaka insects.
And Kuntibhoja, the great car-warrior with a complexion like Indra’s bow; Bhīmasena’s maternal uncle Senajit, the great car-warrior;
Śaṅkha, the son of Virāṭa; and you yourself, O Janārdana, are a treasure.
"O Kṛṣṇa, this great accumulation of the kṣatriyas has been accomplished;
this radiant kingdom, renowned among all kings, has been obtained by the son of Dhṛtarāṣṭra, O Vārṣṇeya. A sacrifice of weapons shall now take place."
"You shall be the knower of this sacrifice, O Janārdana; and you, Kṛṣṇa, shall perform the office of the *adhvaryu* in this rite.
And here, Bibhatsu, he of the monkey-banner, equipped for battle, shall be the *hotṛ*."
The Gāṇḍīva shall be the sacrificial ladle, and the prowess of men shall be the clarified butter.
O Mādhava, the Aindra, Pāśupata, Brāhma,
and Sthūṇākarṇa weapons shall be the mantras employed there by Savyasācin.
Following in his father’s footsteps— or perhaps even surpassing him in prowess—
