the son of Subhadrā will perform the *grāvastotra* there perfectly. Furthermore, Bhīma shall be the *udgātṛ*, and the exceedingly powerful one [Arjuna] the *prastotṛ*.
Roaring in battle, that tiger among men, the destroyer of elephant hosts,
and that righteous King Yudhiṣṭhira himself will remain there, constantly engaged in prayers and burnt offerings, performing the duties of the Brahman priest.

O Madhusūdana, there will be the sounds of conchs, drums, and kettledrums, along with loud lion-roars; he shall be worthy of the Subrahmaṇya invocation. And Nakula and Sahadeva, the illustrious sons of Mādrī, [shall also be present].
Those two of great prowess will properly perform the duties of the *śāmitra* there;
their chariot banners shall serve as the sacrificial posts (*yūpa*) for the sacrifice being spread out,
and they will become the Maitrāvaruṇa and Āgnīdhra priests of great power.
O Govinda, let the spears for this sacrifice— polished, with variegated shafts— be prepared, O Janārdana; likewise, let the barbed arrows, the nalīkas, the nārācas,
and those reinforced with calf-tooth tips be ready.
The lances shall be the Soma-vessels, and the shields the strainers;
the swords here shall be the sacrificial potsherds, and the heads the *puroḍāśa* cakes.
O Kṛṣṇa, blood shall be the oblation in this sacrifice.
The sacrificial fuel and the enclosing sticks were his spears and spotless maces; the members of the assembly were the disciples of Droṇa and of Kṛpa Śaradvat;
and the arrows released by the wielder of the Gāṇḍīva bow were the sacrificial strews.
Employed by the great car-warriors and urged on by Droṇa and the son of Droṇa,
Sātyaki will perform the duties of the *prātiprasthātṛ* priest;
here Dhṛtarāṣṭra’s son is the consecrated sacrificer (*dīkṣita*), and his great army is his wife.

"O mighty-armed one, when the ritual of the Atirātra sacrifice has been commenced, the immensely powerful Ghaṭotkaca will perform the office of the *śamitṛ* (the slayer). And the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) for this sacrifice shall be the majestic Dhṛṣṭadyumna."
Born from the dark purifier (Agni) during the performance of the Vaitāna rite,
O Kṛṣṇa, because I spoke harsh words to the Pāṇḍavas for the sake of pleasing the son of Dhṛtarāṣṭra, I now suffer for that deed.
"O Kṛṣṇa, when you see me slain by Savyasācin, then this sacrifice of his will have its funeral pyre. When the Pāṇḍava drinks the blood of Duḥśāsana..."
O Janārdana, when the two Pāñcāla princes strike down Droṇa and Bhīṣma, then the Soma-pressing will have been properly performed for the roaring one who roars;
at that time, O Janārdana, there shall be the conclusion of the sacrifice.
"O Mādhava, when the mighty Bhīmasena slays Duryodhana, then will the sacrifice of Dhṛtarāṣṭra’s son reach its completion;
and the daughters-in-law and granddaughters-in-law of Dhṛtarāṣṭra shall gather together."
O Keśava, with their lords slain, their sons killed, and their protectors gone,
they will weep together with Gāndhārī amidst the clamor of dogs, vultures, and ospreys;
O Janārdana, that shall be the final purificatory bath (*avabhṛtha*) at this sacrifice.
O bull among Kṣatriyas, O Madhusūdana, let not the Kṣatriyas— those advanced in learning and advanced in age— meet with a futile death on your account;
let the entire circle of the Kṣatriya order go to its end by the sword in a state of prosperity.
O Keśava, Kurukṣetra is the most meritorious place even among the three worlds.
Therefore, O Puṇḍarīkākṣa, perform here whatever you desire,
so that the entire warrior class, O Vārṣṇeya, may attain heaven in its entirety.
"O Janārdana, as long as the mountains and rivers shall endure,
so long shall this eternal sound born of his fame persist;
the Brahmins shall recount the great battle of the Mahābhārata."
O Vārṣṇeya, in the assemblies of the kṣatriyas, this [account] shall bring glory;
for those who hear it, there shall be long life, sons, and wealth, and even for mortals, it shall become a station in heaven.
"O Keśava, O scorcher of foes, always concealing our counsel, bring the son of Kuntī here for battle with me.
Saṃjaya said:
Having heard Karna’s words, Keshava, the slayer of enemy heroes,
then spoke these words with a smile, laughing gently:
"O Karna, does the prospect of attaining the kingdom not cause you distress?"
Indeed, you do not wish to rule the earth that has been given by me;
the victory of the Pāṇḍavas is certain—
of this there is no doubt whatsoever.
The victory-banner of the Pāṇḍava is seen,
the fierce king of monkeys raised aloft;
it is a divine illusion fashioned by Bhauvana.
Raising aloft banners as brilliant as Indra’s,
divine beings who inspire fear are seen there, appearing truly terrifying.
O Karṇa, the glorious banner of Dhanañjaya does not cling to mountains or trees; rising upwards and extending horizontally for the distance of a yojana, it stands in its full form.
When you see him in battle— raised high like fire itself, with white horses and Kṛṣṇa as his charioteer—
manifesting the Aindra weapon as well as both the Agneya and the Maruta weapons.

And when you behold Yudhiṣṭhira, the son of Kuntī, in battle, there will then be neither the Tretā, nor the Kṛta, nor the Dvāpara age; for the roar of the Gāṇḍīva will be like the crash of a thunderbolt.
Engaged in silent recitation and burnt offerings, protecting his own great army—
unassailable like the sun and scorching the enemy host—
at that time there will be neither the Tretā, nor the Kṛta, nor the Dvāpara ages.
When you see the mighty Bhīmasena in battle,
having drunk the blood of Duḥśāsana and dancing on the field of combat like a rutting elephant that has slain its rival, you will know he is invincible.
At that time, there will be no Tretā, no Kṛta, and no Dvāpara ages.
Not even a single one remains unemptied, nor is anything established in emptiness. The world-protectors do not remain, nor are they remembered as being doubled in number.

Neither seven nor nine other such numbers will be found there; in that place, there will be no number at all. When you behold the two sons of Mādrī, those great chariot-warriors, in the midst of battle—
Agitating the army of the sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra like two elephants, they plunged into the clash of weapons, crushing the chariots of the enemy heroes;
at that time, there was neither the Tretā nor the Kṛta, nor the Dvāpara age.
When you see Droṇa, the son of Śantanu, Kṛpa,
King Suyodhana, and Jayadratha the ruler of the Sindhus,
rushing swiftly toward battle in the fray, yet being held back by Savyasācin;
"Then there will be neither the Tretā, nor the Kṛta, nor the Dvāpara ages.
Having gone from here, O Karṇa, speak to Droṇa, the son of Śantanu, and Kṛpa:
'This month is gentle, with fodder and fuel easily obtained.'"
The land is abundant with ripe medicinal herbs and forests, rich in fruit and having few flies;
the water is free from mud, flavorful, and pleasant, being neither too hot nor too cold.
Furthermore, on the seventh day from now, the new moon will occur.
One should engage in battle there, for they say that [the goddess] has Śakra as her deity.
Likewise, you should say to all the kings who have arrived for battle:
"Whatever is desired by you, I shall indeed accomplish it all for you."
The kings and princes, following the will of Duryodhana,
having met their death by the sword, shall attain the highest state.
Sañjaya said:
Having heard those beneficial and auspicious words of Keśava, Karṇa,
after honoring Kṛṣṇa, the slayer of Madhu, spoke:
"O mighty-armed one, knowing me as I am, why do you wish to delude me?"
Regarding this total destruction of the earth that has now arrived,
the omens therein were I, Śakuni, Duḥśāsana,
and King Duryodhana, the son of Dhṛtarāṣṭra.
"Without doubt, O Kṛṣṇa, this great battle between the Pāṇḍavas and the Kurus has arrived— a terrible conflict, a mire of blood. Kings and princes alike have come under the sway of Duryodhana."
"Those who are consumed by the fire of weapons in battle shall go to the abode of Yama.
Indeed, O Madhusūdana, many terrible dreams are seen,
as well as ominous signs and most dreadful portents."
O Vārṣṇeya, these various hair-raising portents seem to proclaim the defeat of Dhṛtarāṣṭra’s son and the victory of Yudhiṣṭhira;
for a fierce and immensely radiant planet has seized the constellation presided over by Prajāpati.
Saturn afflicts living beings excessively as he causes them suffering;
and having made a retrograde motion in Jyeṣṭhā, O Madhusūdana,
Mars seeks Anurādhā as if to appease the constellation presided over by Mitra.
"Surely, O Kṛṣṇa, a great danger has arisen for the Kurus;
for especially, O Vārṣṇeya, does the planet afflict Citrā. The mark of the moon has been displaced, and Rāhu will approach the sun."
These meteors fall from the sky accompanied by thunderclaps and earthquakes;
the elephants groan and the horses shed tears.
O Mādhava, they take no pleasure even in water or fodder.
"When these omens have appeared, O mighty-armed one, they say that a terrible danger threatening the destruction of living beings has arrived;
for even when little has been eaten, a great amount of excrement is seen here."
"O Keśava, O Madhusūdana, among all the armies of Dhṛtarāṣṭra’s sons— among the horses, the elephants, and the men—
the wise say that this is a sign of impending defeat."
"O Kṛṣṇa, they say that the mounts of the Pāṇḍavas are delighted;
even the wild animals keep them to their right, which is a sign of victory for them.
O Keśava, all the wild animals pass to the left of Dhārtarāṣṭra."
Furthermore, incorporeal voices that cause distress to the people are a sign of his defeat. Peacocks, *puṣpaśakuna* birds, swans, cranes, and *cātaka* birds—
Flocks of *jīvaka* birds follow the Pāṇḍavas,
while vultures, crows, cranes, hawks, *yātudhānas*,
and hyenas follow the Kauravas; and swarms of flies also follow the Kauravas.
In the armies of Dhṛtarāṣṭra’s son, there is no sound of kettledrums;
yet the drums of the Pāṇḍavas resound even without being struck,
just as water wells roar like bulls.
O Mādhava, a rain of flesh and blood was showered by the god upon the armies of Dhṛtarāṣṭra’s son as a sign of their defeat;
likewise, a radiant city of the Gandharvas appeared before us.
With its walls, moats, and ramparts, and its beautiful gateways,
Kṛṣṇa stands there like a bolt, obscuring the sun at both the morning and evening twilights, signaling a great danger.
Birds with one wing, one eye, and one leg, dancers of terrible appearance,
emitted a dreadful cry— a sign of impending defeat. A solitary jackal howled dreadfully— a sign of impending defeat.
Black-necked birds, hanging down and terrifying, are flying toward the twilight; that is a sign of defeat.
Furthermore, O Madhusūdana, he first hates the Brāhmaṇas and his elders.
And even servants who are devoted [to him]— that is a sign of his defeat.
O Madhusūdana, the eastern quarter appears reddish, the southern has the color of weapons, and the western resembles an unbaked earthen vessel.
The northern direction has the luster of a conch shell; these are declared to be the colors of the directions.
Yet all the directions are ablaze, O Mādhava, portending great danger for the son of Dhṛtarāṣṭra amidst these signs of portentous omens.
O Acyuta, I saw Yudhiṣṭhira in a dream ascending a palace with a thousand pillars together with his brothers;
they were all seen wearing white turbans and white garments.
I perceive bright seats for all of them,
O Kṛṣṇa; and by me, O Janārdana, at the end of a dream, the earth was seen covered with entrails and fouled with blood.
Mounted upon a heap of bones, Yudhiṣṭhira of immeasurable prowess,
filled with joy, ate rice-pudding with ghee from a golden vessel;
Yudhiṣṭhira was seen by me swallowing the earth.
"Clearly he will enjoy this earth given by you;
Vṛkodara of terrible deeds,
that tiger among men, has ascended a high mountain, mace in hand, as if surveying this very earth."
"He will clearly destroy us all in the great battle;
this is known to me, O Hṛṣīkeśa, for where there is dharma, there is victory. That Dhananjaya, the wielder of the Gāṇḍīva bow, has mounted a pale-white elephant."
O Hṛṣīkeśa, blazing with supreme splendor together with you,
you shall slay all those kings in battle, headed by Duryodhana; of this I have no doubt, O Kṛṣṇa.
Nakula, Sahadeva, and the great car-warrior Sātyaki—
those tigers among men, their arms and necks adorned with pure bracelets and necklaces, and arrayed in white garlands and garments— mounted that supreme vehicle drawn by men.
"O Janārdana, these three high ministers are seen wearing white umbrellas and garments, and they too have white turbans;
O Keśava, recognize them among the armies of Dhṛtarāṣṭra’s son."
"Aśvatthāman, Kṛpa, and Kṛtavarman the Sātvata—
all these kings, O Mādhava, are seen wearing red turbans.
Bhīṣma and Droṇa, O Janārdana, have mounted a chariot yoked with camels."
"O mighty-armed one, O lord, together with me and the son of Dhṛtarāṣṭra,
we have set out toward the direction commanded by Agastya, O Janārdana;
in a very short time, we shall reach the abode of Yama."
"Both I and the other kings, and that entire circle of Kṣatriyas, shall enter the fire of the Gāṇḍīva; of this I have no doubt. Kṛṣṇa said:
"Surely this earth must now face its destruction,
for my words, O Karna, do not reach your heart,
even as the destruction of all beings is at hand, my dear."
"This improper course, appearing as if it were right, does not depart from my heart.
Karṇa said:
"O Kṛṣṇa, may we behold you alive after this great battle."
"O mighty-armed one, we have crossed over [this world] due to the destruction and slaughter of heroes;
or rather, O Kṛṣṇa, our reunion in heaven will surely take place. There, O sinless one, we shall meet with you once again."
Saṃjaya said:
Having spoken thus to Mādhava and having embraced him closely, Karṇa,
dismissed by Keśava, descended from the seat of the chariot.
Then, mounting his own chariot adorned with gold,
the son of Rādhā returned with us, his mind dejected. Thereupon Keśava, together with Sātyaki, proceeded even more swiftly.
Again addressing his driver with the words, "Go! Go!", Vaiśampāyana said: "When Kṛṣṇa’s mediation had failed and he had departed from the Kurus toward the Pāṇḍavas..."
Approaching Pṛthā, the Kṣattṛ spoke slowly as if grieving:
"O mother of living sons, you know my disposition, which has always been one of favor toward you;
yet Suyodhana does not accept my words, even though I cry out."
For that king Yudhiṣṭhira was supported by the Cedis, Pañcālas,
and Kekayas, as well as by Bhīma, Arjuna, Kṛṣṇa, Yuyudhāna, and the Naimiṣeyas; yet,
even while encamped at Upaplavya, he remained devoted solely to dharma.
Out of affection for his kinsmen, he desires [the kingdom] like a weak man longing for strength;
yet this King Dhṛtarāṣṭra, though advanced in years, finds no peace,
and intoxicated by pride in his sons, he persists upon the path of unrighteousness.
A mutual dissension has arisen among Jayadratha, Karṇa, Duḥśāsana, and the son of Subala due to their wicked intellect;
for indeed, by unrighteous means, this kingdom was seized from one who is most righteous.

For whomsoever this dharma shall become a continuous concern, who would not burn with grief while dharma is being forcibly carried away by the Kurus? When Keśava has departed without a peaceful settlement, the Pāṇḍavas will exert themselves in war.
"Then there will come a ruin of the Kurus, destroying their heroes;
thinking of this, I find no sleep by day or by night.
Having heard those words spoken by Kuntī out of concern for the welfare [of her sons], [Yudhiṣṭhira said:]
Wailing piteously and afflicted by grief, he reflected in his mind:
"Fie upon wealth, for the sake of which this great destruction of kinsmen has occurred;
indeed, in this battle, the defeat of these friends will surely follow."
The Pāṇḍavas, Cedis, Pāñcālas, and Yādavas have assembled;
if they should fight with the Bharatas, what indeed could be more painful than that? Behold the certain fault in war, as well as defeat in war.
"For one without wealth, death is better; for there is no victory when one's kinsmen have perished.
As I reflect thus, sorrow arises in my heart.
[The grandfather Śāṃtanava and the preceptor, the lord of warriors—]
And Karṇa, for the sake of Dhṛtarāṣṭra’s son, increases my fear. The preceptor Droṇa would never fight against his own disciples out of personal desire;
how then could he harbor ill-will toward the Pāṇḍavas? And so too with the Grandfather (Bhīṣma).
But this one alone is a man of false vision, following the evil-minded son of Dhṛtarāṣṭra;
constantly pursuing delusion, he is wicked and hates the Pāṇḍavas. He is particularly persistent in his pursuit of great misfortune and is moreover powerful.
That Karṇa has always been on the side of the Pāṇḍavas burns me now. Yet today, I hope that by approaching Karṇa, I may appease his mind regarding the Pāṇḍavas and show him the truth as it is.
There the Blessed One was gratified, and Durvāsas granted me a boon:
that while I was dwelling in my father’s house, there would be an invitation from the gods.
Thus, I am now in the inner apartments of King Kuntibhoja, held in high honor by him.
Reflecting in many ways with a grieving heart, she considered the relative strength of the mantras and the power of the Brahmin’s speech;
and because of her womanhood and her youth, she pondered this again and again.
At that time, protected by her confident nurse and surrounded by her circle of friends,
she avoided any transgression and guarded her father’s reputation,
thinking: "How indeed may I act rightly, and how may I remain free from offense?"
Thinking, "May I become [such]," and having paid homage to that brahmin,
I then approached the god Arka out of curiosity; yet, being but a maiden, I acted thus out of foolishness.
"He who was born from my womb while I was a maiden, and who has been raised by me like a son—
why would he not follow this wholesome advice that is likewise for his brother's benefit?
Having thus reflected, Kuntī resolved upon this supreme course of action.
Having set out for the sake of his duty, he went toward the Bhāgīrathī. Then, on the bank of the Gaṅgā, Pṛthā beheld her son Vṛṣa, who was compassionate, devoted to truth, and standing in attendance.
On the bank of the Gaṅgā, Pṛthā heard the sound of Vedic recitation;
standing behind him as he faced east with his arms raised,
that ascetic woman remained there, waiting for the conclusion of his prayers for the sake of her purpose.
Afflicted by the heat of the sun, the Kuru queen, the daughter of the Vṛṣṇis, stood upon Karṇa’s upper garment, withering like a garland of lotuses;
having performed her prayers until her back was scorched, she turned around, firm in her vows.
Having seen Kuntī, the highly effulgent, proud, and best of the upholders of dharma approached her with joined palms and saluted her according to custom; then,
smiling and bowing low, Vaikartana Vṛṣa spoke to Kuntī.
Karna said: "I am Radheya, the son of Adhiratha, Karna; I salute you. For what purpose have you come? Tell me, what may I do for you?"
Kuntī said:
"O Karṇa, you are the son of Kuntī, not the son of Rādhā; Adhiratha is not your father. You were not born in the family of a charioteer; know this to be my word."
"You were born of me as a son born of an unmarried woman (kānīna), borne within my womb as my first-born.
O dear son, you are Pārtha, born in the palace of Kuntibhoja. You are the sun, the deity Virocana, whose nature is to illuminate."
"O Karṇa, he begot you in me, the best among wielders of weapons—
earrings and armor bound upon you, a divine offspring endowed with splendor. O invincible son, you were born by me in my father's house."
That you, out of delusion, serve the sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra without having informed your brothers— that is not fitting for you, my son, especially so. This,
my son, is the fruit of dharma for men who are firm in their resolve toward dharma.
Since your father and your mother, who possesses singular vision, are pleased with you,
enjoy the prosperity of Yudhiṣṭhira— which was formerly acquired by Arjuna but seized through greed by the wicked sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra— having wrested it back from them.

Today let the Kurus behold the encounter between Karṇa and Arjuna; seeing that meeting with such brotherly affection, let the wicked bow down. Indeed, let Karṇa and Arjuna be to you as Rāma and Janārdana.
"What indeed in this world could be unachievable for you two when joined together?
O Karṇa, you will surely shine resplendent when surrounded by your five brothers,
just as Brahmā shines when surrounded by the Vedas with the Vedāṅgas as the fifth."
"Born with the most excellent virtues, the eldest among your noble kinsmen—do not call yourself 'the Sūta’s son'; you are Pārtha, O hero!
Vaiśampāyana said:
Then Karna heard a voice issuing from the sun, a speech that was difficult to transgress and full of affection, uttered by the Sun-god like a father:
"Pritha has spoken the truth; O Karna, do as your mother says."
"O tiger among men, it would have been better for you had you performed all of this;
yet, even when addressed thus by his mother and by his father Bhānu himself,
the mind of Karṇa, who was firm in truth, did not waver at all."
Karna said:
"I do not lack faith in the words spoken by you, O Kshatriya;
this performance of your command shall be for me a gateway to dharma."
"O lady, the great transgression that you have committed against me has defiled me;
it is that which destroys your fame and renown. Furthermore, though I am born a kṣatriya, I have not attained the honors due to a kṣatriya."
What greater evil could an enemy have wrought against me than this? At the very time for action, you showed no compassion toward me; today, you urge me on when my preparations have long since passed.
"Indeed, you did not previously act for my benefit as a mother would;
today you awaken me, seeking only your own welfare.
For who indeed would not be distressed by Dhanañjaya when he is accompanied by Kṛṣṇa?"
Who would not recognize me today as I have gone to the assembly of the Pārthas, fearing for my life?
Previously unknown as a brother, I have now been revealed at the time of battle. If I go over to the Pāṇḍavas, what will the warrior class say of me?
"Always provided with all my desires and greatly honored,
how could I indeed render that fruitless for the sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra—
those who, having instigated enmity with others, constantly attend upon me?"
They always pay homage to me, just as the Vasus do to Vāsava;
how can I today shatter the hopes of those who, by my very life-force, were capable of confronting their enemies?
How could I abandon those who, with me as their raft, desire to cross the impassable battle— those who, longing for the further shore, seek it when no other shore exists?
For this very moment has arrived for those who live under the protection of Dhṛtarāṣṭra’s son.
I must discharge my debt there, even at the cost of not protecting my life;
for those who have been well-supported and have achieved their purpose, when the time for action arrives,
become unsteady and wicked, disregarding what has been done for them and acting treacherously.
For those who are royal sinners, who have misappropriated the sustenance provided by their master,
neither this world nor the next exists, for they are doers of evil deeds.
For the sake of Dhṛtarāṣṭra’s sons, I shall fight with your sons.
Relying on my strength and power, I would certainly not speak a falsehood to you; yet,
out of regard for compassion and the conduct befitting a virtuous man,
I shall not carry out these words of yours today, even though they serve your purpose.
"However, this undertaking of yours shall not be in vain toward me;
I will not slay your sons in battle, though they be deserving of death and capable of enduring it—
namely Yudhiṣṭhira, Bhīma, and the twins— with the sole exception of Arjuna."
My battle shall be with Arjuna within Yudhiṣṭhira’s army;
for by slaying Arjuna in combat, I would attain my goal,
and even if slain by Savyasācin, I would be endowed with glory.
"O illustrious lady, those five sons of yours shall never perish—
whether they be without Arjuna and with Karṇa, or with both Arjuna and Karṇa— once I have been slain.
Vaiśampāyana said:
Having heard these words of Karṇa, Kuntī, trembling with grief, embraced her son Karṇa—who remained unshaken by his fortitude—and said:
"It must indeed be so; by this, the Kauravas shall go to their destruction."
"O Karṇa, as you say, destiny is indeed more powerful.
O crusher of enemies, you have granted immunity to your four brothers; acknowledge that promise as the means of release from this conflict."
"Health and well-being," said Pṛthā to Karṇa;
Karṇa replied to her with pleasure, and then they both departed in separate directions.
Vaiśampāyana said:

Having arrived at Upaplavya from Hastinapura, Keśava, the subduer of enemies, related everything that had happened regarding the Pāṇḍavas. After conversing for a very long time and deliberating again and again, he spoke.
Having dismissed all the kings headed by Virāṭa, Śauri went to his own residence for the sake of rest; meanwhile,
when the sun had set, the five Pāṇḍava brothers [did likewise].
Having performed their twilight devotions and meditating upon him alone with their minds fixed on him,
they summoned Kṛṣṇa of the Daśārhas and again held counsel together.
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
"O lotus-eyed one, having gone to Nāgapura, what was said by you to the son of Dhṛtarāṣṭra in the assembly? You ought to tell us that.
Vāsudeva said:

"Having gone to Nāgapura, I spoke to the son of Dhṛtarāṣṭra in the assembly hall words that were true, beneficial, and for his own good; yet that evil-minded man did not accept them. Yudhiṣṭhira said:
O Hṛṣīkeśa, when he had fallen onto that wrong path, what did the grandfather, the elder of the Kurus, say to the impatient Duryodhana?
Or, O mighty-armed one, what did the preceptor, the son of Bharadvāja, say?
"What did his father Dhṛtarāṣṭra, or Gandhārī, say to him?
What did our younger father, Kṣattṛ, the best among the upholders of dharma,
say to the son of Dhṛtarāṣṭra as he was tormented by grief for his sons?"
Furthermore, O Janārdana, tell us what all those kings who are seated in the assembly have said according to the truth;
for you have already spoken everything regarding the two leaders of the Kurus.

For those words of Dhṛtarāṣṭra’s son in the assembly of the Kurus— words that were both hostile and improper— did not enter his heart, as he was a dull-witted man overcome by desire and greed, though he considered himself wise.
"O Keśava, that which is unpleasant to my heart does not remain there;
O Lord Govinda, I wish to hear their words.
O Father, act in such a way that Time (Death) may not seize them."
"For you, O Kṛṣṇa, are our refuge; you are our protector and you are our teacher.
Vāsudeva said:
"Listen, O King, to how King Suyodhana was addressed with these words."
"O king of kings, listen to me regarding what occurred in the assembly hall in the midst of the Kurus.
When these words were spoken by me, the son of Dhṛtarāṣṭra laughed.
Then Bhīṣma, becoming greatly incensed, spoke these words."
"O Duryodhana, understand this which I speak to you for the sake of the lineage;
having heard it, O tiger among kings, act for the benefit of your own family. My father, dear one, O King, was the world-renowned Śantanu."
I was his only son, the best among those who possess sons. The thought arose in him: "How might there be a second son?
For the wise declare that one who has an only son is effectively sonless."
"Lest the lineage should come to an end, and so that my fame might spread far and wide, I understood her desire and brought Kālī as a wife,
having made a difficult vow for the sake of my father and the family."

"O you who are well-known to me, I dwell here as one who is not a king and whose vital energy is directed upward (a celibate), abiding by my vow with full confidence. From her was born the mighty-armed and illustrious scion of the Kuru lineage."
"The righteous-souled Vicitravīrya was my younger brother, O King.
When my father had ascended to heaven, I installed him in the sovereignty. Indeed, becoming his servant and a subordinate, I attended upon King Vicitravīrya."
O Indra among kings, I brought home for him wives who were his equals; you have heard many times how I defeated hosts of monarchs. Thereafter, I entered into a duel with Rāma in battle.
For he had been exiled by these citizens out of fear of Rāma;
moreover, being excessively addicted to his wives, he contracted consumption.
And when the lord of the gods did not send rain upon the kingdom that was without a king, [the people sought him out].
Then the subjects, oppressed by the fear of hunger, rushed toward me alone.
The subjects said:
"All the subjects are exhausted; become our king for our well-being."
"Drive away the calamities; may it be well with you, O enhancer of Śantanu’s lineage! All your subjects are being tormented by most dreadful diseases;
O son of Gaṅgā, only a few remain—you ought to protect them."
"O hero, having dispelled diseases, protect your subjects according to dharma. While you live, let the kingdom not go to ruin.
Bhīṣma said:

Even as the subjects were crying out, my mind was not at all agitated, for I was guarding my vow and likewise remembering my virtuous conduct. Then, O Great King, the citizens and my auspicious mother Kālī [approached].
My servants, priests, teachers, and many learned Brahmins,
deeply distressed, constantly said to me, "Become the king!
"Having obtained you, this kingdom protected by Pratīpa will perish."
"O high-minded one, do you indeed become king for our benefit!
Thus addressed, with palms joined in reverence, I was deeply distressed and afflicted;
yet out of respect for my father, O son, I made a solemn promise to them.
"For he was one whose vital energy was drawn upward, a kingless man, yet for the sake of the lineage again and again.
Then, with palms joined in reverence, I sought to appease my mother:
"O Mother, born of Śantanu and upholding the Kuru dynasty, [how could I do this?]"
"O King, lest I should repeatedly make my promise false—
and especially for your sake— do not appoint me to this burden. O mother, you who are so fond of your son, I am your servant and your slave."
Having thus entreated my mother and the people,
O great king, I then besought the great sage Vyāsa regarding my brother’s wife;
together with my mother, I then propitiated that ṛṣi.
I indeed requested a favor for the sake of offspring, and he granted it.
O best of the Bharatas, he then begot three sons;
however, because he was blind and lacked physical faculties, your father was not the king.
The high-souled Pāṇḍu became king, renowned throughout the world.
He was the king, and these sons of yours are the heirs to their father's inheritance. My dear son, do not engage in strife; let half of the kingdom be given to them.
"While I am alive, what man here would rule the kingdom? Do not disregard my words; I always desire your welfare.
O son, O King, there is no distinction for me between you and them."

This is the opinion of your father, of Gāndhārī, and of Vidura; it is what the elders have said, which you ought to hear. Do not disregard my words, lest you destroy yourself, as well as the entire earth.
Vāsudeva said:
After Bhīṣma had spoken, Droṇa, who was skilled in speech, addressed Duryodhana in the midst of the kings, saying, "May you be blessed."

Just as Pratīpa and Śantanu, my dear, rose up for the sake of the lineage, so too did Devavrata Bhīṣma remain steadfast for the sake of the lineage. Then there was King Pāṇḍu, true to his word and master of his senses.
The righteous-souled king of the Kurus, firm in his vows and well-composed,
bestowed the kingdom upon his eldest son, the wise Dhṛtarāṣṭra; likewise, he who increased the Kuru lineage gave it to his younger brother, Vidura.
Then, O King, having established that infallible one upon the throne,
the Kuru prince, being sinless, departed for the forest together with his two wives.
Vidura, however, remained standing nearby and waited upon him with humble devotion.
Like a servant, that tiger among men raised the yak-tail fan;
then, O dear one, all the subjects attended upon Dhṛtarāṣṭra, the lord of people,
according to the prescribed rites, just as they had done for King Pāṇḍu.
Having entrusted the kingdom to Dhṛtarāṣṭra and Vidura,
Pāṇḍu, the conqueror of enemy cities, wandered over the entire earth. He was occupied with the accumulation of the treasury, the distribution of gifts, and the supervision of his dependents.
Vidura, true to his promise, was in charge of the maintenance of all;
and the highly energetic Bhīṣma, the conqueror of enemy cities, supervised the king’s activities regarding peace and war, as well as his personal attendants.
King Dhṛtarāṣṭra, possessed of great strength, sits upon his throne constantly attended by the high-souled Vidura;
how is it that, born in such a lineage, you resolve to bring about the destruction of that family?
"O lord of men, enjoy these pleasures together with your brothers;
I say this not out of any wretchedness, nor for the sake of wealth in any way,
O best of kings— I eat only what has been given by Bhīṣma, and not by you."
"O lord of men, I shall not seek a means of livelihood from you;
where Bhīṣma is, there Droṇa is, so do what Bhīṣma tells you. O crusher of enemies, let half the kingdom be given to the sons of Pāṇḍu."
"O dear one, my teacherhood toward you and toward them has always been equal.
As Aśvatthāman is to me, so too is the one with white horses (Arjuna).
What is the use of much talk? Where there is dharma, there is victory."
When this had been said by Droṇa of immeasurable splendor, O Great King,
Vidura, who is true to his promise and knows the dharma, turned back and looked toward his father’s face, and then spoke these words.
"O Devavrata, understand these words as I speak them:
this Kuru lineage, which had perished, has been raised up again by you.
Yet, you disregard my words as I lament."

"Who is this man named Duryodhana, a defiler of his lineage in this family, whose mind you follow, being yourself overcome by greed— for him who is ignoble, ungrateful, and whose heart is destroyed by avarice?"
"He who transgresses the instruction of his father, who perceives both dharma and worldly interest— these Kurus are surely perishing because of Duryodhana's actions;
O great king, act in such a way that they do not utterly perish."
O you of great splendor, do not destroy me and Dhṛtarāṣṭra, whom you have already fashioned like a painter fashioning a painting; do not let them perish,
just as Prajāpati, having created his offspring, might then withdraw them.

Do not remain indifferent, O mighty-armed one, while witnessing the destruction of your lineage! If your intellect has now perished as ruin stands before you, then go to the forest together with me and Dhṛtarāṣṭra.
"Or, having bound the deceitful and evil-minded son of Dhṛtarāṣṭra, let this kingdom now properly be protected by the Pāṇḍavas. Be gracious, O tiger among kings; a great destruction is foreseen."
Having spoken thus concerning the Pāṇḍavas, the Kurus, and the kings of immeasurable splendor, Vidura, with a dejected mind, ceased speaking;
he then remained lost in thought, sighing again and again.
Then the daughter of King Subala,
fearing the destruction of her lineage, spoke words consistent with dharma and artha to the evil-minded and cruel Duryodhana:
In the presence of the kings, he spoke to his son out of anger:
"Those kings who have entered the royal assembly, as well as the brahmin-sages and the other members of the court."
Listen, for I shall declare your transgression,
you who are sinful along with your ministers and retinue: the kingdom of the Kurus was to be enjoyed by them in succession.
"This is our family tradition passed down through generations.
You, O evil-minded one of cruel deeds,
are destroying the kingdom of the Kurus through your misconduct."
The wise Dhṛtarāṣṭra is established in the kingdom,
and his younger brother is the far-sighted Vidura;
having bypassed these two, how can [you] hold the sovereignty?
O Duryodhana, out of delusion you seek [this] today;
yet both the King and the high-souled Kṣattṛ must remain dependent upon Bhīṣma while he stands firm.
But this high-souled one, the son of the River, the best among men, through his knowledge of dharma, has no desire for the kingdom;
yet this invincible kingdom of Pāṇḍu—
Today his sons alone prevail, and no others;
this entire kingdom belongs to the Pāṇḍavas,
inherited from their grandfather and passed down to their sons and grandsons.
Whatever the high-souled leader of the Kurus, the wise Devavrata, who is true to his promise, says—
that we must all carry out without violating righteousness.
While duly observing their own duties with the permission of the one of great vows,
the king should speak exactly as Vidura says.
That task should be undertaken by your friends,
having appointed them and prioritizing righteousness for a very long time; this kingdom of the Kurus has been obtained through justice.
Let Yudhiṣṭhira, the son of Dharma,
indeed rule, being urged by King Dhṛtarāṣṭra and likewise placed at the forefront by the son of Śaṃtanu.
Vāsudeva said:
"O lord of men, when Gāndhārī had spoken thus, Dhṛtarāṣṭra,
the ruler of people, spoke these words to Duryodhana in the midst of the kings."
"O Duryodhana, my son, listen to this which I shall say to you;
act accordingly for your own welfare, if you have any respect for your father.
In former times, Soma was the lord of creatures and the increaser of the Kuru lineage."
Yayāti, the son of Nahuṣa, was indeed the sixth [son] born from Soma.
He had five sons who were the best among royal sages;
of them, the lord Yadu, possessed of great splendor, became the eldest.
He had three sons: Druhyu, Anu, and Pūru. Of these, Pūru was the youngest, and he was the one who increased our lineage, having been begotten by Śarmiṣṭhā, the daughter of Vṛṣaparvan.
And Yadu, O best of the Bharatas, became the son of Devayānī;
he was the grandson, dear one, of Śukra Kāvya of immeasurable splendor,
the founder of the Yādava lineage, powerful and esteemed for his heroism.

But he, filled with pride and of very dull intellect, despised the Kṣatriyas; deluded by the arrogance of his strength, he did not abide by his father’s command. Out of a groundless greed for the kingdom, he brought about the destruction of his lineage.
And having humiliated his father and his brothers, that unconquered and powerful Yadu became the sole ruler over the earth bounded by the four oceans;
having brought all kings under his control, he dwelt in the city named after the elephant (Hastinapura).
Then his father Yayāti, the son of Nahuṣa, being extremely enraged,
cursed his son, O son of Gāndhārī, and deposed him from the kingdom;
and so did his brothers who followed him, being arrogant in their strength.
Then Yayāti, filled with rage, cursed those sons as well. Thereupon, that best of kings installed his youngest son, Pūru— who remained obedient to his will and was compliant— in the kingdom.

Thus, even an elder brother who is arrogant does not inherit the kingdom; rather, younger brothers inherit the kingdom through service to their elders. In the same way, my grandfather was a knower of all dharmas.
Pratīpa, the protector of the earth, was renowned throughout the three worlds.
While that lion among kings was ruling his kingdom with righteousness,
three illustrious sons, equal to the gods, were born to him.
Devāpi was the eldest; after him came Bāhlīka;
and the third, O dear one, was Śaṃtanu, my wise grandfather.
But Devāpi, that best of kings, possessed great splendor yet suffered from leprosy.
He was righteous and truthful, devoted to serving his father;
he was esteemed by the people of both the city and the countryside, honored by the virtuous,
and dear to the hearts of all, both young and old— Devāpi.
Wise, true to his word, and devoted to the welfare of all beings,
he abided by the instructions of his father as well as those of the brahmins;
he was the beloved brother of Bāhlīka and of the high-souled Śantanu.
And there was supreme brotherly affection among those high-souled ones as they remained united.
Then, in the course of time, that best of kings, having grown old,
had the materials for his consecration prepared according to the scriptures.
And the conqueror caused all auspicious rites to be performed;
yet the brahmins and the elders, together with the people of the city and the countryside,
all sought to prevent the consecration of Devāpi.
Having heard that his consecration had been prevented, the king’s throat choked with tears; the monarch grieved for his son.
Thus he was generous, a knower of dharma, and true to his promise.
"Though he is beloved by his subjects, he is nonetheless afflicted with a skin disease;
the gods do not favor a protector of the earth who has deficient limbs.
Thinking thus, those bulls among the twice-born dissuaded the best of kings.
Then, his soul deeply distressed and overwhelmed by grief for his son,
Devāpi died; seeing him dead,
Bāhlīka abandoned the kingdom and settled in the forest, taking refuge in the family of his maternal uncle.
Having abandoned his father and brothers, he reached that prosperous city. Permitted by Bāhlīka, O King, the world-renowned Śantanu,
upon the death of his father, ruled the kingdom as king.
In that very same way, O Bhārata, the wise Pāṇḍu, having reflected upon this matter, deprived me— the eldest— of the kingdom on the grounds that I was deficient in limb; yet Pāṇḍu,
though he was the younger, obtained the kingdom as king.

Upon the destruction of his sons, O subduer of enemies, this kingdom shall belong to me, who am currently excluded from the succession; how then can you desire the kingdom? For, being the son of one who is not a king and lacking ownership yourself, you wish to seize what belongs to another.
The high-souled prince Yudhiṣṭhira is the rightful heir to this kingdom obtained through justice, and he is the protector of these Kuru people.
He is a ruler of great majesty,
true to his word, ever vigilant,
established in the scriptures, and virtuous toward his kinsmen.
Beloved by his subjects, compassionate toward his friends, with senses conquered, he was the protector of virtuous people; endowed with forgiveness, endurance, self-control, and straightforwardness.
Truthfulness in vows, learning, vigilance,
compassion for living beings, and instruction—
all these royal qualities are present in Yudhiṣṭhira.
"You are not a prince, you are of ignoble conduct, greedy toward your kinsmen, and evil-minded;
this kingdom has come to you by hereditary succession from others."
O ill-behaved one, how will you be able to take it? Free yourself from delusion and give up half the kingdom, along with its mounts and its retinue.
"Therefore, O lord of men, the remainder of your life shall belong only to you and your younger brother.
Vāsudeva said:
When Bhīṣma, Droṇa, Vidura, Gāndhārī, and Dhṛtarāṣṭra had spoken thus, the dull-witted one did not understand;
shaking them off, he rose up in anger, his eyes bloodshot with rage.
The kings, having renounced their lives, pursued him from behind.
And he commanded those evil-minded monarchs again and again: "Set out for Kurukṣetra; today is the day of Puṣya."
Then those rulers of the earth, having appointed Bhīṣma as their commander-in-chief, set forth with their armies, joyful yet impelled by Time. Eleven akṣauhiṇīs of the kings assembled together.
At their head, Bhīṣma, whose banner bears the palm tree, shone resplendent. O lord of the people, do what is appropriate and timely in this matter.
These are the words spoken by Bhīṣma, as well as by Droṇa and Vidura.
O Bhārata, O King, this which occurred in the assembly of the Kurus has been told to you by me in the presence of Gāndhārī and Dhṛtarāṣṭra. At the outset,
O King, I employed conciliation, desiring brotherly affection.
Because of the non-differentiation of the Kuru lineage and for the sake of the increase of my subjects, division is appropriate for me once conciliation is not accepted; likewise,
the recounting of deeds associated with both gods and men is necessary.
When Suyodhana did not heed my words preceded by conciliation,
then, O Bhārata, I brought together all the kings and sowed dissension among them, displaying wonders that were both terrible and dreadful.
O Lord, superhuman deeds have been displayed by me;
having rebuked those kings and treated Suyodhana as if he were a blade of grass, I have repeatedly terrified the son of Rādhā and the son of Subala.
Having repeatedly pointed out the inferiority of the sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra and their faults,
and having divided all the kings through my words and counsel,
I then spoke again with conciliation and the offer of gifts.
Because of the non-differentiation of the Kuru lineage and likewise because of the necessity of their duties,
all those sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra, Bhīṣma, and Vidura should remain submissive, casting aside pride and acting as inferiors to the Pāṇḍavas.
Let them grant you the kingdom, and let them be without power;
as King Bhīṣma and Vidura have said, so let it be.
Let the entire kingdom be yours; relinquish only five villages.
"O best of kings, she must certainly be maintained by your father.
Thus addressed, that evil-minded man did not relinquish his intent;
he saw no other way than the fourth punishment for those sinners.
The lords of men have set out for Kurukṣetra to meet their destruction.
I have told you all this that occurred in the assembly of the Kurus;
they will not surrender the kingdom to you without war, O Pāṇḍava.
"All causes of destruction have arrived for those whose death is imminent.
Vaiśampāyana said:
Having heard the words of Janārdana, Yudhiṣṭhira, the King of Dharma, [spoke].
The righteous-souled one spoke to his brothers in the presence of Keśava:
"You have heard what occurred in the assembly hall in the gathering of the Kurus,
and you have all taken to heart every word spoken by Keśava."
"Therefore, O best of men, arrange my army for me; let these seven akṣauhiṇīs assemble for victory. Learn now of their seven renowned commanders."
Drupada and Virāṭa, Dhṛṣṭadyumna and Śikhaṇḍin,
Sātyaki and Cekitāna, and the heroic Bhīmasena—
all these leaders of the army are warriors who would lay down their lives.
All were knowers of the Vedas and heroes; all were firm in their well-performed vows. They were modest and possessed of statesmanship, all being experts in warfare.
They were skilled in the use of arrows and missiles, as well as combatants with every kind of weapon.
"He who is the leader even of the seven armies, who knows their divisions,
and who could withstand Bhīṣma in battle— who is like a fire with arrows for its flames—
tell me of him here, O Sahadeva, O joy of the Kurus."
"O tiger among men, who in our own opinion is fit to be our commander-in-chief?
Sahadeva replied:
"The lord of the earth [Yudhiṣṭhira] is endowed with [virtues], shares our sorrows as one, and is possessed of great prowess."
Relying upon that knower of dharma, we shall pursue our own respective portions:
the powerful Virāṭa of Matsya, skilled in weapons and fierce in battle,
will withstand Bhīṣma and those great car-warriors in combat.
Vaiśampāyana said:
When Sahadeva had spoken these words, Nakula, who was skilled in speech, immediately thereafter addressed him with this statement.
In age, according to the scriptures, in fortitude, in lineage, and in noble birth; modest, of distinguished family, illustrious, and proficient in all the sciences;
he learned the Veda and the weapons from Bharadvāja—he was invincible and true to his promise.
He who constantly vies with Droṇa and the mighty Bhīṣma,
this commander of the army is worthy of praise at the head of the assembly of kings;
surrounded by sons and grandsons, he is like a tree with a hundred branches.
That lord of the earth, a hero who graces the assembly, performed severe austerities together with his wife out of wrath for the destruction of Droṇa;
that bull among kings always sustains us as if he were our father.
"Let our father-in-law Drupada lead our army at the front;
it is my conviction that he will withstand Droṇa and Bhīṣma as they advance.
For that king is a master of divine weapons and is a friend of the descendant of Aṅgiras."
When the two sons of Mādrī had thus stated their own opinions, O descendant of Kuru,
Savyasācin, the son of Vāsava who is equal to Vāsava himself, spoke these words:
"This man, by the power of his asceticism and by pleasing the ṛṣis..."
A divine person appeared, flame-colored and possessed of great strength;
armed with a bow, clad in armor, and bearing a sword, he rose from the sacrificial fire-pit, having mounted a chariot yoked with excellent celestial horses.
Roaring like a great cloud with the sound of his chariot, the heroic and powerful one— possessing the sturdy frame of a lion, the valorous stride of a lion,
the chest of a lion, mighty arms, and a lion-like breast— is endowed with great strength.

The hero roars like a lion; he has the shoulders of a lion and great splendor. He has beautiful eyebrows, fine teeth, a handsome jaw, and beautiful arms; his face is lovely and his body is well-proportioned. He has beautiful collarbones, wide-set eyes, and beautiful feet that are firmly established.
Impervious to all weapons like a rutting elephant,
truthful and with his senses conquered, he was born for the destruction of Droṇa.
I consider Dhṛṣṭadyumna capable of withstanding the arrows of Bhīṣma.
In battle, Rāma endured those [arrows] whose touch was like that of a thunderbolt, which were like serpents with flaming mouths,
equal in speed to the messengers of Yama, resembling fire upon impact,
and as terrible as the crash of a thunderbolt.
"I do not see any man, O King, who could withstand that one of great vows, except for Dhṛṣṭadyumna; such is the thought fixed in my mind.
He is considered by me to be a swift-handed general, a versatile warrior."
"Clad in impenetrable armor, glorious as a leader of an elephant herd,"—
when Arjuna had spoken thus, Bhīma took up his speech.
Bhīma said:
"O Indra among kings, the Siddhas and the assembled Rishis declare that Śikhaṇḍin, the son of Drupada, was born for the purpose of slaying [Bhīṣma]; for him who,
in the midst of battles, manifests divine weapons."
Men shall behold his form as if that of the high-souled Rāma; O King,
I do not see anyone in battles who could pierce Śikhaṇḍin with a weapon when he stands armored upon his chariot in the fray.
"O King, no one other than the heroic Śikhaṇḍin can withstand Bhīṣma of the great vows in a single combat of chariots; he, I consider, shall be my commander-in-chief.
Yudhiṣṭhira said:

"O dear one, Keśava, whose soul is established in dharma, knows everything regarding the essence and the lack of essence, and the strength and weakness of the entire world— both what has passed and what is yet to come. Let him whom Kṛṣṇa of the Daśārhas calls upon be our commander of the army."

Whether he has mastered the weapons or not, whether he is old or young— he is our root in victory, and he, dear father, is our root in defeat. In him rest our lives and our kingdom, our existence and non-existence, and our happiness and sorrow.

"He is the Ordainer and the Disposer; success is established in him. He whom Kṛṣṇa of the Daśārhas calls upon is fit to be our commander-in-chief. Let that best of speakers speak, for the night is passing away."
Then, having appointed as our commander one who acts under the will of Kṛṣṇa,
we shall set out for the field of battle once the remainder of the night has passed,
with our weapons consecrated and our auspicious rites performed.
Vaiśampāyana said:
Having heard those words of the wise Dharmarāja,
the lotus-eyed one (Kṛṣṇa), looking toward Dhananjaya, spoke.
"O great king, these whom you have named are also mine;
they are the leaders of your army, heroes who fight with valor. Indeed, all of them are capable of crushing your enemies."
For these would strike fear even into Indra in a great battle, let alone into the sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra— those greedy and evil-minded men. Indeed,
O mighty-armed subduer of foes, I too have acted for the sake of your pleasure.

O Bhārata, a great effort was made there so that peace might prevail; the debt toward Dharma has been discharged, and those who wish to speak should not be censured. That foolish and unwise man considers himself to have achieved his purpose.
The son of Dhṛtarāṣṭra, though afflicted by illness, considers himself strong. Let the army be properly arrayed, for they are regarded by you as capable of being slain;
the sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra will not be able to stand when they behold Dhanañjaya.
Bhīmasena, enraged, and the twins who resemble Yama;
the indignant Dhṛṣṭadyumna with Yuyudhāna as his second; Abhimanyu, the sons of Draupadī, and also Virāṭa and Drupada.
And other lords of men, commanders of akṣauhiṇīs, firm in their prowess— our powerful army, invincible and unassailable,
will slay the host of Dhṛtarāṣṭra’s sons in battle; of this there is no doubt.
"I consider Dhṛṣṭadyumna to be the commander-in-chief, O subduer of enemies.
When Kṛṣṇa had spoken thus, those best of men were filled with joy;
from their delighted minds, a great roar arose.
Then, as the troops hurried and rushed about,
there arose from all sides the tumultuous sound of horses and elephants, the rattling of chariot wheels, and the blaring of conchs and drums.
That fierce gathering of forces was like an agitated ocean,
formidable with chariots, infantry, and elephants, as turbulent as if with great waves;
it was filled with those running, challenging one another, and fastening on their armor.
As the Pāṇḍavas set out with their armies in every direction,
their host appeared like the full Ganges, difficult to withstand.
In the vanguard stood Bhīmasena and the two sons of Mādrī, all clad in armor.
The son of Subhadrā, the sons of Draupadī, Dhṛṣṭadyumna the son of Pṛṣata,
the Prabhadrakas, and the Pañcālas, led by Bhīmasena, advanced;
then a roar arose like that of the ocean during the full moon.
The roar of those joyful warriors as they marched forth seemed to touch the very heavens. The delighted and armored combatants were capable of tearing apart the enemy ranks;
in their midst went King Yudhiṣṭhira, the son of Kuntī.

Wagons, market-stalls, and dwellings; all vehicles and draft animals; the treasury, machines, and weapons; those who are physicians and healers; and whatever force is weak, as well as those who are emaciated and frail.
Having gathered those things, the king departed along with his attendants; meanwhile,
the truthful Draupadī, princess of Pañcāla,
returned to Upaplavya accompanied by women and surrounded by male and female servants.
Having made preparations for their primary defense with both stationary and mobile military outposts,
the sons of Pāṇḍu set forth with a vast army,
surrounded by Brahmins and distributing cattle and gold.
Being thus praised, O King, they departed on chariots adorned with jewels:
the Kekayas, Dhṛṣṭaketu, Abhibhū the son of the King of Kāśī,
Śreṇimān, Vasudāna, and the unconquered Śikhaṇḍin.
Joyful, satisfied, clad in armor, bearing weapons, and fully adorned,
they all followed King Yudhiṣṭhira, surrounding him on every side.
Virāṭa, Yajñasena the Somaka, and others took their positions at the rear.
Sudharmā, Kuntibhoja, and the sons of Dhṛṣṭadyumna brought four ten-thousand units of chariots, five times as many horses,
ten times as many infantry, and sixty thousand cavalrymen.
Then Anādhṛṣṭi, Cekitāna, the king of the Cedis, and Sātyaki, having surrounded Vāsudeva and Dhanañjaya, all advanced. Having reached Kurukṣetra, those strikers drew up their armies in battle array.
The Pāṇḍavas appeared like bellowing bulls;
having plunged into Kurukṣetra, those subduers of enemies blew their conchs,
and likewise Vāsudeva and Dhanañjaya blew their two conchs.
Hearing the roar of the Pāñcajanya conch, which was like the crash of a thunderbolt,
all the troops rejoiced on every side;
it was joined by the sound of conchs and drums and the lion-like roars of the swift warriors.
He made the earth, the atmosphere, and the oceans resound.
Then, King Yudhiṣṭhira encamped his army in a level and pleasant region abounding in fodder and fuel.
Having avoided cremation grounds, temples of the gods,
hermitages of the great seers, sacred fords, and shrines,
the lord of the earth [established it] in a region that was sweet, free of saline soil, auspicious, and holy.
Yudhiṣṭhira, the son of Kuntī, caused a camp to be established;
then, having risen again, refreshed and with his mounts rested,
he set forth surrounded by hundreds of thousands of lords of the earth.
Having routed hundreds of the Dhārtarāṣṭra troops stationed in their divisions, Keśava, together with Pārtha, moved about on all sides;
and Dhṛṣṭadyumna, the son of Pṛṣata, measured out the camp.
And the noble car-warrior Satyaki, the powerful Yuyudhana,
having reached the sacred river Hiraṇvatī in Kurukṣetra— a river with excellent landing-stairs, pure water, and free from pebbles and mud— [remained there].
O Bhārata, Keśava had a moat dug there and,
for the sake of protection, stationed his army there after giving them instructions;
such was the arrangement for the camp of the high-souled Pāṇḍavas.
Keśava caused such [ships] to be built for the lords of men—
providing abundant water and timber, most difficult to attack,
and stocked with various kinds of food and provisions by the hundreds and thousands.
There, O Indra among kings, were the highly precious pavilions of the various kings, each situated separately like celestial chariots upon the surface of the earth. There,
hundreds of wise artisans were stationed, having been provided with their wages.

He provided physicians who were highly skilled and equipped with all necessary instruments; likewise, he produced mountain-like heaps of bowstrings, bows, armor, and weapons, as well as honey, clarified butter, juices, and dust.

In every camp, King Yudhiṣṭhira provided abundant water, excellent fodder, and supplies of husks, charcoal, and other necessities. He also prepared great siege engines, iron arrows, javelins, spears, and battle-axes.
At that time, bows, armor, and other equipment were held dear by the men.
Elephants, clad in mail and covered with iron plates of armor, appeared there like mountains, each capable of fighting hundreds and thousands of warriors.
O Bhārata, knowing that the Pāṇḍavas had settled there, their allies,
accompanied by their armies and mounts, hastened to the designated place.
Having observed the vow of celibacy, those Soma-drinkers had bestowed abundant sacrificial fees.
The rulers of the earth assembled for the victory of the sons of Pāṇḍu.
Janamejaya said:
[Regarding] Yudhiṣṭhira, who was approaching with his army, desiring to fight—
It was encamped at Kurukṣetra, protected by Vāsudeva,
joined by Virāṭa and Drupada along with their sons,
and surrounded by hundreds of kings, including the Kekayas and the Vṛṣṇis.
"O one rich in asceticism, having heard that King Duryodhana was like Mahendra protected by the Ādityas— by those great car-warriors— what did he do in response? I wish to hear this in detail."
In that tumultuous uproar which arose in Kurujāṅgala,
the Pāṇḍavas, Vāsudeva, Virāṭa, and Drupada would indeed have caused even the army of the gods to tremble in their encounter.
Dhṛṣṭadyumna the Pāñcālya, the great car-warrior Śikhaṇḍin,
and the valiant Yuyudhāna, who is difficult even for the gods to overcome—
O rich in asceticism, I wish to hear about this in detail.
Whatever actions were performed by the Kurus and the Pāṇḍavas—
Vaiśampāyana said:
When the descendant of Daśārha had departed, King Duryodhana then...
He spoke these words to Karṇa, Duḥśāsana, and Śakuni:
"Adhokṣaja has gone to the sons of Pṛthā with a mission still unaccomplished;
filled with wrath, he will certainly speak to them, without a doubt."
For a conflict between Vāsudeva and the Pāṇḍavas is indeed desired by me;
Bhīmasena and Arjuna alike abide by the counsel of the Daśārha,
and even Ajātaśatru today follows the will of Bhīma and Arjuna.
Previously, he, along with all his brothers, was humiliated by me;
likewise, Virāṭa and Drupada have both been made my enemies.
Furthermore, those two leaders of armies are under the influence of Vāsudeva.
"This conflict that is about to occur will be tumultuous and hair-raising;
therefore, O lords of the earth, prepare all the equipment for battle without delay and let encampments be established at Kurukṣetra."
Having ample space and difficult for enemies to seize,
with water and wood nearby by the hundreds and thousands,
their paths for food and supplies were uncuttable, and they were filled with heaps of jewels.
"Let roads be prepared outside the city, level and filled with various weapons, adorned with banners and flags.
Let the departure be proclaimed today so that it may take place tomorrow; do not delay."
Having promised "So be it," those high-souled ones, appearing joyful, carried out their plan on the following day for the destruction of the rulers of the earth.
Then all those kings, having heard that royal command, [acted accordingly].
Indignant, they rose from their costly seats,
slowly rubbing their arms which resembled iron clubs,
adorned with shining golden bracelets and anointed with sandalwood and aloe.

Binding their turbans with hands resembling white lotuses, those best of chariot-warriors and experts in horsemanship donned their lower garments, upper robes, and all their ornaments. They [prepared] the chariots and the horses.
Those skilled in the training of elephants readied the elephants;
then they prepared many variegated golden armors and various weapons, making them ready in every respect.
And foot soldiers and men brought forth various weapons,
many of them adorned with gold, upon their bodies.
That [battle] was as exalted as a festival, filled with highly rejoicing men.
O Bhārata, the city of Dhṛtarāṣṭra’s son was filled with agitation;
it was like a whirlpool of water consisting of a flood of people, with chariots, elephants, and horses as its fish,
resounding with the blast of conchs and drums, and possessing the jewels of accumulated treasuries.

The great ocean of the Kuru king arose, with its waves of variegated ornaments and armor, its foam of stainless weapons, its surrounding mountains of rows of palaces, and its vast deeps of carriage-roads and marketplaces; it was brought forth by the rising moon of the warriors.
O King, it appeared then like the ocean at the rising of the moon.
Vaiśampāyana said:
Yudhiṣṭhira, calling to mind those words of Vāsudeva, [acted accordingly].
Again he questioned the descendant of Vṛṣṇi: "How did that dull-witted one speak thus?
Now that this time has arrived, O Acyuta, what is appropriate for us? And how should we conduct ourselves so that we do not fall away from our own duty?"
"You understand the opinions of Duryodhana, Karṇa, and Śakuni,
the son of Subala; you know the mind of myself and my brothers,
and you have heard the words of both Vidura and Bhīṣma."
O you of vast wisdom, you have heard in its entirety the wisdom of Kuntī.
Having considered all this and reflected upon it again and again,
O mighty-armed one, tell us without hesitation what is appropriate for us.
Having heard these words of the King of Dharma, which were consistent with righteousness and purpose,
Kṛṣṇa, whose voice resounded like a cloud or a drum, spoke these words:
"I have already spoken words that are beneficial and consistent with righteousness and purpose."
But that [advice] does not take root in the Kuru prince whose intellect is characterized by deceit;
nor does the dull-witted one listen to Bhīṣma or Vidura,
or even to anything I have said— he transgresses it all.
He desires neither righteousness nor fame;
that evil-souled one, relying on Karṇa, considers everything already won. Suyodhana has even ordered my imprisonment.
But that wicked-souled man, transgressing the command, did not obtain his desire;
neither Bhīṣma nor Droṇa spoke words that were appropriate there,
O Acyuta, for they all followed him except for Vidura.
Śakuni, the son of Subala, as well as Karṇa and Duḥśāsana—
those fools spoke improper words to you, that foolish and intolerant man. But what is the use of my repeating those things which the Kauravas said?
In brief, that evil-souled one behaves improperly toward you;
among all these kings who are your soldiers,
whatever is sinful and whatever is unwholesome is entirely established in him.
"Nor do we ever desire peace with the Kauravas through excessive surrender; rather, war must follow immediately thereafter.
Having heard these words of Vāsudeva, all the kings [responded].
O Bhārata, not speaking a word, they gazed intently at the face of the king.
Yudhiṣṭhira, however, perceiving the intention of the rulers of the earth,
ordered the preparations for battle together with Bhīma, Arjuna, and the twins.
Then, when the array had been ordered, the army of the Pāṇḍava broke into shouts of joy and the soldiers rejoiced;
yet Dharmarāja Yudhiṣṭhira beheld the slaughter of those who were not to be slain.
Groaning, he spoke thus to Bhīmasena and Vijaya:
"That for which we have lived in the forest and the suffering I have endured—
that very supreme calamity now approaches us despite all our efforts."

That for which we exerted ourselves has been lost through our own efforts; yet, while we were still striving, a great calamity has come upon us. For how can a battle be waged with those who are incapable of being slain?
"How can there be victory for us by killing our elders and preceptors?
Having heard those words of Dharmarāja, Savyasācin, the scorcher of foes,
repeated to him the speech that had been spoken by Vāsudeva.
The son of Devakī has spoken the words of Kuntī and Vidura;
those words have been heard by you in their entirety, O King.
And it is my firm conviction that neither of them would speak what is unrighteous.
"Furthermore, O son of Kuntī, it is not right for one who has not fought to turn back.
Having heard those words of Savyasācin, Vāsudeva then spoke to Pārtha with a smile, saying, "It is even so."
Then, O great king, those sons of Pāṇḍu, firm in their resolve for battle, spent that night in comfort along with their soldiers. Vaiśampāyana said:
When the night had passed, O Bhārata, King Duryodhana then divided those eleven armies—
consisting of the elite, the middling, and the inferior among men, elephants, chariots, and horses.
The lord of the earth gave these instructions to all those divisions:
"Let them be equipped with undercarriages, quivers, fenders, and javelins; let them have side-saddles, spears, sword-belts, and mallets."
Adorned with banners and flags, equipped with bows and lances, and provided with various colorful ropes, nooses,
and carpets; they were furnished with hair-seizing grips for throwing, as well as oil, molasses, and sand.
All [the chariots] were equipped with jars of venomous serpents, resinous dust, bells, and shields; they were all provided with axes, tree-climbers, iron balls, water,
and stones.
They were all equipped with *śāla* trees and *bhindipāla* missiles, along with mallets smeared with beeswax;
they all possessed arrows, staffs, *sīra* weapons, and poisoned *tomara* spears; they all had winnowing baskets and bags, as well as sickles, hooks, and *tomara* spears.
All [the weapons] were equipped with spikes and saws,
wrapped in tiger skins and covered with leopard skins; they were provided with handles, possessed horns, and were fitted with various types of quivers and weapons.
Equipped with axes and spades, provided with oil, linen, and ghee,
covered with golden nets and adorned with various jewels,
they were well-dressed and beautifully decorated, clad in tiger skins.
With variegated banners and handsome forms, they were like blazing fires;
likewise, the armored heroes were highly skilled in weapons,
of noble birth, knowledgeable about the breeds of horses, and appointed to the office of charioteers.
With their protective amulets fastened, their girth-bands tightened, and their banners and flags raised;
with their ornaments and chariot-fittings secured, and their shields, swords, and spears bound on— all the chariots were yoked to four horses, and all were fully equipped with weapons.
All of them had their mounts bristling with excitement, and all were equipped with bows.
One was the driver of the two lead horses, while the other two were the outriders;
they too were the best among chariot-warriors, as was the charioteer himself, who was likewise an expert in horses.
Like well-guarded cities difficult for enemies to seize,
there were thousands of chariots adorned everywhere with golden garlands;
and just as there were chariots, so too were there elephants, girth-strapped and beautifully decorated.
There were seven men who appeared like mountains rich in jewels:
among them, O King, two were bearers of elephant-goads, two were supreme archers,
two were bearers of excellent swords, and one was the bearer of a spear and a banner.
O King, that army of the Kaurava consisted of thousands of intoxicated elephants, crowded with armor, weapons,
and quivers; they were adorned with various armors, equipped with banners, and beautifully decorated.
There were tens of thousands of horses, fully equipped with riders— well-trained,
well-tempered, adorned with golden trappings and gear— and numbering many hundreds of thousands, all obedient to the control of their riders.

There were foot soldiers there, adorned with golden garlands, possessing various forms and diverse appearances, clad in various armor and bearing weapons; for every chariot there were ten elephants, and for every elephant there were ten horses.
Ten men were the foot-guards for the horse on all sides;
fifty elephants followed the chariot, and one hundred horses followed the elephant.
For every horse, there were seven men whose duty was to mend its wounds.
Five hundred elephants constitute a *senā*, and chariots are the same number;
fifty [horses] and one hundred [horses], and five times that many men [form a *patti*]; ten *senās* make a *pṛtanā*, and ten *pṛtanās* make a *vāhinī*.
Vāhinī, pṛtanā, senā, dhvajinī, sādinī, camū,
akṣauhiṇī, and varūthinī are synonyms used to define it; thus were the divisions arrayed by the wise son of Kuru.
Eleven akṣauhiṇīs were counted there, and indeed seven as well;
the force of the Pāṇḍavas consisted of exactly seven akṣauhiṇīs,
while the force of the Kauravas consisted of eleven akṣauhiṇīs.
Fifty-five men are prescribed as this *patti*;
three of these constitute a *senāmukha*, which is designated as a *gulma*. Ten *gulmas* formed a *gaṇa*, and there were tens of thousands of such *gaṇas*.
Among Duryodhana’s armies, those strikers who were about to fight—
thereupon the mighty-armed King Duryodhana, having carefully observed those brave and intelligent men, appointed them as his generals.
Having duly assembled the leaders of separate *akṣauhiṇī* divisions— those best of men and kings— he consecrated them:
Kṛpa, Droṇa, Śalya, and the great car-warrior Saindhava.
And Sudakṣiṇa the Kāmboja, and Kṛtavarman,
and the son of Droṇa, and Karṇa, and Bhūriśravas,
and Śakuni the son of Subala, and the great car-warrior Bāhlīka.
Day after day and at every moment, O Bhārata,
he repeatedly gave them various instructions in his very presence;
likewise, all those who were their followers were strictly disciplined.
O King, the soldiers became joyful, robust, well-equipped, firm in their resolve for valor, and desirous of doing what was pleasing to the king. Vaiśampāyana said:
Then the son of Dhṛtarāṣṭra, with palms joined in reverence, together with all the lords of the earth, spoke these words to Bhīṣma, the son of Śāntanu:
"Even though this army is very great, it is [powerless] without a leader of the host."
Upon encountering battle, it is shattered like an anthill;
for the intellect of two [opposing sides] is never equal at any time,
and the prowess of leaders indeed competes with one another.
O one of great wisdom, it is heard that all the Brāhmaṇas, with their banners of *kuśa* grass raised high, marched against the Haihayas of immeasurable prowess; and at that time,
O Grandfather, the Vaiśyas and Śūdras followed them as well.
On one side were the three social orders, and on the other were the bulls among the Kṣatriyas;
yet in battles, those three orders were repeatedly broken,
even though all the Kṣatriyas remained steadfast, being born of the lowest [of the twice-born].

But the Kṣatriyas indeed prevail, for their strength is concentrated on one side. Then those best of the twice-born questioned the Kṣatriyas; those knowers of dharma explained the matter to them exactly as it was, O Grandfather.

"In battle, we listen to one who possesses great intelligence, whereas you all remain separate, each acting according to his own intellect. Thereupon, those brahmins appointed a single brahmin as their general.
Having conquered the Kṣatriyas, he was skilled in policies and heroic;
thus, those who appoint as their commander-in-chief one who is skilled, heroic, established in welfare, and stainless, conquer their enemies in battle.
"You are equal to Uśanas and always a well-wisher toward me; steadfast in dharma and incapable of being led astray, please become our commander-in-chief—
just as the sun is among the radiant ones, or the moon among the plants."
Like Kubera among the Yakṣas, like Vāsava among the Maruts,
as Meru is among the mountains, and as Suparṇa is among the birds;
like Kumāra among living beings, and like Havyavāṭ among the Vasus.

For protected by you, we shall surely become unassailable even by the thirty gods, just as the inhabitants of heaven are protected by Śakra. May you go before us, like the son of Agni at the head of the gods.
"We shall follow you, just as bulls follow the leader of the herd.
Having spoken thus, the lord of men fell at his feet, saying:
"Protect us, O tiger among kings; I have come to you for refuge."
Bhīṣma said:
"O mighty-armed descendant of Bharata, it is exactly as you say. For just as you are to me, so too are the Pāṇḍavas."

Moreover, O lord of men, it is for their own welfare that I must speak to you: you must fight on their behalf, according to the agreement that was made. However, I do not see any warrior on earth who is my equal.
Except for that tiger among men, Dhanañjaya, the son of Kuntī—
he, the mighty-armed one, knows all celestial weapons in their entirety—
that Pāṇḍava would never fight me openly in battle.
In a mere moment, by the power of my weapons alone, I could render this world devoid of men— including gods, asuras, and rākṣasas— but,
O lord of men, the sons of Pāṇḍu must not be exterminated by me.
"Therefore, O joy of the Kurus, I shall always slay ten thousand warriors by means of this practice; in this way I will bring about their destruction,
provided that they do not kill me first in the encounter."
"O King, I shall be your commander-in-chief under another condition; you ought to hear it from me here as I wish. O Lord of the Earth, either Karṇa must fight first, or I."
"For the son of the Sūta always vies excessively with me in battle.
Karna said:
"O King, as long as the son of Gaṅgā lives, I shall not fight under any circumstances."
"But once Bhīṣma is slain, I shall fight with the wielder of the Gāṇḍīva.
Vaiśampāyana said:
Then, according to the prescribed rites, he appointed [Droṇa], who had given away abundant sacrificial fees, as the commander-in-chief.
The son of Dhṛtarāṣṭra, having been consecrated, shone resplendently before Bhīṣma. Then, by the king’s command, men calmly sounded kettledrums, conchs, and hundreds of *puṣkara* drums.
Various lion-roars and the sounds of mounts broke forth,
and from a cloudless sky there fell a rain of mud made of blood;
there were thunderclaps, earthquakes, and the sounds of elephants trumpeting.
They struck terror into the hearts of all the warriors;
moreover, bodiless voices arose from the sky, meteors fell,
and jackals, foreboding fear, howled intensely with piercing cries.
When the king consecrated the son of Gaṅgā as commander-in-chief,
O King, these fierce portents appeared by the hundreds.
Then, having appointed Bhīṣma, the crusher of enemy forces, as the generalissimo—
Having caused the best of the twice-born to recite blessings, and having honored them profusely with gold coins and cattle,
he set forth surrounded by his soldiers, increasing in prosperity through their cries of victory,
accompanied by his brothers and placing the son of the River (Bhīṣma) at the head.
With his great army, he went to Kurukṣetra.
Having traversed Kurukṣetra together with Karṇa, the Kaurava king,
O lord of men, caused his camp to be pitched on level ground.
In a region that was sweet and free from saline soil, abounding in fodder and fuel,
the camp shone just like Hāstinapura itself.
Janamejaya said:
To the high-souled Bhīṣma, the son of the River, the best among wielders of weapons,
the grandfather of the Bharatas, and the banner of all the rulers of the earth;
one who is equal to Bṛhaspati in intelligence and equal to the earth in forbearance.
He was like the ocean in depth, like the Himalayas in steadfastness,
like Prajāpati in magnanimity, and like the sun in brilliance;
he was like Mahendra in the destruction of his enemies with showers of arrows.

Having heard that [Arjuna] had been initiated for the long night of the battle-sacrifice— which was terrifying, formidable, hair-raising, and fierce— what did the mighty-armed King Yudhiṣṭhira, who is skilled in all dharmas, say?
"Neither Bhīmasena nor Arjuna, nor even Kṛṣṇa, could prevail.
Vaiśampāyana said:
"The highly intelligent Yudhiṣṭhira was skilled in the matters of duty and purpose in times of distress."

Having summoned all his brothers and Vāsudeva of the Sātvata clan, he who is the best among speakers addressed them with these words of conciliation: "Surround the armies; remain alert and clad in armor."
"Your grandfather will fight first;
therefore, look for my leaders among the seven armies.
Vāsudeva said:
"O bull of the Bharatas, since this time has arrived, you have spoken these meaningful words exactly as you ought to speak. O mighty-armed one, they please me; let that which follows be done."
"Let seven leaders indeed be consecrated in your army.
Vaiśampāyana said: Then, having summoned Drupada, Virāṭa, and the bull of the Śinis (Sātyaki), [he spoke].
Dhrishtadyumna the Panchala, King Dhrishtaketu,
Shikhandin the Panchala, and Sahadeva the Magadha—
these seven great archers, heroes who delight in battle.
Yudhiṣṭhira duly consecrated the leaders of the army,
and he appointed Dhṛṣṭadyumna as the commander-in-chief of the entire host—
he who had been born from the blazing fire for the purpose of Drona’s end.
Of all those high-souled warriors assembled together,
he made Dhananjaya, the conqueror of wealth and master of his senses (Guḍākeśa), the commander-in-chief.
And Arjuna, in turn, was both the leader and the driver of the horses.
The glorious Janārdana, the younger brother of Saṃkarṣaṇa and possessor of great intelligence,
having seen that a battle was imminent and fraught with great danger,
entered the palace of the Pāṇḍava king, armed with his plow.
Together with Akrūra and others—Gada, Sāmba, Ulmuka, and the rest;
