with the sons of Rukmiṇī and the sons of Āhuka, headed by Cārudeṣṇa;
and accompanied by the Vṛṣṇi leaders who had arrived like tigers fierce in their strength.
Protected by the Maruts like Vāsava, the mighty-armed one was clothed in blue silk; resembling a peak of Mount Kailāsa,
he moved with the playful gait of a lion, glorious and with eyes reddened at the corners by intoxication.
Seeing him, Dharmarāja and the immensely radiant Keśava, as well as Pārtha Vṛkodara of terrible deeds, and the wielder of the Gāṇḍīva bow and whatever other kings were there, then rose up.
Having approached, they all paid homage to Halāyudha.
Then King Pāṇḍava touched him on the hand with his own hand;
and all of them, led by Vāsudeva, offered their salutations.
Having saluted the elders Virāṭa and Drupada, Halāyudha,
the subduer of enemies, sat down together with Yudhiṣṭhira.
Then, when those kings had sat down on all sides, [the conversation began].
Looking toward Vāsudeva, the son of Rohiṇī spoke:
"This great, fierce, and terrible destruction of men is about to occur;
I consider this to be certain destiny, and it cannot be avoided."
"It is my hope that I may see you all, together with your friends, emerged from this battle, free from disease and with bodies uninjured;
for the assembled host of kings has undoubtedly been ripened by Time."
"A great slaughter is about to occur, a mire of flesh and blood.
I have said this again and again in private to Vāsudeva:
'O Madhusūdana, maintain an impartial attitude toward your kinsmen.'"
"For as the Pāṇḍavas are to us, so too is King Duryodhana;
let service be rendered to him as well with due propriety," he said again and again.
Yet Madhusūdana did not act upon those words of mine for your sake.
Having observed Dhanañjaya, who is resolved with his whole being,
my mind is certain that victory for the Pāṇḍavas is assured;
for such, O Bhārata, is this firm resolve of Vāsudeva.
"And I cannot bear to look upon the world without Kṛṣṇa;
therefore, I shall follow whatever Keśava intends to do.
For both heroes are my disciples, being experts in the art of mace-fighting."
Therefore, I have equal affection for Bhīma as I do for King Duryodhana;
for that reason, I shall go to visit the sacred fords along the Sarasvatī,
for I cannot bear to witness the destruction of the Kauravas.
Having spoken thus and being permitted by the Pāṇḍavas, the mighty-armed Rāma set out on his pilgrimage to the sacred fords (tīrthayātrā), having turned back Madhusūdana.
Vaiśampāyana said:
At that very time, however, [there was the daughter] of the high-souled Bhīṣmaka,
King Hiraṇyaloman, who was a direct friend of Indra himself,
the highly illustrious Bhoja, and the sovereign lord of the Āhṛtis.
The son of the Lord of the South is renowned in all directions as Rukmin; he,
a disciple of that lion among Kimpuruṣas who dwells on Mount Gandhamādana,
has mastered the entire science of archery in its four divisions.

That mighty-armed one obtained the bow of Mahendra, which was equal in splendor to the Gāṇḍīva; it was comparable to the Śārṅga, divine, inexhaustible, and perfectly proportioned. These three alone are the divine bows of those who roam the heavens.
In that regard, the Gāṇḍīva belongs to Varuṇa, while the Vijaya bow belongs to Mahendra;
but they say the Śārṅga is the divine, radiant bow of Viṣṇu,
which Kṛṣṇa bears and which strikes terror into the armies of his enemies.

The son of Pākaśāsana obtained the Gāṇḍīva bow from the Fire-god at Khāṇḍava; the highly energetic Rukmin received the Vijaya bow from Drumā. Having severed the nooses of Mura and slain Mura by his might, he [obtained it].
Having conquered the subterranean Naraka and recovered the jeweled earrings,
sixteen thousand women, various gems,
and the supreme bow Śārṅga, Hṛṣīkeśa obtained them.
But Rukmin, having obtained the Vijaya bow whose sound was like a thundercloud,
advanced against the Pāṇḍavas as if terrifying the entire world—
he who had formerly been unable to endure them, being arrogant in the strength of his own arms.
The hero, having made a vow before the wise Vāsudeva regarding the abduction of Rukmiṇī— "I shall not return without having slain Keśin"—
then pursued the descendant of Vṛṣṇi, the foremost among all wielders of weapons.
With a vast fourfold army, capable of striking from afar, adorned with various weapons and armor, and swelling like the Ganges,
he approached the Lord Vārṣṇeya, the master of all yogas.
Having made his vow, O King, that monarch was defeated by Vāsudeva;
frustrated and ashamed, he returned to Kuṇḍina,
where that slayer of enemy heroes had already been defeated in battle by Kṛṣṇa.
There he established an excellent city named Bhojakata;
with that great army, abounding in elephants and horses,
that city became renowned on earth by the name Bhojakata, O King.
That King Bhoja, endowed with great heroism, surrounded by a vast army consisting of one *akṣauhiṇī*, approached the Pāṇḍavas. Then,
clad in armor, bearing a sword, arrows, and a bow, equipped with hand-guards, he mounted his chariot.
With his banner the color of the sun, he entered the great army,
well known to the sons of Pāṇḍu and desiring to do what was pleasing to Vāsudeva;
King Yudhiṣṭhira, however, went out to meet him and honored him.
Honored by the sons of Pāṇḍu according to custom and well-received,
he in turn honored them all; then, having rested along with his army,
he spoke in the midst of the heroes to Dhanañjaya, the son of Kuntī.

"I stand here as your ally in battle; if you are afraid, O Pāṇḍava, I shall provide assistance in the fray that will be unbearable for your enemies. Indeed, there is no man here who is my equal in prowess."
"O Pāṇḍava, whatever share you shall give me, I will take it in battle—
even if it be from the heroic Droṇa and Kṛpa, or Bhīṣma and Karṇa;
or indeed, let all these lords of the earth stand aside."
"O Phalguna, having slain your enemies in battle, I shall give [this] to you," he said in the presence of Dharmarāja and Keśava,
while all the lords of the earth and others were listening from every side.
Looking toward Vāsudeva and the Pāṇḍava Dharmarāja,
the wise son of Kuntī smiled and spoke to him with the affection of a friend:
"O hero, while I was fighting with the Gandharvas of immense strength..."
Who was my companion and friend at that time during the expedition to the cattle-stations?
And who was the helper then, as I fought in that terrifying Khāṇḍava forest crowded with gods and dānavas?
In battle with the Nivātakavacas and the Kālakeya Dānavas,
who was my ally then as I fought there?
Likewise, in the city of Virāṭa during the conflict with the Kurus?
O dear one, when I was fighting against many, who became my allies?
Relying in battle upon Rudra, Śakra, Vaiśravaṇa, Yama,
Varuṇa, Pāvaka, as well as Kṛpa, Droṇa, and Mādhava— [who were my helpers then]?
Wielding the divine bow Gāṇḍīva, firm and full of splendor,
equipped with inexhaustible arrows and strengthened by celestial weapons—
he who was born in the lineage of the Kauravas and especially as the son of Pāṇḍu.
How could a disciple, aided by Vāsudeva and pointing to Droṇa [as his protector],
say "I am afraid" while wielding the Gāṇḍīva bow?
How could one such as I utter the disgraceful words, "I am afraid"?

"O tiger among men, even if it were Vajrāyudha himself speaking these words, I am not afraid, O mighty-armed one, nor do I stand in need of assistance. Go as you please and as you see fit, or stay elsewhere."
Having heard those words of the wise Vijaya,
O bull of the Bharata race, Rukmin then turned back his ocean-like army and approached Duryodhana in that very same manner.
In that very manner, the lord of men approached him and spoke;
however, he was then rejected by that one who considered himself a hero.
O great king, only two withdrew from that battle.
When Rāma, the son of Rohiṇī of the Vṛṣṇi clan, and Rukmin, the lord of the earth,
had likewise departed on their pilgrimage to the sacred fords,
the sons of Pāṇḍu sat down once again for counsel.
That assembly of the King of Dharma, crowded with kings,
shone, O Bhārata, like the sky variegated with stars when the moon is present.
Janamejaya said:
"O bull among the twice-born, when the armies were thus arrayed on Kurukṣetra,
what did the Kurus do, impelled as they were by Time?
Vaiśampāyana said:
When the armies had been thus arrayed, O bull of the Bharatas,
King Dhṛtarāṣṭra spoke these words to Sañjaya:
"Come, Sañjaya, tell me everything without leaving anything out."
Regarding what occurred in the encampment of the Kuru and Pāṇḍava armies,
I consider destiny alone to be supreme, and human effort to be useless,
since even though I was aware of the evils of war and the rise of destruction, [I did not prevent it].
Nevertheless, O charioteer, I am unable to restrain my son, who is of deceitful intellect and addicted to evil gambling, nor can I ensure his own welfare; for indeed,
my mind perceives only the faults [of such conduct].
Having encountered Duryodhana, that [battle] will turn back once more.
Such being the case, O Saṃjaya, whatever is destined to happen shall come to pass;
for indeed, in battle, the sacrifice of one's body is honored as the duty of a Kṣatriya.
Saṃjaya said:
"O Great King, this follow-up question you have asked is worthy of you;
however, you ought not to attribute this fault to Duryodhana."
Listen without exception, O King, as I speak:
whatever inauspicious result a man may incur from his own evil conduct,
he cannot attribute that transgression to fate or to time.

"O Great King, he who among men should practice every kind of censurable act deserves to be slain by all the world for performing such reproachable deeds. O best of men, these humiliations have been suffered by the Pāṇḍavas while they were waiting for you."

Listen to me in its entirety regarding that slaughter which occurred in battle among horses, elephants, and kings of immeasurable splendor— all of whom were experienced at gambling and were defeated by their ministers at the dice-game.
"O Great King, remaining steadfast and having heard, as it truly is, the destruction and arising of all the worlds in this great battle, do not be despondent. For indeed,
a person is not the agent of their own auspicious or sinful deeds."

For man is not independent; he is made to act like a wooden machine. Some are directed by a Lord (īśvara), some by chance (yadṛcchā), and others by their past actions (pūrvakarman); thus this [world] is drawn forth in three ways.
"Therefore, having fallen into misfortune, remain steadfast and listen.
Sañjaya said:
"When the high-souled Pāṇḍavas had settled at the Hiraṇvatī..."
O Great King, the Kauravas entered their quarters according to the prescribed rites.
There, King Duryodhana, having by his own prowess established the army,
honored the monarchs and likewise stationed the military outposts.
O Bhārata, having established the defensive arrangements for the warriors there,
the king summoned Karṇa, Duḥśāsana, and Śakuni the son of Subala, and held a consultation with them, O Bhārata.
O great king, O descendant of Bharata, Duryodhana, having conversed with Karṇa, with his brother Duḥśāsana,
and with the son of Subala, O Indra among kings, as well as with Duḥśāsana—
Having summoned the owl into his presence, O King, he spoke these words to it:
"O Owl, go to the Pāṇḍavas along with the Somakas, you son of Kaitava!
Having gone there, speak my words while Vāsudeva listens."
This very thing, contemplated for many years, has now arrived:
the battle between the Pāṇḍavas and the Kurus, which strikes terror into the world—
this great discourse of boastful words that Sañjaya spoke.
O son of Kuntī, the time has now come for you, who roar with Vāsudeva as your ally and accompanied by your younger brothers, in the midst of the Kurus;
let all that was promised by you be fulfilled.
In my name, O son of Kuntī, you should speak thus to the eldest brother:
"Being righteous yourself, how is it that you have set your mind upon unrighteousness, together with all your brothers, the Somakas, and the Kekayas?"

"O bull of the Bharatas, it is my conviction that you are one who desires the entire world to perish like a cruel man, yet you are a giver of fearlessness to all beings; for this verse was heard sung of old."
Then, may it be well with you; when the kingdom had been seized by the gods, Prahlāda—
whose banner of righteousness was always held aloft like the banner of the gods— practiced that vow known as "the cat's vow" (baiḍālavratam), wherein his sins remained concealed.
O lord of men, I shall relate to you here this supreme narrative told by Nārada to my father:
it is said that there was a wicked-souled cat who remained inactive in all his undertakings.
O King, once upon a time, standing on the bank of the Gaṅgā with his arms raised,
he purified his mind and said to all embodied beings for the sake of their conviction: "I am practicing dharma."
After a long time, O lord of the people, the egg-born birds came to trust him; gathering together, they praised that cat. Thus being honored by all those birds, he who was himself a feeder on birds—
He considered his own purpose accomplished and the fruit of his practice achieved. Then, after a long time, mice came to that place and there they saw him, a righteous man observing his vow.
O Bhārata, joined with a great undertaking characterized by deceit,
O King, this was the resolution they reached there:
"We all have many friends, and he is indeed our maternal uncle."
"May he constantly provide protection for the old and the young in every way.
Then they all approached the cat and said this:
"By your grace, we wish to roam about according to our pleasure."
"You are our unwavering refuge; you are our supreme friend.
We have all come together and sought refuge in you. You are eternally devoted to dharma; you are firmly established in dharma."
"O one of great wisdom, protect us as the wielder of the thunderbolt protects the gods.
Thus addressed by all those mice, O lord of the people,
that destroyer of mice then replied to all the mice.
I see no way to combine both ascetic practice and the protection [of the world]. Nevertheless, I must certainly carry out your beneficial command; you, likewise, must always carry out my command.
"I am utterly exhausted by my asceticism, having maintained strict discipline;
yet, when I reflect, I see no power at all for me to go on.
Therefore, dear father, let me be carried comfortably from here to the riverbank."
Having agreed to that, O bull of the Bharatas, the mice then reported all those who were old or young to the cat. Thereupon,
that wicked and evil-minded one began devouring the mice.
It becomes fat, golden-hued, and firm of limb;
meanwhile, the colony of mice there is greatly diminished,
while the cat increases in size, endowed with splendor and strength.
Then all those mice, having gathered together, said to one another:
"Our maternal uncle is constantly increasing, while we are wasting away severely.
Thereupon, a certain mouse named Diṇḍika, who was the wisest among them, spoke.
O King, he spoke these words to the great multitude of mice:
"Go together to the riverbank, especially as a united group;
I shall follow behind you along with my maternal uncle."
Then they all honored him, exclaiming, "Excellent! Excellent! And they carried out the meaningful words of Ḍiṇḍika according to what was right;
however, due to ignorance, he then ate Ḍiṇḍika himself.
Then all of them together deliberated straightforwardly;
there, O King, a certain mouse named Kolika, the eldest among them, spoke these words truthfully in the midst of his kinsmen.
Matula does not desire the Dharma; he has merely assumed the appearance of a crest-lock.
For one who subsists on roots and fruits, the excrement does not become hairy. His limbs are flourishing, yet his retinue is diminishing.
"For seven or eight days now, even Dindika has not been seen.
Upon hearing these words, all the mice fled in every direction,
and that wicked-souled cat also departed just as he had come.
In the same way, O evil-souled one, you too, having adopted the hypocritical vow of a cat,
always behave among your kinsmen like a cat among mice; indeed,
your speech is of one kind, while your action is seen to be quite another.
The Vedas and tranquility were given to you for the purpose of deceiving the world;
O King, casting aside this disguise and resorting to the duty of a Kshatriya,
perform all your tasks, for you are most righteous, O bull among men.
O best of the Bharatas, having acquired the earth through the strength of your own arms,
give gifts to the twice-born and to your ancestors as is fitting; for you have remained devoted to the welfare of your mother, who has suffered for many years.
Wipe away your tears; having conquered in battle, bring about the highest honor. We have not refused the five villages that were sought with such effort;
how then could we fight in battle and provoke the Pāṇḍavas?

Remember the abandonment of Vidura because of your wicked disposition, and recall that burning of the house made of lac; become a man! And remember what you said to Kṛṣṇa as he was approaching the assembly of the Kurus.
"O King, here I stand, ready for both peace and battle.
O lord of men, the time for that battle has now arrived.
It was for this purpose, O Yudhiṣṭhira, that I have performed all these deeds."
"What indeed does a Kṣatriya consider to be a gain greater than battle?
And why were you, born in a Kṣatriya lineage renowned throughout the earth,
O bull of the Bharatas, obtained weapons from Droṇa and Kṛpa?"
Since we are of equal origin and equal strength, you should take refuge in Vāsudeva; and in the presence of the Pāṇḍavas, you should say to Vāsudeva:
"Strive to fight against me for your own sake and for the sake of the Pāṇḍavas."
"Furthermore, that form which you created by means of illusion in the midst of the assembly—
having reproduced that very same thing once more, attack me along with Arjuna!
For whether it be sorcery, illusion, or even terrifying trickery, [I shall overcome it]."
When one has taken up arms in battle, counter-roars arise;
we too could venture forth, and by means of our power of illusion (*māyā*), we could go to heaven or the sky,
enter the netherworld (*rasātala*), or even the city of Indra.
And we could display many forms within our own bodies;
yet, through such successive transformations, one does not attain the human intellect.
For it is by the mind alone that the Creator brings all beings under his control.

And as for what you say, O Vārṣṇeya: "Having caused the sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra to be slain in battle, I shall bestow the supreme kingdom upon the Pārthas"— Saṃjaya has related all of that speech of yours to me.
"Your enmity is with Pārtha, who has me as his companion, that Savyasācin. Having been true to his promise, he exerted his prowess for the sake of the Pāṇḍavas.
Fight today in battle with diligence; let us see—be a man!"

But he who, having recognized the enemy, relies upon pure manliness and causes grief to his foes— he lives a life well-lived. And thus, O Kṛṣṇa, your great fame has become renowned in the world without a cause.
Now we understand that there are indeed eunuchs with horns;
even a king like me would never, under any circumstances, be fit to don armor in battle against you, especially against a servant of Kaṃsa.
O Pāṇḍava, remembering the indignity, the seizure of the kingdom, the exile in the forest,
and the suffering of Draupadī, be a man!
That purpose for which a Kṣatriya woman bears a child— this very moment has arrived.
Displaying your strength, prowess, heroism, supreme lightness of hand with weapons,
and manliness in battle, take vengeance for your anger. You have been tormented, dejected, and have dwelt in misery for a long time.
Whose heart would not burst, having been deprived of sovereignty— especially one born of noble lineage, a hero who coveted the wealth of others,
and whose anger would not blaze up when his kingdom was seized and usurped?
"That great speech which was spoken must now be manifested through action;
for the virtuous know a man to be a base person by his mere boasting when he fails to act.
To remain under the power of enemies and the loss of one's kingdom—this is rebirth."
There are two goals for one who fights; therefore, exert your manly prowess. Either, having defeated us, rule this earth, or, slain by us, you shall go to the world of heroes.
O Pāṇḍava, remember the exile from the kingdom, the suffering, the dwelling in the forest,
and the affliction of Kṛṣṇā; and remember the unpleasant words spoken by those who repeatedly attempted to drive you into exile.
Display your indignation today,
for indignation is indeed manliness; let your wrath, strength, heroism, the application of knowledge, and lightness of hand with weapons be seen here in battle, O Pārtha— be a man!
O Ulūka, speak my words repeatedly to that foolish, beardless Bhīmasena, who eats too much and is devoid of knowledge:
"O Pārtha, you who formerly were a cook in the city of Virāṭa."
The one renowned as Ballava is indeed my own manhood; for it was by me alone, O Vṛkodara, that this was sworn in the midst of the assembly when you were powerless:
"Let the blood of Duḥśāsana be drunk, if it can be done!"
O Kaunteya, that which you say— "I shall swiftly slay the sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra in battle"— the time for that has now arrived.
For you, O Bhārata, are to be placed at the forefront when it comes to food, snacks, and drink.
Where is the battle, and where is the feast? Fight and be a man!
You shall lie slain upon the earth, embracing your mace, O Bhārata. Thus, O Vṛkodara, your boasting in the midst of the assembly was in vain.
"O Ulūka, O descendant of Bharata, speak these words of mine to Nakula:
'Stand firm and fight today; let us see your prowess, O Bharata, as well as your affection for Yudhiṣṭhira and your hatred toward me.'"
Now, remember truly the suffering of Kṛṣṇā;
and in the midst of the kings, Sahadeva, you must speak these words of mine:
"O Pāṇḍava, fight now with diligence in battle, remembering your hardships!"
You should speak these words of mine to both Virāṭa and Drupada:
"Masters have never before been seen by servants, even those of great merit; likewise, servants have never before been seen by masters. For from such a union, offspring are produced."
"This king is unworthy of you," they said,
and thus they came; having united for the purpose of slaying him, as well as me,
fight now with me for your own sake and for the sake of the Pāṇḍavas.

And you should speak these words of mine to Dhṛṣṭadyumna, the Pāñcālya: "This agreement has come to you; it must also be secured by you. Having encountered Droṇa in battle, you will know what is most beneficial."
Fight with your friends; perform this wicked and most difficult deed. Furthermore, O Ulūka, speak these words of mine to Śikhaṇḍin:
"Thinking him to be a woman, that mighty-armed Kaurava will not slay you."
"Let Gāṅgeya, the best of archers, now fight with complete fearlessness. Perform your duty in battle with diligence; let us behold your prowess.
Having spoken thus, the king then laughed and said to Ulūka:
Speak again to Dhanañjaya while Vāsudeva listens:
"The collection of iron has been completed; Kurukṣetra is free of mud. Your horses are well-fed and your warriors are paid; fight tomorrow together with Keśava."
Without having encountered Bhīṣma in combat, why do you boast? Like a fool desiring to climb Mount Gandhamādana, so do you boast, O son of Kuntī; cease your boasting and be a man.

O Pārtha, how can you desire sovereignty here without having conquered in battle the son of a Sūta, who is so difficult to withstand; Śalya, the best among the strong; and Droṇa, the foremost of the powerful, who is equal to the Lord of Śacī in combat?

O Pārtha, you wish to defeat Droṇa, who is highly illustrious, a master of the Brāhma bow, one who has reached the further shore of the two Vedas, a leader in battle, unshakeable, moving through the ranks, and infallible— that is in vain.
For we have never heard of Mount Meru being uprooted by the wind; nor would the wind carry away Meru, nor would the sky fall upon the earth,
nor would the age-cycle turn back, were it otherwise than what you have told me.
For who that desires life, having encountered this crusher of enemies— whether it be Pārtha or the other— could return home in safety? How could anyone,
once targeted by these two or touched by their terrible [power], survive?
One who survives the battle may escape by touching the ground with his feet; but why, like a frog dwelling in a well,
do you not perceive this assembled army of kings?
Invincible, resembling the host of gods,
and guarded by lords of men like the heavens by the thirty deities— [guarded] by those from the east, the west, and the south.
With the Udīcyas, Kāmbojas, Śakas, and Khaśas; with the Śālvas along with the Matsyas, the Kurus, and those from the Middle Country;
with the Mlecchas, Pulindas, Draviḍas, Āndhras, and Kāñcīs.
The vast multitude of various people, swelling in battle like the irresistible current of the Ganges,
stood with me in the midst of that army of elephants.
"O dull-witted fool, why do you wish to fight? We know your two inexhaustible quivers, O Pārtha, and we know your chariot given by Agni, as well as your divine banner in battle, O Bhārata."

Fight without boasting; why do you boast so much, O Arjuna? Success comes from this through repeated practice; it is not achieved by boasting. If action in this world could be accomplished through boasting, O Dhanañjaya, [then everything would be easy].
May all have their goals accomplished; for who would be miserable when speaking thus? I know that Vāsudeva is your ally;
I know that your Gāṇḍīva bow is as tall as a palm tree.
"I know that there is no warrior like you;
knowing this, I maintain this kingdom of yours.
Yet, a human being does not attain success through the mere passage of time."
By the mind alone, the Creator brings even favorable things under his control.
Though you lamented, you have enjoyed the kingdom for thirteen years;
furthermore, I shall rule it again after slaying you along with your kinsmen.
Where was your Gāṇḍīva bow then, when you were won as a slave-stake?
Where, O Phalguna, was the strength of Bhīmasena then? Was it from Bhīmasena with his mace, or from Phalguna with his Gāṇḍīva?
Indeed, there was no liberation then without the blameless Kṛṣṇā; she,
the daughter of Pṛṣata, liberated you when you had fallen into servitude,
having been reduced to a non-human state and established in the labor of slaves.
"What I said to you regarding the sesame seeds being sterile was indeed the truth. For Pārtha then wore his hair in a braid while serving as a cook in the kitchen of Virāṭa in the city of Virāṭa."
O son of Kuntī, that which was done by Bhīmasena was indeed my own manly deed.
In this very way, Kṣatriyas always inflict punishment upon a Kṣatriya;
having bound your hair and assumed the guise of a eunuch, you made the maiden dance.
Neither out of fear of Vāsudeva nor even of you, O Phālguna, shall I restore the kingdom; fight, together with Keśava! For there are no illusions, nor sorcery, nor terrifying deceits here.

When they encounter me in battle with my weapons drawn— against whom even a thousand Vāsudevas or hundreds of Phālgunas would roar in defiance— they shall flee in the ten directions before my unerring arrows.
"Go into battle with Bhīṣma, or pierce a mountain with your head;
or cross with your two arms that ocean of men,
which has the son of Śaradvat for its great fish and the son of Somadatta for its timingila."
A sea with Bhīṣma for its terrifying current, Droṇa for its inaccessible crocodiles, Karṇa and Śalya for its great fish and whirlpools, the king of Kamboja for its submarine fire,
Duḥśāsana for its flood, and Śala and Śalya for its fish.
The mountain Jayadratha, with Suṣeṇa as its peaks, Citrāyudha as its elephants and crocodiles, Purumitra as its depth, Durmarṣaṇa as its waters, and Śakuni as its precipices— [cross this].
When you have plunged into this inexhaustible and ever-increasing torrent of weapons and lost your senses, O ascetic,
you will become one whose all kinsmen have been slain.
Then your mind will experience torment;
then your mind, O Pārtha, having been turned away from the governance of the earth, will feel as if it were impure, like one fallen from the third heaven.
"Be at peace; for a kingdom is very difficult for you to obtain, just as heaven is for one who has not practiced austerities.
Sañjaya said:
Having reached the Pandava’s military camp,
the son of Kitava met with the sons of Pandu and addressed Yudhiṣṭhira;
for he was well-versed in the speech of envoys and spoke exactly as he had been instructed.
"Having heard the command of Duryodhana, you ought not to be angry.
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
"Ulūka, you have no fear; speak without anxiety."
"That which is the thought of the greedy Dhṛtarāṣṭra’s son, who lacks foresight.
Saṃjaya said:
"Then, in the midst of the radiant and high-souled Pāṇḍavas..."
In the presence of all the Sṛñjayas and the illustrious Kṛṣṇa, and in the vicinity of Drupada with his sons and Virāṭa,
he spoke these words in the midst of all the lords of the earth.
"O lord of men, the high-minded King Dhṛtarāṣṭra, son of Dhṛtarāṣṭra, has said this to you in the hearing of the Kuru heroes; listen to it:
'You have been defeated at dice, and Kṛṣṇā has been brought into the assembly hall.'"
A man who considers himself a hero can indeed harbor indignation;
yet for twelve years you were exiled from your home into the forest,
and for one year you lived in the service of Virāṭa, having taken up the role of a servant.

O Pāṇḍava, remember the indignation at the seizure of the kingdom, the exile in the forest, and the suffering of Draupadī; be a man! And remember, O Pāṇḍava, that which was sworn by Bhīmasena when he was powerless.
"Let the blood of Duḥśāsana be drunk, if it can be done!
The offering of iron has been made; Kurukṣetra is now free of mud.
The path is level and the warriors are ready; fight tomorrow, together with Keśava!"
Without having encountered Bhīṣma in combat, why do you boast? Like a fool desiring to climb Mount Gandhamādana, so do you boast, O son of Kuntī; instead of boasting, display your manliness.

O Pārtha, how can you desire sovereignty here in this world without having conquered in battle the son of the Sūta, who is so difficult to withstand; Śalya, the best among the strong; and Droṇa, the foremost of warriors, who is equal to the Lord of Śacī in combat?
O Pārtha, it is in vain that you seek to conquer through battle in war Droṇa— the preceptor in the Brahma-bow, the interval between the two Vedas, the leader of the host, unshakeable, and infallible.
For we have never heard that Mount Meru was ever uprooted by the wind;
nor would the wind carry away Meru, nor would the sky fall upon the earth, nor would the age-cycle (yuga) ever turn back— were it otherwise than what you have told me.

For what person desiring life— whether elephant, horse, or man— who, having obtained these two weapons that crush the enemy, could ever return home in safety? How could one who is targeted by them, or even touched by their terrible power, survive?
One might escape alive from battle by touching the ground with one's feet;
but why, like a frog dwelling in a well, do you not perceive this assembled army of kings?
Invincible, resembling the celestial host,
and protected by lords of men as the heavens are by the thirty gods— [the city] guarded by those from the east, the west, and the south;
With the Udīcyas, Kāmbojas, Śakas, and Khaśas; with the Śālvas, Matsyas, Kurus, and those from the Middle Country; with the Mlecchas, Pulindas, Draviḍas, Āndhras, and Kāñcīs.
The vast multitude of men swelling in battle was like the irresistible current of the Ganges,
and I stood there in the midst of that elephant force.
"O dull-witted one, why do you desire to fight?
Having spoken thus to King Yudhiṣṭhira, the son of Dharma,
Ulūka turned back and addressed Jiṣṇu once more.

Fight without boasting; why do you boast so much, O Arjuna? Success comes through repeated practice; it is not achieved by boasting. If this action could be accomplished in the world through boasting, O Dhanañjaya, [then everything would be easy].
"May all have their goals accomplished; where is there so much misery?
"I know Vāsudeva to be your ally;
I know your Gāṇḍīva bow to be as tall as a palm tree."
"I know this: there is no warrior like you;
yet, knowing [this], I take away your kingdom. For one does not attain supreme success through the mere duty of succession."

For by his mind alone the Creator brings all beings under his control. While you were lamenting, I have enjoyed the kingdom for thirteen years; furthermore, having slain you along with your kinsmen, I shall rule it once more.
Where was your Gāṇḍīva bow then, when you were defeated at the stake for slavery?
And where, O Phalguna, was Bhīmasena’s strength then?
[Consider] both Bhīmasena with his mace and Pārtha with his Gāṇḍīva.
Indeed, there was no liberation for you then without the blameless Kṛṣṇā;
that passionate woman liberated you when you had fallen into servitude,
joined with superhuman beings, and established in the work of slaves.
"What I said to you regarding the sesame seeds being sterile was indeed the truth;
for Pārtha then wore his hair in a braid in the city of Virāṭa,
and he labored in the kitchen of Virāṭa performing the work of a cook."
O son of Kuntī, that prowess of mine displayed by Bhīmasena is exactly how Kṣatriyas always mete out punishment to a Kṣatriya—
whether in a guild, in the inner court, or in the braid of hair— whoever flees in battle.

Neither out of fear of Vāsudeva nor even for your sake, O Phalguna, shall I restore the kingdom; fight, therefore, together with Keśava! For neither illusion, nor sorcery, nor deceptive tricks can terrify me.
When I have taken up my weapons in battle, my roars resound;
even a thousand Vāsudevas or hundreds of Phalgunas,
upon encountering me whose arrows are never in vain, will flee in the ten directions.
"Go to battle with Bhīṣma; split the mountain with your head!
Cross this great and deep ocean of men with your two arms—an ocean where the son of Śaradvat is the vast continent and Vivimśati is the swarm of fish."
The army surged with Bṛhadbala as its great wave, Saumadatti as its *timiṃgila* (whale), Yuyutsu as its water, and Bhagadatta as its wind;
it roared loudly.
The great ocean of Hārdikya, with Duḥśāsana as its flood, Śala and Śalya as its fish, and Suṣeṇa and Citrāyudha as its serpents and crocodiles;

A river with Bhīṣma for its terrifying current, boundless and difficult to approach due to Droṇa as its crocodile, with Karṇa and Śalya as its large fish and whirlpools, the Kāmbojas as its submarine fire at the mouth,
Jayadratha as its mountain, and Purumitra as its depth.
Having plunged into that inexhaustible and greatly swollen torrent of weapons— which is difficult to withstand, from which birds fall,
and in which one loses consciousness through exhaustion— O Śramaṇa.
When you have had all your kinsmen slain,
your mind will then fall into deep distress,
like that of an impure person fallen from the third heaven.
"Turn back, O Pārtha, from the governance of the earth!
For it is extremely difficult for you to rule a kingdom, just as heaven is unattainable by one who has not practiced austerity."
Saṃjaya said:
Ulūka, however, spoke again to Arjuna the words as they had been told,
piercing him like an angry venomous serpent with the probe of his speech.
Hearing those words of his, the Pāṇḍavas were exceedingly enraged;
for they had already been deeply incensed by the insults of the son of Kitava.
They could not remain seated and began to brandish their arms.
Like enraged venomous serpents, they glared at one another.
With his head bowed, Bhīmasena gazed at Keśava,
his eyes red at the corners and hissing like a venomous snake.
Seeing the son of the Wind-god afflicted and violently struck by his rage, the descendant of Daśārha,
as if smiling, addressed the son of Kitava:
"Depart quickly, O son of Kitava, and speak thus to Suyodhana."
"Your words have been heard and their meaning grasped; let it be as you intend.
Having spoken thus, O best of kings, the mighty-armed Keśava once again looked toward the highly wise Yudhiṣṭhira.
In the presence of all the Sṛñjayas and the illustrious Kṛṣṇa, and in the vicinity of Drupada with his son and Virāṭa,
as well as in the midst of all the lords of the earth, he spoke these words.
Ulūka also spoke again to Arjuna the very words he had been told,
piercing him like an angry venomous serpent with the pike of his speech;
and he likewise spoke the same words to all those others, beginning with Kṛṣṇa.
Having heard those wicked and cruel words spoken by Ulūka,
Pārtha became agitated and wiped his forehead.
O King, seeing Pārtha in that state at that time, the assembly [was moved].
O Great King, those great car-warriors of the Pāṇḍavas could not endure that insult against Kṛṣṇa and the high-souled Pārtha;
having heard it, those tigers among men, being steadfast, blazed up with rage.
Dhṛṣṭadyumna, Śikhaṇḍin, and the great car-warrior Sātyaki;
the five Kekaya brothers and the Rākṣasa Ghaṭotkaca; the sons of Draupadī, Abhimanyu, and King Dhṛṣṭaketu.
The valiant Bhīmasena and the two great car-warriors, the twins,
all sprang up from their seats with eyes bloodshot with rage,
grasping their beautiful arms smeared with red sandalwood paste.
Adorned with armlets, bracelets,
and upper-arm ornaments, Vṛkodara, the son of Kuntī, who understood their gestures and intentions, ground his teeth against his teeth and repeatedly licked the corners of his mouth.
He rose up with speed, as if blazing with rage;
suddenly rolling his eyes and grinding his teeth together,
he squeezed one hand with the other and spoke these words to Ulūka.

O fool, you have heard the words that Duryodhana spoke to you, intended as an encouragement for us who are as if powerless; O dull-witted one, listen now to these invincible words as I speak them to you.
In the midst of all the kṣatriyas, whatever you shall say to Suyodhana while the son of the Sūta and his evil-minded father listen,
we shall always do it out of our desire to please our eldest brother.
O man of evil conduct, you do not value that which was endured by you;
yet Hṛṣīkeśa has been sent toward the Kurus, desiring peace,
by the wise Dharmarāja who seeks the welfare of the lineage.
Driven by time, you surely desire to go to the abode of Yama; go then to battle with us, for that will certainly take place tomorrow. I too have vowed the slaughter of you along with your brothers.

O wicked one, it shall come to pass exactly so; there is no need for further deliberation on this point. The ocean, the abode of Varuṇa, might instantly overstep its bounds, and even the mountains might crumble away, but what I have spoken cannot be false.
Even if Yama, Kubera, or Rudra himself were your allies,
O evil-minded one, the Pāṇḍavas will act according to their vow; furthermore,
I shall drink the blood of Duḥśāsana as I desire.
"Whichever Kṣatriya here, emboldened, shall advance against me—
even if he places Bhīṣma at his head— I shall send him to the abode of Yama.
And as for these words that were spoken by me in the assembly of the Kṣatriyas..."
“If this shall come true, then by that truth I swear an oath upon myself.
Having heard these words of Bhīmasena, the impatient Sahadeva,
his eyes bloodshot with rage, then spoke these words.
"O wicked one, listen to my words in this assembly of warriors, which befits a man of noble spirit and heroism— words that you must indeed say to your father:
'There shall never be any dissension between us and the Kurus.'"
If there were no connection between you and Dhṛtarāṣṭra,
you would be a man of enmity born for the destruction of the world and the lineage of Dhṛtarāṣṭra— a doer of evil who destroys his own kin.
"From birth, that sinful man has been our father;
he constantly desires to commit harmful and cruel acts against us. I shall reach the end of that most difficult-to-traverse enmity."
"Having first struck you down while Śakuni looks on,
I shall then slay Śakuni in the sight of all the archers.
Having heard these words of both Bhīma and Sahadeva, [he spoke].
Phalguna, as if smiling, spoke these words to Bhimasena:
"O Bhimasena, there are none who harbor enmity toward you;
those fools, dwelling happily in their homes, have fallen under the power of the noose of death."
"O Supreme among Men, you must not speak harshly to Ulūka;
for what fault do messengers commit when they merely repeat what they have been told?
Having spoken thus to the mighty-armed Bhīma of terrible prowess, [he addressed him].
He addressed his friends, the heroes headed by Dhṛṣṭadyumna:
"You have heard the speech of that wicked son of Dhṛtarāṣṭra,
containing insults toward Vāsudeva and especially toward me."
Having heard this, you have become agitated out of a desire for our welfare;
yet, through the power of Vāsudeva and by your own exertion,
I do not regard the entire body of earthly Kṣatriyas as a significant force.
"Permitted by you,
I shall deliver to Ulūka this reply to his words— whatever I shall say to Suyodhana on the morrow at the head of the army regarding what he has boasted."
"With the Gāṇḍīva bow I shall speak; for those who reply with mere words are indeed eunuchs.
Then all those kings praised Dhanañjaya, and the best of monarchs were struck with wonder by that manner of speech.
Having conciliated them all according to their rank and age,
the King of Dharma then replied with words that were appropriate for the occasion;
for a supreme lord of the earth would not disparage himself.
In this matter, O best of the Bharatas, I shall speak further to you as you are intent on listening— first with conciliation and then with force—
concerning that speech of Duryodhana, O bull of the Bharatas.
With eyes exceedingly red, hissing like a venomous serpent,
as if smiling out of rage and licking the corners of his mouth,
he looked toward Janārdana and his brothers and spoke these words.
Stretching out his massive arm, he addressed the son of Kitava:
"O Ulūka, go, O son of Kitava, and say to Suyodhana—
that ungrateful man, a personification of enmity, the evil-minded defiler of his lineage."

O wicked one, you always behave with constant crookedness toward the Pāṇḍavas. That sinful man who, exerting his own prowess, challenges others fearlessly and fulfills his word— he indeed is a true Kṣatriya.
Having become such a sinful Kṣatriya, you have challenged us to battle;
O lowest of your lineage, O Kaurava, do not go to war by setting aside those worthy and unworthy of honor, relying instead upon your own prowess and that of your servants.
"Challenge the sons of Pṛthā in battle; by all means, be a true Kṣatriya!
He who challenges his enemies by relying on the prowess of others, being himself unable to take up the fight—this alone is a eunuch."
"You, who pride yourself so much upon the prowess of others— how can you, being so powerless, roar so defiantly at us? Furthermore,
those words of mine must also be spoken again to that Suyodhana."
"O evil-minded one, you shall be seen as a dog this very day; become a man!
And as for what you think, O fool—that Janārdana will not fight because he has been chosen by the Pārthas as their charioteer—it is for that reason that you do not fear."
Even at this most wretched hour, I could consume all the kings with my wrath like fire consumes straw; yet,
by the command of Yudhiṣṭhira, I shall do so for the sake of the high-souled Phalguna.
"I shall act as the charioteer for you, who are skilled in combat and self-realized. Whether you leap up into the three worlds or enter the depths of the earth,
wherever you may be, you shall see Arjuna’s chariot before you at dawn."
And as for what you consider to be the vain roaring of Bhīmasena—
let it be understood that the blood of Duḥśāsana has been drunk. Neither Pārtha nor King Yudhiṣṭhira looks upon you.
Neither Bhīmasena nor the twins [could endure] one who speaks such contrary words.
Saṃjaya said:
O bull of the Bharatas, having heard those words of Duryodhana, [the king...]
With his two exceedingly copper-red eyes, he stared intently at the son of Kitava. Then the highly illustrious Guḍākeśa, looking toward Keśava,
raised his massive arm and addressed the son of Kitava.
He who, relying on his own prowess, challenges his enemies fearlessly and fulfills his capacity, he indeed is called a *puruṣa*. But he who challenges his enemies by relying on the prowess of others—

A mere kinsman of the warrior class who is powerless is the lowest of men in this world; yet you, being yourself a coward and a fool, imagine your own prowess to be equal to that of your enemies, and thus desire to revile others.

"You, who boast after having consecrated for death that one of great wisdom— an elder among all kings, whose mind was intent on the welfare of others and whose senses were conquered— your true nature is known to us, O evil-minded defiler of your lineage!"
"The Pāṇḍavas will not kill this son of Gaṅgā out of compassion"—
relying upon whose prowess you boast, O son of Dhṛtarāṣṭra,
I shall slay Bhīṣma first while all the archers look on.
"O Kaitavya, go and meet the Bharatas;
speak thus to Suyodhana, the son of Dhṛtarāṣṭra. "So be it," said Arjuna Savyasācin.
At the end of the night, there will be a conflict,
concerning which he of undaunted spirit and true to his word spoke these words to you in the midst of the Kurus, gladdening them.
"I am the slayer of the Pāṇḍava host, as well as the Śālveyakas; this is my burden. Indeed, I could destroy the world were it not for Droṇa."
No fear exists for you from the Pāṇḍavas; for you have indeed gained the kingdom most completely,
while the Pāṇḍavas have gone to their destruction— this is the implication.
Filled with pride, you do not perceive the calamity that is already present within yourself;
therefore, I shall first strike you down in battle.
O slayer, at sunrise, with your army arrayed, wait in person before the elder of the Kurus and protect that man of true promise, who bears a banner and rides a chariot.

While you all look on, I shall strike Bhīṣma down from his chariot with my arrows, making this island [of safety] yours. When tomorrow dawns, Suyodhana will understand the meaning of my boastful words.
Having seen my grandfather afflicted by a net of arrows,
and having heard what was said in the midst of the assembly by the short-sighted man Bhīmasena, who was provoked to anger, regarding your brother Duḥśāsana—
O Suyodhana, you who are ignorant of dharma, eternally hostile, evil-minded, and a doer of cruel deeds— you shall before long fulfill that vow of yours, [born] of your arrogance,
pride, anger, and harshness.
Of harshness, arrogance, and self-conceit;
of cruelty, severity, and hatred of dharma; of unrighteousness, excessive speech, and the transgression against the elders.

O Suyodhana, you shall before long behold the fierce fruit of your hostility toward the sight of me, of your crookedness, and of your entire attempt at subversion— when I am enraged with Vāsudeva as my companion, O lord of men.
"O fool, for what reason do you still have hope for life, or for the kingdom?
Now that Bhīṣma has been laid to rest, and Droṇa and the Sūta’s son have been struck down,
you shall become hopeless regarding life, the kingdom, and your sons."
O Suyodhana, having witnessed the slaughter of your brothers and sons,
and being struck down by Bhīmasena, you shall remember your evil deeds;
for Keśava will never again make a second vow.
"I speak this truth; indeed, all this shall come to pass.
Yudhiṣṭhira then spoke these words to Ulūka, the son of the gambler:
"Ulūka, my dear, go and deliver my message to Suyodhana."
You ought not to judge my conduct by your own; you know the difference between both the pleasant truth and the untruth. Nor do I desire evil even for a worm or an ant.
How could I ever desire the slaughter of my kinsmen? It was for this very purpose, my dear brother, that I previously requested those five villages.
O man of evil intellect, why do you not foresee this great calamity?

With your soul overwhelmed by desire and out of delusion, you boast in this manner; likewise, you do not accept the beneficial words of Vāsudeva. What is the use of speaking much more now? Fight, together with your kinsmen.
"O son of a gambler, speak to that Kuru prince who acts against my will!
You have heard my words; the matter is understood. Let it be exactly as you intend.
Then Bhīmasena spoke these words again to the prince.
"O owl, speak my words to the evil-minded and sinful man,
to the deceitful, treacherous, wicked, and ill-behaved Suyodhana:
'Either you must dwell in the belly of a vulture, or in the city named after the elephant.'"
"O lowest of men, that which was vowed by me in the midst of the assembly—I shall make those words true; I swear this to you by truth itself.
Having slain Duḥśāsana, I shall drink his blood in battle."
"Having indeed broken your two thighs and having slain your brothers,
O Suyodhana, I shall be the death of all the sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra;
and Abhimanyu will undoubtedly be the death of all those princes."
"I shall satisfy you further with my actions; listen again to my words:
having slain Suyodhana along with all his brothers, I shall indeed trample upon his head while the King of Dharma looks on."
Then Nakula spoke these words, O lord of the earth:
"O Ulūka, speak to Suyodhana, the Kaurava son of Dhṛtarāṣṭra:
'You have heard every word spoken by him exactly as it was.'"
"O Kauravya, I shall act exactly as you instruct me.
Sahadeva also, O King, spoke these meaningful words:
"O Suyodhana, this resolve of yours shall prove to be in vain."
"O Great King, you shall grieve along with your sons, kinsmen, and relatives, for the sorrow that you joyfully mock us. Thus did Virāṭa and Drupada, both aged, speak these words to Ulūka.
"It is always the thought of the virtuous man: 'May I remain in a state of servitude.
Whether those two are slaves or no longer slaves depends on the nature of one's own prowess.
Then Śikhaṇḍin spoke these words to the owl:
"You must say to the king: 'He who is always devoted to sinful deeds—
behold me, O King, performing such terrible deeds in battle— that having encountered my prowess, you consider victory in war possible.'"
"I shall strike down your grandfather from his chariot;
surely I was created by the Great-Souled Creator for the slaying of Bhīṣma.
Therefore, I will kill Bhīṣma while all the archers look on."
Dhṛṣṭadyumna also spoke these words to Ulūka, the son of the gambler: "Suyodhana, the son of the king, must be told my message:
'I shall slay Droṇa, along with his followers and his kinsmen.'"
"I am the doer, and likewise the deed, such as no other shall perform.
To him, Dharmarāja spoke these great words out of compassion:
"O King, I would never in any way desire the slaughter of my kinsmen."
"O evil-minded one, it is solely through your fault that all this has been revealed to you. Furthermore, I must certainly perform the great task for the sake of all.
Therefore, go without delay, my dear Ulūka, if you so intend."
"Stay here, may it be well with you; for we are indeed your kinsmen.
Then, O King, the owl, having taken leave of Yudhiṣṭhira, the son of Dharma, departed for the place where King Suyodhana was.
Then Ulūka, having arrived, spoke all the instructions of Arjuna exactly as they had been stated to the impatient Duryodhana,
as well as the prowess of Vāsudeva, Bhīma, and Dharmarāja.
O Bhārata, having heard these words of Nakula, Virāṭa, Drupada, Sahadeva, Dhṛṣṭadyumna, and Śikhaṇḍin, King Yudhiṣṭhira,
that master of guile, reflected upon those words, O King.

Having been granted permission, he returned once more by the way he had come. But having turned back from the Pāṇḍavas, the son of Kitava went to the son of Dhṛtarāṣṭra and related everything exactly as it had been said in the assembly of the Kurus.
Having heard the words of Keśava and Arjuna, that bull among the Bharatas repeated everything exactly as it had been spoken; he then spoke those words of the son of Kitava.
He addressed Duḥśāsana, Karṇa, and Śakuni, saying:
"Command the king's army as well as the allied forces so that the entire host stands ready before sunrise."
Then, commanded by Karṇa, messengers set out in haste on chariots,
while others went on female camels and excellent, high-speed horses;
at Karṇa’s command, they quickly traversed the entire army.
"Command those kings [to depart] before sunrise," said Yoga.
Saṃjaya said:
Having heard the words of Ulūka, Yudhiṣṭhira, the son of Kuntī, [spoke].
He dispatched the army, led by Dhṛṣṭadyumna,
consisting of foot soldiers, elephants, chariots, and hosts of cavalry—
a fourfold force, formidable and unshakable like the earth.
[The army] was protected by Bhīmasena and others, along with Arjuna and other great chariot-warriors;
it was under the command of Dhṛṣṭadyumna, difficult to assail, and resembled the stillness of the ocean.
At its head stood the great archer, the Pāñcālya prince, who is irrepressible in battle.
Seeking to reach Droṇa, Dhṛṣṭadyumna led the divisions forward;
according to their strength and according to their zeal, he assigned the chariot-warriors—
Arjuna against the Sūta’s son, and Bhīma against Duryodhana.
He assigned Nakula to Aśvatthāman, Śaibya to Kṛtavarman,
and Yuyudhāna of the Vṛṣṇi clan to the ruler of the Sindhus;
and he placed Śikhaṇḍin directly in front of Bhīṣma.
He assigned Sahadeva to Śakuni, Cekitāna to Śala,
Dhṛṣṭaketu to Śalya, and Uttamaujas to Gautama;
he also assigned the five sons of Draupadī to the five Trigarta princes.
He assigned the son of Subhadrā to Vṛṣasena and the remaining kings;
for he indeed considered him capable of overcoming even Pārtha in battle.
Having thus divided those warriors, both individually and collectively, [he assigned them].
The great archer Jvalavarṇa assigned Droṇa as his portion.
Then the wise Dhṛṣṭadyumna, the great archer and commander-in-chief of the armies, having duly arrayed the troops, set his mind on battle.
He deployed the divisions of the Pāṇḍavas exactly as instructed;
striving for the victory of the sons of Pāṇḍu, he stood ready upon the field of battle.
Dhṛtarāṣṭra said:
"O Saṃjaya, when Phalguna had vowed the slaughter of Bhīṣma,
what did my dull-witted sons, Duryodhana and the others, do?
For I see the son of Gaṅgā, my father, as already slain in battle."
Having heard those words spoken by Pārtha, who was aided by Vāsudeva and wielded a firm bow, what did that one of immeasurable wisdom—
the great archer Bhīṣma, the best among strikers— say?
Having obtained the generalship of the Kauravas,
what did the son of Gaṅgā— foremost among leaders and possessed of great intelligence and prowess— do?
Vaiśampāyana said:
Then Sañjaya reported all of that to him exactly as it had been spoken by Bhīṣma, the elder of the Kurus and possessor of immeasurable splendor. Sañjaya said:
O King, having obtained the command of the army, Bhīṣma, the son of Śantanu,
spoke these words to Duryodhana as if to gladden him:
"Having paid homage to Kumāra, the commander of the host who holds the spear in his hand..."
"I shall be your commander-in-chief today, without a doubt;
for I am skilled in military operations and in various battle formations, and I know how to direct the work of both those who are paid and those who are not."
In expeditions, journeys, battles, and in the pacification of what has been acquired,
O Great King, he knows as thoroughly as Bṛhaspati; he also knows the vast military arrays of divine, Gandharva, and human origin.
"By means of them, I shall delude the Pāṇḍavas; let your fever depart.
Therefore, O King, I will fight according to the true principles while protecting your army in accordance with the scriptures; let the fever of your mind pass away."
Duryodhana said:
"O son of Gaṅgā, O mighty-armed one, there is no fear for me even from all the gods and asuras combined; I tell you this truly."
How much more so, then, while you— invincible— are established in the command of the army, and while Droṇa, that tiger among men who delights in battle, stands ready,
and while both of you, the foremost of men, are present; my victory is certain.

"O best of the Kurus, even the sovereignty of the gods is certainly not difficult to attain. However, O Kaurava, I wish to know in full the number of chariot-warriors among the enemy as well as our own, and likewise the number of those who are *atirathas*."
"For the Grandfather is skilled in the matters of others as well as his own;
I wish to hear this together with all these lords of the earth.
Bhīṣma said:
"O Gāndhārin, O Indra among kings, hear the enumeration of the chariot-warriors in your own army— those who are *rathas* and those who are *atirathas*, O protector of the earth;
there are many thousands, millions, and hundreds of millions here."
Hear from me, according to their preeminence, those who are the foremost chariot-warriors in your army: you yourself are the noblest of chariot-warriors at the head of all,
together with your brothers beginning with Duḥśāsana, numbering one hundred.
All of them were skilled in the use of weapons, experts in cutting and piercing;
they were proficient in fighting from the seat of a chariot, on the back of an elephant, with maces, and with sword and shield.
They were disciplined drivers, capable strikers, masters of missiles, and accomplished in bearing heavy burdens.
The disciples of Droṇa and of Kṛpa Śaradvat are skilled in the science of archery; these men,
who have been wronged by the sons of Pāṇḍu, will slay the Pāñcālas— who are intoxicated with war— in battle, for they are high-spirited Dhārtarāṣṭras.
Then, O best of the Bharatas, as your commander-in-chief of all the armies, I shall destroy the enemies, rendering the Pāṇḍavas insignificant;
yet it is not fitting for me to speak of my own merits, for I am already known to you.
Kṛtavarman, however, the Bhoja warrior, an *atiratha* and the best among strikers,
will undoubtedly bring you success in battle. He is unassailable by those skilled in weapons, capable of shooting from afar, and possesses firm weaponry.
He will slay your enemies, just as Mahendra slew the Dānavas.
To me, Śalya, the king of the Madras and a great archer, is considered an Atiratha;
he who indeed constantly vies with Vāsudeva in battle after battle.
"O best of chariot-warriors, having abandoned his own nephews,
this Śalya will fight in battle against Kṛṣṇa, who wields the discus and the mace,
as if flooding his enemies with speeds like the waves of the ocean."
Bhūriśravas, skilled in weapons and a well-wishing friend to you as well,
the son of Somadatta and a great archer who leads the hosts of chariot-warriors,
will cause a very great destruction of the enemies' forces.
"O Great King, the king of the Sindhus is, in my opinion, equal to two chariot-warriors;
O King, that valiant and best of car-fighters will fight in battle.
He was previously tormented by the Pāṇḍavas during the abduction of Draupadī."

Remembering that suffering, the slayer of enemy heroes will fight. For by him, O King, having then undertaken severe asceticism, a boon was obtained that is very difficult to attain: to fight the Pāṇḍavas in battle.
This tiger among chariot-warriors, remembering that enmity in battle,
will fight the Pāṇḍavas, O dear one, having cast away his life-breaths which are so difficult to relinquish.
Bhīṣma said:
Sudakṣiṇa of Kamboja is considered a single-unit chariot-warrior;
desiring the accomplishment of your purpose, he will fight against the enemies in battle for your sake,
O best of kings, for this lion among chariot-warriors.
The Kurus shall behold his prowess in battle, which is like that of Indra; for this multitude of his chariots, O Great King— striking with fierce speed—
is like a swarm of locusts from the land of the Kambojas.
Nīla, a resident of Māhiṣmatī who wears blue armor,
will indeed cause a slaughter of the enemies with his multitude of chariots;
for that king has long held a grudge against Sahadeva.
"O King, O best of the Kurus, he will fight constantly for your sake.
Vinda and Anuvinda of Avanti, those two foremost of chariot-warriors, who have come together,
are skilled in battle, my dear, and possess firm heroism and prowess."
These two tigers among men will consume the enemy host with maces,
spears, swords, iron arrows, and lances hurled from their arms;
eager for battle, they will sport in the fray like two leaders of elephant herds.
O Great King, wandering like the God of Death in the midst of the host,
the five Trigarta brothers are, in my opinion, noble chariot-warriors who have long harbored enmity toward the son of Pṛthā since their time in the city of Virāṭa.
O Indra among kings, like makaras agitating the Ganges with its surging waves,
they will throw the army of the Pārthas into turmoil in battle.
O Indra among kings, those five chariot-warriors of whom Satyaratha is the leader—
"O King, O Bhārata, these will fight in battle remembering the former wrongs committed against them by the son of Pāṇḍu, the younger brother of Bhīmasena, while he,
the one with white horses, was conquering the quarters."
Having been forced to pay the highest tribute in battle by being treated with contempt,
those great chariot-warriors, the preeminent bowmen and leaders among the Kṣatriyas, will slay the best of the Pārthas when they encounter them.
Your son Lakṣmaṇa and Duḥśāsana—
both of them tigers among men who never retreat in battle;
young, delicate, and full of vigor, they are both princes.
O tiger among chariot-warriors, in my opinion those two are the best of car-fighters; they are experts in all forms of combat and are skilled leaders in every respect.
Devoted to the duty of the Kṣatriya, those two heroes will perform great deeds.
O Great King, O bull among men, Daṇḍadhāra alone will fight upon his chariot when he reaches the battle, protected by his own army;
likewise, King Bṛhadbala of Kosala is a most excellent car-warrior.
"O dear one, this chariot is considered by me to possess firm speed and prowess;
he will fight in battle, gladdening his own army— this fierce-weaponed, great archer who is devoted to the welfare of Dhṛtarāṣṭra’s son."
O King, this Kṛpa, the son of Śaradvat, who is considered a single-rank chariot-warrior and a leader among the leaders of chariot-divisions, will fight in battle;
casting aside his dear life, he will consume your enemies.
He who was born from a clump of reeds as the son of the great seer Gautama, the preceptor Śaradvat— invincible like Kārttikeya—
is this man who [leads] a diverse army equipped with various weapons and bows.
"O dear one, he will move about in battle like fire, crushing [the enemy].
Bhīṣma said:
"O lord of men, that Śakuni, your maternal uncle, is a single great car-warrior."

Having incurred enmity with the Pāṇḍavas, he will fight; of this there is no doubt. His troops are invincible in battle, never retreating, equipped mostly with formidable weapons, and equal to the force of the wind in speed.
The son of Droṇa is a great archer, surpassing all other bowmen;
he is a versatile warrior in battle, firm in his mastery of weapons, and a great chariot-fighter (mahāratha).
Indeed, O Great King, he is equal to the wielder of the Gāṇḍīva bow.
Released from his bow, his arrows fly together in close succession.
This hero, O best of chariot-warriors, cannot be fully measured by me;
if he so desired, this man of great fame could consume even the three worlds.
The wrath and energy of that noble-minded one were accumulated through asceticism while he dwelt in the hermitage,
and he was favored by Droṇa with divine weapons;
yet, O bull of the Bharatas, he has one great defect.
O best of kings, I do not consider him to be a *ratha* nor an *atiratha*.
A twice-born man always desires long life and holds his own life exceedingly dear;
for there is no one equal to him in either of the two armies.
With a single chariot alone, he could destroy even the army of the gods;
possessed of a magnificent form, by the sound of his palms he could even shatter mountains.
This hero, the striker of terrible splendor, possesses innumerable virtues.
Irresistible like Yama with staff in hand, he will move about like Time itself;
equal to the fire at the end of an eon in his wrath, lion-necked and high-minded, he,
O Bhārata, shall bring peace to the rear of the battle.
But his father, possessed of great splendor, though old, is superior even to the young;
he will perform great deeds in battle—of this I have no doubt.
Indeed, his father will perform great deeds in battle; there is no doubt.
Fanned by the wind of the force of his weapons and arising from the fuel of the army's dry grass, he—
intent on victory, that bull among men and leader of the hosts of chariot-divisions— will consume the troops of the son of Pāṇḍu.
The son of Bhāradvāja, the performer of fierce deeds for your benefit,
is the aged preceptor and teacher of all consecrated kings;
he shall bring about the end of the Sṛñjayas, though Dhananjaya is dear to him.
This great archer would never slay Pārtha, the doer of effortless deeds, for he remembers his radiant status as a teacher, won over by [Pārtha’s] virtues;
this hero always praises the full extent of Pārtha’s qualities.
Bhāradvāja regards him as even more distinguished than his own son; that powerful one could,
with a single chariot alone, slay the gods, Gandharvas, and Dānavas—
even when they are united in battle— by means of his divine weapons.
O King, that tiger among kings, the Paurava, a great car-warrior (*mahāratha*) who crushes the chariots of enemy heroes, is in my estimation a *ratha*, O hero,
as he scorches the enemy host accompanied by his own army.
He will consume the Pāñcālas as a black-trailed fire consumes dry grass;
that prince, a great car-warrior and the best of charioteers, who is devoted to truth,
O King, will range through your enemy's army like Time itself.
O Indra among kings, his warriors, equipped with diverse armor and weapons,
will range through the battle slaying your enemies. Vṛṣasena, the son of Karṇa, is a great car-warrior and the foremost of your chariot-fighters.
O King,

Jalasandha, the highly energetic Magadha slayer of enemy heroes and foremost of your great car-warriors, will consume the forces of your enemies and give up his life in battle, O best among the mighty.
This one, skilled on the back of an elephant, will fight in battle;
or else, the mighty-armed one, destroying the enemy host from his chariot—
O Great King, this bull among men is, in my opinion, a chariot-warrior.

For your sake, he will give up his life along with his army in the great battle; O King, this man is a valiant warrior and a versatile fighter in combat, and being fearless, he will fight against your enemies.
O King, I consider Bāhlīka to be an *atiratha*, a hero in battle who never retreats, equal to Vaivasvata himself;
for having entered the fray, he would not turn back under any circumstances.

O King, just as the commander-in-chief Satyavat, that great car-warrior of yours who performs wondrous deeds in battle and shatters the chariots of his enemies, always advances in the fray without striking down his foes, O Great King.

Having seen this battle, he feels no distress whatsoever; smiling, he advances against his enemies as they stand in their chariot paths. Valiant among his foes, he performs deeds worthy of a noble man.
O King, during the conflict, that supreme person,
the lord of the Rākṣasas, Alāyudha— the performer of cruel deeds and possessor of great strength—
will slay his enemies for your sake, remembering former enmity.
This Bhagadatta, the heroic and powerful lord of Prāgjyotiṣa, is the best of chariot-warriors among all the Rākṣasa hosts; skilled in illusion and firm in enmity, he will range through the battle.
The best of those who wield the elephant-goad and highly skilled in chariot warfare—
by him there occurred in former times a battle with the wielder of the Gāṇḍīva bow,
O King, for many days, as both were eager for victory.
Then, O son of Gandhārī, honoring the chastiser of Pāka as his friend, he entered into an agreement with that high-souled Pāṇḍava:
"This man, skilled in the art of riding upon the necks of elephants, will fight in battle."
The king, mounted upon Airāvata like Vāsava among the gods—
Bhīṣma said:
"Both brothers, Acala and Vṛṣaka, together..."
Your two chariots, difficult to assail, will destroy the enemies;
they are drawn by those two tigers among men, powerful, firm in their wrath, skilled strikers, the foremost of the Gāndhāras, youthful, handsome, and possessed of great strength.
O King, this Karṇa Vaikartana, who is harsh, boastful, and base, is your beloved friend who is always cruel in battle and incites you to conflict with the Pāṇḍavas.
He is a counselor, a leader, a kinsman, and one who is highly esteemed and exceedingly exalted.
Yet, O King, he is neither a full chariot-warrior (*ratha*) nor even an *atiratha*;
for he is deprived of his natural armor and is devoid of consciousness.
Deprived of his two divine earrings and being perpetually compassionate,
and due to the curse of Rāma and the words of the brahmin,
as well as the loss of his physical faculties, he is therefore considered by me to be a half-charioteer (ardharatha).
"Having encountered Phalguna, he shall not escape with his life.
Sanjaya said:
"Then the mighty-armed Drona, the best among wielders of weapons, spoke."
"It is exactly as you have said; there is nothing false in what you say.
However, because Karṇa is excessively proud in every battle yet is seen to turn his back, and because he is compassionate and negligent, I consider him to be only half a chariot-warrior."
Having heard this, O king of kings, the son of Rādhā, his eyes wide with rage,
spoke to Bhīṣma, piercing him with words like a goad:
"O Grandfather, you cut me to pieces at will with your word-arrows."
Though I am innocent, I have always endured all this at every step out of hatred for Duryodhana alone;
yet you consider me to be powerless, just like a coward.

"In my view, you are but a half-charioteer; of this there is no doubt. O Gāṅgeya, I do not speak falsely regarding the entire world. The King does not realize that you are eternally hostile to the Kurus."
For who indeed, among kings of equal status and noble deeds, would inflict such a destruction of prowess in battle while seeking to create a division,
as you do by attempting to commit an offense through the mere mention of his qualities?
"O Kaurava, the status of a great chariot-warrior (*mahāratha*) among the Kṣatriyas cannot be reckoned by years, nor by grey hair, nor by wealth, nor by kinsmen.
The Kṣatriya order is traditionally held to be superior by strength, while the twice-born are superior by their sacred knowledge."

Vaishyas are traditionally defined by their wealth, while Shudras are distinguished by their age. Yet, driven by desire and hatred, you act out of delusion by arbitrarily seizing chariots and great warriors for yourself.
"O mighty-armed Duryodhana, look well and act rightly! Abandon this evil disposition; Bhīṣma is indeed a source of sin for you.
For once an army is divided, O King, it becomes difficult to reunite."
O tiger among men, even those who are hereditary [servants]—how much more so those gathered from various origins?
O Bhārata, a state of duality has arisen among these warriors in battle; our energy is being destroyed right before our eyes, especially so.
Where is the skill of chariot-warriors, and where is the dull-witted Bhīṣma?
I shall hold back the army of the Pāṇḍavas;
having encountered me, whose arrows are never in vain, they shall flee in the ten directions.
The Pāṇḍavas, together with the Pañcālas, are like bulls facing a tiger. Where is the carnage of battle, or the well-spoken counsels?
And where is Bhīṣma, whose age has passed, who is dull-witted, and deluded by time?
For he always and constantly competes with the entire world,
and that man of vain vision considers no other person at all. Indeed, "one must listen to the elders"— this is the teaching of the scriptures.
"But even those who are exceedingly old are considered by me to be like children;
I alone shall slay the Pāṇḍavas, of this there is no doubt.
O tiger among kings, in a fair fight, the glory shall go to Bhīṣma."
"O lord of men, this Bhīṣma has been made your general by you;
a general is to be approached for his qualities, but never as a mere warrior.
O King, I will not fight in any way while the son of Gaṅgā is alive."
"But once Bhīṣma is slain, I shall be a warrior against all these great car-warriors.
Bhīṣma said:
"This immense burden, as vast as the ocean, has been undertaken by me."
This was long contemplated by the son of Dhṛtarāṣṭra for many years in the midst of battle;
now that this time has arrived— scorching and hair-raising—
you still live because you did not cause a rift between us, O son of a Sūta.
"O son of a Sūta, even though I am old, I would not today fail to display my prowess and shatter your desire for battle and your life itself in this conflict, O child,
were it not for Rāma, the son of Jamadagni, who discharged those great celestial weapons."
Not the slightest distress arose within me; what indeed will you do to me?
Though the virtuous do not approve of such self-praise regarding one's own strength, I shall speak to you, O wretched defiler of your lineage, for I am consumed with indignation.
At the *svayaṃvara* of the King of Kāśī, he defeated the assembled host of earthly kṣatriyas on a single chariot alone and swiftly carried off the maidens. Furthermore,
there are thousands more such distinguished men as these.
By me alone were they, along with their armies, repelled on the field of battle.
Having encountered you, a man of enmity, this great calamity of the Kurus has arrived for their destruction; exert yourself and be a man!
"Fight Pārtha in battle, with whom you vie!
I shall see you released from this conflict, O evil-minded one!
Sañjaya said:
Then the high-minded King Dhṛtarāṣṭra, son of Dhṛtarāṣṭra, said to him:
"Look upon me, O son of Gaṅgā, for a great task is at hand. First, consider this very thing, which is my supreme welfare."
"Both of you shall perform great deeds for me. Furthermore,
I wish to hear more about the best of chariot-warriors among the enemies—
those who are *atirathas* there, as well as the leaders of chariot-divisions (*rathayūthapas*)."
"O Kaurava, I wish to hear of the strengths and weaknesses of our enemies,
for this battle shall take place when the night has turned to dawn.
Bhīṣma said:
"O King, these Rathas have been enumerated, as well as the Atirathas;
now hear, O King, concerning those who are half-Rathas among the Pāṇḍavas,
if you still have curiosity regarding the strength of the Pāṇḍava army today."

"O mighty-armed one, calculate the number of chariots along with these lords of the earth. The Pāṇḍava king himself, that noble son of Kuntī, will move through the battle like fire, O dear one; of this there is no doubt."
But Bhīmasena, O king of kings, is a chariot equal to eight [ordinary] chariots;
there is no one equal to him in battle, whether with mace or even with arrows.
Possessing the strength of ten thousand elephants and full of pride, he is not a mere mortal by his splendor.
But the two sons of Mādrī, those two chariot-warriors and bulls among men,
were endowed with beauty and splendor like the two Aśvins;
standing at the head of the army, they remembered their own suffering.
They will conduct themselves like Rudras; of this I have no doubt.
They shall all be high-souled, rising up like the trunks of *śāla* trees, and they will exceed other men by a span in their stature.
All the sons of Pāṇḍu possess the sturdy build of lions and are endowed with great strength;
they have all practiced celibacy and are all exceedingly ascetic.
These tigers among men are modest, yet they are as fierce in their power as actual tigers.
In speed, in striking, and in combat, they were all truly superhuman;
O bull of the Bharatas, they had all conquered the lords of the earth during their conquest of the quarters.
Furthermore, no men could ever seize their weapons, maces, or arrows.
O Kaurava, they are always able to perform these feats:
stringing even their bows, raising up a heavy mace, or drawing back arrows; likewise in speed, in hitting a target, in eating, and in wrestling with the dust.
Even by those who are but children, you have all been distinguished;
having encountered their army, they will destroy it in battle like tigers fierce with strength— do not come into conflict with them.
Each one of them individually could have slain all those kings in battle,
O Indra among kings, as was witnessed by you at the Rājasūya sacrifice;
they also witnessed the suffering of Draupadī and the harsh words spoken during the gambling match.
Remembering this, they will roam through the battle like Death himself.
O hero, with his blood-red eyes and curly hair, and having Nārāyaṇa as his companion,
there is no chariot-warrior such as he among both armies here on earth.
Indeed, among the gods, or formerly among the Dānavas, Uragas,
Rākṣasas, Yakṣas, or even among men—
I have never heard of any such chariot that has existed or will ever exist.
O Great King, it was joined together just like that of the wise Pārtha:
Vāsudeva as the charioteer and Dhanañjaya as the warrior,
with the divine bow Gāṇḍīva and those horses possessing the speed of the wind.
An impenetrable divine armor, two inexhaustible great quivers,
and the collection of weapons belonging to Mahendra, Rudra, Kubera, Yama,
and Varuṇa, as well as maces of terrifying appearance.

Indeed, the various primary weapons such as the thunderbolt and thousands of Dānavas dwelling in Hiraṇyapura were slain in battle by him with a single chariot; who is there whose chariot is equal to his?
For this mighty-armed one, impetuous, powerful, and of true prowess, will surely strike down your army while protecting his own;
and either I or the Preceptor shall go forth against Dhananjaya.
O Indra among kings, there is no third chariot-warrior in either of the two armies who could withstand him as he rains down showers of arrows,
like a cloud driven by a great wind at the end of the summer heat.
"But the son of Kuntī is well-equipped, having Vāsudeva as his ally;
he is both young and skilled, whereas we both are old.
Saṃjaya said:
Having heard these words of Bhīṣma, the arms of those kings— thick, adorned with golden armlets, and smeared with sandalwood paste— then trembled;
along with their agitated minds, they recalled the events of the past.
[This was said] because the capability of the Pāṇḍava sons was seen directly before one's eyes.
Bhīṣma said:
"O great king, all five sons of Draupadī are great chariot-warriors (mahāratha)."
The son of Virāṭa, Uttara, is also considered by me to be a great chariot-warrior; and Abhimanyu, O Great King, is a leader of the leaders of chariot-divisions,
who in battle would be equal to Pārtha or even Vāsudeva.
Light-handed with his weapons, a versatile fighter, high-minded, and of firm prowess,
he will surely display his valor while remembering the sufferings of his father.
Satyaki of the Madhu clan is a hero, a leader among the leaders of chariot-divisions.
