O King, this Uttamaujas, the indomitable hero among the Vṛṣṇis who has conquered all fear, is likewise considered by me to be a great chariot-warrior. And Yudhāmanyu, the valiant bull among men, is also a noble chariot-warrior.

"O King of kings, O Bhārata, many thousands of chariots, elephants, and horses among these will fight on your side against the Pāṇḍavas, casting away their bodies out of a desire to do what is pleasing to the sons of Kuntī."
O King, challenging one another like Agni and the Maruts,
both Virāṭa and Drupada— those two aged and invincible heroes in battle— are, in my opinion, great car-warriors of immense prowess, bulls among men.

"Though advanced in years, those two remain devoted to the duty of the Kṣatriyas; established on the path of heroes, they will strive to the utmost of their power. O Indra among kings, by virtue of their kinship and their lineage of heroism and strength, they [will act]."
Bound by the noose of affection, both great archers remained devoted to the conduct of the noble; yet,
O bull among men, when they encounter a cause, all men of mighty arms— whether brave or even cowardly— act accordingly.

O lord of men, these two, possessed of firm devotion to Pārtha, have reached a single path; having renounced their lives, they strive with all their might. Both of them, fierce in combat, stand apart with their respective akṣauhiṇī divisions.

Preserving their relationship and protecting their trust, O Bhārata, those two world-heroes and great archers, having renounced their very selves, will perform a great deed. Preserving their trust, they will perform a great deed.
Bhīṣma said: "O King, O Bhārata, the son of the king of the Pañcālas, Śikhaṇḍin, the conqueror of enemy cities, is in my opinion the foremost car-warrior for Pārtha."
"He will fight in battle, destroying the established order and spreading your supreme fame among the armies, O Bhārata. His forces are numerous, as are the Pañcālas and the Prabhadrakas."
With that multitude of chariots, he will perform great deeds.
And Dhṛṣṭadyumna, O Bhārata, the commander-in-chief of all the armies,
is in my opinion an Atiratha, O King— that great car-warrior who is a disciple of Droṇa.
He will fight in the battle, slaughtering his enemies in combat like the enraged Lord Pinākin at the end of a Yuga. Those who delight in war speak of that chariot-army of his.
Because of their great number, they were like the ocean, resembling the hosts of gods in battle. But,
O Indra among kings, I consider the son of Dhṛṣṭadyumna to be only half a chariot-warrior, O monarch, for he is still young and has not yet undergone much training in the duties of a Kṣatriya.
The heroic son of Śiśupāla, the king of the Cedis and a great chariot-warrior (mahāratha),
Dhṛṣṭaketu, a mighty archer and kinsman of the Pāṇḍava—
this brave lord of the Cedis, O Bhārata, is here together with his son.
As a great car-warrior, he will perform a great deed that is difficult to accomplish;
devoted to the duty of a Kṣatriya, this conqueror of enemy cities is esteemed by me. And as for Kṣatradeva, O Indra among kings, he is the foremost of chariot-warriors among the Pāṇḍavas.
Jayanta, Amitaujas, and Satyajit, that great car-warrior—
all these high-souled great car-warriors, the best of the Pāñcālas,
will fight in battle, O dear one, like elephants in rut.
Aja and Bhoja, both valiant great-chariot warriors among the Pāṇḍavas,
world-renowned heroes and mighty archers who have renounced their very selves— these two great-chariot warriors will strive to the utmost of their power for the sake of assisting the Pāṇḍavas.
O Indra among kings, these five Kekaya brothers are swift in the use of weapons, versatile combatants, skillful, firm in their prowess, and fierce in battle;
all of them are noble chariot-warriors, and all possess crimson banners.
Kāśika, Sukumāra, Nīla, and another king named Sūryadatta, Śaṅkha, and Madirāśva—
all these were noble chariot-warriors, all possessing the marks of heroes in battle.
All of them are experts in every weapon, and all are considered by me to be high-souled. O great king, Vārdhakṣemi is regarded by me as a great chariot-warrior;
and King Citrāyudha is considered by me to be the best of chariot-warriors.
For Cekitāna, who shines in battle,
and Satyadhṛti, who is devoted to Kiritin— these two tigers among men are both great car-warriors (mahāratha) of the Pāṇḍavas; in my opinion, these two are preeminent chariot-fighters.

Vyāghradatta, O Indra among kings, and Candrasena, O Bhārata—in my opinion, these two are preeminent chariot-warriors among the Pāṇḍavas; of this there is no doubt. And Senābindu, O Indra among kings, and he who is known by the name Krodhahantṛ—
He who is the equal of Vāsudeva and the conqueror of Bhīmasena will fight here with great prowess against your soldiers,
just as you hold me, Droṇa, and Kṛpa in high esteem.
Likewise, that son of Kāśī, who delights in battle, should be considered the best of chariot-warriors; possessing extremely swift weapons, he is a praiseworthy and supreme ratha,
and I consider this conqueror of enemy cities to be a ratha of single quality [superior to me].

And this youthful son of Drupada, Satyajit, who boasts in battle and is valiant in combat, should be considered an eightfold chariot-warrior (*aṣṭaguṇa-ratha*); for he has attained the status of an *atiratha*,
being equal to Dhṛṣṭadyumna.

Desirous of glory for the Pāṇḍavas, he will perform a supreme deed. Devoted and heroic, this other great chariot-warrior is the King of Pāṇḍya, possessed of great prowess and the upholder of the Pāṇḍavas' burden.
Dṛḍhadhanvan, the great archer and best of chariot-warriors among the Pāṇḍavas;
Śreṇimān, O best of the Kauravas; and King Vasudāna—both of these, O scorcher of foes, are in my opinion Atirathas.
"Two other sons of Virāṭa, Śaṅkha and Śveta, both great chariot-warriors,
will perform great deeds for the sake of assisting the Pāṇḍavas.
Bhīṣma said:

O Great King, Bhārata, the illustrious and great car-warrior Rocamāna among the Pāṇḍavas will fight like an immortal against the enemy forces in battle. And Purujit Kuntibhoja is a great archer of immense strength.
The maternal uncle of Bhīmasena is also, in my opinion, an *atiratha*;
this hero is a great archer, accomplished and skillful,
a versatile combatant, capable, and in my view, a preeminent car-warrior (*rathapuṃgava*).
For he will fight with valor, like Maghavan against the Dānavas;
and all his warriors are renowned, each an expert in battle.
For the sake of his sister's son, that hero will act in the conflict.

O Great King, the son of Bhīmasena, the Rākṣasa lord Haiḍimba, stands ready to perform great deeds for the benefit and welfare of the Pāṇḍavas; in my opinion, this leader of chariot-divisions is a master of many illusions.
"O dear one, he who delights in battle will fight in the encounter with his illusory powers (māyā). And those heroic Rākṣasa ministers who are under his command—
these and many other lords of various realms— "
Assembled for the sake of the Pāṇḍava, with Vāsudeva at their head—

these, O King, are the principal ones among the chariot-warriors, the great chariot-warriors (*atiratha*s), and those who are considered half-chariot-warriors (*ardharatha*s) of the high-souled Pāṇḍava.
O King, they will lead that formidable army of Yudhiṣṭhira in battle,
protected by the heroic Kirīṭin as if by Mahendra himself. O hero, when they come toward you in battle seeking victory, I shall [encounter] them.
Desiring victory, or else death in battle, I shall fight;
I will encounter those two supreme men, Pārtha and Vāsudeva, who bear the Gāṇḍīva bow and the discus, like the sun and moon meeting at the junction of day and night.
"And those noble chariot-warriors who are the soldiers of Pāṇḍu’s son—
I shall encounter them along with their armies at the forefront of the battle.
These are your chariot-warriors and great chariot-warriors."
O King, I have described them to you according to their primary importance;
likewise, O King, lord of the Kauravas, there are some who are half-chariot-warriors among them as well.
"O Bhārata, I shall hold back Arjuna, Vāsudeva, and all the other kings who are there, for as long as I behold them;
however, O mighty-armed one, I will not slay Śikhaṇḍin, the prince of the Pañcālas."
Beholding him with arrows raised, ready to fight back in battle,
the world knows that, desiring to do what was pleasing to my father,
I renounced the kingdom I had obtained and remained firm in my vow of celibacy.
I consecrated Citrāṅgada in the kingdom of the Kauravas, and I consecrated the youth Vicitravīrya as the heir apparent;
having made his devotion to the gods (devavrata) famous among all the kings on earth.

"I would never slay a woman, nor anyone who was previously a woman, under any circumstances. For you have heard, O King, that Śikhaṇḍin was formerly a girl and was born a man; therefore, O Bhārata, I will not fight him."
"But I shall slay all other kings, O bull of the Bharatas,
whom I encounter in battle, yet not the sons of Kuntī, O King.
Duryodhana said:
"O best of the Bharatas, for what reason do you not slay Śikhaṇḍin,
who has raised his arrow and is seen as an assailant in battles?
O mighty-armed one, having previously declared [your intent] to the Pāṇḍavas along with the Somakas..."
"O son of Gaṅgā, O grandfather, tell me that [reason] why you said, 'I shall slay them.
Bhīṣma said:
"Listen, Duryodhana, along with these lords of the earth, to this story."
O bull of the Bharatas, it was for this reason that, having observed Śikhaṇḍin in battle, I would not slay him. My father, the great king Śantanu,
that righteous soul and bull among men, reached his destined end at the appointed time, O best of men.
Then, O best of the Bharatas, fulfilling my vow,
I consecrated my brother Citrāṅgada in the great kingdom.
And when he had met his death, I remained steadfast in the will of Satyavatī.

I consecrated King Vicitravīrya according to the prescribed rites. O Indra among kings, although he was the younger brother, Vicitravīrya, being righteous in soul, looked only to me for guidance after his own consecration by me in accordance with dharma.

"O dear one, desiring to perform his marriage rites, I too set my mind upon it, thinking that he should be wedded to a family of equal status. In this regard, O mighty-armed one, I heard that there were three maidens at a *svayaṃvara*."
At that time, all the daughters of the King of Kāśī were peerless in beauty—
Ambā, Ambikā, and likewise the other, Ambālikā—
and kings from across the earth were summoned, O bull of the Bharatas.
Of them, Ambā was the eldest, Ambikā was the middle one, and Ambālikā, O Indra among kings, was the youngest princess. Then, I went alone on a single chariot to the city of the lord of Kāśī.
O mighty-armed lord of the earth, I saw those three well-adorned maidens and the kings who had assembled there. Then, having summoned all those monarchs standing in the assembly, I spoke.
O bull of the Bharatas, I caused those maidens to ascend the chariot;
and having understood that their dowry was valor, I then placed them upon the chariot and addressed all the kings assembled there.
"Bhīṣma, the son of Śāntanu, is abducting the maiden," they said again and again.
"Therefore, all you kings, strive with your utmost power for her liberation;
for I shall carry her away by force while you look on, O lords of men."

Then those protectors of the earth sprang up with weapons raised, crying out in their anger, "Yoke! Yoke!", and they urged on their charioteers. Those elephant-warriors [advanced] with chariots resembling clouds and with elephants.
Then the protectors of the earth, with their horses adorned with golden trappings, rushed forward with weapons raised.
O lord of the people, all those kings then surrounded me on every side with a vast multitude of chariots.

I warded them off with a great shower of arrows and conquered all those kings, just as the King of the Gods conquers the Dānavas. As they charged forward, [I struck down] their variegated banners adorned with gold.
For with each single arrow, O bull among men, I struck down their horses, elephants, and charioteers upon the earth in battle;
laughing, I felled them with my blazing shafts.
Seeing that agility of mine, they were turned back and broken;
all those kings indeed prostrated themselves and offered praise.
Then, having taken those maidens and having dismissed those monarchs, [I departed].

Then, O Bhārata, having conquered the rulers of the earth, I returned to Hastināpura; therefore, O mighty-armed one, I presented those maidens for the sake of my brother and reported that deed to Satyavatī.
Bhīṣma said:
Then, O best of the Bharatas, having approached and saluted my mother, the daughter of the fisherman and mother of heroes, I spoke these words to her.
"O King, having defeated the rulers of the earth, these daughters of the Lord of Kāśī were won by me as a prize for my prowess for the sake of Vicitravīrya.
Then, O King, with eyes brimming with tears, she smelled his head.
Satyavatī spoke joyfully: "O son, by good fortune you have triumphed!
But when the marriage was about to take place with Satyavatī’s consent, the eldest daughter of the King of Kāśī spoke these words with bashfulness.
"O Bhīṣma, you are a knower of dharma and an expert in all the scriptures;
having heard my words concerning dharma, it behooves you to act accordingly here.
Previously, the lord of Śālva was chosen by me as my husband in my mind."
"And I was chosen by him previously, even before my father was aware of it in secret.
O King Bhīṣma, how could you— being a Kaurava and especially one learned in the sacred scriptures— keep me in your house when my heart is set on another?"

Having determined this with your intellect and mind, O bull of the Bharatas, you ought to begin here that which is appropriate for you, O mighty-armed one. It is evident, O lord of people, that the king of the Śālvas is waiting for me.
Therefore, O best of the Kurus, you ought to grant me your permission. Have mercy on me, O mighty-armed one, O foremost of those who uphold dharma;
for we have heard, O hero, that you are devoted to truth upon this earth.
Bhīṣma said:
Then, having obtained the permission of Kālī Satyavatī,
as well as the ministers, the twice-born brahmins, and the family priests, I [departed].
"O lord of men, I have given my consent for my eldest daughter,
Ambā. Having received permission, that maiden departed for the city of the lord of Śālva,
protected by elderly twice-born men and accompanied by her nurse."
Having traversed that path, she reached the lord of men;
having approached King Śālva, she spoke these words:
"O mighty-armed one, O one of great splendor, I have come here for your sake."
Rejoice in me, O King, who am ever devoted to your pleasure and welfare; wait upon me, O King, and practice the duties of righteousness according to dharma.
For you were meditated upon by my mind, and I have been summoned by you.
O lord of the people, the Lord of Śālva spoke to her as if smiling:
"O lady of excellent complexion, I do not desire you as a wife since you have previously belonged to another. Go back, O blessed one, to the presence of that descendant of Bharata."
"I do not desire you, who have been seized by Bhīṣma by force.
For you were then led away by Bhīṣma after he had conquered you with joy,
having touched you in a great battle after defeating the lords of the earth."
"O woman of excellent complexion, I do not desire you as a wife since you have had another before;
how could a king such as I,
who possesses realized wisdom and prescribes the dharma to others, admit a woman who has belonged to another?"
"Go as you please, O blessed lady; let not this time pass you by.
O King, Ambā, tormented by the arrows of the bodiless god, said to him:
"Do not speak thus, O protector of the earth; this shall never be so."
"I am not pleased, O crusher of foes, that I have been led away by Bhīṣma;
I was carried off by force while weeping, after he had put the lords of the earth to flight.
O Lord of Śālva, accept me, your devoted, young, and innocent bride."
"Indeed, the abandonment of devotees is not praised among the duties of dharma. Having thus taken leave of the son of Gaṅgā, who never retreats in battles,
and having been granted permission by him, I have come to your very home."
"O lord of the people, that mighty-armed Bhīṣma does not desire me;
I have heard that Bhīṣma’s undertaking was for the sake of his brother.
O King, those two sisters of mine, Ambikā and Ambālikā, were taken away."
For Gāṅgeya gave [the kingdom] to his younger brother Vicitravīrya;
O Lord of Śālva, I swear by my head that I do not think of any other man whatsoever except you, O tiger among men.
"O Indra among kings, I have not been previously married to another; I have come to you.
I speak the truth, O Śālva, and I swear this by my own soul. Accept me, O large-eyed one, for I have come to you as a maiden."
"O Indra among kings, she who has never belonged to another and who longs for your favor"—
as the daughter of the King of Kāśī was speaking thus, O best of the Bharatas, Śālva cast her off like a snake sheds its worn-out skin.

O sinless bull of the Bharata race, though he was thus entreated by her with many kinds of words, the lord of Śālva placed no faith in the maiden. Thereupon, the eldest daughter of the king of Kāśī was overcome with indignation.
With tearful eyes and a voice faltering with sobs, she said:
"O Lord of the People, wherever I may go abandoned by you,
may there be for me the refuge of the virtuous, just as I have spoken the truth."
O descendant of Kuru, while she was thus speaking piteously and lamenting, the cruel King Śālva then abandoned her;
Śālva spoke to her again and again, saying, "Go, go!"
"I am afraid of Bhīṣma, O fair-hipped one, and you are under Bhīṣma's protection.
Thus addressed by that short-sighted Śālva,
she departed from the city, dejected and weeping like an osprey.
Bhīṣma said:
As she was departing from the city, O Bhārata, she reflected:
"There is no young woman on earth who is situated in a more precarious position than I."
"I am bereft of my kinsmen and have been rejected by Śālva;
nor is it possible for me to return again to the city named after the elephant (Hastināpura),
for I was permitted [to leave] by Bhīṣma on account of Śālva."
"Should I blame myself, or the invincible Bhīṣma? Or rather, my foolish father, who himself arranged this svayaṃvara for me?
This is a fault of my own making, since I [climbed] from Bhīṣma’s chariot at that time..."

"In the past, when the slaughterous battle was raging, I did not go to the aid of Śālva; this is the resulting fruition of that act, that I have fallen into such distress like a fool. Fie on Bhīṣma! And fie on my dull-witted father, whose mind is so deluded!"

"By whom I have been cast forth like a courtesan for the price of valor—shame on me! Shame on King Śālva! And shame also on the Creator, by whose wicked conduct I have fallen into this supreme calamity!"
In every way, a human being receives his own lot;
however, Bhīṣma, the son of Śāntanu, is the mouthpiece for this misfortune of mine.
Therefore, I see that I must now take retribution against Bhīṣma.
"Whether by asceticism or by battle, that is what I consider to be the cause of my sorrow.
What king indeed would venture to defeat Bhīṣma in combat?
Having thus resolved, she departed from the city.
[She reached] the hermitage of high-souled ascetics of virtuous conduct;
there she dwelt that night, surrounded by the ascetics,
and related everything that had happened to her, O Bhārata.

O mighty-armed one of pure smiles, she related in full detail everything regarding the abduction, the release, and the dismissal by Śālva. Then, there was a great Brāhmaṇa there who was firm in his vows.
Śaikhāvatya, advanced in asceticism and a teacher in both the Śāstra and the Āraṇyaka,
that sage of great austerity spoke to her as she was distressed—
a virtuous young woman sighing and devoted to grief and sorrow.
"This being the case, O blessed one, what indeed can be done by the ascetics dwelling in the hermitage— those highly fortunate, great-souled ones who are constant in their penance?
She then said to him, "O King, let a favor be granted to me."
"I wish to go forth into the religious life here; I shall perform difficult austerities.
Surely these evil deeds were committed by me alone in previous bodies while I was deluded; this is certainly their fruit."
"O ascetics, I cannot bear to go back to my own people,
having been rejected, joyless, and cast out by Śālva. O you who are free from stain, I desire to practice asceticism here."
"O you who resemble gods, have compassion for me.
He consoled that maiden with examples, scriptures, and logical arguments;
he comforted her and, together with the twice-born, pledged to accomplish her purpose.
Bhīṣma said:
Then all those virtuous ascetics became occupied with a task,
reflecting upon that maiden and wondering what ought to be done.

Some ascetics said, "Let her be taken to her father's house," while other best of the twice-born set their minds on reproaching us. Some thought that having gone to the lord of the Śālvas, he should be constrained [to accept her].
"No," some decided, "for she has been rejected by him.
This being the case, O blessed lady, what indeed can be done by wise men?
And all those ascetics of rigid vows spoke again.
"Enough of this wandering life here, O blessed lady; listen to these beneficial words. Go from here, may you be blessed, to your father's very home.
Your father, the king, will provide for whatever must follow next."
"There you shall dwell in happiness, O auspicious lady, endowed with all virtues. And no other refuge would be proper for you, O blessed one, than your father;
for a woman's refuge is her husband or her father, O woman of excellent complexion."
In times of stability, the husband is one's refuge; but in times of adversity, the father is the refuge.
Indeed, this life of renunciation is exceedingly difficult for one so delicate, especially for you, O beautiful lady, who are a princess by birth and a young maiden by nature.

"O blessed one, O woman of excellent complexion, many faults indeed exist for a woman living in a hermitage that would not occur in her father's house. Then those brahmins spoke these words to that ascetic woman.
"Seeing you here alone in this desolate and dense forest, the lords of kings will seek you; therefore, do not set your mind upon such a course. Ambā said:

"It is not possible for me to go again to the city of Kāśī, to my father's house; I shall undoubtedly be held in contempt by my kinsmen. For, O ascetics, I lived differently during my childhood in my father's home."
"I shall not go; may it be well with you—wherever my father may be.
I desire to practice austerities, protected by ascetics, so that even in the next world there may be no such great calamity for me."
"O best of Brahmins, because of this misfortune, I shall perform austerities.
Bhīṣma said:
"While those Brahmins were thus reflecting in various ways,"
The royal seer Hotravāhana, an ascetic, arrived at that forest;
seeing that beautiful woman and hearing [of her situation], his mind became deeply distressed.
Then all those ascetics paid homage to that king.
With honors such as a welcome, a seat, and water, they received him;
then, once he was seated and rested,
the forest-dwellers spoke again concerning the maiden while he listened.
O Bhārata, having heard that story of his mother and of the King of Kāśī,
that royal seer of great splendor became troubled in mind;
having heard her speak thus and having seen her, that man of great asceticism was deeply moved.
Then the high-souled royal sage Hotravāhana, overcome with compassion, rose up trembling; O Lord, the father of this mother took that maiden upon his lap and comforted her.
He questioned her in full about the origin of this calamity from the very beginning,
and she reported to him in detail exactly what had occurred.
Thereupon, that royal seer was overcome with pain and grief.
The one of great asceticism resolved upon that course in his mind;
then, trembling and deeply distressed, he spoke to the afflicted maiden:
"Do not go to your father's house, O blessed lady, for I am the father of your mother."
"I shall indeed sever your suffering; abide with me, my daughter. Your mind has had enough, my child, that you are thus withered away. Go at my word to Rāma, the son of Jamadagni, the ascetic."
Rāma will remove your great suffering and grief;
he will slay Bhīṣma in battle if he does not heed your words. Go to that best of the Bhārgavas, whose splendor is equal to the fire of time.
"That one of great asceticism will establish you on the even path.
Then, shedding tears with a choked voice again and again,
she spoke thus to her father Hotravāhana.
Having saluted him with my head, I shall depart at your command;
perhaps today I might behold that noble one, world-renowned. And how will that descendant of Bhṛgu dispel this intense suffering of mine?
"I wish to hear this, for then I shall indeed go there.
Hotravāhana said:
"O child, you shall see Rāma, the son of Jamadagni, in the great forest."
On Mahendra, the best of mountains, sages learned in the Vedas, as well as Gandharvas and Apsarases, constantly wait upon the mighty Rāma, who is true to his promise and engaged in fierce asceticism.
Go there, may prosperity be yours, and speak these words of mine to him:
first, having saluted with your head that one who is advanced in asceticism and firm in his vows, you should then say again, "O blessed lady, what is the task you desire to have done?"
"When I am invoked, Rāma will do all that for you.
My dear child, Rāma is my friend, full of affection, and my well-wisher—
the heroic son of Jamadagni, the best among all wielders of weapons."
While King Hotravāhana was speaking thus to the maiden,
Akṛtavraṇa, the beloved follower of Rāma, appeared.
Then all those sages rose up by the thousands.
And that king Sṛñjaya Hotravāhana was advanced in years;
then, O best of the Bharatas, having questioned one another according to custom, those forest-dwellers sat down together, surrounding him.

Then, O king of kings, filled with affection, joy, and delight, they recounted various delightful, lovely, and divine stories. Then, at the conclusion of the conversation, the high-souled royal sage Hotravāhana—
He questioned Akṛtavraṇa, the most excellent among the great seers, regarding Rāma:
"O mighty-armed one, where is the powerful son of Jamadagni at this time?
O Akṛtavraṇa, is it possible to see that best of those who know the Vedas?"
Akṛtavraṇa said:
"O Lord, O King, Rāma constantly speaks of you alone,
saying, 'The royal sage Sṛñjaya is my dear friend.'"
"It is my thought that Rāma will be here tomorrow at dawn;
you shall see him arriving here out of a desire to behold you.
And for what purpose, O royal sage, has this maiden come to the forest?"
"To whom does she belong, and who are you? I wish to know this.
Hotravāhana said:
"O Lord, she is my daughter's daughter, the auspicious daughter of the King of Kāśī."
O sinless one, Jyeṣṭhā stood at her *svayaṃvara* together with her two sisters.
This eldest daughter of the Lord of Kāśī is renowned as Ambā;
the other two younger ones, O ascetic, are Ambikā and Ambālikā.
Then, O Brahmarṣi, the entire assembly of the Kṣatriyas gathered in the city of Kāśī for the sake of the maiden, and there a great festival took place. Then,
it is said, the immensely powerful Bhīṣma, the son of Śāntanu, [challenged] the kings...
Having cast them down, the one of great splendor carried off those three maidens; then,
O Bhārata, having conquered the protectors of the earth, the pure-souled Bhīṣma returned to Hastināpura together with the maidens.
Then, having informed Satyavatī that the marriage was ready to take place,
the lord gave orders regarding his brother Vicitravīrya. Thereupon,
seeing that the bride had been obtained for the wedding, he prepared for the ceremony.
O bull among the twice-born, there in the midst of the ministers, she said to the son of Gaṅgā:
"O hero, the lord of Śālva was chosen by me as my husband in my heart.
O knower of dharma, you ought not to give me away when my mind is set on another."
Having heard those words, Bhīṣma consulted with his ministers; having reached a decision and remaining steadfast in the opinion of Satyavatī, he sent her forth.
Once permitted by Bhīṣma, she then departed for Śālva, the lord of Saubha.
O Brahmin, this maiden, filled with joy, spoke these words at that time:
"I have been dismissed by Bhīṣma; establish me in righteousness.
O bull among kings, you were previously chosen by me in my heart."
And Śālva also rejected her, suspecting her character:
"She has reached this penance grove and is intensely devoted to the life of an ascetic;
moreover, she was recognized by me through the proclamation of her lineage."
"And he considers Bhīṣma alone to be the cause of the arising of this suffering.
While the king was speaking thus, the maiden spoke these words. Ambā said:
"O Blessed One, it is exactly as the lord of the earth has said:
Sṛñjaya Hotravāhana is the one who formed my body from his mother.
O rich in asceticism, I do not venture to return to my own city."
Out of fear of being held in contempt and out of shame, O great sage,
whatever the venerable Rāma shall say to me, O best of the twice-born,
that is the most important task for me to perform; such is my thought, O venerable one.
Akṛtavraṇa said:
"O blessed lady, which of these two sorrows do you wish to have remedied?
O frail one, tell me that, my child, so that it may be counteracted."
"O blessed lady, if the lord of Saubha is to be dispatched according to your wish,
the high-souled Rāma will dispatch him out of a desire for your welfare.
Or, if you desire that Bhīṣma, the son of the River, be sent by the wise Rāma..."
"Even Bhārgava might act so as to see him utterly defeated in battle;
having heard the words of Sṛñjaya and yours as well, O lady of pure smiles,
let that which must be done next be considered this very day."
She said:
"O Blessed One, I have been carried away by Bhīṣma while he was unaware;
for Bhīṣma does not know, O Brahmin, that my heart is fixed upon Śālva."
Having reflected upon this with your mind, you yourself should determine the decision according to what is right; let the arrangement be made accordingly—
whether it be with Bhīṣma, that tiger among the Kurus, or rather with the King of Śālva.
"O Brahmin, do whatever is appropriate for both of us.
For I have explained to you exactly how this root of suffering arose;
O Blessed One, you ought to devise a remedy for it with due consideration."
Akṛtavraṇa said:
"O blessed lady, O woman of excellent complexion, it is fitting that you should speak such words regarding dharma; now listen to these words of mine."
"If the son of the River had not indeed led you to Hastināpura,
O timid one, Śālva, incited by Rāma, would have seized you by the hair.
It was because of him, O blessed lady, that you were conquered and carried away, O beautiful woman."
O slender-waisted lady, because of that, King Śālva harbors doubt regarding you;
likewise, Bhīṣma prides himself on his manhood and appears as one who has already achieved victory.
Therefore, it is fitting for you to take retaliatory action against Bhīṣma.
Ambā said:
"O Brahmin, this same great desire has also constantly arisen in my heart:
'I would slay Bhīṣma in battle.'"
"Whether it be Bhīṣma, or the King of Śālva, or whomever you blame for this fault— O mighty-armed one, punish him, on whose account I am so deeply distressed.
Bhīṣma said:
While they were speaking thus,
O best of the Bharatas, that day passed away, as did the night, with its pleasant, cool, and warm breezes.
Then Rāma appeared, as if blazing with splendor.
O King, surrounded by his disciples, that sage— wearing matted hair and bark garments, bow in hand, undepressed in spirit, bearing a sword and an axe,
and free from passion— approached King Sṛñjaya, O tiger among kings.
Then, seeing him, all those ascetics, that king of great austerity,
and that ascetic maiden stood with palms joined in reverence;
they attentively honored Bhārgava with the madhuparka offering.
Having been honored according to custom, he sat down together with them.
Then, O Bhārata, those two— the royal seer Sṛñjaya and the son of Jamadagni— began to converse about events of the past.
Then, at the conclusion of their conversation, the royal sage spoke these sweet and meaningful words at the appropriate time to the mighty Rāma, the best of the Bhṛgus:
"O Lord Rāma, this daughter of my daughter is the daughter of the King of Kāśī."
"O you who are skilled in what must be done, hear from me the truth regarding her task;
let the supreme course of action be told," Rāma replied to her.
Thereupon, she approached Rāma, who was like a blazing fire.
Having saluted Rāma’s feet with her head, that auspicious woman stood before him, touching them with her lotus-petal-like hands;
overcome with grief, she wept, her eyes clouded with tears.
She sought refuge with the descendant of Bhṛgu, who is worthy of being a refuge.
Rāma said:
"O princess, as you are toward this Sṛñjaya, so are you toward me."
"Tell me what causes you mental distress; I shall carry out your word.
Ambā said:
"O Blessed One of great vows, I have today sought refuge in you."
"And O Lord, lift me up from this terrible ocean of grief, which is like a mire.
Bhīṣma said:
"And having beheld her beauty and her youthful age once again,"
Rāma, who was exceedingly delicate, became lost in thought;
reflecting, "What will she say?", that best of the Bhṛgus,
Rāma, meditated for a long time, overwhelmed with compassion.
"Tell me," Rāma said again to her of the pure smile;
she then related everything exactly as it had happened to the descendant of Bhṛgu.
Having heard those words of the princess, the son of Jamadagni then—
Having reached a firm conclusion regarding the matter, he said to that woman of beautiful hips:
"O beautiful lady, I shall send word to Bhīṣma, the best of the Kurus;
having heard my righteous words, that lord of men will surely comply."
"If the son of Jahnavī does not carry out the words spoken by me,
O blessed lady, I shall consume him along with his ministers in battle by the fire of my weapons.
Or, if your mind turns away from that course, O princess..."
"In the meantime, I shall employ the heroic lord of Śālva in this task.
Ambā said:
"O descendant of Bhṛgu, as soon as I heard [your words], I was dismissed by Bhīṣma."
My mind had previously been set upon King Śālva; having approached King Saubhari, I spoke words that were difficult to utter. Yet he did not accept me, suspecting my character.

O descendant of Bhṛgu, having deliberated upon all this with your own intellect, you ought to consider what action is appropriate here. Bhīṣma, who observes great vows, is the root of this calamity of mine.

"O mighty-armed tiger among the Bhṛgus, slay Bhīṣma, by whom I was then forcibly abducted and brought under his control; because of him, I have experienced such sorrow and am now enduring this supreme misery."
"For he, O Bhārgava, is greedy, arrogant, and boastful of his victories;
therefore, O sinless one, it is fitting for you to take retaliatory action against him.
This was done by the descendant of Bharata while I was being carried away, O Lord."
A resolve arose in my heart: "I shall cause the one of great vows to be slain.
Therefore, O sinless Rāma, fulfill this desire of mine today;
slay Bhīṣma, O mighty-armed one, just as Purandara slew Vṛtra.
Bhīṣma said:
Thus addressed, O Lord, with the words "Slay Bhīṣma," Rāma spoke to the weeping maiden who was urging him again and again.
"O lady of excellent complexion, I would certainly not take up a weapon against Kāśya, except for the sake of those who know the Veda; what else may I do for you?
O Queen, both Bhīṣma and Śālva are obedient to my will through my word."

"O lady of faultless limbs, I shall do that which is to come to pass; do not grieve. However, O beautiful woman, I shall by no means take up a weapon, except at the command of the Brahmins—this is the vow I have made."
Ambā said:
"My sorrow must be dispelled by your holiness by whatever means possible;
since that [sorrow] was caused by Bhīṣma, O Lord, destroy it for me without delay."
Rāma said:
"O daughter of Kāśī, speak again; Bhīṣma, though he is worthy of being honored by bowing his head at your feet, shall nevertheless grasp both your feet at my word."
Rāma said: "O Bhīṣma, slay him in battle if you wish to do what is pleasing to me,
like a roaring Asura."
"O Rāma, challenged to battle,
if that which was promised is true, you ought to fulfill it here.
Bhīṣma said:
While Rāma and Ambā were thus conversing, O King,
Akṛtavraṇa addressed these words to the son of Jamadagni:
"O mighty-armed one, you ought not to abandon this maiden who has come to you for refuge."
"O Rāma, slay Bhīṣma in battle like an roaring Asura!
O great sage Rāma, if Bhīṣma is challenged by you in battle,
he will either say, 'I am defeated,' or he will do as you command."
"O descendant of Bhṛgu, the task for this maiden shall be accomplished;
O hero, O Lord, your word shall be made true.
And this was your vow at that time, O Rāma, O great sage."
"O Bhārgava, having indeed conquered all the Kṣatriyas, I made this vow before the Brāhmaṇas:
'If a Brāhmaṇa, a Kṣatriya, a Vaiśya, or even a Śūdra should become a hater of the Veda in battle,
I shall surely slay him.'"
For those who have come for refuge, who are terrified and seeking their lives,
I shall not be able to abandon them while I am alive, by any means whatsoever.
And as for him who will conquer the entire assembled host of Kṣatriyas in battle—
"O Bhārgava, I shall slay that arrogant soul," so said Rāma, the victorious Bhīṣma, the upholder of the Kuru lineage. Therefore, O descendant of Bhṛgu, encounter him in battle and fight with him.
Rāma said:
"O best of sages, I remember the vow I made in the past;
I shall act exactly so that he will obtain [the bride] through peaceful means alone."
"O Great Brahmin, this is a great task that has been on the mind of the daughter of Kāśī:
'I myself will go there, taking the maiden with me, to where he is,
if Bhīṣma, who boasts of his prowess in battle, does not carry out my word.'"
"I have made up my mind that I shall slay this arrogant one;
for the arrows released by me do not merely stick in the bodies of living beings—
this was known to you previously in the battle of the kṣatriyas."
Bhīṣma said:
Having spoken thus, the high-minded Rāma, together with those exponents of the Veda, resolved to depart and rose up.
Then, having stayed there that night, those ascetics—
having offered oblations into the fire and recited their prayers— set out with the desire to kill me.
Then Rāma approached them along with those bulls among brahmins.
O great king, descendant of Bharata, they all then settled at Kurukṣetra together with the maiden, surrounding the Sarasvatī river;
those high-souled ascetics were led by the best of the Bhṛgus.
Bhīṣma said:
Then, O King, on the third day, having established himself on level ground,
that one of great vows sent word to me, saying, "I have arrived."
O king of kings, having heard that the mighty lord, that treasury of splendor, had arrived at the border of my territory, I quickly went forth with speed out of affection,
preceded by a cow and surrounded by brahmins.
Seeing that I had approached him, the powerful son of Jamadagni, together with his god-like officiating priests and domestic chaplains,
accepted my worship and spoke these words.
"O Bhīṣma, with what intention did you bring here this daughter of the King of Kāśī,
who was unwilling, and then release her again? For she has been deprived by you of the attainment of dharma, both high and low."
"O Bhārata, for who indeed would venture to approach this woman once she has been touched by you?
For she was rejected by Śālva, thinking, 'She has been carried off by you,' O Bhārata. Therefore, at my command, accept her, O Bhārata."
"O tiger among men, let this princess obtain her own dharma;
O sinless one, it is not proper for you, a king, to inflict this humiliation. Then, observing that he was dejected in mind, I spoke to him."
"O Brahmana, I would never give her back to my brother under any circumstances. O Bhargava, she previously told me here, 'I belong to Shalva.
And with my permission, she departed for the city of Saubha."

"Neither out of fear, nor out of compassion, nor out of greed, nor from a desire for wealth would I abandon the duty of a Kṣatriya; this is the vow I have undertaken. Then Rāma, his eyes clouded with anger, spoke to me.
"If you do not do as I have said, O bull among the Kurus,
I shall slay you today along with your ministers," Rāma said again and again in his agitation, his eyes clouded with rage.
O tiger among the Bhrigus, I repeatedly entreated that subduer of enemies with my cherished words, yet he did not calm his anger;
even when thus beseeched, he would not show me favor.
Having bowed my head again to that best of brahmins, I asked him:
"What is the reason that you wish to fight me here? For the fourfold science of archery was taught to me, while I was still a child, by you alone."
"O mighty-armed Bhārgava, you have taught me; I am your disciple.
Then Rāma, his eyes bloodshot with anger, said to me:
"O Bhīṣma, do you not recognize me as your preceptor, and yet you do not accept this [instruction]?"
"O Kauravya, O lord of the earth, take this daughter of Kāśya for my sake; otherwise, O joy of the Kurus, no peace shall exist for you. Accept her, O mighty-armed one, and protect your own lineage."
"Indeed, because she has been led astray by you, she does not approach her husband.
To Rāma, the conqueror of enemy cities, who was speaking thus, I replied:
"O Brahmarṣi, this shall not happen again; what is the use of your exertion?"

"O son of Jamadagni, having regard for your ancient dignity, I seek to propitiate you, O Blessed One; for this woman was already abandoned by me long ago. Who indeed would ever [desire] another's wife, who stands like a female serpent?"

Knowing the grave faults of women, one should not keep them in one's house; O you of great splendor, I would not abandon dharma even out of fear of Indra. Be gracious, or whatever your purpose may be, accomplish it without delay.
Moreover, O Lord of pure soul, this verse is heard in the Purāṇa as having been sung by the high-minded and great-souled Marutta:
"Even for a guru who is arrogant and ignorant of what ought and ought not to be done..."
Instruction is necessary for one who has set out upon a wrong path.
Though you were highly honored by me out of affection as my preceptor, you do not know the conduct due to a preceptor; therefore, I shall fight with you.
"I would not slay my preceptor in battle, especially a Brahmin—and one who is particularly advanced in asceticism. Thus have I shown patience toward you.
Yet, seeing this Brahmin with his arrow raised like a mere wretched Kshatriya..."
"He who, enraged in battle, should slay one fighting without fleeing, incurs no guilt for the murder of a Brahmin; such is the certainty in the codes of dharma.
O you whose wealth is asceticism, I am a Kshatriya established in the duty of Kshatriyas."

A man who acts toward another exactly as that other person behaves toward him incurs no unrighteousness and attains prosperity; for he is capable in matters of both worldly interest and dharma, and he understands the requirements of place and time.
It is better to fall into uncertainty regarding what is harmful than to live in certainty;
since you proceed according to what is right even while this matter remains uncertain,
therefore, O Rāma, I shall fight alongside you in the great battle.
Behold my strength of arm and my superhuman prowess! Even though things have come to this pass, O descendant of Bhṛgu, I shall do what is possible; O Brahmin, I will fight with you at Kurukṣetra.
"O Rāma, O great sage, prepare yourself as you wish for this duel.
There, O Rāma, struck by me and covered with hundreds of arrows,
you shall attain the worlds won by victory, purified by weapons in the great battle."
"Go, O lover of battle, and turn back toward Kurukṣetra! O mighty-armed one, rich in asceticism, summon me there for combat.
I shall come there, O mighty-armed one, O rich in asceticism, for the sake of fighting you."
"O Rāma, even at that place where you formerly performed the funeral rites for your father,
there I too shall perform my purification by slaying you, O Bhārgava!
Go there quickly, O Rāma, you who are intoxicated with the pride of battle."
"O you who merely claim to be a Brahmin, I shall remove your ancient pride.
And as for what you boast so often in assemblies, O Rāma—
that the Kṣatriyas in this world have been conquered by me alone— listen to that."
"This is a very great unrighteousness that one should die in bed at home;
that he meets his end in battle—that is his eternal duty.
At such a time, neither Bhīṣma nor any other kṣatriya like me would be born."
"O mighty-armed one, I am he who was born later than those fires that blazed among the grasses— Bhīṣma, the conqueror of enemy cities— who shall utterly destroy your pride and desire for battle."
"O Rāma, I shall remove your pride in battle; of this there is no doubt.
Bhīṣma said:
"Then, O Bhārata, Rāma spoke to me as if laughing."
"By good fortune, Bhīṣma, you desire to fight with me in battle! O Kauravya, I am going now to Kurukṣetra with you;
I shall do what was spoken. Come there, O scorcher of foes!"
There, O Bhīṣma, let your mother Jāhnavī behold you slain by me, covered with hundreds of arrows, and being devoured by vultures, herons,
and cranes; beholding you in such a piteous state, she who is frequented by Siddhas and Cāraṇas.
"O King, today that goddess whom I have slain weeps—
she who was undeserving of such a fate, the highly blessed river, the daughter of Bhagīratha,
who gave birth to you, O dull-witted man, so eager for war and afflicted."
"Come, Bhīṣma, let the battle take place with me this very day!
Take all [the equipment], O Kauravya, chariot and the rest, O bull of the Bharatas!
To Rāma, the conqueror of enemy cities, who was speaking thus, I replied:
Having bowed my head, O King, I replied, "So be it.
Having spoken thus, Rāma departed for Kurukṣetra with a desire to fight;
and having entered the city, I informed Satyavatī.

Then, having had the rites for a safe journey performed by his mother and being greeted with blessings, he addressed the twice-born ones, saying "An auspicious day! and "May there be well-being! O one of great splendor, he mounted a beautiful silver chariot yoked with white horses.
O King, that chariot was well-equipped with its fittings, firmly mounted, covered with tiger-skin,
provided with great weapons, and endowed with all necessary implements;
it was driven by a noble hero who was an expert in the science of horses.
Accompanied by a disciplined charioteer who had witnessed many battles,
I set forth, O best of the Bharatas, clad in beautiful white armor and grasping a white bow.
With a white parasol being held over his head,
and being fanned with white whisks, O lord of men,
he was dressed in white garments, wore a white turban, and was adorned entirely with white ornaments.

Being praised with blessings of victory, O bull of the Bharatas, he departed from Hastināpura and arrived at Kurukṣetra, the field of battle. Then those horses were urged on by that charioteer for the great combat.

O King, those [steeds] possessing the speed of thought and wind bore me away with great force. Having reached Kurukṣetra, both I and the powerful Rāma suddenly displayed our prowess against one another for battle, O King.
Then, while standing within the sight of Rāma, who was performing extreme austerities,
I took up that most excellent and supreme conch and blew it.
Thereupon, O King, the twice-born, the ascetics, and the forest-dwellers [were moved].
Then the gods, together with the hosts of ṛṣis, beheld that divine battle.
Thereupon, celestial garlands appeared again and again,
as did divine musical instruments and masses of clouds.
Then all those ascetics, the followers of Bhārgava,
became spectators, surrounding the field of battle.
Then the goddess, who desires the welfare of all beings, spoke to me.
"O King, your mother is here in her own form; what is this that you intend to do?
O best of the Kurus, I shall go and entreat that son of Jamadagni again and again, saying: 'Do not fight with Bhīṣma, for he is your disciple.'"
"O son, do not, do not persist in this way, O King,
in wishing to fight in battle with the Brahmin son of Jamadagni," he rebuked him.
"Is he not indeed a destroyer of Kṣatriyas, possessing prowess equal to that of Hari?"
"O son, since you wish to fight with Rāma, who is already known to you,
I then saluted the queen with joined palms and spoke to her;
O best of the Bharatas, I related everything exactly as it had occurred at the svayaṃvara."
O Indra among kings, just as Rāma was previously propitiated by me,
and just as was the ancient desire of the daughter of the King of Kāśī,
then my mother, the great river, approached Rāma.
For my sake, the queen asked forgiveness of that seer of the Bhṛgu lineage, saying these words:
"Do not fight with Bhīṣma, who is your disciple. And he said to her as she was entreating him, "Restrain Bhīṣma himself."
"Indeed, he does not fulfill my desire," [thinking thus], I approached him.
Saṃjaya said:
Then Gaṅgā, out of affection for her son, once again approached Bhīṣma.
His eyes clouded with anger, he did not heed her words.
Then the righteous-souled Bhṛgu, the best of sages and a man of great asceticism, appeared;
that foremost of the twice-born challenged him once more to battle.
Bhīṣma said:
Smiling as it were, I replied to him as he stood firm in battle:
"Stationed on the ground, I do not wish to fight you while I am mounted upon my chariot."
"Ascend the chariot, O hero, and fasten on your armor, O mighty-armed one,
if you wish to fight me in battle, O Rāma. Then, smiling upon the field of battle, Rāma spoke to me.
"O Bhīṣma, the earth is my chariot, and the Vedas are my excellent horses. Mātariśvan is my charioteer, and the mothers of the Vedas are my armor.
Well-encased in these, O joy of the Kurus, I shall fight in battle."
Speaking thus, O Gāndhārī, Rāma, whose prowess is truth,
surrounded me on all sides with a great multitude of arrows.
Then I beheld the son of Jamadagni stationed upon a celestial chariot.
Wielding every kind of weapon, glorious, and of wondrous appearance,
it was a holy creation fashioned by the mind, as vast as a city,
yoked with divine horses, armored, and adorned with gold.
O mighty-armed one, with the banner adorned by the mark of the moon, Akrūra— bearing a bow, equipped with quivers, and wearing leather arm-guards and finger-protectors—
acted as the charioteer for Yuyutsu in that encounter.
My friend, a knower of the Vedas and exceedingly dear to Bhārgava, is challenging me to battle; his calling out to me gladdens my heart,
as that descendant of Bhṛgu repeatedly cries, "Come on!"
I alone approached that single Rāma, who was like the rising sun, unassailable, possessed of great strength, and the destroyer of kṣatriyas. Then,
having indeed restrained my horses at a distance of three arrow-flights, I [proceeded].
Having dismounted and laid aside my bow, I approached that best of sages, Rāma, on foot,
desiring to honor that most excellent of the twice-born;
and having saluted him according to the prescribed rites, I spoke these excellent words.
"O Rāma, I shall fight you in battle—you who are distinguished, superior, my elder, and virtuous in character. O Lord, pray grant me victory.
Rāma said:
"O best of the Kurus, this is exactly what must be done by one who desires prosperity;
for this, O mighty-armed one, is the duty of those who fight alongside their superiors.
O lord of the people, I would have cursed you had you not come here in this manner."
"Fight with diligence in battle, O Kaurava, relying upon fortitude.
Yet I do not hope for your victory, for I stand here to defeat you. Go and fight according to dharma; I am pleased with your conduct."
Bhīṣma said: Then,
having paid homage to him, I quickly mounted my chariot and once again blew my gold-adorned conch shell in the midst of battle.
Then, O Bhārata, a battle took place between him and me for many days, O King, each desiring victory over the other. In that combat,
he first struck me with arrows feathered with heron-plumes.
O lord of the people, by nine hundred and sixty arrows possessing the brilliance of fire, my four horses and my charioteer were held in check;
likewise, I myself stood in the battle clad in armor.
Having paid homage to the gods and the Brahmins, O Bhārata,
I addressed him as he stood there in battle, as if with a smile:
"I have honored your status as my teacher, even though you are devoid of all restraint."
Furthermore, O Brahmin, hear from me regarding the perfection in the accumulation of dharma:
those Vedas that reside within your body, that great Brahminhood of yours,
and the immense austerity you have practiced— I do not strike at these.
O Rāma, you who have taken your stand upon the duty of a Kṣatriya—strike!
For a Brāhmaṇa indeed attains the status of a Kṣatriya by the raising of weapons. Behold the power of my bow, and behold the strength of my arms!
"O hero, I shall split this bow of yours, along with its arrow, into two pieces!
O bull of the Bharata race, I then discharged a sharp broad-headed shaft at him;
by that, the tip of his bow was severed and fell to the earth.
And nine hundred straight-knotted arrows,
winged with heron feathers, I discharged toward the chariot of Jamadagni’s son;
driven by the wind, they then became embedded in his body.
Those arrows moved along, dripping blood like elephants;
with all his limbs drenched in gore and blood streaming from his wounds,
Rāma then shone, O King, like Mount Meru discharging its minerals.
At the end of winter, O King, Rāma then shone like an *aśoka* tree adorned with clusters of red blossoms, appearing in some places like a *kiṃśuka* tree; then,
filled with rage, Rāma took up another bow.
He indeed rained down those well-sharpened arrows with golden feathers;
having struck me, those fierce shafts, which pierce the vital organs in many ways, shook me with their great velocity, resembling serpents or the poison of fire.
Then, steadying myself once more in that battle, I,
enraged, covered Rāma with hundreds of arrows.
With those arrows, which resembled fire and the sun and were like venomous serpents, he—
Afflicted by those sharp arrows, Rāma became as if deprived of his senses.
Then, overcome with compassion and censuring myself by my own self, I cried out, "Fie! Fie! upon war and the kṣatriya order, O bull of the Bharatas.
O King, overwhelmed by a surge of grief, I spoke repeatedly:
"Alas! What a sin has been committed by me through this kshatriya duty, that my preceptor, a righteous twice-born man, has been thus afflicted with arrows."
Then, O Bhārata, I did not strike the son of Jamadagni any further.
Then, having scorched the earth at the close of day, the thousand-rayed Sun, like Pūṣan, went to his setting, and the battle ceased.
Bhīṣma said: Then, O lord of the people, the charioteer, who was esteemed for his skill, extracted the arrows from himself, from the horses, and from me.
When the horses had bathed, turned back after finding water, and were no longer distressed,
the battle then commenced at dawn as the sun rose. Seeing me quickly approaching, armored and stationed upon my chariot, [the enemy rallied].
The powerful Rāma made his chariot fully ready.
Then, seeing Rāma approaching with a desire for battle,
I cast aside my excellent bow and suddenly descended from the chariot.
O Bhārata, having likewise offered my salutations and ascended the chariot,
I stood there before the son of Jamadagni, free from fear and eager for battle.
Then he overwhelmed me with a great shower of arrows.
And I covered him with a shower of arrows as he was raining [mine] upon me;
but the son of Jamadagni, filled with rage, O King, once again dispatched feathered shafts at me that were like blazing-mouthed serpents.
O King, with sharp, broad-headed arrows, I suddenly severed them by the hundreds and thousands in the sky again and again. Thereupon,
the powerful son of Jamadagni [discharged] divine weapons.
He urged those [weapons] upon me, but I warded them off with my own weapons, O mighty-armed one, desiring to perform a superior feat. Then, a great roar arose from all sides in the sky.
Then, O Bhārata, I discharged the Vāyavya weapon at the son of Jamadagni; Rāma countered it with the Guhyaka weapon. Thereafter, having consecrated it with mantras, I discharged the Āgneya weapon.
The powerful Rāma warded that off with a Vāruṇa weapon. In this manner, I neutralized the divine weapons of Rāma;
and Rāma, the radiant subduer of enemies, was likewise skilled in the knowledge of divine weapons.
Then, O King, keeping me to his left, the best of the twice-born,
the mighty son of Jamadagni, Rāma, pierced me in the chest in a fit of rage.
Thereupon, O best of the Bharatas, I sank down upon my excellent chariot.
Then, O best of the Bharatas, as I was overwhelmed by dejection and tormented by Rāma’s arrows, the charioteer quickly bore me away for the distance of a *goruta*. Thereupon,
I had indeed fled, severely pierced and unconscious.
Seeing this, all the followers of Rāma, including Akṛtavraṇa and the others, as well as the princess of Kāśī, were filled with joy and cried out, O Bhārata. Then,
having regained consciousness and realizing what had happened, I spoke to the charioteer.
"O charioteer, go where Rāma is; I am ready and my pain has vanished.
Then, O descendant of Kuru, the charioteer carried me away on horses of supreme beauty, which resembled the wind in speed and seemed as if they were dancing as they went.
Then, O Kaurava, having approached Rāma, I, highly incensed and desiring victory, covered that enraged one with a net of arrows.
But Rāma [cut down] those straight-flying arrows even as they were falling upon him.
In that battle, he swiftly severed each one of my arrows with three of his own; then,
in that great conflict, all those well-sharpened arrows of mine were crushed and split in two by Rāma’s shafts by the hundreds.
Then again, desiring to slay him, I discharged a blazing, radiant arrow, equal to Time itself, at Rāma, the son of Jamadagni. Struck deeply by it, he fell under the power of the arrow's severance.
Rāma suddenly fainted and fell to the ground. Then, when Rāma had fallen to the earth, the entire world cried out in lamentation, O Bhārata, as agitated as if at the falling of the sun.
Then, all those ascetics, deeply distressed, suddenly rushed toward the descendant of Bhrigu from Kashi;
embracing him, they then slowly comforted him.
O Kaurava, with hands cooled by water and with blessings of victory, Rāma then rose up and, being overwhelmed, spoke these words:
"Stay, Bhīṣma! You are slain! Having fixed an arrow upon his bow.

Released, it fell swiftly upon my left side in that great battle, by which I was violently shaken like a tree reeling in the wind. Then, O King, having slain the horses with a swift weapon in that great battle, he [advanced].
He confidently showered me with those feathered arrows.
Then, O mighty-armed one, I too released the swift weapon that is irresistible in battle; those arrows were directed from within my body.
05.181.030e Quickly enveloping the sky on all sides for both Rāma and me,
05.181.031a the sun did not shine, being completely covered by a net of arrows;
05.181.031c within that space, the wind roared like one obstructed by clouds.
Then, from the agitation of the wind, from the rays of the sun,
from intense heat, and by its own nature, fire was produced.
Those arrows were set ablaze by that very fire which had arisen from themselves.
Then, O King, all those hundreds of thousands, millions, billions, tens of thousands, as well as kharvas and nikharvas, were reduced to ashes upon the earth,
O Kaurava.
Enraged, Rāma swiftly loosed his arrows upon me;
then, O King, I too severed those shafts in battle with my own snake-like arrows and felled them to the ground like serpents.
Thus did that battle take place at that time, O best of the Bharatas;
and when the twilight had passed, my preceptor withdrew.
Bhīṣma said:

O best of the Bharatas, on another day, after he had once again encountered Rāma, there occurred yet another exceedingly fierce and tumultuous battle. Then that hero, skilled in divine weapons, [discharged] numerous celestial missiles.

Day after day, O Bhārata, that righteous and powerful lord employed those [weapons]; and I, casting aside my life-breaths which are so difficult to abandon, struck down his weapons with counter-weapons in that tumultuous battle.
When his weapons had been struck down in various ways by [the enemy’s] missiles, the descendant of Bhṛgu,
possessed of great splendor and having renounced his life in that battle, became enraged;
he then hurled a spear of terrible form.
The high-souled son of Jamadagni was obstructed by the missiles; he [held] that blazing meteor, as if cast forth by Time,
its tip aflame, pervading the worlds with its splendor.
Then, with my blazing arrows,
I cut that [weapon] as it approached— blazing like the sun at the time of universal destruction— and caused it to fall to the ground in three pieces.
Then a wind blew, fragrant with holy scents;
when she had been cut down, Rāma, blazing with anger,
then hurled twelve other terrible *śakti* weapons.
O Bhārata, it is not possible to describe their form because of its brilliance and its very lightness; however,
I am truly overwhelmed upon seeing them.
From all directions, those [beings] appeared like great meteors from a fire,
diverse in form and blazing with fierce splendor,
like the twelve suns at the dissolution of the world.
Then, O King, having spread out that net consisting of arrows and having displayed it,
I pierced it with a multitude of shafts and loosed twelve more arrows in the battle.
Then I shattered those terrible-looking spears;
thereafter, the high-souled son of Jamadagni hurled other fierce spears with golden shafts.
In that place, the world beholds their forms;
all of them indeed possess sharp blades,
are unsheathed, variegated, and bound with bands of gold.
Just like blazing great meteors,
O lord of men, those fierce weapons were warded off by my shield and struck down by me with my sword in battle.
In that battle, with divine arrows belonging to the son of Jamadagni,
I rained down upon his divine horses and their charioteer,
making them resemble snakes that have cast off their skins.
Seeing his gold-adorned spears cut down,
the high-souled crusher of the lord of the Haihayas, overcome with rage, manifested a divine weapon.
Then, fierce rows of blazing arrows fell like swarms of locusts,
and they covered his body most densely.
"Give me the horses, the charioteer, and the chariot itself.
O King, my chariot was covered on all sides with arrows,
as were the horses and the charioteer.
The yoke, the chariot pole, as well as the wheels, and likewise the axle, were cut by arrows and then shattered. Then,
when that shower of arrows had passed away;
He rained back upon that preceptor a torrent of arrows;
wounded by those shafts, that mass of Brahmanic power released profuse blood incessantly from his body.
Just as Rāma was tormented by a net of arrows,
so too was I deeply and severely pierced;
then, in the afternoon, the battle ceased.
When the sun was seeking the mountain for its setting,
Bhīṣma said:
"Then at dawn, O Indra among kings, when the sun had risen clear and bright..."
The battle between me and the descendant of Bhṛgu resumed once more.
Then, standing upon his whirling chariot, Rāma— the best among strikers—
rained down showers of arrows upon me, like Śakra raining upon a mountain.
By that shower of arrows, my friend the charioteer was struck;
he fell upon the floor of the chariot, causing my mind great distress. Then, that charioteer of mine entered into a state of profound despondency.
Struck by the arrows on the ground,
he fell down and lost consciousness; then, O Indra among kings, the charioteer gave up his life, tormented by Rāma’s shafts, and in a mere moment, fear entered me as well.

Then, O King, when the charioteer had been slain, as I was discharging my arrows with a distracted mind, Rāma loosed shafts equal to death itself. Thereupon, that descendant of Bhṛgu [struck] me, who was overwhelmed by the calamity of my charioteer and utterly confounded.
Drawing his bow with great force, he struck me deeply with an arrow. O King, that blood-drinker, having fallen upon my collarbone,
entered the depths of the earth along with me, O Indra among kings.
O bull of the Bharatas, thinking me slain, Rāma then roared loudly like a cloud and rejoiced again and again. O King, when I had thus fallen, Rāma was filled with joy.
Together with those followers, he let out a great roar. As for those Kauravas who were stationed at my side,
as well as the people who had come there desiring to witness that battle— they all cried out.
When I was struck down, they then experienced the utmost agony. Then, O lion among kings, having fallen, I beheld eight twice-born ones who were radiant like the sun and fire.
They stood surrounding me on all sides,
holding me with their own arms in the midst of the battle;
and being protected by those brahmins, I did not touch the ground.

For I was stationed in the atmosphere by those brahmins, like kinsmen; and while sleeping in the sky, I was sprinkled with drops of water. Then, O King, those brahmins, having taken hold of me, spoke.
"Do not fear," they all said together, repeatedly adding, "May it be well with you.
Then, comforted by their words, I suddenly rose up and beheld my mother, the best of rivers, seated upon a chariot.
And my horses were indeed held back by her,
O Indra among the Kauravas, in that great river;
and having honored the feet of my mother, I spoke.
Likewise, I mounted the chariot of Ṛṣṭiṣeṇa;
she protected my chariot, the horses, and the equipment. Having joined my palms in reverence, I sent her back once again.

Then, O Bhārata, having myself yoked those horses swift as the wind, I fought with the son of Jamadagni when the day had ended. Then, O best of the Bharatas, [I encountered] that one of great strength and impetuous speed.
In that battle, I released an arrow at Rāma that pierced his heart;
then, oppressed by the force of the arrow, he fell to the earth. Abandoning his bow on his knees, Rāma fell under the sway of unconsciousness.
Then, when Rāma, who possessed many thousands [of cows], had fallen,
clouds covered the sky, raining down much blood;
and meteors fell by the hundreds, accompanied by thunderclaps and earthquakes.
Svarbhānu suddenly eclipsed the blazing sun;
harsh winds blew and the earth trembled;
vultures, crows, and herons flew about, filled with joy.
In the blazing quarter, a jackal repeatedly let out a dreadful howl;
drums, though unstruck, resounded with a fierce noise.
O best of the Bharatas, such were the terrible portents that occurred.
When the high-souled Rāma had fallen to the earth as if unconscious,
O Kauravya, he suddenly rose up and rushed toward me once more for battle, overwhelmed and frantic with rage.
Taking up his palm-tree-sized bow and an arrow, the mighty-armed Bhārgava— though possessed by rage— abided by the counsel of the great seers and spoke these words to him: "O Rāma!"
He of immeasurable soul took up an arrow resembling the Destroyer at the end of time.
Then the sun, its orb of rays dimmed, sank below the horizon, shrouded in a mass of dust.
The night, with its pleasantly cool breezes, set in;
then we withdrew from the battle.
Thus, O King, did the withdrawal take place.
Then again, in Vimala, it was most terrible for twenty days every morning;
likewise, there were another three days.
Bhīṣma said:
Then, O king of kings, at night, having bowed my head in salutation to the Brahmins, the ancestors, and all the deities, I spoke.
O lord of the people, having retired to my bed at night amidst the creatures that roam by night, I reflected in my mind upon this most terrible battle with the son of Jamadagni.
Many days have passed today since this great calamity began;
yet, O Brahmin, I am unable to defeat the immensely powerful Rāma,
the son of Jamadagni, in battle at the front of the fray.
"If I am able to conquer the powerful son of Jamadagni,
may the gracious deities reveal themselves to me during the night.
Then, O king of kings, I lay down to sleep at night, wounded by arrows.
On my right side, as if at the time of dawn,
I was then raised up and supported by those foremost brahmins who had fallen with me from the chariot, and I was comforted with the words, "Do not fear."
"O Great King, those very ones, having appeared to me in a dream, surrounded me and spoke these words; listen to them, O best of the Kurus:
'Arise! Do not fear, O son of Gaṅgā; there is no danger whatsoever for you.'"
"O tiger among men, we shall protect ourselves, for you are our very bodies.
Rāma, the son of Jamadagni, will by no means defeat you in battle;
rather, you alone, O bull of the Bharatas, shall be the victor over Rāma in combat."
"O King of kings, O sinless one, this weapon, which is very dear to you, will recognize you; it will attend upon you of its own accord,
by means of which you shall subdue your enemies of great prowess, O Kaurava."
For this was known even to you during your previous assumption of a body,
O Bhārata— the sleep called *Prasvāpa*, created by Viśvakṛt for Prajāpati.
Indeed, not even Rāma knows this, nor does any man anywhere on earth.
"Remember that, O mighty-armed one, and apply it with great care. By means of that weapon, O lord of men, Rāma shall not meet his destruction,
nor shall you ever incur the burden of sin, O giver of honor."
Afflicted by the power of your arrows, that son of Jamadagni will fall asleep;
then, having conquered him, you yourself shall raise him up again in battle with your beloved weapon, Bhīṣma-saṃbodhana.
"Act thus, O Kauravya; having mounted your chariot at dawn, we consider one who is fast asleep and one who is dead to be equal. Furthermore, O King, Rāma must never be killed."
"Therefore, let this Prasvāpa weapon that has arisen be employed," having said this,
O King, all those best of the twice-born vanished;
they were eight in number, identical in form, and possessed radiant bodies.
Bhīṣma said:
"Then, O Bhārata, when the night had passed, I awoke;
and reflecting upon that dream, I attained the highest joy."

Then, O Bhārata, there occurred between me and him a tumultuous, wonderful battle that caused the hair of all living beings to stand on end. Then the descendant of Bhṛgu rained down upon me a shower consisting of arrows.
O Bhārata, I warded him off with a net of arrows; then,
exceedingly enraged and possessed of great ascetic power, he once again hurled a *śakti* at me out of the very same anger he had felt yesterday.
With a touch like Indra’s thunderbolt and a radiance resembling the staff of Yama,
blazing like fire in battle and licking all directions with its flames,
it was then, O tiger among the Bharatas, like a celestial mansion moving through the sky.
O Bhārata, she struck me swiftly on the shoulder; then,
O mighty-armed one with eyes like those of a wounded deer, terrible blood flowed from my wound like red chalk-ore from a mountain, having been struck by Rāma.
Then, filled with intense rage toward the son of Jamadagni,
I dispatched an arrow resembling Death itself and like the venom of a serpent.
Struck by it on the forehead, that hero, the best of the twice-born, [stood firm].

O Great King, he shone like a mountain with its peaks. Enraged, he drew back his bow with great force and fixed upon it a terrible arrow, resembling the Destroyer at the end of time, which was capable of annihilating his enemies.
That fierce arrow, hissing like a venomous serpent, fell upon his chest;
O King, I then descended to the earth, stained with blood.
Having regained consciousness once more, [I addressed] the wise son of Jamadagni.
I hurled a stainless spear, blazing like a thunderbolt.
It fell upon the chest of that foremost of the twice-born;
he became overwhelmed, O King, and a trembling seized him.

Then his friend, the brahmin Akṛtavraṇa, a man of great asceticism, embraced him and comforted him in many ways with auspicious words. Having been thus consoled, Rāma was then filled with wrath and indignation.
Then he of great vows manifested the supreme Brahmā weapon. Thereupon, to counter it, I discharged the most excellent Brahmā weapon itself; it blazed forth as if displaying the end of an eon.
O best of the Bharatas, there occurred a meeting between those two Brahma-missiles in mid-air; without reaching either Rāma or me, O best of the Bharatas,
they then manifested in the sky as nothing but pure radiance.
And all living beings, O lord of the people, fell into distress;
and the ṛṣis, along with the gandharvas and the deities, O Bhārata,
experienced supreme anguish, oppressed by the fiery energy of the weapon.
Then the earth, with its mountains, forests, and trees, trembled;
and all living beings, being tormented, fell into the deepest despair. O King, the sky blazed forth and the ten directions were filled with smoke.
Then those who travel through the sky were unable to remain in the atmosphere. While the world, including the gods, asuras, and rākṣasas, raised a cry of "Alas!",
O Bhārata, I desired to yoke [the chariot], thinking, "Now is the opportunity."
"By the word of those who discourse on Brahman, the beloved weapon Prasvāpa appeared in my mind as soon as it was thought of. Bhīṣma said:
Then, O King, a great tumultuous roar arose in the heavens, saying,
"O Bhīṣma, do not release the Prasvāpa weapon! O joy of the Kauravas,
I did indeed discharge that weapon at the descendant of Bhṛgu.
While I was employing the Prasvāpa weapon, Nārada spoke these words:
"O Kauravya, these hosts of gods stationed in the celestial firmament are restraining you today; do not employ the Prasvāpa."

"Rāma is an ascetic, devoted to Brahman, a Brāhmaṇa, and your preceptor; O Kauravya, do not show him disrespect in any way whatsoever. Then I beheld those eight expounders of Brahman stationed in the sky.
Smiling at me, O Indra among kings, they spoke these words slowly:
"O best of the Bharatas, do exactly as Narada has said. For this, O bull of the Bharatas, is the supreme good for the worlds."
Then, having withdrawn that sleep-inducing weapon from the battle,
he ignited the Brahmāstra in that combat according to the prescribed rites.
Thereupon, Prince Rāma became enraged.
Seeing that weapon indeed turned back, he suddenly uttered these words: "I have been defeated by Bhīṣma; I am one of very dull intellect."
Then the son of Jamadagni beheld his father,
and likewise his father's father, and yet another beyond him;
they stood surrounding him on all sides.
Then they spoke to him with words of consolation:
"O child, do not ever again commit such a rash act,
especially by going into battle against Bhīṣma, who is a kṣatriya."
"O descendant of Bhṛgu, this is the duty of a Kṣatriya, namely battle;
whereas for Brāhmaṇas, Vedic study and the observance of vows are the supreme wealth. It was for a certain reason that we were invited by you."
The wielding of weapons is most fierce, and that task has been accomplished by you. My child, this much was sufficient in your combat with Bhīṣma;
O mighty-armed one, enough of this struggle—withdraw from this battle.
"Sufficient for you, may it be well with you, is this wielding of the bow.
Cast it aside, O invincible Bhārgava, and practice ascetic penance.
Here is Bhīṣma, the son of Śāntanu, who has been restrained by all the gods."
Thus urged repeatedly by Rāma, "Desist from this battle;
do not fight with your preceptor," it is not right for you, O best of the Kurus, to seek to defeat Rāma in combat.
"O Gāṅgeya, show honor to this Brāhmaṇa on the field of battle! We are indeed your superiors; therefore, we restrain you.
Bhīṣma is one of the Vasus; by good fortune, my son, you still live."
"This son of Śantanu, the son of Gaṅgā, is the highly illustrious Vasu.
O Rāma, how can he be conquered by you in battle? Turn back!
This Arjuna, the best of the Pāṇḍavas and the mighty son of Purandara—"
The heroic Nara, Prajāpati, the ancient and eternal primordial deity,
renowned throughout the three worlds as Savyasācin and possessed of great prowess—
his death at the proper time was indeed ordained by the Self-Existent One.
Thus addressed by his ancestors, Rāma spoke this to them:
"I shall not turn back from battle; such is the vow I have undertaken. Never before have I retreated at the forefront of the fray."
"O grandfathers, let the son of the River (Bhīṣma) be withdrawn from battle at your pleasure;
but I shall by no means turn back from this fight.
Then, O King, those sages headed by Ṛcīka [spoke] at that time.
Accompanied by Nārada himself, they approached and spoke thus:
"Turn back from the battle, dear son; honor these best of the twice-born.
Out of regard for the duty of a Kṣatriya, I said to them, "No."

This is my vow in this world: I shall never turn my back on battle, nor retreat even when struck from behind by arrows. Neither out of greed, nor out of weakness, nor out of fear, nor for the sake of wealth, would I do so.
"‘I would rather abandon the eternal dharma’— this was my firm resolve.
Then, O King, all those sages headed by Nārada,
as well as my mother Bhāgīrathī, arrived in the midst of the battle."

"Likewise equipped with arrows and a bow, and likewise firm in my resolve, I stand in battle to fight. Then, having gathered together once more in the encounter, they spoke to Rāma, the descendant of Bhṛgu.
"The hearts of the brahmins are indeed as soft as fresh butter; be appeased, O Bhārgava!
Rāma, Rāma, turn back from this battle, O best of the twice-born!
For Bhīṣma cannot be slain by you, and you cannot be slain by Bhīṣma, O Bhārgava."
Speaking thus, they all blocked the field of battle and laid down their weapons before the descendant of Bhṛgu. Then I once again addressed those eight exponents of the Veda.
I beheld eight blazing planets, as if they had risen together.
Standing in the midst of battle, they spoke these words to me with affection:
"Go to Rāma, O mighty-armed one; do what is beneficial for the world by honoring your preceptor."
Seeing that Rāma had indeed turned back at the word of his friend,
and desiring to act for the welfare of the worlds, I too accepted his speech.
Then, having approached Rāma, I, who was severely wounded, paid him homage.
And Rāma, the great ascetic, smiling with affection, said to me:
"There is no kṣatriya walking this earth who is your equal in this world. Go, Bhīṣma; I have been greatly gratified by you in this battle."
And right before my eyes, Bhārgava summoned that maiden and spoke in a piteous voice in the midst of those ascetics.
Rāma said:
"O beautiful lady, this is evident to all the people:
that I have indeed exerted great manly effort to the utmost of my power;
yet, I am simply unable to defeat Bhīṣma, the foremost of weapon-wielders, in battle."
Displaying supreme weapons to demonstrate my excellence beyond measure, I say:
