"This is my highest power; this is my greatest strength. Go wherever you wish, O blessed lady; what else shall I do for you?"
"Seek refuge with Bhīṣma alone; no other recourse exists for you, for I have been utterly defeated by Bhīṣma as he discharged his great celestial weapons.
Bhīṣma said:
Having spoken thus, the high-minded Rāma then sighed and remained silent; thereupon the maiden addressed the descendant of Bhṛgu:
"O Blessed One, it is exactly as the Blessed One has said."
"This Bhīṣma of noble intellect is invincible in battle even by the gods;
yet you have performed my task to the best of your power and to the best of your energy, having displayed your prowess and various weapons in the fray."
Furthermore, he cannot be surpassed in battle even by the most subtle means;
nor shall I ever go back to Bhīṣma again under any circumstances.
However, O ascetic, I shall go to that place where Bhīṣma is.
"O descendant of Bhṛgu, I myself shall strike you down in battle. Having spoken thus, the maiden departed with eyes agitated by rage,
her resolve fixed on asceticism as she contemplated my death.
Then, O Bhārata, that best of the Bhrigus, Rāma, having taken leave of me, departed for Mount Mahendra with those sages just as he had come,
while I, being praised by the twice-born, mounted my chariot.

Having entered the city, O Great King, I reported everything as it had happened to my mother Satyavatī, and she rejoiced at me. Then I appointed wise men to investigate the circumstances regarding the maiden.
Day after day, indeed, my diligent attendants, established in my welfare and seeking what is dear to me, reported her every word, gesture,
and movement; for as soon as that maiden set out for the forest, resolved upon asceticism, [I learned of it].
At that very moment, I became distressed and dejected, as if I had lost my senses.
For no Kṣatriya could ever defeat me in battle by prowess,
O dear one, except for a knower of Brahman who is refined by austerity and firm in his vows.
Moreover, O King, I reported this matter to Nārada and to Vyāsa out of fear; both of them said to me:
"O Bhīṣma, you should not feel despondent regarding the daughter of the King of Kāśī."

Who would dare to turn back destiny by means of human effort? But that maiden, O Great King, having entered the circle of hermitages and taken up residence on the bank of the Yamunā, performed superhuman austerities.
Without food, emaciated, parched, with matted hair and covered in dirt and mud,
subsisting on air for six months and remaining as motionless as a pillar,
she whose wealth is her asceticism reached the bank of the Yamunā for another year.
The spirited woman completed her stay in the water without food; she completed another year by subsisting on a single withered leaf,
remaining for a year with fierce resolve, standing balanced on the tip of her big toe.
In this manner, she scorched heaven and earth for twelve years;
yet even though she was being restrained by her kinsmen, she could not be turned back.
Thereupon, she went to Vatsabhūmi, a land frequented by *siddhas* and *cāraṇas*.
She wandered day and night through the sacred regions of that hermitage belonging to the high-souled ascetics of virtuous conduct; there, the princess of Kāśī, bathing her limbs, roamed at will.
O great king, [they stayed] at Nanda’s hermitage, then at the auspicious Ulūka hermitage,
at Cyavana’s hermitage, and indeed at the abode of Brahmā;
at Prayāga, at the sacrificial ground of the gods, and in the forests of the gods as well.
Likewise, O King, at Bhogavatī, as well as in the hermitage of Kauśika;
in the hermitage of Māṇḍavya, O King, and likewise in the hermitage of Dilīpa;
and at Rāmahrada, O Kauravya, and in the hermitage of Pailagārgya.

O lord of the people, at those sacred fords (tīrtha), the daughter of Kāśī then bathed her limbs, having undertaken intense austerity. As she emerged from the water, O descendant of Kuru, my mother spoke to her:
"Why do you distress yourself, O blessed lady? Tell me the truth of this.
Then, O King, that blameless woman, with palms joined in reverence, said to her:
"O fair-eyed one, Bhīṣma was not defeated by Rāma in battle."
"Who else would dare to conquer that lord of the earth when he has raised his weapon?
Therefore, O Goddess, I shall perform most terrible austerities for the destruction of Bhīṣma;
I shall wander the earth so that I may slay the king."
"May this fruit of my vow appear in my body in the next world, just as it is for me now.
Then the river flowing to the ocean replied, "O beautiful woman, you act with crookedness.
O lady of faultless limbs, O frail one, this desire cannot be attained by you."
"O Princess of Kāśī, if you are indeed performing this vow for the destruction of Bhīṣma,
yet you release your body while still established in that vow,
O auspicious lady, you shall become a river— crooked and possessing water only during the rainy season."
"Difficult to ford and unknowable, flowing for eight months but not for the four months of the rains,
filled with fearsome crocodiles, terrible, and inspiring dread in all beings"—
having spoken thus, O King, he then turned back from the daughter of Kāśi.
My highly fortunate mother,
that beautiful woman, would sometimes for eight months and sometimes for ten months not even drink water, O lady of excellent complexion, as if smiling.
O descendant of Kuru, out of a longing for sacred fords, that daughter of the King of Kāśī ran hither and thither, falling down repeatedly; thus,
O Bhārata, she became the river famous as Ambā in Vatsabhūmi.

O King, through that asceticism, she was born as half a portion; she became the river Vārṣikī in the land of the Vatsas— a river full of crocodiles, difficult to ford, and winding— and at that time, she also became a maiden.
Bhīṣma said:
Then all those ascetics, seeing her firmly resolved upon penance, O dear one, turned her back and asked, "What is your purpose?"
Then the maiden spoke to those sages, who were advanced in asceticism:
"I have been rejected by Bhīṣma and deprived of my duty as a wife.
O you whose wealth is asceticism, my consecration is for his destruction, not for the sake of worldly life."
"Having slain Bhīṣma, I shall attain peace"—this was my firm resolve. It is because of him that I have reached this eternal abode of suffering;
deprived of the world of my husband, I am here neither woman nor man.
"O you whose wealth is asceticism, I shall not turn back from battle without having slain the son of Gaṅgā;
this is the resolve in my heart for the sake of which I have exerted myself. Disgusted with my state as a woman, I am firmly resolved upon attaining manhood."
"I desire to act against Bhīṣma; I am not to be restrained," she said again.
Then the god, the wielder of the trident, the lord of Umā, revealed himself in his own form to that beautiful woman in the midst of those great ṛṣis.
Being invited to choose a boon, she then chose my defeat;
the god replied to that high-minded woman, "I shall slay him.
Thereupon, that maiden spoke again to Rudra.
"O Lord, how might my victory in battle come to pass? O Lord of Umā, my mind is deeply pacified by this womanhood of mine. And yet, O Lord of Beings, the defeat of Bhīṣma was promised by you."
"O you whose banner is the bull, act in such a way that this may become true:
so that, having encountered him in battle, I may slay Bhīṣma, the son of Śantanu.
To her, Mahādeva, whose banner is the bull, spoke as follows.
"O blessed lady, my speech has never spoken falsehood; it shall come true.
You shall slay Bhīṣma in battle and attain manhood. And you shall remember all of this when you have passed into another body."
"Born into the lineage of Drupada, you shall become a great chariot-warrior;
swift in the use of weapons and a versatile combatant, you shall be highly esteemed.
O auspicious lady, all this shall come to pass exactly as I have said."
"After some lapse of time, you shall later become a man.
Having spoken thus, the one of great splendor, Kapardin whose banner is the bull,
vanished right there while the brahmins were looking on.
Then, while those great seers were looking on, that blameless woman of excellent complexion gathered wood from that forest,
constructed a very large funeral pyre, and set fire to it.
O Great King, with a mind blazing with rage, she said, "For the sake of Bhīṣma's slaughter," and entered the fire; O King,
the eldest daughter of the King of Kāśī entered the river Yamunā.
Duryodhana said:
"O Gāṅgeya, how did Śikhaṇḍin, having been a girl at that time, become a man? O best of warriors, O grandfather, tell me that."
Bhīṣma said:
O Indra among kings, the queen of that monarch Drupada was his beloved chief wife,
yet she was childless, O lord of the people.
At that very time, O great king, Drupada, the lord of the earth,
sought to gratify Śaṅkara for the sake of offspring;
having resolved upon our destruction, he undertook severe ascetic penance.

He obtained a daughter from Mahādeva, saying, "May there be a son for me. [The god asked: "O Blessed One, I desire a son as a counter-measure against Bhīṣma. Being thus addressed by the God of gods, he replied: "She shall become both female and male."
"Turn back, O protector of the earth; this shall never be otherwise. Having returned to the city, he said this to his wife:
"O Queen, a great effort has been made by me through asceticism for the sake of a son."
"Having been a maiden, you shall become a man," so was I told by Śambhu.
Though entreated again and again, Śiva replied, "It is destiny.
For that shall not be otherwise; indeed, what is to be must happen just so.

Then, having become self-restrained at the time of her season, that high-minded wife of King Drupada approached Drupada for union. In due course, she conceived a child by means of the methods prescribed by sacred ordinance.
O protector of the earth, as Nārada told me regarding that daughter of Pṛṣata, so it was:
then the lotus-eyed queen conceived that embryo. O descendant of Kuru, King Drupada [treated] his beloved wife with affection.
Out of affection for his son, the mighty-armed one then attended to him with great care;
and the Kuru prince obtained every desire according to his wishes. Then, for King Drupada, the lord of the earth, who was childless—
In due time, O lord of men, that queen, the consort of Drupada, gave birth to a daughter of preeminent beauty. To that illustrious Drupada, who was childless, she [gave birth].
"O Indra among kings, he proclaimed, 'A son has been born to me. Then, O lord of men, King Drupada performed all the rites for a son for her while she remained concealed,
just as one would for a son."
And that queen of Drupada guarded the secret with every effort, addressing him as "son";
indeed, no one in the city knew her [secret] except for the son of Pṛṣata.
For, having faith in those words of the god of wondrous splendor,
he covered that girl [with clothes] and declared, "It is a male.
Then the king had all the birth-rites performed for him.

They knew her as Śikhaṇḍin, for she was treated according to the rules prescribed for males; however, I alone learned this through a spy, from the words of Nārada, from the speech of the gods, and likewise through Ambā’s own ascetic power.
Bhīṣma said:
Drupada made a great effort regarding all his kinsmen;
consequently, [his daughter] attained supreme proficiency in writing and other arts as well as in the crafts.
O Indra among kings, he became a disciple of Droṇa in the science of archery.
O great king, his mother, a woman of excellent complexion,
then urged the king on behalf of her daughter’s marriage, just as she would for a son.
Then, seeing that maiden who had reached the bloom of youth, the son of Pṛṣata (Drupada) thought her to be a woman and fell into anxiety together with his wife. Drupada said:
"This daughter of mine has reached her youth, increasing my sorrow;
yet she was concealed by me at the word of the wielder of the trident.
O Great Queen, that shall not prove false in any way whatsoever."
"How indeed could the Creator of the three worlds make that false?
His wife said, "O King, if it pleases you, I shall speak; listen to my words."
"O son of Pṛṣata, having heard this now, you should proceed with your own duty.
O King, let the formal taking of a wife be performed for him according to the rules;
my mind is certain that those words will come true."
Bhīṣma said: Then,
having made a firm resolve regarding that matter, the couple chose the daughter of the lord of Daśārṇa as their bride.
Then King Drupada, that lion among kings,
having carefully considered all the kings according to their lineage,
[chose] the daughter of the king of the Daśārṇas.
He chose Śikhaṇḍin as his wife;
that king who was known as Hiraṇyavarman, the ruler of the Daśārṇas,
gave his daughter to that Śikhaṇḍin.
And that king among the Daśārṇas was a great lord of the earth—
Hiraṇyavarman, invincible, possessing a vast army and a high mind.
When the marriage had then been performed, O best of kings, that maiden...
And that maiden Śikhaṇḍinī reached her youth;
having taken a wife, Śikhaṇḍin returned again to Kāmpilya,
for she did not know that he was a woman for some time.
Having learned that Śikhaṇḍinī was indeed a girl, the daughter of Hiraṇyavarman,
feeling ashamed, informed her nurses and her friends that she was the daughter of the Pāñcāla king, Śikhaṇḍinī.
Then, O tiger among kings, those nurses from Daśārṇa fell into great distress from grief, and they sent word [to their master]. Thereupon, the messengers reported everything to the lord of Daśārṇa.
When that king heard of the deception exactly as it had occurred, he became enraged.
But Śikhaṇḍin, O great king, then lived in the royal household like a man,
filled with joy and never drawing attention to his womanhood.
Then, O bull of the Bharatas, having heard that after a few days had passed,
Hiraṇyavarman, O king of kings, was overcome with distress due to his wrath.
Thereupon, the king of the Daśārṇas was filled with intense anger.
He dispatched a messenger to the residence of Drupada. Then, having approached Drupada, the messenger of Kāñcanavarman set him aside alone in a secluded spot and spoke these words in private.
"O King, the king of Daśārṇa spoke these words to you:
'O sinless one, provoked by this insult and deceived by you, he says:
"O King, you surely hold me in contempt; this is surely the result of your evil counsel."'"
"O evil-minded one, because you out of delusion asked for my daughter as a bride for your own son, receive today the fruit of that deception.
Here I take you away along with your kinsmen and ministers; stand firm!"
Having disregarded my prowess, my lineage, and my conduct,
you have initiated an unprecedented deception among men. Perform all your duties and enjoy unsurpassed pleasures.
"I shall go quickly to rescue you along with your kinsmen.
Bhīṣma said:
"O King, when Drupada had been addressed thus by the messenger at that time..."
Like a captured thief, his speech did not flow;
he made a strenuous effort with relatives and consolations,
sending messengers with sweet words, declaring, "This is not so."
Then that king, having once again ascertained the truth of the matter,
set out in haste, thinking that the daughter of the Pañcāla king was still a maiden.
Thereupon, he dispatched messengers to his friends of immeasurable prowess.
Then, O best of kings, having heard from the nurses that account of his daughter’s abduction,
Drupada, the most excellent of monarchs, assembled his forces and set his mind upon marching against Drupada, O Bhārata.
Then, O king of kings, that lord of the earth, Hiraṇyavarman, consulted with his allies regarding the Pāñcāla monarch. There, a firm resolution was reached by those high-souled kings.
"O King, if it be true that Śikhaṇḍinī is indeed a girl,
we shall bind the King of the Pāñcālas and bring him home,
having installed another lord of men as king over the Pāñcālas."
"We shall have King Drupada killed along with Śikhaṇḍin.
Then that lord, having recognized the messenger, dispatched the Kṣattṛ once more to the son of Pṛṣata, saying: "I am going to kill you; remain firm!"
By nature timid and a sinner,
King Drupada, the lord of the earth, was seized by intense fear;
having dispatched a messenger to the king of Daśārṇa, Drupada was emaciated by grief.
Having met his wife in private, the lord of men spoke these words,
overcome by great fear and struck in his heart by grief—
the King of Pañcāla speaking to the beloved mother of Śikhaṇḍin.
"My very powerful relative, King Hiraṇyavarman, leading his army, will march against me in anger.
What shall I, a fool, do now regarding this maiden?"
"For the lord of men will soon arrive with his ministers;
indeed, Śikhaṇḍin, your son, is suspected of being a girl. Having thus ascertained the truth, he [the king] came together with his friends, his army, and his followers.
"Thinking 'I have been deceived,' he wishes to rescue me;
what is the truth here, O fair-hipped one, and what is false? Tell me, O beautiful lady.
Having heard your words, O auspicious one, I shall act accordingly."
"For I have fallen into doubt, as has this young Śikhaṇḍinī;
and you too, O Queen of excellent complexion, have encountered great distress. Therefore, for the sake of our complete liberation, tell the truth to me who asks."
"O lady of beautiful hips, O lady of radiant smiles, I shall act accordingly regarding this task;
do not fear for Śikhaṇḍin, for I will manage that matter according to the truth. O lady of excellent limbs, I have been deceived by ritual action regarding the duty of a son."
"I have deceived the king of Daśārṇa, that lord of the earth.
Tell me this, O highly fortunate lady, so that I may do what is beneficial in this matter;
for even though the king knew [the truth], he did so only for the sake of proclaiming it to others."
Urged by the light, the queen replied to the lord of the earth.
Bhīṣma said:
Then, O lord of men, the mother of Śikhaṇḍin spoke according to the truth.
O mighty-armed one, she reported to her husband regarding the maiden Śikhaṇḍinī:
"O King, out of fear of my co-wives, I, who am childless,
declared that this daughter born as Śikhaṇḍinī was indeed a son."

"And by you as well, O best of men, this was approved out of affection for me; thus, O bull among kings, the duty toward a daughter has been fulfilled by you. Furthermore, O King, you have taken as your wife the daughter of the lord of Daśārṇa."

"And previously you stated, before seeing the meaning of the god's words, that she would be born a girl and later become a man; thus this was overlooked by you. Having heard this, Drupada Yajñasena [reflected].
Having reported the entire truth to those learned in mantras,
O King, the king deliberated upon the mantra regarding whatever was appropriate for the protection of his subjects.
O lord of men, having personally brought about a deception regarding that king of Daśārṇa, he established a connection with him by proving his capability.
With his mind one-pointedly fixed on the mantra, he reached a firm resolve;
O Bharata, O Indra among kings, during that time of calamity, he protected the city— which was naturally well-guarded and adorned on all sides— thoroughly.
O bull of the Bharatas, in his conflict with the lord of Daśārṇa, the king, together with his wife, fell into the utmost distress. [The king thought:
"How may I avoid this great war with my own kinsman?"
Having thus reflected in his mind, he then worshipped the deities. But seeing him at that time, O King, so devoted to the gods as he performed the worship, the queen,
his wife, spoke these words.
The devotion toward the gods is always true and esteemed by the virtuous;
yet for us, who worship them most fervently, it has led us to this ocean of suffering.
Therefore, let all the deities be worshipped with abundant sacrificial fees.
"O Lord, let the fires also be offered for the purpose of repelling the Daśārṇas;
and with your mind, O Master, contemplate a retreat without fighting. By the grace of the gods, all this shall come to pass."
"O large-eyed king, act accordingly upon that which has been deliberated with you by your ministers for the sake of this city's preservation.
For destiny, O ruler of the earth, when joined with human effort, succeeds most effectively."
Because they are mutually contradictory, there can indeed be no establishment of either one.
Therefore, O lord of the people, having made arrangements for the city together with your ministers, worship the deities as you desire.
Seeing those two conversing in this manner, utterly devoted to grief, the high-minded maiden Śikhaṇḍinī was then as if filled with shame.
Thereupon she reflected: "Both of these are suffering on my account."
Thinking, "These two," she then set her mind upon destroying her own life.
Having thus made this resolution, being utterly overcome by grief,
she abandoned her home and went to a dense, uninhabited forest.
O King, that forest is protected by the powerful Yakṣa Sthūṇākarṇa;
out of fear of him alone, people avoid that forest.
Therein lies the abode of Sthūṇa, plastered with lime and clay.
O King, having entered that city— which was thick with the smoke of parched grain offerings and adorned with high walls and gateways— Śikhaṇḍinī, the daughter of Drupada,
emaciated her body by not eating for many days.
The Yakṣa Sthūṇa, endowed with honey-colored eyes, revealed himself to her and said:
"For what purpose is this undertaking of yours? Tell me without delay; I shall accomplish it.
She replied to the Yakṣa again and again, "It is impossible."
Then that Guhyaka replied to her, "I shall do so. "O daughter of a king, I am an attendant of the Lord of Wealth and a granter of boons;
I will give you even what is not to be given. Tell me what you wish to say."
Then, O Bhārata, Śikhaṇḍin reported all of that in its entirety to Sthūṇākarṇa, the chief of the Yakṣas:
"O Yakṣa, my father has fallen into calamity; he will soon perish."
"The enraged lord of Daśārṇa will indeed march against him—
he who is of great strength and great energy, that king clad in golden armor.
Therefore, O Yakṣa, protect me, as well as my father and my mother."
"For you have indeed promised me the removal of my suffering:
'O Yakṣa, by your grace, may I become an irreproachable man,' as long as that king does not return to my city."
"O great Yakṣa, O Guhyaka, show favor to this extent!
Bhīṣma said:
"Then, O bull of the Bharatas, having heard the words of Śikhaṇḍin, that Yakṣa—"
Oppressed by fate, he reflected in his mind and said:
"O Kaurava, that which was destined must indeed come to pass for my sorrow. O blessed lady, I shall fulfill your desire, but understand my condition."

"I shall give you back your own manhood and I will bear your womanhood for a certain period of time; I will restore this male organ of yours to you. You must return at the appointed time; I tell you this truly."

"I am a lord whose will is accomplished, able to assume any form at will and traveling through the air. By my grace, protect the city and all your kinsmen alone. O daughter of a king, I shall assume your female form."
"Give me your word of truth; I shall do what is pleasing to you.
Śikhaṇḍin said, "O Blessed One, I shall give back this mark of yours once again."
"O night-stalker, maintain this womanhood for a short period of time.
Once King Hemavarman of Daśārṇa has departed,
I shall become a maiden again, and you shall become a man."
Bhīṣma said:
Having spoken thus, O King, those two made an agreement there,
and then they transferred [their powers] to one another without mutual malice.
O lord of men, the Yakṣa Sthūṇa assumed the female form,
and Śikhaṇḍin received that radiant Yakṣa-body.
Thereupon, O King, Śikhaṇḍin, the prince of the Pañcālas, attained manhood.
He entered the city joyfully and approached his father;
he related everything exactly as it had happened to Drupada and, in private, O King, he told his mother about the favor granted by the Yakṣa.
Having heard that from him, Drupada experienced supreme joy; together with his wife, he then recalled the words of Maheśvara. Thereupon, O King, he dispatched a messenger to the lord of Daśārṇa.
"This man is my son; may you grant me your faith," he said.
Then the King of Daśārṇa, filled with grief and indignation, suddenly approached Drupada, the King of Pañcāla.
Then, having reached Kāmpilya, the lord of Daśārṇa sent forth,
after honoring him, an envoy who was the best among the knowers of Brahman.
"O envoy, speak in my name to that lowest of kings, the Pāñcālya."
"O evil-minded one, since you have chosen my daughter for the sake of your own daughter, you shall today behold the fruit of that arrogance; of this there is no doubt.
Thus addressed by him, O best of kings, that brahmin—
Urged by the king of Daśārṇa, the messenger set out for the city;
then, in that city, he encountered Drupada, the domestic priest.
To him, the Pāñcāla king offered a cow and the guest-offering (arghya), treating him with great honor.
O Indra among kings, he caused him, along with Śikhaṇḍin, to reach that honor;
yet he did not accept that worship and spoke these words,
which had been uttered by that heroic king Kāñcanavarman.
"O man of base conduct, since I have been deceived by you for the sake of your daughter,
reap the fruit of that evil deed, O evil-minded one!
Give me battle today, O lord of men, at the forefront of the fray!"

"I shall immediately uproot you along with your ministers, sons, and kinsmen. Having been addressed with these reproachful words by the messenger of the lord of Daśārṇa, who was accompanied by a priest, the king was indeed made to hear them in the midst of his ministers.
O best of the Bharatas, Drupada, bowing with affection, said:
"O Brahmin, regarding the words you have spoken to me on behalf of our kinsman,
the messenger himself will deliver the reply."
Then Drupada also dispatched a messenger— a Brahmin who had mastered the Vedas— to the high-souled Hiraṇyavarman;
and having met with that king, the lord of Daśārṇa, at that time, [the messenger delivered his message].
O King, he repeated those words spoken by Drupada:
"Let the truth be clearly ascertained; this boy is indeed my son.
This has been said falsely by someone else, and therefore it is not to be believed."
Then that king, having heard [the report] from Drupada,
being filled with deliberation, dispatched young women of most excellent and very beautiful form.
Having been sent to determine whether Śikhaṇḍin was a woman or a man, they learned his true nature and reported everything to the king with joy.
O Indra among the Kauravas, [he gave] the high-souled man Śikhaṇḍin to the king of Daśārṇa;
then, having performed the arrival ceremony, that king was filled with joy.
Having met with his kinsman, he dwelt there joyfully.
And the lord of men, being delighted, gave wealth to Śikhaṇḍin—
elephants, horses, cows, and many hundreds of female slaves.
Having been honored, he departed after sending back his daughter,
while King Hemavarman was pleased and his offenses had been subdued.
Once the King of Daśārṇa had returned, Śikhaṇḍinī appeared joyful.
Then, after some time, Kubera, whose vehicle is man,
while traveling through the worlds, came to the residence of Sthūṇa. He was passing over that house.
The protector of wealth gazed upon the residence of the yakṣa Sthūṇa,
which he observed to be well-adorned and variegated with strings of garlands.
It was honored with parched grain and perfumes, as well as canopies, and was scented with incense;
it was further adorned with banners and flags.
Having seen that place adorned on all sides with offerings of food, drink, meat, and oblations, and filled with garlands of jewels, gems, and gold; 05,193.033b*0590_01.
Rich with the fragrance of various flowers, sprinkled, swept, and made beautiful,
the lord of the yakṣas then spoke to those yakṣas who were his followers: "O you of immeasurable prowess, this residence of Sthūṇa is well-adorned."
"And why does that one of very dull intellect not approach me today?
Since this person of weak soul does not approach me despite knowing [me],
it is my opinion that a great punishment should be inflicted upon him."
The Yakṣas said:
"O King, a daughter named Śikhaṇḍinī was born to King Drupada.
For some particular reason, he bestowed upon her the characteristics of a man."

Having assumed the characteristics of women, he remains in the house as a woman; because of that, he who possesses a female form does not approach you out of shame. For this reason, O King, Sthūṇa does not see you today.
"Having heard this, act according to what is right; let the celestial chariot remain here.
Bhīṣma said:
"Then the lord of the Yakṣas said, 'Let a pillar be brought.'"
"I shall inflict punishment upon him," he said again and again. O lord of the earth, having been summoned, he approached the lord of the Yakṣas;
O great king, assuming the form of a woman, he stood there filled with shame.
O descendant of Kuru, the Giver of Wealth (Dhanada), being greatly incensed, cursed him:
"O Guhyakas, let this sinful man remain in womanhood exactly as it is!
Then the high-souled Lord of the Yakṣas spoke:
Because you, O evil-minded one, disregarded the Yakṣas here as mere servants, and because you, O doer of evil deeds, accepted the female marks for Śikhaṇḍin; [therefore...]
"O one of very wicked intellect, because this which was not to be done has been committed by you,
therefore from this day forward you shall be a woman and he likewise a man. Then, it is said, the yakṣas propitiated Vaiśravaṇa.
"Bring an end to the curse for the sake of Sthūṇa," he said again and again.
Then the high-souled lord of the Yakṣas replied to all his followers and the hosts of Yakṣas, O dear one, with the desire to bring an end to the curse.
"When Śikhaṇḍin is slain in battle, he shall regain his own form;
let the Yakṣa Sthūṇa be free from anxiety"—
having spoken thus, the blessed Lord, who is worshipped by Yakṣas and Rākṣasas, [departed].
He departed together with all those who move in the blink of an eye;
but Sthūṇa, having received the curse, remained right there at that time.
And when the appointed moment arrived, Śikhaṇḍin indeed came to that night-walker.
Having approached, he spoke these words: "O Blessed One, I have arrived.
Then Sthūṇa said to him again and again, "I am pleased," upon seeing the prince Śikhaṇḍin come with such sincerity.
He related everything exactly as it had happened to Śikhaṇḍin.
The Yakṣa said:
"O prince, I have been cursed by Vaiśravaṇa on your account."
"Go now as you wish; wander through the worlds at your pleasure.
I believe this was ordained of old and cannot be avoided:
your departure and the sight of the descendant of Pulastya."
Bhīṣma said:
Thus addressed by the Yakṣa Sthūṇa, O Bhārata,
Śikhaṇḍin returned to the city filled with great joy.
Drupada, together with his son Śikhaṇḍin, whose purpose had been accomplished, honored the twice-born, the deities, the sacred shrines, and the crossroads with various costly perfumes and garlands.
And the King of Pañcāla, together with his kinsmen, attained supreme joy; O bull among the Kurus, O great king, he then gave Śikhaṇḍin— his son who had previously been a woman— to Droṇa as a pupil.
The prince Śikhaṇḍin, along with you all and Dhṛṣṭadyumna the son of Pṛṣata, mastered the fourfold science of archery (dhanurveda). But my spies,
dear one, reported this to me exactly as it happened.
"O Great King, those who were joined by me to Drupada in the forms of one dull-witted, blind, and deaf—
thus was this son of Drupada born, O best of the Kauravas, Śikhaṇḍin, the most excellent of chariot-warriors, both woman and man."
O bull of the Bharatas, this is Śikhaṇḍin, born in the lineage of Drupada, who was formerly the eldest daughter of the Lord of Kāśī, renowned by the name Ambā.
I will not strike him while he stands before me with bow in hand, eager for battle.
"Even for a moment I would look upon her, yet I would not strike her;
this is my constant vow, renowned even throughout the earth:
[I do not strike] a woman, one who was previously a woman, one whose name is feminine, or one who has the form of a woman."
"I shall not release my arrows," O joy of the Kauravas;
"I shall not slay Śikhaṇḍin for this reason"—
this is the truth, O dear one, regarding the birth of Śikhaṇḍin that I know.
Therefore, I shall not slay him, even though he is an assailant in battle;
for if Bhīṣma were to kill a woman, he would be killing himself as well. Thus, I will not kill him, even upon seeing him standing in the fray.
Saṃjaya said:
Having heard this, King Duryodhana, the descendant of Kuru,
reflected for a moment and then considered it appropriate toward Bhīṣma.
Saṃjaya said:
When the night had turned to dawn, your son once again questioned the grandfather in the midst of his entire army.
O son of Gaṅgā, this supreme army of the son of Pāṇḍu—
which abounds in men, elephants, and horses, and is crowded with great chariot-warriors such as Bhīma, Arjuna, and other mighty archers— [is formidable].
Guarded by those resembling the world-protectors, led by Dhṛṣṭadyumna,
it was unassailable, irresistible, and like a surging ocean—
an ocean of an army that could not be shaken even by the gods in a great battle.
O Gāṅgeya of great splendor, in what length of time could you consume [the enemy],
or the preceptor who is a great archer, or Kṛpa of immense strength,
or Karṇa who boasts in battle, or the son of Droṇa, the best of the twice-born?
"O mighty-armed one, all of you here in my army are indeed experts in divine weapons. I desire to know this, for there is a great curiosity constantly in my heart; you ought to tell it to me."
Bhīṣma said:
"O best of the Kurus, O lord of the earth, this is worthy of you,
since you inquire about the relative strength and weakness of both your enemies and your own."

"Listen, O King, to what my supreme power in battle may be, as well as the prowess of my weapons in combat and the strength of my arms, O mighty-armed one. Other people should be fought with straightforward warfare alone."
"It is the settled rule of dharma that a master of illusion should fight with illusory warfare. O mighty-armed one, I shall slay the army of the Pāṇḍavas,
making my portion each day from the forenoon onwards."
"O one of great luster, having set aside ten thousand warriors as my share,
and one thousand chariot-fighters— this is the portion I consider mine. Arrayed according to this rule, I shall remain ever-vigilant."
"O Bhārata, I could destroy this great army in this much time,
were I to discharge my mighty weapons while standing in battle;
I could slay hundreds of thousands in a single month, O Bhārata."
Saṃjaya said:
O king of kings, having heard those words of Bhīṣma, King Duryodhana then questioned Droṇa, the best of the Aṅgirasas.
"O Teacher, in what length of time could you slay the soldiers of the son of Pāṇḍu? To him Droṇa replied, as if smiling:
"I am old, O best of the Kurus, and my vital strength and activity are diminished."

"With the fire of my weapons, I could consume the army of the Pāṇḍavas, just as Bhīṣma, the son of Śāntanu, did in a month; such is my thought. This is my supreme power; this is my greatest strength."
Kṛpa, the son of Śaradvat, declared that he could achieve it in just two months;
the son of Droṇa, however, promised the destruction of the army in ten nights;
and Karṇa, the knower of great weapons, pledged to do so in five nights.
Having heard those words of the Sūta’s son, the son of the River Ganges laughed a loud laugh and spoke these words: "Indeed,
you shall not [conquer] Pārtha in battle while he still bears arrows, sword, and bow."
"O son of Rādhā, you think thus because you encounter Acyuta as he rises up on his chariot joined by Vāsudeva;
yet it is possible for you to speak even more than this, according to your desire."
Vaiśampāyana said:
Having heard this, O best of the Bharatas, the son of Kuntī summoned all his brothers to a private place and spoke these words.
Those who are my spies among the armies of Dhṛtarāṣṭra’s son have provided me with this report after the night has passed:
it is said that Duryodhana questioned the son of the River (Bhīṣma), who is of great vows.
"O Lord, in what length of time could you slay the army of the Pāṇḍavas?
"In a month," replied that evil-minded son of Dhṛtarāṣṭra.
And within that same amount of time, Droṇa also gave his promise.
We have heard that Gautama declared it would take double that time;
however, the son of Droṇa, a master of great weapons, promised to do it in ten nights.
Likewise, Karṇa, an expert in divine weapons, was questioned in the assembly of the Kurus.
He vowed to slay that army within five days;
therefore, O Arjuna, I also wish to hear your words as to how long it will take you to destroy the enemies in battle.
Thus addressed by the king, Dhanañjaya Guḍākeśa looked toward Vāsudeva and replied with these words:
"All these high-souled men are masters of weapons and versatile in combat."

"Without a doubt, O Great King, they would surely destroy your army. Let the distress of your mind depart; I speak the truth when I say that, with Vāsudeva as my companion, I could slay them all from a single chariot."

It is my conviction that in a mere twinkling of an eye, he can [perceive] even the three worlds together with the gods, including all things moving and stationary—the past, the present, and the future.
As long as this Hari desires it, so long does it exist; it cannot be otherwise.

"That terrible and great weapon which Paśupati bestowed upon me during the duel at Kairāta— that very same one now resides within me. It is that with which Paśupati destroys all beings at the end of a Yuga."
O tiger among men, he employs this very thing against me;
neither Bhīṣma the son of Gaṅgā, nor Droṇa, nor Gautama, nor the son of Droṇa knows of it, O King— how much less the son of a Sūta?
"However, it is not right to slay common folk in battle with divine weapons;
we shall conquer our enemies through fair combat alone.
O King, these tigers among men are your allies."
All are experts in divine weapons, all are lovers of battle;
all uphold the vow of heroes, and all are firm in their vows of virtuous conduct. Having performed the purificatory ablutions at the conclusion of Vedic study, all of these are unconquered.
O Pāṇḍava,
Śikhaṇḍin, Yuyudhāna, Dhṛṣṭadyumna the son of Pṛṣata,
Bhīmasena, both the twins, Yudhāmanyu, and Uttamaujas— these would destroy even the army of the gods in battle.
Both Virāṭa and Drupada are equal to Bhīṣma and Droṇa in battle;
likewise the mighty-armed Śaṅkha and the exceedingly powerful Haiḍimba;
and his son Añjanaparvan, who possesses great strength and prowess.
The mighty-armed Śaineya, skilled in battle, is your ally; so too are the powerful Abhimanyu and the five sons of Draupadī. Indeed, you yourself are capable of destroying even the three worlds.
"O Kaurava, I know this of you: that man whom you might look upon with anger, O you who possess the splendor of Vāsava, would clearly and swiftly cease to exist.
Vaiśampāyana said:
Then, at the clear dawn, urged by the son of Dhṛtarāṣṭra,
Duryodhana, the kings set out toward the Pāṇḍavas;
having all bathed, they were pure, wearing garlands and white garments.
Having taken up their weapons and raised their banners, they had the benedictions pronounced and offered oblations into the fires;
all were knowers of the Vedas, heroes, and all were firm in their vows of good conduct; all were performers of ritual acts and all bore the marks of battle-readiness.
In battles, those of great strength, desiring to conquer the higher worlds,
were all single-minded and full of faith in their supreme goal:
Vinda and Anuvinda of Avanti, along with the Kekayas and the Bāhlikas.
All of these set forth with Bhāradvāja at their head: Aśvatthāman, the son of Śantanu, Jayadratha the king of the Sindhus,
and those chariot-warriors from the south, the west, and the mountains.
Śakuni, the king of the Gāndhāras, along with those from the east and the north in their entirety—
the Śakas, Kirātas, Yavanas, Śibis, and Vasātis—
surrounded that great car-warrior, accompanied by their respective armies.
All these great car-warriors marched forth in the second division: Kṛtavarman with his army, the mighty Trigartas,
and King Duryodhana surrounded by his brothers.
Śala, Bhūriśravas, Śalya, Kausalya, and Bṛhadbala—
these followed behind, led by the son of Dhṛtarāṣṭra. Having traveled along a level road, those great car-warriors prepared for battle.
In the western half of Kurukṣetra, they stood ready in their armor. Duryodhana, O Bhārata, had his camp constructed so that it was adorned like a second Hāstinapura.
O Indra among kings, even those men who dwell in cities and are highly skilled do not perceive any difference between a city and a camp;
for the lord of the earth constructs fortresses for kings that are exactly like them.
The Kuru prince caused [the ground] to be prepared by the hundreds and thousands;
leaving aside a circular area of five yojanas,
O King, those army encampments entered that field of battle in groups of hundreds.
There, those protectors of the earth quickly entered thousands of well-stocked tents according to their zeal and according to their strength.
Among those high-souled kings together with their armies, King Duryodhana [remained].
He ordered unsurpassed food and drink for all those outside [the palace],
including the elephants, horses, and men, as well as those who live by their crafts and others who had followed there— the *sūtas*, *māgadhas*, and bards.
The Kuru king beheld with due ceremony all those merchants, courtesans, and the people who had come as spectators.
Vaiśampāyana said:
Thus addressed by Sañjaya, Dhṛtarāṣṭra, deeply distressed in mind,
remained there reflecting upon his vast anxieties along with Gāndhārī and Vidura;
and likewise did King Yudhiṣṭhira, the son of Kuntī and son of Dharma.
O Bhārata, he urged on the heroes headed by Dhṛṣṭadyumna;
then he commanded Dhṛṣṭaketu, the slayer of enemies and commander-in-chief of the Cedis, Kāśis, and Karūṣas, who was a leader of firm prowess.
Virāṭa, Drupada, Yuyudhāna, Śikhaṇḍin, and the two great archers of the Pañcālas, Yudhāmanyu and Uttamaujas—
those heroes, clad in variegated armor and wearing earrings of refined gold, [stood there].
Sprinkled with clarified butter and blazing like fires upon their altars,
those great archers shone like flaming planets.
Then that bull among men, having honored his army according to its rank, [proceeded].
The lord of the earth gave orders for those divisions to set out;
the son of Pāṇḍu dispatched Abhimanyu, Bṛhanta, and all the sons of Draupadī, as well as these men headed by Dhṛṣṭadyumna.
Yudhiṣṭhira dispatched Bhīma, Yuyudhāna, and the Pāṇḍava Dhanañjaya as his second division of the army. As they loaded their equipment, moved about, and rushed forward, [the enemy watched].
The roar of the joyful warriors there seemed to touch the very heavens. Then,
following them, the lord of the earth himself set out, accompanied by Virāṭa and Drupada, as well as other rulers of the world.
The army of Bhīmadhanvāyana, led by Dhṛṣṭadyumna,
appeared like the full Ganges— calm yet flowing.
Then the wise one once again arrayed his forces.
Deluding the flow of the intellect of Dhṛtarāṣṭra’s sons,
the Pāṇḍava [Arjuna] [fought] the sons of Draupadī, those great archers, as well as Abhimanyu,
Nakula, Sahadeva, and all the Prabhadrakas.
Ten thousand horses, two thousand elephants,
ten thousand foot soldiers, and five hundred chariots—
Bhīmasena, the invincible, was appointed as the foremost of this force.
In the center, however, were Virāṭa and Jayatsena of Magadha,
as well as the two great car-warriors (mahāratha) of the Pañcālas, Yudhāmanyu and Uttamaujas—
both heroic, high-souled, and bearing maces and bows.

Then Vāsudeva and Dhanañjaya followed into the midst [of the army]. Seeing them, all the lords of the earth, as well as all the gods stationed in the intermediate space led by Indra, thought that [the enemy] was already lost.
The men, having taken up their weapons, became exceedingly enraged. Twenty thousand of their banners were manned by heroes;
there were five thousand elephants and rows of chariots on all sides.
And those heroic foot-soldiers, bearing bows, swords, and maces,
followed by the thousands from behind and by the thousands from the front,
where Yudhiṣṭhira himself was in that army, that ocean of forces.
There, O Bharata, those protectors of the earth were for the most part stationed;
there were thousands of elephants, tens of thousands of horses,
as well as thousands of chariots and foot soldiers.
Cekitāna, O bull among kings, marched forth with his vast army;
and Dhṛṣṭaketu, the ruler and leader of the Cedis, advanced;
as did Sātyaki, the great archer and preeminent chariot-warrior of the Vṛṣṇis.
Surrounded by a hundred thousand chariots, the powerful one advanced,
driving them forward; while Kṣatradeva and Brahmadeva, those two bulls among men stationed upon their chariots, followed behind, protecting his rear.
There were carts, market stalls, and dwellings, as well as all kinds of vehicles and draft animals;
there too were thousands of elephants and tens of thousands of horses,
along with all the non-essential property, the womenfolk, and whatever was frail or weak.
Having secured the transporters of the accumulated treasuries as well as the granaries,
Yudhiṣṭhira set out slowly with his elephant division. Satyadhṛti, the son of Suci, who is difficult to vanquish in battle, followed him.
Śreṇimān and Vasudāna, or the powerful son of Kāśya—
twenty thousand chariots were their followers,
as well as tens of millions of horses adorned with small bells.
Twenty thousand elephants with tusks as long as plow-poles were there for combat— noble breeds with temples flowing [with musth], moving like clouds;
and sixty thousand other elephants, O Bhārata.
The armies of the high-souled Yudhiṣṭhira that were in the battle followed behind the king like clouds pouring down rain, their temples and faces streaming with rut,
moving like shifting mountains.
Such was the terrible power of that wise son of Kuntī,
relying upon which he attacked Suyodhana, the son of Dhṛtarāṣṭra;
behind him followed other men by the hundreds, thousands, and tens of thousands.
Roaring, their armies set forth by the thousands; there,
thousands of men, filled with joy, sounded thousands of kettledrums and tens of thousands of conchs by the thousands and tens of thousands.
